x: Matthew 6:24 "No one can serve two masters. You cannot serve God and money." Hebrews 13:5 "Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, I will never leave you nor forsake you." Luke 12:15 "Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions." Proverbs 11:28 "Whoever trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous will flourish like a green leaf." Matthew 6:19-20 "Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy, but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven." 1 Timothy 6:17-18 "Charge them not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy." Philippians 4:11-12 "I have learned, in whatever situation I am, to be content... I know how to be brought low, and I…

t: What the Bible Says About Grief & Loss
x: What the Bible says about grief and loss, how Scripture gives permission to mourn, and the hope it holds out in sorrow.

p: What the Bible Says About Grief & Loss
x: Grief is one of the most misunderstood experiences in Christian community, often mistaken for a failure of faith rather than what it actually is: love confronting loss. The clearest evidence against the idea that grief signals weak faith is Jesus Himself. At the tomb of Lazarus, knowing full well He was about to raise His friend from the dead within minutes, Jesus still wept (John 11:35). If grief were incompatible with faith or foreknowledge of a good outcome, the Son of God would have had no reason to weep. He wept anyway — because grief is the appropriate human response to death and loss, not a symptom of doubting God's power or presence. Scripture distinguishes Christian grief not by its absence but by its character: "that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13). This verse does not instruct believers not to grieve — it assumes they will — but…

p: What the Bible Says About Grief & Loss
x: God's posture toward the grieving is not distant sympathy but active nearness. Scripture describes Him as "the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction" (2 Corinthians 1:3-4) — comfort that is personal, present, and comprehensive rather than a general theological statement about suffering. Grief does not push a person away from God; it places them exactly where His comfort is most explicitly promised. Scripture also teaches that death, for those in Christ, is not the final word. Revelation's vision of a day when God "will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more" (Revelation 21:4) does not erase present grief but reframes its horizon. The pain of separation is real and is not minimized by future hope — but it is held within a larger story where separation is not eternal for those united to Christ. Romans 8:38-39 extends this…

p: What the Bible Says About Grief & Loss
x: Grieving with hope does not mean grieving less intensely or resolving faster — it means carrying sorrow within a larger story that does not end at the grave. Psalm 30:5's promise that "weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning" is not a guarantee of a quick timeline but an assurance that night, however long, is not the final state. For some griefs, the morning does not arrive fully until the resurrection itself; even so, the promise stands. Practically, this means allowing space for lament without shame, staying connected to community rather than withdrawing, and continuing to bring the rawest parts of grief honestly to God in prayer, as the psalmists modeled. God is not offended by tears, questions, or even anger directed at Him in grief — He draws nearer to the brokenhearted, not further away, and He has demonstrated, in the tears of His own Son, that grief and…

p: What the Bible Says About Grief & Loss
x: Revelation 21:4 "He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore." 1 Thessalonians 4:13 "We do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope." John 11:35 "Jesus wept." Psalm 30:5 "Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning." 2 Corinthians 1:3-4 "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction." Romans 8:38-39 "For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord." Romans 12:15 "Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep."
A study of the seven I AM statements of Jesus in John's Gospel, from the bread of life to the true vine.

t: What Are the I AM Statements?
x: Seven times in the Gospel of John, Jesus applies the phrase "I am" (Greek: ego eimi) to Himself, followed by a specific image: bread of life, light of the world, the door, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life, the way and the truth and the life, and the true vine. John selected these seven declarations carefully — his Gospel states its purpose plainly near the end: "these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name" (John 20:31). Each I AM statement is a piece of evidence in that case, a claim Jesus made about His own identity that His hearers could weigh for themselves. The phrase "I am" carries far more weight than an ordinary self-introduction. In Exodus 3:14, when Moses asked God's name at the burning bush, God answered, "I AM WHO I AM... say this to the people of Israel, 'I AM has sent…

t: I Am the Bread of Life
x: The Statement In John 6:35, after miraculously feeding five thousand people with five loaves and two fish, Jesus declared: "I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst." The crowd had followed Him across the Sea of Galilee seeking more physical food, but Jesus redirected their hunger toward something eternal. He was not merely a provider of bread — He was claiming to be the bread itself, the sustenance that satisfies the deepest need of the human soul. The context of this statement is critical. The crowd wanted a sign like the manna Moses gave (John 6:30-31). Jesus corrected them: it was not Moses but the Father who gave the bread from heaven, and now the Father was giving the true bread — not a substance that spoils, but a Person who gives eternal life. Jesus was claiming to be the ultimate answer to humanity's deepest…

t: I Am the Light of the World
x: The Statement During the Feast of Tabernacles in Jerusalem, when massive golden candelabras illuminated the Temple courts in remembrance of God's pillar of fire that guided Israel through the wilderness, Jesus stood and declared: "I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life" (John 8:12). The timing was no accident — surrounded by ceremonial light celebrating God's past guidance, Jesus claimed to be the living fulfillment of that very light. In the Old Testament, light is consistently associated with God's presence, truth, and salvation: "The LORD is my light and my salvation" (Psalm 27:1); "The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light" (Isaiah 9:2). The contrast Jesus draws is absolute: light versus darkness, life versus death. There is no middle ground. This was a direct challenge to the religious leaders who…

The Statement In John 10:9, Jesus declared: "I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture." This statement comes in the context of an extended metaphor about shepherds, sheep, and sheepfolds. In first-century Palestine, sheep pens often had a single opening with no gate — the shepherd himself would lie across the entrance at night, literally becoming the door with his own body. Jesus was not merely pointing to a way of salvation — He was claiming to be the exclusive access point between humanity and God, replacing the entire Old Testament system of mediated access through the Tabernacle and Temple. He is not a door among many; He is the door — singular, definite, exclusive. The promise attached to this claim is threefold: salvation ("he will be saved"), freedom ("will go in and out"), and provision ("find pasture"). The door is not…

The Statement In John 10:11, Jesus declared: "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep." This statement would have been electrifying to His Jewish audience, because throughout the Old Testament, God Himself is described as the Shepherd of Israel: "The LORD is my shepherd" (Psalm 23:1). By claiming to be the Good Shepherd, Jesus was claiming the role that belonged exclusively to God. The word "good" (Greek: kalos) means not just morally good but beautiful, noble, ideal — the model shepherd against whom all others are measured, contrasted with hired hands who abandon the sheep when danger comes (John 10:12-13). The defining characteristic of the Good Shepherd is that He "lays down his life for the sheep" — a clear reference to the cross. Jesus did not lose His life accidentally. "No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord" (John 10:18).…

t: I Am the Resurrection and the Life
x: The Statement Standing before a grieving Martha, whose brother Lazarus had been dead for four days, Jesus made one of His most stunning declarations: "I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die" (John 11:25-26). Martha believed in a future resurrection — Jesus redirected her faith from a distant theological event to His own person: the resurrection is not merely something that will happen — it is Someone standing in front of you. He is not saying He will perform resurrections (though He did, moments later) — He is saying He is resurrection itself. The timing of this statement is profoundly pastoral. Jesus said these words not in a theological lecture but at a graveside, to a woman weeping over her brother. He wept with her (John 11:35). He proved His claim minutes later by…

t: I Am the Way, the Truth, and the Life
x: The Statement On the night before His crucifixion, in the intimacy of the Upper Room, Jesus told His troubled disciples: "I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6). Thomas had just asked, "Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?" Jesus' answer was not a map or a set of instructions — it was Himself. This threefold claim is perhaps the most comprehensive of all Jesus' self-declarations: He does not merely show the way (as a prophet might), teach the truth (as a philosopher might), or offer life (as a healer might). He is these things in His very person. The exclusive conclusion — "No one comes to the Father except through me" — follows necessarily from the claim itself. If Jesus is the way (not a way), then all other paths are dead ends. This is not arrogance but logic: if the claim is true, exclusivity…

The Statement In His final extended teaching before the cross, Jesus told His disciples: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit" (John 15:1-2). The vine was one of the most recognized symbols in Israel — it represented God's chosen people throughout the prophets, but Israel had been called an unfaithful vine that produced wild grapes (Isaiah 5:1-7). Jesus now claims to be the true vine — the faithful Israel, the genuine article that replaces the failed original. This statement uniquely emphasizes the organic, living connection between Jesus and His followers. A branch has no life independent of the vine and cannot produce fruit by effort alone — it produces fruit only by remaining connected to the source of life. Jesus repeats the word…

t: What the Bible Says About Identity & Self-Worth
x: What the Bible says about identity and self-worth: being made in God's image and who we are in Christ.

p: What the Bible Says About Identity & Self-Worth
x: Every human being is constantly answering the question "who am I?" — whether consciously or not — and the answer we give shapes everything from our decisions to our emotional stability. The world offers a shifting menu of answers: you are what you achieve, what you look like, what others think of you, what you own, or what mistakes define your past. Each of these foundations is inherently unstable, because achievements can be lost, opinions change, appearances fade, and mistakes accumulate. An identity built on any of them is an identity perpetually under threat. Scripture roots identity somewhere entirely different: not in performance or perception, but in what God has declared to be true. This declaration begins at creation itself — humanity is made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), a status assigned prior to any accomplishment or failure, simply by virtue of being made by Him. Long…

p: What the Bible Says About Identity & Self-Worth
x: Scripture describes the believer's identity in Christ with a cluster of specific, concrete terms: chosen, not accidental (1 Peter 2:9); adopted as a child and heir, not merely tolerated (Romans 8:16-17); crucified and alive in Christ, no longer defined by the old self (Galatians 2:20); and God's own workmanship, purposefully created for good works prepared in advance (Ephesians 2:10). None of these statuses are earned through performance — they are given, received by faith, and then lived out rather than achieved. This reframes the entire project of "finding yourself" that dominates contemporary culture. The world's instruction is to look inward and discover an authentic self through self-exploration and self-expression; Scripture's instruction is to look to Christ and receive an identity that is both more stable and more true than anything self-discovery could produce, because it is…

p: What the Bible Says About Identity & Self-Worth
x: Worth established at creation was confirmed decisively at the cross. The willingness of God to send His Son to die for humanity is the highest possible statement of value — not because humanity earned that worth through goodness, but because God assigned it through love. This means self-worth is not a fragile calculation dependent on daily performance; it was settled, once and permanently, at Calvary, for anyone who receives it by faith. Practically, living from this identity means learning to interrupt the reflexive question "am I enough?" with the settled truth of what God has already declared. When performance fails, when others' opinions turn critical, when the past resurfaces with old shame, the anchor is not self-improvement but remembering — chosen, adopted, a new creation, an heir. Identity rooted in God's declaration does not fluctuate with circumstances the way identity rooted…

p: What the Bible Says About Identity & Self-Worth
x: Ephesians 2:10 "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them." 1 Peter 2:9 "But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession." 2 Corinthians 5:17 "Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come." Galatians 2:20 "I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me." Romans 8:16-17 "The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God, and if children, then heirs." Jeremiah 1:5 "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you." Genesis 1:27 "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them."
The judges of Israel — Othniel, Ehud, Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah, Samson and the rest — deliverers God raised up in the cycle of sin, oppression and rescue.

The book of Judges covers the turbulent centuries between Joshua's conquest and Israel's first king — roughly 1200 to 1050 BC. Joshua's generation had seen God part the Jordan and topple Jericho, but Judges opens with a sobering notice: "there arose another generation after them who did not know the LORD or the work that he had done for Israel" (Judges 2:10). With no central government, no king, and the tribes only loosely confederated, Israel repeatedly drifted into the religion of the Canaanite peoples they had failed to fully dispossess. What follows is not a list of successes but a downward spiral the book itself narrates as a repeating pattern: Israel does evil and worships other gods; the LORD hands them over to an oppressor; Israel cries out in misery; God raises up a judge — a deliverer empowered by His Spirit — who defeats the enemy and leads the nation back to Him; the land…

Story Othniel appears twice in Scripture. Before the period of the judges proper, he won Achsah, the daughter of Caleb, as his wife by capturing Kiriath-sepher (Judges 1:12-13) — so he enters the book of Judges already proven in Caleb's own family circle. His actual judgeship, told in just five verses, follows the book's cycle for the first time: Israel forgot the LORD and served the Baals and the Asheroth, so He sold them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, for eight years. When Israel cried out, the Spirit of the LORD came upon Othniel; he judged Israel, went out to war, and the LORD gave Cushan-rishathaim into his hand. The land had rest forty years, until Othniel died. Legacy and Lessons Othniel's account is brief, but it establishes the template every later judge is measured against: sin, oppression, a cry for help, Spirit-empowered deliverance, and rest.…

Story Israel's relapse brought Eglon, king of Moab, who allied with Ammon and Amalek to seize the City of Palms and oppress Israel for eighteen years. When Israel cried out, the LORD raised up Ehud, a Benjaminite the text specifically notes was left-handed. Ehud strapped a short double-edged sword to his right thigh — concealed, since guards expected a weapon on a right-handed man's left side — and brought Israel's tribute to the obese king. Dismissing his attendants under the pretense of a private message from God, Ehud drove the blade into Eglon, slipped out, and locked the doors behind him; the servants delayed entering, assuming the king was relieving himself. Ehud escaped, rallied Israel's hill country with a trumpet blast, and seized the fords of the Jordan, cutting off the fleeing Moabites and killing about ten thousand of them. The land had rest eighty years. Legacy and Lessons…

Story Shamgar's entire account is a single verse. Judges 3:31 says only that he was the son of Anath, that he struck down six hundred Philistines with an ox goad — a long, pointed pole used to prod oxen while plowing — and that he too saved Israel. Unlike the other judges, no sin, no named oppressor, no length of rule, and no years of rest are recorded around him; he is simply noted and the narrative moves on. He is remembered once more, in the Song of Deborah, as a marker of how dangerous the roads had become "in the days of Shamgar" (Judges 5:6) — a passing reference that suggests he was a known figure to the book's first readers even though almost nothing of his story survives. Legacy and Lessons Little is recorded of Shamgar, and that is worth saying plainly rather than filling in. What is recorded is enough: an ordinary farming tool, in the hand of someone willing to use it, became…

Story After Ehud's death, Israel again did evil, and the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin, king of Canaan, whose commander Sisera oppressed Israel cruelly for twenty years with nine hundred iron chariots. Deborah, a prophetess and the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time, holding court under a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel. She summoned Barak of Kedesh and relayed God's command: muster ten thousand men from Zebulun and Naphtali to Mount Tabor, where the LORD would give Sisera into his hand. Barak agreed only on the condition that Deborah go with him; she agreed, but told him that because of this the honor of the day would belong to a woman instead. The LORD threw Sisera's army into a panic before Israel; Sisera himself fled on foot to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, who gave him milk, let him fall asleep, and then drove a tent peg through his temple —…

Story Midian, Amalek, and the people of the east oppressed Israel seven years, devastating crops and driving the nation into caves and dens in the hills. When Israel cried out, God first sent a prophet to confront their idolatry, and then the angel of the LORD found Gideon threshing wheat in a winepress, hiding from the Midianites, and called him "mighty man of valor." Gideon protested that his clan was the weakest in Manasseh and he the least in his father's house. After confirming signs — fire consuming an offering on the rock, then the famous dry-and-wet fleece tests — Gideon tore down his father's altar to Baal by night, too afraid of the townspeople to do it in daylight. When he mustered an army, God pared it down from thirty-two thousand to three hundred, first dismissing the fearful and then selecting by how men drank from a stream, so Israel could not boast that its own strength…

Story After the violent, self-appointed kingship of Abimelech — who is not counted among the judges, since he seized power rather than being raised up by God — Tola son of Puah, of the tribe of Issachar, "arose to save Israel." He lived in Shamir, in the hill country of Ephraim, and judged Israel twenty-three years before he died and was buried there. Scripture records no oppressor, no battle, and no particular crisis under his judgeship — only that he rose to save Israel and led for more than two decades. Legacy and Lessons Very little is told of Tola, and the honest reading is that little was meant to be told — not every faithful leader's story includes a dramatic battle. Coming right after Abimelech's bloody, illegitimate reign, more than two decades of stable, undramatic leadership may have been exactly the deliverance Israel needed at that moment. Key Verses Judges 10:1 — After…

Story Jair the Gileadite judged Israel twenty-two years. His entire notice centers on his household: thirty sons, who rode thirty donkeys and possessed thirty towns in the land of Gilead, remembered in the text as "Havvoth-jair" — a name the writer says was still in use "to this day." He died and was buried in Camon. As with Tola, no oppression or deliverance is recorded. Legacy and Lessons The detail about Jair's sons, donkeys, and towns is a mark of prosperity and settled regional influence rather than military achievement — a large household functioning as a kind of clan leadership across Gilead. His brief record is another reminder that Scripture values faithful, stable governance even when it produces no battle to narrate. Key Verses Judges 10:3 — After Tola, Jair the Gileadite judged Israel twenty-two years. Judges 10:4 — He had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys and had…

Story Israel relapsed into idolatry again, worshiping the gods of the surrounding nations, and the LORD let the Ammonites and Philistines crush Gilead for eighteen years. When Israel cried out, God first rebuked them for turning to Him only in trouble, then relented as they repented and put away their foreign gods. Jephthah, a mighty warrior, was the son of a prostitute and had been driven out by his half-brothers and denied any inheritance; he fled to the land of Tob, where a band of men gathered around him. When Ammon threatened, the very elders of Gilead who had rejected him came begging him to lead them, and Jephthah agreed on the condition that he would remain their head if he won. He first tried diplomacy, sending the Ammonite king a detailed appeal to Israel's history, but was refused. Then, with the Spirit of the LORD upon him, Jephthah made a vow: whatever came out of his house…

Story Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel after Jephthah. His notice centers entirely on his family: he had thirty sons and thirty daughters, sent his daughters out in marriage to families outside his own clan, and brought in thirty young women from outside for his sons — a record of deliberate, far-reaching marriage alliances. He judged Israel seven years, then died and was buried in Bethlehem. No oppression, battle, or deliverance is recorded. Legacy and Lessons Like Tola and Jair before him, Ibzan's short record emphasizes family and alliance-building rather than military rescue — a reminder that not every judge's contribution to Israel's good came on a battlefield. Building stability through relationships and leadership during a settled interval mattered too, even though Scripture gives it only three verses. Key Verses Judges 12:8 — After Jephthah, Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel.…

Story Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel ten years, then died and was buried at Aijalon in the land of Zebulun. That is the complete record Scripture gives of him — no family detail, no battle, no crisis, nothing beyond his tribe, the length of his rule, and where he was buried. Legacy and Lessons Elon's is the briefest notice of any judge in the book — two verses in total. That God still saw fit to record his name, tribe, and years of service, with almost nothing else said, is itself worth noting: obscurity to later readers is not the same as obscurity to God, who remembers faithful service however little of it survives in writing. Key Verses Judges 12:11 — After Ibzan, Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel ten years. Judges 12:12 — Elon died and was buried at Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.

Story Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite judged Israel. Like Jair, his record notes a large and prosperous household: forty sons and thirty grandsons who rode on seventy donkeys. He judged Israel eight years, then died and was buried at Pirathon, in the land of Ephraim, in what the text identifies as "the hill country of the Amalekites" — an older, pre-Israelite place-name still used to locate it. He is the last of the minor judges named before the book turns to Samson. Legacy and Lessons Abdon closes the sequence of minor judges on the same note Tola opened it with: unremarkable, undramatic years of leadership and family stability, worth recording even without a crisis attached to them. Taken together, the six minor judges are a reminder that the quiet, largely unrecorded faithfulness of many ordinary leaders sustained Israel in between its most famous and most dramatic deliverances.…

Story Israel relapsed once more, and the LORD gave them into the hand of the Philistines for forty years. The angel of the LORD appeared to Manoah's barren wife, announcing that her son would be a Nazirite to God from the womb — no razor, no wine, no unclean food, per the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6 — and would "begin to deliver Israel from the hand of the Philistines." Samson's strength came from the Spirit of the LORD rushing upon him at decisive moments, not from his hair itself; his uncut hair was only the outward sign of a consecration he kept breaking in every other way. His life was a string of compromising entanglements with Philistine women against his parents' wishes, though the text notes the LORD was using the conflict to confront the Philistines. A failed marriage and a betrayed riddle led him to kill thirty Philistines for their garments and burn their fields; he later…
The kings of Israel and Judah, from Saul, David and Solomon through the divided kingdom to the exile.

t: The Kings of a Divided Kingdom
x: Israel's monarchy began around 1050 BC when the people demanded a king "such as all the other nations have" (1 Samuel 8:5) — a request God granted, though it was, in a real sense, a rejection of His own direct rule over them. Saul, David, and Solomon reigned in succession over a single united kingdom, each ruling roughly forty years. Saul's disobedience cost him the dynasty; David's faithfulness (despite serious failure) earned his family an everlasting covenant promise, later fulfilled in Christ; and Solomon's wisdom built the Temple but his divided loyalty planted the seeds of collapse. When Solomon's son Rehoboam alienated the northern tribes around 930 BC, the united kingdom permanently split in two. The northern kingdom kept the name Israel, set up its own capital and worship system under Jeroboam, and was ruled by nineteen kings across roughly two centuries — every single one of…

His Reign Saul was Israel's first king — tall, handsome, and initially humble. When Samuel anointed him, Saul was hiding among the baggage, overwhelmed by the weight of what God was calling him to. The Spirit of God came upon him powerfully, and his early reign showed genuine promise. He rallied Israel against the Ammonites at Jabesh-Gilead with decisive courage, and the nation united behind their new king with hope. But Saul's character contained a fatal flaw: he feared people more than he feared God. When pressured by circumstances at Gilgal, he offered sacrifices instead of waiting for Samuel as commanded. When sent to destroy the Amalekites completely, he spared the best livestock and King Agag, then lied about it. Samuel's devastating verdict — "To obey is better than sacrifice" — marked the beginning of Saul's unraveling. Saul's final decades were marked by paranoia, jealousy…

His Reign David's reign as king represents both the golden age of Israel and a cautionary tale about the dangers of unchecked power. Anointed as a shepherd boy, he waited over a decade before ascending to the throne — first ruling Judah from Hebron, then uniting all twelve tribes under his leadership in Jerusalem. He conquered the Jebusite stronghold, made it his capital, and brought the Ark of the Covenant there with dancing and celebration. God made an everlasting covenant with David — promising that his throne would be established forever, a promise ultimately fulfilled in Jesus Christ. David's military victories expanded Israel's borders to their greatest extent, and as a psalmist, he gave Israel its hymnbook, expressing the full range of human emotion in worship to God. Yet David's sin with Bathsheba and murder of Uriah revealed that even the greatest king was capable of the most…

His Reign Solomon inherited a united, prosperous kingdom from his father David and asked God for the one thing that would define his reign: wisdom. God was so pleased with this request — that Solomon asked for wisdom to govern rather than wealth or long life — that He granted all three. Solomon's wisdom became legendary, attracting the Queen of Sheba and rulers from across the known world to hear his insight. Solomon's greatest achievement was building the Temple in Jerusalem — the permanent dwelling place of God among His people that David had dreamed of but was not permitted to construct. The dedication of the Temple, with God's glory filling the building so that the priests could not stand, marked the pinnacle of Israel's worship life. Yet Solomon's end contradicts his beginning. Despite his unmatched wisdom, he married seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines — many from…

His Reign Rehoboam inherited the most prosperous kingdom in the world from his father Solomon, yet managed to tear it in two within days of his coronation. When the northern tribes came to him requesting relief from Solomon's heavy taxation and forced labor, Rehoboam faced a defining leadership decision. The older counselors — men who had served his father — advised compassion: "If you will be a servant to this people today, they will be your servants forever." Instead, Rehoboam rejected their wisdom and turned to his young friends who had grown up with him in palace privilege. Their advice was brutal arrogance: "My little finger is thicker than my father's waist." Rehoboam delivered this threat to the assembled tribes, and in that moment, ten of twelve tribes permanently seceded, creating the divided kingdom of Israel and Judah. Rehoboam's reign over the remaining kingdom of Judah was…

His Reign Jeroboam was one of Solomon's capable officials whom God chose to rule the ten northern tribes after the kingdom divided. Through the prophet Ahijah, God promised Jeroboam a dynasty like David's — if he would walk in God's ways and keep His commandments. But Jeroboam's faith crumbled under political anxiety. Fearing that his people would return to Rehoboam if they continued worshipping at the Temple in Jerusalem, he constructed two golden calves — one at Dan and one at Bethel — and told Israel, "Here are your gods who brought you up out of Egypt." Jeroboam's sin became so foundational to Israel's apostasy that subsequent writers refer to it repeatedly as "the sin of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin." Every wicked king of the northern kingdom is measured against this standard, and this pattern of idolatry persisted for two centuries until Israel's final…

His Reign Ahab is remembered as the most wicked king in Israel's history — a man who "did more to provoke the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger than all the kings of Israel who were before him." His marriage to Jezebel, a Phoenician princess devoted to Baal, introduced institutionalized pagan worship into Israel on an unprecedented scale. Together they built a temple to Baal in Samaria and actively hunted down the prophets of the LORD. Ahab's confrontation with Elijah at Mount Carmel exposed the emptiness of Baal worship, yet even this spectacular display of God's power did not permanently turn Ahab's heart. His coveting of Naboth's vineyard — and Jezebel's murder of Naboth to obtain it — revealed a king who believed his power entitled him to whatever he desired. Yet even Ahab experienced a moment of genuine repentance. When Elijah delivered God's judgment for Naboth's murder, Ahab tore…

His Reign Jehoshaphat was one of Judah's best kings — a man who sought the LORD, removed idols, and sent teachers throughout the land to instruct the people in God's law. His reign brought peace and prosperity to Judah, and even surrounding nations feared the God of Jehoshaphat. He reformed the judicial system, establishing judges in every fortified city with the charge: "Consider carefully what you do, because you are not judging for mere mortals but for the LORD." His finest hour came when a vast army of Moabites, Ammonites, and Meunites marched against Judah. Jehoshaphat's response was not military strategy but prayer and fasting: "We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you." God's answer came through a Levite prophet: "The battle is not yours but God's." Judah went out singing, and God set ambushes that destroyed the enemy armies. Yet Jehoshaphat's fatal weakness was his…

His Reign Hezekiah inherited a kingdom in spiritual ruin from his father Ahaz, who had shut the Temple doors, set up altars to foreign gods, and even sacrificed his own children in pagan rituals. In his very first month as king, Hezekiah reopened and purified the Temple, reinstated proper worship, and called the nation to celebrate Passover for the first time in generations. Hezekiah's greatest test came when Sennacherib of Assyria — the superpower that had already destroyed the northern kingdom — surrounded Jerusalem with an overwhelming army. Hezekiah's response was to take Sennacherib's threatening letter, spread it before the LORD in the Temple, and pray one of Scripture's most honest prayers of desperation. God's answer was decisive: that very night, the angel of the LORD struck down 185,000 Assyrian soldiers, and Sennacherib retreated in disgrace to be murdered by his own sons.…

His Reign Josiah became king at eight years old, inheriting a nation steeped in idolatry after the disastrous reigns of his grandfather Manasseh and father Amon. Yet at sixteen, he "began to seek the God of his father David," and at twenty, he began purging Judah of its high places, Asherah poles, and carved images. The turning point came when Josiah was twenty-six. During Temple repairs, the high priest Hilkiah discovered the Book of the Law — likely Deuteronomy — buried and forgotten in the Temple itself. When Josiah heard its words read aloud, he tore his robes in grief, recognizing how far the nation had drifted from God's commands. Josiah led the most thorough national repentance in Judah's history. He read the entire Book of the Law publicly, renewed the covenant, destroyed every idol and high place in the land, and celebrated a Passover unprecedented since the days of the judges.…

t: What the Bible Says About Loneliness
x: What the Bible says about loneliness, God's presence with His people, and the gift of community.

p: What the Bible Says About Loneliness
x: Loneliness is not the same experience as simply being alone. A person can live in the middle of a crowded city, surrounded by coworkers, family, and acquaintances, and still feel profoundly isolated — unseen, unknown, and disconnected at the level that actually matters. Conversely, solitude chosen and inhabited well can be restorative rather than lonely. What defines loneliness is not physical proximity to others but the absence of felt connection, understanding, and belonging. This desire for connection is not a modern psychological invention or a weakness to overcome — it is woven into the created order itself. Before sin entered the world, before anything else in creation was declared "not good," God said of Adam's solitude: "It is not good that the man should be alone" (Genesis 2:18). Community was built into humanity's design from the very beginning, which means the ache of…

p: What the Bible Says About Loneliness
x: God's promised presence is the foundational answer to loneliness, though it does not replace the need for human community. "I will never leave you nor forsake you" (Hebrews 13:5) is not a poetic sentiment but a covenant guarantee — the loneliest circumstance a believer can face is never a circumstance of true abandonment. Psalm 139's declaration that there is nowhere a person can go where God's presence does not reach — not heaven, not the depths, not the farthest sea — means isolation from other people, however painful, is never isolation from God. At the same time, Scripture never treats divine presence as a substitute for the human community God also designed us to need. The church exists precisely as the family of God, a body whose members belong to one another (Romans 12:5) and are commanded to bear one another's burdens (Galatians 6:2). God's answer to loneliness is not merely…

p: What the Bible Says About Loneliness
x: Because loneliness often distorts self-perception into believing connection is unavailable or unwanted, the biblical response is rarely passive waiting but active, sometimes uncomfortable movement toward others. Stepping into community — a small group, a shared meal, a vulnerable conversation — is frequently the very thing loneliness makes hardest to do, which is precisely why it requires deliberate choice rather than waiting for the feeling of readiness to arrive first. This does not mean every attempt at connection resolves loneliness instantly, or that community is always easy to find or sustain. But God settling "the solitary in a home" (Psalm 68:6) describes His consistent pattern of provision — He is not indifferent to isolation, and He works, often through ordinary means like a church community, a friend's invitation, or a small act of hospitality, to bring the lonely into…

p: What the Bible Says About Loneliness
x: Psalm 68:6 "God settles the solitary in a home; he leads out the prisoners to prosperity." Matthew 28:20 "And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age." Psalm 139:7-10 "Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend to heaven, you are there!" Hebrews 13:5 "For he has said, I will never leave you nor forsake you." Isaiah 43:2 "When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they shall not overwhelm you." Psalm 25:16 "Turn to me and be gracious to me, for I am lonely and afflicted." Genesis 2:18 "Then the LORD God said, 'It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him.'"

t: What the Bible Says About Lust & Sexual Sin
x: What the Bible says about lust and sexual sin, God's design for sexuality, and the path to purity and forgiveness.

p: What the Bible Says About Lust & Sexual Sin
x: Jesus deepened the conversation about sexual sin far beyond mere physical action when He taught that "everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart" (Matthew 5:28). This teaching locates the real battleground of sexual purity not primarily in behavior but in the heart and mind — the desires, fantasies, and gaze that precede any physical act. This is sobering because it means the fight against lust cannot be won simply by avoiding certain actions; it requires the deeper work of transforming what the heart desires and where the mind wanders. Scripture treats sexual sin with particular seriousness — not because it is uniquely unforgivable, but because of its unique relationship to the body. Paul writes that "the sexually immoral person sins against his own body" (1 Corinthians 6:18) in a way other sins do not, because the body of the…

p: What the Bible Says About Lust & Sexual Sin
x: The Bible's consistent strategy for sexual temptation is flight, not fight. Paul's instruction to "flee from sexual immorality" (1 Corinthians 6:18) and his warning to "make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires" (Romans 13:14) both assume that willpower alone, tested repeatedly against temptation, eventually fails. Job's resolve — "I have made a covenant with my eyes" (Job 31:1) — models proactive avoidance rather than reactive resistance: deciding in advance what will not be looked at, rather than trusting in-the-moment discipline when temptation actually arrives. Purity, in Scripture's vision, is not merely a list of prohibitions but a positive pursuit — filling the mind with what is true, honorable, and pure (Philippians 4:8) so there is less room for what is not. Walking by the Spirit, Paul writes, is how the desires of the flesh are not gratified (Galatians 5:16) —…

p: What the Bible Says About Lust & Sexual Sin
x: Practically, guarding purity begins with guarding the inputs — what is watched, read, followed, and dwelt on — because the mind cannot easily unsee or unthink what it has repeatedly exposed itself to. This is not legalism; it is the wisdom of Psalm 119:9's question, "How can a young man keep his way pure? By guarding it according to your word" — purity is guarded proactively through Scripture-shaped vigilance, not discovered accidentally through good intentions alone. Real accountability — a specific person who asks specific, direct questions regularly — interrupts the pattern of hiding that allows sexual sin to persist unaddressed. Combined with a clear plan for fleeing specific temptations (removing access, changing habits, avoiding known triggers) rather than merely resolving to try harder next time, this forms the practical shape of Scripture's counsel: flee, fill the mind with what…

p: What the Bible Says About Lust & Sexual Sin
x: Matthew 5:28 "But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart." 1 Thessalonians 4:3-4 "For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality; that each one of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor." Job 31:1 "I have made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I gaze at a virgin?" Romans 13:14 "But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires." Galatians 5:16 "But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh." Psalm 119:9 "How can a young man keep his way pure? By guarding it according to your word." 1 Corinthians 6:19-20 "Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you... You are not your own, for you were bought with a price."
What the Bible teaches about marriage and family: God's design, love and respect, raising children, and grace at home.

Marriage is the first human institution — established in Genesis 2, before government, before the church. God said "it is not good that man should be alone" and created woman as his ezer (helper/strength). Ephesians 5:22-33 is the most comprehensive NT passage on marriage. Paul grounds the husband-wife relationship in the mystery of Christ and the church — marriage is meant to be a living picture of the gospel. The Deuteronomy 6 model ("when you sit, walk, lie down, and rise") shows that faith-formation happens in the ordinary rhythms of life, not just formal instruction. In the ancient world, Paul's instructions were radical — calling husbands to sacrificial love and elevating wives as co-heirs of grace (1 Peter 3:7) was countercultural. The Bible presents no perfect families — Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, David all had dysfunction. Grace is always available, and God can redeem broken family…

Genesis 1:27-28 — "Male and female he created them… Be fruitful and multiply." Marriage and family are part of creation's design. Malachi 2:14-16 — God calls Himself a witness to the marriage covenant and hates faithless divorce. 1 Corinthians 13:4-7 — The "love chapter" defines the quality of love that sustains a marriage. Proverbs 31:10-31 — A portrait of a godly woman: industrious, wise, generous, and feared the Lord. Joshua 24:15 — "As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD." 3 John 1:4 — "I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth."

Marriage as a Living Picture (Ephesians 5) — Marriage reflects the relationship between Christ and the church. How does viewing your role this way change how you approach it, whether as husband or wife? Quick to Listen, Slow to Speak (James 1:19) — Healthy communication starts with genuinely hearing before responding. Where could you grow in listening more and reacting less this week? Faith Woven Into Ordinary Moments (Deuteronomy 6:6-7) — God's instruction was to teach His Word in the normal rhythms of daily life, not just formal settings. What everyday moments in your family could become faith-building conversations? Not Letting the Sun Go Down (Ephesians 4:26) — Scripture warns against carrying anger into the next day. Is there unresolved conflict in your marriage or family you need to address now rather than later? The Legacy You're Building (Deuteronomy 6, Psalm 78) — Faith is…
Studies of men of the Bible, from Abraham, Moses and David to Peter and Paul: flawed, faithful and used by God.

Scripture never flatters its heroes. The men whose stories anchor the Old and New Testaments are not marble statues of virtue — they are shepherds who lied, kings who murdered, prophets who despaired, and persecutors who became apostles. What sets them apart is not the absence of failure but the presence of God, who called imperfect men and patiently shaped them into instruments of His purpose. Their stories span the whole arc of redemptive history: Abraham's covenant journey out of Ur, Moses leading a nation out of slavery, David's rise from shepherd boy to king after God's own heart, Joseph's suffering turned to providence, Daniel's unwavering integrity in a pagan court, Elijah's fire and fear on the same mountain, Paul's conversion from persecutor to preacher, Peter's failure redeemed into leadership, Joshua's courage inherited from decades of faithful following, and Gideon's…

His Story Abraham's story begins with a call to leave everything familiar — his country, his people, his father's household — for a land God would show him. He obeyed without knowing the destination, launching a journey of faith that would span decades and test him in ways he could not have anticipated. Central to that journey was God's promise of a son, a promise that seemed to grow more impossible with each passing year as Abraham and Sarah aged well beyond childbearing years. The wait for Isaac was marked by very human stumbles — Abraham's attempt to secure an heir through Hagar, and his repeated lies about Sarah being his sister out of fear for his own safety. Yet through it all, God remained faithful to His covenant, and Isaac was finally born when Abraham was a hundred years old, the promise arriving precisely on God's timetable rather than Abraham's. The ultimate test came on…

His Story Moses was born under a death sentence, hidden by his mother, and set adrift on the Nile — only to be raised in the household of the very Pharaoh who had ordered his death. Straddling two worlds, Hebrew by birth and Egyptian by upbringing, Moses lived decades before God would use that unlikely position to prepare him for a mission he could not yet imagine. After killing an Egyptian and fleeing to Midian, Moses spent forty years shepherding flocks in obscurity before God met him at a burning bush and called him to lead Israel out of slavery. What followed was a relationship of unmatched intimacy — Scripture says God spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. Yet even Moses, humbled beyond any other man on earth, was barred from entering the Promised Land after striking the rock at Meribah in anger rather than trusting God's word. Moses led Israel through the…

His Story David was the youngest of Jesse's sons, overlooked and left tending sheep while his brothers were considered for kingship. Yet when Samuel came to anoint Israel's next king, God directed him past every impressive elder brother to the boy in the field, declaring that man looks on the outward appearance but the LORD looks on the heart. David's rise was neither swift nor easy. After defeating Goliath, he spent nearly a decade as a fugitive fleeing King Saul's jealous rage, repeatedly refusing opportunities to force his way to the throne even when Saul's life was in his hands. In the wilderness years, David wrote many of the psalms that would become Scripture's deepest expressions of trust, lament, and worship. When David finally became king, God established an everlasting covenant through him. Yet David's reign was marred by grave sin — his affair with Bathsheba and the murder of…

His Story Joseph was his father Jacob's favored son, a status that bred deep resentment among his brothers. At seventeen, that jealousy turned violent — sold into slavery and carried off to Egypt, torn from everything familiar. Yet Scripture repeats a striking refrain through Joseph's darkest years: "the LORD was with Joseph," even when every earthly circumstance suggested otherwise. In Egypt, Joseph rose to prominence in Potiphar's household, only to be falsely accused and thrown into prison. Even there, his gift for interpreting dreams eventually brought him before Pharaoh, and he was elevated to prime minister of Egypt, second only to Pharaoh himself — a stunning reversal from slave and prisoner to the most powerful man in the nation outside the throne. When famine drove his brothers to Egypt for grain, Joseph finally revealed his identity to the very men who had betrayed him. Rather…

His Story Daniel was taken captive from Jerusalem as a teenager during Nebuchadnezzar's first siege, transported to Babylon, and enrolled in a program designed to erase his Jewish identity and replace it with Babylonian loyalty. Given a new name — Belteshazzar — and immersed in pagan learning, Daniel faced immediate pressure to compromise. Yet from his very first recorded act — resolving not to defile himself with the king's food — Daniel established a pattern of quiet, unwavering faithfulness that would define his entire life. For over seventy years, Daniel served in the highest levels of multiple pagan governments — Babylonian and Persian — without compromising his devotion to God. His ability to interpret dreams and visions brought him influence with kings, yet he never used his position for personal gain. When his enemies sought to destroy him, the only accusation they could find…

His Story Elijah burst onto the biblical stage without genealogy or introduction — a wild prophet from Gilead who stood before King Ahab and declared that no rain would fall except by his word. In an era when Israel had plunged into Baal worship under Ahab and Jezebel's influence, Elijah stood as God's solitary voice of truth. His ministry was characterized by dramatic divine interventions: ravens bringing food, a widow's jar of oil that never emptied, and a dead boy raised to life. The pinnacle of Elijah's ministry came on Mount Carmel, where he challenged 450 prophets of Baal to a contest of divine power. After their god failed to respond to hours of frantic prayer, Elijah drenched his altar with water and prayed a simple, confident prayer. Fire fell from heaven, consuming the sacrifice, the stones, and even the water in the trench. The people fell on their faces crying, "The LORD, He…

His Story Before he was Paul the apostle, he was Saul the persecutor — a Pharisee of Pharisees, trained under Gamaliel, consumed with zeal for the traditions of his fathers. He oversaw the stoning of Stephen, dragged believers from their homes, and traveled to distant cities to imprison followers of "the Way." By his own admission, he was the chief of sinners, a man whose religious devotion had become a weapon against the very God he claimed to serve. Everything changed on the road to Damascus when a blinding light knocked him to the ground and the risen Christ spoke: "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" In that moment, the persecutor became the persecuted, and the enemy of the church became its greatest champion. Paul's conversion was so dramatic, so inexplicable by human means, that it stands as one of history's strongest testimonies to the reality of the resurrection. Paul's…

His Story Simon Peter was a rough-handed fisherman from Galilee — impulsive, passionate, and prone to speaking before thinking. When Jesus called him from his nets, Peter left everything to follow, and from that moment became the most prominent of the twelve disciples. He was the first to confess Jesus as "the Christ, the Son of the living God," and Jesus responded by declaring that upon this rock-like confession, He would build His church. Yet Peter's boldness was matched by his failures. He walked on water, then sank in doubt. He declared he would die for Jesus, then denied knowing Him three times before a servant girl. The night of Jesus' arrest, Peter's confidence shattered completely, and he wept bitterly at the depth of his cowardice. On the shores of Galilee after the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter with a threefold question — "Do you love me?" — matching each of Peter's three…

His Story Joshua served as Moses' assistant for forty years before being commissioned to lead Israel into the Promised Land. He was one of only two spies — along with Caleb — who believed God could deliver Canaan into Israel's hands when the other ten returned with a report of fear. That faith, tested through decades of wilderness wandering while an entire generation died around him, positioned Joshua to inherit the mantle of leadership when Moses could go no further. God's charge to Joshua rings across the centuries: "Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened, and do not be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go." This was not a suggestion but a command — because the task ahead was genuinely terrifying. Joshua's courage was not the absence of fear but obedience in the face of it. Under Joshua's leadership, the walls of Jericho fell, the sun stood still at…

His Story When the angel of the LORD appeared to Gideon, he found him threshing wheat in a winepress — hiding from the Midianites who had oppressed Israel for seven years. The greeting was startling: "The LORD is with you, mighty warrior." Gideon's response was incredulous. He saw himself as the least member of the weakest clan in Manasseh. Yet God saw something in Gideon that Gideon could not see in himself. Gideon's journey from fearful farmer to victorious leader was marked by hesitation and testing. He asked for signs — the famous fleece, wet then dry — not from lack of faith but from honest wrestling with a calling that seemed impossibly beyond him. God patiently accommodated Gideon's weakness, confirming His word again and again until Gideon was ready to move. The climax came when God reduced Gideon's army from 32,000 to just 300 men — deliberately making victory impossible by…
The miracles of Jesus and what they reveal about His authority over nature, sickness, evil spirits and death.

In Hebrew thought, a name was never a mere label — it revealed character, nature, and reputation. When Scripture gives God a name, it is unveiling something true about who He is, often in response to a specific human need or crisis. The root of Elohim is "El," meaning strength, might, or power. As Elohim, God is presented as the supreme Creator who spoke the universe into existence by the sheer authority of His word. He is not a distant clockmaker but an intimately involved architect who designed every star, every creature, and every human soul with intentionality and purpose.
