Discovering the money, the brothers are terrified and see it as a sign of God's judgment on them for what they did to Joseph (vv. 27-28). Jacob refuses at first to let Benjamin go, grieving that he has already lost Joseph and Simeon (vv. 36-38).
m: ten brothers bowing before a ruler they do not recognize, fulfilling a dream they mocked twenty years earlier, an accusation of spying that forces the very confession the brothers have avoided for two decades, we are verily guilty concerning our brother spoken while the accused stands listening in…

x: With the famine continuing, Jacob finally agrees to send Benjamin to Egypt after Judah pledges personal responsibility for his safety (vv. 8-14). The brothers return to Egypt bringing gifts and double the silver, and are brought to Joseph's house, where they fearfully explain the money found in their sacks (vv. 15-22). Joseph's steward reassures them and releases Simeon, and Joseph, overcome with emotion at seeing Benjamin, has to leave the room to weep in private (vv. 23-30). Joseph hosts the brothers at a feast, seating them in birth order to their astonishment and favoring Benjamin, but he still conceals his identity from them (vv. 31-34).
m: a famine that finally forces Jacob's hand where fear alone could not, Judah offering himself as surety for Benjamin in the same breath that proves how far he has come from the brother who sold Joseph for silver, a steward's casual mention of the God of Israel as the source of the money's mysterious…

x: Joseph tests his brothers one final time by having his silver cup planted in Benjamin's sack, then sending his steward to overtake them and accuse them of theft (vv. 1-6). When the cup is found in Benjamin's sack, the brothers tear their clothes in despair and return with him to the city (vv. 12-13). Judah pleads before Joseph, recounting how their father's life is bound up in the boy and offering himself as a slave in Benjamin's place rather than let his father suffer further loss (vv. 18-34). Judah's willingness to sacrifice himself for Benjamin marks a complete transformation from the brother who once proposed selling Joseph in chapter 37.
m: a silver cup deliberately planted in the youngest brother's sack as the final test of whether these men have actually changed, a rash vow that whoever has it shall die spoken before anyone knows the cup will be found on Benjamin, torn clothes and a return to the city rather than the abandonment…

x: Unable to control himself any longer, Joseph sends everyone but his brothers out of the room and reveals his identity to them, weeping so loudly the Egyptians hear it (vv. 1-2). The brothers are terrified, but Joseph reassures them, telling them not to be grieved or angry with themselves, because God sent him ahead of them to preserve life during the famine (vv. 4-8). Joseph tells them to hurry back and bring their father Jacob and the whole family down to Egypt to live in Goshen, promising to provide for them through the remaining years of famine (vv. 9-13). Pharaoh confirms the invitation and sends wagons and provisions for the journey, and when Jacob hears that Joseph is alive, his spirit revives (vv. 16-28).
m: a revelation that comes only after Joseph can no longer restrain himself, weeping loudly enough that the Egyptians outside the room can hear it, three separate statements crediting God rather than the brothers for sending Joseph to Egypt, an invitation for the whole family to come down and be…

x: Jacob sets out for Egypt, and God speaks to him in a vision at Beersheba, telling him not to be afraid to go down, promising to make him into a great nation there and to bring him back again (vv. 1-4). The chapter then lists the seventy members of Jacob's family who go down to Egypt, son by son (vv. 8-27). Judah is sent ahead to meet Joseph, and when Joseph arrives he falls on his father's neck and weeps for a long time (vv. 28-29). Joseph instructs his family to tell Pharaoh they are shepherds so they will be settled in Goshen, since shepherds are detestable to the Egyptians, keeping the family together and separate (vv. 31-34).
m: a stop at Beer-sheba, the same place Abraham and Isaac once worshipped, before Jacob will take a single step further toward Egypt, God's doubled call, Jacob, Jacob, promising both to go down with him and to bring him back up again, a genealogy totaling exactly seventy souls entering Egypt, a number…

x: Joseph presents five of his brothers and then his father Jacob before Pharaoh, who grants the family the land of Goshen to settle in (vv. 1-10). Joseph provides his father and brothers with food during the famine (vv. 11-12). As the famine intensifies, Joseph administers Egypt's crisis, collecting money, then livestock, and finally land from the Egyptians in exchange for grain, until Pharaoh owns nearly everything and the people become his tenants under a fifth-of-the-harvest tax (vv. 13-26). Israel settles and multiplies greatly in Goshen, and as Jacob nears death he makes Joseph swear to bury him in Canaan with his fathers (vv. 27-31).
m: five brothers coached to present themselves specifically as shepherds so Pharaoh will settle them apart in Goshen, Jacob blessing Pharaoh twice in an audience where the lesser is technically blessing the greater, a famine administration in which Joseph systematically buys up money, livestock, land…

x: As Jacob nears death, Joseph brings his two sons Ephraim and Manasseh to him, and Jacob formally adopts them as his own, giving them equal standing with his other sons in the inheritance (vv. 1-6). Jacob recalls Rachel's death and burial near Bethlehem before blessing the boys (v. 7). When Jacob crosses his hands to lay his right hand on the younger Ephraim instead of the firstborn Manasseh, Joseph tries to correct him, but Jacob insists he knows what he is doing, prophesying that the younger will become greater (vv. 13-19). The scene continues Genesis' recurring pattern of God's sovereign choice overturning the expected birth order.
m: two grandsons formally adopted as Jacob's own sons, elevating Joseph to a double portion no other son receives, a dying man's eyes too dim to see clearly yet his hands crossed deliberately rather than by accident, Joseph's protest at the crossed hands met with Jacob's own insistence, I know it, my…

x: Jacob gathers his twelve sons to tell them what will happen to them in the days to come, delivering a prophetic blessing over each one in turn (v. 1). Reuben is denounced for defiling his father's bed and loses his preeminence, while Simeon and Levi are condemned for their violence at Shechem (vv. 3-7). Judah is blessed with his brothers' praise and the promise that the scepter and ruler's staff will not depart from him until the coming of one to whom obedience belongs (vv. 8-12). The remaining brothers each receive shorter blessings characterizing their tribes' futures — Zebulun by the sea, Issachar's labor, Dan's judging, Joseph's fruitfulness, and Benjamin's fierceness among them (vv. 13-27). Jacob then instructs his sons to bury him with his fathers in the cave at Machpelah and dies (vv. 29-33).
m: twelve sons gathered to hear not farewells but futures, that which shall befall you in the last days, Reuben's birthright forfeited in a single sentence for defiling his father's bed, Simeon and Levi's violence at Shechem answered with a scattering that becomes judgment for one and blessing for the…

x: Joseph mourns his father's death and has him embalmed, then leads a large procession back to Canaan to bury Jacob in the cave at Machpelah, as he had sworn to do (vv. 1-14). After their father's death, Joseph's brothers fear he will now take revenge on them, but Joseph weeps at their fear and reassures them that though they intended evil against him, God intended it for good, to preserve many lives (vv. 15-21). Joseph lives to see his great-grandchildren through Ephraim and Manasseh's line (vv. 22-23). Before he dies at 110, Joseph makes his brothers swear to carry his bones out of Egypt when God eventually brings Israel back to the land he promised (vv. 24-26).
m: a father embalmed for forty days and mourned for seventy before a funeral procession of Egyptian officials, chariots and horsemen escorts his body all the way back to Canaan, brothers newly afraid of revenge the moment their father is gone, inventing or recalling a deathbed instruction to plead for…

x: The book opens with Jacob's family, seventy in number, thriving in Egypt after Joseph's death until a new king who does not know Joseph comes to power (vv. 1-8). Fearing Israel's growing numbers, Pharaoh forces the people into harsh slave labor building the cities of Pithom and Raamses, but the more they are oppressed the more they multiply (vv. 9-14). When that fails, Pharaoh orders the Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah to kill every baby boy at birth, but they refuse out of reverence for God and are blessed for it (vv. 15-21). Pharaoh then escalates to a public decree that every Hebrew son is to be thrown into the Nile (v. 22).
m: five verbs of growth in one verse echoing both the creation mandate and the promise to Abraham, a dynasty change introduced as a king who did not know Joseph, oppression that backfires so badly that affliction only multiplies the people further, two midwives who fear God enough to lie to a king and…

x: A Levite couple hides their newborn son for three months, then sets him adrift on the Nile in a basket, where Pharaoh's daughter finds and adopts him, naming him Moses (vv. 1-10). As a grown man, Moses kills an Egyptian he sees beating a Hebrew, and when the deed becomes known he flees to Midian (vv. 11-15). There he defends the daughters of the priest Reuel (Jethro) at a well, marries Zipporah, and has a son, Gershom (vv. 16-22). Years later, after the king of Egypt dies, God hears the groaning of enslaved Israel and remembers His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (vv. 23-25).
m: eighty years of a life compressed into twenty-five verses, an ark built for a baby using the same word Genesis used for Noah's vessel, a rescue engineered by a sister who positions her own mother to be hired as the nurse, a premature deliverance by the sword answered by a countryman's question of…

x: While tending sheep near Horeb, Moses encounters God in a bush that burns without being consumed, and is told to remove his sandals because he stands on holy ground (vv. 1-6). God declares that He has seen Israel's suffering and will send Moses to bring the people out of Egypt into a land flowing with milk and honey (vv. 7-10). When Moses protests his own inadequacy, God promises His presence, and when Moses asks for God's name, God answers with the self-existent name later rendered LORD, telling Moses this is His name forever (vv. 11-15). God then instructs Moses to gather Israel's elders, predicts that Pharaoh will resist even after mighty signs, and promises that Israel will leave Egypt with the Egyptians' wealth (vv. 16-22).
m: a bush that burns without being consumed, ground made holy by presence rather than by any quality of the dirt itself, a name whose form deflects definition back onto God's own self-existence, a first objection about identity answered not with reassurance about Moses but with a promise of…

x: God gives Moses three miraculous signs to prove his calling — a staff that becomes a serpent, a hand that turns leprous and is healed, and water that becomes blood — but when Moses still protests that he is not eloquent, God grows angry and appoints his brother Aaron as his spokesman (vv. 1-17). Moses receives Jethro's blessing to return to Egypt, and God warns him that He will harden Pharaoh's heart and that Moses is to tell Pharaoh that Israel is God's firstborn son (vv. 18-23). On the way, in a strange and abrupt episode, the LORD seeks to kill Moses, and Zipporah saves him by circumcising their son (vv. 24-26). Aaron meets Moses in the wilderness, and together they gather Israel's elders, perform the signs before the people, and the Israelites believe and bow in worship (vv. 27-31).
m: three signs matched to three objections, a rod, a hand and river water, a question about who made the mouth thrown back at a man who says he cannot speak, an anger kindled only after the plain request to send someone else, a firstborn son named as Israel's identity before a single plague has fallen…

x: Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh to let Israel go into the wilderness to worship the LORD, but Pharaoh refuses, claiming he does not know this God, and retaliates by making the Israelites gather their own straw while still producing the same quota of bricks (vv. 1-14). When the Israelite foremen are beaten for failing to meet the quota, they appeal to Pharaoh, only to be dismissed as lazy, and they turn in anger on Moses and Aaron for making their situation worse (vv. 15-21). Moses, discouraged, brings his complaint to God, asking why He sent him at all when conditions for the people have only worsened (vv. 22-23).
m: a first audience with Pharaoh answered by the question of who the LORD even is, a labor quota left standing while the raw material for meeting it is withdrawn, foremen beaten for a shortfall created by the order itself, the very people who had bowed in worship two chapters earlier now cursing the…

x: God reassures Moses, revealing Himself by His covenant name the LORD and renewing His promise to free Israel from bondage, take them as His people, and bring them into the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (vv. 1-8). Moses relays this to Israel, but the people are too broken by their harsh labor to listen, so God again commands him to go and speak to Pharaoh (vv. 9-13). The narrative pauses for a genealogy tracing the tribes of Reuben, Simeon, and especially Levi down to Moses and Aaron, establishing their family line (vv. 14-27). The chapter closes by returning to God's command and Moses' renewed objection that he is not a skilled speaker (vv. 28-30).
m: a name given a fuller unveiling than the patriarchs themselves received, seven first-person promises stacked one after another as though redemption were a single continuous sentence, a people too crushed by their own bondage to hear good news when it is spoken to them, a lineage inserted…

x: God tells Moses that he will function as God to Pharaoh, with Aaron as his prophet, and warns that He will harden Pharaoh's heart so His judgments may multiply against Egypt; Moses is eighty and Aaron eighty-three when they begin (vv. 1-7). Aaron's staff becomes a serpent before Pharaoh, and though Egypt's magicians duplicate the feat, Aaron's serpent swallows theirs, yet Pharaoh's heart remains hard (vv. 8-13). The LORD then strikes the Nile through Aaron's staff, turning all its water to blood, killing the fish and fouling the river, but the magicians reproduce this too and Pharaoh is unmoved for seven days (vv. 14-25).
h: The First Plague: Water to Blood (vv.14-25)
m: a relationship defined in terms of authority before a single word is spoken to Pharaoh, a rod that becomes a serpent and then swallows the serpents produced by rival magic, imitation power that can reproduce a plague but not reverse it, a river turned to blood on the very site where Hebrew infants…

x: God sends a plague of frogs that overrun Egypt; when Pharaoh begs Moses to remove them and promises to let Israel go, Moses prays them away, but Pharaoh hardens his heart once the relief comes (vv. 1-15). Next, Aaron strikes the dust to produce gnats, a plague even Egypt's magicians cannot replicate, and they acknowledge it as the finger of God, though Pharaoh still will not yield (vv. 16-19). God then sends swarms of flies but spares Goshen where Israel lives, and Pharaoh again offers a partial compromise before reneging as soon as the flies are gone (vv. 20-32).
m: Frogs, gnats and flies applied as successive pressure, magicians who imitate the first and cannot reproduce the second, a distinction drawn between Israel and Egypt, and a heart hardened again after each reprieve

x: God strikes Egypt's livestock with a fatal disease while sparing Israel's animals entirely, yet Pharaoh's heart remains hard (vv. 1-7). Moses then throws ashes into the air, producing painful boils on people and animals throughout Egypt, even afflicting the magicians themselves (vv. 8-12). Finally God sends the most devastating plague yet, a hailstorm mixed with fire that destroys crops, livestock, and people left in the open, sparing only Goshen; Pharaoh admits his sin and asks Moses to pray, but once the storm stops he and his officials harden their hearts again (vv. 13-35).
m: Livestock, boils and hail escalating from property to persons, Egypt's own magicians struck, a warning issued before the hail so that some could shelter, and a confession withdrawn as soon as the rain stopped

x: God explains that He has hardened Pharaoh's heart so that His signs will be remembered for generations, then sends a devastating swarm of locusts that consumes everything the hail had left; Pharaoh briefly confesses his sin and asks forgiveness, but hardens his heart again once the locusts are blown away (vv. 1-20). God next covers Egypt in a thick darkness for three days while Israel's homes remain filled with light; Pharaoh offers to let the people go if they leave their flocks behind, a condition Moses refuses (vv. 21-27). The chapter ends with Pharaoh warning Moses never to appear before him again on pain of death (v. 28).
m: Locusts and darkness stripping what the hail had left, officials pleading with Pharaoh before Israel does, negotiation over who is permitted to go, and a darkness described as something that could be felt

x: God tells Moses that one final plague remains: at midnight, every firstborn in Egypt will die, from Pharaoh's own son to the firstborn of slaves and livestock, while not even a dog will bark against Israel, showing that the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and His people (vv. 1-7). God also instructs the Israelites to ask their Egyptian neighbors for articles of silver and gold before they leave (v. 2). Moses, held in high regard by Pharaoh's officials, delivers this warning and leaves Pharaoh's presence in fierce anger, while the chapter notes that the LORD had hardened Pharaoh's heart so that all these wonders would be multiplied in Egypt (vv. 8-10).
m: one plague announced as the last, back wages requested in silver and gold for four centuries of unpaid labor, a coming distinction so exact that not even a dog barks on Israel's side of it, a warning delivered and then a departure made in great anger, and a hardening reaffirmed as the reason the…

x: The LORD institutes the Passover, instructing each household to select an unblemished lamb, apply its blood to the doorposts, and eat it roasted with unleavened bread, so that the destroyer will pass over homes marked by the blood (vv. 1-13). This meal is established as a perpetual memorial, alongside the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread (vv. 14-20). At midnight the LORD strikes down every firstborn in Egypt, producing a great cry of anguish throughout the land, and Pharaoh finally summons Moses and Aaron and orders Israel to leave immediately (vv. 29-33). The Israelites plunder the Egyptians of silver, gold, and clothing as they depart, and a company of roughly 600,000 men plus women and children, along with a mixed multitude, leaves Rameses after 430 years in Egypt (vv. 34-42). The chapter closes with further regulations for who may eat the Passover meal (vv. 43-51).
m: a calendar reset so that redemption itself becomes Israel's new starting point, a lamb selected on the tenth and killed on the fourteenth without a bone broken, blood applied to a doorframe as the one thing that turns judgment aside, a meal eaten in traveling clothes with a staff already in hand…

x: God commands that every firstborn male, whether of Israel's people or livestock, is to be consecrated to Him, and instructs Israel to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread annually as a reminder of the exodus, treating it as a sign on their hand and forehead (vv. 1-16). Rather than leading Israel along the shorter route through Philistine territory, where they might face war and lose heart, God guides them by way of the wilderness toward the Red Sea, and the people leave Egypt armed for battle, with Moses carrying Joseph's bones as he had sworn (vv. 17-19). The LORD leads them visibly, going before them in a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night (vv. 20-22).
h: The Pillar of Cloud and Fire (vv.20-22)
m: a firstborn claimed as God's own on the strength of firstborns once spared, a longer road chosen deliberately because the shorter one led past a war the people were not ready to face, a coffin carried the length of a wilderness journey to answer a four-hundred-year-old oath, a father instructed to…

x: God directs Israel to camp in a position that will lure Pharaoh into pursuing them, so that His glory will be displayed when Pharaoh's army is destroyed (vv. 1-4). Pharaoh, regretting he let Israel go, chases them with his chariots, and the terrified Israelites cry out and blame Moses, who tells them to stand still and watch the LORD fight for them (vv. 5-14). At God's command Moses stretches his staff over the sea, which divides so Israel crosses on dry ground while the pillar of cloud shields them from the pursuing Egyptians (vv. 15-22). When Moses stretches his hand out again, the waters return and destroy Pharaoh's entire army, and Israel, seeing this great deliverance, fears the LORD and believes in Him and in Moses (vv. 23-31).
m: a camp positioned to look trapped so that a king's confidence would be his own undoing, a command to stop crying out and start marching forward, a wind that blows all night to open what a hand merely gestures toward, chariot wheels that come off mid-pursuit as the army realizes too late whom it is…

x: Moses and Israel sing a song celebrating the LORD's triumph over Pharaoh's army, praising His holiness, power, and faithfulness, and anticipating that He will bring Israel to His holy dwelling place (vv. 1-18). Miriam the prophetess leads the women in the same refrain with tambourines and dancing (vv. 19-21). Three days into the wilderness, Israel finds no water until they reach Marah, where the water is bitter; Moses throws in a piece of wood at God's direction and the water becomes drinkable, and the LORD gives them a statute there and tests their obedience (vv. 22-26). The people then arrive at Elim, where they find twelve springs and seventy palm trees and camp by the water (v. 27).
m: a song sung on a shore still littered with the wreckage of an army, praise moving from a single victory outward to nations who have not yet even heard the news, water made undrinkable three days after the greatest deliverance in the nation's history, a tree shown by God turning bitterness sweet…

x: In the wilderness of Sin, the Israelites grumble against Moses and Aaron, longing for the food they had in Egypt, so God promises to rain bread from heaven, testing whether the people will follow His instructions (vv. 1-4). Each evening quail cover the camp and each morning a flaky substance called manna appears on the ground, which the people are to gather daily in a set amount, with a double portion on the sixth day so none needs to be gathered on the Sabbath (vv. 13-30). Some disobey and try to gather on the Sabbath or keep leftover manna overnight, and it spoils or cannot be found. A jar of manna is kept as a memorial for future generations, and Israel eats manna for the next forty years until reaching the border of Canaan (vv. 31-36).
m: a month out from slavery and already the flesh pots of Egypt remembered more fondly than the whip, bread provided daily as both gift and test of whether the law will be walked in, a portion doubled on the sixth day so the seventh can be kept without gathering, manna spoiling overnight for the…

x: When Israel finds no water at Rephidim, the people quarrel with Moses and God instructs him to strike the rock at Horeb, from which water flows out for the people (vv. 1-7). Amalek then attacks Israel, and as long as Moses holds up his hands with the staff of God, Joshua and the army prevail in battle, with Aaron and Hur supporting Moses' arms when he grows tired (vv. 8-13). The LORD tells Moses to record this victory as a lasting memorial and declares that He will eventually blot out Amalek entirely, and Moses builds an altar there, naming it after the LORD as Israel's banner of victory (vv. 14-16).
m: water struck from a rock that God says he will be standing on when it is struck, a place named twice for the same complaint, once for testing and once for quarreling, a battle whose outcome tracks not the sword in the valley but a pair of raised hands on the hill, arms grown too heavy to hold up…

x: Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, comes to the wilderness camp bringing Zipporah and their two sons, and rejoices upon hearing all that the LORD has done for Israel, offering sacrifices and sharing a meal with Moses and the elders (vv. 1-12). Watching Moses spend the whole day personally judging every dispute brought to him, Jethro warns that this pace will wear him out and advises him to appoint capable, God-fearing, trustworthy men as judges over groups of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens, reserving only the hardest cases for himself (vv. 13-23). Moses follows this counsel, establishing a tiered system of judges, and Jethro then returns to his own land (vv. 24-27).
m: a father-in-law's visit turning into the clearest lesson in Scripture on delegation, a whole nation waiting from morning to evening for one man's judgment, an outsider's blunt diagnosis that the thing Moses is doing is not good and will wear him away, a fourfold qualification for leaders, able…

x: Three months after leaving Egypt, Israel camps before Mount Sinai, and God proposes a covenant through Moses: if the people obey Him and keep His covenant, they will be His treasured possession, a kingdom of priests, and a holy nation, and the people agree to all He has spoken (vv. 1-8). God tells Moses He will come to him in a thick cloud so the people can hear Him speak and trust Moses as well, and instructs the people to consecrate themselves, wash their clothes, and stay away from the mountain for three days (vv. 9-15). On the third day, amid thunder, lightning, thick cloud, and a loud trumpet blast, the LORD descends on the mountain in fire, and Moses goes up and down relaying warnings that no one but Moses and Aaron may cross the boundary to approach God directly (vv. 16-25).
m: an arrival at the very mountain where the bush once burned, fulfilling a promise made to Moses before he ever returned to Egypt, an offer framed as identity before it is framed as obligation, eagles' wings before commandments, a people's unanimous yes given before they have heard a single specific…

x: From Mount Sinai, God speaks the Ten Commandments directly to the assembled nation of Israel, establishing the moral foundation of the covenant relationship. The first four commandments govern Israel's relationship with God (vv. 1-11), and the remaining six govern relationships with others (vv. 12-17). Terrified by the thunder, lightning, and trumpet blast accompanying God's voice, the people ask Moses to serve as mediator so God would no longer speak to them directly (vv. 18-21).
h: The First Table: Duties Toward God (vv.3-11)
The Second Table: Duties Toward Neighbor (vv.12-17)
m: words spoken audibly to an entire nation rather than delivered through an intermediary, a preamble of rescue placed before a single command is given, four commandments ordering the relationship with God followed by six ordering relationships with neighbors, prohibitions reduced in places to two or…

x: God begins a section of case law governing Israel's covenant community, opening with regulations for the release of Hebrew servants after six years of service (vv. 1-11). The laws then turn to crimes deserving the death penalty — murder, striking or cursing one's parents, and kidnapping — followed by principles of proportional justice for personal injuries, summarized as life for life, eye for eye (vv. 12-27). The chapter closes with laws about liability when an ox gores a person or when negligence with a pit or animal causes harm or death, establishing that even property owners bear responsibility for the safety of others (vv. 28-36).
m: case law applying the commandments to disputes an agrarian society would actually face, a servant who may choose permanent bondage marked by a pierced ear at the doorpost, a sharp line drawn between premeditated murder and accidental killing by whether a city of refuge is available, eye for eye and…

x: This chapter continues Israel's case law with regulations on theft and restitution, requiring thieves to repay what they stole, often multiple times over (vv. 1-15). It then addresses seduction, moves to capital offenses such as sorcery, bestiality, and sacrificing to other gods, and commands compassionate treatment of foreigners, widows, and orphans, warning that God Himself will hear their cry if they are mistreated (vv. 16-24). Further laws forbid charging interest on loans to the poor and require a borrowed cloak taken in pledge to be returned by sunset, and the chapter closes with instructions on offering the firstfruits and firstborn to God and a call to be a holy people (vv. 25-31).
m: restitution scaled to the animal and its recoverability, four-fold for a sheep and five-fold for an ox already sold, capital penalties reserved for sorcery, bestiality and sacrifice to other gods, a repeated appeal to Israel's own memory of being strangers as the reason to treat strangers well, a…

x: God gives Israel laws promoting justice — prohibiting false testimony, bribery, and perverting justice for the poor, and requiring fair treatment even of an enemy's stray animal (vv. 1-9). He commands a sabbatical year for the land every seventh year and weekly Sabbath rest for people and animals alike, along with three annual feasts — Unleavened Bread, Harvest, and Ingathering — when all Israel's men are to appear before Him (vv. 10-19). The LORD then promises to send an angel ahead of Israel to guard them and lead them into the land, warning them not to worship the gods of the nations they will displace, and promising to gradually drive out those nations and establish Israel's borders (vv. 20-33).
m: false witness and majority pressure treated as equally corrupting to justice, an obligation to help even an enemy's struggling animal, a sabbath year that lets the land itself rest while the poor eat what grows unattended, three annual pilgrimage feasts marking the agricultural and redemptive…

x: Moses relays all of God's words and laws to the people, who agree to obey, and he formalizes the covenant by sprinkling sacrificial blood on the altar and on the people, calling it the blood of the covenant (vv. 1-8). Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders then go up the mountain and see God, eating and drinking in His presence without harm (vv. 9-11). Moses ascends further into the cloud that covers the mountain, where the glory of the LORD appears like a consuming fire, and he remains there receiving instructions for forty days and forty nights (vv. 12-18).
m: a covenant sealed with blood divided between an altar and a crowd, half on one and half thrown on the other, tying both parties into a single agreement, seventy-four elders who see God and are simply not struck down for it, a pavement like sapphire described beneath his feet, a book of the covenant…

x: God calls the Israelites to bring voluntary offerings of gold, silver, fine materials, and skins so that a sanctuary can be built for Him to dwell among His people, built exactly according to the pattern He shows Moses (vv. 1-9). He then gives detailed instructions for the ark of the covenant, a gold-covered chest topped with a mercy seat and two cherubim, where God will meet with Moses (vv. 10-22). The chapter continues with specifications for the table of showbread and the golden lampstand, both to be placed inside the sanctuary (vv. 23-40).
m: a sanctuary requested only from those who give willingly, materials from gold to acacia wood listed before a single instruction on assembly, an ark whose two cherubim face each other and look down at the very spot God promises to meet Moses, bread kept perpetually before God's presence representing…

x: God gives Moses detailed instructions for the Tabernacle's structure — ten linen curtains embroidered with cherubim, an outer covering of goat-hair curtains, and a wooden frame of acacia boards set in silver bases (vv. 1-30). A veil woven with cherubim is to separate the Most Holy Place, where the ark will rest, from the Holy Place, and a screen is to cover the entrance to the tent (vv. 31-37).
m: ten inner curtains joined by fifty gold clasps into what the text insists on calling one tabernacle, four successive layers of covering moving from woven cherubim inward to weatherproof skins outward, a framework of gilded acacia standing in silver sockets on three sides, a veil separating the holy…

x: God prescribes the bronze altar for burnt offerings, complete with horns and bronze utensils, to stand before the Tabernacle (vv. 1-8). He then details the dimensions of the surrounding courtyard, its linen curtains, posts, and entrance gate (vv. 9-19). The chapter closes with instructions for pure oil to keep a lamp burning continually, tended by Aaron and his sons (vv. 20-21).
m: a bronze altar with horns on each corner positioned as the very first thing anyone entering the courtyard would meet, a courtyard whose linen walls run a hundred fifty feet by seventy-five and stand only shoulder height, a single gate on the east side as the only way in, oil kept burning from…

x: God instructs Moses to set apart Aaron and his sons as priests and to have skilled craftsmen design sacred garments that reflect dignity and honor (vv. 1-5). These include an ornate ephod, a breastpiece set with twelve gemstones representing Israel's tribes and containing the Urim and Thummim for seeking God's guidance, a blue robe hung with bells and pomegranates, and a gold plate on the turban inscribed as holy to the LORD (vv. 6-39). Simpler garments are also prescribed for Aaron's sons, including undergarments to preserve modesty when they serve at the altar (vv. 40-43).
m: garments made for glory and for beauty rather than for utility alone, two shoulder stones and twelve breastplate stones carrying the whole nation's names into the priest's presence with God, bells and pomegranates alternating on a robe's hem so the priest's movement inside the holy place is…

x: God prescribes an elaborate seven-day ordination ceremony for Aaron and his sons, involving washing, special garments, and a series of sacrifices — a bull for sin, one ram as a burnt offering, and a second ram whose blood is applied to their ears, thumbs, and toes to consecrate them fully to priestly service (vv. 1-37). Instructions follow for the continual daily offering of two lambs at the Tabernacle, morning and evening (vv. 38-42). The chapter closes with God's promise to meet with Israel there and dwell among them as their God, the very reason the Tabernacle and priesthood exist (vv. 43-46).
m: a seven-day ordination built from washing, clothing, anointing and three distinct sacrifices, blood applied to an ear, a thumb and a big toe so that hearing, doing and walking are each separately consecrated, a sin offering whose flesh is burned outside the camp while its fat alone goes to the…

x: God instructs the building of a gold altar of incense, to be placed before the veil, where Aaron will burn incense every morning and evening and make atonement once a year (vv. 1-10). He also commands a census tax — a half-shekel ransom paid by every Israelite — and prescribes a bronze basin where priests must wash before serving at the altar or entering the Tabernacle (vv. 11-21). The chapter concludes with the precise recipes for the holy anointing oil and the incense, both reserved exclusively for sacred use and forbidden to be copied for ordinary purposes (vv. 22-38).
m: an incense altar kept so small it is easy to miss beside the ark it stands nearest to, a ransom of exactly half a shekel charged alike to rich and poor at every census, a bronze laver positioned between altar and tent so that cleansing always follows atonement and precedes service, an anointing oil…

x: God appoints Bezalel and Oholiab, filling them with His Spirit and skill to craft all the furnishings of the Tabernacle and the priestly garments (vv. 1-11). He then reaffirms the command to keep the Sabbath as a perpetual sign of the covenant between Him and Israel, warning that anyone who profanes it is to be cut off from the people (vv. 12-17). The chapter closes with God giving Moses the two stone tablets of the covenant law, written by God's own hand (v. 18).
m: The first man in Scripture said to be filled with the Spirit, and filled for craftsmanship rather than prophecy, the Sabbath set as a limit on even holy work, and tablets written with the finger of God

x: While Moses is on the mountain, the people grow impatient and pressure Aaron into making a golden calf, which they worship and celebrate with a feast, prompting God to threaten to destroy the nation until Moses intercedes on their behalf (vv. 1-14). Moses comes down, breaks the stone tablets in anger at the scene, burns and grinds the calf into powder, and makes the people drink it in water (vv. 15-20). When Moses calls for those loyal to the LORD, the Levites respond and execute about three thousand people involved in the idolatry (vv. 25-29). Moses then returns to God to intercede once more, offering to be blotted out himself in the people's place, but God sends a plague upon them for their sin while still preserving the nation (vv. 30-35).
m: A covenant broken within weeks of being made, a leader who blames the people he led, tablets shattered deliberately, an intercession that appeals to God's reputation rather than Israel's merit, and a mediator offering to be blotted out

x: After the golden calf incident, God tells Moses He will send an angel to lead Israel to the promised land but will not go among them Himself, lest He consume them for their stubbornness, prompting the people to mourn and remove their ornaments (vv. 1-6). Moses meets with God at the tent of meeting outside the camp, speaking with Him face to face as a friend, and pleads for God's own presence to go with Israel rather than an angel alone, a request God grants (vv. 7-17). Moses then asks to see God's glory, and God agrees to let His goodness pass by while hiding Moses in the cleft of a rock, allowing him to see only His back (vv. 18-23).
h: An Angel Instead of My Presence (vv.1-6)
Face to Face, as a Man Speaketh unto His Friend (vv.7-11)
m: An offer of an angel instead of God's own presence, a leader who refuses to move without it, conversation described as between friends, and a request to see glory answered by a hand over a cleft in the rock

x: Moses cuts two new stone tablets and returns to the mountain, where the LORD passes before him and proclaims His own name, describing Himself as compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love, while also holding the guilty accountable (vv. 1-9). Moses worships and intercedes for the people, and God renews the covenant, repeating warnings against alliances with the Canaanites and their idols and reiterating instructions for Israel's annual feasts (vv. 10-26). Moses remains on the mountain forty days without food or water while God writes the words of the covenant on the new tablets (vv. 27-28). When Moses comes down, his face shines so brightly from being in God's presence that he must wear a veil except when speaking directly with the LORD (vv. 29-35).
h: Forty Days Without Bread or Water (vv.27-28)
m: New tablets cut by human hands, the self-description of God most quoted inside the Old Testament itself, a covenant renewed with the same terms that were broken, and a face that shone and had to be veiled

x: Moses reminds the people to keep the Sabbath, then relays God's instructions for the Tabernacle, calling for freewill offerings of gold, silver, fine fabrics, and skins from anyone whose heart moves them (vv. 1-19). The people respond with remarkable generosity, men and women alike bringing materials and offering their skills willingly (vv. 20-29). Moses again identifies Bezalel and Oholiab as the Spirit-filled craftsmen chosen to lead the work and teach others their skills (vv. 30-35).
m: The Sabbath stated before the building begins, offerings taken only from willing hearts, skill named as a gift rather than a qualification, and craftsmen announced publicly to the people who will fund them

x: Bezalel, Oholiab, and the other skilled craftsmen begin constructing the Tabernacle, and the people continue bringing so many materials that Moses has to command them to stop giving (vv. 1-7). The chapter then details the actual construction of the curtains, coverings, wooden frames, bars, and the veil and screen, carried out exactly as the LORD had commanded Moses (vv. 8-38).
m: Giving that had to be stopped by proclamation, curtains counted and measured, frames and bases and bars itemized, and a veil that divides what the rest of the structure exists to house

x: Bezalel constructs the ark of the covenant with its gold mercy seat and cherubim, the table for the bread of the Presence, and the golden lampstand, each built to the specifications God had given (vv. 1-24). He then makes the altar of incense and prepares the sacred anointing oil and incense (vv. 25-29).
h: The Anointing Oil and the Incense (v.29)
m: Furnishings made in the order of their nearness to God, gold beaten rather than cast, a lampstand from a single talent, and anointing oil and incense prepared last

x: Bezalel builds the bronze altar and the bronze basin, the latter made from the mirrors of the women who served at the entrance of the Tabernacle, and completes the courtyard with its curtains and posts (vv. 1-20). The chapter closes with a detailed accounting of all the gold, silver, and bronze contributed and used in the Tabernacle's construction, recorded under Ithamar's oversight (vv. 21-31).
m: The altar a worshipper met before anything else, a laver made from donated mirrors, a courtyard that marks a boundary, accounts published rather than assumed, and silver traceable to a census of 603,550 men

x: The skilled workers complete the priestly garments — the ephod, breastpiece with its twelve stones, robe, tunics, turban, and the gold plate inscribed as holy to the LORD — each made exactly as God had commanded (vv. 1-31). All the finished components of the Tabernacle are then brought to Moses, who inspects the work, finds it done precisely as instructed, and blesses the people (vv. 32-43).
m: Garments that state doctrine rather than merely cover, twelve names carried on the shoulders and twelve stones over the heart, an inscription reading HOLINESS to the LORD, and a completion described in the language of Genesis

x: God instructs Moses to set up the Tabernacle on the first day of the new year, anoint all its furnishings, and consecrate Aaron and his sons as priests (vv. 1-16). Moses erects the Tabernacle exactly as the LORD had commanded, placing the ark, table, lampstand, and altars each in their proper place (vv. 17-33). When the work is finished, the cloud covers the tent and the glory of the LORD fills the Tabernacle so completely that even Moses cannot enter, and from then on the cloud's movement over the Tabernacle guides Israel's travels through the wilderness (vv. 34-38).
m: A tabernacle raised on the first day of the second year, every item placed as commanded, obedience recorded eight times in one chapter, a cloud that settles, and a glory so full that even Moses cannot enter

x: The LORD, speaking to Moses from the Tent of Meeting, gives Israel instructions for the burnt offering, the first of the sacrificial laws (vv. 1-2). If the offering is a bull from the herd, the worshiper presents a male without defect, lays a hand on its head so it is accepted as atonement, and kills it before the LORD; Aaron's sons then sprinkle the blood on the altar, cut the animal into pieces, wash the entrails and legs, and burn the whole animal on the wood as a pleasing aroma to the LORD (vv. 3-9). The same pattern applies to an offering from the flock, a sheep or goat, killed on the north side of the altar (vv. 10-13). Those too poor to offer an animal may bring turtledoves or young pigeons, which the priest kills, drains of blood, and burns whole on the altar (vv. 14-17). In every case the offering is wholly consumed, signifying the worshiper's complete surrender to God.
h: The Burnt Offering from the Herd (vv.1-9)
The Burnt Offering from the Flock (vv.10-13)
m: three tiers of animal, cattle, flock and birds, set side by side so that wealth never determines whether a worshipper can approach, a hand laid on the animal's head transferring identification before a single cut is made, an offering consumed entirely rather than shared with anyone, blood handled…

x: The LORD instructs Israel on the grain offering, made of fine flour with oil and frankincense, of which the priest burns a token portion on the altar while the remainder belongs to Aaron and his sons as a most holy portion (vv. 1-3). Grain offerings may also be baked in an oven as unleavened cakes or wafers, cooked on a griddle, or prepared in a pan, but every kind must be brought to the priest for burning (vv. 4-10). No grain offering may contain yeast or honey, though these may be presented separately as firstfruits, and every offering must be seasoned with salt as a sign of the enduring covenant (vv. 11-13). A firstfruits grain offering of roasted, crushed new grain, mixed with oil and frankincense, is also described, with the priest again burning a memorial portion as a food offering to the LORD (vv. 14-16).
h: No Leaven, No Honey, Always Salt (vv.11-13)
m: The one offering with no death in it, grain as the fruit of human labor given back, a memorial portion burned and the rest fed to the priests, leaven and honey excluded while salt is required, and firstfruits given before the harvest is enjoyed

x: The LORD gives instructions for the peace offering, a voluntary sacrifice of fellowship that may be brought from the herd, male or female without defect; the worshiper lays a hand on its head, kills it at the Tent of Meeting, and the priests sprinkle its blood on the altar (vv. 1-5). The same offering may come from the flock as a lamb or a goat, following the identical procedure of laying on hands, killing, and sprinkling blood (vv. 6-16). In every case the fat covering the entrails, the two kidneys, and the covering of the liver are burned on the altar as a food offering of pleasing aroma to the LORD, since all fat belongs to him (vv. 3-4, 9-10, 14-16). The chapter closes with a permanent statute for every generation: Israel must never eat fat or blood (v. 17).
h: The Peace Offering from the Herd (vv.1-5)
A Perpetual Statute: Neither Fat Nor Blood (v.17)

x: The LORD tells Moses that when anyone sins unintentionally against one of his commands, a sin offering must be brought to make atonement (vv. 1-2). If the anointed priest sins and brings guilt on the people, he must offer a young bull, laying his hand on its head before killing it; he then brings its blood into the Tent of Meeting, sprinkles it seven times before the veil, puts blood on the horns of the incense altar, and burns the fat on the altar while the rest of the bull is carried outside the camp and burned (vv. 3-12). If the whole congregation sins unknowingly, the elders lay hands on a bull on the people's behalf and the same blood ritual is followed, so that the priest may make atonement and the people may be forgiven (vv. 13-21). A ruler who sins must bring a male goat, with blood applied to the horns of the burnt offering altar rather than the incense altar (vv. 22-26). An…
h: When One of the Common People Sins (vv.27-35)

x: The chapter lists specific unintentional sins that require a sin offering: failing to testify after hearing a public call for witnesses, unknowingly touching an unclean carcass or human uncleanness, and thoughtlessly swearing an oath one later forgets (vv. 1-4). Once a person recognizes his guilt, he must confess the sin and bring a female lamb or goat, or, if that is unaffordable, two turtledoves or pigeons — one for the sin offering and one for a burnt offering (vv. 5-10). The LORD then addresses guilt offerings for unintentional misuse of holy things, requiring a ram plus restitution of the value lost plus one-fifth (vv. 14-16), and for any unwitting violation of a command, requiring a ram without defect so that the…

If He Cannot Afford a Lamb (vv.7-13)
The Trespass Offering: Restitution with a Fifth Added (vv.14-16)

x: The LORD gives laws for restitution when someone sins against a neighbor through fraud, robbery, extortion, or a false oath over a lost item: the offender must repay the full amount plus a fifth and bring a ram as a guilt offering, and the priest will make atonement (vv. 1-7). Aaron and his sons are then instructed on the burnt offering: the fire on the altar must burn continually, day and night, and the priest must remove the ashes each morning in special garments before carrying them outside the camp (vv. 8-13). A separate grain offering is prescribed for Aaron's own ordination day, to be wholly burned rather than eaten (vv. 19-23). Finally, the law of the sin offering specifies that it must be slaughtered where the…
h: The Law of the Burnt Offering for Priests (vv.8-13)

x: The law of the guilt offering is given: it is slaughtered like the burnt offering, its fat burned on the altar, and its meat eaten by the priests as a most holy portion, with the officiating priest keeping the hide of any burnt offering he presents (vv. 1-10). The law of the peace offering follows, distinguishing a thanksgiving offering — accompanied by various breads and eaten the same day — from a vow or freewill offering, which may also be eaten the next day but must be burned if any remains on the third day, since eating it then makes the offering unacceptable (vv. 11-18). Meat that touches anything unclean, or is eaten by someone unclean, defiles the offering and brings guilt on the offerer (vv. 19-21). Israel is forbidden to eat the fat of any ox, sheep, or goat, or any blood at all, on penalty of being cut off from the people (vv. 22-27). The priest's portion of every peace…
h: The Law of the Guilt/Trespass Offering (vv.1-10)
The Law of the Peace Offering (vv.11-21)
The Wave Offering and Heave Offering (vv.28-36)

x: Moses assembles the congregation and carries out the ordination of Aaron and his sons exactly as the LORD commanded (vv. 1-5). He washes them, dresses Aaron in the priestly garments — tunic, sash, robe, ephod, breastpiece with the Urim and Thummim, and turban with its gold plate — and anoints the tabernacle, the altar, and Aaron himself with oil (vv. 6-12). Aaron's sons are then clothed, and Moses offers a bull as a sin offering, applying its blood to the altar and burning its fat while the rest is burned outside the camp (vv. 13-17). A ram is offered as a burnt offering, and a second ram, the ram of ordination, provides blood that Moses applies to the right ear, thumb, and big toe of Aaron and his sons before he waves portions of the meat and bread before the LORD (vv. 18-29). Moses sprinkles Aaron and his sons and their garments with oil and altar blood to consecrate them, then…
m: seven separate movements, washing, clothing, anointing, sin offering, burnt offering, ram of consecration and week-long seclusion, assembled into a single ordination, oil poured rather than sprinkled on Aaron's head, an ear, a thumb and a great toe each marked with blood, priests requiring their…

x: On the eighth day, Moses summons Aaron, his sons, and the elders of Israel, and directs Aaron to offer a calf as a sin offering and a ram as a burnt offering for himself, and to have the people bring a goat, calf, lamb, and grain offering, so that the LORD's glory may appear (vv. 1-6). Aaron approaches the altar and offers the sin offering and burnt offering for himself, following the prescribed procedures of blood application and burning (vv. 7-14). He then offers the people's sin offering, burnt offering, grain offering, and peace offerings, waving the breast and thigh before the LORD as Moses instructed (vv. 15-21). Aaron lifts his hands and blesses the people, and after he and Moses come out of the Tent of Meeting, the glory of the LORD appears to the whole assembly (vv. 22-23). Fire goes out from the LORD's presence and consumes the burnt offering and fat on the altar, and the…
h: The Eighth Day — Aaron's First Ministry (vv.1-4)
Aaron's Blessing and the Glory of God (vv.22-24)
m: an eighth day arriving only after seven of confinement, exactly the order Moses gives Aaron, offer for thyself first and then for the people, divine fire descending to consume the offering, the same fire that will consume Nadab and Abihu one chapter later, a blessing pronounced before the people…

x: Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorized fire before the LORD that he had not commanded, and fire comes out from the LORD and kills them on the spot (vv. 1-2). Moses tells Aaron that this shows the LORD will be shown holy by those who come near him, and Aaron remains silent; Moses then has the bodies carried outside the camp and forbids Aaron and his remaining sons from any mourning rites, on pain of death, lest the LORD's anger fall on the whole congregation (vv. 3-7). The LORD tells Aaron that priests must never drink wine or strong drink when entering the Tent of Meeting, so that they can distinguish holy from common and clean from unclean, and can teach Israel the statutes (vv. 8-11). Moses instructs Aaron and his remaining sons on eating the remaining grain offering and the priests' portions of the peace offerings in a clean place (vv. 12-15). Moses is angry to learn that…
h: The Sin of Nadab and Abihu (vv.1-3)
No Wine, and the Duty to Distinguish (vv.8-11)
The Dispute over the Sin Offering (vv.16-20)

x: The LORD gives Moses and Aaron dietary laws for Israel, beginning with land animals: any animal that has a split hoof and chews the cud may be eaten, while the camel, rock hyrax, hare, and pig are named as unclean because each lacks one of the two marks (vv. 1-8). Among water creatures, only those with fins and scales are permitted; all others are detestable (vv. 9-12). A list of unclean birds follows, including eagles, vultures, ravens, owls, and the stork, while most winged, jumping insects such as locusts and grasshoppers are permitted (vv. 13-23). Contact with the carcasses of unclean animals, and of a list of small unclean creeping things such as the weasel, rat, and lizard, brings uncleanness on a person or object until evening, and requires washing of clothes or breaking of clay vessels (vv. 24-38). Even the carcass of a clean animal that dies naturally conveys uncleanness to…
m: two criteria required together rather than either alone for a land animal to be called clean, a short list of named exceptions including a pig that looks clean on the outside while failing the inward test, unclean birds identified not by a rule but by their diet of carrion and death, insects…

x: The LORD gives Moses laws for a woman's purification after childbirth: if she bears a son, she is ceremonially unclean seven days, the boy is circumcised on the eighth day, and she remains in a state of blood purification for thirty-three more days, during which she may not touch anything holy or enter the sanctuary (vv. 1-4). If she bears a daughter, both periods are doubled, to two weeks of uncleanness and sixty-six days of purification (v. 5). When her purification is complete, she is to bring a year-old lamb for a burnt offering and a young pigeon or turtledove for a sin offering, so the priest can make atonement for her and she is cleansed (vv. 6-7). A woman who cannot afford a lamb may instead bring two turtledoves or two pigeons, one for each offering (v. 8).
h: Purification After Bearing a Male Child (vv.1-4)
Purification After Bearing a Female Child (v.5)
m: the shortest chapter in the book covering one of the most universal human experiences, an eight-day interruption for circumcision inserted into a forty-day period of uncleanness, an unexplained doubling of both stages for a daughter compared to a son, one offering required regardless of the child's…

x: The LORD gives Moses and Aaron detailed procedures for priests to diagnose suspected skin disease: when a person has a swelling, rash, or bright spot, the priest examines it, and if the hair has turned white and the sore appears deeper than the skin, he pronounces the person unclean, but if the case is uncertain he isolates the person for seven days, then examines again to see whether the condition has spread (vv. 1-8). Similar diagnostic rules follow for chronic leprosy, boils, and burns that have become suspicious sores, each judged by depth, color, and the presence of white hair (vv. 9-28). Special rules address itching sores on the head or beard and bald patches on the head or forehead, each evaluated the same way for infection (vv. 29-44). A person diagnosed as unclean must wear torn clothes, leave his hair unkempt, cover his upper lip, call out a warning that he is unclean, and…
h: Leprosy of the Head or Beard (vv.29-37)
The Unclean Person Outside the Camp (vv.45-46)
m: the longest chapter in the book built entirely around diagnosis rather than cure, a priest rather than a physician deciding what counts as disease, a paradox in which a partial outbreak is unclean but a body covered head to foot is pronounced clean, quarantine periods measured in matched sets of…

x: The LORD gives the ritual for a leper's cleansing: the priest examines the healed person outside the camp, then has two live birds, cedar wood, scarlet yarn, and hyssop brought; one bird is killed over fresh water, and the living bird, dipped in its blood with the wood, yarn, and hyssop, is used to sprinkle the person seven times before being released into the open field (vv. 1-7). The cleansed person washes his clothes, shaves off all his hair, and bathes, then waits seven more days before shaving again and bathing a second time (vv. 8-9). On the eighth day he brings two male lambs, one ewe lamb, grain, and oil so the priest can offer a guilt offering, sin offering, and burnt offering, applying blood and oil to his right ear, thumb, and big toe as in the priests' own ordination (vv. 10-20). A reduced offering of one lamb and two birds is provided for those too poor to afford the full…
m: a two-bird ceremony in which one bird dies and the other is dipped in its blood before being released alive, a total shaving of every hair on the body marking the start of a new eighth day, blood applied to the same ear, thumb and toe once marked at a priest's own ordination, a poverty provision…

x: Moses and Aaron receive laws governing bodily discharges that render a person ceremonially unclean (vv. 1-2). A man with a chronic discharge defiles anything he lies or sits on, and anyone who touches him, his bedding, or his seat must wash and remain unclean until evening (vv. 3-12); once the discharge stops he counts seven days, washes, and brings two birds to the priest on the eighth day for atonement (vv. 13-15). A seminal emission brings uncleanness until evening for both partners (vv. 16-18). A woman's monthly period brings seven days of uncleanness that spreads to anything and anyone she touches (vv. 19-24), and an irregular or prolonged discharge extends that uncleanness until she is cleansed and brings the same bird offering (vv. 25-30). The chapter closes by explaining that these laws separate Israel from uncleanness so they do not defile the tabernacle that dwells among them…
m: four separate sources of bodily uncleanness gathered into one chapter, a chronic discharge that renders unclean anything the sufferer sits or lies upon, an ordinary seminal emission requiring nothing more than washing and a wait until evening, an unspecified length given to chronic bleeding that…

x: After the deaths of Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu, the Lord warns Aaron not to enter the Most Holy Place at will, but only on the appointed day, dressed in holy linen, with a bull for his own sin offering (vv. 1-5). Two goats are presented for the people, and Aaron casts lots to designate one for the Lord and one as the scapegoat (vv. 6-10). He sacrifices the bull for himself and his household, burning incense so its cloud covers the mercy seat, then sprinkles its blood there (vv. 11-14). He repeats the process with the people's goat, cleansing the Holy Place, the tent, and the altar from Israel's uncleanness and sin (vv. 15-19). Aaron then lays both hands on the live goat, confesses all Israel's iniquities over it, and sends it into the wilderness to carry their sins away (vv. 20-22). After washing and changing garments, he offers the burnt offerings and completes atonement for himself…
h: The Warning: Do Not Enter Freely (vv.1-2)
The Blood Brought Within the Veil (vv.15-19)

x: The Lord commands that any Israelite who slaughters an ox, lamb, or goat must bring it to the door of the tent of meeting as an offering to the Lord, so that Israel no longer sacrifices to goat idols in the open field (vv. 1-7). The same requirement applies to any burnt offering or sacrifice, whether by a native Israelite or a resident foreigner (vv. 8-9). Eating blood in any form is strictly forbidden, because the life of a creature is in its blood, and blood on the altar is what makes atonement for the soul (vv. 10-12). Anyone who hunts game must pour out its blood and cover it with dust rather than eat it (vv. 13-14). Anyone who eats an animal that died naturally or was killed by wild beasts must wash and remain unclean until evening, or else bear the guilt (vv. 15-16).
m: a law confining every slaughter to the Tabernacle so that no sacrifice is ever offered in an open field, blood forbidden to eat on the ground that it is life itself, given by God for the altar rather than for the table, the single verse tying every sacrifice in the book back to one principle, the…

x: The Lord tells Israel not to follow the practices of Egypt where they lived or Canaan where they are going, but to keep His statutes and ordinances, by which a person shall live (vv. 1-5). He then lists forbidden sexual relations with close relatives — parents, siblings, in-laws, aunts, granddaughters, and a wife's sister taken as a rival (vv. 6-18). He forbids relations with a woman during her menstrual uncleanness, adultery with a neighbor's wife, and giving one's children to Molech (vv. 19-21). Homosexual relations and bestiality are also forbidden as detestable and perverse (vv. 22-23). The chapter closes with a warning that the nations before Israel defiled themselves and the land with these very practices, and the land vomited them out; Israel must not defile the land the same way lest it vomit them out as well (vv. 24-30).
h: The Framework: Neither Egypt Nor Canaan (vv.1-5)
The Land Vomits Out Its Inhabitants (vv.24-30)

x: The Lord calls all Israel to be holy because He is holy, then works through a wide range of everyday commands (vv. 1-2). Israel must honor parents, keep the sabbaths, reject idols, and leave the edges of their fields and vineyards for the poor and the foreigner (vv. 3-10). They must not steal, lie, swear falsely, oppress a neighbor, withhold a hired worker's wages, curse the deaf, or put a stumbling block before the blind (vv. 11-14). Judges must judge fairly without favoritism, and no one may slander, endanger a neighbor's life, hate a brother in his heart, or take vengeance — instead they are to love their neighbor as themselves (vv. 15-18). Further laws forbid mixing kinds of animals, seed, and cloth, regulate fruit trees and offerings, and prohibit eating blood, divination, pagan mourning cuts, and tattoos (vv. 19-28). Israel must not prostitute a daughter, must keep the sabbaths…
m: a single command, ye shall be holy for I the LORD your God am holy, spelled out across nearly every area of daily life, gleaning laws that leave the edges of every field for the poor and the stranger, four and five-word prohibitions on stealing, lying and false dealing packed one after another with…

x: The Lord commands that anyone who gives a child to Molech be stoned to death, and He will personally cut off both that person and any who look the other way and fail to execute him (vv. 1-5). Turning to mediums and spiritists likewise brings being cut off, for Israel is to sanctify itself and be holy (vv. 6-8). Cursing one's parents carries a death sentence (v. 9), and death is likewise prescribed for adultery, for various forms of incest with a father's wife, daughter-in-law, or a woman and her mother, for homosexual relations, and for bestiality (vv. 10-16). Additional incest with a sister, aunt, or uncle's or brother's wife brings being cut off or left childless (vv. 17-21). Israel must keep all these statutes so the land does not vomit them out as it did the nations before them, and they must distinguish clean animals from unclean, being holy because the Lord who set them apart from…
m: penalties assigned to the very acts chapter eighteen only prohibited, Molech worship carrying a death sentence that falls on the community too if it looks away, cursing a parent treated as capital while some of the incest laws instead carry childlessness or being cut off, a scale of consequence…

x: The Lord instructs that ordinary priests may defile themselves for the death of only their closest relatives, and even then must not adopt pagan mourning practices like shaving the head or cutting the flesh, since they are holy to God (vv. 1-6). Priests may not marry a prostitute or a divorced woman, and a priest's daughter who becomes a prostitute is to be burned (vv. 7-9). The high priest is held to an even higher standard: he must never disorder his hair, tear his clothes, or go near a dead body, even for his own parents, and he must marry only a virgin from his own people (vv. 10-15). Finally, no descendant of Aaron who has a physical defect — blindness, lameness, deformity, or similar conditions — may approach the altar to offer sacrifices, though he may still eat the priestly food, so that the sanctuary is not profaned (vv. 16-24).
h: Priests and Defilement by the Dead (vv.1-6)
m: a graduated scale of holiness rising from ordinary Israelite to priest to high priest, priests forbidden the mourning customs common to their culture, the high priest denied even those small exceptions for his own father or mother, marriage restrictions narrowing further the higher the office…

x: The Lord instructs Aaron and his sons to keep away from the holy offerings while ceremonially unclean, on penalty of being cut off, and describes the sources of uncleanness — skin disease, discharge, contact with the dead — that require washing and waiting until evening (vv. 1-9). Only a priest's own household, not a hired worker or outside guest, may eat the holy food, and anyone who eats it unwittingly must make restitution (vv. 10-16). Offerings brought to the Lord, whether burnt offerings, vow offerings, or freewill offerings, must be male animals without any defect — not blind, injured, maimed, or diseased (vv. 17-25). A newborn animal must remain with its mother seven days before it can be offered, a mother and her young may not be slaughtered on the same day, and a thanksgiving offering must be eaten the same day it is sacrificed (vv. 26-30). The chapter closes with a call to…
h: Priestly Holiness in Eating Holy Things (vv.1-9)
Who May and May Not Eat Holy Things (vv.10-16)
m: uncleanness disqualifying a priest from holy food until evening rather than permanently, a household member's status, whether slave, guest or married-out daughter, determining who may eat what belongs to the priest alone, sacrificial animals held to the same standard of wholeness demanded of the…

x: The Lord gives Moses Israel's calendar of appointed feasts, beginning with the weekly sabbath as a day of rest (vv. 1-3). Passover falls on the fourteenth day of the first month, followed by seven days of Unleavened Bread with holy convocations on the first and last days (vv. 4-8). During the harvest, Israel is to bring a sheaf of firstfruits to the priest to be waved before the Lord, and fifty days later celebrate the Feast of Weeks with two loaves of bread and offerings, again leaving the edges of the fields for the poor and the foreigner (vv. 9-22). The seventh month opens with the Feast of Trumpets, a day of rest and remembrance (vv. 23-25), followed on the tenth day by the Day of Atonement, when Israel must deny themselves and do no work (vv. 26-32). The month closes with the seven-day Feast of Tabernacles, when Israel lives in temporary shelters to remember how the Lord made their…
h: These Are the Feasts of the LORD (vv.1-2)
The Sabbath — Foundation of All Feasts (v.3)

Feast 4: Pentecost / Feast of Weeks — 50 Days After Firstfruits (vv.15-22)
Feast 6: Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur) — 10th of Tishri (vv.26-32)
m: seven appointed times named the LORD's rather than Israel's own, a long gap in the calendar between Pentecost and Trumpets left conspicuously unfilled, feasts falling into two clusters, spring and fall, that later readers line up against a first and second coming, a wave sheaf offered the very day…

x: The Lord commands Israel to supply pure olive oil so Aaron can keep a lamp burning continually in the tent of meeting, and to set out twelve loaves of showbread on the golden table each sabbath for the priests to eat (vv. 1-9). A man whose mother is Israelite and father Egyptian blasphemes the Lord's name during a fight in the camp and is placed in custody until God's will is known (vv. 10-12). The Lord commands that he be stoned outside the camp, and establishes that anyone, native or foreigner, who blasphemes must be put to death (vv. 13-16). This leads into laws of retribution — life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth — applied equally to native Israelite and foreigner alike (vv. 17-22). Moses relays the command, and Israel stones the blasphemer as the Lord instructed (v. 23).
h: The Law of Retaliation — Lex Talionis (vv.17-22)
m: a lamp kept burning continually just outside the same veil the previous chapters described from the inside, twelve loaves of showbread replaced every Sabbath and eaten only by the priests, a blasphemer of mixed Israelite and Egyptian parentage held in custody until Moses can inquire of God…

x: On Mount Sinai the Lord institutes the sabbath year: every seventh year the land itself is to rest, with no sowing or pruning, and whatever grows on its own is left for all to eat (vv. 1-7). After seven sabbath cycles, the fiftieth year is the Year of Jubilee, announced by trumpet on the Day of Atonement, when liberty is proclaimed throughout the land, property returns to its original family, and prices between neighbors are set fairly according to the years remaining until Jubilee (vv. 8-17). The Lord promises a triple harvest in the sixth year so Israel can trust Him through the sabbath year (vv. 18-22). Land is never sold permanently since it belongs to the Lord, and a poor Israelite's property, or the man himself, may be redeemed by a near relative or released at Jubilee, with different rules for houses in walled cities, villages, and Levitical towns (vv. 23-34). Israel must support…

God's Provision for the Sabbath Year (vv.18-22)

x: The Lord repeats the ban on idols and the call to keep His sabbaths and revere His sanctuary, then sets before Israel the blessings of obedience: timely rain, abundant harvests, peace and safety in the land, victory over enemies, fruitfulness, and God's own presence dwelling among them (vv. 1-13). If Israel refuses to listen, He warns of escalating judgment delivered in stages — first terror, disease, and defeat before enemies; then failed crops and a sky of iron; then wild animals devouring their children and livestock; then war, siege, and even the horror of eating their own children; and finally exile among the nations while the land finally enjoys the sabbaths Israel denied it (vv. 14-39). Yet if the exiled people confess their sin and humble their uncircumcised hearts, the Lord promises to remember His covenant with Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham and not utterly destroy them, because He…
m: two commands, no idols and keep my sabbaths, standing in for the whole of the law before any blessing or curse is named, blessings for obedience listed before five escalating cycles of discipline for continued refusal to listen, the phrase seven times more recurring at each new stage of judgment…

x: The Lord gives Moses rules for redeeming vows in which a person is dedicated to Him, setting valuations by age and sex, with reduced rates for the poor as the priest assesses their ability to pay (vv. 1-8). An animal dedicated by vow cannot be exchanged for another, good for bad, without both becoming holy (vv. 9-13). A house or field dedicated to the Lord is valued by the priest, and the owner may redeem it by adding a fifth to its value; a field not redeemed before the Jubilee permanently becomes the priests' possession (vv. 14-25). Firstborn animals already belong to the Lord and cannot be dedicated again, though an unclean firstborn may be redeemed (vv. 26-27). Anything devoted entirely to the Lord is most holy and cannot be sold or redeemed, and a person so devoted cannot be ransomed (vv. 28-29). The tithe of the land's produce and of the herds and flocks belongs to the Lord, and…
h: Valuation of Persons Dedicated by Vow (vv.1-8)
m: a system of fixed valuations substituting money for a person no one could actually lay on an altar, an animal already fit for sacrifice forbidden from ever being exchanged once vowed, redemption of a house or field always costing a fifth more than the original valuation, a firstborn animal excluded…

x: God commands a census of all Israelite men age twenty and older able to serve in the army, counted by tribe and clan in the second year after the exodus (vv. 1-3). Each tribe's total is recorded, yielding an army of 603,550 men (vv. 20-46). The Levites are excluded from the fighting count and are instead set apart to camp around the tabernacle and care for its service, since unauthorized approach to it brings danger (vv. 47-53). The chapter closes noting Israel's obedience in carrying out everything the Lord commanded (v. 54).
m: a census confined to men twenty and older able to go to war, the largest tribe Judah counted first among the twelve even though the order follows something other than birth, Levites deliberately excluded from the military count and assigned instead to guard the Tabernacle itself, a death penalty…

x: God directs each tribe to camp under its own standard at a set distance from the tabernacle, with three tribes grouped together on each of the four sides — Judah's group to the east, Reuben's to the south, Ephraim's to the west, and Dan's to the north (vv. 1-31). The Levites camp immediately around the tabernacle itself, forming a protective inner ring between the people and God's dwelling (v. 17). The total number of fighting men from all twelve tribes is 603,550, matching the census of chapter 1 (v. 32). Israel breaks camp and marches in this same order, each tribe in its assigned position, exactly as the Lord commanded Moses (vv. 33-34).
h: The East Side — Camp of Judah (vv.1-9)
The South Side — Camp of Reuben (vv.10-16)
The Center — The Tabernacle and Levites (v.17)
The West Side — Camp of Ephraim (vv.18-24)
The North Side — Camp of Dan (vv.25-31)
m: four camps of three tribes each arranged on the four sides of a Tabernacle that never moves from the center, Judah given the position of honor facing the sunrise and the order to set out first, Reuben's camp marching second despite Reuben's own birthright long since forfeited, the Tabernacle and…

x: Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu die for offering unauthorized fire before the Lord, leaving Eleazar and Ithamar to serve as priests alongside their father (vv. 1-4). God sets the tribe of Levi apart to assist Aaron and care for the tabernacle, dividing them into three clans — Gershon, Kohath, and Merari — each assigned specific furnishings and duties to guard and carry (vv. 5-37). The Levites are formally given to serve in place of Israel's firstborn sons, who technically belonged to God since the exodus (vv. 11-13, 40-45). Because the Levites (22,000) fall short of the number of firstborn Israelites (22,273), the extra 273 are redeemed with a five-shekel payment collected and given to Aaron (vv. 46-51).
h: The Sons of Aaron, and Two Who Died (vv.1-4)
The Levites Instead of the Firstborn (vv.11-13)
m: a priestly genealogy that opens by naming two sons and then removing them in the same breath, Nadab and Abihu dead without children, an entire tribe of Levites handed over to Aaron as a gift rather than hired as staff, redemption of the firstborn grounded explicitly in the night the LORD spared…

x: God instructs Moses and Aaron to count the Kohathites, Gershonites, and Merarites between the ages of thirty and fifty, defining the service each clan will perform in transporting the tabernacle (vv. 1-3, 21-23, 29-30). The Kohathites carry the most sacred objects — the ark, table, lampstand, and altars — but only after Aaron and his sons have carefully covered each item, since handling or even seeing the holy things unwrapped brings danger (vv. 4-20). The Gershonites are responsible for the tabernacle's curtains, coverings, and hangings, while the Merarites carry the frames, bars, pillars, and bases (vv. 24-28, 31-33). The chapter closes with the total count of all three clans eligible for this service: 8,580 men (vv. 34-49).
h: The Kohathites and the Covered Holy Things (vv.1-20)
m: holy objects wrapped in a fixed sequence of coverings before the men assigned to carry them are even allowed to approach, a repeated warning that seeing or touching what is uncovered brings death even to the Levites entrusted with carrying it, tent pegs and frame pieces inventoried by name rather…

x: God commands the removal of anyone with a serious skin disease, a discharge, or defilement from contact with a corpse outside the camp, so that the place where He dwells among His people remains undefiled (vv. 1-4). Laws follow requiring confession and full restitution plus a fifth for wrongs done to another person, with unclaimed restitution going to the priest (vv. 5-10). The bulk of the chapter details a ritual for a husband who suspects his wife of unfaithfulness but has no proof — she drinks water mixed with dust from the tabernacle floor, and its effect, or lack of one, reveals guilt or innocence (vv. 11-31). The ritual functions to protect an innocent wife from baseless suspicion while leaving true guilt exposed to God's judgment rather than to accusation alone.
m: three categories of uncleanness ordered entirely outside the camp because God himself dwells in its midst, restitution for wrongdoing requiring both confession and a payment increased by a fifth, sin against a person treated as sin against the LORD, an unusual test involving bitter water for a wife…
