x: God gives instructions for the Nazirite vow, a period of special consecration in which a man or woman abstains from wine and anything from the grapevine, lets their hair grow uncut, and avoids contact with the dead (vv. 1-8). If the vow is broken through unavoidable defilement, prescribed offerings restore the person before the vow resumes; when the vow period ends, further offerings mark its completion and the hair is shaved and burned (vv. 9-21). The chapter closes with the priestly benediction God gives Aaron and his sons to pronounce over Israel, invoking the Lord's blessing, protection, favor, and peace on His people (vv. 22-26). God declares that by pronouncing His name over Israel this way, the priests place His blessing on them (v. 27).
m: a vow of consecration open to any Israelite of either sex rather than reserved to priest or Levite, three restrictions, no wine or anything from the grapevine, no razor, no contact with the dead, matching in severity what is normally expected only of the high priest, a defilement that resets the…

x: Over twelve consecutive days, the leader of each of Israel's twelve tribes brings forward an identical offering to dedicate the newly completed tabernacle and its altar (vv. 1-88). Each leader's gift includes a silver plate and basin filled with grain offering, a gold dish of incense, animals for burnt, sin, and peace offerings, and covered carts with oxen to help the Levites transport the tabernacle (vv. 12-88). Though every tribe brings the exact same offering, the text records each leader and gift individually by name and day, honoring each tribe's generosity rather than reporting only the totals (vv. 12-83). The chapter ends with Moses entering the tent of meeting and hearing the voice of the Lord speaking to him from above the atonement cover between the cherubim (v. 89).
h: Wagons and Oxen for the Levites (vv.1-9)
God Speaks from the Mercy Seat (v.89)
m: the longest chapter in the book built around twelve offerings that are, deliberately, all identical, six wagons and twelve oxen distributed unevenly to Gershon and Merari for the loads they actually carry while the Kohathites receive none because their burden must be borne on the shoulder, one…

x: God instructs Aaron to set up the seven lamps of the lampstand so they light the area in front of it (vv. 1-4). The Levites undergo a purification ritual — sprinkled with water, shaved, and washed — before the Israelites lay hands on them and they are presented to the Lord as a wave offering, formally dedicating them to tabernacle service in place of Israel's firstborn (vv. 5-19). God sets their active service between ages twenty-five and fifty, after which they may assist but no longer carry the full workload (vv. 23-26). The chapter closes noting that Moses, Aaron, and the community carried out everything just as the Lord commanded (vv. 20-22).
m: seven lamps lit facing forward so the Holy Place is never served in darkness, a Levite cleansing ceremony involving sprinkled water, a full shave and washed clothes before a single duty is performed, the whole congregation laying hands on the Levites so the nation's own obligation is transferred to…

x: In the second year after leaving Egypt, Israel keeps the Passover as commanded, but men defiled by contact with a corpse cannot participate, so God institutes a second Passover a month later for anyone unclean or on a journey at the original time (vv. 1-14). The chapter then turns to the cloud that covers the tabernacle from the day it was set up, appearing like fire at night; whenever the cloud lifted, Israel set out, and wherever it settled, they camped (vv. 15-19). Whether the cloud stayed a few days, a month, or a year, the Israelites obeyed its movement precisely, never setting out or staying based on their own judgment (vv. 20-23). This section highlights Israel's obedience to divine guidance rather than their own timing during the wilderness years.
m: a second Passover kept exactly one year after the first, ceremonially unclean men who ask to be included rather than accepting exclusion, a provision built for the genuinely prevented and fenced against anyone merely unwilling, a cloud settling over the Tabernacle from the very day it is first…

x: God instructs Moses to make two silver trumpets for summoning the community, signaling the camps to set out, and sounding alarms in battle, each with its own distinct pattern of blasts (vv. 1-10). On the twentieth day of the second month, the cloud lifts from the tabernacle and Israel sets out from Sinai for the first time, tribe by tribe in the order established in chapter 2 (vv. 11-28). Moses invites his brother-in-law Hobab to join them as a guide, and as the ark sets out ahead of the people, Moses asks the Lord to rise up against His enemies and to return and rest among Israel's many thousands when it stops (vv. 29-36). This marks the end of Israel's roughly year-long stay at Sinai and the true beginning of the journey toward the Promised Land.
m: two silver trumpets whose different blasts distinguish a full assembly from a leaders' meeting and one tribal division's departure from another's, a strict rule that only Aaron's sons may sound them, a departure carried out in the exact camp order fixed two chapters earlier, an invitation to Hobab…

x: Israel complains about hardship, and fire from the Lord burns at the edge of the camp until Moses intercedes (vv. 1-3). The rabble among them craves meat, complaining that the manna has grown monotonous, which prompts weeping throughout the camp and provokes the Lord's anger and Moses' own despair over the burden of leading the people alone (vv. 4-15). God tells Moses to gather seventy elders to share the burden of leadership, placing His Spirit on them so they prophesy, including two who remain in the camp rather than at the tent (vv. 16-30). The Lord then sends a wind that brings vast quantities of quail, but while the meat is still being eaten a plague strikes the people, and the place is named Kibroth Hattaavah, meaning graves of craving, marking Israel's discontent (vv. 31-34).
h: The Spirit on the Seventy Elders (vv.24-30)
m: a first complaint met with fire at the very edge of the camp, a craving for meat that turns nostalgic about food eaten as slaves, Moses pouring out a burden so heavy he asks to be killed rather than carry it, seventy elders suddenly prophesying once God's Spirit is distributed from what already…

x: Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses over his Cushite wife and challenge whether the Lord has spoken through Moses alone rather than through them as well (vv. 1-2). The Lord defends Moses' unique standing, explaining that while He speaks to other prophets in visions and dreams, He speaks with Moses face to face, plainly and directly, making Moses the most humble man on earth (vv. 3-8). God's anger burns against Miriam and Aaron, and Miriam is struck with a skin disease, while Aaron pleads with Moses not to hold the sin against them (vv. 9-13). Moses intercedes and asks God to heal her, and after seven days of quarantine outside the camp, Miriam is restored and the people move on (vv. 14-16).
h: Miriam and Aaron Speak Against Moses (vv.1-2)
m: a challenge to Moses' authority disguised as a complaint about his marriage, a parenthetical statement calling Moses the meekest man on the face of the earth right where he might be expected to defend himself, God distinguishing Moses from every other prophet by speaking to him mouth to mouth…

x: God directs Moses to send one leader from each tribe to scout the land of Canaan, and Moses instructs them to assess the land's quality, the strength of its cities, and the character of its people (vv. 1-20). After forty days exploring the land, the spies return carrying a cluster of grapes so large it takes two men to carry it, along with pomegranates and figs, confirming the land's richness (vv. 21-24, 27). Ten of the spies report that the land's inhabitants are too strong to overcome, describing fortified cities and people of great size that leave them feeling like grasshoppers by comparison (vv. 28-33). Caleb alone urges the people to go up and take the land, insisting they are well able to do it (v. 30).
h: Caleb's Faith vs. the Majority's Fear (vv.30-33)
m: twelve tribal leaders sent to spy out a land already promised rather than merely rumored, a single cluster of grapes so large it takes two men on a pole to carry it back as evidence, an honest report of walled cities and giant inhabitants delivered alongside an evil report that slanders the land…

x: The people weep through the night and grumble against Moses and Aaron, wishing they had died in Egypt or in the wilderness rather than face the inhabitants of Canaan, and they talk of choosing a new leader to take them back (vv. 1-4). Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes and urge the people not to rebel, insisting the Lord is with them and the land is exceedingly good, but the assembly threatens to stone them (vv. 5-10). The Lord's glory appears, and though He threatens to destroy the nation, Moses intercedes, appealing to God's reputation among the nations and His steadfast character, and the Lord relents from destroying them outright but still pronounces judgment (vv. 11-19). Because of their unbelief, that entire generation of adults twenty and older, except Caleb and Joshua, is sentenced to wander and die in the wilderness over the next forty years, one year for each day the spies…
h: God's Anger and Offer to Moses (vv.10b-12)
m: an entire congregation weeping all night and proposing to elect a new leader back to Egypt, Joshua and Caleb tearing their clothes and nearly stoned for insisting the land is good, an offer to make of Moses a greater nation refused by an intercessor arguing God's own reputation and God's own words…

x: God gives regulations for grain, drink, and animal offerings to accompany sacrifices once Israel enters and settles the land, extending hope even after the previous chapter's judgment by speaking of a future beyond the wilderness (vv. 1-16). Laws follow regarding offerings from the land's first produce and provisions for unintentional sin, both for the community and for individuals, along with a warning that defiant, willful sin cuts a person off from the people (vv. 17-31). The narrative interrupts with an account of a man found gathering wood on the Sabbath, whom the community holds in custody until the Lord instructs that he be put to death outside the camp as a deliberate violation (vv. 32-36). The chapter closes with the command that Israelites attach tassels with a blue cord to the corners of their garments as a visual reminder to keep all of God's commands rather than following…
m: a sentence of forty years' death opened, in its very next breath, with when ye be come into the land, grain and drink offerings scaled to whichever animal accompanies them, a single law repeated for native Israelite and resident stranger alike, a stark distinction drawn between unintentional sin…

x: Korah, along with Dathan, Abiram, and 250 prominent leaders, rises up against Moses and Aaron, accusing them of exalting themselves above the rest of the congregation, which they claim is entirely holy (vv. 1-3). Moses proposes a test: Korah and his followers will offer incense before the Lord the next day, and God Himself will show who is truly chosen (vv. 4-19). When Moses warns the people to move away from the tents of the rebels, the ground opens and swallows Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and their households alive, and fire consumes the 250 men offering incense (vv. 20-35). Despite this display of judgment, the people accuse Moses and Aaron of causing the deaths the next day, provoking a plague that kills many more until Aaron makes atonement by standing between the living and the dead with incense (vv. 41-50).
m: a Kohathite Levite already entrusted with the holiest objects in Israel demanding the priesthood on top of it, a theology of all the congregation are holy twisted into a denial that God appoints specific leaders at all, Dathan and Abiram calling Egypt itself a land flowing with milk and honey…

x: Following the rebellion of chapter 16, God instructs each tribal leader to place a staff, inscribed with his name, before the ark, with Aaron's staff representing the tribe of Levi (vv. 1-7). Overnight, Aaron's staff alone sprouts, buds, blossoms, and produces ripe almonds, visibly confirming that God has chosen Aaron and his line for the priesthood (vv. 8-9). God commands that the staff be kept permanently before the ark as a sign to end the people's grumbling against the appointed leadership, so that further deaths from complaint might be prevented (vv. 10-11). The people, still shaken by the recent judgment, cry out in fear that anyone who comes near the tabernacle will die, showing how deeply the events had impressed on them the danger of approaching God without proper mediation (vv. 12-13).
m: twelve rods laid before the ark overnight with each leader's own name carved into his, one rod alone sprouting, budding, blossoming and bearing ripe almonds in stages a living tree normally takes months to complete, eleven dead sticks returned to their owners beside the one that came alive, a rod…

x: God lays out the responsibilities of Aaron, his sons, and the Levites for guarding the sanctuary and bearing responsibility for any offense connected to it, with priests alone permitted to handle the altar and its most holy things (vv. 1-7). As compensation for this service, the priests receive a portion of the offerings brought to the tabernacle, including the best of the grain, oil, wine, and firstfruits (vv. 8-19). Rather than receiving a territorial inheritance like the other tribes, the Lord declares Himself to be Aaron's inheritance and portion among the Israelites (v. 20). The Levites in turn receive a tithe from the rest of Israel for their service, and they themselves give a tenth of what they receive to the priests (vv. 21-32).
m: an entire chapter addressed to Aaron directly rather than to Moses, priests and Levites literally bearing the iniquity of the sanctuary so ordinary Israelites do not, provisions listed in such detail, firstfruits, firstborn redemption, devoted things, that the priesthood's abundance is impossible…

x: God instructs Israel to bring an unblemished red heifer that has never been yoked, which is slaughtered outside the camp and completely burned along with cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet material, its ashes kept for use in a purification ritual (vv. 1-10). Anyone who touches a dead body becomes ceremonially unclean for seven days and must be purified using water mixed with the heifer's ashes on the third and seventh days, or else remain defiled and cut off from the community (vv. 11-13, 16-20). This provision extends even to those present in a tent where someone dies or who touch a bone or a grave, showing how thoroughly death defiles under this system (vv. 14-16). The ritual points to the seriousness with which God treats the presence of death among a people called to reflect His life and holiness.
m: a red heifer never yoked and without blemish burned entirely outside the camp rather than on the altar, ashes mixed with running water into what the text calls the water of separation, contact with a corpse, a bone or even a grave in an open field all defiling for seven days, the very act of…

x: Miriam dies and is buried at Kadesh, and when the community has no water, the people again quarrel with Moses, wishing they had died as their brothers did before the Lord (vv. 1-5). God instructs Moses to speak to a rock in the sight of the people so it will yield water, but Moses instead strikes the rock twice with his staff in anger, and though water gushes out abundantly, God tells Moses and Aaron that because they did not trust Him enough to honor Him as holy before Israel, neither will enter the Promised Land (vv. 6-13). The king of Edom refuses Israel passage through his territory despite Moses' request, forcing Israel to go around (vv. 14-21). At Mount Hor, Aaron is stripped of his priestly garments, which are placed on his son Eleazar, and Aaron dies there, mourned by the whole community for thirty days (vv. 22-29).
h: Water from the Rock at Meribah (vv.2-13)
m: Miriam's death recorded in a single unadorned sentence after decades of leading Israel in worship, water struck twice from a rock God had only commanded to be spoken to, a leader barred from the very land he has led an entire nation toward because of one act of disbelief before their eyes, a…

x: Israel defeats the king of Arad after vowing to devote his cities to destruction if God gave them victory (vv. 1-3). When the people again grow impatient and speak against God and Moses on the journey, the Lord sends venomous snakes among them, and many die from the bites (vv. 4-6). At the people's plea, Moses intercedes, and God instructs him to make a bronze serpent and put it on a pole, so that anyone bitten who looks at it lives (vv. 7-9). Israel then defeats Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan, taking possession of territory east of the Jordan and settling in the plains of Moab (vv. 21-35).
m: the same battlefield, Hormah, that swallowed Israel's presumptuous attack in chapter fourteen now delivering its first real victory, fiery serpents sent in judgment for a complaint almost identical to complaints already judged a generation earlier, a bronze serpent lifted on a pole that Jesus…

x: Balak, king of Moab, alarmed by Israel's size and recent victories, sends elders to hire the prophet Balaam to curse Israel, but God initially forbids Balaam from going (vv. 1-14). When Balak sends more distinguished officials with a greater reward, God permits Balaam to go but tells him he may only speak what God tells him (vv. 15-20). On the road, the angel of the Lord blocks the way with a drawn sword, visible to Balaam's donkey but not to Balaam himself, and the donkey balks and is beaten three times before the Lord opens its mouth to speak to Balaam (vv. 21-30). When Balaam's own eyes are opened, he sees the angel and is warned that the donkey's resistance saved his life; Balaam then continues to Moab, committed to speaking only what God gives him (vv. 31-41).
m: a Moabite king too frightened to fight Israel by the sword turning instead to a diviner four hundred miles away to curse it by words, a foreign prophet consulting the LORD not once but repeatedly in hope of a different answer, God's outward permission to go granted even while his anger burns at the…

x: Balaam has Balak build seven altars and offer sacrifices, then meets with God before delivering his first oracle, which blesses rather than curses Israel and marvels that no one can curse what God has not cursed (vv. 1-10). Frustrated, Balak takes Balaam to another location to try again, but Balaam's second oracle declares that God does not lie or change His mind like a man, and that He has beheld no misfortune in Jacob because the Lord their God is with them (vv. 11-24). Balak, upset that Balaam will neither curse nor stay silent about Israel, tries yet another location, but Balaam maintains that he can only speak what God puts in his mouth (vv. 25-30).
m: A hired curse that keeps emerging as blessing, seven altars as an attempt to manage God, a word its speaker cannot reverse, a God unlike a man in changing His mind, and a change of vantage point that changes nothing

x: Balaam, now certain that it pleases the Lord to bless Israel, no longer resorts to omens but simply looks out over the encamped tribes as the Spirit of God comes upon him (vv. 1-2). His third oracle praises the beauty and strength of Israel's encampment and pronounces blessing on those who bless Israel and a curse on those who curse them (vv. 3-9). Enraged, Balak dismisses Balaam without payment, but before leaving, Balaam delivers a fourth oracle describing a star that will come out of Jacob and a scepter that will rise out of Israel, a distant prophecy pointing toward a future ruler who will overcome Israel's enemies (vv. 10-19). Balaam closes with additional oracles concerning Amalek and other neighboring peoples before he and Balak go their separate ways (vv. 20-25).
h: Third Oracle: Israel's Beauty and Power (vv.1-9)
Fourth Oracle: The Star and Scepter (vv.14-19)
m: divination abandoned entirely as the Spirit of God comes upon Balaam directly for his third oracle, an oracle that pronounces Israel's own encampment beautiful before repeating the Abrahamic promise nearly word for word, a furious king dismissing the very prophet he paid, a final oracle offered…

x: While camped at Shittim, Israelite men begin relationships with Moabite women and are drawn into worshiping their gods, provoking the Lord's anger and a plague against the people (vv. 1-3, 9). God commands that the leaders of the offenders be executed, and as Moses and the community weep at the entrance of the tent, an Israelite man brazenly brings a Midianite woman into his tent in full view of everyone (vv. 4-6). Phinehas, grandson of Aaron, follows them and kills both with a spear, an act of zeal that stops the plague, which had already killed 24,000 people (vv. 7-9). Because of his zeal for God's honor, the Lord grants Phinehas and his descendants a covenant of lasting priesthood (vv. 10-13).
m: seduction succeeding at Baal-Peor where three chapters of failed curses could not, Israelite men yoking themselves to a local god through Moabite women's invitation to sacrificial feasts, a plague spreading through the camp even while the people weep openly at the Tabernacle entrance, a single…

x: Following the plague at Peor, God commands a second census of all Israelite men twenty and older able to serve in the army, organized tribe by tribe as in chapter 1 (vv. 1-4, 51). The total comes to 601,730, remarkably close to the number from the first census nearly forty years earlier, even though this is now an entirely new generation, since none of those counted the first time remained alive except Caleb and Joshua (vv. 63-65). The chapter also records the Levite census separately, since they receive no land inheritance, and notes several family lines, including a brief mention of Zelophehad, who had no sons (vv. 57-62, 33). The land is to be divided among the tribes by lot, in proportion to each tribe's size (vv. 52-56).
m: a second census taken only after the entire generation counted in the first has died exactly as decreed, a total of six hundred one thousand seven hundred thirty men landing within two thousand of the number counted thirty-eight years earlier, one tribe, Simeon, collapsing by well over half while…

x: The five daughters of Zelophehad approach Moses, asking that their father's inheritance not disappear simply because he had no sons, and the Lord rules in their favor, establishing that daughters may inherit when there is no son, with further rules for inheritance when there are no children at all (vv. 1-11). God tells Moses to view the Promised Land from a mountain, reminding him that he will not enter it because of his and Aaron's failure to honor God at the waters of Meribah (vv. 12-14). Moses asks the Lord to appoint a new leader so the community will not be left without guidance, and God chooses Joshua, commissioning him publicly before Eleazar the priest and the whole assembly with the laying on of hands (vv. 15-23).
m: five sisters petitioning publicly for their dead father's inheritance because he left no son, a divine ruling that reshapes the law of inheritance rather than simply denying their claim, Moses told to view the promised land from a mountain he will never descend into, a request for a successor that…

x: God instructs Moses to remind Israel to present the food offerings due Him at their appointed times, beginning with the regular daily burnt offering presented each morning and evening (vv. 1-8). Additional offerings are prescribed for the Sabbath, doubling the daily offering, and for the beginning of each month, marked by a larger set of sacrifices (vv. 9-15). The chapter then details the offerings for Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, and for the Feast of Weeks, each requiring specific combinations of animals, grain, and drink offerings beyond the regular daily sacrifice (vv. 16-31). Together these instructions establish a rhythm of continual worship woven into the calendar of daily, weekly, monthly, and festival life.
m: a daily offering called God's own bread offered morning and evening as the framework around which every other sacrifice is added, a Sabbath offering that doubles the daily rather than replacing it, a new moon offering scaled by exact fractions of an ephah and hin per animal, Passover and Unleavened…

x: God prescribes the offerings for the Feast of Trumpets on the first day of the seventh month, marked by trumpet blasts and a distinct set of sacrifices beyond the regular offerings (vv. 1-6). Ten days later, the Day of Atonement requires solemn rest from work along with its own specified offerings, described here purely in terms of sacrifice rather than the fuller ritual detailed in Leviticus 16 (vv. 7-11). The Feast of Tabernacles begins five days after that and lasts eight days, requiring an unusually large and gradually decreasing number of bulls sacrificed each day, alongside rams, lambs, and grain and drink offerings (vv. 12-38). The chapter closes noting that these offerings are in addition to whatever vows or freewill offerings the people bring on their own (v. 39).
m: a first day of the seventh month set apart specifically for trumpet blasts, a tenth day requiring souls afflicted and no work at all, its public offerings kept explicitly separate from the more elaborate atonement ritual already given in Leviticus, a seven-day feast of booths whose bull count…

x: God gives Moses instructions for Israel regarding vows, establishing that a man who makes a vow or binding oath must keep every word of it without breaking his promise (vv. 1-2). For a young woman still in her father's house, her father may nullify a vow on the day he hears of it, but if he says nothing, it stands (vv. 3-5). Similarly, a wife's vow may be nullified by her husband on the day he hears it if he disapproves, but if he remains silent, the vow stands and he bears any guilt for later revoking it (vv. 6-15). A widow or divorced woman, however, is bound by any vow she makes, since no husband has authority to release her from it (v. 9).
h: Moses Speaks to the Tribal Heads (v.1)
A Widow or Divorced Woman's Vow (v.9)
m: vow law addressed to tribal leaders as a matter of communal governance rather than only private devotion, a man's own vow left with no possibility of annulment by anyone, a father or husband able to void a daughter's or wife's vow only on the very day he first hears of it, silence functioning as…

x: The Lord instructs Moses to take vengeance on the Midianites for their role in seducing Israel into idolatry and immorality at Peor before Moses himself dies (vv. 1-2). Israel sends 12,000 men into battle, kills the Midianite kings along with Balaam, and takes the women, children, livestock, and plunder captive, burning their towns (vv. 3-12). Moses is angry that the officers spared the women, since it was Moabite and Midianite women who led Israel into sin at Peor, and he orders that only the young girls be kept alive (vv. 13-18). The plunder and captives are carefully divided between the soldiers and the rest of the community, with a portion set aside for the Lord, and remarkably, not a single Israelite soldier is lost in the battle (vv. 25-54).
m: a war explicitly named the LORD's vengeance on Midian rather than Israel's own, a force of only twelve thousand men sent under a priest rather than a general, Balaam found among the Midianite dead despite never having cursed Israel by a single word, Moses' fury at officers who spared the very women…

x: The tribes of Reuben and Gad, who own large herds, request the fertile grazing land of Jazer and Gilead east of the Jordan rather than crossing into Canaan proper (vv. 1-5). Moses initially rebukes them, fearing they will discourage the rest of Israel from crossing over just as the unfaithful spies once did, and warns that their unwillingness to fight would provoke God's anger against the whole nation again (vv. 6-15). The two tribes clarify that they intend to build fortified towns for their families and livestock, then send their fighting men ahead of the other tribes to help conquer Canaan before returning east (vv. 16-19). Moses agrees on the condition that they keep this promise, and the land is granted to Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh (vv. 20-42).
m: Reuben and Gad requesting land east of the Jordan for the sake of their livestock before a single tribe west of the river has received its own inheritance, Moses drawing a direct line back to the ten spies and the forty years their unbelief cost the nation, a compromise in which the two tribes…

x: This chapter records the full itinerary of Israel's journey, listing by name the roughly forty-two stopping points from their departure out of Egypt to their arrival on the plains of Moab by the Jordan (vv. 1-49). Written down at the Lord's command, the list traces four decades of wilderness wandering and includes brief notes such as the death of Aaron on Mount Hor in the fortieth year (vv. 2, 38-39). As Israel nears the land, God commands them to drive out all the inhabitants of Canaan, destroy their idols and high places, and take possession of the land by lot according to tribe and family size (vv. 50-54). God warns that if they fail to remove the Canaanites, those who remain will become like irritants and troubles to them, and Israel will suffer the same judgment intended for the land's former inhabitants (vv. 55-56).
h: Kadesh to the Plains of Moab (vv.37-49)
m: forty-two stations written down by Moses at God's own command rather than left to memory, an itinerary from Egypt to Sinai covering roughly two months while the following thirty-eight years of wandering are compressed into a bare list of names, Aaron's death recorded here a second time with his…

x: God defines the borders of the land Israel is about to inherit, describing the southern boundary along the edge of Edom and the wilderness of Zin, the western boundary along the Mediterranean coast, the northern boundary running toward the entrance of Hamath, and the eastern boundary along the Jordan and the Sea of Galilee down to the Dead Sea (vv. 1-12). Moses is told this land is to be divided among the nine and a half remaining tribes, since Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh have already received their inheritance east of the Jordan (vv. 13-15). The Lord names Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and one leader from each of the remaining tribes to oversee the actual division of the land (vv. 16-29).
h: The Nine and a Half Tribes (vv.13-15)
m: precise borders drawn by God rather than left to conquest to define, a southern line running through the Wilderness of Zin and the Brook of Egypt to the Mediterranean, a western border stated in a single phrase, the Great Sea, a northern extent reaching to Lebo-hamath that later becomes the…

x: God commands that the Levites, who receive no tribal territory, be given forty-eight cities scattered throughout the other tribes' land, along with surrounding pasture for their livestock (vv. 1-8). Six of these cities are designated as cities of refuge, three on each side of the Jordan, where a person who kills someone accidentally may flee for protection from the victim's avenger until a fair trial can take place (vv. 9-15). The chapter distinguishes carefully between deliberate murder, which carries the death penalty regardless of refuge, and unintentional killing, for which the slayer may live safely in the city of refuge until the death of the high priest (vv. 16-28). Rules against accepting a ransom for a murderer's life or for release from a city of refuge underscore that bloodshed defiles the land and demands proper justice rather than a payoff (vv. 29-34).
h: The Death of the High Priest (vv.25-28)
m: forty-eight Levitical cities distributed proportionally by every tribe rather than granted as a single inheritance, six of those forty-eight set apart specifically as cities of refuge, three on each side of the Jordan, murder distinguished from manslaughter by weapon, motive and premeditation…

x: Leaders from the clan of Manasseh raise a concern with Moses: if Zelophehad's daughters, who inherited their father's land in chapter 27, marry men from another tribe, their inheritance would transfer to that tribe and permanently reduce Manasseh's allotted territory (vv. 1-4). The Lord rules that the concern is valid and that Zelophehad's daughters must marry within their own tribe so that each tribe retains the inheritance assigned to it (vv. 5-9). Zelophehad's daughters obey, marrying within their father's clan, keeping their inheritance within the tribe of Manasseh (vv. 10-12). The book closes by noting that these are the commands and regulations the Lord gave Israel through Moses on the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho, ending the book on a note of settled order after decades of wandering (v. 13).
m: tribal leaders raising a problem chapter twenty-seven's ruling left unresolved, land passing permanently out of a tribe if an inheriting daughter marries outside it, God affirming the concern exactly as he had affirmed the daughters' own claim two chapters earlier, a solution that grants freedom to…

x: Moses opens his farewell address on the plains of Moab, reviewing how the LORD had commanded Israel at Horeb to appoint capable leaders as judges over the tribes to share the burden of leadership (vv. 9-18). He recounts sending twelve spies into Canaan from Kadesh-barnea; despite their report of a good land, the people refused to go up and rebelled against the LORD's command (vv. 22-33). As judgment, that entire generation except Caleb and Joshua was barred from entering the land (vv. 34-38), and a later attempt to enter anyway ended in defeat by the Amorites (vv. 41-44). The chapter frames Israel's forty years of wandering as the consequence of that unbelief.
m: an eleven-day journey remembered as a forty-year one before the address even properly begins, a whole land already described in its fullness, hill country, coast, Lebanon, before a single step toward it is described, judges appointed the same way Jethro once counseled but retold now as Moses' own…

x: Moses continues recounting the wilderness years, describing how Israel wandered around Mount Seir for many years before God directed them north, instructing them not to provoke Edom, Moab, or Ammon since He had given those lands to Lot's and Esau's descendants (vv. 1-23). God then commands Israel to cross the Arnon and take the land of Sihon, king of the Amorites, when he refused to let Israel pass through peacefully (vv. 24-37). Israel defeats Sihon completely, capturing his cities and livestock, marking the first military victory of the conquest era.
m: thirty-eight years of wandering compressed into a handful of verses ending at a single named brook, three separate nations, Edom, Moab and Ammon, that Israel is explicitly forbidden to attack because God gave their land to someone else first, parenthetical notes about vanished giants elsewhere…

x: Moses recounts Israel's defeat of Og, king of Bashan, whose kingdom included sixty fortified cities (vv. 1-11), after which the conquered territory east of the Jordan is divided among the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, with instructions for their fighting men to help the other tribes conquer Canaan first (vv. 12-20). Moses commissions Joshua to lead the people across the Jordan (vv. 21-22), then recalls pleading with God to let him enter the promised land himself; God refuses, telling him to view the land from Pisgah instead (vv. 23-29).
h: The Defeat of Og King of Bashan (vv.1-7)
The Condition for the Transjordan Tribes (vv.18-20)
m: a giant king's iron bed preserved as physical evidence long after the giant himself is gone, sixty fortified cities taken from Bashan in a single campaign, land distributed to two and a half tribes on the explicit condition that their warriors first help conquer everyone else's, a charge to Joshua…

x: Moses urges Israel to keep God's statutes without addition or subtraction, reminding them of what they witnessed at Baal-peor and warning them not to forget what they saw at Horeb (vv. 1-14). He warns sharply against making any carved image of God, since Israel saw no form when the LORD spoke to them from the fire, and against turning to worship the sun, moon, or stars (vv. 15-19). Moses foresees future exile for disobedience but promises that God will still be found by those who seek Him with all their heart, since He is a merciful God who keeps His covenant (vv. 25-31). He closes by appointing three cities of refuge east of the Jordan (vv. 41-43) and setting the stage for repeating the law (vv. 44-49).
h: Exile Foretold, and the Way Back (vv.25-31)
Cities of Refuge East of Jordan (vv.41-43)
m: a covenant explained rather than merely repeated for a generation that mostly never heard it delivered at Horeb, a nation asked whether any other people has a god so near or laws so righteous, no image permitted of anything because Israel heard only a voice at the mountain and saw no form to copy…

x: Moses gathers Israel to restate the covenant made at Horeb, reminding the new generation that it applies to them and not only their fathers (vv. 1-5). He repeats the Ten Commandments essentially as first given at Sinai, covering worship of God alone, the prohibition of idols, keeping the Sabbath, honoring parents, and the commands against murder, adultery, theft, false witness, and coveting (vv. 6-21). Moses recalls how the people, terrified by the fire and voice at the mountain, asked him to hear from God on their behalf and relay His words to them, a request God approved (vv. 22-33).
h: God Spoke and Added No More (v.22)
m: a covenant Moses insists was made not with the dead fathers but with the very people standing there that day, the Ten Commandments restated nearly word for word from Sinai with the Sabbath's reason changed to remembering slavery in Egypt, God adding no more once the ten words are spoken, a people…

x: Moses urges Israel to fear the LORD and keep His commandments so that they and their children may live long in the land (vv. 1-3). He gives the great confession known as the Shema, declaring the LORD to be one, and commanding Israel to love Him with all their heart, soul, and strength, teaching these words diligently to their children at every opportunity throughout the day (vv. 4-9). Moses warns that once settled in the land of plenty they did not build, they must not forget the LORD who brought them out of slavery in Egypt, and must not test Him or follow other gods as the surrounding nations do (vv. 10-19). He instructs parents to explain to their children why they keep these laws, since the LORD rescued Israel from Egypt for their good and for righteousness (vv. 20-25).
h: The Word in Every Sphere of Life (vv.6-9)
m: the Shema, hear O Israel, the LORD our God is one, standing as the single sentence Jesus later calls the first and greatest commandment, God's words commanded into every posture of daily life, sitting, walking, lying down, rising, cities and vineyards and wells Israel will inherit without having…

x: Moses commands Israel to devote to complete destruction seven Canaanite nations they will encounter, forbidding treaties or intermarriage with them because such alliances would turn Israel's hearts to other gods (vv. 1-5). He explains that the LORD did not choose Israel for their size or merit, since they were the fewest of all peoples, but simply because He loved them and kept the oath made to their ancestors (vv. 6-8). Moses promises that obedience will bring blessing, fruitfulness, health, and victory over enemies, and urges Israel not to fear the nations ahead of them, since the God who defeated Pharaoh will fight for them too (vv. 9-24).
m: seven named nations marked for complete destruction not from ethnic hatred but to prevent Israel's own children being turned to other gods, Israel's election traced to nothing in Israel itself, they were the fewest of all peoples, but to God's own love and an oath sworn long before, blessing…

x: Moses reminds Israel to remember the whole way the LORD led them through the wilderness these forty years, humbling them and testing them, even feeding them manna to teach them that people live not on bread alone but on every word from God's mouth (vv. 1-5). He describes the good land they are entering, one of streams, wheat, and abundance, where they will lack nothing (vv. 6-9). Moses' central warning follows: when they eat and are full and their houses and herds increase, they must not become proud and forget the LORD, telling themselves that their own power produced this wealth, for it is God who gives the ability to produce it, in fulfillment of His covenant (vv. 10-18). He closes with a warning that forgetting God and following other gods will lead to Israel's destruction, just as it destroyed the nations before them (vv. 19-20).
h: Remember — He Gives Power to Get Wealth (vv.18-20)
m: forty years of wilderness reinterpreted as education rather than punishment, hunger deliberately allowed before manna is given so the lesson of dependence can land, a good land described in such lavish detail, brooks, wheat, honey, iron in the stones, that its abundance itself becomes the coming…

x: Moses corrects any assumption that Israel will possess the land because of their own righteousness, telling them plainly it is because of the wickedness of the nations there and to fulfill God's oath to the patriarchs, and reminding them that they are a stubborn people (vv. 1-6). He recounts their rebellion at Horeb with the golden calf while he was on the mountain receiving the tablets, and how he interceded, fasting forty days and nights, to turn aside God's anger and prevent their destruction (vv. 7-21). Moses lists further rebellions at Taberah, Massah, Kibroth-hattaavah, and Kadesh-barnea as evidence of Israel's persistent unfaithfulness, and recalls again pleading on their behalf (vv. 22-29).
m: a warning issued in advance against ever crediting the conquest to Israel's own righteousness, the same claim demolished three times in three consecutive verses, a golden calf built at the very base of the mountain where the law was still being written above them, an offer to make of Moses a…

x: Moses recalls being told to cut two new stone tablets and build an ark, after which God rewrote the Ten Commandments on them (vv. 1-5). He notes that the LORD set apart the tribe of Levi to carry the ark, minister before Him, and bless in His name, receiving no land inheritance since the LORD Himself is their inheritance (vv. 6-9). Moses then draws a broad conclusion from all he has recounted: circumcise your hearts and stop being stubborn, for the LORD, who shows no partiality and loves the foreigner, requires Israel simply to fear Him, walk in His ways, love Him, and serve Him with all their heart and soul (vv. 12-22).
h: The New Tablets and the Ark (vv.1-5)
m: new tablets cut and carried up the mountain a second time after Moses himself broke the first pair, Levi set apart at this point in the story specifically to carry the ark rather than to inherit land, five requirements condensed into a single rhetorical question, what doth the LORD thy God require…

x: Moses calls Israel to love the LORD and keep His commandments always, reminding the generation that saw firsthand what God did to Pharaoh's army and to Dathan and Abiram, who were swallowed by the earth for their rebellion (vv. 1-7). He contrasts Egypt, watered by irrigation, with Canaan, a land watered by rain from heaven that the LORD personally cares for throughout the year, with blessing tied to obedience and drought and famine tied to turning to other gods (vv. 8-17). Moses instructs Israel to keep His words on their hearts, teach them to their children, and bind them as reminders in daily life, then closes the section by setting blessing and curse before Israel, blessing for obedience and curse for disobedience, to be pronounced from Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal once they enter the land (vv. 18-32).
h: Love and Obey — Remember What You Saw (vv.1-7)
Obedience Brings Strength and Long Life (vv.8-9)
The Land Depends on God's Rain (vv.10-12)
Blessing and Curse — Gerizim and Ebal (vv.26-32)
m: an appeal addressed specifically to those who personally witnessed the plagues and the Red Sea rather than to their children, a land explicitly contrasted with Egypt because it depends on rain from heaven rather than on foot-worked irrigation canals, blessing and rain tied to obedience so directly…

x: Moses commands Israel to destroy every place where the Canaanite nations worshiped their gods, their altars, pillars, and carved images, once they take possession of the land (vv. 1-3). Unlike the pagan practice of worshiping anywhere, Israel is told to bring their offerings, tithes, and sacrifices only to the one place the LORD will choose to put His name, where the whole community will eat and rejoice before Him (vv. 4-14). Meat for ordinary meals may be eaten anywhere, but Israel is repeatedly warned not to eat blood and not to imitate the worship practices of the nations they are displacing, nor add to or take away from what God has commanded (vv. 15-32).
h: One Place of Worship, Not Every Man His Own (vv.8-14)
The Tithe, the Levite, and the Blood (vv.17-28)
Do Not Worship God Like the Pagans (vv.29-32)
m: every pagan worship site marked for total destruction, altars torn down, pillars broken, names erased, before a single word is said about how Israel itself should worship, a single chosen place established in deliberate contrast to every man doing what is right in his own eyes, ordinary meat…

x: Moses warns Israel that even a prophet or dreamer who performs a sign that comes true must be rejected and put to death if he urges the people to follow other gods, because the LORD is testing whether Israel loves Him with all their heart (vv. 1-5). He extends the same warning to a family member or close friend who secretly entices someone to serve other gods; such a person is to be shown no pity, and the one enticed must be the first to strike (vv. 6-11). Finally, if an entire town is found to have turned to idolatry, Moses commands a thorough investigation and, if confirmed, the destruction of that town and everything in it as a permanent judgment against apostasy (vv. 12-18).
h: The False Prophet — Signs That Lead Astray (vv.1-5)
The Enticing Family Member or Friend (vv.6-11)
m: a prophet whose predicted sign actually comes true still to be rejected if it leads toward another god, five separate negatives, no consent, no listening, no pity, no sparing, no concealing, aimed at the very closest relationships, a brother, a child, a wife, a friend as one's own soul, an entire…

x: Moses forbids Israel from practices of pagan mourning rites, since they are a people holy to the LORD and set apart from other nations (vv. 1-2). He then lists which animals, birds, and water creatures may and may not be eaten, distinguishing clean from unclean, and repeats the earlier command against boiling a young goat in its mother's milk (vv. 3-21). The chapter closes with instructions to tithe a tenth of all produce each year, eating it in the LORD's presence, or converting it to money if the distance is too great, and setting aside a special tithe every third year to provide for the Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows (vv. 22-29).
h: Clean and Unclean — Birds and Insects (vv.11-20)
Animals Found Dead; Kid in Mother's Milk (v.21)
m: an identity, ye are the children of the LORD your God, given before a single food law is stated, pagan mourning practices, cutting the body and shaving the head for the dead, forbidden specifically because Israel belongs to God rather than to grief's usual customs, the same clean and unclean animal…

x: Moses institutes a sabbatical year in which every seventh year, all debts owed by fellow Israelites must be canceled, though this need not apply to foreigners (vv. 1-6). He commands generosity toward the poor, warning against a hard heart or a stingy eye that withholds help simply because the year of release is near, since the poor will always be present in the land (vv. 7-11). Hebrew servants who have served six years must be freed in the seventh, sent away with generous provisions rather than empty-handed, though a servant who loves his master may choose to stay permanently (vv. 12-18). The chapter closes with instructions to dedicate every firstborn male animal to the LORD, eating it before Him each year unless it has a defect (vv. 19-23).
h: The Year of Release — Debt Cancellation (vv.1-6)
m: a debt release every seven years described as belonging to the LORD rather than merely to the calendar, an ideal of no poor among you made explicitly conditional on obedience rather than promised outright, a warning against the wicked thought that calculates the release year before deciding whether…

x: Moses instructs Israel to keep the Passover in the month of Abib, commemorating their hurried departure from Egypt, and to observe the seven days of Unleavened Bread that follow it (vv. 1-8). Seven weeks later they are to keep the Feast of Weeks with a freewill offering, and in the fall the Feast of Tabernacles for seven days, both occasions marked by rejoicing that includes servants, Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows (vv. 9-15). All Israelite men are required to appear before the LORD at these three pilgrimage feasts, none empty-handed (vv. 16-17). The chapter closes with instructions to appoint judges and officials in every town to render honest judgment without bribery or partiality, and a prohibition against planting sacred trees or setting up sacred pillars near the LORD's altar (vv. 18-22).
m: three pilgrimage feasts, Passover, Weeks and Tabernacles, each requiring every male to appear at the one chosen place rather than nowhere in particular, unleavened bread eaten specifically because Israel left Egypt in haste, giving scaled proportionally to each man's own blessing rather than fixed…

x: Moses forbids sacrificing any animal with a defect and prescribes the death penalty, on the testimony of two or three witnesses, for anyone in Israel found worshiping other gods (vv. 1-7). For legal cases too difficult for local judges, Moses establishes a central court of priests and a judge at the place the LORD chooses, whose rulings must be followed without deviation (vv. 8-13). Anticipating Israel's eventual request for a king, Moses lays out requirements in advance: the king must be an Israelite chosen by the LORD, must not multiply horses, wives, or silver and gold for himself, and must write out a copy of the law to read all his life so that his heart does not grow proud above his fellow Israelites (vv. 14-20).
h: The Supreme Court for Difficult Cases (vv.8-13)
m: a blemished sacrifice called an abomination before a single word is said about human justice, idolaters prosecuted only after diligent inquiry and only on the testimony of two or three witnesses rather than one, the accusing witnesses required to throw the first stones themselves, a supreme court…

x: Moses reaffirms that the Levitical priests receive no land inheritance but instead live from the offerings made to the LORD, since He is their inheritance (vv. 1-8). He forbids Israel from adopting the occult practices of the surrounding nations, including child sacrifice, divination, sorcery, mediums, and consulting the dead, because these are detestable to the LORD, who is driving out the nations for such practices (vv. 9-14). In their place, Moses promises that the LORD will raise up a prophet like himself from among Israel, whose words carry God's own authority, while warning that anyone who speaks presumptuously in the LORD's name or in the name of other gods must be put to death (vv. 15-22). This promised prophet is understood in the New Testament as ultimately fulfilled in Christ.
m: an entire tribe left with no land inheritance because the LORD himself is stated to be their inheritance, a list of forbidden occult practices, divination, sorcery, necromancy and child sacrifice, running to eight distinct terms in two verses, a promised prophet like Moses raised up from among…

x: Moses instructs Israel to set apart three cities of refuge once they possess the land, so that someone who kills another accidentally can flee there and be protected from revenge, and commands that three more be added later if the land's borders expand (vv. 1-10). He distinguishes this protection from the case of premeditated murder, where the elders must hand the killer over to be put to death without pity (vv. 11-13). Moses also forbids moving a neighbor's boundary marker and requires at least two or three witnesses to establish any charge, with the penalty a false witness intended for the accused applied instead to the false witness himself, so that others will hear and be afraid to do likewise (vv. 14-21).
h: Cities of Refuge and the Roads to Them (vv.1-10)
m: roads and equal spacing commanded to the cities of refuge so that distance itself never determines a man's guilt, the same refuge explicitly denied to anyone who lies in wait out of hatred rather than kills by accident, a boundary stone protected by law as though moving it were theft of land…

x: Moses gives instructions for warfare, telling Israel not to be afraid of enemy armies with more horses and chariots, since the LORD who brought them out of Egypt goes with them into battle (vv. 1-4). Before a battle, officers are to exempt anyone who has just built a house, planted a vineyard, become engaged, or is simply afraid, so that fear does not spread through the ranks (vv. 5-9). Moses distinguishes how Israel is to treat distant cities, offering terms of peace before attacking, from the nearby Canaanite cities, which are to be completely destroyed so their idolatrous practices cannot corrupt Israel (vv. 10-18). The chapter closes by commanding that fruit trees be spared during a siege, since trees are not the enemy (vv. 19-20).
m: a priest, not a general, addressing the army before battle with a fourfold command against fear, four separate exemptions sending home the man with an undedicated house, an unharvested vineyard, an unconsummated betrothal or a fearful heart, peace offered to distant cities before any siege begins…

x: Moses provides for an unsolved murder, instructing the elders of the nearest town to perform a ritual with a heifer to atone for the bloodshed and clear the community of guilt (vv. 1-9). He then addresses several difficult family situations: how a soldier may take a captive woman as a wife only after a month of mourning for her family, the requirement that a firstborn son's inheritance rights not be denied out of favoritism toward another wife's son, and the procedure for parents to bring a persistently rebellious son before the elders for judgment (vv. 10-21). The chapter closes by requiring that the body of an executed criminal not remain hanging on a tree overnight, since it would defile the land (vv. 22-23).
m: an unsolved murder answered by a heifer ceremony performed by the nearest city's elders rather than left unaddressed, a captive woman granted a full month to mourn her parents before any marriage and, if later unwanted, released rather than sold, a firstborn son's double portion protected from a…

x: Moses commands Israel to help a neighbor's stray ox, sheep, or lost property rather than ignoring it, and forbids a woman from wearing men's clothing or a man wearing women's clothing (vv. 1-5). He gives further scattered laws: releasing a mother bird before taking her young, building a parapet around a new roof to prevent injury, not planting two kinds of seed together or plowing with an ox and donkey yoked as a pair, and putting tassels on the corners of garments (vv. 6-12). The remainder of the chapter addresses sexual purity in detail, including false accusations against a bride, adultery, the assault of an engaged or unengaged woman, and forbidden relationships, treating chastity and marriage as matters that touch the whole community's holiness (vv. 13-30).
h: The Bird's Nest — Compassion for Animals (vv.6-7)
Betrothed Woman in the Field — Rape (vv.25-27)
m: a neighbor's stray ox or lost garment that cannot simply be ignored, an active duty to help lift a fallen animal rather than merely avoiding harm, a roof railing required specifically so a fall does not bring blood on the builder's own house, mixed seed, mixed plowing animals and mixed fabric all…

x: Moses lists who may and may not be admitted into the assembly of the LORD, including restrictions on Ammonites and Moabites due to their hostility toward Israel, alongside instructions welcoming Edomites and Egyptians after a few generations (vv. 1-8). He gives rules for keeping the military camp ritually clean, including provisions for bodily discharges and burying human waste outside the camp, since the LORD moves among them there (vv. 9-14). Moses closes with a range of further laws: not returning an escaped slave to his master, forbidding cult prostitution, prohibiting bringing the wages of prostitution into the LORD's house, forbidding interest charged to fellow Israelites, requiring that vows be kept once made, and permitting a hungry traveler to eat from a neighbor's field or vineyard but not to harvest it (vv. 15-25).
m: emasculated men, those of illegitimate birth, and Ammonites and Moabites permanently barred from the assembly while Edomites and Egyptians are readmitted after only three generations, camp sanitation regulated down to a tool for covering waste because the LORD himself is said to walk in the camp…

x: Moses addresses divorce, permitting a certificate of divorce under certain conditions but forbidding a woman's first husband from remarrying her after she has married another (vv. 1-4). He commands that a newly married man be exempted from military service and work obligations for a year to bring happiness to his wife, and forbids taking a millstone as loan collateral since it is a person's livelihood (vv. 5-6). The chapter continues with protections for the vulnerable: kidnapping is a capital offense, care must be taken with skin diseases, a poor man's pledge must be returned by evening, wages must be paid promptly, parents and children are not to be punished for each other's sins, and foreigners, orphans, and widows must not be denied justice or the gleanings of the harvest (vv. 7-22).
m: a divorce law that regulates rather than commands the practice, forbidding a woman's return to her first husband once she has remarried, a full year exempted from war and public duty for a newly married man so he can, in the text's own words, cheer up his wife, a millstone forbidden as collateral…

x: Moses limits corporal punishment to forty lashes so that a guilty person is not degraded beyond what the offense warrants, and instructs that an ox should not be muzzled while treading grain (vv. 1-4). He establishes levirate marriage, requiring a man to marry his deceased brother's childless widow to preserve the family line, with a public rite of shaming for a brother who refuses (vv. 5-10). Further laws follow regarding an unusual case of a woman intervening in a fight, and honest weights and measures in commerce, since dishonest scales are detestable to the LORD (vv. 11-16). The chapter closes by commanding Israel to remember what Amalek did in attacking the weak and weary at the rear of the column, and to blot out Amalek's memory once settled in the land (vv. 17-19).
m: a limit of forty stripes on corporal punishment specifically so the punished man is not degraded beyond recognition as a brother, an ox permitted to eat while it treads the grain rather than being muzzled through its labor, levirate marriage requiring a surviving brother to raise up his dead…

x: Moses instructs that once in the land, Israel is to bring the firstfruits of the harvest to the LORD's chosen place, reciting a confession that recounts their ancestor's humble beginnings, their slavery in Egypt, and God's deliverance and gift of a land flowing with milk and honey (vv. 1-11). He also commands a declaration to be made when the third-year tithe has been fully given to the Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows, affirming obedience to God's commands (vv. 12-15). The chapter closes with a mutual declaration: Israel affirms the LORD as their God and pledges obedience, while the LORD declares Israel His treasured people, set high above all nations in praise, fame, and honor (vv. 16-19).
m: a firstfruits ceremony that only begins once Israel is actually settled in the land, a worshipper's confession opening with a Syrian ready to perish was my father and moving through slavery, deliverance and gift in a handful of verses, a third-year tithe declaration built around three negatives…

x: Moses and the elders command Israel to set up large stones plastered with the words of the law on Mount Ebal as soon as they cross the Jordan, and to build an altar of uncut stones there for offerings (vv. 1-8). He then instructs that upon entering the land, six tribes are to stand on Mount Gerizim to pronounce blessings and six on Mount Ebal to pronounce curses (vv. 11-13). The Levites recite twelve specific curses covering idolatry, dishonoring parents, moving boundary markers, and various forms of sexual sin and secret injustice, with the people affirming each one, showing that the law's demands reach into hidden as well as public life (vv. 14-26).
h: The Stones of the Law at Ebal (vv.1-8)
The Ceremony of Blessings and Curses (vv.11-26)
m: great stones plastered and inscribed with the entire law set up specifically on Ebal, the mountain of cursing, rather than Gerizim, an altar of uncut stones built alongside those inscribed stones with no iron tool ever lifted against them, a formal declaration that this very day Israel has become…

x: Moses sets out at length the blessings that will follow obedience to the LORD: fruitfulness in family, field, and flock, victory over enemies, and prosperity in every undertaking, along with Israel's rise to prominence among the nations (vv. 1-14). He then details the curses that will follow disobedience at even greater length, including disease, drought, defeat, oppression, and ultimately exile among foreign nations, expressed as a chilling reversal of every named blessing (vv. 15-68). The chapter's warnings culminate in a description of siege conditions so severe that captivity will feel plausible only as national judgment for turning away from the LORD, underscoring the seriousness of the covenant Israel is entering.
m: fourteen verses of blessing set against fifty-four verses of curse, a structural imbalance that already forecasts which path Moses expects Israel to take, blessing promised in the city and the field, coming in and going out, everywhere without exception, a siege prophecy specific enough to name a…

x: Moses gathers Israel in Moab to enter into covenant with the LORD, reminding them of everything they saw in Egypt and during forty years of wilderness provision, yet noting that only now have their eyes and hearts truly begun to understand (vv. 1-9). The covenant includes not only those present but also future generations, and Moses warns against anyone who hears these words and still turns secretly to worship other gods, since the LORD will not forgive such presumption (vv. 10-21). He describes a devastated future land that will prompt other nations to ask why the LORD did this, with the answer being Israel's abandonment of the covenant, then closes by noting that secret things belong to the LORD while revealed things belong to Israel to obey (vv. 22-29).
h: Ye Have Seen All That the LORD Did (vv.1-9)
m: a covenant explicitly distinguished from the one made at Horeb rather than a mere repetition of it, evidence for that covenant drawn from forty years of clothes and shoes that never wore out rather than from any new miracle, an admission that Israel saw everything yet was given no heart to…

x: Moses looks ahead to a time when Israel, scattered among the nations for disobedience, will return to the LORD with all their heart, and promises that God will then restore their fortunes, gather them back, and circumcise their hearts to love Him fully (vv. 1-10). He insists that God's command is not too difficult or distant, but very near, already in their mouth and heart to be obeyed (vv. 11-14). Moses closes his address by setting life and prosperity against death and adversity, urging Israel to choose life by loving the LORD, obeying His voice, and holding fast to Him, since He is their life and the guarantee of their days in the land (vv. 15-20).
m: restoration promised even from the outmost parts of heaven once a scattered people calls the blessing and the curse to mind and returns with all the heart, a commandment described as neither too high to reach nor too far across the sea to fetch but already near, in the mouth and in the heart, a…

x: At 120 years old, Moses tells Israel that he can no longer lead them and that the LORD Himself will go before them and destroy the nations ahead, encouraging both Israel and Joshua, his successor, to be strong and courageous (vv. 1-8). He writes down the law and commands that it be read publicly to all Israel every seven years during the Feast of Tabernacles, so that every generation, including children, will learn to fear the LORD (vv. 9-13). The LORD then tells Moses that after his death Israel will turn to other gods, and instructs him to write a song as a witness against them for that future unfaithfulness (vv. 14-22). Moses commissions Joshua directly and commands the Levites to place the book of the law beside the ark as a permanent witness (vv. 23-29).
h: Moses' Charge to Israel and Joshua (vv.1-8)
m: a leader at one hundred twenty admitting plainly that he can no longer go out and come in, the same charge, be strong and of a good courage, given first to the whole nation and then to Joshua personally, a written law entrusted to the priests with instructions for public reading every seven years…

x: Moses recites a song calling heaven and earth to witness, praising the LORD as a faithful Rock whose work is perfect, in contrast to Israel, whom he compares to a warped and crooked generation despite God's care for them like the apple of His eye (vv. 1-14). He describes how Israel grew fat and prosperous and then abandoned the God who made them, provoking Him to jealousy with foreign gods, so that God hid His face from them and let them face hardship at the hands of their enemies (vv. 15-27). Yet the song ends with the LORD's promise to vindicate His people and take vengeance on their adversaries, since He alone kills and makes alive and no one can deliver out of His hand (vv. 28-43). Moses then urges the people to take these words to heart, since they are not empty but their very life (vv. 44-47).
m: heaven and earth summoned as witnesses that will outlast the audience actually listening, God pictured first as a faithful rock of perfect work before Israel is ever called a perverse and crooked generation, an eagle stirring her nest as the image for how God found and carried Israel through the…

x: Before his death, Moses pronounces a blessing over each tribe of Israel, beginning by recalling the LORD's coming from Sinai with His holy ones to give Israel the law as a possession (vv. 1-5). He addresses the tribes individually, including Reuben, Judah, Levi, Benjamin, Joseph, Zebulun and Issachar, Gad, Dan, Naphtali, and Asher, speaking words of blessing, protection, and future prosperity suited to each (vv. 6-25). The blessing closes with praise of Israel's uniqueness among the nations, since there is no one like the God of Jeshurun, who rides through the heavens to help His people and is their refuge and everlasting arms (vv. 26-29).
m: a dying leader's blessing on all twelve tribes given as his very last recorded words, Reuben's blessing reduced to bare survival rather than the prominence his birthright once promised, Levi praised specifically for choosing covenant loyalty over family ties at the golden calf, Joseph receiving by…

x: Moses climbs Mount Nebo to Pisgah's peak, where the LORD shows him the whole promised land, from Gilead to Dan and west to the Mediterranean Sea, while reminding him that he will not cross over into it himself (vv. 1-4). Moses dies there in Moab at 120 years old, his eyesight and strength undiminished, and the LORD buries him in a valley whose exact location remains unknown (vv. 5-7). Israel mourns him for thirty days, and Joshua, filled with the spirit of wisdom through Moses' laying on of hands, takes up leadership of the people (vv. 8-9). The book closes noting that no prophet since has arisen in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face (vv. 10-12).
m: a single mountain vantage point from which God shows Moses the entire land he will never set foot in, a death described as happening according to the word of the LORD and a burial performed by God himself in a grave no one has ever located, an old man whose eye was not dim nor his strength abated…

x: After the death of Moses, the LORD commissions Joshua as Israel's new leader, promising to give the people every place they set foot, from the wilderness to Lebanon and from the Euphrates to the Mediterranean (vv. 1-4). God vows never to fail or abandon Joshua as He was with Moses, and commands him three times to be strong and courageous, tying success to careful obedience to the law rather than military strength (vv. 5-9). Joshua relays the command to the officers, telling the people to prepare supplies for crossing the Jordan within three days, and reminds the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh of their pledge to fight alongside their brothers first (vv. 10-15). The people respond with total obedience, echoing God's own charge back to Joshua to be strong and courageous (vv. 16-18).
m: Moses' death and Joshua's commission delivered in the same breath, territory promised as far as every place the sole of the foot will tread, three commands to be strong and courageous each carrying a different emphasis, meditation on the law day and night tied directly to prosperity and success…

x: Joshua sends two spies from Shittim to scout Jericho, and they lodge at the house of Rahab, a prostitute (v. 1). When the king of Jericho demands the men be handed over, Rahab hides them on her roof and misdirects the pursuers, having already concluded that the LORD has given Israel the land after hearing how He dried up the Red Sea and defeated Sihon and Og (vv. 2-11). She asks the spies to swear an oath sparing her family when Israel conquers the city, and they agree on the condition that she keep silent and mark her house with a scarlet cord in the window (vv. 12-20). Rahab lowers the men down the city wall by a rope, they hide three days in the hills, and they return safely to Joshua reporting that the land's inhabitants are already terrified of Israel (vv. 21-24).
h: The Covenant and the Scarlet Cord (vv.12-21)
m: Two spies sent quietly after the twelve who failed at Kadesh a generation earlier, Rahab hiding strangers on her roof under stalks of flax, a pagan woman's confession that the LORD is God in heaven above and earth beneath, a scarlet cord tied in a window as an act of faith before any promise is…

x: After three days camped by the Jordan, the officers instruct the people to follow the ark of the covenant, carried by the priests, keeping a distance of about two thousand cubits behind it (vv. 1-4). Joshua tells the people to consecrate themselves because the LORD will do wonders among them the next day, and God promises to exalt Joshua before all Israel just as He was with Moses (vv. 5-7). As the priests carrying the ark step into the Jordan, the water flowing downstream is cut off and piles up far upstream near Adam, while the water below drains away, letting Israel cross on dry ground opposite Jericho (vv. 8-16). The priests stand firm in the middle of the riverbed until the entire nation has passed over (v. 17).
m: The Jordan crossed at flood stage rather than at a season that would make it easy, consecration commanded the day before the miracle rather than after it, the ark going ahead of the people as the proof the living God is among them, waters cut off and standing in a heap far upstream, and Joshua…

x: After all Israel has crossed the Jordan, the LORD tells Joshua to select twelve men, one from each tribe, to carry twelve stones from the riverbed where the priests stood and set them up as a memorial (vv. 1-9). The purpose is so that when future generations ask what the stones mean, their parents can tell them how the LORD dried up the Jordan just as He had the Red Sea (vv. 6-7, 21-24). The Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh cross armed for battle ahead of the rest, about forty thousand strong, and the LORD exalts Joshua in the sight of all Israel so the people fear him as they had feared Moses (vv. 12-14). Once the priests step out of the riverbed with the ark, the Jordan's waters return to their place, and the people camp at Gilgal on the tenth day of the first month (vv. 15-20).
m: Twelve stones taken from the exact spot where the priests' feet stood, a question children are expected to ask built into the memorial's whole purpose, two monuments raised, one in the riverbed and one at Gilgal, so the miracle is remembered from two directions, waters returning to their place the…

x: When the kings of the Amorites and Canaanites hear that the LORD dried up the Jordan for Israel, their courage fails them (v. 1). At Gilgal, the LORD instructs Joshua to circumcise the new generation, since the men born during the wilderness years had never been circumcised, removing what God calls the reproach of Egypt (vv. 2-9). Israel then keeps the Passover, and the day after eating the produce of the land, the manna stops falling, since the people now have food from Canaan itself (vv. 10-12). Near Jericho, Joshua encounters a man with a drawn sword who identifies himself as commander of the LORD's army; Joshua falls facedown in worship and is told to remove his sandals because he is standing on holy ground (vv. 13-15).
h: The Commander of the LORD's Army (vv.13-15)
m: Canaanite kings' hearts melting before a single battle is fought, circumcision restoring a covenant sign an entire generation had gone without, a name, Gilgal, explained as the rolling away of Egypt's reproach, manna ceasing the day after the first Passover eaten in the land, and a commander of the…

x: The LORD instructs Joshua on how Israel is to take Jericho: the armed men, with seven priests blowing ram's-horn trumpets before the ark, are to march around the city once a day for six days in silence (vv. 1-11). On the seventh day they march around it seven times, and when the priests sound a long blast and the people shout, the wall collapses and Israel takes the city (vv. 12-20). Everything in Jericho is devoted to destruction except Rahab and her household, who are spared for hiding the spies, and the silver, gold, and articles of bronze and iron, which are placed in the LORD's treasury (vv. 21-25). Joshua pronounces a curse on anyone who rebuilds the city, and his reputation spreads throughout the land (vv. 26-27).
m: A battle plan that looks absurd by any military standard, silence commanded for six days before a single shout on the seventh, the number seven governing days, priests, trumpets and circuits alike, Rahab named the one exception to a city otherwise placed under total destruction, and a curse…

x: After the fall of Jericho, Achan of the tribe of Judah secretly keeps some of the devoted plunder—silver, gold, and a fine robe—in violation of God's command (vv. 1, 20-21). Unaware of this, Israel sends a small force against the little city of Ai and is routed, losing thirty-six men (vv. 2-5). Joshua tears his clothes and pleads with God, who reveals that Israel has been defeated because someone took what was set apart for destruction (vv. 6-15). Lots are cast until Achan is exposed; he confesses, and he, his family, and his possessions are stoned and burned in the Valley of Achor (vv. 16-26).
h: Judgment in the Valley of Achor (vv.24-26)
m: A private theft turned into a public defeat at a city Israel should have easily taken, Joshua's grief answered bluntly with get thee up rather than more prayer, a lot narrowing tribe by clan by household until it lands on one man, a confession that echoes I saw, I coveted, I took, the same…

x: After the defeat at Ai, the LORD commands Joshua to attack again, this time with a strategy: a large ambush force hides behind the city while Joshua leads the main body in a feigned retreat (vv. 1-13). The king of Ai pursues, leaving the city undefended, so the ambush rises to set it ablaze; the trapped army is destroyed and its king executed (vv. 14-29). Joshua then leads Israel to Mount Ebal, builds an altar of uncut stones as Moses commanded, offers sacrifices, and writes a copy of the law of Moses on the stones (vv. 30-32). He reads the entire law—blessings and curses—before all the assembled people, including women, children, and foreigners (vv. 33-35).
m: The same words, fear not, neither be thou dismayed, repeated to restore confidence after failure, plunder permitted at Ai that had been forbidden at Jericho, an ambush strategy directed by God rather than a purely miraculous victory, a spear held outstretched until the destruction is complete, and…

x: Hearing of Israel's victories, the kings of Canaan unite against Joshua, but the Gibeonites take a different approach: they disguise themselves with worn-out sandals, patched wineskins, and moldy bread to pose as travelers from a distant land (vv. 3-13). Israel's leaders sample their provisions but fail to inquire of the LORD, and they make a treaty of peace with them, sworn by oath (vv. 14-15). Three days later Israel learns the Gibeonites live nearby, yet honors the oath because it was sworn in the LORD's name, even as the people grumble (vv. 16-21). Joshua confronts the Gibeonites, who admit they lied out of fear for their lives, and he sentences them to perpetual service as woodcutters and water carriers for Israel and the altar of the LORD (vv. 22-27).
m: A Canaanite coalition uniting for open war while one city chooses deception instead, moldy bread and worn sandals used as evidence Israel examines without ever asking counsel of the LORD, an oath sworn in God's name that binds Israel even after the deception is discovered, a congregation murmuring…

x: When the king of Jerusalem hears that Gibeon made peace with Israel, he forms a coalition of five Amorite kings to attack the city, and Gibeon appeals to Joshua for help (vv. 1-6). Joshua marches all night from Gilgal, routs the coalition, and the LORD hurls hailstones on the fleeing army that kill more than the sword does (vv. 7-11). Joshua then asks the LORD to make the sun and moon stand still so Israel can finish the battle in daylight, an event with no equal before or since (vv. 12-14).
