The five kings are found hiding in a cave at Makkedah, executed, and Joshua presses on to conquer a series of southern cities, including Makkedah, Lachish, Eglon, Hebron, and Debir (vv. 16-43).
h: Joshua's Night March and God's Promise (vv.6-9)
The Battle and the Sun Standing Still (vv.10-15)
m: A treaty ally's appeal answered by an all-night march rather than delay, hailstones killing more of the enemy than Israel's own swords, a sun commanded to stand still so a day of battle could be finished, captured kings made to have Israel's captains put their feet on their necks, and a systematic…

x: In the north, Jabin king of Hazor rallies a huge coalition of kings and their armies, as numerous as sand on the seashore, with many horses and chariots, to fight Israel at the waters of Merom (vv. 1-5). The LORD tells Joshua not to be afraid and promises victory; Israel attacks by surprise, routs the coalition, and hamstrings their horses and burns their chariots as commanded (vv. 6-9). Joshua captures Hazor, kills its king, and burns the city, the only one of the northern cities burned in this campaign (vv. 10-15). The chapter closes with a summary of Joshua's long campaign to take the whole land, leaving only a remnant of the Anakim in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod, and the land finally has rest from war (vv. 16-23).
m: A northern coalition described as sand on the seashore complete with a technology Israel has never faced before, horses hamstrung and chariots burned rather than kept as captured strength, Hazor alone burned among the northern cities as the coalition's head, a chain of obedience traced from God to…

x: This chapter closes the conquest narrative with a summary list of defeated kings. It first records the two Amorite kings Moses defeated east of the Jordan—Sihon of Heshbon and Og of Bashan—whose territory was given to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh (vv. 1-6). It then lists thirty-one kings that Joshua and Israel defeated west of the Jordan, from Jericho and Ai through the cities of the south and north (vv. 7-24). The list stands as a record of the LORD's faithfulness in giving Israel the land he promised.
h: Kings Defeated East of the Jordan — Under Moses (vv.1-6)
Kings Defeated West of the Jordan — Under Joshua (vv.7-24)
m: A ledger of victories rather than a narrative, two campaigns under two leaders, territory described by boundary and terrain, thirty-one kings counted one at a time, and a tally that closes the conquest account

x: The LORD tells the aging Joshua that much land still remains unconquered—the territory of the Philistines, Geshurites, and other regions—yet instructs him to go ahead and divide it among the tribes by inheritance, trusting God to complete the conquest (vv. 1-7). The chapter then reviews the territory Moses had already assigned east of the Jordan to Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh, including the former kingdoms of Sihon and Og (vv. 8-31). It closes by repeating that the tribe of Levi received no land inheritance, because the LORD, the God of Israel, is itself their inheritance (vv. 32-33).
h: Thou Art Old, and Much Land Remains (vv.1-7)
The Eastern Allotment, and Levi's Portion (vv.8-14)
Half Manasseh, and the LORD as Levi's Inheritance (vv.29-33)
m: An old leader and a great deal of unconquered ground, land allotted by faith before it is held, the eastern tribes' inheritance recorded from Moses' day, and one tribe given no territory at all

x: As the tribes gather at Gilgal to receive their inheritance west of the Jordan by lot, Caleb, now eighty-five years old, comes forward to remind Joshua of the promise Moses made him at Kadesh-barnea forty-five years earlier (vv. 6-9). Caleb recalls that he and Joshua alone among the twelve spies brought back a faithful report, while the other ten caused the people's hearts to melt in fear (vv. 7-8). Though decades have passed, Caleb declares he is still as strong as the day Moses sent him and asks for the hill country of Hebron, home of the powerful Anakim (vv. 10-12). Joshua blesses him and gives him Hebron as his inheritance, because he wholly followed the LORD (vv. 13-15).
m: A pause over one man before any boundary is drawn, forty-five years between a promise and its keeping, an eighty-five-year-old asking for hill country rather than easy land, and a phrase repeated three times

x: This chapter details the extensive boundaries of Judah's inheritance, running from the southern wilderness near Edom up to the Mediterranean coast and the Jordan (vv. 1-12). Caleb drives the three sons of Anak out of Hebron and then captures Debir, offering his daughter Achsah in marriage to whoever takes the city; his kinsman Othniel succeeds and wins her (vv. 13-17). Achsah persuades Caleb to add springs of water to the dry land given her, and he grants her both the upper and lower springs (vv. 18-19). The chapter closes with long lists of Judah's towns and villages, though it notes that Judah could not dislodge the Jebusites living in Jerusalem (v. 63).
h: The Hill Country and the Wilderness (vv.48-62)
m: Judah allotted first and most fully, a boundary described like a survey rather than a summary, a daughter who asks for springs, town lists by region, and a city left unconquered in the last verse

x: The allotment for the descendants of Joseph begins with a general southern boundary before turning to Ephraim's specific inheritance in the central hill country (vv. 1-4). Ephraim's territory is marked out with towns and borders reaching toward Gezer and the Mediterranean (vv. 5-9). Despite the conquest, Ephraim fails to drive out the Canaanites living in Gezer, and instead lets them remain as forced laborers among them, a compromise repeated elsewhere in the land (v. 10).
m: Joseph's double portion realized as two allotments, the fertile central highlands, Shiloh and Shechem and Bethel inside the territory, and Canaanites left in place under tribute

x: The other half of the tribe of Manasseh receives its inheritance, beginning with Machir's descendants and the special case of Zelophehad's five daughters, who—as promised earlier in Numbers—receive a land inheritance among their father's brothers since he had no sons (vv. 1-6). Manasseh's territory stretches on both sides of the Jordan and includes towns within Issachar and Asher's borders, though Manasseh cannot yet drive out the Canaanites in cities like Beth-shean and Taanach, who have iron chariots (vv. 7-13). The tribes of Joseph complain to Joshua that one allotment is too small for so large a people, and Joshua tells them that if they are so numerous, they should go up into the forested hill country and clear it themselves rather than fear the Canaanites' iron chariots (vv. 14-18).
h: The Border, and Towns Within Other Tribes (vv.7-13)
m: Daughters who inherit because they asked and were granted, a tribe complaining its portion is too small, an answer that points at uncleared forest, and iron chariots offered as the reason it cannot be done

x: With seven tribes still lacking territory, Joshua gathers Israel at Shiloh, where the tabernacle is set up, and rebukes the people for their slowness to take possession of the land the LORD has given them (vv. 1-3). He sends men to survey the remaining land and divide it into seven written portions, which are then assigned by casting lots before the LORD at Shiloh (vv. 4-10). The lot falls first to Benjamin, whose territory lies between Judah and the tribes of Joseph, and the chapter closes with a detailed list of Benjamin's boundaries and cities, including Jericho and the border near Jerusalem (vv. 11-28).
h: The Tabernacle Set Up at Shiloh (v.1)
m: The tabernacle set up at Shiloh where it stayed three centuries, seven tribes still holding nothing, a rebuke about slackness rather than opposition, surveyors sent out to write a description, and Benjamin's small portion between Judah and Ephraim

x: The remaining allotments are assigned by lot: Simeon receives towns within Judah's territory since Judah's portion proved too large, followed by Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, and Naphtali, each described with its boundaries and cities (vv. 1-39). Dan receives the last allotment, but when the tribe struggles to take its assigned territory, its people go on to capture the city of Leshem in the north and rename it Dan (vv. 40-48). Finally, Israel gives Joshua himself an inheritance in the hill country of Ephraim; at the LORD's command, he receives and rebuilds the town of Timnath-serah, where he settles (vv. 49-51).
m: Simeon's towns inside Judah's territory, the northern tribes that would become Galilee, Dan's portion and later migration, and Joshua receiving his own inheritance last of anyone

x: The LORD instructs Joshua to designate cities of refuge, as Moses had commanded, where a person who kills someone accidentally and without malice can flee from the avenger of blood and receive a fair hearing before the elders (vv. 1-6). Three cities are appointed west of the Jordan—Kedesh, Shechem, and Hebron—and three more east of the Jordan—Bezer, Ramoth, and Golan (vv. 7-8). Anyone who kills unintentionally may live safely in these cities until standing trial and until the death of the current high priest, after which he may return home, reflecting God's justice tempered with mercy for the unintentional offender (v. 9).
m: Six cities spaced so nobody was more than a day from one, a hearing at the gate instead of pursuit, protection that ends at the death of the high priest, and a distinction drawn between accident and intent

x: The heads of the Levite families come to the leaders of Israel at Shiloh and remind them that the LORD commanded through Moses that Levi be given cities to live in along with pasturelands, since Levi receives no territorial inheritance of its own (vv. 1-3). Forty-eight cities in all are allotted to the various Levitical clans out of the other tribes' territories, including the six cities of refuge already named (vv. 4-42). The chapter closes with a triumphant summary: the LORD gave Israel all the land he swore to their fathers, granted them rest from their enemies on every side, and not one word of all his good promises failed—everything came to pass (vv. 43-45).
m: Forty-eight towns for the tribe with no territory, distributed through every other tribe rather than gathered, thirteen for the priestly line near where the temple would stand, and a summary that not one promise failed

x: With the land conquered and divided, Joshua commends the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh for their faithful service and sends them home east of the Jordan with his blessing and a share of the plunder (vv. 1-9). On the way, they build a large, conspicuous altar by the Jordan, and when the rest of Israel hears of it, the western tribes assume it is a rival altar for sacrifice and prepare to go to war over what they see as apostasy (vv. 10-12). A delegation led by Phinehas confronts the eastern tribes, who explain that the altar is not for sacrifice but a witness for future generations, so their descendants will not be cut off from worshiping the LORD alongside their brothers (vv. 13-29). Satisfied by the explanation, Phinehas and the delegation return home, war is averted, and the altar is named Witness between the tribes (vv. 30-34).
m: Eastern tribes released after keeping their word, an altar built by the Jordan, nine tribes mustering for civil war, a delegation sent to ask before attacking, and an answer that satisfies everyone

x: Now old and well along in years, Joshua summons the leaders of Israel and reminds them that the LORD has fought for them, driving out great nations before them, and urges them to be very strong to keep and obey all that is written in the Book of the Law (vv. 1-6). He warns them not to associate with the nations remaining among them or invoke, swear by, serve, or bow down to their gods, but to hold fast to the LORD as they have done to this day (vv. 7-8). Joshua reminds them that the LORD has kept every good promise he made, and warns that just as surely as the good promises have been fulfilled, the LORD will bring every disaster on them if they transgress the covenant and go after other gods, until they perish from the good land he has given them (vv. 14-16).
h: The LORD Hath Fought for You (vv.1-5)
m: A farewell that warns rather than celebrates, not one promise failed, intermarriage named as the danger, and remaining nations described as snares and scourges

x: Joshua assembles all the tribes of Israel at Shechem and recounts, speaking for the LORD, the nation's history from Abraham's call, through the exodus and wilderness years, to the conquest of the land, emphasizing that it was God, not their own sword or bow, who gave them victory (vv. 1-13). He calls the people to fear the LORD and serve him in sincerity and truth, putting away any other gods, and declares that he and his household will serve the LORD no matter what others choose (vv. 14-15). The people twice affirm their commitment to serve the LORD, and Joshua renews the covenant at Shechem, recording it in the Book of the Law and setting up a large stone as a witness (vv. 16-27). The chapter closes with the deaths of Joshua at a hundred and ten years old and of Eleazar the priest, and the burial of Joseph's bones at Shechem, brought up from Egypt generations earlier (vv. 29-33).
m: A covenant renewal at Shechem where Abraham built an altar, history retold as God's initiative throughout, a choice put to the people, an answer Joshua tells them they cannot keep, and three burials to close the book

x: After Joshua's death, Israel asks the LORD who should lead the fight against the Canaanites, and He names Judah, who enlists Simeon as an ally (vv. 1-3). Judah defeats the Canaanites and Perizzites at Bezek, capturing King Adoni-Bezek, who admits his mutilation is fitting payback for his own cruelty toward seventy kings (vv. 5-7), then burns Jerusalem and takes Hebron and Debir, where Caleb gives Achsah in marriage to Othniel along with springs of water (vv. 10-15). Judah also takes Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron, though iron chariots block the valley (vv. 18-19). The chapter closes by listing tribe after tribe failing to fully drive out the Canaanites, a pattern of incomplete obedience that sets up Israel's later compromise (vv. 21-36).
m: A prologue explaining the whole book's later cycles by one repeated verb, did not drive out, Adoni-bezek recognizing divine justice in his own mutilation, a spy shown mercy the way Rahab once was but building a pagan city instead of joining Israel, Asher's reversal recorded in one devastating…

x: The angel of the LORD comes up from Gilgal to Bochim, rebuking Israel for making covenants with the Canaanites instead of tearing down their altars, and warns these nations will remain as thorns and their gods a snare (vv. 1-3); the people weep and offer sacrifices there (vv. 4-5). After Joshua's generation dies, a new generation arises that does not know the LORD or His works, and Israel serves the Baals and Ashtaroth, provoking His anger (vv. 6-13). God hands them to raiders, then raises up judges who deliver them, yet each generation relapses into idolatry once the judge dies (vv. 14-19). The chapter closes with the LORD leaving the remaining nations to test Israel's obedience (vv. 20-23), establishing the cycle of sin, oppression, and deliverance that structures the rest of Judges.
h: Joshua's Death and the Lost Generation (vv.6-10)
m: An angel's rebuke delivered at a place later named for the weeping it caused, a covenant renewed at Gilgal answered by disobedience rather than gratitude, a generation that knew not the LORD rising the moment eyewitnesses to His works had died, a cycle of sin, oppression, crying out, deliverance…

x: The LORD leaves several nations in Canaan to test Israel and to train generations unfamiliar with war (vv. 1-4), and Israel intermarries with the Canaanites and serves their gods, forgetting the LORD (vv. 5-7). He hands them over to Cushan-Rishathaim of Mesopotamia for eight years, until Othniel, Caleb's nephew, is empowered by the Spirit and delivers Israel, giving the land forty years of rest (vv. 8-11). Israel relapses, and the LORD strengthens Eglon of Moab against them for eighteen years, until the left-handed Ehud assassinates Eglon in his upper room with a hidden two-edged sword and escapes before the body is found (vv. 12-26). Ehud then rallies Israel at the Jordan fords and strikes down about ten thousand Moabites, securing eighty years of peace (vv. 27-30). The chapter closes with Shamgar killing six hundred Philistines with an ox goad (v. 31).
h: Shamgar — One Verse, One Ox Goad (v.31)
m: Nations left deliberately to teach war to a generation that had never fought one, Othniel's story told as the cycle in its purest and briefest form, a left-handed weakness turned into Ehud's actual weapon, a very fat king and a hidden dagger described in more physical detail than any other…

x: After Ehud's death Israel again does evil, and the LORD sells them to Jabin king of Canaan, whose commander Sisera oppresses them with nine hundred iron chariots for twenty years (vv. 1-3). Deborah the prophetess, who judges Israel beneath her palm tree, summons Barak with the LORD's command to gather ten thousand men at Mount Tabor for victory over Sisera at the river Kishon; Barak agrees only if she goes too, so Deborah warns the honor will instead go to a woman (vv. 4-9). The LORD throws Sisera's army into confusion, and the whole force falls by the sword while Sisera flees on foot (vv. 14-16). He hides in Jael's tent, where she gives him milk, then drives a tent peg through his temple as he sleeps (vv. 17-21). Barak finds Sisera already dead, and Israel prevails until Jabin is destroyed (vv. 22-24).
m: Deborah alone among the judges shown actually adjudicating disputes under her palm tree, Barak's condition for going answered with a prophecy that costs him the honor of the victory, discomfited used of Sisera's army the same way it is used of a rout only God can cause, an alliance of convenience…

x: Deborah and Barak sing a victory hymn praising the LORD, who marched from Seir with the earth trembling before Him, recalling how the roads stood empty and rulers were absent until Deborah arose as a mother in Israel (vv. 1-9). The song rouses Deborah and Barak to lead their captives (vv. 10-12), then names the tribes who answered — Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir, Zebulun, Issachar — while rebuking Reuben, Gilead, Dan, Asher, and the town of Meroz for staying behind (vv. 13-23). Jael is pronounced most blessed of women for striking Sisera dead with a tent peg after luring him with milk (vv. 24-27), and the song closes with Sisera's mother waiting in vain at her window for a son who will never return, before praying the LORD's enemies perish like this while His friends shine like the rising sun (vv. 28-31).
h: Speak, Ye That Ride on White Asses (vv.9-13)
m: A victory hymn possibly composed within hours of the battle it celebrates, the same God who marched from Sinai marshaled again against Sisera, three classes of listener called to speak in turn, the wealthy, the magistrates and the ordinary traveler, tribes praised for fighting and tribes named for…

x: Because Israel does evil, the LORD hands them over to Midian for seven years; the Midianites and their allies strip the land bare, driving the people into caves and dens until Israel cries out for help and a prophet rebukes them for forsaking the LORD (vv. 1-10). The angel of the LORD then appears to Gideon threshing wheat in hiding and calls him a mighty man of valor, commissioning him to save Israel despite his protest that his clan is the weakest in Manasseh and he is the least in his family (vv. 11-16). Gideon asks for a sign, and fire from a rock consumes his offering before the angel vanishes, leaving Gideon awestruck that he has seen the LORD face to face and unharmed (vv. 17-24). That night the LORD orders Gideon to tear down his father's altar to Baal and its Asherah pole and build an altar to the LORD instead; he obeys under cover of darkness, and though the townsmen demand…
m: A prophet sent to name the sin before any deliverer is sent to address the suffering, a mighty man of valour found threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from raiders, an objection about being least in the poorest family in the smallest clan met without correction, a father's own logic defending…

x: The LORD tells Gideon his army of 32,000 is too large, since Israel might boast that its own strength saved it, so 22,000 fearful men are sent home, leaving 10,000 (vv. 1-3). Still too many, the LORD has Gideon sift the rest at the water, keeping only the 300 who lap water from their hands and sending the remaining 9,700 away (vv. 4-8). That night the LORD sends Gideon down to the enemy camp, where he overhears a Midianite soldier's dream of a barley loaf overturning a tent, interpreted as Gideon's coming victory, and Gideon worships before returning to rally his men (vv. 9-15). He arms his 300 with trumpets, torches, and empty jars, dividing them into three companies (v. 16). At his signal in the night, they smash their jars, blow their trumpets, and shout, throwing the vast Midianite camp into panic so that the enemy turns swords on each other and flees (vv. 19-22). Israel then…
m: An army called too many rather than too few before a single battle is fought, two rounds of reduction that leave three hundred out of thirty-two thousand, a barley-cake dream overheard in the enemy's own camp before Gideon ever gives an order, an attack carried out with trumpets, empty jars and…

x: Gideon defuses Ephraim's anger over being left out of the battle with diplomatic flattery (vv. 1-3), then presses on across the Jordan with his exhausted 300, chasing the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna (v. 4). When Succoth and Penuel refuse to feed his weary men, he vows to punish them (vv. 5-9), and after capturing the kings and routing the remaining army at Karkor, he returns and carries out that punishment, disciplining Succoth's elders and destroying Penuel's tower and men (vv. 10-17). Learning that Zebah and Zalmunna had killed his own brothers, Gideon personally executes the two kings when his young son is too afraid to do it (vv. 18-21). Israel then offers Gideon a hereditary kingship, but he refuses, insisting the LORD alone shall rule over them (vv. 22-23) — though he then requests the plunder's gold earrings and makes an ephod that all Israel worships, becoming a snare to…
m: A diplomatic answer that calls Ephraim's gleanings greater than Gideon's own vintage, faint yet pursuing describing an army too exhausted to stop, two Israelite towns punished with thorns and a broken tower for refusing bread to their own deliverer, kingship refused in a sentence that gets the…

x: Abimelech persuades his mother's kin in Shechem to back him as sole ruler over Gideon's seventy sons, and funded by silver from Baal-berith's temple he hires reckless men and murders all but the youngest brother, Jotham, who escapes into hiding (vv. 1-6). From Mount Gerizim, Jotham denounces Shechem with a parable of trees seeking a king, where only the worthless bramble accepts, warning that fire will consume both Abimelech and Shechem if their alliance was built on treachery (vv. 7-21). After three years, God sends a spirit of division between Abimelech and Shechem; the citizens rebel under Gaal, but Abimelech, warned by his officer Zebul, ambushes and defeats them, then destroys the city itself, killing its people and burning about a thousand more who take refuge in a stronghold (vv. 22-49). Moving on to attack Thebez, Abimelech is fatally struck on the head by a millstone dropped by…
m: Seventy brothers murdered on one stone to clear a path to a crown none of them held, the oldest fable in the book handed to trees that each refuse a throne before a bramble accepts it, an evil spirit sent by God between conspirators as their punishment rather than as a mystery, a millstone dropped…

x: After Abimelech, Tola of Issachar judges Israel twenty-three years (vv. 1-2), followed by Jair the Gileadite, whose thirty sons ride thirty donkeys and control thirty towns known as Havvoth-jair, for twenty-two more years (vv. 3-5). Israel again turns to idols, serving the gods of the surrounding nations, so the LORD's anger delivers them into the hands of the Philistines and Ammonites, who oppress Israel severely for eighteen years, especially east of the Jordan (vv. 6-9). When the people cry out and confess their sin, the LORD initially refuses to save them again, telling them to cry to the gods they chose instead (vv. 10-14), but relents in compassion after Israel puts away its foreign gods and pleads for deliverance (vv. 15-16). As the Ammonites mass for battle in Gilead, Israel gathers at Mizpah, and the leaders of Gilead ask who will lead the fight, promising that man headship…
m: Two minor judges given forty-five years of unremarked stability between two chapters of chaos, an idolatry catalogue naming seven nations' gods as the most comprehensive in the book, God answering confession by naming seven past deliverances that match the seven gods just named, a command to go and…

x: Jephthah, a mighty warrior but the son of a prostitute, is driven out by his half-brothers and takes refuge with a band of outcasts in Tob (vv. 1-3). When Ammon attacks, Gilead's elders come begging him to lead them, and he agrees on the condition that he becomes their permanent head if God grants victory (vv. 4-11). Jephthah first tries diplomacy, sending Ammon's king a detailed historical argument that Israel never took Ammonite or Moabite land but only territory won from the Amorites under Sihon, appealing to the LORD as judge, but the king refuses to listen (vv. 12-28). The Spirit of the LORD comes on Jephthah as he marches to battle, and he vows that whatever comes out of his house to meet him on his safe return will be offered to the LORD as a burnt offering (vv. 29-31). He crushes the Ammonites in a great slaughter (vv. 32-33), but returning home he is met by his only child, his…
m: An outcast son of a prostitute recalled by the same brothers who expelled him, diplomatic negotiation with Ammon built on a careful reading of Israel's own three hundred years of history, a rash vow made after the Spirit had already come upon him, not to secure victory but as though it still needed…

x: After Jephthah's victory over Ammon, the Ephraimites confront him for not being called to the fight and threaten to burn his house down (v. 1); when Jephthah explains that he had called them and they refused to help (vv. 2-3), war breaks out and Gilead defeats Ephraim, killing 42,000 men at the Jordan fords by testing their pronunciation of the word Shibboleth (vv. 4-6). Jephthah judges Israel six years before he dies (v. 7), and three minor judges follow in succession — Ibzan of Bethlehem for seven years (vv. 8-10), Elon the Zebulunite for ten years (vv. 11-12), and Abdon son of Hillel for eight years (vv. 13-15) — each noted briefly for family and burial rather than military exploits.
m: A grievance and a threat delivered in the same breath by a tribe that arrives only after the fighting is over, force chosen over the diplomacy Gideon once used for the identical complaint, a pronunciation Ephraim's dialect could not produce turned into a password and then a death sentence…

x: During a forty-year Philistine oppression, the Angel of the LORD appears to the barren wife of Manoah of the tribe of Dan and announces she will bear a son who is to be a Nazirite from birth, set apart to begin delivering Israel from the Philistines (vv. 1-5). She reports the encounter to Manoah, who prays that the messenger would return to instruct them further, and the angel appears to her again before Manoah meets him and repeats the earlier instructions (vv. 6-14). When Manoah offers a sacrifice, the angel ascends in the flame, revealing himself to be divine and leaving both parents in awe, though Manoah's wife reasons calmly that God would not have accepted their offering if he intended to kill them (vv. 15-23). The son is born and named Samson, and as he grows the Spirit of the LORD begins to stir him at Mahaneh-dan (vv. 24-25).
h: Manoah's Prayer and the Second Appearance (vv.8-14)
m: Forty years of oppression recorded with no mention of Israel crying out at all, an angel's announcement given to an unnamed woman before her husband ever hears it, Nazirite restrictions placed on a mother's own diet before her son is even born, a name refused as secret and wonderful rather than…

x: Samson goes down to Timnah and insists on marrying a Philistine woman there despite his parents' objections, not realizing God is using the request to create an opportunity against the Philistines (vv. 1-4). On the way, he kills a young lion barehanded with the Spirit's sudden strength but tells no one, and later finds a swarm of bees and honey in the lion's carcass, which he eats and shares without revealing its source (vv. 5-9). At his wedding feast, Samson poses a riddle about the lion and honey to thirty Philistine companions, wagering garments on the answer, and when they cannot solve it, they threaten his bride until she pries the answer from him and tells them (vv. 10-18). Furious that his riddle was betrayed, Samson kills thirty men in Ashkelon to pay his debt and storms off, leaving his bride to be given to his best man instead (vv. 19-20).
m: A demand for a Philistine wife justified only afterward as something of the LORD working an occasion against them, a lion torn apart bare-handed and its carcass later robbed of honey in a first, casual violation of a vow Samson never seems to notice breaking, a riddle wagered on thirty garments and…

x: After Samson discovers his wife has been given to another man, he retaliates by tying torches to 300 foxes and burning the Philistines' grain fields, vineyards, and olive groves (vv. 1-5); the Philistines respond by burning his wife and father-in-law, and Samson strikes back with great slaughter before retreating to the rock of Etam (vv. 6-8). Three thousand men of Judah, resigned to Philistine rule, come and bind Samson to hand him over (vv. 9-13), but when the Philistines close in, the Spirit of the LORD comes upon him, he snaps his ropes, and kills a thousand men with a donkey's jawbone (vv. 14-17). Afterward, desperately thirsty, he cries out to God, who splits open a hollow place and provides water (vv. 18-19); the chapter closes noting Samson judged Israel twenty years (v. 20).
m: Three hundred foxes and torches turned into an act of agricultural warfare, escalating retaliation that burns a wife for the very threat once made against her, three thousand men of Judah arriving not to fight the Philistines but to hand their own deliverer over, a fresh jawbone found and used…

x: Samson visits a prostitute in Gaza and escapes a trap by tearing out the city gates and carrying them off (vv. 1-3), then falls for Delilah, who is bribed by the Philistine lords to discover the source of his strength (vv. 4-5). After three false answers, Samson's persistent pestering wears him down and he reveals that his strength depends on his uncut Nazirite hair; Delilah has it shaved off while he sleeps, and he wakes not realizing the LORD has left him (vv. 6-20). The Philistines blind him, bind him, and set him grinding grain in prison, but as his hair grows back he prays for strength one final time and pulls down the temple of Dagon, killing more Philistines in his death than in his life (vv. 21-30); his family recovers his body and buries him (v. 31).
m: City gates torn out and carried thirty-eight miles as proof his strength survives his own moral failure, three lies told to a woman clearly trying to betray him before a fourth answer finally does, a sentence naming its own tragedy, he wist not that the LORD was departed from him, hair beginning to…

x: Micah confesses to his mother that he stole 1,100 pieces of silver from her, and she dedicates part of it to make a carved and cast idol for him (vv. 1-4). Micah sets up a private shrine complete with an ephod and household idols and installs his own son as priest (v. 5), and the narrator notes that in those days Israel had no king, so everyone did what was right in their own eyes (v. 6). A young Levite from Bethlehem later comes looking for a place to live, and Micah hires him as his personal priest for an annual wage, food, and clothing, concluding that God is sure to bless him now that he has a Levite serving his shrine (vv. 7-13).
m: Stolen silver confessed, cursed and blessed in the same breath before it is melted into an idol dedicated to the LORD, a private shrine violating nearly every law it touches while its owner believes it pleases God, the book's own thesis stated for the first time, no king in Israel, every man did…

x: The tribe of Dan, still without their full allotted territory, sends out five spies who lodge with Micah and learn from his Levite priest that their journey is favored by the LORD (vv. 1-6); they find the peaceful, undefended city of Laish and report that God has given it into Israel's hand (vv. 7-10). Six hundred armed Danites march north, and along the way the spies lead them to Micah's house, where they steal his idols and persuade his Levite to become priest for an entire tribe instead of one man (vv. 11-20); when Micah pursues them, he is powerless against their numbers and returns home stripped of his gods and his priest (vv. 21-26). The Danites then destroy the unsuspecting city of Laish, rebuild it as Dan, and set up Micah's idol, establishing an idolatrous priesthood that continues there for generations (vv. 27-31).
h: The Danite Spies and Micah's Priest (vv.1-6)
Laish Burned and the Idol Set Up (vv.27-31)
m: Spies sent to find easier prey after Dan failed to conquer the land it was actually allotted, a peaceful, unsuspecting people scouted and reported good because they had no ally near enough to help them, a theft carried out brazenly while six hundred armed men wait at the gate, my gods which I made…

x: A Levite from Ephraim travels to Bethlehem to retrieve his concubine, and after several days of hospitality from her father, the two set out late in the day and are forced to stop for the night at Gibeah in Benjamin rather than a foreign city (vv. 1-15). An old man finally takes them in, but wicked men of the city surround the house demanding to abuse the Levite; when the Levite pushes his concubine out to them instead, they abuse her through the night, and she is found dead or dying at the doorstep in the morning (vv. 16-28). The Levite cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them throughout Israel's tribes to provoke outrage and summon a response to this atrocity, described as unlike anything seen since Israel came out of Egypt (vv. 29-30).
h: Four Days of Delay and the Road North (vv.5-12)
The Dismemberment and Call to Action (vv.29-30)
m: A refrain, there was no king in Israel, opening a chapter deliberately built to echo Sodom, four days of hospitality that delay a departure into exactly the danger it was avoiding, an old man's warning that reveals he already knows what Gibeah is, a demand at the door identical to Sodom's answered…

x: Israel unites as one body at Mizpah after hearing how the Levite's concubine was raped and killed at Gibeah, and the assembly demands that Benjamin hand over the guilty men of Gibeah for justice (vv. 1-13). When Benjamin refuses and instead musters for battle, the tribes inquire of God and attack, but Benjamin's skilled fighters, including left-handed slingers, inflict heavy losses on Israel in the first two days of fighting (vv. 14-25). After weeping, fasting, and seeking the Lord a third time, Israel receives God's promise of victory and sets an ambush against Gibeah (vv. 26-33). The ambush succeeds, the city is set ablaze, and the Benjamite army is routed and nearly annihilated, with only six hundred men escaping to the rock of Rimmon while Israel destroys the rest of Benjamin's cities and people (vv. 34-48).
h: The Demand Refused and the Armies Numbered (vv.12-17)
The Third Day — Victory Through Ambush (vv.26-48)
m: Four hundred thousand men assembled against one tribe rather than against a foreign oppressor, a Levite's account that emphasizes the threat to himself over the crime against her, a lawful demand for the guilty refused by the whole tribe protecting them, two defeats costing forty thousand men…

x: Having nearly destroyed the tribe of Benjamin, Israel weeps at Bethel over their oath never to give their daughters to Benjamin in marriage, now threatening the tribe's extinction (vv. 1-7). Discovering that Jabesh-gilead had failed to join the assembly at Mizpah, they send troops to destroy the city, sparing 400 young virgins to give as wives to the 600 surviving Benjamite men, though this leaves 200 still unmarried (vv. 8-14). To solve the remaining shortfall without technically breaking their oath, the elders instruct the Benjamites to seize wives for themselves from the young women dancing at the yearly feast at Shiloh (vv. 15-23). Benjamin is restored to its territory and the tribes disperse, and the book closes with its defining verdict on the era: there was no king in Israel, and everyone did what was right in their own eyes (vv. 24-25).
h: Israel's Grief and the Oath Problem (vv.1-7)
m: A rash oath at Mizpah discovered to threaten an entire tribe with extinction, grief expressed with no apparent awareness that Israel's own violence caused it, a second oath activated to justify slaughtering Jabesh-gilead for the sake of finding brides, an abduction planned at a legitimate feast…

x: After the deaths of her husband and both sons in Moab, Naomi decides to return to Bethlehem and urges her daughters-in-law, Orpah and Ruth, to go back to their own families. Orpah eventually agrees, but Ruth refuses to leave Naomi, pledging her lifelong loyalty and adopting Naomi's people and God as her own (vv. 16-17). The two women arrive in Bethlehem together, destitute, just as the barley harvest is beginning — setting up the harvest-field encounter with Boaz in chapter 2.
m: A famine that sends a family from the house of bread to the country of Israel's enemy, three burials that empty Naomi of husband and both sons, a blessing offered to daughters-in-law from a woman with nothing left to give, Ruth's vow that moves from geography to God to death itself, and a name…

x: Ruth asks Naomi's permission to glean leftover grain in the fields, and she happens to end up working in a field belonging to Boaz, a wealthy relative of Naomi's late husband Elimelech (vv. 1-3). Boaz notices her, learns of her loyalty to Naomi, and treats her with extraordinary generosity — inviting her to stay in his field, drink from his workers' water, eat at his table, and instructing his young men not to touch her while deliberately leaving extra grain for her to gather (vv. 4-16). Ruth returns home with an abundant amount of barley, and when Naomi learns whose field it was, she recognizes God's continuing kindness and identifies Boaz as one of their family redeemers (vv. 17-23).
m: Gleaning laws that provide dignity through labor rather than charity, a chance encounter the narrator names as providence, Boaz's instructions that each exceed what the law required, an ephah of barley too large to be accidental, and Naomi's bitterness giving way the moment she hears the word…

x: Naomi devises a plan to secure Ruth's future, instructing her to wash, perfume herself, dress well, and go to the threshing floor after Boaz has eaten and lain down for the night (vv. 1-5). Ruth uncovers his feet and lies down, and when Boaz wakes startled at midnight, she asks him to spread his garment over her as her kinsman-redeemer (vv. 6-9). Boaz responds with honor, blessing her for choosing him over younger men and affirming her reputation as a worthy woman, but he discloses that a nearer kinsman has first right to redeem the family (vv. 10-13). He sends her home before daylight with six measures of barley as a pledge of his intent, and Naomi assures Ruth that Boaz will settle the matter that very day (vv. 14-18).
m: A threshing floor plan that is bold without being improper, feet uncovered at midnight and a startled question in the dark, kindness named greater the second time than the first, a nearer kinsman acknowledged before any promise is made, and six measures of barley sent to Naomi by name

x: Boaz goes to the city gate and, before ten elders as witnesses, offers the nearer kinsman the chance to redeem Elimelech's land; the man agrees until Boaz explains that redeeming the land also means marrying Ruth to preserve her dead husband's name, at which point he declines and transfers his right by removing his sandal (vv. 1-8). Boaz then publicly declares that he has acquired the land and taken Ruth as his wife, and the elders and people bless the union, comparing Ruth to Rachel and Leah (vv. 9-12). The LORD gives Ruth conception, and she bears a son, Obed, whom the women of Bethlehem celebrate as a restorer of Naomi's life and provider for her old age (vv. 13-17). The chapter closes with a genealogy tracing ten generations from Perez through Boaz and Obed to Jesse and David, placing this Moabite widow in the ancestral line of Israel's greatest king (vv. 18-22).
h: Birth of Obed and Restoration of Naomi (vv.13-17)
m: A legal transaction conducted in public at the gate with ten witnesses, land offered before the obligation that comes with it is disclosed, a nearer kinsman who saves his own name by losing it from the record, a sandal ceremony the narrator has to explain to his own readers, and a genealogy that…

x: Elkanah, an Ephraimite with two wives, favors the childless Hannah even as her rival Peninnah torments her year after year on their family's trips to Shiloh (vv. 1-7). Deeply distressed, Hannah prays silently at the tabernacle and vows that if the LORD gives her a son she will dedicate him to God for life, with no razor ever touching his head (vv. 10-11). Eli the priest first mistakes her moving lips for drunkenness, then blesses her once she explains her grief (vv. 12-17). The LORD remembers Hannah, and she conceives and names her son Samuel (vv. 19-20). After he is weaned, she brings the boy to Eli and leaves him at Shiloh to serve the LORD for as long as he lives, fulfilling her vow (vv. 24-28).
m: Renewal beginning not with a warrior or a political revolution but with a barren woman's prayer, the LORD stated twice to have shut up her womb rather than left it to chance, lips moving with no voice heard mistaken by the priest for drunkenness, a name explained by a wordplay, because I have asked…

x: Hannah offers a prayer of praise celebrating the LORD who humbles the proud and exalts the lowly, promising that God will one day give strength to His king and anointed (vv. 1-10). Meanwhile Eli's sons Hophni and Phinehas, serving as priests, abuse their office by seizing meat meant for sacrifice and treating the LORD's offerings with contempt (vv. 12-17). Samuel, by contrast, grows up ministering faithfully before the LORD, wearing a linen ephod, while Hannah visits yearly bringing him a small robe (vv. 18-19). Eli rebukes his sons but they ignore him, so a man of God warns Eli that his sons will die on the same day and his priestly line will lose its honor, while the LORD will raise up a faithful priest in their place (vv. 27-35).
m: A song that moves from one woman's relief to a cosmic declaration about how God reverses every human condition, sons called worthless men who knew not the LORD despite serving as priests in His own house, meat stolen from sacrifices before the fat could even be burned to God, a rebuke that is…

x: The LORD calls to young Samuel three times in the night as he lies near the ark, and each time Samuel runs to Eli, thinking the old priest had summoned him (vv. 4-8). Eli finally realizes God is speaking and instructs Samuel to answer, "Speak, LORD, for your servant is listening" (v. 9). The LORD then reveals that He is about to judge Eli's house forever, because Eli knew of his sons' sin and failed to restrain them (vv. 11-14). Though afraid, Samuel reports the full message to Eli the next morning, and Eli accepts it as the LORD's will (vv. 15-18). As Samuel grows, the LORD continues to speak through him, and all Israel comes to recognize him as a true prophet (vv. 19-21).
h: The Word of the LORD Was Rare (vv.1-3)
m: A rare and precious word of the LORD opening the chapter as a statement of spiritual famine rather than mere quiet, three calls mistaken for Eli before a fourth is finally recognized as God's own voice, speak, LORD, for thy servant heareth answered by a message that will make both ears of anyone…

x: Israel suffers an initial defeat against the Philistines at Aphek, losing about four thousand men, so the elders send for the ark of the covenant from Shiloh, hoping it will guarantee victory (vv. 1-4). Its arrival in camp draws a great shout from Israel and terrifies the Philistines, who nonetheless rally and fight hard, routing Israel a second time with thirty thousand casualties, and capturing the ark while killing Eli's sons Hophni and Phinehas (vv. 5-11). A messenger runs to Shiloh and reports the disaster to Eli, who falls backward from his seat and dies upon hearing the ark is taken (vv. 12-18). Phinehas's wife, going into labor at the news, names her newborn son Ichabod, declaring that Israel's glory has departed because the ark of God is gone (vv. 19-22).
m: An ark fetched into battle as equipment rather than sought after in repentance, Philistines more theologically alert than Israel in recognizing these are the Gods that smote the Egyptians, four pieces of news delivered in ascending severity with only the last one killing Eli, a name given at birth…

x: After capturing the ark at Aphek, the Philistines carry it to Ashdod and set it in the temple of their god Dagon, but the next morning they find the idol fallen face down before it (vv. 1-3). They set Dagon upright again, yet the following morning he is found fallen once more, this time with his head and hands broken off on the threshold (v. 4). The LORD then strikes the people of Ashdod with tumors, prompting them to move the ark to Gath, where the same affliction strikes both small and great, and then to Ekron, whose people cry out in terror as death spreads through the city (vv. 6-12). The episode shows that the God of Israel remains sovereign even over pagan idols and enemy territory.
m: An idol found fallen on its face before the ark and set back up only to fall again, this time dismembered at the threshold, a war trophy that turns out to defend itself without any human army, the hand of the LORD named as the keyword of a plague that moves city to city with the ark itself, Ashdod…

x: After seven months the Philistines consult their priests, who advise sending the ark back with a guilt offering of five golden tumors and five golden mice, and testing whether cows pulling the cart go straight to Israel without human guidance (vv. 1-9). The cows head directly to Beth-shemesh, lowing as they go, confirming that Israel's God, not chance, caused their affliction (vv. 10-12). The Israelites there rejoice, sacrifice the cows as a burnt offering, and set the ark on a great stone alongside the gold objects (vv. 13-15). But when some men of Beth-shemesh look inside the ark, the LORD strikes seventy of them dead, teaching the people to fear His holiness (v. 19). Shaken, they send word to Kiriath-jearim asking its residents to come take the ark away (vv. 20-21).
h: The Philistines' Plan to Return the Ark (vv.1-9)
Five Golden Emerods, and the Men Struck (vv.17-21)
m: Philistine priests knowing the Exodus story well enough to warn their own people against hardening their hearts like Pharaoh, cows overriding every natural instinct toward their calves to walk straight toward Israel, a town that rejoices at the ark's arrival in one verse and asks to be rid of it…

x: The ark is brought to Kiriath-jearim and remains there twenty years while Israel mourns after the LORD (vv. 1-2). Samuel calls the nation to repent, telling them to put away their foreign gods and serve the LORD alone, and the people obey, gathering at Mizpah to fast and confess their sin (vv. 3-6). When the Philistines advance to attack the assembled Israelites, Samuel offers a sacrifice and cries out to the LORD, who answers with thunder that throws the Philistine army into confusion, letting Israel pursue and defeat them (vv. 7-11). Samuel then sets up a memorial stone called Ebenezer, declaring that the LORD has helped Israel thus far (v. 12), and goes on to judge Israel faithfully for the rest of his life, traveling a circuit between Bethel, Gilgal, Mizpah, and his home in Ramah (vv. 15-17).
h: Twenty Years, and the Gathering at Mizpeh (vv.1-9)
m: Twenty years summarized as a nation lamenting after the LORD before any revival actually begins, a condition set rather than a rally led, if ye do return unto the LORD with all your hearts, thunder from heaven doing the fighting while Israel only pursues what is already routed, a memorial stone…

x: When Samuel grows old, he appoints his sons Joel and Abijah as judges, but they take bribes and pervert justice, prompting the elders of Israel to come to Ramah and demand a king like the other nations (vv. 1-5). Samuel is displeased, but the LORD tells him the people are not rejecting Samuel but rejecting God's own kingship over them, and instructs him to grant their request after warning them of its cost (vv. 6-9). Samuel details how a king will conscript their sons for war and labor, take their daughters for his household, seize their best fields, and take a tenth of their crops and flocks, reducing them to servitude (vv. 11-17). Despite the warning, the people insist on having a king to fight their battles like the other nations, so the LORD tells Samuel to grant their request (vv. 19-22).
h: God's Response: Rejection of Divine Kingship (vv.6-9)
m: Samuel's own sons repeating Eli's failure by turning aside after dishonest gain, a demand for a king named by God as rejection of Himself rather than of Samuel, a warning built entirely on the repeated word take, sons, daughters, fields, a tenth of everything, until you yourselves are servants, a…

x: Kish of Benjamin sends his son Saul, a strikingly tall and handsome young man, to search for lost donkeys, and after searching several regions without success Saul's servant suggests they consult a local seer for guidance (vv. 1-6). Unknown to Saul, the LORD had told Samuel the day before that he would send a Benjamite whom Samuel was to anoint as ruler over Israel to save the people from the Philistines (vv. 15-16). When Samuel meets Saul at the city gate, the LORD confirms this is the man, and Samuel invites him to a feast, seats him in the place of honor, and reassures him that the donkeys are found and that Israel's desire rests on him (vv. 17-20). Saul, surprised by this attention given his small tribe, stays the night and is led out by Samuel the next morning to receive a private word from God (vv. 21-27).
m: A search for lost donkeys turning out to be God's chosen route to a royal appointment, Saul described as taller than anyone else in Israel, the kind of king appearance alone would choose, girls at a well giving the future king his walking directions without knowing who he is, a word, captain, used…

x: Samuel anoints Saul with oil and kisses him, declaring that the LORD has appointed him ruler over Israel, then gives him three confirming signs he will encounter on his way home, including a company of prophets whose Spirit will come upon him and change him into another man (vv. 1-8). Each sign happens exactly as foretold, and when Saul meets the prophets he too begins to prophesy, so astonishing those who know him that it becomes a proverb, "Is Saul also among the prophets?" (vv. 9-12). Samuel then summons Israel to Mizpah, reminds them they have rejected God by demanding a king, and casts lots that select Saul, who is found hiding among the baggage out of reticence (vv. 17-23). Presented before the people, Saul is hailed as king, though some worthless men despise him and withhold their loyalty (vv. 24-27).
m: Oil poured and a kiss given as the formal acts of an anointing kept private before it is ever made public, three confirming signs all fulfilled the same day exactly as Samuel described them, a proverb born from bewilderment, is Saul also among the prophets, rather than from reverence, a king found…

x: Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabesh-gilead and demands the right eye of every man as a condition of surrender, so the city's elders beg for seven days to seek help from Israel (vv. 1-3). When messengers reach Saul and the people weep, the Spirit of God comes upon him in anger, and he cuts oxen into pieces and sends them throughout Israel, warning that anyone who fails to follow him and Samuel will suffer the same fate (vv. 5-7). Saul musters a massive army, and the next morning his forces strike the Ammonite camp and scatter them so thoroughly that no two remain together (vv. 8-11). When the people want to execute those who had opposed Saul's kingship, Saul refuses, crediting the LORD's salvation, and the nation goes to Gilgal to confirm him as king with rejoicing (vv. 12-15).
h: Not a Man Shall Be Put to Death (vv.12-15)
m: A demand to gouge out every right eye designed as a calculated insult to the whole nation, seven days granted by an enemy confident enough in Israel's helplessness to allow the delay, oxen cut in pieces and sent throughout Israel echoing the Levite's dismembered concubine, three companies attacking…

x: Samuel reminds Israel that he has given them the king they demanded, and calls on them and the LORD's anointed to testify that he has never defrauded, oppressed, or taken a bribe from anyone (vv. 1-5). He recounts the LORD's righteous acts, from bringing their fathers out of Egypt to raising up judges whenever Israel cried out after falling into idolatry (vv. 6-11). He rebukes them for demanding a king when Nahash threatened them, even though the LORD was already their king, but promises that both king and people can still prosper if they fear and obey the LORD (vv. 12-15). To prove his point, Samuel calls down thunder and rain during the dry wheat harvest, terrifying the people into confessing that asking for a king added to their sins (vv. 16-19). Samuel nonetheless reassures them that the LORD will not abandon His people if they serve Him faithfully, warning that both they and their…
h: Fear Not, Only Serve the LORD (vv.20-25)
m: A public challenge to name any ox or ass Samuel ever took, answered by the people's unanimous acquittal, deliverers named one after another to prove God provided leaders long before any king was demanded, the demand for a king traced to a specific crisis rather than to genuine necessity, thunder…

x: Two years into Saul's reign, his son Jonathan strikes a Philistine garrison at Geba, provoking the Philistines to muster a vast army at Michmash and driving frightened Israelites into hiding (vv. 1-6). Saul waits at Gilgal for the seven days Samuel had appointed, but when Samuel does not arrive and the people begin to scatter, Saul grows impatient and offers the burnt offering himself (vv. 8-9). Samuel arrives just afterward and rebukes Saul for not keeping the LORD's command, declaring that his kingdom will not endure and that the LORD has already sought a man after His own heart to replace him (vv. 13-14). Saul is left with only about six hundred men, and the chapter closes by noting that the Philistines had stripped Israel of blacksmiths, leaving nearly the whole army without swords or spears (vv. 19-22).
h: The Garrison Smitten and the People Hiding (vv.1-7)
m: Credit for Jonathan's attack claimed by Saul in the same breath as the trumpet blast, a nation dissolving into caves and pits rather than a battle actually being fought, seven days waited to the letter before a sacrifice offered one day too soon, thou hast done foolishly answered not with removal…

x: Without telling his father, Jonathan and his armor-bearer climb toward a Philistine outpost, trusting that the LORD can save by many or by few, and take it as a sign that God has given the Philistines into their hand when the garrison invites them up (vv. 6-12). The two strike down about twenty men, sending trembling and confusion through the Philistine camp that Saul's watchmen notice from a distance (vv. 13-16). Saul rallies his forces, and the LORD grants a great deliverance as the Philistines panic and Hebrews who had defected rejoin Israel in the pursuit (vv. 20-23). Saul's rash oath forbidding anyone to eat until evening weakens his own troops and nearly costs Jonathan his life when he unknowingly tastes honey, but the people intervene to rescue him (vv. 24-45). The chapter closes summarizing Saul's family and his ongoing wars against Israel's surrounding enemies (vv. 47-52).
m: A declaration of faith made without presuming on the outcome, there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few, an attack by two men producing an earthquake and an army turning its swords on itself, an oath interrupting the very pursuit it was meant to secure, honey untouched on the…

x: Samuel relays the LORD's command that Saul completely destroy the Amalekites, sparing nothing, in judgment for how they had opposed Israel after the exodus (vv. 1-3). Saul defeats them but spares King Agag along with the best sheep and cattle, destroying only what was worthless, which prompts the LORD to tell Samuel that He regrets making Saul king (vv. 8-11). When Samuel confronts him, Saul insists he obeyed, blaming the people for keeping the livestock to sacrifice, but Samuel declares that obedience is better than sacrifice and that Saul's rejection of the LORD's word means the LORD has rejected him as king (vv. 20-23). Saul confesses his sin and begs forgiveness, but Samuel tells him the kingdom has already been torn from him and given to a better neighbor, then personally executes Agag before the LORD (vv. 24-33). Samuel never sees Saul again, though he grieves for him, and the…
h: Saul's Failed Repentance and the Kingdom Torn Away (vv.24-35)
m: A command given in full and obeyed in part, the bleating that gave it away, obedience weighed against sacrifice, a robe torn as a sign, and a confession more concerned with honor than with restoration

x: The LORD tells Samuel to stop mourning for Saul and sends him to Bethlehem to anoint a new king from among the sons of Jesse, using a sacrifice as cover so Saul will not hear of it (vv. 1-5). As Jesse's sons pass before him, Samuel is drawn to Eliab's appearance, but the LORD corrects him: God does not look at outward appearance as man does, but looks at the heart (vv. 6-7). Seven sons are rejected before Jesse sends for the youngest, David, who is out tending sheep; when he arrives, the LORD tells Samuel this is the one, and Samuel anoints him in the presence of his brothers as the Spirit of the LORD comes upon him from that day forward (vv. 8-13). Meanwhile the Spirit departs from Saul and an evil spirit troubles him instead, so his servants bring in David - described as skilled, brave, and favored by the LORD - to soothe Saul by playing the harp, and David becomes his armor-bearer…
m: Grief rebuked as something that must not paralyze obedience any longer, man looking on the outward appearance while the LORD looks on the heart stated as the chapter's own thesis, seven older sons passed over before the youngest is even sent for from the sheep, a father who did not think to bring…

x: The Philistines and Israel face off across the valley of Elah, and the Philistine champion Goliath - over nine feet tall and heavily armored - comes out morning and evening for forty days daring Israel to send a man to fight him, leaving Saul and the army terrified (vv. 1-11, 16). David, the youngest of Jesse's sons, is sent to the camp with food for his brothers and hears Goliath's taunts; indignant that the giant would defy the armies of the living God, he asks what reward awaits the man who kills him, drawing a rebuke from his brother Eliab (vv. 12-30). Brought before Saul, David volunteers to fight, citing how the LORD delivered him from a lion and a bear while shepherding, and Saul reluctantly agrees, though David removes Saul's armor as untested and instead takes his staff, sling, and five stones (vv. 31-40). Facing Goliath's scorn and curses, David declares he comes in the name…
m: Forty days of a champion's defiance met by silence from every man in Saul's army including the king who stands head and shoulders above them all, an errand to deliver provisions placing David at the battlefield by nothing more than an ordinary chore, a reward asked about only after the theological…

x: After David's victory, Jonathan's soul is knit to David's in deep friendship, and the two make a covenant, with Jonathan giving David his robe, armor, sword, and bow (vv. 1-4). David serves successfully under Saul, but when the women celebrate his return singing that Saul has slain his thousands and David his ten thousands, Saul grows jealous and suspicious that only the kingdom remains for David to gain (vv. 5-9). The next day, tormented by an evil spirit, Saul twice hurls a javelin at David while he plays the harp, and afterward, fearing David because the LORD is with him, removes him to command a thousand men, where David continues to succeed and grow in the people's love (vv. 10-16). Saul then offers his daughter Merab to David as a trap meant to expose him to the Philistines, but she is given to another man instead; when Michal, Saul's other daughter, is found to love David, Saul…
h: David's Success and the Women's Song (vv.5-9)
m: A crown prince's soul knit to David's and royal robe and armor handed over as though the throne itself is being surrendered, a celebration song turned into a threat the moment Saul starts counting thousands against ten thousands, a spear hurled twice at a man playing the harp for the very king who…

x: Saul orders Jonathan and his servants to kill David, but Jonathan intervenes, persuading his father that David is innocent and has served him well, so Saul swears David will not be put to death and David returns to court (vv. 1-7). After David defeats the Philistines again, an evil spirit comes upon Saul and he hurls his javelin at David while he plays the harp, but David escapes and flees that night (vv. 8-10). Saul sends men to watch David's house and kill him in the morning, but his wife Michal lets him down through a window and places an idol in the bed with goat's hair to buy him time, then tells Saul David threatened her when he demands to know why she let his enemy escape (vv. 11-17). David flees to Samuel at Ramah, and when Saul's messengers arrive to seize him, the Spirit of God comes upon them and they prophesy instead; this happens with two more waves of messengers, and…
m: An oath sworn in the LORD's name broken within verses of being made, the same spear-and-harp scene repeated until David finally does not return to it, an idol placed in a bed as a decoy revealing spiritual compromise even inside David's own household, three companies of messengers overcome by the…

x: David flees to Jonathan asking what he has done to deserve Saul's murderous intent, and Jonathan doubts it, so the two devise a plan: David will hide during the New Moon feast while Jonathan gauges his father's mood and signals the verdict through arrows shot near a boy sent to retrieve them (vv. 1-23). Jonathan and David also reaffirm their covenant, with Jonathan asking David to show unfailing kindness to his family in the future (vv. 14-17, 42). At the feast, Saul notices David's empty seat and, on hearing Jonathan's excuse that David went to a family sacrifice in Bethlehem, erupts in fury, cursing Jonathan and declaring David must die because he threatens Jonathan's claim to the throne; when Jonathan objects, Saul hurls his javelin at him too (vv. 24-34). The next morning Jonathan carries out the arrow signal, confirming to David that he must flee, and the two part in grief, weeping…
m: Three anguished questions, what have I done, what is mine iniquity, what is my sin, opening a chapter neither man can yet fully believe needs asking, a New Moon feast turned into a deliberate test of a father's intentions, a prince who already knows David will be king and asks only that his own…

x: Fleeing alone, David arrives at Nob and asks the priest Ahimelech for food, claiming to be on a secret mission for Saul; since no ordinary bread is available, Ahimelech gives him the consecrated showbread after confirming the men have kept themselves ritually pure (vv. 1-6). Doeg the Edomite, one of Saul's servants, is present and witnesses the exchange (v. 7). David also asks for a weapon and is given the sword of Goliath, which had been kept behind the ephod (vv. 8-9). Fleeing further to Gath, David grows afraid when Achish's servants recognize him as the man celebrated for defeating tens of thousands of Philistines, so he pretends to be insane, scratching at the gate and drooling on his beard, until Achish dismisses him as a madman unworthy of his attention (vv. 10-15).
m: A lie told to a trembling priest to obtain bread reserved only for those who serve at the altar, Doeg the Edomite noted in a single ominous verse that plants a detail for later, Goliath's own sword taken from behind the ephod and carried by the very man who once used a sling against it, madness…

x: David escapes to the cave of Adullam, where his family joins him along with about four hundred men who are in distress, in debt, or discontented, and he becomes their leader (vv. 1-2). He arranges for his parents' safety with the king of Moab, then, at the prophet Gad's instruction, moves into the land of Judah (vv. 3-5). Saul, sitting with his spear among his servants, laments that no one has warned him of David's movements, and Doeg the Edomite volunteers that Ahimelech the priest gave David food, Goliath's sword, and a word from the LORD at Nob (vv. 6-10). Saul summons Ahimelech, rejects his defense that David was simply his trusted, loyal son-in-law, and orders his guards to kill the priests; when they refuse, Doeg himself kills eighty-five priests and puts the entire city of Nob to the sword, including women, children, and livestock (vv. 11-19). Only Ahimelech's son Abiathar…
m: Four hundred men in distress, in debt and discontented gathering to a rejected king in a cave rather than to any court, Saul's paranoia appealing to tribal loyalty before it ever appeals to evidence, a priest's entirely reasonable defense ignored the moment it is given, royal guards refusing to…

x: When David hears that the Philistines are raiding Keilah, he inquires of the LORD twice and, despite his men's fear, is told to attack, and he defeats the Philistines and rescues the town, with Abiathar joining him there carrying an ephod (vv. 1-6). Saul plans to besiege David in Keilah, but David inquires of the LORD through the ephod and learns that the men of Keilah would hand him over, so he and his roughly six hundred men leave before Saul arrives (vv. 7-13). David hides in the wilderness of Ziph, where Saul searches for him daily without success; Jonathan visits him there, encourages him in God, and affirms that David will be king while Jonathan serves under him, and the two renew their covenant (vv. 14-18). The Ziphites betray David's location to Saul, who nearly traps David and his men on a mountain in Maon, but a message about a Philistine invasion forces Saul to break off the…
m: A fugitive doing the king's actual job, saving a city from Philistine raiders while the king hunts him instead, David inquiring of the LORD before every move in deliberate contrast to Saul's paranoid impulse, a city just rescued willing to hand its rescuer over the moment Saul asks, Jonathan's last…

x: Saul takes three thousand men to hunt David near En-gedi and, without knowing it, enters the very cave where David and his men are hiding; David's men urge him to kill Saul as an act of the LORD's providence, but David instead only cuts off a corner of Saul's robe and immediately feels convicted for even that, refusing to harm the LORD's anointed (vv. 1-7). After Saul leaves the cave, David calls out and bows before him, holding up the piece of robe as proof that he had the chance to kill him but spared his life, insisting he means Saul no harm and appealing to the LORD to judge between them (vv. 8-15). Saul weeps, admits David is more righteous than he is, and acknowledges that David will indeed become king, asking him to swear not to wipe out his descendants; David swears the oath, and the two part ways (vv. 16-22).
m: A king entering a cave to relieve himself with no idea his hunted enemy is hiding in its recesses, a conscience troubled even by cutting a robe's corner when killing was the option every man around him urged, judgment deliberately left to the LORD rather than taken by David's own hand, Saul's own…

x: Samuel dies and is mourned by all Israel, and David moves into the wilderness of Paran (v. 1). David sends men to greet the wealthy but surly Nabal during sheep-shearing, politely asking for provisions in return for having protected his shepherds, but Nabal insults David and refuses, prompting David to arm four hundred men to take revenge (vv. 2-13, 21-22). A servant warns Nabal's wife Abigail, a wise and beautiful woman, and she quickly gathers a generous supply of food and rides out to intercept David without telling her husband (vv. 14-20). Abigail falls before David, takes the blame on herself, and pleads with him not to shed blood or take vengeance into his own hands, reminding him the LORD will make him a lasting house and future king; David blesses her for restraining him and accepts her gift (vv. 23-35). When Abigail tells the now-sober Nabal what happened the next morning, his…
m: Samuel's death marking the end of an era in one brief, almost passing notice, a wealthy fool's contempt echoing Saul's own dismissive language toward the son of Jesse, Abigail's intervention arriving as the thing that restrains David from bloodguilt where his own conscience had restrained him with…

x: The Ziphites again betray David's location to Saul, who marches into the wilderness of Ziph with three thousand men to hunt him down (vv. 1-4). David sneaks into Saul's camp at night with Abishai and finds Saul and his army in a supernaturally deep sleep, spear stuck in the ground beside him (vv. 5-7). Abishai urges David to let him kill Saul with a single spear thrust, but David refuses to harm the LORD's anointed, trusting God to deal with Saul in his own time (vv. 8-11). David takes only the spear and water jug as proof, then calls out from a distant hilltop, rebuking Abner for failing to protect the king (vv. 12-16). Saul again confesses his sin, but David, having learned from experience, simply goes on his way rather than trusting Saul's unstable repentance (vv. 17-25).
m: A second betrayal by the Ziphites leading to a second chance David again refuses, a deep sleep sent by God over an entire army rather than mere carelessness, Abishai's offer to end it with one spear-thrust turned down on the same principle as the cave, Saul's missing spear and water jug serving as…

x: Convinced that Saul will eventually kill him, David despairs of finding safety in Israel and takes his six hundred men to live among the Philistines under King Achish of Gath (vv. 1-4). Achish grants David the town of Ziklag, which becomes his base for sixteen months (vv. 5-7). From there David raids longtime enemy peoples, destroying every inhabitant so no survivor can report the truth to Achish (vv. 8-9), and deceives Achish into believing he has been raiding Judah itself, making the Philistine king trust him as a loyal, permanent servant (vv. 10-12) — a risky deception that keeps David alive while he waits for God's timing to bring him to the throne.
m: A statement of despair rather than faith, I shall now perish one day by the hand of Saul, opening a chapter where David's plan actually works precisely because it is human rather than divine, Ziklag requested specifically to avoid the constant surveillance of living in Gath's royal city, raids…

x: As the Philistines mass for battle, King Achish orders David and his men to fight alongside him, forcing David into an uncomfortable position against his own people (vv. 1-2). With Samuel now dead, Saul finds himself terrified at the Philistine army and unable to get any answer from God through dreams, priests, or prophets (vv. 3-6). In desperation, Saul disguises himself and seeks out a medium at Endor, despite having outlawed such practices himself (vv. 7-10). The medium conjures Samuel's spirit, who rebukes Saul and delivers a crushing message: because of Saul's disobedience, the kingdom has been given to David, and tomorrow Saul and his sons will die in battle (vv. 11-19). Saul collapses in terror and, urged by the woman and his servants, finally eats before facing his last night (vv. 20-25).
m: God's silence answering Saul through no channel at all, dreams, Urim or prophets, after years of Saul ignoring every channel God actually used, a ban on mediums broken by the very king who once enforced it, a disguise and a night journey concealing a king from his own kingdom rather than from an…

x: As the Philistine armies gather at Aphek for war against Israel, David marches with Achish's forces in the rear guard (vv. 1-2). The Philistine commanders object loudly, refusing to let a Hebrew, especially David, celebrated in song for killing his ten thousands, fight alongside them for fear he might turn against them in battle (vv. 3-5). Achish reluctantly agrees, telling David he personally trusts him but must send him back to avoid alienating the other commanders (vv. 6-7). David protests but is sent back to Ziklag while the Philistines continue on to Jezreel (vv. 8-11) — God providentially sparing David from choosing between his Philistine hosts and his own people.
m: A dilemma David's own deception created resolved by Philistine commanders rather than by any plan of his own, a pagan king swearing by the LORD to testify that David has been upright, the women's song of thousands and ten thousands remembered at exactly the moment it becomes dangerous rather than…

x: David and his men return to Ziklag to find it burned and their wives and children carried off by Amalekite raiders, leaving the men so grieved that they speak of stoning David, though he strengthens himself in the Lord his God (vv. 1-6). He inquires of the Lord through the priest Abiathar and is told to pursue, with the promise of a certain rescue (vv. 7-8). Of the six hundred men who set out, two hundred too exhausted to cross the brook Besor stay behind while David presses on with the rest (vv. 9-10). Along the way they find an abandoned Egyptian servant of an Amalekite, and after feeding him he guides them to the raiding party (vv. 11-15). David attacks and routs the Amalekites, recovering his wives, the other captives, and all the plunder, with nothing missing (vv. 16-20). When some of his men object to sharing the spoil with the two hundred who stayed behind, David overrules them…
m: A homecoming to a burned city and captured families discovered only after three days of marching, David encouraging himself in the LORD his God at the exact moment his own men speak of stoning him, an abandoned Egyptian slave, left to die by his own master, becoming the guide who leads David…

x: The Philistines overwhelm Israel's army on Mount Gilboa, and as the men of Israel flee, Saul's sons, including Jonathan, are killed in the fighting (vv. 1-2). Badly wounded by archers, Saul asks his armor-bearer to kill him rather than let him fall into enemy hands, but the armor-bearer refuses out of fear, so Saul falls on his own sword; his armor-bearer then does the same (vv. 3-6). Nearby towns are abandoned as the Philistines advance, and the next day they find Saul's body, cut off his head, display his armor in the temple of Ashtaroth, and fasten his body to the wall of Beth-shan (vv. 7-10). Hearing of this disgrace, the valiant men of Jabesh-gilead travel all night to retrieve the bodies, burn them, and bury the bones with a seven-day fast, giving their fallen king an honorable end (vv. 11-13).
m: A battle whose outcome Samuel had already named years before it is fought, Jonathan dying alongside a father whose rebellion was never his own, a king asking his armor-bearer to finish what the archers could not before falling on his own sword, a head cut off and armor displayed in a temple exactly…

x: An Amalekite messenger arrives at David's camp in Ziklag and reports that Saul and Jonathan died at Gilboa, falsely claiming he killed Saul himself at the king's request (vv. 1-10). David and his men mourn and fast, and David orders the Amalekite executed for daring to kill God's chosen king (vv. 11-16). David then composes a lament for Saul and Jonathan and calls for it to be taught throughout Judah (vv. 17-18), praising their strength and unity in life and death and grieving especially the depth of his friendship with Jonathan (vv. 19-27).
m: An Amalekite's claim to have killed Saul contradicting the account already given in the previous book, David unable to fathom how anyone could stretch out a hand against the LORD's anointed, mourning that covers Saul, Jonathan, the people of the LORD and the house of Israel rather than only a…

x: David inquires of the LORD and moves to Hebron, where the men of Judah anoint him king (vv. 1-4). Meanwhile Abner, Saul's army commander, makes Saul's son Ish-bosheth king over the rest of Israel at Mahanaim (vv. 8-10), setting the two houses on a collision course. War breaks out; a contest of twelve young men from each side at Gibeon ends in mutual slaughter, and Abner's forces are routed by Joab's men (vv. 12-17). Asahel, Joab's younger brother, pursues Abner in the retreat and is killed by him despite repeated warnings to turn aside, planting a blood feud that resurfaces later (vv. 18-23).
m: A kingship begun by inquiry, shall I go up, rather than by seizure, a rival throne set up at Mahanaim for a puppet king who lasts two years against David's seven and a half, twelve champions from each side dying together in a combat meant to settle nothing and settling nothing, Abner's warnings to…

x: As the war between the two houses drags on, David grows steadily stronger while Saul's house weakens (v. 1). Abner, angered by Ish-bosheth's accusation involving Saul's concubine Rizpah, opens negotiations to bring all Israel over to David, who agrees on the condition that his wife Michal be restored to him first (vv. 12-16). Abner meets with David in peace and departs safely, but Joab, without David's knowledge, lures him aside at the gate and kills him in revenge for his brother Asahel (vv. 26-27). David publicly curses the act, mourns Abner with a lament, and refuses to eat until sundown, convincing the people he had no part in the murder (vv. 31-37).
m: A list of sons at Hebron that reads as a genealogy and a foreshadowing of every tragedy still to come, Abner's rage revealing he has always known God's sworn purpose to set David's throne over all Israel, a defection born of anger rather than conviction the moment Abner is accused over a concubine…
