x: With Abner dead, Ish-bosheth loses heart and all Israel is troubled (v. 1). Two of his own raiding captains, Baanah and Rechab, sneak into his house at midday, kill him as he rests, and carry his head to David at Hebron expecting a reward (vv. 5-8). David reminds them how he had executed the Amalekite for merely claiming to kill Saul, then orders them executed as well, their hands and feet cut off and bodies hung by the pool at Hebron, while Ish-bosheth's head is buried in Abner's tomb (vv. 9-12). The chapter also recalls how Jonathan's son Mephibosheth was crippled as a child when his nurse fled with him after news of Saul and Jonathan's deaths (v. 4).
m: Hands growing feeble the moment the one man propping up a puppet kingdom is gone, two captains sneaking in during the heat of the day pretending to fetch wheat before murdering a king in his own bed, God's name invoked to frame an assassination as justice rather than crime, David tracing the same…

x: The elders of Israel come to David at Hebron, recall his past leadership of Israel, and anoint him king over the whole nation at age thirty (vv. 1-5). David leads his men against the Jebusite stronghold of Jerusalem, captures it, and makes it his capital, known afterward as the city of David (vv. 6-9). Hiram of Tyre sends cedar, carpenters, and masons to build David a palace, and David recognizes that the LORD has established his kingdom for the sake of His people Israel (vv. 11-12). When the Philistines hear David has become king, they attack twice; both times David inquires of the LORD before responding and defeats them decisively (vv. 17-25).
m: A threefold argument, kinship, proven leadership, divine appointment, made before David is anointed a third time over the whole nation, a taunt about the blind and the lame answered by a water shaft climbed to take a supposedly impregnable city, a name, Zion, replacing Jebus as David makes the city…

x: David gathers thirty thousand men to bring the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim toward Jerusalem, but when the cart shakes, Uzzah reaches out to steady it and is struck dead, leaving David angry and afraid to move the ark further (vv. 6-9). He leaves it at the house of Obed-edom for three months, and when Obed-edom is blessed instead of harmed, David resumes the procession, this time with sacrifices offered as the ark moves (vv. 12-13). David dances before the LORD with all his might as the ark enters Jerusalem, and his wife Michal watches from a window and despises him for it in her heart, leading to her being childless for the rest of her life (vv. 14-16, 20-23).
m: A new cart chosen instead of the poles and Levite shoulders God had actually commanded, Uzzah struck dead for steadying what he was never meant to touch, three months of anger and fear before David tries again, this time correctly, dancing before the LORD with all his might stripped of royal robes…

x: David, now settled in his palace, tells the prophet Nathan he wants to build a house for the ark, and Nathan initially encourages him (vv. 1-3). That night the LORD tells Nathan that David will not build God a house; instead God will build David a house, raising up his offspring after him and establishing his throne forever, with that offspring building the temple (vv. 5-16). David responds with a prayer of humble gratitude, marveling that God would speak of his house so far into the future, and asks God to keep His promise and let His name be magnified forever (vv. 18-29).
h: David's Desire to Build a Temple (vv.1-3)
m: A king at rest noticing the contrast between his own cedar house and the curtains the ark still dwells within, Nathan's initial approval overturned that same night by a message he never expected to carry, a wordplay on house running through the whole chapter, David wanting to build God one and God…

x: David defeats and subdues the Philistines, then conquers Moab, measuring out captives with a cord for execution or survival (vv. 1-2). He strikes down Hadadezer of Zobah and the Arameans who come to Hadadezer's aid, placing garrisons in Damascus and dedicating the silver, gold, and bronze he takes to the LORD (vv. 3-12). He also defeats the Edomites in the Valley of Salt and stations garrisons throughout Edom (vv. 13-14). The chapter closes by noting that the LORD gave David victory everywhere he went, listing his chief officials, and summarizing that David administered justice and righteousness to all his people (vv. 15-18).
m: A refrain repeated twice, the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went, framing every conquest in the chapter, Moab's prisoners measured by a line with two-thirds executed for reasons the text never fully explains, chariot horses hamstrung rather than multiplied in deliberate restraint of…

x: David asks whether anyone remains of Saul's house so he can show kindness for Jonathan's sake, and learns through Saul's former servant Ziba of Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son, who is lame in both feet (vv. 1-4). David summons Mephibosheth, who bows before him in fear, but David restores to him all of Saul's land and grants him a permanent place at the king's own table, treating him like one of his sons (vv. 7-11). Ziba and his household are appointed to farm the land for Mephibosheth's benefit, while Mephibosheth himself settles in Jerusalem, eating continually at the king's table despite his disability (vv. 12-13).
m: A question no ancient king asked, is there yet any left of the house of Saul that I may shew him kindness, David seeking survivors to bless rather than to eliminate, Mephibosheth falling on his face expecting execution and receiving fear not instead, land restored and a permanent seat at the king's…

x: When the Ammonite king Nahash dies, David sends envoys to console his son Hanun, but Hanun's officials convince him the men are spies, so he shaves off half their beards, cuts their garments at the hip, and sends them home in humiliation (vv. 1-5). Realizing they have angered David, the Ammonites hire Aramean mercenaries; Joab leads Israel's army and splits his forces to fight the Ammonites and Arameans on two fronts at once, putting both armies to flight (vv. 9-14). Hadadezer regroups the Arameans for a second battle, but David personally crosses the Jordan and leads Israel to a decisive victory, after which the Arameans make peace with Israel and refuse to help Ammon again (vv. 17-19).
m: Ambassadors sent in genuine kindness reinterpreted by advisors as spies sent to search out the city, beards shaved and garments cut at the hips as a humiliation calculated to provoke war rather than merely insult, Joab facing enemies in front and behind and dividing his best troops toward the…

x: In the spring, when kings normally went to war, David stays behind in Jerusalem while Joab besieges the Ammonite city of Rabbah (v. 1). From his rooftop David sees Bathsheba bathing, sends for her, and sleeps with her while her husband Uriah is at the front; she conceives (vv. 2-5). Hoping to cover the pregnancy, David recalls Uriah from battle so he will sleep with his wife, but Uriah refuses out of loyalty to his fellow soldiers, so David sends him back with a sealed letter ordering Joab to place him where the fighting is fiercest and then withdraw support (vv. 6-15). Uriah dies as arranged, and after Bathsheba's mourning ends David marries her, though the chapter closes noting that what he had done displeased the LORD (v. 27).
m: A king tarrying at home in the season when kings go forth to battle, the seeds of the whole chapter's disaster planted in that one detail, a woman's purification noted specifically so no reader could later doubt whose child she carried, Uriah's loyalty to the ark and to Israel in the field standing…

x: The LORD sends Nathan to confront David with a parable about a rich man who steals a poor man's only lamb, and when David angrily condemns the man, Nathan reveals that David himself is that man (vv. 1-7). Nathan pronounces judgment: violence will never leave David's household, and what he did in secret will be exposed publicly; David confesses his sin against the LORD, and Nathan tells him that though he is forgiven, the child born to Bathsheba will die (vv. 9-14). David fasts and pleads for the child, but after the child dies he rises, worships, and resumes life, later comforting Bathsheba, who bears Solomon (vv. 15-25). The chapter closes with Joab summoning David to finish capturing Rabbah so David receives credit for the victory (vv. 26-31).
m: A parable about a stolen lamb crafted precisely enough to draw David into pronouncing his own sentence, thou art the man landing after an indictment that begins by listing gifts rather than accusations, a confession reduced to five words, I have sinned against the LORD, with no qualification…

x: Amnon, David's son, becomes obsessed with his half-sister Tamar and pretends to be sick to lure her into his room, then rapes her despite her protests (vv. 1-14). His desire immediately turns to hatred, and he has her thrown out in disgrace, leaving her desolate in her brother Absalom's house (vv. 15-20). David is furious but takes no action against Amnon, so Absalom nurses his hatred in silence for two years (v. 22). At a sheep-shearing feast, Absalom has his servants kill Amnon and then flees to his grandfather in Geshur, where he stays three years (vv. 23-38). The chapter closes with David's grief for Amnon giving way to a longing to see Absalom again (v. 39).
m: A craftiness that turns a father's love into the very mechanism that delivers a daughter into a trap, Tamar arguing on every ground, moral, personal, practical, before being overpowered anyway, love that turns to hatred greater than the love itself the instant the sin is finished, a father's anger…

x: Joab notices David's longing for Absalom and sends a wise woman from Tekoa to tell a fabricated story that maneuvers David into pardoning his own exiled son in principle (vv. 1-20). David agrees to let Absalom return to Jerusalem but insists he not appear in the king's presence, leaving him in a kind of exile within the city for two more years (vv. 21-24, 28). Absalom is described as strikingly handsome, with a notable head of hair, and fathers three sons and a daughter named Tamar (vv. 25-27). Frustrated at being kept away from the king, Absalom burns Joab's field to force a meeting, and Joab finally brings him before David (vv. 29-33). David kisses Absalom, restoring him outwardly, but the reconciliation is incomplete, planting seeds of future rebellion.
h: Joab's Scheme and the Wise Woman of Tekoa (vv.1-20)
m: A king's heart torn between longing for an exiled son and an inability to act without appearing to excuse murder, a wise woman's fictional case built to mirror David's own situation closely enough that he cannot see the trap until it closes, restoration granted halfway, let him not see my face…

x: Absalom spends four years at the city gate intercepting petitioners and quietly courting Israel's loyalty away from his father (vv. 1-6). He then travels to Hebron under a false pretext and proclaims himself king, drawing conspirators including David's trusted counselor Ahithophel (vv. 7-12). When David learns of the revolt he flees Jerusalem on foot, weeping, leaving ten concubines behind to keep the house (vv. 13-17, 30). He sends the ark back to the city rather than use it as a talisman, trusting God's will over its presence, and sends his friend Hushai back to Absalom's court to undermine Ahithophel's counsel (vv. 24-29, 32-37).
h: David on the Mount of Olives (vv.30-37)
m: A conspiracy that begins with chariots and runners and a seat at the city gate rather than with any act of violence, every petitioner's complaint validated and every fault laid at the king's door before Absalom ever asks to be made judge, a religious vow used as the pretext to reach Hebron, the…

x: As David flees, Ziba meets him with supplies and falsely claims that his master Mephibosheth hopes to reclaim Saul's kingdom, prompting David to hand over all of Mephibosheth's property to Ziba (vv. 1-4). Shimei, a relative of Saul, curses David and pelts him with stones, calling him a man of bloodshed, but David refuses to let his men kill him, trusting God to judge the insult (vv. 5-14). Absalom enters Jerusalem and, on Ahithophel's advice, publicly lies with David's remaining concubines on the palace roof to make his rebellion irreversible in the eyes of Israel (vv. 20-22). Ahithophel's counsel is prized as though it came from God himself, underscoring how dangerous his defection to Absalom truly is (v. 23).
m: Provisions offered by Ziba wrapped around a devastating and unverified accusation against his own master, Shimei's cursing built on a theology that is wrong about David's guilt yet not entirely wrong about divine discipline, a king who tells his men to leave the cursing alone because the LORD hath…

x: Ahithophel urges Absalom to let him pursue David immediately with a small force while David is weary and unprepared, a plan that could end the rebellion in one stroke (vv. 1-4). Hushai, David's secret ally, counters with advice to gather all Israel first for an overwhelming assault, appealing to Absalom's pride, and the text notes that the Lord had determined to defeat Ahithophel's better counsel to bring disaster on Absalom (vv. 5-14). Hushai warns David through secret messengers to cross the Jordan that night, and after a narrow escape David's men do so (vv. 15-22). Seeing his advice rejected, Ahithophel goes home and hangs himself, while David makes his way safely to Mahanaim (vv. 23-24).
m: Two counselors offering competing strategies, one militarily sound and one only flattering, with Absalom choosing the worse of the two, a narrator's own verdict stated outright, the LORD had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, a message relayed through a servant girl and hidden down…

x: David organizes his army into three divisions under Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, and though he wants to go out with them himself, his men insist he stay behind, and he charges them all to deal gently with Absalom for his sake (vv. 1-5). The battle in the forest of Ephraim is fierce, and the forest itself claims more lives than the sword; Absalom's army is defeated (vv. 6-8). Absalom's hair catches in the branches of a large tree as he rides beneath it, leaving him suspended and helpless, and Joab kills him with javelins despite David's explicit order to spare him (vv. 9-15). News of the victory reaches David, but when he learns his son is dead he is overcome with grief, weeping bitterly for Absalom (vv. 24-33).
m: A public order given in front of the whole army, deal gently for my sake with the young man, even with Absalom, a forest that kills more men than the sword through its own terrain, hair or branches catching a rider left hanging between the heaven and the earth, a monument built by a man with no son…

x: Joab confronts David for mourning Absalom so publicly that it humiliates the very soldiers who saved his life and kingdom that day, warning that David risks losing all his support if he doesn't show his men favor (vv. 1-7). David heeds the rebuke, returns to sit at the gate, and the army comes before him again (v. 8). As David returns toward Jerusalem, Judah and Israel argue over who has the greater right to escort the king home, a rivalry that hints at the deeper division to come (vv. 9-15, 41-43). Along the way David shows mercy to Shimei, who had cursed him, restores Mephibosheth's property after hearing his side against Ziba, and honors the aged Barzillai for his loyalty (vv. 16-39).
m: An army ashamed of its own victory because the king's public grief outweighs any celebration, Judah won back by an offer of command that creates the deadly rivalry the next chapter will resolve by murder, a curse-giver spared on a day of restoration rather than vengeance though a different…

x: Sheba, a troublemaker from the tribe of Benjamin, blows a trumpet and calls Israel to abandon David, while Judah alone stays loyal to the king (vv. 1-2). David orders Amasa to muster Judah, but when he delays, Joab takes charge of the pursuit and treacherously kills Amasa, his rival for command, then continues after Sheba (vv. 4-13). Joab besieges Sheba in the city of Abel, and a wise woman from the city negotiates with him, then has the townspeople throw Sheba's head over the wall to end the siege (vv. 14-22). The chapter closes with a list of David's chief officials, showing the kingdom's administration restored to order (vv. 23-26).
m: A cry of secession, we have no part in David, growing directly out of the tribal jealousy the previous chapter never resolved, ten concubines left in a widowhood that is neither marriage nor freedom because of what was done to them in public, a greeting and a beard grasped as if for a kiss…

x: A three-year famine leads David to seek God, who reveals it is due to Saul's earlier slaughter of the Gibeonites in violation of Israel's ancient covenant with them (vv. 1-2). David asks the Gibeonites what will atone for the wrong, and they request seven of Saul's male descendants be handed over for execution, which David does, sparing only Mephibosheth (vv. 3-9). Rizpah, mother of two of the executed men, guards their bodies from scavengers for months until David has them properly buried along with the bones of Saul and Jonathan (vv. 10-14). The chapter closes with four battles against Philistine giants descended from Rapha, in which David's mighty men kill each giant in turn (vv. 15-22).
m: A three-year famine traced back to an oath Saul broke against Gibeonites who had deceived Israel decades earlier, seven descendants handed over for execution while Mephibosheth alone is spared because of an oath to Jonathan, Rizpah's vigil over unburied bodies moving David to give them proper…

x: David sings this psalm of deliverance, nearly identical to Psalm 18, describing God as his rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, and stronghold in his time of distress (vv. 1-4). He recounts how he cried out to God from the grip of death and how the earth itself seemed to shake as God came down to rescue him (vv. 5-16). He praises God for rewarding his righteousness and integrity, and for training him for battle and giving him strength against his enemies (vv. 21-40). The song closes with praise for God's exaltation of David as king and his steadfast covenant love shown to David and his descendants forever (vv. 47-51).
m: A cascade of titles opening the song, rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, horn of salvation, each reflecting a different way God was actually experienced, nine verses of cosmic storm and earthquake answering the cry of one man drowning, rescue attributed to delight rather than merit, he delivered me…

x: David's last words are recorded as an oracle describing the ideal ruler who governs in the fear of God, bringing blessing like sunlight after rain (vv. 1-4). He affirms that God's everlasting covenant with his house is his true security, even while acknowledging his own house is not yet all it should be before God (vv. 5). The chapter catalogs David's mightiest warriors, led by an elite group of three who performed legendary feats, including three men who broke through Philistine lines just to bring David water from the well at Bethlehem, which he refused to drink and poured out to the Lord instead (vv. 8-17). The list continues through thirty more mighty men, including Uriah the Hittite, honoring the loyal soldiers who stood with David throughout his reign (vv. 18-39).
m: Four titles claimed at once, son of Jesse, raised on high, anointed of the God of Jacob, sweet psalmist of Israel, before the oracle itself even begins, an admission that his own house has not perfectly lived up to the ideal he is describing, three men breaking through enemy lines for water David…

x: David's anger prompts him to order a census of Israel and Judah, against Joab's objection, apparently reflecting misplaced trust in military numbers rather than God (vv. 1-9). Convicted afterward, David confesses his sin, and God gives him a choice of three punishments through the prophet Gad: famine, military defeat, or plague (vv. 10-13). David chooses to fall into God's hands rather than man's, and a plague kills seventy thousand people before God stops the destroying angel at the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite (vv. 14-16). David buys the threshing floor and oxen at full price, refusing to offer God a sacrifice that costs him nothing, and builds an altar there — the site that would become the Temple mount (vv. 18-25).
h: David's Census — The Sin of Pride (vv.1-9)
David's Conviction and the Three Choices (vv.10-14)
m: God's anger against Israel never explained before David is permitted to be tempted into a census Joab himself recognizes as prideful, numbers that reveal the sin themselves, eight hundred thousand and five hundred thousand counted as trust placed in military strength rather than in God, three…

x: David, now old and served by the young Abishag as a caretaker, is dying, and his son Adonijah moves to seize the throne, winning support from Joab and the priest Abiathar and holding a sacrificial feast for his allies (vv. 1-10). Nathan the prophet and Bathsheba separately warn David of the plot and remind him of his earlier oath that Solomon would succeed him (vv. 11-27). David swears again that Solomon will reign and orders Zadok, Nathan, and Benaiah to anoint him king at Gihon (vv. 28-37). Solomon is anointed and enthroned amid public celebration that reaches Adonijah's feast and scatters his guests in fear (vv. 38-49). Adonijah grabs the horns of the altar seeking protection, and Solomon spares his life on condition of loyalty, sending him home (vv. 50-53).
m: A power vacuum created by a king too old even to keep warm, Adonijah exalting himself the same way Absalom once did and inviting only allies who would not object, Nathan and Bathsheba timing two independent reports to force a decision before a coup becomes irreversible, Solomon anointed publicly at…

x: As he nears death, David charges Solomon to be strong and to keep the law of Moses so their line will endure, then instructs him to deal with Joab's bloodguilt, to show kindness to Barzillai's sons, and to bring down Shimei, who had cursed him (vv. 1-9). David dies after forty years as king, and Solomon's rule is firmly established (vv. 10-12). When Adonijah asks to marry Abishag, Solomon reads it as a renewed bid for the throne and has him executed, then banishes Abiathar from the priesthood, fulfilling an old prophecy against Eli's house (vv. 13-27). Joab flees to the altar for refuge but is killed there on Solomon's order, and Benaiah takes his place over the army (vv. 28-35). Shimei is confined to Jerusalem under penalty of death; when he later leaves the city, Solomon has him executed as well, and the kingdom is secured in Solomon's hand (vv. 36-46).
m: A deathbed charge that pairs be strong and shew thyself a man with instructions for settling old scores, forty years of reign summarized in one transitional sentence, a request for Abishag read by Solomon as a claim on the kingdom itself, a priest exiled rather than executed because his sanctuary…

x: Solomon marries Pharaoh's daughter, and though he loves the Lord and walks in David's ways, the people still sacrifice at high places since the temple has not yet been built (vv. 1-3). At Gibeon, God appears to Solomon in a dream and offers to give him whatever he asks; Solomon requests an understanding heart to govern God's people rather than long life, riches, or victory over enemies (vv. 4-9). Pleased with this request, God grants him unmatched wisdom and, because he did not ask for them, riches and honor besides, promising long life if he remains obedient (vv. 10-14). Solomon wakes, worships in Jerusalem, and holds a feast (v. 15). He then demonstrates his wisdom by resolving a dispute between two women over a living infant, ordering the child cut in two to expose the true mother, whose plea to spare the child reveals her — and all Israel stands in awe of the wisdom God has given…
m: A foreign marriage alliance and a genuine love for the LORD held in the same breath without resolution, an open-ended offer answered with a request for a listening heart rather than knowledge or riches, wisdom granted alongside riches and honor that were never actually requested, two prostitutes…

x: The chapter lists Solomon's chief officials — priests, scribes, a recorder, and household leaders — and his twelve district governors, who each supply provisions for the royal court for one month of the year (vv. 1-19). Judah and Israel are as numerous as the sand of the sea, eating, drinking, and rejoicing, while Solomon rules a vast territory from the Euphrates to the border of Egypt and receives tribute from surrounding kings (vv. 20-21). His daily provisions are described in striking abundance, and he keeps thousands of horses and chariots, with Judah and Israel dwelling securely under their own vines and fig trees throughout his reign (vv. 22-28). God gives Solomon wisdom and understanding beyond that of the wise men of the East and of Egypt; he speaks three thousand proverbs and composes over a thousand songs, and people from every nation come to hear his wisdom (vv. 29-34).
m: A sophisticated bureaucracy listed office by office including the man who will matter again in chapter twelve, twelve administrative districts drawn deliberately across rather than along the old tribal boundaries, provisions for a single day's court described in numbers that read as staggering…

x: Hiram, king of Tyre, who had loved David, sends envoys to Solomon on hearing he has become king (v. 1). Solomon explains that David could not build a temple because of constant warfare, but now that God has given him rest on every side, he intends to build a house for the Lord's name as God promised through David, and he asks Hiram to supply cedar cut by skilled Sidonian woodcutters (vv. 2-6). Hiram rejoices, blesses the Lord for giving David such a wise son, and agrees to provide cedar and cypress timber, floated by sea to wherever Solomon directs, in exchange for wheat and oil for his household (vv. 7-11). The Lord gives Solomon wisdom as promised, and Solomon and Hiram make a peace treaty between them (v. 12). Solomon conscripts a labor force of thirty thousand Israelites, sending them to Lebanon in monthly shifts of ten thousand under Adoniram, along with seventy thousand…
m: A Phoenician alliance initiated by Hiram before Solomon even asks for it, rest named as the precondition for building rather than an incidental blessing, a workforce of over one hundred eighty thousand men mobilized for a single national project, Adoniram named as the overseer who will be stoned…

x: In the fourth year of his reign, Solomon begins building the temple, whose dimensions, porch, side chambers, and windows are described in detail, all of it built with stone shaped off-site so that no hammer or tool is heard at the building site (vv. 1-10). The Lord tells Solomon that if he walks in His statutes and keeps His commandments, He will fulfill His promise to David and dwell among the people of Israel (vv. 11-13). Solomon finishes the house, lining the interior with cedar and the floor with cypress, and overlaying the innermost sanctuary — a twenty-cubit cube — with pure gold, where he places two olive-wood cherubim whose outstretched wings span the room and touch in the middle (vv. 14-28). The walls and doors throughout are carved with cherubim, palm trees, and flowers and covered in gold, and the inner court is built of stone and cedar (vv. 29-36). The foundation is laid in…
h: The Interior: Gold, Cedar, and Cherubim (vv.14-38)
m: A date anchored to four hundred eighty years after the Exodus rather than left as an undated year of Solomon's reign, dimensions exactly double the tabernacle's signaling continuity rather than replacement, a conditional promise interrupting the construction narrative in its own middle, cherubim…

x: Solomon spends thirteen years building his own palace complex, including the House of the Forest of Lebanon, a porch of pillars, a throne porch for judging cases, his own residence, and a house for Pharaoh's daughter, all built of costly hewn stone (vv. 1-12). He brings in a skilled bronze craftsman, also named Hiram, from Tyre, who casts the two great bronze pillars for the temple porch, named Jachin and Boaz, and tops them with ornate capitals (vv. 13-22). Hiram also makes the massive bronze "sea" resting on twelve oxen, ten wheeled bronze stands and basins, and all the temple's bronze tools and vessels in such quantity that their weight is never measured (vv. 23-47). Solomon then furnishes the temple with gold: the altar, table, lampstands, and an array of gold implements, and finally brings in the silver and gold David had dedicated, completing the work for the house of the Lord…
h: The Two Pillars: Jachin and Boaz (vv.15-22)
m: A palace complex that took thirteen years against the temple's seven, a second Hiram, a craftsman rather than a king, described in the same language once used of Bezalel, two named pillars proclaiming He establishes and In Him is strength rather than serving as structural supports, a bronze sea…

x: Solomon assembles Israel's elders and tribal leaders to bring the ark of the covenant up from the city of David into the temple, where the priests set it beneath the wings of the cherubim in the Most Holy Place (vv. 1-9). As the priests withdraw, a cloud fills the house — the glory of the Lord — so that they cannot continue ministering (vv. 10-11). Solomon addresses the assembly, recounting how God chose David and now him to build a house for His name, then kneels and spreads his hands toward heaven in a lengthy dedicatory prayer (vv. 12-21). He acknowledges that no house can contain God, and pleads with Him to hear and forgive whenever Israel — or even a foreigner — prays toward this place, whether in matters of sin, defeat, drought, famine, or exile (vv. 22-53). Solomon rises, blesses the assembly, and offers a vast sacrifice of oxen and sheep, dedicating the temple with a…
h: The Ark Brought to the Temple (vv.1-11)
m: An ark carried into the Most Holy Place until a cloud fills the house and drives the priests out from ministering, a question that undercuts the whole building project before the prayer continues, will God indeed dwell on the earth, seven petitions offered for seven different kinds of national…

x: After Solomon finishes both the temple and his palace, the Lord appears to him a second time, as He did at Gibeon, consecrating the temple and promising to establish his throne forever if he obeys — but warning that if Israel turns to other gods, the Lord will cut them off from the land and cast off the temple, making it a byword among the nations (vv. 1-9). At the end of twenty years of building, Solomon gives Hiram of Tyre twenty cities in Galilee, but Hiram is unimpressed with them and calls the region Cabul (vv. 10-14). The chapter recounts Solomon's building projects — Millo, the wall of Jerusalem, Hazor, Megiddo, Gezer, and store and chariot cities — accomplished using forced labor drawn from Israel's remaining Canaanite peoples, while Israelites serve as soldiers and officials (vv. 15-23). Solomon offers sacrifices three times a year and builds a fleet at Ezion-geber that, with…
m: A second appearance to Solomon bookending twenty years of building the way the first appearance opened his reign, a promise and a warning delivered in the same conditional sentence, twenty cities in Galilee handed to Hiram and rejected as Cabul in an awkward diplomatic moment, a building program…

x: Hearing of Solomon's fame, the Queen of Sheba travels to Jerusalem with a great caravan of spices, gold, and precious stones to test him with hard questions, and he answers all of them (vv. 1-3). Overwhelmed by his wisdom, his palace, his food, and the order of his court, she is left breathless, tells Solomon the reports she heard did not do justice to the reality, and blesses the Lord for setting him on Israel's throne (vv. 4-9). She gives Solomon a vast quantity of gold and spices, and he gives her gifts in return before she returns to her own country (vv. 10-13). The remainder of the chapter catalogs Solomon's wealth: his enormous annual gold income, gold shields and an ivory throne overlaid with gold, a fleet trading with Tarshish, and horses and chariots imported from Egypt, concluding that Solomon exceeded all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom, with silver as common in…
m: A queen who travels thousands of miles with hard questions and finds the half was not told her, wealth catalogued in numbers deliberately excessive, six hundred sixty-six talents of gold in a single year, silver counted so common it was nothing accounted of, horses imported from Egypt and sold on…

x: In his old age, Solomon's foreign wives turn his heart toward their gods, and he builds high places for Chemosh and Molech near Jerusalem (vv. 1-8). Because Solomon broke the covenant despite two direct warnings, God announces He will tear away the kingdom, though for David's sake this waits until Solomon's son reigns, and one tribe remains (vv. 9-13). God raises up adversaries, including Hadad the Edomite and Rezon of Damascus (vv. 14-25), and the prophet Ahijah tears his garment into twelve pieces, giving Jeroboam ten as a sign that ten tribes will become his (vv. 26-39). Solomon tries to kill Jeroboam, who flees to Egypt until Solomon dies after forty years as king (vv. 40-43), setting up the coming split of the kingdom.
m: The same verb once used of Solomon loving the LORD now describing his love for many strange women, seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines each a small compromise accumulated over decades, judgment tempered by mercy for David's sake so the kingdom is rent but not in Solomon's own lifetime…

x: Rehoboam travels to Shechem to be made king, where the people ask him to lighten the harsh labor Solomon placed on them (vv. 1-5). Rejecting the elders' advice, Rehoboam follows his young friends' counsel and answers harshly, promising even heavier burdens (vv. 6-15). Ten tribes revolt, killing Rehoboam's labor overseer and making Jeroboam king over Israel in the north, leaving Rehoboam only Judah and Benjamin (vv. 16-20); God stops him from attacking his brothers through the prophet Shemaiah (vv. 21-24). Fearing the people will return their allegiance to Jerusalem, Jeroboam sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan and appoints unauthorized priests, permanently corrupting Israel's worship (vv. 25-33) — the definitive split into the northern and southern kingdoms, the fruit of Solomon's earlier sin.
m: A reasonable request for lighter labor answered with a crude boast about scorpions instead of whips, elders counseling service rejected for the counsel of peers who had grown up with the king, an old rebellion cry revived word for word, what portion have we in David, a prophet's this thing is from…

x: A man of God travels from Judah to Bethel and confronts Jeroboam at his idolatrous altar, prophesying that a future king named Josiah will one day desecrate it, with the altar splitting apart as an immediate sign (vv. 1-3). When Jeroboam orders him seized, the king's hand withers instantly and is restored only through the prophet's prayer (vv. 4-6). Under strict orders from God, the man refuses the king's hospitality, but an old prophet in Bethel lies to him, claiming an angel countermanded God's instructions, and he accepts the invitation to eat (vv. 7-19). For that disobedience a lion kills him on the road home, though it leaves his body and donkey untouched (vv. 20-28). The old prophet buries him with honor, while Jeroboam presses on unchanged (vv. 29-34) — a warning that even partial disobedience brings serious consequence.
m: A king named three hundred years before his birth as the prophecy against Bethel's altar, a hand withered and restored in the same scene as the sign that confirms the word, an old prophet's lie stated plainly by the narrator before the man of God ever believes it, a lion that kills without eating…

x: When Jeroboam's son Abijah falls ill, Jeroboam sends his wife in disguise to the blind prophet Ahijah, but God reveals her identity in advance and Ahijah delivers a devastating message: because of Jeroboam's idolatry, God will wipe out his house, and the child will die the moment she reaches home (vv. 1-16). The boy dies as she crosses the threshold, closing out Jeroboam's twenty-two-year reign (vv. 17-20). Rehoboam's reign in Judah is marked by the same idolatry, provoking God to let Egypt's King Shishak plunder the temple and palace treasures, including Solomon's gold shields, which Rehoboam replaces with bronze (vv. 21-28), amid ongoing war between the two kings (vv. 29-31) — both kingdoms sliding into judgment under compromised worship.
m: A disguise sent to a prophet who already knows she is coming before she arrives, heavy tidings delivered to a queen still standing at the door in her costume, a child's death timed to the exact moment her feet cross the threshold, Judah descending into the same abominations the Canaanites were…

x: Abijam becomes king of Judah and reigns three years, following his father's sinful example rather than David's wholehearted devotion, though God preserves his line for David's sake (vv. 1-8). His son Asa succeeds him and reigns forty-one years, removing male shrine prostitutes and idols from the land and even deposing his grandmother Maacah as queen mother for making an idol, which he destroys (vv. 9-13). Asa's heart remains loyal to the Lord throughout his life, though the high places are never eliminated, and war continues against Baasha of Israel, prompting Asa to bribe Ben-hadad of Syria into breaking his treaty with Baasha (vv. 14-22). Meanwhile in the northern kingdom, Nadab is assassinated by Baasha, who wipes out Jeroboam's entire house and then reigns in his place, continuing the same pattern of sin (vv. 25-34).
m: A lamp preserved in Jerusalem for David's sake regardless of which king currently holds the throne, Asa's own grandmother deposed from the queen mother's position for making an idol, silver and gold taken from the temple treasury to bribe Syria rather than trusted to the LORD, a prophecy against…

x: The prophet Jehu condemns King Baasha for following Jeroboam's sins and pronounces the same destruction on his house (vv. 1-7). Baasha's son Elah is assassinated by his officer Zimri, who wipes out Baasha's family but reigns only seven days before Omri's forces besiege him and he burns the palace down around himself (vv. 8-20). Israel splits between rival claimants Tibni and Omri until Omri prevails, buys the hill of Samaria, and builds it as Israel's new capital (vv. 21-28). Omri is called more evil than any king before him, but his son Ahab surpasses him further, marrying Jezebel and building Baal a temple in Samaria (vv. 29-33). The chapter closes with Hiel of Bethel rebuilding Jericho at the cost of his sons' lives, exactly as Joshua had prophesied (v. 34) — a chapter of relentless political violence and deepening apostasy.
m: A prophecy against Baasha delivered in language almost identical to the one once spoken against Jeroboam, a king found drinking himself drunk while his own army is in the field, a seven-day reign ending in a burned palace and a name that becomes proverbial for treachery, Ahab's evaluation topping…

x: Elijah announces to Ahab that there will be no rain except by his word, then obeys God's command to hide by the Brook Cherith, where ravens bring him food each morning and evening (vv. 1-7). When the brook dries up, God sends him to a widow in Zarephath who is preparing what she expects to be her last meal, but Elijah promises her flour and oil will not run out, and they don't, sustaining the household through the famine (vv. 8-16). When the widow's son later dies, Elijah cries out to God and stretches himself over the boy three times, and the child's life is restored, proving to the widow that Elijah truly speaks God's word (vv. 17-24).
m: A prophet erupting onto the scene with no genealogy and no introduction before pronouncing a drought by his own word, ravens, unclean birds by the law's own definition, commanded to feed him morning and evening, God's provision found in enemy territory through a Gentile widow rather than among…

x: After three years of drought, God sends Elijah back to confront Ahab, meeting Obadiah along the way, a God-fearing official who had hidden a hundred prophets from Jezebel's purge (vv. 1-16). Elijah challenges 450 prophets of Baal to a contest on Mount Carmel: two altars, two sacrifices, and whichever god answers by fire is God (vv. 17-24). The prophets of Baal cry out and cut themselves for hours with no response, while Elijah rebuilds the LORD's altar, drenches it with water, and prays a simple prayer that brings down fire consuming the sacrifice, wood, stones, and even the water in the trench (vv. 25-38). The people fall down declaring, "The LORD, he is God," and Elijah has the false prophets executed (vv. 39-40), then prays for rain and outruns Ahab's chariot to Jezreel as the drought breaks (vv. 41-46).
m: A famine so severe the king himself searches for grass to keep his horses alive, a governor who hid a hundred prophets at personal risk introduced alongside the one prophet everyone is hunting, a question that names Israel's condition exactly, how long halt ye between two opinions, mockery aimed at…

x: Fearing Jezebel's death threat after the Carmel victory, Elijah flees into the wilderness and, exhausted and afraid, asks God to let him die under a broom tree (vv. 1-4). An angel feeds him twice, and on that strength he travels forty days to Horeb, the mountain of God (vv. 5-8). There, rather than appearing in a powerful wind, earthquake, or fire, God speaks to Elijah in a still, small voice (vv. 9-14). God corrects Elijah's belief that he is the only faithful one left, revealing seven thousand in Israel who have not worshiped Baal, and commissions him to anoint Hazael as king over Syria, Jehu as king over Israel, and Elisha as his own successor (vv. 15-18), who leaves everything to follow him (vv. 19-21).
m: A prophet who called fire from heaven fleeing in terror from a single messenger's threat, an angel's answer to despair given as food and sleep rather than rebuke, forty days and nights of strength drawn from one meal echoing Moses at the same mountain, wind, earthquake and fire all passing before…

x: Ben-hadad of Syria besieges Samaria with thirty-two allied kings and demands Ahab's silver, wives, and children, which Ahab initially concedes, but he refuses a second, more humiliating demand, backed by the elders of Israel (vv. 1-12). A prophet promises Ahab victory to prove that the LORD is God, and Israel's small force routs the Syrians while Ben-hadad escapes (vv. 13-21). Warned that Syria will return, Ahab prepares, and when Ben-hadad's advisors claim Israel's God is only a god of the hills, God grants an even greater victory in the valley at Aphek to prove otherwise (vv. 22-30). Ben-hadad begs for mercy, and Ahab spares his life and makes a treaty with him instead of destroying him as God intended (vv. 31-34). A prophet in disguise tricks Ahab into pronouncing judgment on himself, then reveals that because Ahab freed a man devoted to destruction, his own life and people will pay…
m: Total submission demanded and then a second demand for anything pleasant in the king's own eyes going further still, victory granted through two hundred thirty-two young servants against a massive coalition so Ahab would know that I am the LORD, Syrian advisors reducing God to a deity of the hills…

x: Ahab desires Naboth's vineyard next to his palace, but Naboth refuses to sell his ancestral inheritance, leaving Ahab sulking in his bed (vv. 1-4). Jezebel takes charge, forging letters in Ahab's name that arrange a public fast where false witnesses accuse Naboth of cursing God and the king, resulting in his stoning (vv. 5-14), after which Jezebel tells Ahab to go take possession of the vineyard (vv. 15-16). God sends Elijah to confront Ahab there, pronouncing that dogs will lick Ahab's blood where they licked Naboth's, and that Jezebel will be eaten by dogs at Jezreel, with disaster coming on his entire house (vv. 17-26). When Ahab humbles himself, tearing his clothes and fasting, God delays the judgment until after his lifetime, bringing it instead on his son (vv. 27-29).
m: A refusal grounded in covenant law rather than stubbornness or bargaining, a king who sulks in bed over land he cannot legally buy, a plot built on a false fast and two witnesses accusing an innocent man of cursing God and the king, arise take possession given without any explanation of how Naboth…

x: After three years of peace, Jehoshaphat of Judah joins Ahab of Israel in planning an attack to reclaim Ramoth-gilead from Syria, and four hundred prophets Ahab gathers all promise victory (vv. 1-12). Micaiah, the one true prophet Ahab despises, is summoned and describes a vision of Israel scattered like sheep without a shepherd, revealing that a lying spirit has filled the mouths of Ahab's prophets to lure him to his death (vv. 13-23). Struck by Zedekiah and imprisoned on bread and water, Micaiah insists his word will be proven true (vv. 24-28). Ahab disguises himself for battle, but a stray arrow finds him anyway, and he bleeds to death propped up in his chariot, with dogs later licking his blood exactly as earlier prophesied (vv. 29-40). The chapter closes noting Jehoshaphat's mostly faithful reign in Judah and the start of Ahaziah's evil reign in Israel (vv. 41-53).
h: The Alliance and the Question of Prophecy (vv.1-9)
m: Four hundred prophets unanimous in one voice against Micaiah's single dissent, a coaching note asking Micaiah to agree before he is even questioned, a vision of a lying spirit sent to persuade Ahab's prophets, offered as the reason four hundred voices could all be wrong together, a disguise that…

x: After Ahab's death, King Ahaziah of Israel falls through a lattice in his upper chamber and, injured, sends messengers to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether he will recover (vv. 1-2). An angel directs Elijah to intercept the messengers with word that Ahaziah will die for consulting a foreign god instead of Israel's own (vv. 3-4). When Ahaziah learns Elijah's identity from the messengers' description, he twice sends a captain with fifty soldiers to arrest him, and both companies are consumed by fire from heaven at Elijah's word (vv. 9-12). A third captain humbly begs for his life, and an angel instructs Elijah to go with him safely to deliver the verdict to the king in person (vv. 13-15). Ahaziah dies without an heir just as Elijah foretold, and his brother Jehoram becomes king (vv. 17-18).
m: A king injured by a fall who sends to a Philistine god before he ever thinks to ask Israel's own, is it not because there is not a God in Israel repeated as the question that damns the inquiry, fire falling twice on captains who command rather than request, a third captain's plea on his knees…

x: Elijah and Elisha travel from Gilgal to Bethel, Jericho, and the Jordan, where Elijah parts the water with his mantle so they cross on dry ground (vv. 1-8). Before being taken up, Elijah asks what he can do for Elisha, who requests a double portion of his spirit; Elijah says this will be granted only if Elisha witnesses his departure (vv. 9-10). A chariot and horses of fire appear in a whirlwind and carry Elijah to heaven, and the grieving Elisha tears his clothes and picks up the fallen mantle (vv. 11-13). Elisha strikes the Jordan with it, the water parts as it had for Elijah, and the watching sons of the prophets recognize that Elijah's spirit now rests on him (vv. 14-15). Elisha then purifies Jericho's water with salt (vv. 19-22), and when youths at Bethel mock him, two bears maul forty-two of them as a sign of God's judgment (vv. 23-24).
h: The Translation and the Double Portion (vv.9-12)
m: A journey retracing Israel's conquest route in reverse as though Elijah is walking backward through its history, three refusals to be left behind answered each time with as the LORD liveth and as thy soul liveth, a double portion requested as a firstborn's inheritance rather than as raw power, a…

x: Jehoram of Israel allies with Jehoshaphat of Judah and the king of Edom to put down Moab's rebellion against Israelite rule, but their armies nearly perish from lack of water after a seven-day march through the wilderness (vv. 1-10). At Jehoshaphat's request they consult Elisha, who despite rebuking Jehoram calls for a musician and, under the Lord's hand, prophesies that the dry streambed will fill with water and that Moab will be defeated (vv. 11-19). Water flows in from the direction of Edom, and the Moabites, seeing it reddened by the morning sun, mistake it for blood from a battle between the allied kings and rush in to plunder, only to be routed (vv. 20-24). The allied armies devastate Moab's cities and land as Elisha foretold (v. 25). When the king of Moab fails to break through the Edomite line, he sacrifices his own son as a burnt offering on the city wall, and the horrified…
m: A qualified evaluation, evil, but not like his father and his mother, describing partial reform that removes excess while keeping the system, an alliance with Judah echoing the same yoking Jehoshaphat once made with Ahab, a musician's music calming the prophet's spirit before any word comes, water…

x: Elisha multiplies a widow's small jar of oil to fill many borrowed vessels, providing enough to pay off her creditors and live on the rest (vv. 1-7). A wealthy Shunammite woman builds Elisha a room to stay in, and he promises that she, though barren and married to an old husband, will have a son within a year (vv. 8-17). Years later the boy dies suddenly, and the woman travels to fetch Elisha, who returns with her, prays, and stretches himself over the child until he revives (vv. 18-37). Elisha also purifies a pot of stew that had been made poisonous by wild gourds, telling the company to eat safely (vv. 38-41). Finally, he multiplies twenty loaves of barley bread and fresh grain to feed a hundred men with some left over, according to the Lord's word (vv. 42-44).
h: The Shunammite's Son: Death and Raising (vv.18-37)
m: Two questions, what shall I do for thee and what hast thou in the house, beginning a miracle with what a widow already owns rather than what she lacks, a Shunammite woman's hospitality sustained rather than sporadic, earning a promise she initially refuses to trust, a boy's death met with as the…

x: Naaman, a valued Syrian army commander who has leprosy, learns from a captured Israelite servant girl of a prophet in Samaria who could heal him (vv. 1-4). He travels to Elisha, who sends a messenger telling him simply to wash seven times in the Jordan (vv. 8-10). Naaman is enraged at the lack of ceremony and nearly leaves, but his servants persuade him to try it, and after washing his flesh is restored like a child's (vv. 11-14). He returns to confess the God of Israel and offer a gift, which Elisha refuses, though Naaman asks to take Israelite soil home with him (vv. 15-19). Elisha's servant Gehazi secretly chases Naaman down, lies to obtain silver and clothing, and is struck with Naaman's leprosy as punishment for his greed and deceit (vv. 20-27).
h: Naaman's Need and the Slave Girl's Faith (vv.1-7)
m: A commander introduced with every credential and then one devastating qualifier, but he was a leper, a captive slave girl possessing the one thing her master's whole army lacks, an instruction so simple it insults a man ready to attempt something difficult instead, seven dips in a muddy river…

x: When a borrowed axe head sinks in the Jordan during building work, Elisha makes it float by throwing in a stick (vv. 1-7). He repeatedly warns the king of Israel of Syrian ambushes by divine insight, prompting the king of Syria to send an army to capture him at Dothan (vv. 8-14). Elisha's servant is terrified at being surrounded, but Elisha shows him the unseen horses and chariots of fire protecting them, then strikes the Syrian troops with blindness and leads them into Samaria, where the king feeds them and sends them home instead of killing them (vv. 15-23). Ben-hadad of Syria later besieges Samaria until famine grows so severe that two women resort to eating their own sons, and the horrified king vows to kill Elisha, who calmly awaits his messenger (vv. 24-33).
h: Elisha and the Syrian Army at Dothan (vv.8-23)
m: A borrowed axe head recovered because a poor man's integrity mattered enough for a miracle, a servant's panic at Dothan answered with eyes opened to horses and chariots of fire already surrounding the city, more that be with us than that be with them stated before the servant can even see it, a…

x: Amid Samaria's famine, Elisha prophesies that by the next day fine flour and barley will sell at ordinary prices at the city gate; the king's officer scoffs that this couldn't happen even if the Lord opened windows in the sky, and Elisha tells him he will see it happen but not eat any of it (vv. 1-2). Four leprous men at the gate, facing death either way, decide to surrender to the besieging Syrian camp, only to find it deserted — the Lord had made the Syrians hear the sound of a great army and they fled, abandoning everything (vv. 3-7). The lepers loot the camp before reporting the news to the city, and after scouts confirm the Syrians are gone, the people rush out to plunder the camp, causing food prices to collapse exactly as Elisha foretold (vv. 8-16). The doubting officer, put in charge of the gate, is trampled to death by the surging crowd, fulfilling Elisha's word against him…
m: A prophecy of overnight abundance answered with an officer's cynicism even if the LORD made windows in heaven, four lepers reasoning their way into the enemy camp because staying anywhere else guarantees death, an empty Syrian camp abandoned because God made an army of noise no one actually needed…

x: The Shunammite woman, warned earlier by Elisha of a coming seven-year famine, returns from Philistia to find her land seized, but the king restores it along with back produce after Gehazi happens to be recounting Elisha's miracles at court (vv. 1-6). Elisha travels to Damascus, where the ailing King Ben-hadad sends Hazael to ask if he will recover; Elisha weeps as he foresees the atrocities Hazael will commit against Israel, and tells him he will become king (vv. 7-13). Hazael returns and smothers Ben-hadad with a wet cloth, seizing the throne of Syria as Elisha prophesied (v. 15). Jehoram of Judah, who married Ahab's daughter, reigns wickedly and loses Edom and Libnah to revolt before his son Ahaziah succeeds him (vv. 16-24). Ahaziah allies with Israel's King Joram against Hazael at Ramoth-gilead, and after Joram is wounded he goes to recover at Jezreel, where Ahaziah visits him (vv.…
h: Hazael and the Death of Ben-hadad (vv.7-15)
m: A land restored at the precise moment a king happens to be asking about the miracle that would prove the claim, Elisha weeping over Hazael before Hazael has done any of the things being wept over, a paradoxical answer, he will recover and he will surely die, describing illness and murder in the…

x: Elisha sends a young prophet to secretly anoint Jehu king over Israel at Ramoth-gilead, charging him to destroy the house of Ahab in judgment for the blood of the prophets and to see Jezebel devoured by dogs (vv. 1-10). Jehu's fellow officers proclaim him king, and he drives furiously to Jezreel, where the wounded King Joram and visiting King Ahaziah go out to meet him (vv. 11-21). When Joram asks whether he comes in peace, Jehu denounces Jezebel's idolatry and kills Joram with an arrow, casting his body onto Naboth's plot in fulfillment of Elijah's earlier word, while Ahaziah flees but is mortally wounded and dies at Megiddo (vv. 22-28). Jezebel, painted and adorned, taunts Jehu from a window, and at his command her own eunuchs throw her down to her death, her body trampled by horses (vv. 30-33). When Jehu later orders her buried, his men find that dogs have already eaten her flesh…
m: An anointing carried out in secret and fled from immediately because it amounts to treason against a reigning king, a watchman's identification made from nothing but the way a chariot is driven, what peace answered with a question that names the sin rather than the greeting offered, a body thrown…

x: Jehu forces Samaria's elders to execute all seventy of Ahab's sons, whose heads are piled at the city gate, and he goes on to kill everyone remaining of Ahab's house along with his officials and priests, fulfilling Elijah's prophecy against that dynasty (vv. 1-11). He also slaughters forty-two relatives of Ahaziah of Judah and, joined by Jehonadab son of Rechab, wipes out any survivors of Ahab's family still in Samaria (vv. 12-17). Under the pretense of holding a great sacrifice to Baal, Jehu gathers all of Baal's worshipers into his temple and has them massacred, then destroys the temple and turns it into a latrine (vv. 18-27). Though the Lord commends Jehu for carrying out this judgment and promises his descendants the throne for four generations, Jehu fails to remove Jeroboam's golden calves at Bethel and Dan or to fully follow the law (vv. 28-31). As a result, the Lord begins…
m: A challenge to choose a champion from seventy sons that Jehu already knows will never be answered, two heaps of heads displayed at the gate as evidence turned into indictment, forty-two relatives killed simply for traveling toward a court that no longer exists, a solemn assembly for Baal announced…

x: After her son Ahaziah's death, Athaliah destroys the rest of the royal family and seizes Judah's throne, but the infant Joash is rescued by his aunt Jehosheba and hidden in the temple for six years (vv. 1-3). In the seventh year, the priest Jehoiada arms the temple guard, brings out young Joash, crowns and anoints him, and the people proclaim him king (vv. 4-12). Athaliah rushes to the temple crying treason but is seized and executed outside its gates (vv. 13-16). Jehoiada then leads the people in covenants to serve the Lord and support the king, and the crowd tears down the temple of Baal and kills its priest (vv. 17-18). Joash is enthroned in the palace, and the city rests quietly after Athaliah's violent end (vv. 19-21).
m: A grandmother destroying her own grandchildren's lives to seize a throne that was never legally hers, one infant hidden in the temple for six years while the Davidic line hangs by a single thread, David's own spears and shields brought out of storage for a coup carried out on the Sabbath, treason…

x: Joash becomes king of Judah at age seven after being hidden in the temple during Athaliah's purge, and does what is right throughout the years the priest Jehoiada instructs him, though the high places are never removed (vv. 1-3). Finding that the priests have collected temple-repair funds for years without making repairs, Joash sets up a chest by the altar so offerings go directly toward paying the workmen, who carry out the repairs with such integrity that no formal accounting of the funds is required (vv. 4-16). When Hazael of Syria threatens Jerusalem, Joash strips the temple and palace treasuries of gold to buy him off rather than face him in battle (vv. 17-18). The chapter closes with Joash's own officials conspiring against him and assassinating him, after which his son Amaziah reigns in his place (vv. 19-21).
m: Righteousness explicitly qualified as lasting only as long as Jehoiada the priest instructed him, twenty-three years passing with temple repair money collected but no repairs made, a chest with a hole in its lid replacing an accounting system that had failed for decades, temple treasures stripped…

x: Jehoahaz becomes king of Israel and continues in the sins of Jeroboam, bringing Syrian oppression under Hazael and Ben-hadad that reduces Israel's army to a small remnant of horsemen, chariots, and infantry; when Jehoahaz seeks the LORD, God provides a measure of relief, though the nation still does not turn from its idolatry (vv. 1-9). His son Jehoash succeeds him and, on visiting the dying Elisha, weeps over him as Israel's true defense; Elisha has him shoot an arrow eastward as a sign of victory over Syria, then strike the ground with arrows, and rebukes him for stopping at three strikes instead of five or six, limiting his future victories to three partial ones (vv. 10-19). Elisha dies and is buried, and in a later year a man's corpse revives the moment it touches Elisha's bones as it is hastily buried in his tomb (vv. 20-21). The chapter closes noting that the LORD continued to…
h: Jehoash of Israel and Elisha's Death (vv.10-21)
m: An army reduced to fifty horsemen and ten chariots yet not abandoned because of a covenant made centuries earlier with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the chariot of Israel and the horsemen thereof spoken twice, once at Elijah's departure and once at Elisha's, an arrow shot eastward named the arrow of…

x: Amaziah becomes king of Judah, does what is right though the high places remain, and executes his father's assassins while sparing their children as the Law required (vv. 1-6). He defeats Edom and takes Sela (v. 7), then rashly challenges Jehoash of Israel to battle despite Jehoash's warning parable of the thistle and the cedar (vv. 8-10); Judah is routed, and Jehoash breaks down part of Jerusalem's wall and plunders the temple and palace treasuries (vv. 11-14). A conspiracy later forces Amaziah to flee to Lachish, where he is assassinated, and his son Azariah succeeds him (vv. 17-21). The chapter closes with Jeroboam II's prosperous but spiritually empty forty-one-year reign over Israel, in which he restores Israel's borders as the LORD had spoken through Jonah (vv. 23-29).
m: Justice executed on assassins while their children are deliberately spared in explicit obedience to the law of individual responsibility, a challenge to war answered with a parable about a thistle that asked for a cedar's daughter, success in Edom souring into the arrogance that provokes Amaziah's…

x: Azariah (Uzziah) becomes king of Judah and reigns fifty-two years, doing what is right yet leaving the high places standing; the LORD strikes him with leprosy, forcing his son Jotham to govern the household and judge the land (vv. 1-7). In the north, Israel spirals into instability: Zechariah, the last of Jehu's dynasty, is assassinated by Shallum after only six months, fulfilling God's word to Jehu, and Shallum is himself killed within a month by Menahem, whose brutal reign includes paying tribute to Pul of Assyria (vv. 8-22). Pekahiah succeeds his father Menahem but is murdered by his own captain Pekah, who seizes the throne and later loses Israelite territory to Tiglath-pileser of Assyria (vv. 23-31). The chapter closes in Judah with Jotham's generally faithful reign, though the high places remain and the LORD begins sending Rezin of Aram and Pekah of Israel against Judah (vv. 32-38).
m: A long and mostly faithful reign remembered chiefly for a leprosy contracted the moment a king tried to burn incense that belonged only to the priests, four generations promised to Jehu's dynasty fulfilled exactly and no further, five kings in rapid succession and four of five transitions…

x: Ahaz becomes king of Judah and plunges into deep apostasy, walking in the ways of Israel's kings and even sacrificing his son in the fire (vv. 1-4). When Rezin of Aram and Pekah of Israel besiege Jerusalem, Ahaz appeals to Tiglath-pileser of Assyria for rescue, stripping the temple and palace treasuries to pay for the alliance (vv. 5-9). After seeing a pagan altar in Damascus, Ahaz has the priest Uriah build a replica in Jerusalem, displaces the bronze altar of the LORD, and rearranges the temple's furnishings to please the king of Assyria (vv. 10-18). He dies and is succeeded by his son Hezekiah (vv. 19-20).
m: An evaluation refusing Ahaz even the qualified praise weaker kings received, his own son made to pass through the fire in the exact abomination that drove out the Canaanites, an altar copied from Damascus and installed while the LORD's own altar is quietly moved aside, temple fittings dismantled…

x: Hoshea, the last king of Israel, conspires with Egypt against Assyria, prompting Shalmaneser to imprison him and besiege Samaria for three years before the city falls and Israel is deported to Assyria, Halah, the Habor River, and the cities of the Medes (vv. 1-6). The chapter then explains at length why this judgment fell: Israel had walked in the customs of the nations, worshiped other gods and the starry host, built high places and Asherah poles, practiced divination and child sacrifice, and rejected every prophet's warning to turn back, so that only Judah was left (vv. 7-23). The king of Assyria resettles the land with foreign peoples from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim, who at first do not fear the LORD; when lions attack them, an exiled priest is sent back to teach them how to worship Him (vv. 24-28). The result is a syncretistic religion that persists to the…
m: A last king's slight improvement over his predecessors still not enough to avert judgment, more space given to explaining why Samaria fell than to describing how, an indictment unfolding systematically through pillars, Asherah poles and rejected prophets, foreign settlers sent lions until an exiled…

x: Hezekiah becomes king of Judah and does what is right as David had done, removing the high places, smashing the sacred pillars and Asherah poles, and destroying the bronze serpent Moses had made because Israel had turned it into an idol (vv. 1-4). He trusts in the LORD as no king before or after him did, rebels against Assyria, and defeats the Philistines, while the narrative recalls how Israel had already fallen to Assyria for its unfaithfulness (vv. 5-12). When Sennacherib invades Judah, Hezekiah first tries to buy him off by stripping the temple and palace treasuries (vv. 13-16), but Sennacherib's field commander, the Rabshakeh, still comes to Jerusalem and delivers a taunting speech before the people on the wall, mocking Hezekiah's trust in the LORD and Egypt's ability to help (vv. 17-35). Hezekiah's officials tear their clothes at the blasphemy, and the people stay silent as…
h: Hezekiah's Reforms and the Fall of Israel (vv.1-12)
m: A king praised above every king before or after him for trusting the LORD, a bronze serpent Moses himself had made destroyed because it had become an idol under its own name, tribute paid first and temple doors stripped of their gold before the real crisis even begins, a rabshakeh's speech built to…

x: When Hezekiah hears the Rabshakeh's threats, he tears his clothes, goes into the temple, and sends his officials to Isaiah, who assures him that Sennacherib will hear a rumor, return home, and fall by the sword (vv. 1-7). Sennacherib, now fighting Libnah and warned of Tirhakah of Cush's approach, sends Hezekiah a letter repeating the threat (vv. 8-13). Hezekiah spreads the letter out before the LORD in the temple and prays that God would deliver Jerusalem so that all the kingdoms of the earth would know He alone is God (vv. 14-19). Isaiah responds with an oracle declaring that Sennacherib will not enter the city or even shoot an arrow at it, and that a remnant of Judah will yet take root and bear fruit (vv. 20-34). That night the angel of the LORD strikes down 185,000 in the Assyrian camp; Sennacherib withdraws to Nineveh, where his sons assassinate him while he worships his god, and…
h: The Letter Spread Before the LORD (vv.8-19)
The Destruction of the Assyrian Army (vv.35-37)
m: A message sent to Isaiah phrased as labor that cannot be completed rather than as a request for rescue, a letter spread out before the LORD rather than merely read, a prayer that concedes the enemy's own evidence instead of disputing it, Jerusalem personified as a virgin daughter mocking the very…

x: Hezekiah becomes deathly ill, and when Isaiah tells him to prepare to die, he prays and weeps, prompting the LORD to grant him fifteen more years of life and to confirm it with the sign of the sun's shadow retreating ten steps (vv. 1-11). When envoys from Merodach-baladan of Babylon arrive, Hezekiah foolishly shows them all his treasures and armory (vv. 12-13). Isaiah rebukes him, prophesying that everything in the palace, along with some of Hezekiah's own descendants, will one day be carried off to Babylon (vv. 14-18). Hezekiah accepts the word with relief that peace will last in his own lifetime, and the chapter closes by noting his engineering works, including the water tunnel, before his death and succession by his son Manasseh (vv. 19-21).
h: The Babylonian Envoys and the Sentence (vv.12-21)
m: A death sentence reversed before the prophet who delivered it has even left the middle court, weeping turned toward the wall answered with fifteen added years and a shadow moved backward as the sign, envoys shown every treasure in the house for no better reason than that they had heard the king was…

x: Manasseh becomes king of Judah at twelve and reigns fifty-five years, rebuilding the high places his father Hezekiah had destroyed, erecting altars to Baal and an Asherah pole inside the temple itself, worshiping the starry host, sacrificing his own son in the fire, and practicing sorcery and divination (vv. 1-9). Through his prophets the LORD declares that such disaster will fall on Jerusalem that the ears of all who hear of it will tingle, and that Judah will be measured by the same standard of judgment used against Samaria and the house of Ahab (vv. 10-15). Manasseh also fills Jerusalem with innocent blood, making his reign, along with his son and successor Amon's, the low point of Judah's kings; Amon reigns only two years before his own officials assassinate him, and the people of the land install his young son Josiah as king (vv. 16-26).
m: A fifty-five year reign, the longest of any king of Judah, judged the most wicked precisely because of what it undid, an Asherah image placed inside the very temple built to house the name of the LORD, judgment pronounced as irreversible, the line of Samaria and the plummet of Ahab's house applied…

x: Josiah becomes king of Judah at eight years old and reigns thirty-one years, doing what is right as David had (vv. 1-2). In the eighteenth year of his reign he sends Shaphan the secretary to oversee repairs to the temple, and during the work the high priest Hilkiah discovers the Book of the Law (vv. 3-8). When Shaphan reads it aloud to him, Josiah tears his clothes in alarm at how far Judah has strayed and orders the priests to inquire of the LORD about it (vv. 9-13). The prophetess Huldah confirms that disaster is indeed coming on Jerusalem for its idolatry, but because Josiah's heart was tender and he humbled himself before the LORD, she promises he will die in peace before he sees it (vv. 14-20).
h: Josiah, the Repairs, and the Book Found (vv.1-11)
m: A verdict with no qualification attached at all, turned not aside to the right hand or to the left, accounts left unaudited because the workmen dealt faithfully without needing to be checked, a book of the law found by accident in the middle of ordinary temple repairs, Huldah consulted rather than…

x: Josiah gathers the people and reads them the Book of the Covenant, renewing Judah's commitment to the LORD (vv. 1-3). He then leads the most sweeping reformation in Judah's history, removing idolatrous vessels and priests from the temple, tearing down the Asherah and the high places from Geba to Beersheba, defiling Topheth where children had been sacrificed, and destroying the altar at Bethel in fulfillment of an old prophecy (vv. 4-20). He celebrates a Passover unlike any kept since the days of the judges, and no king before or after him turned to the LORD with such wholehearted devotion (vv. 21-25). Yet the LORD's fierce anger against Judah does not relent because of the sins Manasseh had committed, and He resolves to remove Judah from His sight as He had Israel (vv. 26-27). Josiah is killed in battle against Pharaoh Necho at Megiddo, and the chapter closes with the brief, evil reigns…
h: Bethel, the Passover, and Josiah's Death (vv.15-37)
m: An entire book of the covenant read aloud to elders, priests, prophets and people together before a single reform begins, cleansing that starts inside the temple itself before it ever reaches the countryside, a three-hundred-fifty-year-old shrine built for Solomon's foreign wives finally torn down…

x: Jehoiakim becomes a vassal of Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon but later rebels, bringing raiding bands of Chaldeans, Arameans, Moabites, and Ammonites against Judah as the LORD's judgment for the innocent blood Manasseh had shed (vv. 1-7). His son Jehoiachin reigns only three months before Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem and he surrenders (vv. 8-12). Nebuchadnezzar strips the temple and palace of their treasures and deports Jehoiachin, the royal family, the officials, the craftsmen and smiths, and some ten thousand leading citizens to Babylon, leaving only the poorest people in the land (vv. 13-16). He installs Jehoiachin's uncle Mattaniah as a puppet king under the new name Zedekiah, who also does evil and eventually rebels against Babylon (vv. 17-20).
m: Rebellion against Babylon after three years of vassalage triggering raiders sent by the commandment of the LORD rather than mere political consequence, judgment traced explicitly back to Manasseh's innocent blood which the LORD would not pardon, an eighteen-year-old king surrendering along with his…

x: In Zedekiah's ninth year Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem, and by the eleventh year famine is so severe in the city that the wall is finally breached (vv. 1-4). Zedekiah flees but is captured near Jericho, forced to watch his sons executed, then blinded and taken in bronze shackles to Babylon (vv. 5-7). Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, burns the temple, the palace, and every great house in Jerusalem, tears down the city walls, and deports most of the remaining population, leaving only the poorest to work the land (vv. 8-12). He also carries off or breaks up all the temple's bronze, silver, and gold articles, including the great pillars and the bronze sea, and executes the chief priest Seraiah and other leading officials at Riblah (vv. 13-21). Gedaliah is appointed governor over those left in the land, but he is soon assassinated by Ishmael, and the remaining people flee to Egypt…
h: The Temple Plundered and the Aftermath (vv.13-30)
m: An eighteen-month siege ending in a breach and a king's flight by night through a garden gate, sons killed in front of Zedekiah as the last thing his own eyes ever see before they are put out, temple bronze and gold catalogued item by item in a grief that is almost liturgical in its detail, leaders…

x: The chapter opens with a rapid genealogy from Adam through Seth to Noah's three sons (vv. 1-4), then traces the nations descended from Japheth, Ham, and Shem, including Nimrod (v. 10) and the earth's division in Peleg's day (v. 19). The line narrows through Shem to Abraham (vv. 24-27), branches to the sons of Ishmael and Keturah (vv. 28-33), then settles on Isaac's sons Esau and Israel (v. 34). The remainder traces Esau's descendants and the clans of Seir (vv. 35-42), closing with the kings and chiefs who ruled Edom before Israel had a king (vv. 43-54), setting the covenant line within the wider sweep of world history.
h: The Sons of Japheth, Ham and Shem (vv.5-23)
Ishmael and the Sons of Keturah (vv.28-33)
Esau, and the Dukes of Edom (vv.34-54)
m: Ten generations from Adam to Noah covered in four verses with no dates and no narrative at all, a table of nations arranged in reverse order so the line that matters comes last, the whole human race narrowed to one man by verse twenty-seven through simple omission, Ishmael and Keturah's sons listed…

x: The chapter begins by naming the twelve sons of Israel (vv. 1-2), then focuses on Judah's line: Er's wickedness and death, and Tamar's sons Perez and Zerah (vv. 3-4). Perez's descendants are traced through Hezron and Ram down to Jesse and his sons, ending with David as the seventh and youngest, alongside his sisters Zeruiah and Abigail (vv. 5-17). The genealogy then follows Caleb and Hezron's other branches, including Machir of Gilead (vv. 18-24) and the line of Jerahmeel (vv. 25-41), and closes with further descendants of Caleb linked to towns such as Kiriath-jearim and Bethlehem, along with the Kenite clan of Rechab (vv. 42-55). The chapter's real interest is establishing David's ancestry within Judah's tribe.
h: The Sons of Israel, and the Sons of Judah (vv.1-8)
The Sons of Caleb, and Hezron's Line (vv.18-24)
m: Eleven tribes named in one sentence and set aside for six chapters so Judah can be taken up immediately, Er's wickedness and Tamar's deception recorded without being smoothed over in the first eight verses, nine verses carrying the entire line the whole book depends on, from Ram to Jesse to David…

x: The chapter lists David's sons born in Hebron, including Amnon, Absalom, and Adonijah, along with the length of his reigns there and in Jerusalem (vv. 1-4), then names his Jerusalem-born sons, including Solomon (vv. 5-9). The royal line is then traced in unbroken succession from Solomon through Rehoboam, Asa, Hezekiah, and Josiah (vv. 10-14), whose own sons include Jehoiakim and Zedekiah (v. 15). The chapter closes by following the line through the exile to Jeconiah and Zerubbabel (vv. 17-19) and on through several more post-exilic generations (vv. 20-24), preserving the Davidic, messianic line even after the monarchy's collapse.
h: The Line of Jeconiah After the Exile (vv.17-24)
m: David's sons divided by birthplace, Hebron and Jerusalem, with nothing recorded about what any of them did, fourteen reigns from Solomon to Josiah listed with no distinction made between the worst kings and the best, four sons of Josiah named in one place found nowhere else in scripture, Jeconiah…

x: Judah's family lines continue through Shobal, Ashhur of Tekoa, and Caleb's descendants (vv. 1-20), interrupted by Jabez's brief prayer asking God to bless him, enlarge his territory, and keep him from harm — a request God grants (vv. 9-10). The genealogy of Shelah's line and the guilds of linen workers and potters follows (vv. 21-23), then shifts to Simeon's much smaller tribe, listing its clans, cities such as Beersheba and Ziklag, and its slower growth compared to Judah (vv. 24-33). The chapter closes with Simeonite raids that displaced Hamite settlers near Gedor and Amalekites at Mount Seir, securing new pasturelands in Hezekiah's day (vv. 34-43).
m: Terse entries naming fathers of towns rather than fathers of sons throughout most of the chapter, a register that stops dead for two verses to quote a man's prayer by name, oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed and enlarge my coast, craftsmen and linen workers and potters recorded by trade rather…

x: The tribe of Reuben's genealogy opens with a note that his birthright passed to Joseph's sons because he defiled his father's bed, though the ruling scepter belonged to Judah (vv. 1-2). Reuben's descendants are traced down to Beerah, who was carried into exile by Assyria, and the tribe's settlements in Gilead are described (vv. 3-10).
