Gad's genealogy and territory in Bashan follow (vv. 11-17), then the combined forces of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh — over 44,000 warriors — defeat the Hagrites in battle because they trusted God (vv. 18-22). The chapter closes with the half-tribe of Manasseh's leaders and the sobering report that all three tribes were later exiled by Assyria for turning to idolatry (vv. 23-26).
m: A birthright forfeited in the opening verses and explained rather than merely noted, Reuben's line ending with a name carried away captive by Assyria, a war credited explicitly to prayer rather than to the numbers the register has just finished counting, because they put their trust in him, and the…

x: The chapter traces the tribe of Levi in detail, beginning with the sons of Levi - Gershon, Kohath, and Merari - and the family of Amram, whose children are Aaron, Moses, and Miriam (vv. 1-3). It follows the high priestly line from Aaron down through Zadok to Jehozadak, who goes into exile when the LORD hands Judah and Jerusalem over to Nebuchadnezzar (vv. 4-15). The wider Levitical genealogy is then repeated in more detail (vv. 16-30) before turning to the singers David appoints for the house of the LORD: Heman from the Kohathites, Asaph his kinsman from the Gershomites, and Ethan from the Merarites, each ministering with song before the tabernacle (vv. 31-48). Aaron and his descendants are set apart for the most holy duties, offering sacrifices and incense and making atonement for Israel (vv. 49-53). The chapter closes with a lengthy record of towns and pasturelands assigned to the…
h: The Line of the High Priests (vv.1-15)
m: Eighty-one verses, the longest genealogical chapter in the book, dedicated entirely to the tribe responsible for worship, twenty-three generations of high priests traced in one unbroken line from Aaron to the exile, Samuel placed inside the Kohathite Levites rather than in Ephraim where an earlier…

x: The chapter surveys several of Israel's less-prominent tribes: Issachar's clans and their large fighting force (vv. 1-5), Benjamin's descendants and their mighty warriors (vv. 6-11), and a brief notice of Naphtali (v. 13). Manasseh's genealogy through Machir and Gilead includes Zelophehad's daughters (vv. 14-19), while Ephraim's line records the deaths of two sons killed by raiders from Gath, Ephraim's mourning, and the birth of Beriah in the aftermath, along with his daughter Sheerah who built several towns (vv. 20-24). The chapter ends with Asher's descendants and fighting men, numbering 26,000 (vv. 30-40), rounding out the military strength of the tribes settled across the land.
h: Ephraim, and the Sons Slain at Gath (vv.20-29)
m: A chapter whose attention swings unevenly from one tribe to the next, Naphtali given a single verse while others receive whole genealogies, muster numbers embedded directly into a family tree as though compiling an army roster alongside a lineage, sons slain at Gath in a raid gone wrong recorded…

x: The chapter details Benjamin's genealogy beginning with Bela and his brothers (vv. 1-5), then traces family heads who settled in Geba, Moab, and Jerusalem, including the builders of Ono and Lod (vv. 6-28). It turns to the family of Gibeon, whose descendants include Ner, Kish, and ultimately King Saul and his son Jonathan (vv. 29-33). The line continues through Jonathan's son Merib-baal down through many generations to Azel's sons and the skilled archers of Ulam (vv. 34-40), preparing the reader for Saul's death narrated in chapter 10.
m: A second and far longer treatment of Benjamin than the tribe received in the previous chapter, families tracked by where they resettled and remarried after near destruction in Judges twenty, a list narrowing at last to one household, Kish and Saul and his four sons, Jonathan's own line followed ten…

x: The chapter opens by noting Israel's exile to Babylon for unfaithfulness before listing those who resettled Jerusalem after the return: laypeople from Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh (vv. 1-9), followed by the priests and their genealogies (vv. 10-13). The Levites are detailed next, including the singers, gatekeepers, and those responsible for the tabernacle's vessels, storerooms, and daily provisions such as the showbread and incense (vv. 14-34). The chapter closes by repeating the genealogy of Gibeon's family down to Saul and his sons (vv. 35-44), setting up the account of Saul's death in the following chapter.
m: A pivot clause turning nine chapters of descent into the reason for writing them at all, carried away to Babylon for their transgression, priests and Levites counted by name to establish exactly who may serve in a temple still being rebuilt, eighteen verses on gatekeeping alone, more than most…

x: The Philistines defeat Israel at Mount Gilboa, killing Saul's sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua before Saul, badly wounded by archers, takes his own life rather than be captured (vv. 1-5). With Saul's whole house dead, Israel abandons nearby towns and the Philistines occupy them (vv. 6-7). The Philistines strip Saul's body, display his armor in their temple, and fasten his head in the house of Dagon, until the men of Jabesh-gilead recover and bury the bones (vv. 8-12). The chapter closes with the Chronicler's verdict: Saul died for his unfaithfulness to the Lord and for consulting a medium instead of seeking God, so the kingdom turned to David (vv. 13-14).
m: A whole reign compressed into one chapter, the chapter in which the king dies, no anointing, no jealousy and no pursuit of David included at all, a body stripped and its head fastened in the temple of Dagon as a trophy of religious triumph, Jabesh-gilead's rescue of the bones told exactly as in the…

x: All Israel gathers to David at Hebron, recalling that the Lord had already appointed him shepherd of His people, and the elders anoint him king in a covenant before the Lord (vv. 1-3). David and his men capture the fortress of Jebus, renaming it the City of David after Joab leads the assault and becomes commander (vv. 4-9). The remainder of the chapter catalogs David's mighty men, headed by the exploits of his top three warriors — including the men who broke through Philistine lines to draw water from Bethlehem's well for David, who then poured it out to the Lord rather than drink it (vv. 10-19) — followed by Abishai, Benaiah, and the long roster of the Thirty (vv. 20-47).
h: The Three, and the Water of Bethlehem (vv.10-19)
The Roll of the Mighty Men (vv.20-47)
m: Seven years of civil war with the house of Saul omitted entirely so all Israel anoints David at once, a promotion offered to whoever takes Jerusalem first turning Joab into chief before a single battle is fought, three men breaking through a Philistine garrison for water David only longed for aloud…

x: The chapter lists the warriors who joined David during his outlaw years, beginning with ambidextrous Benjamite archers who came to him at Ziklag despite being kinsmen of Saul (vv. 1-7), followed by fierce Gadite fighters who crossed the flooded Jordan to reach him (vv. 8-15). When men of Benjamin and Judah arrive, David questions their intentions before Amasai, moved by the Spirit, pledges their loyalty and is made a captain (vv. 16-18); Manassites also defect to David's side (vv. 19-22). The chapter closes with a tribe-by-tribe census of the armies that gathered at Hebron to make David king over all Israel, totaling well over 300,000 men who celebrate together with food and drink (vv. 23-40).
m: A chapter with no parallel in Samuel added specifically to prove all Israel, not one tribe, supported David, Benjamites from Saul's own tribe defecting to the very man Saul was hunting, warriors of Issachar praised not for strength but for understanding the times, a host described as like the host…

x: David consults with Israel's leaders and the whole assembly agrees to bring the ark of God back from Kiriath-jearim, since it had been neglected during Saul's reign (vv. 1-4). As the procession moves the ark on a new cart with music and celebration, the oxen stumble and Uzza reaches out to steady it (vv. 8-9). The Lord strikes Uzza dead for touching the ark, and the place is named Perez-uzza; fearful and angry, David leaves the ark at the house of Obed-edom instead of bringing it to Jerusalem (vv. 10-13). The ark remains there three months, during which the Lord blesses Obed-edom's household (v. 14).
m: A decision to move the ark justified as a correction of Saul's own neglect, for we enquired not at it in the days of Saul, a new cart chosen anyway, the very method the Philistines once used and not the one the law prescribed, celebration described in full, singing, harps, cymbals and trumpets…

x: Hiram king of Tyre sends cedar, masons, and carpenters to build David a house, and David recognizes that the Lord has established his kingdom for the sake of Israel (vv. 1-2). David takes more wives and fathers additional sons in Jerusalem, whose names are listed, including Solomon (vv. 3-7). When the Philistines hear David is king and come seeking him, he inquires of God before each engagement: first defeating them at Baal-perazim and burning their abandoned idols (vv. 8-12), then striking them from Gibeon to Gezer after God instructs him to circle around and attack at the sound of marching in the treetops (vv. 13-16). David's fame spreads to every nation as the Lord brings fear of him upon them (v. 17).
m: Hiram's builders read as proof the LORD had confirmed David's kingdom for the people's sake rather than his own, thirteen sons listed at Jerusalem including Solomon with no mention at all of his mother, two Philistine battles both begun by asking rather than assuming the answer already known, a…

x: David prepares a tent for the ark in Jerusalem and, having learned from the earlier tragedy, insists that only Levites may carry it, as God commanded (vv. 1-2). He assembles the Levite clans under their chiefs and directs the priests and Levites to consecrate themselves for the task, acknowledging that the first attempt failed because they did not follow the prescribed order (vv. 3-15). Singers and musicians — Heman, Asaph, and Ethan — are appointed with cymbals, harps, and lyres, alongside gatekeepers and priests who sound trumpets before the ark (vv. 16-24). The ark is carried up to Jerusalem with sacrifices, shouting, and instruments, while Michal watches David dance before the Lord and despises him in her heart (vv. 25-29).
h: None Ought to Carry the Ark But the Levites (vv.1-15)
The Singers and the Order of the Procession (vv.16-24)
The Ark Comes Up, and Michal Despises (vv.25-29)
m: A second attempt that begins with research rather than repetition of the first mistake, the rule stated outright before it is followed, none ought to carry the ark of God but the Levites, four thousand priests and Levites gathered by family so the correction is executed rather than merely…

x: With the ark set in its tent, David offers burnt and peace offerings, blesses the people, and distributes bread, meat, and wine to every Israelite (vv. 1-3). He appoints Asaph and fellow Levites to minister before the ark with music and thanksgiving, giving them a psalm that calls Israel to remember God's wondrous works and His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (vv. 4-22). The psalm calls all the earth to declare God's glory, worship Him in holiness, and rejoice that the Lord reigns, closing with praise for His enduring mercy (vv. 23-36). David then leaves Asaph's family ministering before the ark in Jerusalem while Zadok and the priests continue sacrifices at the tabernacle in Gibeon, and all the people return home (vv. 37-43).
h: O Give Thanks Unto the LORD (vv.7-22)
Sing Unto the LORD, All the Earth (vv.23-36)
m: Bread, meat and wine distributed to every man and woman in Israel before a single note of the psalm is sung, a psalm delivered into Asaph's hand that readers of the Psalter will recognize almost word for word as Psalm 105, touch not mine anointed and do my prophets no harm read by exiles as a…

x: David tells the prophet Nathan he wants to build a house for the ark since he himself lives in a house of cedar, and Nathan initially encourages him (vv. 1-2). That night the Lord tells Nathan that David will not build Him a house; instead, God has always dwelt in a tent and will build David a house through his offspring, who will build the temple and receive an everlasting throne (vv. 3-14). Nathan reports this word to David exactly as given (v. 15). David responds with a prayer of humble astonishment, marveling that God would do such great things for him and his house and reaffirming God's unique covenant relationship with Israel (vv. 16-22), closing by asking the Lord to fulfill His promise and bless his house forever (vv. 23-27).
h: Thou Shalt Not Build Me an House (vv.1-6)
The Promise of a House and a Throne (vv.7-15)
Who Am I, O LORD God (vv.16-27)
m: An embarrassment about accommodation, I dwell in a house of cedars while the ark remains under curtains, corrected the same night Nathan first approved it, a question with a history attached, did I ever ask any judge why he had not built me a house of cedars, a wordplay on house turning David's…

x: David continues extending his kingdom through a string of military victories (v. 1). He subdues the Philistines, taking Gath from their control, then defeats Moab, whose people become tribute-paying servants (vv. 1-2). Marching north, he defeats Hadadezer king of Zobah, capturing chariots and horses; when the Syrians of Damascus come to Hadadezer's aid, David kills twenty-two thousand of them and makes both nations tributaries (vv. 3-6). He brings the captured gold and bronze to Jerusalem - bronze Solomon later uses for temple furnishings - and receives gifts from Tou king of Hamath, all of which David dedicates to the LORD (vv. 7-11). Abishai then strikes down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt, bringing Edom under garrison as well (vv. 12-13). The chapter closes noting that the LORD gives David victory wherever he goes and that he reigns with justice and equity, then…
h: Tou of Hamath, and David's Officers (vv.9-17)
m: Eight verses covering campaigns in four directions with the Chronicler's attention fixed on what came back rather than how the fighting went, temple furniture named directly, brass Solomon will later use for the sea and the pillars, taken from these very wars, a refrain repeated as the chapter's…

x: After Ammon's king Nahash dies, David sends envoys to console his son Hanun, but Hanun's officials wrongly suspect them of spying, so Hanun shaves the men and cuts off their robes before sending them home in disgrace (vv. 1-4). David tells the humiliated men to wait in Jericho until their beards grow back (v. 5). Realizing they have angered David, the Ammonites hire thousands of Aramean chariots and troops (vv. 6-7). Joab engages the Arameans while his brother Abishai faces the Ammonites, and both enemy forces flee before them (vv. 8-15). When the Arameans regroup under Hadadezer's general Shophach, David personally leads Israel across the Jordan, defeats them, and kills Shophach; Hadadezer's allies then make peace with David and refuse to help Ammon again (vv. 16-19).
h: Joab and Abishai Divide the Army (vv.6-15)
m: Condolences sent in genuine kindness reinterpreted by advisors as espionage before any war is declared, beards shaved and garments cut as a diplomatic insult severe enough to trigger a war on its own, a two-front battle answered by the best speech Joab gives anywhere, let the LORD do that which is…

x: In spring, the season when kings typically went to war, Joab leads Israel's army to besiege and destroy Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, while David stays behind in Jerusalem (v. 1). David takes the enormous crown from Ammon's king, claims a large amount of plunder, and subjects the city's people to forced labor, his policy toward all the Ammonite cities (vv. 2-3). The rest of the chapter recounts three later battles with the Philistines: Sibbekai kills the giant Sippai at Gezer (v. 4), Elhanan kills Goliath's brother Lahmi (v. 5), and David's nephew Jonathan kills a taunting six-fingered, six-toed giant at Gath (vv. 6-7). All these giants descend from the Rephaim of Gath and fall by the hand of David and his men (v. 8), echoing David's own earlier triumph over Goliath.
h: The Sons of the Giant at Gath (vv.4-8)
m: Three chapters of Bathsheba and Uriah in Samuel compressed to nothing at all here, the omission louder than anything the chapter actually records, David tarried at Jerusalem kept without the sentence that follows it in the other book, a crown weighing a talent of gold taken from Rabbah's king…

x: Satan incites David to census Israel and Judah over Joab's objections; Joab reluctantly complies, tallying over 1.1 million fighting men (vv. 1-6). Displeased, God strikes Israel, and David confesses his sin; the prophet Gad offers him a choice of three years of famine, three months of military defeat, or three days of plague (vv. 7-13). David chooses to fall into God's mercy, and a plague kills 70,000 before the LORD halts the destroying angel just as it reaches Jerusalem, standing at Ornan the Jebusite's threshing floor (vv. 14-15). Seeing the angel, David begs that judgment fall on him rather than the people (vv. 16-17). Following Gad's instruction, David buys the threshing floor at full price, refusing to offer God a sacrifice that costs him nothing, and builds an altar there; fire falls from heaven in answer, and the plague stops (vv. 18-27). David worships at this new site instead…
h: Satan Provoked David to Number Israel (vv.1-8)
m: Satan named outright as the one who provoked the census, a different opening clause than the parallel account in Samuel, Joab objecting and overruled anyway before Levi and Benjamin are quietly left out of his own count, three choices reduced to a preference about whose hand should hold the sword…

x: David declares that the site he has chosen will be the house of the LORD God and the altar of burnt offering for Israel (v. 1). He gathers foreign laborers to cut stone and stockpiles iron, bronze beyond measure, and cedar timber from the Sidonians and Tyrians, reasoning that Solomon is young and inexperienced and the house must be built with great magnificence, so he prepares all he can before his death (vv. 2-5). Summoning Solomon, David explains that he himself was barred from building the temple because he shed much blood in war, but that a son will be born to him who will be a man of peace - Solomon - to whom God will give rest from every enemy and an everlasting throne (vv. 6-10). David prays God will grant Solomon wisdom and discretion to keep the law, then reports the vast supplies of gold, silver, bronze, iron, timber, and stone he has already gathered along with skilled…
h: This Is the House of the LORD God (vv.1-5)
Thou Shalt Not Build, Solomon Shall (vv.6-16)
m: A site named in one sentence before David starts buying materials he will never use himself, a reason for the refusal given in David's own words nowhere else in scripture, thou hast shed blood abundantly and made great wars, a name explained as its own argument, Solomon, a man of rest, for a house…

x: Now old and full of years, David makes his son Solomon king over Israel (v. 1). He gathers the leaders of Israel, the priests, and the Levites, and numbers the Levites thirty years old and up at thirty-eight thousand, assigning twenty-four thousand to oversee the work of the house of the LORD, six thousand as officers and judges, four thousand as gatekeepers, and four thousand to praise the LORD with the instruments David has made (vv. 2-5). David then organizes the Levites into divisions according to the three sons of Levi - Gershon, Kohath, and Merari - listing the heads of their families (vv. 6-23). Because the ark now has a permanent resting place and the Levites no longer need to carry the tabernacle and its furnishings, the age for service is lowered from thirty to twenty (vv. 24-27). Their new duties are defined as assisting the sons of Aaron in the service of the temple courts…
h: The Levites from Thirty Years Old (vv.1-6)
The New Charge from Twenty Years Old (vv.24-32)
m: Thirty-eight thousand Levites numbered and divided by function rather than by tribe, irregular entries left uneven rather than rounded because the register is a working duty roster and not a composition, an age lowered from thirty to twenty explained by the job itself changing, the Levites shall no…

x: Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu die without children before their father, leaving Eleazar and Ithamar to serve as priests (vv. 1-2). David, together with Zadok from Eleazar's line and Ahimelech from Ithamar's, organizes the priesthood into twenty-four courses for their appointed service; because more leading men are found among Eleazar's descendants, sixteen heads of families are drawn from his line and eight from Ithamar's, with the order determined by casting lots and recorded by Shemaiah the scribe (vv. 3-6). The twenty-four lots are then listed by name, beginning with Jehoiarib and Jedaiah and continuing through Harim, Malchijah, Abijah, Jeshua, Immer, and the rest, establishing the fixed rotation by which each family enters the house of the LORD to serve (vv. 7-19). The chapter closes with a further list of the remaining Levites - descendants of Kohath and Merari - who likewise cast…
h: The Twenty-Four Courses of the Priests (vv.1-19)
The Rest of the Sons of Levi (vv.20-31)
m: Two of Aaron's four sons removed from the record in the first two verses for dying without children, a rota drawn by lot specifically to forestall any dispute over precedence, twenty-four courses established that were still running a thousand years later when Zechariah served in Luke's Gospel…

x: David and the army commanders set apart the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun to minister through music, prophesying with lyres, harps, and cymbals (v. 1). Asaph's sons serve under his direction; Jeduthun's sons give thanks and praise under their father's guidance; and Heman, described as the king's seer, is given fourteen sons and three daughters by God, all of whom join their father in the service of song (vv. 2-6). All of them are trained and skilled singers under their fathers' instruction for the service of the house of God, playing cymbals, harps, and lyres under the king's direction alongside Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman (v. 6). Counting these musicians together with their kinsmen skilled in song, the total comes to two hundred eighty-eight, and lots are cast for their order of service without regard to whether each was young or old, teacher or pupil (vv. 7-8). The remainder of…
h: The Twenty-Four Courses of the Singers (vv.9-31)
m: Musicians described three times in eight verses as prophesying with harps, psalteries and cymbals rather than merely playing them, Heman called the king's seer and credited with children serving under his own direction, two hundred eighty-eight singers organized into twenty-four courses mirroring…

x: This chapter organizes the temple's support staff into three groups. First, the descendants of Korah and Merari are listed as gatekeepers, including Obed-edom's unusually large and blessed family of sixty-two able men, and lots are cast to assign each family to a specific gate, east, north, south, and west, plus additional posts at the storehouse and causeway (vv. 1-19). Next, Levites are appointed as treasurers over the temple's treasuries and the dedicated gifts contributed from war plunder by David, Samuel, Saul, Abner, and Joab (vv. 20-28). Finally, Izharite and Hebronite Levites are appointed as officers and judges over Israel's civil and religious affairs on both sides of the Jordan, including 1,700 men over the western tribes and 2,700 over Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh in the east (vv. 29-32).
m: Gatekeepers organized by family and by reason, one man chosen specifically because he was a wise counselor, Obed-edom returning from chapter thirteen with sons the register credits directly to God's blessing on his house, a duty roster for the east, north, south and storehouse gates settled by lot…

x: This chapter catalogs David's military and administrative structure. Twelve army divisions of 24,000 men each rotate monthly guard duty under commanders including Jashobeam, Benaiah, and Asahel's son Zebadiah (vv. 1-15). A ruler is named over each of the twelve tribes (vv. 16-22), followed by a note that David never finished numbering men under twenty, trusting God's promise to multiply Israel like the stars, and that Joab's earlier census was left out of the official record because it brought divine wrath (vv. 23-24). Royal stewards are then listed over the king's treasuries, storehouses, farmland, vineyards, olive and sycamore groves, herds, camels, donkeys, and flocks (vv. 25-31). The chapter closes with David's inner circle of counselors and officials, including Jonathan, Ahithophel, Hushai, and Joab as army commander (vv. 32-34).
h: The Stewards of the King's Substance (vv.25-34)
m: An army organized as a rotating militia of twenty-four thousand a month rather than a standing force, commanders drawn directly from the mighty men who once took Jerusalem, two tribes missing from the list of princes with no explanation offered, a census admitted to have been left unfinished and…

x: David assembles all the officials of Israel at Jerusalem - tribal leaders, commanders, stewards, and mighty warriors - and tells them he had desired to build a house of rest for the ark, though God told him he could not since he was a man of war who had shed blood (vv. 1-3). He explains that God chose him from his father's house to be king, chose Judah as leader among the tribes, and among his own sons chose Solomon for the throne of the LORD's kingdom, promising an everlasting reign if he keeps God's commandments (vv. 4-7). David charges Israel and Solomon to observe all of God's commandments, urging Solomon to know God intimately and serve Him with a whole heart and willing mind, since the LORD searches every heart (vv. 8-10). He hands Solomon the detailed plan for the temple, which he says came to him by the LORD's own hand, covering its rooms, treasuries, courts, and the gold and…
h: Know Thou the God of Thy Father (vv.9-10)
The Pattern Given by the Spirit (vv.11-21)
m: An old and full-of-days king standing up on his own feet, a detail with visible effort in it, to deliver one final public speech, a refusal and its reason repeated in front of the whole assembly, thou hast been a man of war and hast shed blood, two verses to Solomon alone that are the sharpest…

x: David tells the assembly that Solomon is young and the work ahead is great, since the temple is not for man but for the LORD God, and that he has already provided vast quantities of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and precious stones from his own treasury out of devotion to God's house; he then asks who else will consecrate themselves to give willingly (vv. 1-5). The tribal and family leaders, commanders, and officials respond by giving generously, and the people rejoice at their wholehearted offering, as does David (vv. 6-9). David blesses the LORD before the assembly, praising His greatness and power, acknowledging that everything already belongs to Him, describing human life as fleeting as a shadow, and praying that God preserve this generosity in the people's hearts and give Solomon a whole heart to keep His commandments (vv. 10-19). The assembly worships and offers sacrifices the…
h: Blessed Be Thou, LORD God of Israel (vv.10-19)
Solomon Made King, and David's Death (vv.20-30)
m: A personal contribution offered first and described as proper good rather than royal treasury, willingly repeated three times in one verse to describe the mood of an entire assembly's giving, a prayer arguing that nothing given was ever truly theirs to begin with, all things come of thee and of…

x: Solomon is established as king with the Lord's favor, and he leads all Israel to the high place at Gibeon, where the tabernacle Moses built stood, though David had already brought the ark to Jerusalem (vv. 1-4). There Solomon offers a thousand burnt offerings on the bronze altar, and that night God appears to him, inviting him to ask for anything (vv. 5-7). Rather than requesting wealth, honor, or victory over his enemies, Solomon asks for wisdom and knowledge to govern God's people well (vv. 8-10). Pleased with this request, God grants him unmatched wisdom along with riches and honor surpassing any king before or after him (vv. 11-12). The chapter closes by describing Solomon's growing wealth and power - his chariots and horsemen, his abundance of silver, gold, and cedar, and his trade in horses and chariots with Egypt and neighboring kings (vv. 13-17).
h: Solomon at the Tabernacle in Gibeon (vv.1-6)
Chariots, Silver and the Horse Trade (vv.14-17)
m: Political intrigue from the opening chapters of Kings omitted entirely so Solomon's very first act is worship rather than politics, an explanation supplied for why the king sacrifices at Gibeon rather than in Jerusalem, an open question, ask what I shall give thee, answered by naming what has…

x: Solomon resolves to build a temple for the LORD's name and a palace for his own kingdom, conscripting a large workforce of burden-bearers, stonecutters, and overseers (vv. 1-2). He writes to Huram, king of Tyre, asking for the same help Huram once gave David, explaining that the temple must be great because Israel's God is greater than all gods, though no house can truly contain him (vv. 3-6). He requests a craftsman skilled in gold, silver, bronze, and dyed fabrics, plus cedar and other timber from Lebanon, offering generous payment in wheat, barley, wine, and oil (vv. 7-10). Huram replies with praise for Israel's God and sends the skilled craftsman Huram-abi, along with a plan to raft timber to Joppa (vv. 11-16). Solomon then numbers the foreign residents in the land, 153,600 in all, and assigns them as laborers, stonecutters, and overseers (vv. 17-18).
h: The Levy and the Letter to Huram (vv.1-10)
Huram's Answer and the Foreign Workforce (vv.11-18)
m: Two houses determined at once, one for the LORD and one for the king's own kingdom, with the labor counted before a single stone is cut, a letter to Huram built around a disclaimer, who is able to build him an house, seeing the heaven of heavens cannot contain him, a Gentile king's reply opening…

x: Solomon begins construction on Mount Moriah, at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, in the second month of his fourth year as king (vv. 1-2). The main hall measures sixty cubits by twenty, with a gold-covered porch towering above it (vv. 3-4). The interior is paneled and overlaid with fine gold, decorated with palm trees, chains, and precious stones, and cherubim are carved into the gold-covered walls (vv. 5-7). The Most Holy Place, a perfect twenty-cubit cube, is covered in six hundred talents of gold and holds two golden cherubim whose wings stretch the full width of the room (vv. 8-13). A blue, purple, and crimson veil embroidered with cherubim separates the space, and two great bronze pillars, decorated with chains and a hundred pomegranates, are set up at the entrance and named Jachin and Boaz (vv. 14-17).
h: The Site, and the Overlaying of the House (vv.1-7)
The Most Holy House, the Cherubim and the Two Pillars (vv.8-17)
m: A single verse tying three separate moments to one patch of ground, Moriah, the threshing floor and the temple now rising on it, a date given to the exact day construction began, cherubim twenty cubits across spanning the whole width of the holy place wing to wing, a veil worked with cherubim in…

x: Huram casts the temple's furnishings in bronze: a great altar twenty cubits square, and the massive round Sea, resting on twelve bronze oxen and rimmed with lily-shaped blossoms, holding about three thousand baths of water (vv. 1-5). Ten lavers are added for washing sacrifices, alongside ten golden lampstands, ten tables, and a hundred gold basins, set within the courts enclosed by bronze doors (vv. 6-9). Huram-abi completes the bronze work for Solomon — the two pillars with their capitals and four hundred pomegranates, the stands and basins, and the Sea with its oxen — casting it all in the clay ground between Succoth and Zeredah in such quantity that the weight of the bronze could not be calculated (vv. 10-18). Solomon then furnishes the interior with the gold altar, the tables for the bread of the Presence, the lampstands, and every lamp, tong, basin, and door made of pure gold (vv.…
h: The Brasen Altar, the Sea and the Lavers (vv.1-10)
Huram's Work Finished, and the Vessels of Gold (vv.11-22)
m: Furnishings listed by function starting in the courtyard, a bronze altar four times the area of the one it replaced, a distinction drawn precisely, lavers for washing what is offered and the sea for the priests to wash themselves, brass cast in the plain of Jordan in quantities the text declines to…

x: Solomon completes all the work for the house of the LORD and brings in the silver, gold, and vessels David had dedicated, placing them in the temple treasuries (v. 1). He assembles the elders, tribal heads, and leaders of Israel in Jerusalem to bring the ark up from Zion during the autumn feast, and the priests and Levites carry up the ark, the tent of meeting, and the holy vessels while Solomon and the whole congregation sacrifice sheep and oxen too many to count (vv. 2-6). The priests set the ark in its place beneath the outstretched wings of the cherubim in the Most Holy Place; its carrying poles are long enough to be seen from the Holy Place but not from outside, and nothing is inside the ark except the two tablets Moses placed there at Horeb (vv. 7-10). As the priests come out, the Levitical singers - Asaph, Heman, Jeduthun, and their relatives, dressed in fine linen with cymbals…
h: The Ark Brought Up to the Finished House (vv.1-10)
The Singers, the Trumpets and the Cloud (vv.11-14)
m: The one thing the whole building was for finally carried inside once construction is finished, staves left visible and an ark holding nothing but the two tables from Horeb offered as evidence rather than assertion, the division that opened the book, ark in one place and altar in another, resolved…

x: Solomon acknowledges that the LORD dwells in thick darkness even as he has built him a house to dwell in forever, then blesses the assembled congregation and recounts how God chose Jerusalem and David, and has now fulfilled his promise through Solomon by building the temple and placing the ark inside it (vv. 1-11). Standing on a bronze platform before the altar, he kneels with hands spread toward heaven and prays that God, who cannot truly be contained by any house, would still hear every prayer made toward this place (vv. 12-21). He asks God to judge disputes brought before the altar, to forgive and restore Israel after defeat, drought, famine, plague, or siege brought on by sin, and to hear even the prayers of foreigners and soldiers who pray toward the temple (vv. 22-35). Finally, he pleads that if the people are ever carried into captivity and repent, turning back toward Jerusalem…
h: The Prayer Begins, at the Brasen Scaffold (vv.12-21)
The Seven Cases Brought to This House (vv.22-35)
If They Sin and Are Carried Captive (vv.36-42)
m: A paradox stated to the assembly before the prayer even begins, the LORD hath said he would dwell in the thick darkness, yet I have built an house of habitation, a brasen scaffold supplied only by Chronicles for Solomon to kneel on before the whole congregation, a question left open rather than…

x: When Solomon finishes praying, fire falls from heaven to consume the offerings and the LORD's glory fills the temple so completely that the priests cannot enter, prompting the people to bow and worship, declaring God's mercy endures forever (vv. 1-3). Solomon and the people dedicate the house with an enormous sacrifice of 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep, and the priests and Levites minister with music and trumpets before all Israel (vv. 4-7). The dedication feast lasts seven days, followed by a solemn assembly, and the people go home rejoicing over God's goodness to David, Solomon, and Israel (vv. 8-11). The LORD appears to Solomon by night, promising that if his people humble themselves, pray, seek his face, and turn from wickedness, he will hear from heaven, forgive their sin, and heal their land (vv. 12-14). But he also warns that turning to other gods will bring uprooting from the…
h: Fire from Heaven, and the Dedication Feast (vv.1-11)
The Second Appearance, and What Was Promised (vv.12-18)
m: Fire from heaven reported only by Chronicles, consuming the offering the moment the prayer ends, twenty-two thousand oxen and a hundred twenty thousand sheep counted across seven days of dedication and seven of feasting, a nighttime answer opening with I have heard thy prayer before it ever reaches…

x: After twenty years spent building the temple and his own palace, Solomon rebuilds the cities Huram had given back to him, along with Tadmor, Hamath's store cities, and fortified towns such as Beth-horon and Baalath (vv. 1-6). He conscripts the surviving Canaanite peoples for forced labor but keeps Israelites as soldiers and officers rather than servants (vv. 7-10). He moves Pharaoh's daughter out of David's palace, judging it unfit for her because the ark of the LORD had been there, and he maintains the regular schedule of offerings and priestly and Levitical courses established by Moses and David (vv. 11-16). Finally, Solomon sends ships from Ezion-geber with Huram's experienced sailors to Ophir, bringing back four hundred fifty talents of gold (vv. 17-18).
h: Cities Built, Peoples Levied, and Pharaoh's Daughter (vv.1-11)
The Ordered Worship, and the Voyage to Ophir (vv.12-18)
m: Twenty years of building given a hard stop before the account turns to fortified cities and administration, foreign peoples made bondservants while Israelites serve only as soldiers and officers, a scruple only Chronicles keeps, Pharaoh's daughter moved out of David's own city because it was too…

x: The queen of Sheba comes to Jerusalem with a great caravan of spices, gold, and precious stones to test Solomon with hard questions, and finds that his wisdom exceeds even the report she had heard, leaving her breathless at his household, temple, and offerings (vv. 1-6). She blesses the LORD for setting Solomon on the throne to rule with justice, and gives him a vast gift of gold and spices before returning home (vv. 7-12). The chapter then catalogs Solomon's extraordinary wealth — annual gold income of 666 talents, gold shields and targets, an ivory throne overlaid with gold and flanked by lions, ships bringing exotic goods from Tarshish, and silver made as common as stone in Jerusalem (vv. 13-28). It closes by noting Solomon's other recorded acts and his forty-year reign, ending with his death and burial and the succession of his son Rehoboam (vv. 29-31).
h: The Weight of Gold and the Ivory Throne (vv.13-21)
Solomon's Renown, His Sources and His Death (vv.22-31)
m: A queen undone not by answers to her hard questions but by the ordinary arrangements, the seating, the food, the ascent to the house of the LORD, six hundred sixty-six talents of gold in one year with silver counted as nothing at all, an ivory throne with lions on its steps judged like none made in…

x: At Shechem, Israel asks the newly crowned Rehoboam to lighten the heavy labor and taxation Solomon had imposed, promising to serve him if he does (vv. 1-4). Rejecting the elders' advice to speak kindly to the people, Rehoboam instead follows his young advisors and threatens to make the burden even heavier, boasting that his little finger will be thicker than his father's waist (vv. 5-11). His harsh answer fulfills God's word spoken through Ahijah, and the ten northern tribes reject the house of David, stoning Rehoboam's labor officer and forcing the king to flee back to Jerusalem (vv. 12-18). Only Judah remains loyal to Rehoboam, and Israel's rebellion against David's line continues to the writer's own day (v. 19).
h: The Petition at Shechem, and the Two Counsels (vv.1-11)
The Rough Answer, and the Break (vv.12-19)
m: A coronation turned into a negotiation the moment Rehoboam arrives at Shechem instead of Jerusalem, two counsels offered, one treating loyalty as something bought with kindness and one escalating into a boast about scorpions, a narrator's own aside naming the cause of God behind a king's foolish…

x: Rehoboam musters 180,000 warriors from Judah and Benjamin to force Israel back under his rule, but the prophet Shemaiah delivers God's word forbidding the fight, since the division is the LORD's doing, and the king obeys (vv. 1-4). Rehoboam instead fortifies Judah, building up fifteen cities such as Bethlehem, Etam, Hebron, and Lachish, stocking them with supplies, shields, and spears (vv. 5-12). Priests and Levites, and other Israelites who set their hearts to seek the LORD, leave Jeroboam's kingdom and its idolatrous priesthood for Judah and Jerusalem, strengthening Rehoboam's realm for three years while it still walked in the way of David and Solomon (vv. 13-17). The chapter closes with Rehoboam's family details — his wives, especially his favorite Maachah, and his many children — including his choice of Abijah as his intended successor (vv. 18-23).
h: The War Called Off, and the Cities Fortified (vv.1-12)
The Priests and Levites Move South (vv.13-17)
The Household, and the Naming of an Heir (vv.18-23)
m: A hundred eighty thousand men mustered for reconquest and stopped by one prophetic word, this thing is done of me, fifteen cities fortified and named individually as the defensive policy chosen instead of war, priests and Levites migrating south in a story of movement rather than of royal policy…

x: Once Rehoboam's kingdom is secure, he and all Israel abandon the LORD's law, so in his fifth year God allows Shishak of Egypt to invade with a massive army and seize Judah's fortified cities before reaching Jerusalem (vv. 1-4). The prophet Shemaiah tells Rehoboam and the princes that they have been abandoned to Shishak because they abandoned the LORD, and when they humble themselves, God relents from full destruction, though he still lets Judah become subject to Egypt so they will know the difference between serving him and serving foreign kings (vv. 5-8). Shishak plunders the temple and palace treasures, including Solomon's gold shields, which Rehoboam replaces with bronze ones (vv. 9-11). Because Rehoboam humbled himself, some good remains in Judah, and the chapter closes with a summary of his seventeen-year reign, his failure to set his heart on seeking the LORD, and his death and…
h: Shishak Comes Up, and Shemaiah's Word (vv.1-8)
The Golden Shields Replaced with Brass (vv.9-16)
m: A verdict given before the invasion even starts, when Rehoboam had strengthened himself he forsook the law of the LORD, an Egyptian campaign whose record on a relief at Karnak makes this one of the earliest points where scripture and outside history touch, a prophetic principle stated plainly, ye…

x: When war breaks out between Abijah of Judah and Jeroboam of Israel, Abijah stands on Mount Zemaraim and calls out to Jeroboam and Israel's vastly larger army, arguing that the LORD gave the kingdom to David's line forever and that Israel's golden calves and unauthorized priests stand against God's covenant, while Judah still keeps proper priests, sacrifices, and the lampstand (vv. 1-12). Jeroboam sets an ambush behind Judah's army, but when Judah cries out to the LORD and the priests sound their trumpets, God routs Israel before them, and Judah kills five hundred thousand of Israel's chosen men (vv. 13-18). Judah prevails because they relied on the LORD, and Abijah captures Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron from Jeroboam, who never regains his strength and eventually dies at the LORD's hand (vv. 19-20). The chapter closes noting Abijah's many wives and children (v. 21).
h: The Ambush, the Cry and the Rout (vv.13-22)
m: Three verses in Kings expanded here into a full battlefield address that is the most compact statement of the book's own theology, a covenant of salt claimed for David's line before a single argument about the actual battle, an accusation aimed at worship rather than at politics, the sons of Aaron…

x: After Abijah's death, his son Asa reigns in a decade of peace, during which he removes foreign altars, high places, idols, and Asherah poles, and calls Judah to seek the LORD and keep his law (vv. 1-5). Using the years of rest, he builds fortified cities with walls and gates and raises a large army of spearmen and archers from Judah and Benjamin (vv. 6-8). When Zerah the Ethiopian invades with an enormous army and three hundred chariots, Asa cries out to the LORD for help, confessing that God can aid the weak against the mighty just as easily as the strong, and asking that no man prevail against him (vv. 9-11). The LORD strikes down the Ethiopians before Asa, and Judah pursues them, plundering the surrounding cities and carrying off vast flocks and camels before returning to Jerusalem (vv. 12-15).
h: Asa's Reforms, and the Quiet Years (vv.1-8)
Zerah the Ethiopian, and the Prayer at Mareshah (vv.9-15)
m: Ten years of rest spent on demolition and construction at once, a king's own words supplying the reasoning, let us build these cities while the land is yet before us because we have sought the LORD, an invading host counted at a million met by a prayer that argues from God's indifference to odds…

x: The Spirit of God comes on Azariah son of Oded, who meets Asa and warns that the LORD will be found by Judah only as long as they seek him, recalling the years Israel spent without the true God, a teaching priest, or the law, and the chaos that followed (vv. 1-7). Encouraged, Asa removes the detestable idols from Judah, Benjamin, and the towns he had taken from Ephraim, and repairs the altar of the LORD (v. 8). He gathers Judah, Benjamin, and many who had defected from Israel at Jerusalem, where they sacrifice from the plunder and enter a covenant to seek the LORD wholeheartedly, under penalty of death for refusal, sealing it with oaths, shouting, and trumpets (vv. 9-15). Asa also removes his grandmother Maachah as queen mother for making an idol, which he burns at the Kidron, and though the high places remain, his heart stays fully devoted to the LORD, bringing peace until his…
h: The Covenant at the Feast, and Maachah Deposed (vv.8-19)
m: A prophet meeting a returning army with a condition rather than a congratulation, the LORD is with you while ye be with him, judges-era chaos described as the alternative to seeking God, an oath sworn with a loud voice, shouting, trumpets and cornets after seven hundred oxen and seven thousand…

x: In his thirty-sixth year, Asa responds to Baasha's fortification of Ramah by paying Ben-hadad of Syria with treasury silver and gold to break his alliance with Israel, rather than trusting the Lord (vv. 1-6). The seer Hanani rebukes him for relying on Syria instead of God, who had shown Himself strong for Asa against the far larger Ethiopian army, and warns that wars will follow from now on (vv. 7-9). Enraged, Asa imprisons Hanani and oppresses some of his own people (v. 10). Two years later he grows severely diseased in his feet and again seeks physicians instead of the Lord, dying in his forty-first year and receiving an honored burial (vv. 12-14).
h: Hanani's Rebuke, and the Diseased Feet (vv.7-14)
m: A blocked road answered by treasury gold sent to buy a foreign alliance rather than by prayer, a strategy that works exactly as intended and is condemned anyway, a seer's rebuke built entirely on the king's own history, the Ethiopians and Libyans once defeated by a different reliance, the…

x: Jehoshaphat succeeds his father Asa and strengthens Judah's defenses against Israel, walking in David's early ways rather than seeking the Baals (vv. 1-4). Because the Lord establishes his kingdom, Judah brings him tribute and he grows wealthy and honored, removing high places and Asherah poles from the land (vv. 5-6). In his third year he sends officials, Levites, and priests throughout Judah's cities to teach the Book of the Law among the people (vv. 7-9). As a result, the fear of the Lord falls on the surrounding kingdoms so that none make war against him, and even Philistines and Arabians bring tribute (vv. 10-11). The chapter closes cataloging his fortified cities, storehouses, and the vast army of commanders serving him (vv. 12-19).
h: The Teaching Circuit, and the Fear on the Nations (vv.7-13)
m: A verdict given early, the LORD was with Jehoshaphat because he walked in the first ways of David his father, a qualifier, first, doing real work by pointing past both kings' later failures, a teaching circuit with no parallel in Kings, princes, Levites and priests carrying the book of the law…

x: Jehoshaphat, now allied by marriage with Ahab of Israel, travels to Samaria and is persuaded to join Ahab's campaign against Ramoth-gilead, though he first asks to inquire of the Lord (vv. 1-4). Ahab's four hundred prophets unanimously promise victory, but at Jehoshaphat's request the reluctant Micaiah is summoned and, despite pressure to agree with the others, predicts Israel scattered like sheep without a shepherd (vv. 5-16). Micaiah explains that a lying spirit sent by the Lord has deceived Ahab's prophets to lure him to his death, for which Zedekiah strikes him and Ahab has him imprisoned (vv. 18-27). Ahab disguises himself for battle, yet a stray arrow finds him anyway, and he dies that evening propped up in his chariot, exactly as Micaiah foretold (vv. 29-34).
h: The Alliance, and the Four Hundred Prophets (vv.1-11)
Micaiah, the Lying Spirit and the Prison (vv.12-27)
Ramoth-gilead, the Disguise and the Random Arrow (vv.28-34)
m: An alliance committed to before it is ever inquired about, I am as thou art and my people as thy people, spoken before any word from the LORD is sought, four hundred prophets unanimous against Micaiah's single dissent, a lying spirit that volunteers itself in a heavenly council as the explanation…

x: Jehoshaphat returns safely to Jerusalem, where the seer Jehu son of Hanani confronts him for allying with wicked Ahab and loving those who hate the Lord, though he commends him for removing the Asherah poles and seeking God (vv. 1-3). Jehoshaphat then travels among the people from Beersheba to Ephraim, turning their hearts back to the Lord, and appoints judges in every fortified city of Judah (vv. 4-5). He charges them to judge not for man but for the Lord, who shows no partiality and takes no bribes, urging them to act in the fear of the Lord (vv. 6-7). In Jerusalem he also establishes Levites, priests, and family heads to handle religious and royal disputes, instructing them to deal courageously and faithfully (vv. 8-11).
h: Jehu's Rebuke on the Road Home (vv.1-3)
m: A chapter with no parallel in Kings recording both a rebuke and a reform in the same breath, a question that names the sin directly, shouldest thou help the ungodly and love them that hate the LORD, a verdict deliberately mixed, nevertheless there are good things found in thee, judges charged with…

x: When the Moabites, Ammonites, and people from Mount Seir advance against Judah, Jehoshaphat is alarmed and proclaims a fast, gathering the nation to seek the Lord at the temple (vv. 1-4). He prays publicly, recalling God's past faithfulness to Israel and confessing that Judah has no power against this vast army, so their eyes are on Him alone (vv. 5-12). The Spirit comes upon the Levite Jahaziel, who announces that the battle belongs to God and Judah need only stand still and watch Him deliver them (vv. 14-17). The next morning, as singers go out praising the Lord ahead of the army, God sets the invading forces against one another until none survive, and Judah spends days gathering plunder at what becomes known as the Valley of Beracah (vv. 20-26). The chapter closes summarizing Jehoshaphat's generally faithful reign and his ill-advised shipbuilding alliance with wicked King Ahaziah of…
h: The Invasion, the Fast and Jehoshaphat's Prayer (vv.1-13)
The Singers Sent Out First, and the Valley of Berachah (vv.20-30)
The Reign Summed Up, and the Ships Broken (vv.31-37)
m: A king's fear named honestly before his response to it, Jehoshaphat feared and set himself to seek the LORD, a prayer built as a legal argument citing jurisdiction, promise and the irony of nations Israel was once forbidden to invade, an answer that reassigns the whole battle, the battle is not…

x: Jehoram succeeds his father Jehoshaphat and secures the throne by murdering all his brothers and some officials (vv. 1-4). He walks in the ways of Ahab's house through his marriage to Ahab's daughter, doing evil in the Lord's sight, though God preserves David's line because of His covenant (vv. 5-7). During his reign Edom and Libnah revolt from Judah's rule because he has forsaken the Lord (vv. 8-10). The prophet Elijah sends him a letter condemning his idolatry and the murder of his brothers, and predicting a plague on his family and a severe intestinal disease for himself (vv. 12-15). The Lord then stirs up Philistine and Arabian raiders who plunder the palace and carry off his sons and wives, and Jehoram dies in agony from the foretold disease after two years, unmourned and buried outside the tombs of the kings (vv. 16-20).
h: Jehoram Kills His Brothers, and Judah Follows Israel (vv.1-11)
Elijah's Letter, and a Death Without Mourning (vv.12-20)
m: Brothers given wealth and cities by their own father killed the moment the firstborn is strengthened enough to do it, a marriage explaining the whole direction of a reign, he had the daughter of Ahab to wife, a covenant with David alone keeping the book from reading as a simple ledger of what was…

x: After Arab raiders kill his older brothers, Ahaziah becomes king at a young age and follows the wicked counsel of his mother Athaliah and the house of Ahab (vv. 1-4). He joins Joram of Israel in battle against Hazael of Syria at Ramoth-gilead, and while visiting the wounded Joram in Jezreel he is caught up in Jehu's God-ordained purge of Ahab's house and is killed (vv. 5-9). When Athaliah learns her son is dead, she seizes power by destroying the rest of the royal family, but Ahaziah's infant son Joash is secretly rescued by his aunt Jehoshabeath and hidden in the temple for six years under Athaliah's usurped reign (vv. 10-12).
h: Ahaziah, and the House of Ahab's Counsel (vv.1-9)
Athaliah Destroys the Seed Royal, and Joash Is Hidden (vv.10-12)
m: A king reigning only because raiders had already killed every older brother who might have taken the throne first, a mother named outright as his counsellor to do wickedly, a numerical difference between this book and Kings that has never been fully resolved, a destruction credited to God for the…

x: In the seventh year of Athaliah's usurped reign, the priest Jehoiada makes a covenant with military commanders and gathers the Levites and family heads to Jerusalem to install the hidden young Joash as king (vv. 1-3). He organizes guards throughout the temple and palace, arms them with David's old weapons, and presents Joash publicly, anointing him and crowning him as the people acclaim their new king (vv. 4-11). When Athaliah hears the commotion and rushes to the temple crying treason, Jehoiada has her led out and executed away from the sanctuary (v. 15). He then renews the covenant between the Lord, the king, and the people, and the crowd tears down the temple of Baal and kills its priest (vv. 16-17). Jehoiada restores proper Levitical worship and gatekeeping, and Joash is enthroned amid citywide rejoicing and quiet (vv. 18-21).
h: The Covenant with the Captains, and the Crowning in the Temple (vv.1-11)
Athaliah's Cry, and the Covenant Renewed (vv.12-21)
m: An operation described as a national religious assembly here rather than the palace-guard coup of the parallel account in Kings, a covenant cited before any action is taken, the king's son shall reign as the LORD hath said of the sons of David, Athaliah's own cry, treason, treason, naming exactly…

x: Joash becomes king at seven and does what is right throughout the lifetime of the priest Jehoiada, who arranges his marriages (vv. 1-3). He orders the priests and Levites to collect funds for repairing the temple, and when they are slow to act he has a chest set up at the gate to gather the tax Moses had prescribed, funding a full restoration of the temple and its vessels (vv. 4-14). After Jehoiada dies at a very old age, the princes of Judah persuade Joash to abandon the temple for the worship of Asherah poles and idols, provoking God's wrath (vv. 17-18). When Jehoiada's son Zechariah, filled with the Spirit, denounces this apostasy, Joash has him stoned to death in the temple courtyard, showing no gratitude for his father's kindness (vv. 20-22). Judah is then defeated by a small Syrian force, and Joash, left badly wounded, is assassinated in his own bed by his own servants avenging…
h: The Chest at the Gate, and the House Repaired (vv.1-14)
Jehoiada Dies, and Zechariah Is Stoned in the Court (vv.15-22)
The Syrian Raid, and the King Killed in His Bed (vv.23-27)
m: A verdict bounded explicitly by another man's lifetime, right all the days of Jehoiada the priest, a first fundraising method that fails and the text says why without excusing anyone, the Levites hastened it not, a chest set outside that works because it removes the human middleman entirely, the…

x: Amaziah begins his reign doing what is right, though not wholeheartedly, executing his father's assassins but sparing their children in keeping with the Law of Moses (vv. 1-4). He musters Judah's army and hires a hundred thousand mercenaries from Israel, but a man of God warns him the Lord is not with Israel and he should dismiss them despite the money already paid (vv. 5-10). Trusting God's promise instead, Amaziah defeats Edom at the Valley of Salt, but afterward foolishly adopts the defeated nation's gods and worships them, provoking a prophet's rebuke that he silences by threat (vv. 11-16). Amaziah then rashly challenges Joash of Israel to battle despite Joash's warning parable, and Judah is routed at Beth-shemesh, with Jerusalem's wall broken down and the temple treasures plundered (vv. 17-24). He lives fifteen more years but is eventually assassinated in a conspiracy after he…
h: The Hired Israelites Sent Home, and the Valley of Salt (vv.1-13)
The Gods of Edom, and the Challenge to Joash (vv.14-28)
m: The book's most exact verdict, right in the sight of the LORD but not with a perfect heart, given before a single event of the chapter unfolds, murderers' children spared in deliberate obedience to a statute the text quotes directly, a hundred talents already spent on hired troops sent home anyway…

x: The people make the sixteen-year-old Uzziah king after his father Amaziah, and he reigns fifty-two years in Jerusalem, doing what is right in the eyes of the LORD as his father had done (vv. 1-4). He seeks God in the days of Zechariah, who instructs him in the fear of God, and as long as he seeks the LORD, God grants him success (v. 5). He wages successful war against the Philistines, tearing down the walls of Gath, Jabneh, and Ashdod and building new towns in their territory, and receives tribute from the Ammonites as his fame spreads to Egypt (vv. 6-8). He fortifies Jerusalem with towers, digs cisterns and builds towers in the wilderness for his herds, keeps farmers and vinedressers because he loves the soil, and raises a large trained army equipped with shields, spears, armor, and engines of war for shooting arrows and stones from the towers (vv. 9-15). But when he grows strong…
h: The Reign That Prospered, and the Engines on the Towers (vv.1-15)
The Censer in the Temple, and the Leprosy (vv.16-23)
m: Fifty-two years of prosperity tied explicitly to a duration rather than to a fixed character, as long as he sought the LORD, God made him to prosper, achievements itemized like a state record, broken cities, dug wells, an army of over three hundred thousand and engines invented for the towers, a…

x: Jotham becomes king at twenty-five and reigns sixteen years in Jerusalem, doing what is right before the Lord as his father Uzziah had done — but unlike Uzziah, he never enters the temple to burn incense, even though the people continue their corrupt ways (vv. 1-2). He builds the upper gate of the temple, does extensive work on the wall of Ophel, and constructs cities, forts, and towers throughout Judah's hill country and forests (vv. 3-4). He defeats the Ammonites in battle, and they pay him heavy tribute in silver, wheat, and barley for three years (v. 5). Jotham grows powerful because he orders his life before the Lord his God (v. 6), and the chapter closes noting his death and the succession of his son Ahaz (vv. 7-9).
h: Jotham's Accession, and the Line He Did Not Cross (vv.1-4)
The Ammonite Tribute, and a Verdict Without Qualification (vv.5-9)
m: One clause carrying an entire comparison to his father, right according to all that Uzziah did, howbeit he entered not into the temple of the LORD, a standing observation slipped in even during praise, the people did yet corruptly, Ammonite tribute specified for three years running as the chapter's…

x: Ahaz becomes king at twenty and reigns wickedly, walking in the ways of Israel's kings, casting metal images for the Baals, and even burning his own sons as offerings in the Valley of Ben-Hinnom, sacrificing on the high places and under every green tree (vv. 1-4). Because of this the Lord hands him over to the king of Syria and to Pekah of Israel, who kills 120,000 men of Judah in one day and carries off 200,000 captives (vv. 5-8). The prophet Oded confronts the returning army for their cruelty against their own kinsmen, and Ephraimite leaders intervene, clothing, feeding, and returning the captives to Jericho (vv. 9-15). Edom and the Philistines also raid Judah, and Ahaz's appeal to Assyria for help brings only further distress rather than relief (vv. 16-21). In his desperation Ahaz sacrifices to the very gods of Damascus that defeated him, shuts the temple doors, and sets up altars to…
h: Ahaz, the Defeats, and Oded's Word at Samaria (vv.1-15)
The Appeal to Assyria, and the Altar from Damascus (vv.16-27)
m: Child sacrifice in the valley of Hinnom named as the exact practice that once justified expelling the land's previous inhabitants, casualties given with a cause attached each time, because they had forsaken the LORD God of their fathers, an appeal to Assyria answered in four words, but he helped…

x: Hezekiah becomes king at twenty-five and immediately reopens and repairs the doors of the temple that his father Ahaz had shut (vv. 1-3). He summons the priests and Levites, telling them their fathers were unfaithful and brought disaster on Judah, and commands them to consecrate themselves and cleanse the temple of the uncleanness it has accumulated (vv. 4-11). The Levites respond eagerly, sanctifying the temple in sixteen days and reporting to Hezekiah that all its vessels have been cleansed and prepared before the Lord's altar (vv. 12-19). The king then leads the assembly in sin offerings and burnt offerings for the whole nation, restoring the singing and instruments established under David, while the people worship joyfully (vv. 20-30). The chapter closes with abundant freewill offerings brought by the people and rejoicing over how quickly God had prepared their hearts for this work…
h: The Doors Opened, and the Charge to the Levites (vv.1-11)
The Sin Offering for All Israel, and the Song Restored (vv.20-30)
More Offered Than the Priests Could Handle (vv.31-36)
m: Doors shut by a father reopened as the first act of a son's reign in its very first month, an instruction to the Levites paired with a diagnosis, our fathers have trespassed and turned away their faces from the habitation of the LORD, sixteen days dated precisely to carry the accumulated refuse of…

x: Hezekiah sends letters throughout Israel and Judah, including Ephraim and Manasseh, inviting everyone to Jerusalem to keep the Passover in the second month, since the priests were not yet consecrated in sufficient numbers and the people had not gathered in time for the usual date (vv. 1-5). Runners carry the king's appeal from town to town, urging the people to return to the Lord so He will show mercy to the remnant who escaped Assyria; most mock the messengers, but some from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humble themselves and come, and God gives Judah one heart to obey (vv. 6-12). A great crowd assembles in Jerusalem, tears down the city's remaining pagan altars, and keeps the Passover as the priests and Levites hurriedly sanctify themselves (vv. 13-17). Since many worshippers had not properly purified themselves, Hezekiah prays for the Lord to pardon those who seek Him sincerely, and…
h: The Letters Sent Through All Israel (vv.1-12)
The Passover Kept, and a Prayer for the Unprepared (vv.13-22)
m: A Passover kept a month late using a provision Numbers itself makes for exactly this case, letters sent into territory Assyria had already annexed inviting a shattered kingdom's remnant back to Jerusalem, an appeal built on catastrophe rather than on strength, turn again unto the LORD and he will…

x: Following the Passover, the people fan out across Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh, smashing sacred pillars, cutting down Asherah poles, and tearing down every high place and altar before returning home (v. 1). Hezekiah reorganizes the priests and Levites into divisions for offering sacrifices and leading worship at the temple, and dedicates his own resources for the regular offerings prescribed in the Law (vv. 2-3). He also commands the people of Jerusalem to support the priests and Levites, and they respond with such abundant firstfruits and tithes of grain, wine, oil, honey, and livestock that the gifts pile up in heaps for months (vv. 4-8). When Hezekiah asks about the surplus, the chief priest Azariah reports that since the offerings began, the priests have had more than enough and a great store remains (vv. 9-10). Hezekiah has storage chambers prepared and appoints Levite…
h: The Storehouses, the Distribution and the Verdict (vv.11-21)
m: A festival ending in demolition rather than dispersal, images broken and high places thrown down as far as Ephraim and Manasseh, giving encouraged with a stated purpose, that they might be encouraged in the law of the LORD, contributions piling in heaps for months faster than the system built to…

x: After Hezekiah's faithful reforms, Sennacherib of Assyria invades Judah's fortified cities, so Hezekiah blocks the outside water sources, repairs the walls, arms the people, and assures them that a greater power is with Judah than the arm of flesh backing Assyria (vv. 1-8). Sennacherib's messengers mock Hezekiah's trust in the Lord, boasting that no god of any nation has delivered its people from Assyria and insulting God directly in letters and shouted taunts (vv. 9-19). Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah cry out to heaven, and the Lord sends an angel who destroys the Assyrian camp, forcing Sennacherib to retreat home in shame, where his own sons later kill him (vv. 20-22). Hezekiah grows wealthy from the gifts that follow, but later becomes proud during an illness and the visit of Babylonian envoys, and God tests him before he humbles himself (vv. 24-31). The chapter closes noting his…
h: The Invasion, the Water Stopped and the Wall Built (vv.1-8)
The Assyrian Argument at the Wall (vv.9-19)
The Angel, and the Gifts Brought to Jerusalem (vv.20-23)
The Sickness, the Envoys, and What God Left Him to Learn (vv.24-33)
m: An invasion arriving after all Hezekiah's reforms rather than in place of them, faithfulness proving no immunity from trial, an Assyrian argument allowed to run at length because it is a genuinely good one, why should this god succeed where every other nation's god has failed, a religious reform…

x: Manasseh becomes king at twelve and undoes his father Hezekiah's reforms, rebuilding the high places, erecting altars to Baal and the host of heaven, and even placing a carved idol inside the temple itself (vv. 1-7). He sacrifices his own children in the fire, practices sorcery and divination, and leads Judah into worse evil than the nations the Lord had driven out before Israel, ignoring every warning (vv. 6-10). As judgment, the Assyrians capture him with hooks and chains and carry him to Babylon, where in his distress he humbles himself and prays to the Lord, who hears him and restores him to his kingdom (vv. 11-13). Recognizing that the Lord is God, Manasseh removes the foreign idols, rebuilds the Lord's altar, and orders Judah to serve Him, though the people continue sacrificing at the high places (vv. 15-17). His son Amon then reigns briefly but does not humble himself as his…
h: The Hooks, the Prayer and the Restoration (vv.10-17)
The Prayer Recorded, and Amon's Two Years (vv.18-25)
m: Fifty-five years, the longest reign of any king of Judah, spent cataloguing nine verses of exactly what it restored, a carved image set in the very house of which God had said, in Jerusalem shall my name be forever, a section found only in Chronicles that changes the whole shape of the reign…

x: Josiah becomes king at eight and reigns thirty-one years, doing right in the Lord's eyes without turning aside (vv. 1-2). At sixteen he begins seeking the God of his ancestor David, and at twenty he starts purging Judah and Jerusalem of high places, Asherah poles, and idols, extending the destruction as far as Naphtali before returning to Jerusalem (vv. 3-7). In his eighteenth year he sends officials to repair the temple, and the money collected is faithfully distributed to the workmen (vv. 8-13). While retrieving the funds, the priest Hilkiah discovers the Book of the Law and gives it to Shaphan the scribe, who reads it to the king (vv. 14-18). Hearing its words, Josiah tears his clothes in grief and sends a delegation to inquire of the Lord (vv. 19-21). They consult the prophetess Huldah, who confirms coming judgment on Judah but promises Josiah he will die in peace because his heart…
h: The Purge, and the Repair Begun (vv.1-13)
The Book Found, and the Clothes Torn (vv.14-21)
Huldah's Answer, and the Covenant Read to the People (vv.22-33)
m: A reform staged deliberately across three ages, seeking at sixteen, purging at twenty, repairing at twenty-six, a reach into territory no king of Judah had governed for a century, only possible because Assyrian power was already collapsing, a book found by accident during ordinary repair work and…

x: Josiah keeps a Passover to the Lord in Jerusalem, organizing the priests and Levites by their divisions according to the instructions of David and Solomon (vv. 1-6). He and his officials provide an enormous number of animals from the royal and private herds for the offerings, and the priests and Levites carry out the sacrifice and preparation with great care and order (vv. 7-15). The text notes that no Passover like it had been kept since the days of the prophet Samuel, making it the most carefully observed celebration among all the kings of Israel (vv. 18-19). Later, when Pharaoh Neco marches through the region to fight at Carchemish, Josiah unwisely goes out to intercept him despite Neco's warning that God had sent him and was not directed at Judah, and Josiah is fatally wounded by archers at Megiddo (vv. 20-23). He dies and is mourned deeply throughout Judah and Jerusalem, with…
h: The Passover Prepared, and the Provision for It (vv.1-9)
The Service Kept as It Had Not Been Since Samuel (vv.10-19)
Megiddo, and the Lamentations for Josiah (vv.20-27)
m: A single line quietly ending an era, no more shall there be a burden upon your shoulders, retiring the Levites' carrying duty for good, provisioning measured in numbers precisely because generosity is what is being counted, a service so procedural that everything being exactly where the writing…

x: Judah's final kings each reign briefly and badly: Jehoahaz is deposed by Egypt after three months, Jehoiakim is bound and taken by Nebuchadnezzar after doing evil for eleven years, and the boy king Jehoiachin is likewise carried to Babylon after only three months on the throne (vv. 1-10). Zedekiah, the last king, does evil, refuses to humble himself before the prophet Jeremiah, and rebels against Nebuchadnezzar despite having sworn loyalty to him in God's name (vv. 11-13). The priests and people compound the guilt by defiling the temple and mocking the messengers God repeatedly sends until there is no remedy left (vv. 14-16). The Lord finally hands them over to the Babylonians, who kill many in the temple, burn the city and its palaces, and carry the survivors and the temple's treasures into exile, fulfilling Jeremiah's prophecy of seventy years (vv. 17-21). The book ends on a note of…
h: The Messengers Mocked, and the Land Keeping Sabbath (vv.15-21)
Cyrus, and a Book That Ends on a Command to Go Up (vv.22-23)
m: Four kings compressed into twenty-three years, each installed and deposed at the convenience of whichever empire is nearest, an age given differently here than in the parallel account in Kings with neither book explaining the divergence, a compassion named as God's motive for sending messenger…

x: In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, the LORD fulfills Jeremiah's prophecy by stirring Cyrus to issue a decree freeing the Jewish exiles to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the Temple (vv. 1-4). God stirs the spirits of the heads of Judah, Benjamin, the priests, and the Levites to go up, while their neighbors strengthen their hands with silver, gold, goods, and freewill offerings (vv. 5-6). Cyrus also brings out the sacred Temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had carried off to Babylon, entrusting them to Sheshbazzar through the treasurer Mithredath (vv. 7-8), and the chapter closes with an inventory of 5,400 vessels restored to Jerusalem (vv. 9-11).
h: Those Whose Spirit God Had Raised (vv.5-6)
m: Jeremiah's seventy years reaching their term, a pagan emperor's spirit stirred to issue the decree, willing returnees rather than conscripts, and stolen vessels handed back by the hands that held them

x: Ezra records a census of the exiles who return from Babylon to Judah and Jerusalem under Zerubbabel's leadership, listing them by family, town of origin, and role (vv. 1-35). The priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants are counted separately, along with the descendants of Solomon's servants (vv. 36-58). Some families cannot prove their genealogical descent from Israel and are barred from serving as priests until a priest can consult the Urim and Thummim to settle the question (vv. 59-63). The whole assembly totals about 42,360 people, plus servants, singers, and livestock, and many of the leaders give generously toward rebuilding the temple once they arrive in Jerusalem (vv. 64-70).
h: The Register of Those Who Returned (vv.1-2)
Those Who Could Not Prove Their Genealogy (vv.59-70)
m: A register kept by name and family, organization by clan and then by town, a shortage of Levites that will recur, those unable to prove their descent, and giving offered before anything is built

x: When the seventh month arrives, the returned exiles gather in Jerusalem, and Jeshua and Zerubbabel rebuild the altar to resume burnt offerings despite their fear of the surrounding peoples (vv. 1-3). They keep the Feast of Tabernacles and reinstate the regular offerings, though the Temple's foundation is not yet laid (vv. 4-6). Builders are hired and materials brought from Sidon and Tyre, and in the second year the Levites are appointed to oversee the work (vv. 7-9). When the foundation is finally laid, priests and Levites praise the LORD with trumpets and cymbals as the people shout for joy, while older men who remember Solomon's Temple weep at the smaller sight, mingling grief and celebration (vv. 10-13).
h: Cedar from Lebanon, the Foundation Laid (vv.7-11)
m: An altar rebuilt before any walls or houses, the festival calendar restored before the building exists, cedar fetched from Lebanon as Solomon had, and weeping and shouting that could not be told apart

x: When the returned exiles begin rebuilding the temple, neighboring peoples ask to join the project, claiming to worship the same God, but Zerubbabel and the Jewish leaders refuse their help (vv. 1-3). In response, these adversaries discourage and intimidate the builders and bribe officials to obstruct the work throughout the reigns of Cyrus and into the reign of Darius (vv. 4-5). The chapter then jumps ahead to describe later opposition under Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes: enemies write a letter accusing Jerusalem of being a rebellious city that will stop paying tribute if rebuilt, and Artaxerxes orders the work halted by force (vv. 6-23). As a result, construction on the temple stops completely until the second year of Darius's reign (v. 24).
h: Weakening the Hands of the People (vv.4-5)
m: An offer of partnership refused on theological rather than ethnic grounds, hands deliberately weakened, true facts assembled into a misleading letter, and sixteen years of silence

x: Encouraged by the preaching of the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, Zerubbabel and Jeshua resume construction on the temple in Jerusalem without a fresh royal permit (vv. 1-2). The regional governor Tattenai and his colleague Shethar-bozenai arrive, question the elders about who authorized the rebuilding, and ask for the names of those in charge (vv. 3-4). Because God is watching over the elders, the officials do not stop the work outright but instead send King Darius a letter describing the project and recounting the Jews' explanation, that Cyrus originally decreed the temple be rebuilt and had its sacred vessels returned (vv. 5-16). The letter closes by asking Darius to search the royal archives and confirm whether Cyrus really issued that decree (v. 17).
h: We Are the Servants of the God of Heaven (vv.11-17)
m: Two prophets restarting what politics had stopped, a governor's enquiry that turns into vindication, an unusually fair official report, and elders who name their fathers' sin as part of their defense

x: Darius orders a search of the royal archives and finds Cyrus's original decree authorizing the Temple's rebuilding at Jerusalem, with its dimensions and funding specified (vv. 1-5). He commands the governor Tattenai to leave the work alone and fund it fully from the royal treasury, with severe penalties for interference (vv. 6-12). The elders finish the Temple, aided by the preaching of Haggai and Zechariah, completing it in the sixth year of Darius (vv. 13-15). The people dedicate it with sacrifices and joy, restore the priestly divisions, and celebrate Passover and Unleavened Bread, rejoicing that the LORD turned the king's heart toward them (vv. 16-22).
m: A decree found in the wrong archive, a hostile enquiry producing state funding, a temple finished seventy years after its destruction, twelve goats for twelve tribes when only two had returned, and a Passover kept

x: In the reign of Artaxerxes, Ezra the priest and scribe is introduced through his priestly genealogy tracing back to Aaron (vv. 1-6).
