He leads a company of Israelites, priests, Levites, and Temple servants on the four-month journey from Babylon to Jerusalem, because he had set his heart to study, obey, and teach the law of the LORD (vv. 7-10). Artaxerxes issues a letter granting Ezra authority to take silver, gold, and vessels to Jerusalem, draw funds from the royal treasury, exempt Temple personnel from taxation, and appoint judges to teach and enforce God's law (vv. 11-26). Ezra blesses the LORD for putting this favor in the king's heart and strengthening him to gather leaders for the journey (vv. 27-28).
h: Blessed Be the LORD God of Our Fathers (vv.27-28)
m: A genealogy traced to Aaron, a scribe who studied and did and then taught, royal authority granted beyond anything asked for, the hand of God named three times as the explanation, and a response that is doxology rather than triumph

x: Ezra lists the family heads and roughly 1,500 men who journeyed with him from Babylon (vv. 1-14). Finding no Levites among those gathered at the river Ahava, he sends for ministers to join the company (vv. 15-20). He proclaims a fast to seek God's protection for the journey, ashamed to ask the king for a military escort after declaring that God's hand is on those who seek him (vv. 21-23). Ezra entrusts the silver, gold, and sacred vessels to twelve chief priests, carefully weighing and recording everything as a holy offering (vv. 24-30). The company departs and God delivers them from ambush along the way; in Jerusalem the treasure is weighed again and found exact, and offerings are made to the LORD (vv. 31-36).
h: Those Who Went Up With Ezra (vv.1-14)
I Was Ashamed to Require Soldiers (vv.21-23)
Delivered from the Hand of the Enemy (vv.31-36)
m: A nine-hundred-mile journey with no escort, Levites recruited because none had volunteered, a fast called because asking for soldiers would contradict a public testimony, and treasure weighed out in front of witnesses

x: Ezra learns that the returned exiles, including priests and Levites, have intermarried with the surrounding pagan peoples and adopted their detestable practices (vv. 1-2). Devastated, he tears his garment, pulls out his hair, and sits appalled until the evening sacrifice, when he falls to his knees and prays (vv. 3-5). He confesses that Israel's guilt towers to the heavens, recalling how their ancestors' sins brought conquest and exile, and marvels that God has shown grace by leaving a remnant and restoring the Temple (vv. 6-9). He acknowledges that intermarrying with the peoples of the land now defies God's clear command through the prophets, and closes in humble shame, admitting that Israel stands guilty before the LORD with no excuse (vv. 10-15).
h: The Princes Chief in This Trespass (vv.1-2)
Our Iniquities Are Increased Over Our Head (vv.6-9)
Shall We Break Thy Commandments Again? (vv.10-15)
m: Intermarriage found among the leaders first, a prohibition about covenant loyalty rather than ancestry, a prayer that identifies with sin it did not commit, and a confession that asks for nothing

x: As Ezra weeps and confesses before the Temple, a large crowd of men, women, and children gathers around him in tears (v. 1). Shecaniah proposes a covenant to put away the foreign wives according to the law and urges Ezra to act, so Ezra makes the leaders swear to do it (vv. 2-5). A proclamation summons the exiles to Jerusalem within three days, on pain of forfeiting property and standing in the community (vv. 6-9). Given the size of the task and the winter rain, the assembly appoints leaders to examine each case at scheduled times over the following months (vv. 10-15). The investigation runs into the new year, and the chapter closes with a list of priests, Levites, singers, and other Israelites found guilty, who pledge to put away their wives (vv. 16-44).
h: Shecaniah: Yet Now There Is Hope (vv.1-4)
The Book Ends Without a Conclusion (v.44)
m: A remedy proposed by the people rather than imposed, a covenant made in the rain, cases examined one at a time over three months, 113 names recorded, and a book that stops without a conclusion

x: Nehemiah, serving as cupbearer to King Artaxerxes in the Persian capital of Susa, learns from his brother Hanani that Jerusalem's wall lies in ruins and its gates have been burned, leaving the returned exiles in disgrace (vv. 1-3). The news drives him to days of weeping, fasting, and prayer (v. 4). His prayer opens by praising God's covenant faithfulness, then moves into confession of Israel's sin and a plea for God to remember His promise to restore a repentant people (vv. 5-9). He closes by asking God to grant him success and favor with the king, since he serves as royal cupbearer (vv. 10-11).
m: A cupbearer with daily access to a king, news that arrives four months before anything is said about it, mourning before petition, and a prayer that quotes God's own promise back to him

x: Four months after hearing the news, Nehemiah's evident sorrow prompts King Artaxerxes to ask what is troubling him, and Nehemiah, after a quick prayer, requests letters granting safe passage and timber to rebuild Jerusalem's gates and walls (vv. 1-8). Arriving in Judah, he keeps his plans quiet at first and surveys the broken walls alone by night before revealing his intentions to the officials and people (vv. 11-16). He challenges the community to rebuild and end their disgrace, testifying that God's hand has been on him throughout, and the people respond with resolve to begin the work (vv. 17-18). When Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem mock the plan and accuse them of rebellion, Nehemiah answers that the God of heaven will grant success and that these outsiders have no claim in Jerusalem (vv. 19-20).
h: So I Prayed to the God of Heaven (vv.4-8)
Let Us Rise Up and Build (vv.17-20)
m: Sadness shown before a king at personal risk, a prayer lifted between a question and its answer, requests specific enough to prove months of planning, and a wall inspected at night before anyone is told

x: The rebuilding of Jerusalem's wall is recorded gate by gate and section by section, beginning at the Sheep Gate and proceeding around the entire circuit back to the Sheep Gate again (vv. 1-32). Priests, goldsmiths, perfumers, merchants, rulers, and even women are named among those who repaired specific stretches, often working near their own homes (vv. 8-12). Some sections receive extra praise for eager effort, while a few nobles are noted for not lending their shoulders to the work (v. 5). The chapter reads as an honor roll showing that rebuilding the wall was a shared project spanning every class and trade in the community.
h: Round the City, Gate by Gate (vv.6-15)
m: Forty teams named with the section each built, a high priest working alongside goldsmiths and perfumers, daughters recorded among the builders, men building opposite their own houses, and one group who would not work

x: Sanballat and Tobiah ridicule the rebuilding project, and Nehemiah responds by praying for God to turn their scorn back on them while the workers press on until the wall reaches half its height (vv. 1-6). When the surrounding enemies conspire to attack Jerusalem, Nehemiah again prays and posts an armed guard, steadying a people who have grown fearful and discouraged (vv. 7-14). From that point the builders work with a weapon in one hand and a tool in the other, with a trumpeter ready to rally them at the first sign of attack (vv. 15-18). Nehemiah has half the men stand guard while the rest labor, and no one removes their clothes at night as they stay ready to defend the city (vv. 19-23).
h: Mockery: Even a Fox Would Break It (vv.1-6)
The Strength of the Bearers Is Decayed (vv.10-14)
m: Opposition escalating from mockery to conspiracy to discouragement from within, prayer paired with a posted guard at every stage, families stationed by their own gaps, and a trowel in one hand with a weapon in the other

x: A crisis breaks out among the people as families mortgage their fields and sell their children into slavery just to buy food and pay the king's tax, while wealthy Jewish nobles charge them interest (vv. 1-5). Nehemiah becomes angry, confronts the nobles and officials publicly, and demands they return the confiscated fields, vineyards, and money along with the interest they have collected (vv. 6-11). The nobles agree and swear an oath before the priests to keep their promise, and Nehemiah symbolically shakes out his robe to picture what should happen to anyone who breaks it (vv. 12-13). He then describes his own example as governor, refusing the food allowance he was entitled to and instead feeding many at his own table for twelve years, out of reverence for God (vv. 14-19).
h: A Great Cry Against Their Brethren (vv.1-5)
Twelve Years Without the Governor's Allowance (vv.14-18)
Think Upon Me, My God, for Good (v.19)
m: Exploitation found inside the community while enemies waited outside, usury and debt-slavery among brothers, an assembly called against the nobles, and a governor who declined his allowance for twelve years

x: When Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem the Arabian hear that Nehemiah has finished the wall except for the gates, they invite him to a meeting in the plain of Ono, intending to harm him, but Nehemiah refuses four times, insisting he cannot leave the work he is doing (vv. 1-4). Sanballat then sends an open letter accusing him of plotting rebellion and wanting to be king, hoping to frighten him into stopping, but Nehemiah denies the charge and prays for strength (vv. 5-9). The hired prophet Shemaiah urges Nehemiah to hide in the temple to save his life, but Nehemiah recognizes the scheme as a trap meant to discredit him and refuses, asking God to remember Tobiah, Sanballat, and the prophetess Noadiah for their intimidation (vv. 10-14). The wall is completed in just fifty-two days, and the surrounding nations lose confidence, recognizing that the work was accomplished by God (vv. 15-16). The…
h: Four Invitations to the Plain of Ono (vv.1-4)
m: Four invitations to a meeting that was an ambush, an open letter designed to be read by others, a prophet paid to give bad counsel, a refusal that names the work as the reason, and fifty-two days

x: With the wall finished, Nehemiah appoints gatekeepers, singers, and Levites, and puts his brother Hanani and the commander Hananiah in charge of Jerusalem, instructing them to keep the gates shut until well after sunrise (vv. 1-3). Because the city is large but still thinly populated, Nehemiah is prompted by God to gather the nobles, officials, and people for registration, and he finds the genealogical record of those who first returned from exile under Zerubbabel (vv. 4-5). The rest of the chapter reproduces that list — priests, Levites, temple servants, and lay families identified by clan and hometown — along with the totals of livestock, servants, and gifts given toward the work (vv. 6-73). The record establishes who legitimately belongs to the restored covenant community before the population of Jerusalem is addressed in chapter 11.
h: Gatekeepers, Singers and a Delegated Command (vv.1-4)
m: A wall finished and a city still empty, command delegated to two men, a register recovered rather than compiled, descent that some could not prove, and giving recorded by household

x: The people gather as one at the Water Gate and ask Ezra to bring out the Book of the Law, which he reads aloud from a wooden platform from early morning until midday while the Levites move through the crowd explaining its meaning (vv. 1-8). Hearing the Law read plainly, the people weep, but Nehemiah, Ezra, and the Levites tell them not to grieve because the day is holy and the joy of the Lord is their strength (vv. 9-12). The next day the family heads study further with Ezra and discover the command to keep the Feast of Booths, so the people build shelters and celebrate with a joy not seen since the days of Joshua (vv. 13-17). The Law is read publicly each day of the festival, closing with a solemn assembly on the eighth day (v. 18).
h: Bring the Book: The People Ask (vv.1-6)
The Joy of the LORD Is Your Strength (vv.9-12)
m: A book asked for rather than imposed, six hours of reading from a wooden platform, Levites who gave the sense, weeping redirected into feasting, and a feast kept as it had not been since Joshua

x: Two days later the people assemble again in fasting and sackcloth, confessing their sins and the sins of their ancestors as the Law is read for a quarter of the day and confession and worship fill another quarter (vv. 1-3). The Levites lead a sweeping prayer that retraces God's faithfulness from creation through the call of Abraham, the exodus from Egypt, the giving of the Law at Sinai, and the wilderness years into the conquest of the land (vv. 5-25). It then traces a repeated cycle in the time of the judges and kings: the people rebel, God disciplines them through their enemies, they cry out, and He mercifully delivers them, again and again (vv. 26-31). The prayer closes by acknowledging that God has been just in bringing the hardship of exile and continued foreign rule on them because of their unfaithfulness, even as they still live as servants in their own land (vv. 32-37), and on…
m: The longest prayer in the Old Testament, history recited as a cycle of faithfulness against rebellion, God called ready to pardon in the middle of the indictment, justice conceded to be on God's side, and a covenant proposed at the end

x: The document is sealed first by Nehemiah and a long list of priests, Levites, and leaders, followed by the rest of the people who join them in a binding oath to follow God's Law given through Moses (vv. 1-29). They pledge specifically not to intermarry with the surrounding peoples, to honor the Sabbath by refusing to trade on it, and to observe the sabbatical year by forgiving debts every seventh year (vv. 30-31). The community also commits to fund the temple with an annual tax, a rotation for supplying wood for the altar, and the firstfruits and tithes required by the Law (vv. 32-37). Levites are assigned to collect the tithes, and the people conclude with a shared resolve not to neglect the house of their God (vv. 38-39).
h: Levites and Chiefs of the People (vv.9-27)
Entering into a Curse and an Oath (vv.28-31)
We Will Not Forsake the House of Our God (vv.32-39)
m: A covenant signed rather than felt, eighty-four names beginning with the governor, commitments itemized down to firewood, nothing new legislated, and a motto that closes the document

x: Since Jerusalem needs residents to match its rebuilt walls, the leaders already live there while the rest of the people cast lots so that one in ten families relocates to the holy city, and the community blesses those who volunteer to go (vv. 1-2). The chapter then lists the heads of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin who settled in Jerusalem, along with the priests, Levites, gatekeepers, and temple servants stationed there for worship (vv. 3-24). A final section records the towns and villages throughout the countryside where the remaining people of Judah and Benjamin continued to live, from Beersheba in the south to the Valley of Hinnom (vv. 25-36).
h: The Chief of the Province in Jerusalem (vv.3-19)
The Villages of Judah and Benjamin (vv.25-36)
m: A fortified city that nobody wanted to live in, one household in ten brought by lot, volunteers blessed publicly, inhabitants recorded by role, and a survey of the countryside from Beersheba northward

x: The chapter opens with genealogical lists of the priests and Levites who served from the days of Zerubbabel down through the high priesthood of Jaddua, preserving the record of who ministered at each generation (vv. 1-26). For the dedication of the completed wall, the Levites and singers are gathered from throughout the region and the priests and people purify themselves, the wall, and the gates (vv. 27-30). Nehemiah then sends two great choirs in opposite directions along the top of the wall, each followed by leaders and musicians, until both processions meet at the temple to offer sacrifices and rejoice (vv. 31-42). The celebration is marked by such great joy, with women and children joining in, that the sound is heard far outside the city, and the chapter closes with men appointed to manage the storerooms for tithes and offerings that support the priests, Levites, singers, and…
h: The Joy of Jerusalem Heard Afar Off (vv.40-43)
m: Genealogies establishing unbroken service across generations, two choirs marching opposite ways along the top of the wall, a rampart once dismissed as fox-work carrying processions, joy audible at a distance, and storerooms organized for what comes after

x: When the Book of Moses is read publicly, the people learn that Ammonites and Moabites are permanently barred from the assembly for their past hostility, and Israel separates itself from all foreigners (vv. 1-3). Nehemiah, returning from a stay in Persia, discovers that the priest Eliashib has given Tobiah a room in the temple courts once used for offerings and tithes, and he angrily throws out Tobiah's belongings and restores the chamber (vv. 4-9). He also finds the Levites unsupported and their temple duties abandoned, so he rebukes the officials, restores their provisions, and appoints trustworthy treasurers (vv. 10-14). Seeing merchants trading and people treading winepresses on the Sabbath, Nehemiah rebukes the nobles, shuts the city gates before each Sabbath, and threatens force against traders who linger outside the walls (vv. 15-22). He confronts men who have married foreign…
h: Read in the Book of Moses (vv.1-3)
The Levites Gone to Their Fields (vv.10-14)
Shut the Gates Before the Sabbath (vv.15-22)
m: A return that finds every commitment broken, an enemy housed in the temple storeroom, Levites gone back to their fields for lack of support, gates shut before the Sabbath, and a book that ends asking to be remembered

x: King Ahasuerus, ruling over 127 provinces from India to Cush, holds a lavish 180-day display of his kingdom's wealth in the third year of his reign, followed by a seven-day banquet for all the people of Susa with wine flowing freely (vv. 1-8). Queen Vashti hosts a separate feast for the women, and on the last day, the king, merry with wine, sends for her to display her beauty before his guests wearing her royal crown (vv. 9-11). When Vashti refuses to come, the king becomes furious and consults his legal advisors on how to respond (vv. 12-15). Memucan warns that Vashti's defiance will embolden wives throughout the empire to despise their husbands, and urges the king to issue an irrevocable decree removing her as queen and giving her position to someone else (vv. 16-19). The king agrees, and letters go out across the empire declaring that every man should rule his own household (vv.…
h: The King's Feasts: 180 Days and Seven (vv.1-9)
Memucan's Counsel and the Irrevocable Decree (vv.13-20)
The Letters Sent to Every Province (vv.21-22)
m: An empire displayed over 180 days, a queen who refuses a summons, advisers who turn a domestic quarrel into imperial policy, and a vacancy created without anyone intending it

x: After his anger cools, King Ahasuerus's attendants propose a search for a new queen by gathering beautiful young women from across the empire (vv. 1-4). Among them is Esther, a Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai, a descendant of exiles from Jerusalem, who instructs her not to reveal her Jewish identity (vv. 5-10). Esther wins favor with Hegai, the keeper of the king's harem, and receives special treatment as she and the other candidates undergo months of preparation before appearing before the king (vv. 8-9, 12-14). When her turn comes, Esther pleases everyone who sees her, and the king loves her more than any other woman, crowning her queen in the seventh year of his reign (vv. 15-17). Mordecai continues watching over her from his post at the king's gate, still keeping her heritage secret, and there uncovers a plot by two royal chamberlains to assassinate the king (vv. 19-21).…
h: A Search for a New Queen (vv.1-4)
m: A search conducted across 127 provinces, a Benjaminite of Saul's line raising his orphaned cousin, a Hebrew name kept hidden behind a Persian one, and a loyalty recorded and then forgotten

x: After Haman is promoted above all the king's officials, Mordecai alone refuses to bow to him, revealing that he is a Jew, which enrages Haman enough to plot the destruction of Mordecai's entire people rather than Mordecai alone (vv. 1-6). Lots (Pur) are cast to select a date for the massacre, landing on the thirteenth of Adar (v. 7). Haman tells the king that a certain people scattered through the provinces refuse to obey his laws and offers a huge sum of silver for their destruction; the king hands over his signet ring and gives Haman free rein to deal with them as he wishes (vv. 8-11). A decree is drafted, sealed, and sent to every province, ordering the annihilation of all Jews — young and old, women and children — on that single day, while the city of Susa is thrown into confusion even as the king and Haman sit down to drink (vv. 12-15).
h: The Lot Cast, the King Bought (vv.7-11)
Letters Sealed with the King's Ring (vv.12-15)
m: An old enmity revived between Amalek and the house of Saul, one man's refusal answered with a plan to kill a nation, a lot cast to choose the day, and a king who sells a people without asking who they are

x: When Mordecai learns of Haman's decree to destroy the Jews, he tears his clothes and mourns publicly in sackcloth and ashes. He sends word to Esther urging her to approach the king on behalf of her people, warning that deliverance will come from elsewhere if she stays silent, and suggesting that she may have been placed in her royal position for exactly this moment (vv. 13-14). Esther agrees to go to the king uninvited — a potentially fatal risk — but first asks Mordecai to gather all the Jews of Susa to fast with her for three days (vv. 15-17).
h: Mordecai in Sackcloth at the Gate (vv.1-3)
Esther Sends Clothes; Hathach Sends Word (vv.4-9)
Who Knoweth Whether Thou Art Come for Such a Time (vv.10-14)
m: Public mourning in every province, a queen insulated from the crisis until told, position reframed as responsibility rather than safety, and a decision made without any guarantee

x: On the third day, Esther approaches the king's inner court uninvited, risking her life, but he extends his golden scepter and grants her favor, inviting her to name any request (vv. 1-3). Rather than stating her petition, she invites the king and Haman to a banquet that day, and there again defers, asking them to return the next day for a second banquet (vv. 4-8). Haman leaves the first banquet elated, but his joy turns to fury when he passes Mordecai at the king's gate and Mordecai still refuses to honor him (v. 9). At home, Haman boasts to his wife Zeresh and friends about his wealth, his many sons, and his unique invitation to Esther's banquets, yet admits none of it satisfies him as long as Mordecai remains unpunished (vv. 10-13). Zeresh and his friends suggest building a gallows seventy-five feet high and asking the king to hang Mordecai on it the next morning; pleased with the…
m: Three days of fasting before one step through a door, a scepter held out, a request deferred twice for no stated reason, and a man whose triumph is ruined by the sight of one unbowed head

x: Unable to sleep, the king orders the royal chronicles read aloud and learns that Mordecai once exposed a plot against his life yet was never rewarded (vv. 1-3). Just as Haman arrives to ask permission to hang Mordecai, the king asks him what should be done for a man the king wishes to honor; assuming he means himself, Haman describes an elaborate public honor — royal robes, a royal horse, and a procession through the city (vv. 4-9). To his horror, the king commands Haman himself to carry out this honor for Mordecai, and Haman complies before rushing home in humiliation (vv. 10-11). His wife and advisers warn him that his downfall before Mordecai has begun, and as they speak the king's attendants arrive to summon Haman to Esther's second banquet (vv. 12-14).
m: A king who cannot sleep, a chronicle read at random, a reward twelve years overdue, a question answered by the wrong man about himself, and an enemy made to lead the horse

x: At Esther's second banquet, the king again asks what she wishes, and Esther finally reveals that she and her people have been sold for destruction, explaining that she would have stayed silent over mere slavery but not over annihilation (vv. 1-4). When the king demands to know who is responsible, Esther identifies Haman as the enemy standing before them, terrifying him (vv. 5-6). The king storms out in anger, and when he returns to find Haman fallen across Esther's couch pleading for his life, he interprets it as an assault on the queen (vv. 7-8). Learning of the gallows Haman built for Mordecai, the king orders Haman hanged on it, and his wrath is satisfied (vv. 9-10).
h: The Second Banquet: Let My Life Be Given Me (vv.1-4)
Who Is He, and Where Is He? (vv.5-6)
Haman Falls at the Queen's Feet (vv.7-8)
m: A petition that finally names its subject, a queen revealing she is among the condemned, a king's fury turned on his favorite, and a gallows used by the man who built it

x: King Ahasuerus gives Esther the estate of Haman, and when she reveals Mordecai's relation to her, the king grants him the royal signet ring he had taken back from Haman (vv. 1-2). Esther falls at the king's feet weeping and pleads again for her people, asking him to revoke Haman's plot against the Jews (vv. 3-6). Since a decree sealed with the king's ring cannot be legally reversed under Persian law, the king authorizes Esther and Mordecai to write a new edict in his name to counter it (vv. 7-8). Royal scribes draft the decree in the languages of every province, and couriers carry it on swift horses throughout the empire, granting the Jews the right to assemble and defend themselves, destroying any armed force that attacks them on the thirteenth day of Adar, the very day set for their destruction (vv. 9-14). Mordecai leaves the palace in royal robes as the city of Susa shouts for joy…
h: Haman's House and the King's Ring (vv.1-2)
Write Ye Also for the Jews (vv.7-12)
Couriers on Royal Horses; Susa Rejoices (vv.13-17)
m: A signet ring changing hands, Persian law that cannot be repealed and must be answered instead, couriers sent on royal horses, and a city that had been perplexed now rejoicing

x: On the very day set for their destruction, the tables turn and the Jews gain mastery over their enemies throughout the provinces, aided by officials who now fear Mordecai's growing power (vv. 1-4). In Susa the Jews kill five hundred men along with Haman's ten sons, and throughout the empire tens of thousands more, while taking no plunder (vv. 5-10, 16). At Esther's request the king grants the Jews of Susa a second day to act and orders Haman's sons' bodies hanged publicly (vv. 11-15). Mordecai then writes to establish the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar as an annual celebration of feasting and gift-giving called Purim, named after the "pur," or lot, Haman cast to set the day of destruction (vv. 17-28). Esther and Mordecai confirm this observance with full royal authority as a lasting institution (vv. 29-32).
h: Five Hundred in Susa, and Haman's Ten Sons (vv.6-10)
m: The appointed day turned inside out, plunder authorized and three times refused, a second day requested in Susa, and a festival named after the lot that was meant to destroy them

x: The book closes briefly, noting that King Ahasuerus levied tribute across his empire, including the coastlands, and that his acts and the full account of Mordecai's greatness are recorded in the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia (vv. 1-2). Mordecai is described as second in rank only to the king, esteemed among the Jews and popular with his people, using his position to seek their welfare and speak peace to all his descendants (v. 3).
m: A three-verse epilogue, a reader pointed to the Persian chronicles for verification, and a book that opens with a king displaying his own glory closing with a man seeking the good of his people

x: The narrator introduces Job, a man from the land of Uz who is blameless, upright, and extraordinarily wealthy, with seven sons, three daughters, and vast flocks and herds (vv. 1-3). His sons take turns hosting feasts, and Job regularly offers sacrifices afterward in case they sinned in their hearts (vv. 4-5). In a heavenly scene, God points out Job's righteousness to Satan, who counters that Job only serves God because of his blessings and asks permission to test him (vv. 6-11). God allows Satan to strike everything Job owns, but not Job himself (v. 12). Four messengers arrive in rapid succession reporting the loss of his oxen, donkeys, sheep, camels, and finally all ten of his children in a collapsing house (vv. 13-19). Job tears his robe, shaves his head, and falls down worshiping, blessing the Lord's name rather than cursing him, and does not sin in all of this (vv. 20-22).
m: four descriptive words, perfect, upright, God-fearing and evil-avoiding, applied at once to introduce a man before a single event happens to him, a heavenly council convened where God himself raises Job's name to Satan rather than the reverse, an accusation reduced to a single transactional…
d: Satan Takes Job's Property and Children (vv13–22)

x: The scene shifts back to the heavenly court, where Satan again presents himself before the Lord, who commends Job's continued integrity even though Satan incited him against Job without cause (vv. 1-3). Satan argues that Job only endures because his own body has been spared, and asks permission to strike his flesh directly, confident Job will curse God to his face (vv. 4-5). The Lord permits it, limiting Satan only from taking Job's life, and Job is afflicted with painful sores from head to foot (vv. 6-7). Scraping himself with broken pottery while sitting in ashes, Job is confronted by his wife, who urges him to curse God and die, but he rebukes her and does not sin with his words (vv. 8-10). His three friends — Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar — hear of his suffering, travel to comfort him, and are so shocked by his appearance that they sit with him in silence for seven days and nights…
m: the same heavenly council convened a second time with God adding that Job was destroyed without cause, a proverb, skin for skin, used to argue that a man will trade anything external to save his own body, boils covering Job from the sole of his foot to his crown so completely his own friends fail…

x: Having endured seven days of silence, Job finally speaks, opening his mouth to curse the day of his birth rather than curse God (vv. 1-3). He wishes that day had been blotted from existence — swallowed by darkness, excluded from the calendar, and barren of any joy (vv. 4-10). Job asks why he did not die at birth, reasoning that death would have brought him the same rest enjoyed by kings, princes, and slaves alike, free from turmoil and oppression (vv. 11-19). He closes by questioning why God gives life and light to those in bitter misery who long for death more than hidden treasure, describing his own constant sighing, dread, and lack of any peace or rest (vv. 20-26).
h: Why Give Light to the Miserable? (vv.20-26)
m: a curse aimed deliberately at the day of Job's birth rather than at God himself, language that inverts the words of creation, let there be light answered point for point by let that day be darkness, death portrayed not as punishment but as the great equalizer where kings and prisoners alike find…

x: Eliphaz the Temanite offers the first response to Job's outburst, gently noting that Job has strengthened many others in their troubles but now grows impatient and terrified when trouble touches him personally (vv. 1-5). He appeals to Job's own reputation for godliness as reason for confidence, insisting from experience that the innocent are never truly destroyed and that those who sow trouble reap what they plant (vv. 6-11). Eliphaz then recounts a terrifying night vision in which a spirit passed before him and a voice asked whether any mortal can be righteous before God, since even his angels are charged with error (vv. 12-18). He concludes that human beings, who live in fragile houses of clay, are crushed like moths and perish without gaining wisdom, implying Job's suffering points to hidden sin (vv. 19-21).
m: Eliphaz opening gently by reminding Job of the same counsel Job once gave to others now struggling to take it himself, a theology built on a single observed claim, who ever perished being innocent, a lion's fate used as proof that even the mightiest wicked eventually fall, a terrifying night vision…

x: Eliphaz continues his argument, insisting no holy one will answer Job's complaint and warning that resentment and envy destroy the foolish, not the righteous (vv. 1-5). He reasons that trouble does not spring from the ground but is born into mankind as surely as sparks fly upward, so Job should instead seek God, who does great and unsearchable things and lifts up the lowly while frustrating the schemes of the crafty (vv. 6-16). Eliphaz calls Job blessed for being corrected by God, since the Almighty who wounds also heals, and promises deliverance from famine, war, slander, and wild beasts if Job accepts this discipline (vv. 17-23). He assures Job that in humble submission his home would be secure, his descendants numerous, and his life would end at a full age like grain gathered in season, urging him to accept this wisdom (vv. 24-27).
m: a proverb offered as settled fact, man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward, used to minimize rather than acknowledge Job's grief, a hymn to God's power and justice that is true in every line yet aimed to imply Job simply hasn't sought God properly, suffering reframed entirely as…

x: Job responds to Eliphaz, arguing that if his grief and misfortune could be weighed, they would outweigh the sand of the sea, explaining why his words have sounded so wild (vv. 1-4). He insists no one complains without cause, comparing his longing for death to a natural craving, and wishes God would simply grant him relief by ending his life since he has never denied the words of the Holy One (vv. 5-13). Job rebukes his friends for withholding the kindness a suffering man deserves, comparing them to deceptive desert wadis that promise water but run dry just when travelers need them most (vv. 14-21). He challenges them to point out any actual wrongdoing on his part rather than treating his desperate words as mere wind, insisting his righteousness and honesty remain intact (vv. 22-30).
m: grief measured against the sand of the sea and found immeasurably heavier, a donkey and an ox that only cry out when something is genuinely lacking, offered as proof that Job's own outcry is proportional rather than dramatic, friends compared to seasonal desert streams that run dry precisely when…
d: Job Replies: My Complaint Is Just (vv1–30)

x: Job continues by describing human life on earth as hard labor like that of a hired servant, marked by months of futility and nights of sorrow with no relief when he lies down (vv. 1-6). He reflects that his life is but a breath that will soon vanish like a cloud, never to return, and so he refuses to hold his complaint back, asking why God treats him — a mere mortal — like a monster requiring constant watching (vv. 7-16). Job questions why God pays such close attention to humanity, testing them every moment and terrifying him with dreams rather than granting even a moment's peace to swallow his own spit (vv. 17-19). He closes by asking why, if he has sinned, God does not simply pardon his guilt instead of making him a target, since he will soon lie down in the dust and be gone (vv. 20-21).
h: The Brevity and Misery of Life (vv.1-6)
m: human life compared to hired labor and hard military service, endless nights of tossing set against days that fly by swifter than a weaver's shuttle, Job turning from his friends to address God directly for the first time in the book, Psalm eight's wonder, what is man, that thou art mindful of him…
d: Job Continues: My Life Has No Hope (vv1–21)

x: Bildad the Shuhite speaks up, rebuking Job for his long, wind-like words and insisting that God never perverts justice, so if Job's children died, they must have sinned and been given over to the consequence (vv. 1-4). He urges Job to earnestly seek God and, if he is pure and upright, God will restore him so completely that his former prosperity will seem small compared to his future (vv. 5-7). Bildad appeals to the wisdom of earlier generations, comparing the godless to reeds that wither without water and to a spider's web that offers no real security, doomed to be forgotten (vv. 8-19). He concludes that God does not reject a blameless man nor uphold evildoers, and promises that if Job is innocent, God will yet fill his mouth with laughter while those who hate him are put to shame (vv. 20-22).
m: an opening that dismisses Job's own words as a strong wind before offering a single argument, a foundational premise, doth God pervert judgment, used to conclude that Job's dead children must have deserved their fate, an appeal to inherited tradition on the grounds that we are but of yesterday and…

x: Job answers Bildad by agreeing in principle that God is just but questioning how any mortal could win a case against him, since God's wisdom and power are too vast to resist — moving mountains, shaking the earth, commanding the sun and stars (vv. 1-10). Job laments that God passes by unseen, snatches away without being questioned, and crushes both Rahab's helpers and, it seems, the innocent and guilty alike without distinction (vv. 11-24). He compares his fleeting days to a runner or a swooping eagle, insisting that even if he tried to appear cheerful he cannot escape dread, since God plunges him into misery no matter how clean his hands are (vv. 25-31). Job's deepest complaint is that God is not a man he can confront in court, and there is no arbiter or mediator to stand between them so he could speak without fear (vv. 32-35).
m: Job agreeing with Bildad's premise that God is just while drawing from it a far more terrifying conclusion, an inventory of divine power, moving mountains, shaking the earth, commanding the sun, that outstrips anything the friends have said about God, a confession that even innocence would not help…
d: Job Replies: There Is No Arbiter (vv1–35)

x: Job, weary of his life, resolves to voice his complaint freely, asking God directly why he contends with him and whether it pleases God to oppress the work of his own hands while smiling on the schemes of the wicked (vv. 1-3). He asks whether God sees as limited humans do, needing to search out iniquity, when God already knows Job is not guilty and that no one can deliver him from his hand (vv. 4-7). Job marvels that the same hands that formed him like clay, knit him together with bones and sinews, and granted him life now seem bent on destroying him completely (vv. 8-17). He asks why he was ever born at all if only to suffer like this, and pleads for God to leave him alone for his few remaining days so he might find a little comfort before descending into the darkness of death (vv. 18-22).
m: a demand to know why God contends with him rather than simply naming the charge, one of the most intimate descriptions of creation in Scripture, fashioned like clay, poured like milk, curdled like cheese, fenced with bones and sinews, a paradox in which Job cannot win either way, if I be wicked…
d: Job Continues: I Loathe My Life (vv1–22)

x: Zophar the Naamathite speaks next, the bluntest of the three, accusing Job of empty and mocking talk and insisting Job's claim to be pure in God's sight cannot go unanswered (vv. 1-4). He wishes God himself would speak and reveal the depths of wisdom, arguing that God is actually exacting less punishment than Job's guilt deserves (vv. 5-6). Zophar declares that God's greatness is unsearchable — higher than the heavens, deeper than Sheol, broader than the sea — and that no one can resist or fully know him (vv. 7-12). He urges Job to put away any iniquity in his hand, promising that if he does, his life will grow brighter than noonday, secure and untroubled, while the wicked have no such hope and only look toward death (vv. 13-20).
m: the harshest of the three friends opening not with sympathy but with a direct accusation of lying, a wish that God himself would speak against Job and a claim that God exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth, a genuinely exalted description of God's unsearchable wisdom, higher than…

x: Job answers Zophar with biting sarcasm, telling his friends that wisdom will not die with them and that he understands these things just as well as they do, even though he — a righteous man whom God once answered — has become a laughingstock (vv. 1-6). He points out that even the animals, birds, fish, and earth itself know that the hand of the Lord controls all creation and holds the life and breath of every living thing (vv. 7-10). Job insists that true wisdom and power belong to God alone, who tears down what cannot be rebuilt, controls the waters, and strips kings, priests, counselors, and judges of their strength and understanding (vv. 11-21). He describes God as the one who makes nations rise and fall, deprives their leaders of understanding, and leaves them groping in darkness like drunkards with no light (vv. 22-25).
m: sarcasm opening the reply, no doubt but ye are the people, and wisdom shall die with you, before Job claims equal standing with his accusers, the tabernacles of robbers prosper named as an observation that directly undercuts the friends' whole theology, creation itself called on as a witness, ask…
d: Job Replies: The LORD Has Done This (vv1–25)

x: Job insists he has seen and understood everything his friends have said and is not inferior to them, but he wants to argue his case directly with God rather than with them, since they are worthless physicians who invent lies on God's behalf (vv. 1-5). He challenges them to stop pretending to defend God through deceit and partiality, warning that God's own splendor would terrify them if he examined their arguments, calling their maxims as fragile as ashes and clay (vv. 6-12). Job resolves to state his case boldly even at the risk of his life, declaring that even if God kills him he will still hope in God and defend his own integrity before him, confident that no godless person would even dare approach God this way (vv. 13-19). He asks God for only two things — to remove his heavy hand and stop terrifying him — so he can ask why God hides his face, treats him as an enemy, and makes him…
m: friends dismissed outright as forgers of lies and physicians of no value, a direct challenge that their silence would be wiser than their speech, one of the most famous verses in all of Scripture, though he slay me, yet will I trust in him, spoken in the very breath that insists on maintaining his…
d: Job Replies: The LORD Has Done This (vv1–28)

x: Job reflects that every human born of woman lives only a short, trouble-filled life, springing up like a flower and vanishing like a shadow, so he asks why God bothers to bring such a fleeting creature to judgment (vv. 1-6). He notes that even a felled tree has hope of sprouting again at the scent of water, but when a person dies, they lie down and do not rise until the heavens themselves are no more (vv. 7-12). Job longs for God to hide him in Sheol until his wrath passes and then remember him, wondering aloud whether a man can live again after death and vowing to wait out his hard service until his release comes (vv. 13-15). He closes by imagining that if God simply stopped counting his sins, he might have hope, but instead watches God wear away human hope like water wearing down stone, leaving a man unaware of what becomes of his own children (vv. 16-22).
m: man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble, opening one of Scripture's most quoted meditations on mortality, a tree's capacity to sprout again after being cut down set bitterly against a man who lies down and riseth not, a sudden flash of resurrection hope, if a man die, shall…
d: Job Continues: Man Born of Woman (vv1–22)

x: Eliphaz responds a second time, now sharply accusing Job of speaking with empty, wind-filled arguments that undermine true piety and reveal his own guilt through his own words (vv. 1-6). He rebukes Job for assuming he possesses secret wisdom beyond what wise men far older than Job's own father already hold, and for turning his rage against God with such reckless speech (vv. 7-13). Eliphaz repeats the claim that no human being — born of woman — can be pure before God, since even the heavens and God's holy ones are not flawless in his sight (vv. 14-16). Drawing on the tradition of the ancestors, Eliphaz describes in vivid detail the torment awaiting the wicked man: haunted by terror, doomed to the sword, stripped of lasting wealth, and consumed by the very deception he conceives in his own heart (vv. 17-35).
m: a second speech opening with open accusation rather than gentle counsel, thine own mouth condemneth thee, and not I, turning Job's own protests of innocence into further proof of guilt, rhetorical questions demanding whether Job predates Adam or sat in God's secret council, angels themselves called…
d: Eliphaz Accuses: Job Does Not Fear God (vv1–35)

x: Job replies to Eliphaz calling his friends miserable comforters whose windy words never end, insisting that if their roles were reversed he could pile up empty arguments too, but would instead offer real comfort and relief (vv. 1-5). He describes God as the one who has worn him out, torn his household apart, and turned into an adversary who gnashes his teeth and locks eyes on him like an attacking warrior, wounding him without pity (vv. 6-14). Wrapped in sackcloth with his face reddened from weeping, Job protests that no violence stains his hands and his prayer remains pure, and he begs the earth not to cover the injustice done to him (vv. 15-18). Remarkably, he appeals past his human accusers to a witness and advocate in heaven, an intercessor who will plead his case with God as a friend pleads for a friend, since his own remaining years are few (vv. 19-22).
m: a verdict on his friends that has become proverbial, miserable comforters are ye all, an offer of what real comfort would have looked like, I would strengthen you with my mouth, delivered as a rebuke of what they actually provide, some of Scripture's most violent imagery describing God tearing him…
d: Job Replies: Miserable Comforters Are You All (vv1–22)

x: Job continues, describing his spirit as broken, his days fading, and the grave already awaiting him amid the mockery of those around him, and he challenges God directly to put up a pledge for him since no one else will stand as his guarantor (vv. 1-5). He laments that God has made him a byword among people, someone others spit at, while his body wastes to a shadow, even though upright and innocent people are appalled at how the godless treat him (vv. 6-9). Job sees no wisdom among his friends and mourns that his plans and heart's desires are shattered, accusing them of falsely calling darkness light (vv. 10-12). He closes by concluding that if his only home left is the grave and his only family the worm and corruption, then his hope has nowhere left to go but down into the dust of death (vv. 13-16).
m: a spirit broken enough to say the graves are ready for me, a request for God himself to stand as surety since no human friend will vouch for him, Job reduced to a public byword even as he insists the righteous shall hold on his way and grow stronger, corruption and the worm addressed as father…
d: Job Continues: My Spirit Is Broken (vv1–16)

x: Bildad answers again, irritated that Job dismisses his friends as senseless beasts, and insists the created order will not be rearranged just to accommodate Job's anger (vv. 1-4). He then paints an elaborate portrait of the wicked man's downfall: his lamp is snuffed out, his own schemes trap his feet in nets and snares, and terror dogs him on every side (vv. 5-11). Bildad describes calamity devouring the wicked man's body, dragging him from the safety of his tent to the king of terrors, while fire and burning sulfur consume his dwelling and his roots wither both above and below ground (vv. 12-16). He concludes that such a man's memory perishes from the earth, leaving no name, no children, and no descendants, so that people east and west are horrified and recognize his fate as the just end of one who does not know God (vv. 17-21).
h: The Elaborate Fate of the Wicked (vv.5-21)
m: Bildad offended enough by Job's earlier comment about animals to open with open irritation rather than argument, an accusation that Job tears himself in anger and expects the earth to be forsaken for his sake, an elaborate, unbroken poem describing the wicked man's destruction with no conditional…
d: Bildad Speaks: God Punishes the Wicked (vv1–21)

x: Job asks his friends how much longer they will torment and crush him with words, insisting that even if he had truly erred, that would be his concern alone and not grounds for their contempt (vv. 1-6). He describes feeling as though God himself has wronged him, blocking his path, stripping away his honor, tearing him down like an uprooted tree, and treating him as an enemy surrounded by siege troops (vv. 7-12). Job catalogs his total isolation — abandoned by relatives, friends, servants, and even his own wife and children, reduced to skin and bones, and begs his friends to show pity since God's hand alone has struck him (vv. 13-22). In the book's climactic declaration, Job wishes his words were permanently engraved in rock, then affirms that he knows his Redeemer lives and will stand on the earth at the last, and that even after his body is destroyed he will see God with his own eyes…
h: I Know That My Redeemer Lives (vv.23-27)
m: friends accused of vexing his soul and breaking him in pieces with words ten times over, total abandonment catalogued in devastating detail, brothers estranged, servants unresponsive, his own breath offensive to his wife, young children despising him, a request that his words be engraved with an…

x: Zophar answers a second time, admitting his agitated feelings compel him to respond, and reasserts the ancient teaching that the joy of the wicked has always been brief, however high their stature may rise (vv. 1-11). He describes wickedness as sweet in the mouth but turning to venom in the stomach, so that the wealth a wicked man swallows he is ultimately forced to vomit back up and never enjoy (vv. 12-19). Because his appetite is never satisfied, disaster overtakes him at the height of his abundance, as God unleashes burning anger, arrows, and terror upon him even as he tries to flee (vv. 20-25). Zophar concludes that darkness, unkindled fire, and floodwaters will consume the wicked man's house and treasures on the day of God's wrath, declaring this the inheritance God allots to every wicked person (vv. 26-29).
m: Zophar visibly agitated by Job's warning about a coming judgment and rushing to answer defensively, a thesis stated as ancient and self-evident, the triumphing of the wicked is short, and the joy of the hypocrite but for a moment, wickedness pictured as sweet food that turns to the gall of asps…
d: Zophar Speaks: Wickedness Receives Just Retribution (vv1–29)

x: Job asks his friends simply to listen and let that itself serve as their comfort, warning them to be appalled once they truly grasp what he is about to say (vv. 1-6). He directly challenges the friends' theology by asking why the wicked go on living, growing old and powerful, with secure households, thriving livestock, and children who dance and sing to music, all while telling God to leave them alone (vv. 7-16). Job questions how often the wicked actually suffer the sudden ruin his friends describe, arguing that the same death comes to both the prosperous and the embittered, and that punishing a wicked man's children after his own death does nothing to correct him personally (vv. 17-26). He closes by exposing what he believes are their real, wrongheaded assumptions, pointing out that in the real world the wicked are often honored at death and spared calamity, so their attempts to…
h: The Observable Prosperity of the Wicked (vv.7-16)
Job's Final Verdict on the Friends (vv.27-34)
m: a request simply to be listened to before being mocked, let this be your consolations, a single demolishing question, wherefore do the wicked live, become old, yea, are mighty in power, answered with an inventory of the wicked's actual observable prosperity, established children, safe houses, music…
d: Job Replies: The Wicked Do Prosper (vv1–34)

x: Eliphaz delivers his third and sharpest speech, now accusing Job of specific wrongdoing rather than vague sinfulness — exploiting his brothers, stripping the needy of clothing, and sending widows and orphans away empty-handed (vv. 4-9). He argues that God's greatness makes human righteousness irrelevant to him, so Job's suffering must reveal hidden guilt (vv. 2-5, 12-14), and points to the sudden ruin of the wicked in the past as proof (vv. 15-20). Eliphaz then urges Job to reconcile with God, submit to his instruction, and cast away his gold, promising that repentance will restore his delight in God and bring answered prayer (vv. 21-30).
h: The Way of the Wicked and the Righteous Who Watch (vv.15-20)
m: a final speech that abandons theory for outright fabrication, specific crimes invented against a man God himself has already called blameless, taking pledges from brothers, stripping the naked, withholding water from the hungry, an accusation that Job believes thick clouds hide him from God's…
d: Eliphaz Speaks: Job's Wickedness Is Great (vv1–30)

x: Job responds to Eliphaz by longing to find God's dwelling place so he could lay his case before him directly, confident he would be heard and vindicated rather than overpowered (vv. 2-7). Yet God seems to elude him in every direction — east, west, north, and south (vv. 8-9). Job insists God already knows the path he has taken and that testing him would prove him genuine, since he has followed God's ways and treasured his commands more than his own daily bread (vv. 10-12). But God is unchangeable and does whatever he wills, carrying out his purposes for Job's life, which leaves Job terrified and unsettled in his presence (vv. 13-17).
m: a longing that has nothing to do with relief from pain and everything to do with reaching God himself, oh that I knew where I might find him, a search in every direction, forward, backward, left, right, that turns up nothing, one of the Bible's purest statements of faith without sight, when he hath…

x: Job asks why the Almighty does not set fixed times for judging evil, then catalogs the oppression the wicked inflict on the powerless: stealing land and livestock, driving away the needy, and forcing the poor into hiding and hard labor without adequate food, clothing, or shelter (vv. 1-12). He describes evildoers who thrive in darkness — the murderer, adulterer, and thief who avoid the light because it exposes their crimes (vv. 13-17). Job acknowledges that the wicked do eventually meet the same end as everyone else, snatched away like the rest despite their apparent security (vv. 18-24), and closes by challenging anyone to prove his account false (v. 25).
h: Those Who Rebel Against the Light (vv.13-17)
m: a single opening question that names the whole problem of unpunished evil, why, seeing times are not hidden from the Almighty, do they that know him not see his days, boundary stones moved and a widow's ox taken while the poor are reduced to gleaning others' fields and sleeping naked in the cold…

x: In his brief final speech, Bildad marvels at God's dominion and awesome might, which establishes order even in the heights of heaven, and asks who could ever count his armies or escape his light (vv. 2-3). He presses his core argument once more: if even the moon and stars are not pure in God's sight, how much less can a mortal human being — a mere maggot or worm — be righteous or pure before him (vv. 4-6).
m: the shortest speech in the entire book, six verses, marking the visible exhaustion of the friends' theology, an argument reduced to a single point, God's greatness against man's smallness, even the moon and stars called impure before him and man himself called a worm, a kernel of real truth about…
d: Bildad Speaks: Man Cannot Be Righteous (vv1–6)

x: Job opens with biting sarcasm, asking Bildad how his empty words have actually helped someone powerless and without wisdom (vv. 2-4). He then describes God's overwhelming power in far greater terms than his friends have offered: the dead tremble beneath the waters, God stretches the northern skies over empty space and hangs the earth on nothing, and locks the waters in the clouds without bursting them (vv. 5-10). God's rebuke shakes the pillars of heaven, his power stills the sea and crushed the sea monster Rahab, and his hand pierced the fleeing serpent (vv. 11-13). Job concludes that all of this is merely the outer fringe of God's ways — only a faint whisper of his true power (v. 14).
m: sarcasm opening the reply to a six-verse speech, how hast thou helped him that is without power, before Job delivers a hymn to God's majesty that outstrips anything his accusers have managed, God's dominion extending even into Sheol where the dead themselves tremble, the earth described as hanging…
d: Job Replies: God's Majesty Is Unsearchable (vv1–14)

x: Job resumes his speech, swearing by God — who he says has denied him justice — that he will never speak wickedness or concede that his friends are right; he will hold to his integrity until he dies (vv. 2-6). He wishes his enemy's fate to match that of the wicked, since the godless have no real hope when God cuts their life short (vv. 7-10). Job then turns to describe that fate in detail: the wicked man's children die by the sword or hunger, his stored-up wealth passes to the righteous, his fragile house collapses, and terror sweeps him away suddenly like a flood or whirlwind (vv. 11-23).
m: an oath of integrity sworn by the very God Job believes has wronged him, till I die I will not remove mine integrity from me, a refusal to concede his friends' accusations even under continued suffering, a description of the wicked man's fate, children by the sword, houses fragile as a moth's web…

x: Job marvels at humanity's skill in mining silver, gold, iron, and copper from hidden places deep in the earth, tunneling where no bird or beast has gone (vv. 1-11). But he asks where wisdom itself can be found, since it exists nowhere among the living and cannot be purchased with gold, silver, or the finest gems (vv. 12-19). Wisdom is hidden from every living creature; only God knows the way to it, for he sees to the ends of the earth and, in setting the limits of wind, rain, and storm, established and examined wisdom itself (vv. 20-27). The chapter closes with the memorable conclusion that fearing the Lord is wisdom, and turning from evil is understanding (v. 28).
m: an extended survey of human mining technology, silver found, gold refined, iron extracted, mountains overturned, offered as proof of nearly limitless human ingenuity, a central question that all that ingenuity cannot answer, but where shall wisdom be found, the deep and the sea both denying they…

x: Job longs for the months now gone, when God's friendship lit his path and his household still surrounded him (vv. 2-6). He recalls being honored at the city gate, where young men stepped aside and elders rose in his presence (vv. 7-10), because he rescued the poor, the orphan, and the dying, defended the widow, served as eyes for the blind and feet for the lame, and broke the grip of the wicked on their prey (vv. 11-17). He had expected to die at home in peace after a long, honored life, with people hanging on his counsel like farmers waiting for rain (vv. 18-25).
m: an elegy for a vanished life opening with when God preserved me and his candle shined upon my head, elders rising to their feet and princes falling silent the moment Job appeared at the city gate, righteousness described entirely in terms of active advocacy for the poor, the widow, the blind, the…

x: Job contrasts his former honor with his present humiliation: he is now mocked by young men from outcast families he once would not have trusted with his sheep dogs, and they attack and spit on him because God has loosened his restraints (vv. 1-15). His soul pours itself out in unrelenting suffering — pain gnaws his bones through the night, and God has flung him into the mud until he resembles dust and ashes (vv. 16-19). He cries out but God gives no answer, tossing him about in the storm and clearly bringing him toward death (vv. 20-23). Job protests that he wept for the unfortunate and grieved for the poor, yet trouble came instead of the good he expected, leaving him in constant mourning (vv. 24-31).
m: a chapter of pure reversal answering chapter twenty-nine point for point, mocked now by the very outcasts whose fathers he would once have disdained to set with his sheepdogs, a body in open revolt, bones pierced at night, skin disfigured, pain that never rests, a cry that goes specifically…

x: In his final defense, Job declares he made a covenant with his own eyes never to look on a woman with lust, confident that God has counted every one of his steps and would find his integrity if weighed on honest scales (vv. 1-6). He then works through a long series of self-curses, inviting disaster on himself if he is guilty of deceit, adultery, mistreating his servants, denying justice to the poor, the widow, or the orphan, trusting in wealth, worshiping the sun or moon, gloating over an enemy's ruin, neglecting travelers, or hiding his sin (vv. 7-34). He closes by wishing his accuser would put the charges in writing so he could answer them like a prince, and even that his own land would testify against him if he had wronged it (vv. 35-40).
m: sexual purity governed at the level of the eyes themselves, I made a covenant with mine eyes, before any outward act is even addressed, servants treated with justice on the explicit ground that master and servant were made in the same womb, generosity toward the poor, the fatherless and the naked…

x: After Job's three friends fall silent, unable to answer him, Elihu — a younger man who has held his tongue out of respect for age — grows angry, both at Job for justifying himself over God and at the friends for condemning Job without refuting him (vv. 1-5). He explains that it is not age but the Spirit of God within a person that gives true understanding, so age alone does not guarantee wisdom (vv. 6-9). Having waited and listened in vain for the friends to answer Job, Elihu declares himself full of words he can no longer contain, comparing himself to wine with no vent, and promises to speak honestly, without flattery, since he serves God rather than man (vv. 10-22).
m: a fourth voice introduced abruptly and never mentioned again after this speech or in the book's epilogue, anger described as kindled four times in five verses, once at Job for justifying himself over God and three times at the friends for condemning him without a real answer, a long deferral to age…

x: Elihu, a younger bystander, presents himself as Job's equal — formed from the same clay, no more terrifying than Job himself (vv. 1-7) — then quotes back Job's claim to be innocent yet treated as God's enemy (vv. 8-11). Countering Job's charge that God never speaks, Elihu insists God speaks through dreams and night visions that turn a person from pride (vv. 14-18), and through pain that chastens the body while preserving the soul from the pit (vv. 19-22). If a mediating messenger pleads a person's uprightness, God is gracious and finds a ransom, restoring health and favor (vv. 23-28) — one of the book's clearest anticipations of Christ. Elihu closes by inviting Job to answer, since God does all this to rescue and enlighten a life, not destroy it (vv. 29-33).
m: Elihu positioning himself as Job's equal, made by the same Spirit and formed from the same clay, rather than as another distant accuser, Job's own words quoted back to him with apparent accuracy, I am clean without transgression, he counteth me for his enemy, a claim that God does in fact speak…

x: Elihu addresses the wise, quoting Job's claim that God has denied him justice though he is innocent (vv. 1-9). He insists it is unthinkable for God to act wickedly, since God repays each person according to their deeds and depends on no one for His authority over the earth (vv. 10-15). God shows no partiality to princes or the rich, sees every human path, and needs no lengthy investigation before judging, since all are the work of His hands (vv. 16-30). Elihu closes harshly, declaring that Job speaks without knowledge and wishing him tested further because his answers sound like those of wicked men (vv. 34-37) — a conclusion that oversteps into cruelty.
h: Should God Repay on Your Terms (vv.31-33)
m: Job's positions paraphrased once more, I am righteous, and God hath taken away my judgment, before Elihu turns to defend God's justice as inherent rather than delegated, an argument that God cannot answer to anyone because no one appointed him over the earth in the first place, an insistence that…

x: Elihu takes up Job's question of what advantage there is in avoiding sin (vv. 1-3), answering that human sin or righteousness affects other people, not God, who is too high above creation to be harmed or enriched by anyone's conduct (vv. 4-8). People cry out under oppression, yet rarely turn toward God as their maker who gives songs even in the night, so their empty cries go unanswered (vv. 9-13). Elihu tells Job that even though he cannot see God, his case is still before Him and he should trust, but then accuses Job of speaking without knowledge (vv. 14-16).
h: Why God Does Not Answer Cries (vv.9-13)
m: a question attributed to Job, what advantage have I, how am I better off than if I had sinned, answered first by insisting human conduct affects other humans rather than diminishing or enriching God at all, a distinction drawn between crying out in raw pain, which anyone does, and genuinely seeking…

x: Elihu opens his final speech claiming perfect knowledge to defend God's righteousness (vv. 1-4), declaring that God is mighty yet never despises anyone, watching continually over the righteous and establishing them (vv. 5-7). His most original insight follows: when the righteous are bound by affliction, God uses the suffering to show them their sin, open their ears to instruction, and call them back — so that obedience brings prosperity and refusal brings ruin (vv. 8-15). Elihu warns Job that he has been filled with the judgment of the wicked rather than learning from his trial (vv. 16-21), then turns to praise God's unsearchable greatness as displayed in the water cycle, clouds, and thunder — imagery that anticipates God's own appearance from the storm (vv. 22-33).
m: a claim to speak on God's behalf with perfect knowledge that borders on presumption even as its content proves genuinely insightful, a direct challenge to Job's complaint of divine inattention, he withdraweth not his eyes from the righteous, Elihu's most original idea, suffering as discipline that…

x: Elihu's heart trembles at the thunder of God's voice, which rolls across the whole earth with lightning that no one can hold back (vv. 1-5). God commands snow and rain, halts human labor, and drives animals to shelter, sending each storm for correction, provision, or mercy (vv. 6-13). He challenges Job to stand still and consider these wonders — can Job command the clouds, understand their balance, or spread out the sky as God does? (vv. 14-20). Elihu closes by declaring that fair weather comes from the north with terrible majesty, and that the Almighty, excellent in power and abundant in justice, cannot be fully found out — so people rightly fear him, however wise they consider themselves (vv. 21-24).
m: a heart trembling at the sound of God's own thunder before a single further argument is made, weather itself, snow, frost, whirlwind, described as serving multiple purposes at once, whether for correction, or for his land, or for mercy, a repeated challenge to Job, stand still, and consider the…

x: After thirty-seven chapters of human argument, the LORD himself answers Job out of the whirlwind, opening with a direct challenge: who is this that obscures counsel with words lacking knowledge? (vv. 1-3). God does not explain Job's suffering or address the friends' arguments; instead He interrogates Job with a relentless barrage of questions about creation. Where was Job when God laid the earth's foundations while the morning stars sang together? (vv. 4-7). Who shut up the sea behind doors and set its boundaries? (vv. 8-11). Has Job ever commanded the dawn, entered the springs of the sea, seen the gates of death, or walked through the storehouses of snow and hail? (vv. 12-30). Can he bind the Pleiades, loose Orion's belt, or govern the ordinances of the heavens, and does he provide for the raven and hunt prey for the lion? (vv. 31-41). Every question exposes the vast gulf between Job's…
h: The Deep, Death, Light, and Darkness (vv.16-21)
m: God breaking thirty-seven chapters of human argument by speaking out of a whirlwind, an opening rebuke that names Job's words as without knowledge rather than sinful, where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth answered by the detail that morning stars sang and sons of God shouted for…

x: God continues His interrogation of Job, turning from cosmic phenomena to the animal kingdom. Does Job know when the mountain goats and deer give birth, or number their months, though God tends their cycles in remote places no human ever sees? (vv. 1-4). God set the wild donkey free to roam the wilderness, scorning the city and ignoring every driver's shout, and the wild ox refuses to serve or trust any man (vv. 5-12). The ostrich, deprived of wisdom, deals carelessly with her eggs and young, yet outruns a horse when she rises up (vv. 13-18). The war horse is described in soaring detail — clothed with strength, laughing at fear, and charging fearlessly into battle at the sound of the trumpet (vv. 19-25). The hawk and eagle fly and nest by God's instinct alone, not Job's wisdom, spotting prey from unreachable heights (vv. 26-30). Each creature lives entirely outside human control, proof…
m: God's interrogation shifting from cosmic phenomena to animals that live entirely outside human control, mountain goats and wild donkeys whose reproductive cycles God oversees without any need of human awareness, a wild ox too powerful and untameable to ever serve a man's field, an ostrich called…

x: God concludes His first speech by demanding a response: shall the one who argues with the Almighty now answer him? (vv. 1-2). Job, humbled, admits he is of small account and has nothing to say, covering his mouth and refusing to speak further — real submission, though not yet the fuller repentance still to come (vv. 3-5). God speaks again from the whirlwind with a sharper, moral challenge: has Job discredited God's justice by insisting on his own righteousness? (vv. 6-8). If Job can bring down the proud and hide the wicked in the dust as God does, then God will admit Job can save himself by his own strength (vv. 9-14). God then describes Behemoth, a creature of immense power — muscular loins, a tail like a cedar, bones like bronze, lying secure among the lotus trees and drinking in whole rivers without alarm — a beast only its Maker can approach, proving that if Job cannot master…
m: a direct challenge to answer, shall he that contendeth with the Almighty instruct him, met by Job's first brief and still incomplete submission, I am vile, what shall I answer thee, a second speech that turns the question from intellectual to moral, wilt thou condemn me, that thou mayest be…

x: God devotes this entire chapter to Leviathan, the climactic creature of His second speech. Can Job draw him out with a fishhook, put a rope through his nose, or make him a servant through covenant or plea? (vv. 1-6). One attempt to touch him is enough to end the battle forever (vv. 7-9). The theological turn comes next: if no one is fierce enough to rouse Leviathan, who then can stand before God himself, who owes nothing to anyone since everything under heaven already belongs to Him? (vv. 10-11). God then describes Leviathan's invulnerability at length — his sealed rows of scales, fire and smoke pouring from his mouth and nostrils, a heart hard as stone, and total indifference to sword, spear, arrow, or club (vv. 12-30). He churns the deep like a boiling pot and leaves a shining wake behind him, king over every proud creature, with nothing on earth to equal him (vv. 31-34). The argument…
m: an entire chapter devoted to a single terrifying creature no hook, rope, covenant or weapon can subdue, a cumulative catalogue of invulnerability, scales sealed like armor, fire from the mouth, a heart hard as stone, that leaves Leviathan entirely beyond any human power to touch, a theological…

x: Job answers God with the theological high point of the book: he confesses that God can do all things and that no purpose of His can be thwarted, admitting he spoke of things too wonderful for him, which he did not understand (vv. 1-3). Where before he had only heard of God secondhand, now his own eyes have seen Him, and he repents in dust and ashes (vv. 4-6). God then rebukes Eliphaz and his two companions, declaring that they, unlike Job, have not spoken rightly about Him, and instructs them to offer seven bulls and seven rams while Job — the very man they accused — prays on their behalf (vv. 7-9). When Job prays for his friends, the LORD restores his fortunes, giving him twice what he had before: 14,000 sheep, 6,000 camels, 1,000 oxen, and 1,000 donkeys (vv. 10-12). He is given seven sons and three daughters, remarkably beautiful and granted an inheritance alongside their brothers…
m: a confession that moves from secondhand hearing to direct sight, I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear, but now mine eye seeth thee, repentance expressed not over specific invented sins but over speaking of things too wonderful to understand, God's own astonishing verdict that Job, who…

x: A wisdom psalm opening the Psalter, contrasting two ways of life. The blessed person avoids the counsel of the wicked and instead delights in and meditates on God's instruction (vv. 1-2), growing like a tree planted by flowing water that bears fruit and does not wither (v. 3). The wicked have no such stability; they are compared to chaff that the wind blows away and will not survive God's judgment or stand among the righteous (vv. 4-5). The psalm closes with its central claim: the LORD watches over the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked leads to ruin (v. 6).
m: Two ways of life, blessedness, the righteous vs. the wicked, delight in God's Word, divine judgment

x: A royal and messianic psalm. The nations and their rulers conspire and rage against the LORD and his anointed king, plotting to throw off his authority (vv. 1-3), but God in heaven laughs at their defiance and installs his chosen king on Zion (vv. 4-6). The king declares God's decree naming him as son, promising him the nations as an inheritance and the ends of the earth as his possession, with power to break rebellious nations (vv. 7-9). The psalm ends with a warning to earth's rulers to serve the LORD with reverence and submit to his son, pronouncing blessing on all who take refuge in him (vv. 10-12).
h: He That Sitteth in the Heavens Shall Laugh (vv.4-6)
m: God's sovereign rule, rebellion of nations, the Anointed King (Messiah), divine sonship, judgment, refuge in God

x: A lament, traditionally set during Absalom's rebellion against David. David describes how many enemies have risen against him, mocking that God will not save him (vv. 1-2), yet affirms that the LORD is a shield around him, his glory, and the one who lifts his head (v. 3). He cries out and is answered from God's holy hill (v. 4), then describes lying down to sleep and waking again only because the LORD sustains him, giving him courage even surrounded by thousands of enemies (vv. 5-6). He asks God to strike down his attackers (v. 7), and closes affirming that salvation belongs to the LORD, with a blessing pronounced over God's people (v. 8).
h: Many Are They That Rise Up (vv.1-2)
Thou, O LORD, Art a Shield (vv.3-4)
I Laid Me Down and Slept (vv.5-6)
m: Enemies surrounding, trust in God as shield, prayer answered, fearless sleep, salvation belongs to God

x: An evening prayer of trust. David calls on God, who has vindicated him before, to answer him again in distress (v. 1), and rebukes those who dishonor him and chase empty pursuits (v. 2), reminding them that the LORD sets apart the faithful for himself (v. 3). He counsels quiet reflection instead of sin, and trust in the LORD over anxious searching (vv. 4-5). Though others ask where good can be found, David finds joy in God's favor greater than any harvest of grain or wine (vv. 6-7), and closes lying down to sleep in peace because the LORD alone keeps him secure (v. 8).
h: How Long Will Ye Love Vanity (vv.2-3)
Stand in Awe, and Sin Not (vv.4-5)
More Than in the Time That Their Corn Increased (vv.6-7)
I Will Both Lay Me Down in Peace (v.8)
m: Prayer in distress, God's favor vs. worldly gain, joy that surpasses material prosperity, peaceful sleep, safety in God

x: A morning prayer for help against enemies. David asks God to hear his cry and consider his words as he lays his requests before him at daybreak (vv. 1-3), noting that God takes no pleasure in wickedness and that the arrogant cannot stand in his presence (vv. 4-6). In contrast, David will enter God's house through his abundant mercy and worship with reverence (v. 7), asking to be led in righteousness because of his enemies' deceit and corruption (vv. 8-9). He prays for their downfall because of their rebellion (v. 10), then closes with confidence that those who take refuge in the LORD will rejoice, and that he blesses and shields the righteous (vv. 11-12).
h: In the Morning Will I Direct My Prayer (vv.1-3)
Thou Hatest All Workers of Iniquity (vv.4-6)
I Will Come into Thy House (vv.7-8)
There Is No Faithfulness in Their Mouth (vv.9-10)
Let All Those That Put Their Trust in Thee Rejoice (vv.11-12)
m: Morning prayer, God's holiness vs. wickedness, deceitful enemies, worship in reverence, divine protection as shield and favor

x: A penitential lament written in physical and emotional distress. David pleads for mercy, describing bones that shake and a soul in deep anguish, and asks how long his suffering will continue (vv. 1-3). He begs for deliverance for the sake of God's steadfast love, reasoning that the dead cannot praise him (vv. 4-5), and describes nights spent weeping until his bed is soaked with tears, worn out by grief over his adversaries (vv. 6-7). The tone shifts abruptly at the end as David declares that the LORD has heard his weeping and accepted his prayer, so that his enemies will be ashamed and turn back in sudden disgrace (vv. 8-10).
