h: O LORD, Rebuke Me Not in Thine Anger (vv.1-3)
In the Grave Who Shall Give Thee Thanks (vv.4-5)
All the Night Make I My Bed to Swim (vv.6-7)
The LORD Hath Heard the Voice of My Weeping (vv.8-10)
m: Suffering under divine discipline, physical and emotional anguish, tears, prayer heard, sudden confidence, enemies put to shame

x: A lament in which David appeals to God for vindication against a pursuer, traditionally identified as Cush the Benjaminite. He asks for rescue like a lion's prey being torn apart (vv. 1-2), then protests his innocence, inviting judgment if he has wronged the one who is at peace with him (vv. 3-5). He calls on God to rise up in judgment and take his seat over the nations, since he tests the hearts and minds of all people and is angered by wickedness every day (vv. 6-11). The wicked dig a pit for others but fall into it themselves, and their violence returns on their own heads (vv. 14-16), leading David to close in praise of God's righteousness (v. 17).
h: Save Me from All Them That Persecute Me (vv.1-2)
Arise, O LORD, in Thine Anger (vv.6-9)
He Is Fallen into the Ditch (vv.14-16)
m: False accusation, appeal to divine justice, self-imprecation (inviting judgment on self if guilty), the wicked trapped by their own schemes, God as righteous judge

x: A hymn of praise celebrating God's glory in creation and the honored place he has given humanity within it. David marvels that the majestic name of the LORD fills the earth and is even proclaimed through the praise of children (vv. 1-2). Considering the heavens, moon, and stars, he wonders why God pays any attention to human beings at all (vv. 3-4), yet answers that God made mankind only slightly lower than the heavenly beings, crowning them with honor and giving them authority over the created world, including flocks, herds, birds, and fish (vv. 5-8). The psalm closes exactly as it began, repeating the wonder at God's majestic name filling all the earth (v. 9).
h: Out of the Mouth of Babes (v.2)
Thou Hast Put All Things Under His Feet (vv.5-8)
m: God's majesty in creation, human dignity and purpose, dominion mandate, the paradox of human smallness and greatness, Messianic fulfillment

x: A thanksgiving and praise psalm, the first half of an acrostic that continues into Psalm 10. David praises God with his whole heart for his wonderful deeds, recounting how his enemies were driven back and perished under God's righteous judgment (vv. 1-5). The LORD reigns as an everlasting judge who governs the world with justice and serves as a stronghold for the oppressed, so that those who know his name can trust him (vv. 7-10). David calls the nations to sing God's praise, since he remembers the cry of the afflicted and does not forget the needy (vv. 11-12, 18), and asks for mercy from his own enemies while affirming that the nations who forget God will be turned back to judgment (vv. 13-17).
h: I Will Praise Thee with My Whole Heart (vv.1-6)
A Refuge in Times of Trouble (vv.7-10)
Sing Praises to the LORD, Which Dwelleth in Zion (vv.11-14)
The Heathen Is Sunk in the Pit (vv.15-16)
m: Wholehearted praise, God as righteous judge, refuge for the oppressed, nations judged, the wicked trapped by their own schemes, hope for the poor

x: A lament that continues Psalm 9's acrostic pattern, wrestling with why God seems distant while the wicked prosper. The psalmist describes the wicked pursuing the poor, boasting in greed, and arrogantly assuming that God does not see or will never call them to account (vv. 1-6). Their speech is full of cursing and deceit, and they lie in ambush to prey on the helpless and innocent, convinced God has hidden his face and forgotten (vv. 7-11). The psalmist pleads for God to rise up, not forget the afflicted, and break the power of the wicked, since the helpless commit themselves to him (vv. 12-15). The psalm ends in confidence that the LORD is king forever, that he hears the desire of the afflicted, and that he will defend orphans and the oppressed so that no one on earth can terrify them further (vv. 16-18)
h: Arise, O LORD, Lift Up Thine Hand (vv.12-15)
The LORD Is King for Ever (vv.16-18)
m: God's apparent absence, the arrogance and cruelty of the wicked, oppression of the poor, practical atheism, God as defender of the fatherless

x: A psalm of trust in the face of pressure to flee danger. Advisers urge David to escape like a bird to the mountains because the wicked are preparing to attack the upright in secret (vv. 1-3), but he refuses, recalling that the LORD is enthroned in his holy temple, watching and testing all of humanity (vv. 3-4). God tests both the righteous and the wicked and hates those who love violence, promising to rain fiery judgment on the wicked as their portion (vv. 5-6). The psalm closes with the assurance that the LORD is righteous, loves righteous deeds, and that the upright will see his face (v. 7).
h: How Say Ye to My Soul, Flee (vv.1-3)
The LORD Is in His Holy Temple (vv.4-5)
The Upright Shall Behold His Face (v.7)
m: Refusing fear-based flight, God's sovereign observation from heaven, testing of the righteous, judgment on the wicked, beholding God's face

x: A lament over the collapse of honesty and loyalty in society. David observes that the godly and faithful seem to have vanished, replaced by people who flatter and deceive their neighbors (vv. 1-2), and asks God to silence proud, boastful speech, particularly from those who claim their words give them power over others (vv. 3-4). Because of the oppression of the poor and needy, the LORD promises to rise up and provide the safety they long for (v. 5). God's own words are described as pure, like silver refined seven times over, utterly trustworthy compared to human speech (v. 6). The psalm ends with confidence that God will guard the needy from this deceitful generation, even while the wicked continue to strut about and vileness is celebrated among people (vv. 7-8).
h: Help, LORD, for the Godly Man Ceaseth (v.1)
They Speak with a Double Heart (vv.2-4)
Now Will I Arise, Saith the LORD (v.5)
The Words of the LORD Are Pure Words (v.6)
m: The disappearance of godly people, corrupt speech (flattery, lies, boasting), God's pure words contrasted with human deception, divine intervention for the oppressed

x: A short lament built around the repeated question 'how long.' David asks how long God will seem to forget him, hide his face, and leave him to wrestle with sorrow and the taunts of his enemy (vv. 1-2). He pleads for God to look on him and answer before he is overcome, worried that his enemy will rejoice if he falls (vv. 3-4). The psalm turns in its final lines from anguish to settled trust, as David affirms his confidence in God's steadfast love, rejoices in the salvation he expects, and resolves to sing to the LORD for his goodness (vv. 5-6).
h: I Will Sing unto the LORD (vv.5-6)
m: God's apparent forgetfulness, "how long?" repeated, the journey from despair to praise, trust in steadfast love, the decision to sing

x: A wisdom psalm lamenting the corruption of humanity apart from God, closely paralleled later in Psalm 53. It opens by describing the fool who denies God in his heart, leading to universal corruption in which no one does good (vv. 1-3). These evildoers consume God's people carelessly and never call on the LORD, yet the psalm warns that great terror will overtake them because God is present with the righteous (vv. 4-5). Though the wicked mock the plans of the poor, the LORD himself is their refuge (v. 6). The psalm closes with a longing for Israel's salvation and restoration to come out of Zion (v. 7).
h: There Is None That Doeth Good (vv.2-3)
Have All the Workers of Iniquity No Knowledge (vv.4-6)
Oh That the Salvation of Israel Were Come (v.7)
m: Practical atheism ("no God"), universal human corruption, God's search for the righteous, none found good, God as refuge for the poor, longing for Zion's salvation

x: A wisdom psalm describing the character required to dwell in God's presence. It opens with the question of who may stay in God's tent and live on his holy hill (v. 1), then answers with a list of qualities: walking blamelessly, doing what is right, and speaking truth honestly from the heart (v. 2). Such a person does not slander others, harm a neighbor, or spread reproach, but honors those who fear the LORD while despising those who reject him, and keeps promises even when it costs something (vv. 3-4). This person also refuses to profit from exploitative lending or bribery against the innocent, and the psalm concludes that whoever lives this way will never be shaken (v. 5).
h: Who Shall Abide in Thy Tabernacle (v.1)
He That Doeth These Things Shall Never Be Moved (v.5b)
m: Requirements for dwelling with God, ethical character, truthful speech, integrity in relationships, financial justice, keeping vows

x: A psalm of trust with strong messianic overtones, later quoted regarding Christ's resurrection (Acts 2:25-28). David seeks refuge in God, declaring that apart from him he has no good thing, and delights in the faithful people of the land rather than in other gods (vv. 1-4). He describes the LORD as his chosen portion and cup, with his life's boundaries falling in pleasant, secure places (vv. 5-6). Because God counsels him and remains at his right hand, David's heart is glad and his body rests secure, confident that God will not abandon him to death or let his faithful one see decay (vv. 7-10). The psalm ends celebrating the path of life found in God's presence, with fullness of joy and eternal pleasures (v. 11).
h: The Lines Are Fallen unto Me in Pleasant Places (vv.5-6)
I Have Set the LORD Always Before Me (vv.7-8)
Thou Wilt Not Leave My Soul in Hell (vv.9-11)
m: God as refuge and portion, satisfaction in God alone, rejection of idolatry, counsel and guidance, resurrection hope, fullness of joy in God's presence

x: A lament in which David appeals for vindication from a place of integrity. He asks God to hear his righteous cause, having tested his heart at night and found no wickedness or deceit in it (vv. 1-3), and affirms that he has kept himself from violent paths and held to God's ways (vv. 4-5). He calls on God, who answers those who seek him, to guard him like the pupil of an eye and hide him under the shadow of his wings from the wicked who surround him like predators (vv. 6-9). His enemies are arrogant, close their hearts to pity, and hunt him down like a lion stalking prey (vv. 10-12). David asks God to rise up and confront them, since their reward is only in this life, while he looks forward to seeing God's face in righteousness and being satisfied when he awakens in his likeness (vv. 13-15).
h: Keep Me as the Apple of the Eye (vv.6-9)
Like a Lion Greedy of His Prey (vv.10-12)
Deliver My Soul from the Wicked (vv.13-14)
I Shall Be Satisfied, When I Awake (v.15)
m: Innocence before God, divine testing and approval, enemies like lions, apple of God's eye, shadow of God's wings, satisfaction in God's presence vs. worldly satisfaction

x: A lengthy royal psalm of thanksgiving, closely paralleled in 2 Samuel 22, celebrating God's deliverance of David from Saul and other enemies. David opens with an outpouring of love for the LORD as his rock, fortress, and deliverer, describing how he cried out in the grip of death and was heard from God's temple as the earth itself shook (vv. 1-7). What follows is a dramatic theophany of smoke, darkness, thunder, and lightning as God comes down to rescue him because he delights in him (vv. 8-19), and David affirms that God rewards him according to his righteousness and deals with each person according to their own character (vv. 20-27). God arms him for battle, sets him above his enemies, and makes the nations submit to him (vv. 28-45). The psalm closes in praise of God, the living Rock, who grants great victories to his king and shows steadfast love to David and his descendants forever…
h: The Sorrows of Death Compassed Me (vv.4-6)
He Drew Me Out of Many Waters (vv.16-19)
I Have Kept the Ways of the LORD (vv.20-24)
With the Merciful Thou Wilt Shew Thyself Merciful (vv.25-29)
He Teacheth My Hands to War (vv.30-42)
A People Whom I Have Not Known (vv.43-45)
m: Comprehensive deliverance, theophany (God appearing in storm), God as rock/fortress/deliverer, divine warrior, gentleness that makes great, Messianic kingship

x: A hymn combining creation and God's law. The heavens are described as declaring God's glory without needing words, their message going out to the whole earth, with the sun pictured as a bridegroom running its joyful course across the sky (vv. 1-6). The psalm then turns to praise God's instruction: his law revives the soul, his testimony makes the simple wise, his precepts bring joy, and his commands give light to the eyes (vv. 7-9), describing them as more desirable than gold and sweeter than honey, and a great reward to those who keep them (vv. 10-11). David asks to be cleared of hidden faults and kept from willful sin, and closes with the well-known prayer that the words of his mouth and the meditation of his heart would be pleasing to the LORD, his rock and redeemer (vv. 12-14).
h: The Law of the LORD Is Perfect (vv.7-11)
Cleanse Thou Me from Secret Faults (vv.12-14)
m: Two books of revelation (creation and Scripture), the heavens' wordless testimony, the perfection and value of God's law, hidden faults, presumptuous sins, acceptable worship

x: A royal psalm offered as a pre-battle prayer for the king. The people ask the LORD to answer the king in the day of trouble, send help from the sanctuary, and remember his offerings favorably (vv. 1-3), granting his heart's desire and the success of his plans (v. 4), so that the people can shout for joy and raise banners in God's name (v. 5). The psalm turns to confidence that the LORD saves his anointed and answers him from heaven with mighty acts of deliverance (v. 6). Some trust in military strength like chariots and horses, but the singers trust in the name of the LORD their God, so their enemies will collapse while they rise and stand firm (vv. 7-8). It closes with a final plea for the LORD to save the king and answer when they call (v. 9).
h: The LORD Hear Thee in the Day of Trouble (vv.1-5)
Now Know I That the LORD Saveth His Anointed (v.6)
m: Community praying for the king, trust in God's name vs. military power, pre-battle liturgy, confidence in God's anointed, salvation through divine intervention

x: A royal thanksgiving psalm celebrating victories God has granted the king. The king rejoices in the strength the LORD gives, having received his heart's desire and requests (vv. 1-2), met with rich blessings and a crown of gold placed on his head (v. 3). He asked for life and God granted him length of days that stretches on forever, along with glory, splendor, and majesty (vv. 4-5), making him supremely blessed and joyful in God's presence (v. 6), because his trust rests in the LORD's steadfast love rather than his own strength (v. 7). The psalm turns to describe God's judgment on the king's enemies, who will be consumed and their descendants removed from the earth for plotting evil they could not carry out (vv. 8-12), closing with a call to praise God's power (v. 13).
h: The King Shall Joy in Thy Strength (vv.1-7)
Thine Hand Shall Find Out Thine Enemies (vv.8-12)
m: King's joy in divine strength, answered prayer, blessings received, trust in God's steadfast love, judgment on enemies, divine exaltation

x: A lament that turns to praise, quoted by Jesus from the cross and understood as messianic. It opens with the anguished cry of feeling forsaken by God despite the trust of past generations, followed by description of being mocked and scorned by onlookers who taunt that God should rescue him if he delights in him (vv. 1-8). The suffering intensifies into vivid physical imagery: bones out of joint, strength dried up, surrounded by enemies compared to bulls, lions, and dogs, hands and feet pierced, garments divided and gambled for (vv. 12-18). After pleading for rescue, the psalm shifts dramatically in tone, as the sufferer vows to declare God's name to his people and praise him in the assembly (vv. 19-22). It closes looking far beyond the immediate crisis, anticipating that all the ends of the earth and generations not yet born will turn to and worship the LORD (vv. 27-31).
h: My God, Why Hast Thou Forsaken Me (vv.1-2)
Thou Art He That Took Me Out of the Womb (vv.9-11)
They Pierced My Hands and My Feet (vv.14-18)
Deliver My Soul from the Sword (vv.19-21)
I Will Declare Thy Name unto My Brethren (vv.22-26)
All the Ends of the World Shall Remember (vv.27-31)
m: Divine abandonment, extreme suffering, mockery, physical torment describing crucifixion, pierced hands and feet, garments divided, the pivot from lament to worldwide praise, universal kingdom

x: A psalm of trust, among the most beloved in Scripture — David pictures the LORD as a shepherd who provides everything he needs (v. 1), leads him to rest and refreshment (vv. 2-3), and stays present even through danger and the darkest valley (v. 4). The psalm closes with God as a gracious host who prepares a table and anoints David's head even in the presence of enemies (v. 5), with goodness and mercy following him for the rest of his life and beyond (v. 6).
h: The Valley of the Shadow of Death (v.4)
I Will Dwell in the House of the LORD (v.6)
m: God as Shepherd, complete provision, rest and restoration, fearlessness in danger, abundance in God's presence, lifelong goodness and mercy, eternal dwelling with God

x: A royal and liturgical psalm likely used in temple worship. It opens by declaring that the earth and everything in it belong to the LORD, since he founded it upon the seas (vv. 1-2). It then asks who may ascend God's holy hill, answering that it is the one with clean hands and a pure heart, who does not chase false things or swear deceitfully, and such a person receives blessing from God (vv. 3-5). The psalm closes with a dramatic call for the gates to lift up so the King of glory may enter, repeating the question of his identity and answering that he is the LORD, strong and mighty in battle, the LORD of hosts himself (vv. 7-10).
h: Who Shall Ascend into the Hill of the LORD (vv.3-6)
Lift Up Your Heads, O Ye Gates (vv.7-10)
m: God's universal ownership, entrance requirements for worship, the King of Glory entering His gates, God as warrior-king, the LORD of hosts

x: An acrostic lament and prayer for guidance. David lifts up his soul in trust, asking not to be put to shame or let his enemies triumph over him (vv. 1-3), and asks to be taught God's paths and truth, since God is the source of his salvation (vv. 4-5). He asks God to remember his mercy rather than the sins of his youth (vv. 6-7), affirming that the LORD is good and upright, instructing sinners and guiding the humble in his ways (vv. 8-10). He asks forgiveness for his guilt despite its size, for the sake of God's name (v. 11), and describes the blessings given to those who fear the LORD, including instruction, prosperity, and friendship with God (vv. 12-14). The psalm closes with pleas for relief from affliction, loneliness, and many enemies, asking God to guard his integrity and redeem Israel out of all its troubles (vv. 16-22).
h: Unto Thee, O LORD, Do I Lift Up My Soul (vv.1-7)
Good and Upright Is the LORD (vv.8-10)
For Thy Name's Sake, Pardon Mine Iniquity (vv.11-15)
m: Guidance, forgiveness of sins (youth and present), waiting on God, divine instruction, the "secret" of the LORD, covenant faithfulness, loneliness and affliction

x: A psalm in which David appeals to his own integrity while asking for vindication. He asks God to judge him, testing his heart and mind, since he has walked in faithfulness and trusted the LORD without wavering (vv. 1-3). He describes avoiding the company of the deceitful and the wicked, choosing instead to wash his hands in innocence and go around God's altar proclaiming thanksgiving (vv. 4-7). He expresses love for the place where God's glory dwells (v. 8), and asks not to be swept away with sinners and violent men whose hands are full of bribes (vv. 9-10). The psalm closes with a renewed statement of his own integrity and confidence that his foot stands on level ground, prompting praise in the assembly (vv. 11-12).
h: I Have Not Sat with Vain Persons (vv.4-5)
I Will Wash Mine Hands in Innocency (vv.6-8)
Gather Not My Soul with Sinners (vv.9-10)
My Foot Standeth in an Even Place (vv.11-12)
m: Integrity, self-examination before God, separation from evildoers, love for God's house, worship at the altar, standing on level ground

x: A psalm of trust and longing for God's presence. David declares that with the LORD as his light and salvation he has nothing to fear, even if an army surrounds him or war breaks out (vv. 1-3). His single request is to dwell in God's house all his days, gazing on his beauty and seeking him in his temple, confident that God will shelter him and set him safely on a rock in times of trouble (vv. 4-5). He anticipates offering sacrifices with shouts of joy (v. 6), then pleads for God to hear him, not hide his face, and not abandon him even if his own parents were to forsake him (vv. 7-10). He asks to be taught God's way and protected from his adversaries, closing with the encouragement to wait for the LORD and take heart (vv. 11-14).
h: The LORD Is My Light and My Salvation (vv.1-6)
Hide Not Thy Face Far from Me (vv.7-12)
m: God as light and salvation, fearlessness, one supreme desire (God's presence), divine shelter, seeking God's face, abandonment by parents but not God, waiting on the LORD

x: A lament that turns into praise. David cries out to God as his rock, fearing that silence from God would leave him no different than the dead, and lifts his hands toward the sanctuary (vv. 1-2). He asks not to be dragged away with the wicked, whose friendly words mask malice, and asks God to repay them according to their deeds since they disregard his works (vv. 3-5). The tone shifts abruptly as David blesses the LORD for hearing his plea for mercy, calling him his strength and shield in whom his heart trusts, so that he is helped and his heart leaps for joy (vv. 6-7). The psalm closes asking God to save his people and shepherd them as their inheritance forever (vv. 8-9).
h: Draw Me Not Away with the Wicked (vv.3-5)
The LORD Hath Heard the Voice of My Supplications (vv.6-7)
m: Fear of God's silence, separation from the wicked's fate, God as rock and shield, answered prayer producing praise, shepherd-king theology

x: A hymn celebrating the LORD's power displayed through a violent storm, likely composed for temple worship. It opens calling on heavenly beings to ascribe glory and strength to the LORD, worshiping him in the splendor of his holiness (vv. 1-2). The bulk of the psalm describes the voice of the LORD sweeping across the waters, breaking cedar trees, shaking the wilderness, and stripping forests bare — a thunderstorm portrayed as a display of divine majesty (vv. 3-9). While the storm rages, everyone in God's temple cries 'Glory' (v. 9). The LORD is enthroned over the flood as king forever, and the psalm closes with a prayer that he would give strength to his people and bless them with peace (vv. 10-11).
h: Give unto the LORD the Glory (vv.1-2)
The LORD Sitteth upon the Flood (vv.10-11)
m: The voice of the LORD (sevenfold), God's glory in the storm, creation responding to God, God enthroned over chaos, peace for God's people

x: A thanksgiving psalm composed for the dedication of David's house. He praises God for lifting him up and healing him after crying out for help, restoring him from the brink of death (vv. 1-3), and calls on the faithful to sing praise, since God's anger is brief but his favor lasts a lifetime, turning weeping into joy (vv. 4-5). David recalls a time of complacency when he thought he would never be shaken, until God hid his face and he was dismayed (vv. 6-7). He describes pleading with God, reasoning that the dead cannot praise him, so his mourning was needed to be turned into dancing (vv. 8-11). The psalm closes with his resolve to give thanks to the LORD forever for this reversal (v. 12).
h: What Profit Is There in My Blood (vv.8-10)
Thou Hast Turned My Mourning into Dancing (vv.11-12)
m: Healing and restoration, mourning turned to dancing, the brevity of God's anger vs. the permanence of His favor, complacency shattered, joy in the morning

x: A lament and prayer of trust. David commits his life into God's hands, asking to be delivered from those who have set a trap for him, and famously entrusts his very spirit into God's keeping (vv. 1-5). He describes his affliction — grief, physical weakness, and being scorned by neighbors and forgotten like the dead — yet still trusts in the LORD as his God (vv. 9-14). He asks to be rescued from his pursuers and for his enemies' lying lips to be silenced, mindful of how great God's goodness is stored up for those who fear him (vv. 15-20). The psalm closes by praising God's steadfast love shown in a besieged city, and encourages all who hope in the LORD to be strong and take heart (vv. 21-24).
h: In Thee, O LORD, Do I Put My Trust (vv.1-8)
Oh How Great Is Thy Goodness (vv.19-22)
m: Trust in distress, committing one's spirit to God, God's goodness stored up for His people, God as a strong city of refuge

x: A wisdom and penitential psalm on the blessing of forgiveness, closely tied to David's experience of confessing sin. It opens declaring the happiness of the one whose transgression is forgiven and whose sin the LORD no longer counts against them (vv. 1-2). David recalls the physical toll of concealing his sin — bones wasting away, strength drained — until he acknowledged his guilt and God forgave him (vv. 3-5). He counsels the godly to pray while God may be found, promising protection amid trouble, and God offers to instruct and guide the one who listens rather than being stubborn like a horse or mule (vv. 6-9). The psalm closes contrasting the many sorrows of the wicked with the steadfast love surrounding those who trust the LORD, calling the righteous to rejoice (vv. 10-11).
h: Blessed Is He Whose Transgression Is Forgiven (vv.1-2)
I Will Guide Thee with Mine Eye (vv.8-9)
m: Blessedness of forgiveness, confession versus silence, God as hiding place, divine guidance, the physical toll of unconfessed sin

x: A hymn of praise calling the righteous to sing joyfully to the LORD with instruments and a new song (vv. 1-3), praising his word as right and all his work as faithful, since he loves righteousness and justice and the earth is full of his steadfast love (vv. 4-5). By his word the heavens were made and the waters gathered, so all the earth is called to stand in awe of him (vv. 6-9). The LORD frustrates the plans of nations, but his own purposes stand firm forever, and he watches all humanity from heaven, understanding every heart and deed (vv. 10-15). No king is saved by the size of his army, and a warhorse offers no guarantee of victory, but the LORD's eye watches over those who fear him and hope in his steadfast love, delivering them from death and keeping them alive in famine (vv. 16-19). The psalm closes with a request that God's steadfast love rest on the worshipers as they put their…
h: Sing unto Him a New Song (vv.1-3)
By the Word of the LORD Were the Heavens Made (vv.6-9)
The Counsel of the LORD Standeth for Ever (vv.10-12)
There Is No King Saved by the Multitude of an Host (vv.16-17)
The Eye of the LORD Is upon Them That Fear Him (vv.18-19)
Our Soul Waiteth for the LORD (vv.20-22)
m: Singing a new song to God, creation by God's word, God's sovereign plan over nations, trust in God rather than military might, hope in God's steadfast love

x: An acrostic thanksgiving psalm, according to its heading composed after David feigned madness before Abimelech. He resolves to praise the LORD continually and invites others to join him in exalting God's name together (vv. 1-3), recounting how he sought the LORD and was delivered from his fears, with angels encamping around those who fear him (vv. 4-7). He invites readers to taste and see that the LORD is good, promising that those who fear him lack nothing good, unlike young lions who may go hungry (vv. 8-10). The psalm turns instructional, teaching the fear of the LORD through keeping the tongue from evil, turning from evil to do good, and seeking peace, since God's eyes and ears are toward the righteous but he opposes evildoers (vv. 11-16). It closes affirming that the LORD is near the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit, redeeming his servants so that none who take refuge…
h: I Will Bless the LORD at All Times (vv.1-7)
The Eyes of the LORD Are upon the Righteous (vv.15-18)
Many Are the Afflictions of the Righteous (vv.19-22)
m: Tasting God's goodness, the angel of the LORD encamping around the faithful, the many afflictions of the righteous, Messianic prophecy (no broken bones), the fear of the LORD as wisdom

x: An extended lament asking God to fight on David's behalf against enemies who repay his kindness with hostility. He calls on the LORD as a warrior to take up shield and spear against his pursuers, asking that they be like chaff driven by the wind and pursued by the angel of the LORD (vv. 1-6). He recalls that when his enemies were sick he mourned for them as for a friend or brother, yet they now rejoice at his misfortune and mock him without cause (vv. 11-16). He pleads for rescue from his life from the lions, promising to give thanks in the great congregation (vv. 17-18). He asks that his enemies not be allowed to gloat, wink maliciously, or claim to have swallowed him up (vv. 19-25), closing with a prayer that those who delight in his vindication would shout for joy, and a vow that his tongue would speak of God's righteousness and praise all day long (vv. 27-28).
h: They Rewarded Me Evil for Good (vv.11-18)
Let Them Not Rejoice Over Me (vv.19-28)
m: Enemies repaying evil for good, false accusation, plea for divine warrior intervention, vindication of the righteous, betrayal by former friends

x: A psalm contrasting human wickedness with God's boundless goodness. It opens describing the mindset of the wicked, who have no fear of God before their eyes, flatter themselves too much to detect or hate their own sin, and plot evil even while lying in bed (vv. 1-4). In sharp contrast, God's steadfast love and faithfulness are described as reaching to the heavens and skies, his righteousness like mighty mountains and his judgments like the deep sea, sustaining both people and animals (vv. 5-6). David marvels at the preciousness of God's steadfast love, under which people take refuge and feast abundantly, drinking from the river of his delights and seeing light in his light (vv. 7-9). The psalm closes with a prayer for God's love to continue toward those who know him, and confidence that evildoers will ultimately fall and not rise again (vv. 10-12).
h: Thy Mercy Is in the Heavens (vv.5-9)
Let Not the Foot of Pride Come Against Me (vv.10-12)
m: The wickedness of the wicked (no fear of God), God's steadfast love reaching to the heavens, the river of God's delights, the fountain of life, seeing light in God's light

x: An acrostic wisdom psalm counseling patience and trust in the face of the wicked's apparent success. David repeatedly urges the reader not to fret over evildoers, since they will soon fade like grass, and instead to trust in the LORD, delight in him, and commit one's way to him, allowing him to act (vv. 1-7). He contrasts the wicked, whose power and possessions will not last, with the righteous, whose steps the LORD establishes and who will inherit the land even through momentary falls (vv. 16-24). Looking back over a long life, David testifies that he has never seen the righteous utterly forsaken or their children begging for bread, since the LORD does not abandon his faithful ones (vv. 25-28). The psalm closes urging the reader to wait for the LORD and keep his way, promising that he will exalt the patient and that the salvation of the righteous comes from him, their refuge in trouble…
h: The Wicked Have Drawn Out the Sword (vv.12-15)
A Little That a Righteous Man Hath (vv.16-22)
I Have Been Young, and Now Am Old (vv.23-26)
Depart from Evil, and Do Good (vv.27-31)
I Have Seen the Wicked in Great Power (vv.32-36)
m: "Fret not" (repeated), trust and delight in the LORD, commit your way to God, the meek inheriting the earth, the righteous not forsaken, the brevity of the wicked's prosperity

x: A penitential lament in which David describes overwhelming guilt and physical suffering under what he understands as God's discipline. He describes his body wasting away because of his sin, with no soundness in his flesh, wounds that fester, and a heart in constant turmoil, groaning and utterly bowed down (vv. 1-8). His friends and companions stand aloof because of his affliction, while those who seek his life set traps and speak deceit against him all day (vv. 11-12). He describes himself as deaf and mute before his accusers, silently waiting on God rather than defending himself, confessing his iniquity and expressing sorrow over his sin (vv. 13-18). The psalm closes with a plea for God not to forsake him despite his many, powerful enemies, asking for speedy help from the God of his salvation (vv. 19-22).
h: Rebuke Me Not in Thy Wrath (vv.1-2)
There Is No Soundness in My Flesh (vv.3-8)
My Groaning Is Not Hid from Thee (vv.9-10)
My Lovers and My Friends Stand Aloof (v.11)
They Also That Seek My Hurt (v.12)
I Was as a Man That Heareth Not (vv.13-14)
In Thee, O LORD, Do I Hope (vv.15-16)
m: Suffering under divine discipline, graphic physical description of illness, sin acknowledged as the cause, friends and kinsmen withdrawing, patient waiting on God in silence

x: A meditation on the brevity of life. David resolved to guard his words and stay silent while the wicked were near him, but keeping quiet only intensified his inner anguish until he had to speak (vv. 1-3). He asks God to show him how fleeting his life is, since even a full life amounts to little more than a breath, and everyone goes about like a passing shadow, storing up wealth without knowing who will receive it (vv. 4-6). Placing his hope in the LORD, he asks for deliverance from his transgressions and relief from the weight of God's discipline, comparing his fading strength to a moth-eaten garment (vv. 7-11). The psalm closes asking God to hear his prayer, since he is a temporary resident on earth like his ancestors, and to look away so he may know a measure of gladness before he departs from this life (vv. 12-13).
h: I Will Keep My Mouth with a Bridle (vv.1-3)
Make Me to Know Mine End (vv.4-6)
Remove Thy Stroke Away from Me (vv.9-11)
I Am a Stranger with Thee (vv.12-13)
m: Guarding the tongue, the brevity and vanity of human life, prayer for understanding life's shortness, pilgrimage and sojourning, the discipline of God

x: A psalm combining thanksgiving with a later plea for help. David describes waiting patiently for the LORD, who lifted him out of a pit of destruction and set his feet on solid rock, putting a new song of praise in his mouth (vv. 1-3). Rather than sacrifice, God desires an open, obedient ear, and David responds that he has come to do God's will, since God's instruction is written on his heart, and he has proclaimed God's righteousness openly in the assembly (vv. 6-10). He then turns to present trouble, describing evils that surround him, more numerous than he can count, so that his courage fails, and pleads urgently for God's help (vv. 11-13). He asks for the shame of his enemies but joy for those who seek God, and describes himself as poor and needy, trusting that the LORD takes thought for him and asking him not to delay (vv. 14-17).
h: He Brought Me Up out of an Horrible Pit (vv.1-3)
Many, O LORD, Are Thy Wonderful Works (vv.4-5)
I Have Not Hid Thy Righteousness (vv.9-10)
Mine Iniquities Have Taken Hold upon Me (vv.12-17)
m: Patient waiting for God, deliverance from the pit, the new song, sacrifice versus obedience, Messianic prophecy (Christ's incarnation and will), delight in God's will

x: A lament and expression of trust that closes Book I of the Psalter. It opens pronouncing blessing on the one who considers the weak, promising that the LORD will deliver, protect, and sustain such a person, even restoring them from sickness (vv. 1-3). David then describes his own affliction, asking for healing and mercy while confessing his sin, and describes enemies who speak falsely to his face while spreading malicious rumors and hoping for his death behind his back (vv. 4-9). He notes that even a close friend who shared meals with him has turned against him, a betrayal later applied to Judas (v. 9; John 13:18). He asks God to raise him up in order to repay his enemies, finding assurance that God is pleased with him since his enemy has not triumphed over him (vv. 10-12). The psalm closes with a doxology blessing the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting, marking…
h: Blessed Is He That Considereth the Poor (vv.1-3)
Heal My Soul, for I Have Sinned (v.4)
Mine Enemies Speak Evil of Me (vv.5-8)
Raise Me Up, That I May Requite Them (vv.10-12)
Blessed Be the LORD God of Israel (v.13)
m: Compassion for the poor, betrayal by a friend, God's faithfulness, healing, Messianic prophecy

x: A lament expressing deep longing for God, likely from a worshiper exiled far from the temple, sharing a refrain with Psalm 43. The psalmist compares his soul's thirst for God to a deer panting for water, remembering how he once led festive worship processions to God's house, and now weeps day and night while others taunt him asking where his God is (vv. 1-4). He addresses his own soul directly, asking why it is downcast, and urges it to hope in God, who will again be praised (v. 5). From a distant region near the Jordan and Hermon, he recalls being overwhelmed like one caught in crashing waves, yet still trusts that the LORD commands his steadfast love by day and gives him a song by night (vv. 6-8). He asks God why he seems forgotten and mourns under the enemy's oppression, closing again with the refrain urging his soul to hope in God despite its distress (vv. 9-11).
h: The LORD Will Command His Lovingkindness (v.8)
m: Spiritual thirst, longing for God's presence, despair and hope, memory of worship, self-counsel

x: A lament that continues directly from Psalm 42, sharing its refrain and likely composed as a single unit. The psalmist pleads for God to vindicate him against an unfaithful people and rescue him from deceitful and unjust men, asking why God seems to have rejected him while he walks in mourning under oppression (vv. 1-2). He asks God to send out his light and truth to lead him back to the holy hill and God's dwelling place, where he can approach the altar with joy and praise God with the harp (vv. 3-4). The psalm closes exactly as Psalm 42 does, repeating the refrain in which the psalmist questions his own downcast soul and resolves to hope in God, since he will again praise him as his salvation (v. 5).
h: Send Out Thy Light and Thy Truth (v.3)
Then Will I Go unto the Altar of God (v.4)
m: Prayer for vindication, light and truth as guides, longing for worship, hope in God

x: A communal lament in which the people recall God's past deliverance while struggling to understand present defeat. They recount stories heard from their ancestors of how God drove out nations and planted Israel in the land, not by their own sword but by God's power and favor (vv. 1-3), and affirm that their boast is always in God rather than their own weapons (vv. 4-8). Yet the psalm turns to describe a bitter reversal: God has now rejected and humbled them, allowing them to be defeated and scattered among the nations, an object of scorn (vv. 9-16). The people insist that this suffering has come despite their faithfulness to the covenant and without turning from God, describing themselves as sheep destined for slaughter (vv. 17-22). The psalm closes with an urgent plea for God to wake up, stop hiding his face, and redeem them because of his steadfast love (vv. 23-26).
h: We Have Heard with Our Ears (vv.1-3)
Through Thee Will We Push Down Our Enemies (vv.4-8)
All This Is Come upon Us, Yet Have We Not Forgotten Thee (vv.17-22)
m: National suffering, innocent suffering, faithfulness despite defeat, bold appeal to God, martyrdom

x: A royal wedding psalm celebrating a king's marriage, understood by later New Testament writers as pointing to Christ (Hebrews 1:8-9). The poet describes his heart stirred by a noble theme and addresses the king as the most excellent of men, blessed by God forever, urging him to ride out victoriously for truth and justice (vv. 1-5). The king's throne is described as established by God forever, his rule marked by righteousness and gladness above his companions, and his royal robes fragrant with spices from ivory palaces (vv. 6-9). The psalm then turns to address the bride, urging her to forget her own people and honor her lord, describing her arrival in splendor with her attendants amid joy and gladness (vv. 10-15). It closes anticipating that the king's sons will become princes throughout the land, and that his name will be remembered and praised by the nations forever (vv. 16-17).
h: My Heart Is Inditing a Good Matter (vv.1-2)
Gird Thy Sword upon Thy Thigh (vv.3-5)
Thy Throne, O God, Is For Ever (vv.6-9)
Instead of Thy Fathers Shall Be Thy Children (vv.16-17)
m: The King's beauty and glory, the royal bride, Messianic kingship, divine throne, the marriage of Christ and His Church

x: A psalm of trust known as a Song of Zion. It opens declaring that God is a refuge and strength, an ever-present help in trouble, so there is no need to fear even if the earth gives way, mountains fall into the sea, and its waters roar and foam (vv. 1-3). A river brings joy to the city of God, his holy dwelling, and because God is present within her she will not fall, receiving his help at the break of day (vv. 4-5). Nations rage and kingdoms totter, but God's voice alone melts the earth, giving rise to the refrain that the LORD of hosts is with his people, the God of Jacob their fortress (vv. 6-7). Onlookers are invited to see the works of the LORD, who brings desolation on the nations, ends wars, and destroys weapons of war (vv. 8-9). The psalm closes with the well-known command to be still and know that he is God, exalted among the nations and over all the earth, repeating the earlier…
h: God Is Our Refuge and Strength (vv.1-3)
m: God as refuge, fearlessness in chaos, God's sovereign power, "Be still and know," divine presence in the city of God

x: An enthronement hymn calling all peoples to celebrate God's kingship. It opens summoning the nations to clap their hands and shout to God with cries of joy, since the LORD Most High is to be feared as great king over all the earth (vv. 1-2). He is praised for subduing nations under Israel and choosing their inheritance (vv. 3-4). The psalm describes God ascending amid shouts of joy and the sound of trumpets, and calls repeatedly for singing praise to him as king over all the earth and all nations (vv. 5-7). The psalm closes picturing God seated on his holy throne while the nobles of the peoples gather with the people of the God of Abraham, since the rulers of the earth belong to him and he is highly exalted (vv. 8-9).
h: Clap Your Hands, All Ye People (vv.1-4)
God Is Gone Up with a Shout (vv.5-7)
m: Universal kingship of God, exuberant praise, God's ascension, nations gathered to God, joyful worship

x: A Song of Zion celebrating the security of God's holy city. It opens declaring that the LORD is great and greatly to be praised in the city of God, his holy mountain, beautiful in elevation and the joy of the whole earth (vv. 1-2). God has made himself known within its citadels as a fortress (v. 3), and when kings gathered against the city they were struck with astonishment, panic, and trembling like a woman in labor, fleeing in fear (vv. 4-7). What the worshipers had only heard about, they now witness firsthand in the city of the LORD, which God establishes forever (v. 8). Inside the temple, the people meditate on God's steadfast love, and his praise and righteousness reach to the ends of the earth (vv. 9-10). The psalm closes urging the people to walk about Zion, count its towers, and consider its ramparts, so they can tell the next generation that this God is their God forever, who…
h: As We Have Heard, So Have We Seen (v.8)
We Have Thought of Thy Lovingkindness (vv.9-11)
m: The glory of Zion, God as defender of His city, the beauty of God's dwelling, generational testimony, God as eternal guide

x: A wisdom psalm on the folly of trusting in wealth in light of death. The psalmist calls all people, rich and poor alike, to hear this teaching on the emptiness of riches (vv. 1-4), and asks why he should fear those who trust in their wealth, since no one can ransom another or pay God a price to live forever (vv. 5-9). The wise and the foolish alike die and leave their wealth to others, so that human beings without understanding are compared to the beasts that perish (vv. 10-12, 20). The psalmist contrasts this with his own hope that God will redeem his soul from the power of death (v. 15). He closes urging the reader not to be overawed when someone grows rich, since they will carry nothing with them when they die, and again warns that a person without understanding is like the animals that perish (vv. 16-20).
h: They That Trust in Their Wealth (vv.5-9)
Be Not Thou Afraid When One Is Made Rich (vv.16-20)
m: The futility of wealth against death, death as the great equalizer, redemption that only God can provide, the distinction between the wise and the foolish

x: A psalm of judgment in which God himself summons the earth to witness his verdict on his covenant people. The mighty God speaks and calls heaven and earth to judge his people, coming in fire and storm as a consuming presence (vv. 1-6). God clarifies that he does not need Israel's sacrifices for food, since every animal already belongs to him; what he desires is genuine thanksgiving and the honoring of vows, calling on the afflicted to cry out to him in trouble (vv. 7-15). He then rebukes the wicked who recite his statutes while hating discipline, tolerating theft and adultery, and slandering even close family, warning that his patience is not the same as approval (vv. 16-21). The psalm closes with a warning to those who forget God, and a promise that whoever offers genuine thanksgiving honors him and will see his salvation (vv. 22-23).
h: I Will Take No Bullock out of Thy House (vv.7-15)
m: God as judge of His people, true worship vs. empty ritual, God's self-sufficiency, thanksgiving as true sacrifice, hypocrisy exposed

x: A penitential psalm, David's prayer of confession after Nathan confronted him over his sin with Bathsheba and Uriah (superscription). He appeals to God's steadfast love and mercy to blot out his transgressions and cleanse him from his sin, admitting his guilt is constantly before him and that his sin is ultimately against God himself (vv. 1-4). He asks God to purify him thoroughly and to create in him a clean heart and a renewed, steadfast spirit, pleading not to be cast away from God's presence (vv. 7-11). He longs for the joy of salvation restored so he can teach other transgressors God's ways (vv. 12-13), recognizing that God desires a broken and contrite heart more than any sacrifice (vv. 16-17), and closes praying for the well-being of Zion and for future acceptable sacrifices (vv. 18-19).
h: Have Mercy upon Me, O God (vv.1-6)
Create in Me a Clean Heart (vv.10-12)
The Sacrifices of God Are a Broken Spirit (vv.13-17)
Build Thou the Walls of Jerusalem (vv.18-19)
m: Repentance, confession, divine mercy, cleansing from sin, inner transformation, the broken heart, restoration of joy

x: An imprecatory psalm directed at Doeg the Edomite, who betrayed David to Saul (superscription; 1 Samuel 22). David rebukes the powerful man who boasts in evil and loves lies and destructive speech more than truth and righteousness (vv. 1-4). He declares that God will tear him down, uproot him from his tent, and remove him from the land of the living, while the righteous watch, fear God, and laugh at one who trusted in wealth rather than in God (vv. 5-7). By contrast, David compares himself to a flourishing olive tree in God's house, trusting in God's steadfast love forever and vowing to thank and wait on God's name among the faithful (vv. 8-9).
h: I Am Like a Green Olive Tree (vv.8-9)
m: The power of the tongue, false security in wealth, judgment of the wicked, trust in God's steadfast love, contrast between the wicked and the righteous

x: A wisdom psalm, essentially a variant of Psalm 14. The fool denies God in his heart and lives corruptly, and when God looks down from heaven he finds no one who does good, not even one (vv. 1-3). The wicked who devour God's people and never call on him will be struck with great terror, for God scatters the bones of those who besiege the righteous, putting them to shame (vv. 4-5). The psalm closes longing for salvation to come out of Zion, when God restores his people's fortunes and Jacob rejoices (v. 6).
h: The Fool Hath Said in His Heart (v.1)
Have the Workers of Iniquity No Knowledge (v.4)
There Were They in Great Fear (v.5)
Oh That the Salvation of Israel (v.6)
m: Universal human depravity, atheistic folly, God's sovereign observation, total corruption, hope for salvation from Zion

x: A brief lament from when the Ziphites betrayed David's hiding place to Saul (superscription; 1 Samuel 23). David asks God to save and vindicate him by his name and might, since ruthless men who do not regard God are seeking his life (vv. 1-3). He affirms that God is his helper and sustainer, trusting that God will repay his enemies' evil, and vows to offer a freewill sacrifice and give thanks to God's good name (vv. 4-6). The psalm ends confident that God has delivered him from trouble, letting him look in triumph on his enemies (v. 7).
h: Save Me, O God, by Thy Name (vv.1-2)
Strangers Are Risen Up Against Me (v.3)
m: Crying out for deliverance, God's name as salvation, betrayal by allies, confidence in God's help, vow of thanksgiving

x: A lament over betrayal, likely from Absalom's rebellion. David asks God to hear his anguished complaint as enemies oppress him and dread overwhelms him, making him wish for wings like a dove so he could fly away to the wilderness and escape the storm of violence filling the city (vv. 1-8). He describes the city gripped by strife and oppression, but his deepest pain is that the one attacking him is not an enemy but a close friend and companion with whom he once walked to worship together (vv. 9-14). He calls down judgment on his betrayers even as he cries to God morning, noon, and night, confident God will hear and redeem him (vv. 15-19). He contrasts his friend's smooth, treacherous words with the violence hidden in his heart, then resolves to cast his burden on the LORD, trusting God to sustain the righteous and bring the bloodthirsty and deceitful to ruin (vv. 20-23).
h: Oh That I Had Wings Like a Dove (vv.4-8)
I Have Seen Violence and Strife in the City (vv.9-11)
Evening, and Morning, and at Noon (vv.16-19)
Cast Thy Burden upon the LORD (vv.22-23)
m: Betrayal by a close friend, desire to escape, the pain of broken trust, casting burdens on the LORD, God's faithfulness amid human treachery

x: A lament of trust from when the Philistines seized David in Gath (superscription; 1 Samuel 21). David asks for mercy as enemies trample and attack him all day long, yet declares that whenever he is afraid he will trust in God rather than fear what mere flesh can do to him (vv. 1-4). He describes his adversaries twisting his words and lying in wait for his life, but trusts that God has kept count of his wanderings and even collected his tears (vv. 5-8). Confident that his enemies will retreat when he calls, he repeats his refrain of trust in God's word rather than fear of man, and closes vowing to fulfill his thank offerings for having been delivered from death so he may walk before God in the light of the living (vv. 9-13).
h: Be Merciful unto Me, O God (vv.1-2)
In God I Will Praise His Word (vv.3-4)
Put My Tears into Thy Bottle (v.8)
m: Trust in the midst of fear, God's Word as anchor, divine record of suffering, tears stored by God, confidence over fear of man

x: A lament that turns to praise, written while David hid from Saul in a cave (superscription; 1 Samuel 22 or 24). He takes refuge under the shadow of God's wings until destruction passes, crying out to the Most High who sends help from heaven against those who trample him (vv. 1-3). Surrounded by enemies whose words are sharp as swords, he prays that God's glory would be exalted above the heavens even as they set a trap that will catch themselves instead (vv. 4-6). His heart grows steadfast and he resolves to sing and awaken the dawn with praise, declaring he will thank God among the nations for a steadfast love reaching to the heavens (vv. 7-10), and closes repeating his prayer that God be exalted above all the earth (v. 11).
m: Refuge under God's wings, steadfast heart, praise in the midst of danger, God's glory above all, faithfulness and mercy reaching to the heavens

x: An imprecatory psalm confronting corrupt rulers who, instead of judging righteously, devise violence in their hearts and deal it out with their hands (vv. 1-2). David compares them to venomous, deaf serpents who refuse to heed any voice of correction from birth (vv. 3-5). He calls on God to break their strength like a lion's teeth and make them vanish like water draining away or grass trampled underfoot (vv. 6-8). He anticipates the righteous rejoicing when they see God's vengeance carried out, so that onlookers will conclude there truly is reward for the righteous and a God who judges on earth (vv. 9-11).
m: Corrupt judges, injustice, innate human wickedness, divine vengeance, God as righteous Judge, vindication of the righteous

x: A lament from when Saul sent men to watch David's house in order to kill him (superscription; 1 Samuel 19). David pleads for deliverance from bloodthirsty enemies who lie in wait against him though he is guilty of no offense, comparing them to snarling dogs that prowl the city at night (vv. 1-7). He trusts that God, his strength and fortress, laughs at the nations' scheming and will let him look in triumph on his foes, and asks God not to destroy them outright but to make an example of their downfall so all will know God rules over Jacob to the ends of the earth (vv. 8-13). After repeating the picture of enemies prowling and growling like hungry dogs, David resolves to sing of God's strength and steadfast love every morning, since God has been his fortress and refuge in the day of distress (vv. 14-17).
h: Thou, O LORD, Shalt Laugh at Them (vv.8-10)
They Go About the City Again (vv.14-15)
I Will Sing of Thy Power (vv.16-17)
m: Deliverance from enemies, innocence under persecution, God as fortress and defense, morning praise, God's sovereign laughter over the wicked

x: A communal lament after a military defeat, prayed during David's wars with Aram and Edom (superscription; 2 Samuel 8). David laments that God has rejected and broken the nation, shaking the land like an earthquake, and pleads for God to heal what he has torn (vv. 1-3). He recalls God's promise of a banner to rally those who fear him and asks for deliverance by God's right hand (vv. 4-5). God then answers in an oracle claiming sovereignty over the surrounding territories, portioning out Shechem and Succoth and declaring Moab, Edom, and Philistia subdued under him (vv. 6-8). David asks who will lead him against fortified Edom now that God seems to have rejected them, since human help is worthless, and closes trusting that with God's help they will act valiantly and tread down their foes (vv. 9-12).
h: O God, Thou Hast Cast Us Off (vv.1-3)
A Banner Because of the Truth (vv.4-5)
Gilead Is Mine, and Manasseh Is Mine (vv.6-8)
Who Will Bring Me into the Strong City (vv.9-10)
Through God We Shall Do Valiantly (vv.11-12)
m: National defeat and divine discipline, God's sovereignty over all nations, hope after setback, the futility of human help, confidence in God's ultimate victory

x: A psalm of prayer and trust, likely written by David during a time of exile or distress far from Jerusalem. He cries to God from the ends of the earth, asking to be led to a rock higher than himself and recalling God's past faithfulness as shelter and strong tower (vv. 1-3). He longs to dwell in God's presence forever, sheltered under his wings (v. 4), and reflects on vows God has already heard (v. 5). The psalm turns to intercession for the king, asking that his life and reign be extended under God's steadfast love and faithfulness (vv. 6-7), closing with a vow to keep praising God's name and fulfilling his vows day after day (v. 8).
h: From the End of the Earth (vv.1-2)
A Shelter and a Strong Tower (vv.3-4)
The Heritage of Them That Fear Thy Name (v.5)
Thou Wilt Prolong the King's Life (vv.6-7)
m: Crying out from a distance, the rock higher than I, God as shelter and strong tower, longing for God's presence, prayer for the king, eternal praise

x: A psalm of quiet trust, in which David describes waiting in silence for God alone as his rock, salvation, and defense, unshaken despite hostile plots against him (vv. 1-4). He renews that same resolve mid-psalm, urging his own soul to wait only for God and inviting the people to pour out their hearts before him as a refuge (vv. 5-8). David then warns against putting confidence in human status, oppression, or increasing riches, since people of every rank are ultimately insubstantial (vv. 9-10). The psalm closes with the twin truths David has heard from God himself — that power belongs to God, and that steadfast love belongs to the Lord, who repays everyone according to what they have done (vv. 11-12).
h: How Long Will Ye Imagine Mischief (vv.3-4)
Pour Out Your Heart Before Him (v.8)
Men of Low Degree Are Vanity (vv.9-10)
m: Waiting on God alone, soul silence before God, God as rock and fortress, the vanity of human trust, power and mercy belong to God

x: A psalm of ardent longing, written by David in the wilderness of Judah — he describes an intense thirst for God like a parched traveler in a dry and waterless land, recalling how he has beheld God's power and glory in the sanctuary (vv. 1-2). Because God's steadfast love is better than life itself, David resolves to praise him with lifted hands as long as he lives, and to meditate on him through the night (vv. 3-6). He clings to God as his help and refuge, satisfied as if feasting on the richest food, while those seeking his life will be brought down and destroyed (vv. 7-10). The psalm ends with confidence that the king will rejoice in God and all who swear by him will boast, while liars will be silenced (v. 11).
h: Thy Lovingkindness Is Better Than Life (vv.3-5)
They Shall Go into the Lower Parts of the Earth (vv.9-10)
The King Shall Rejoice in God (v.11)
m: Thirsting for God, God's love better than life, soul satisfaction in God, nighttime meditation, clinging to God, joy under God's wings

x: A psalm of lament turning to confident praise, David asks God to protect him from enemies who plot in secret and aim bitter words like arrows at the innocent, believing no one will see their schemes (vv. 1-6). He trusts that God will turn their own weapons against them, shooting them down suddenly so their own tongues bring about their ruin (vv. 7-8). Witnessing this reversal, people everywhere will recognize it as God's doing and stand in awe (v. 9). The psalm closes with the righteous rejoicing and taking refuge in the Lord, with all the upright in heart giving him glory (v. 10).
h: They Whet Their Tongue Like a Sword (vv.3-6)
m: Secret plots of enemies, the tongue as weapon, God's sudden counter-attack, divine poetic justice, the righteous rejoicing in God's judgment

x: A psalm of thanksgiving and praise, celebrating God as the one who hears prayer, forgives overwhelming sin, and welcomes those he chooses to dwell near him in his courts (vv. 1-4). David praises God's awesome deeds of deliverance, the confidence he inspires to the ends of the earth, and his power in setting the mountains in place and stilling the roaring seas (vv. 5-8). The psalm turns to God's care for creation — visiting the earth with rain, enriching it, and preparing grain for the people (vv. 9-10). It closes with a vivid picture of abundance: the year crowned with God's goodness, pastures overflowing with flocks, and valleys covered with grain, all shouting and singing for joy (vv. 11-13).
h: Praise Waiteth for Thee in Zion (vv.1-2)
Blessed Is the Man Whom Thou Choosest (v.4)
By Terrible Things Wilt Thou Answer Us (vv.5-8)
m: Praise for answered prayer, atonement for sin, the blessedness of God's chosen ones, God's sovereignty over nature, abundant provision, the joy of creation

x: A psalm of corporate and personal praise, calling all the earth to shout for joy and sing of God's glorious name and awesome works (vv. 1-4). It recalls God's mighty acts in Israel's history — turning the sea into dry land so his people could cross on foot — and praises his ongoing rule over the nations (vv. 5-7). The psalm then shifts to testimony of refining trials: God tested his people like silver, let them pass through fire and water, yet ultimately brought them into abundance (vv. 8-12). The psalmist personally vows to bring offerings and declares what God has done for his own soul, testifying that God heard his prayer because he did not cling to sin, and closing in praise that God did not turn away his prayer or his steadfast love (vv. 13-20).
h: Make a Joyful Noise unto God (vv.1-4)
He Turned the Sea into Dry Land (vv.5-7)
Thou Hast Tried Us, as Silver Is Tried (vv.8-12)
I Will Pay Thee My Vows (vv.13-15)
Come and Hear, All Ye That Fear God (vv.16-20)
m: Universal praise, God's awesome deeds, testing and refining through trials, personal testimony of answered prayer, the condition for being heard by God

x: A brief missionary psalm, asking God to bless his people and make his face shine on them so that his ways would be known throughout the earth and among all nations (vv. 1-2). Twice the psalmist calls all peoples to praise God, envisioning the nations glad and singing because God judges with justice and guides them (vv. 3-5). The psalm closes by connecting the earth's harvest to God's blessing, praying that God would continue to bless his people so that the whole earth would revere him (vv. 6-7).
h: Then Shall the Earth Yield Her Increase (vv.6-7)
m: God's blessing for global mission, all nations praising God, God's righteous governance, harvest blessing, the Aaronic benediction extended to the world

x: A triumphant psalm of God as divine warrior and king, opening with a prayer that God would arise and scatter his enemies while the righteous rejoice before him (vv. 1-4). He is celebrated as a father to the fatherless and defender of widows, who leads prisoners into freedom and provided for his people during the wilderness march from Sinai (vv. 5-10). The psalm recalls historic victories — kings fleeing armies, spoil being divided, and God's triumphant ascent to his dwelling place on Zion, a hill he chose over all others, escorted by thousands of chariots and angels (vv. 11-18). It praises God as the one who daily carries his people's burdens and holds power even over death, promising to bring his people back from every distant place and to deal with his enemies (vv. 19-23). The psalm closes with a procession of praise into the sanctuary — singers, musicians, and tribal leaders —…
h: Thou, O God, Didst Send a Plentiful Rain (vv.7-14)
Who Daily Loadeth Us with Benefits (vv.19-23)
m: God as warrior-king, the march of God through history, care for the vulnerable, the ascension of God, gifts for men, God's victorious procession, universal praise

x: A psalm of deep lament with strong messianic overtones, David describes himself sinking in overwhelming floodwaters, worn out from crying out and hated without cause even though he bears reproach for God's sake — famously declaring that zeal for God's house has consumed him (vv. 1-9). His fasting, mourning, and devotion have made him a joke to his own family and a target of mockery at the city gate, yet he keeps praying for God's steadfast love to answer him (vv. 10-18). He describes being given gall for food and vinegar to drink in his thirst, isolated with no one to comfort him (vv. 19-21). The psalm turns to an extended imprecation, asking God to bring judgment on his tormentors and blot them from the book of the living (vv. 22-28). It closes with David turning to praise despite his suffering, promising to glorify God with thanksgiving, calling the humble and all creation to rejoice…
h: Save Me, O God, for the Waters Are Come In (vv.1-4)
My Sins Are Not Hid from Thee (vv.5-6)
The Zeal of Thine House Hath Eaten Me Up (vv.7-12)
Hear Me, O LORD, for Thy Mercy Is Good (vv.13-18)
Let Their Table Become a Snare (vv.22-28)
I Will Praise the Name of God with a Song (vv.29-36)
m: Suffering for God's sake, rejection and reproach, Messianic suffering, imprecation against enemies, praise over sacrifice, hope for Zion's salvation

x: A brief, urgent plea for help, nearly identical to the closing verses of Psalm 40. David asks God to hurry to his rescue and to turn back in shame those who seek his life and mock him (vv. 1-3). He prays that those who seek God would instead rejoice and continually praise him (v. 4). The psalm ends with David's own confession of need — poor and needy, he begs God, his only help and deliverer, not to delay (v. 5).
m: Urgency of prayer, pleading for speed, shame on enemies, joy for God-seekers, poverty and neediness before God

x: An individual lament and psalm of trust, likely voiced by an aging worshiper in David's tradition. The psalmist takes refuge in God and asks never to be put to shame, appealing to him as a strong rock of habitation (vv. 1-3), and recalls that he has trusted God since his youth and even from birth (vv. 5-6). Now that old age has come and strength is failing, he begs God not to forsake him while enemies watch for his downfall, assuming God has abandoned him, and asks for their disgrace (vv. 9-13). He resolves to keep hoping and praising God's righteousness and mighty acts even though he cannot fully recount them, asking only to be kept alive long enough to declare God's power to the next generation (vv. 14-18). The psalm closes with confidence that God will revive him from deep distress, prompting a vow of joyful praise on the harp and lyre and constant talk of God's righteousness (vv.…
h: In Thee, O LORD, Do I Put My Trust (vv.1-4)
Thou Art My Trust from My Youth (vv.5-8)
Cast Me Not Off in the Time of Old Age (vv.9-13)
I Will Go in the Strength of the Lord GOD (vv.14-16)
Now Also When I Am Old (vv.17-21)
My Tongue Shall Talk of Thy Righteousness (vv.22-24)
m: Trust from youth to old age, fear of being forsaken in weakness, God's faithfulness across a lifetime, declaring God's works to the next generation, continued praise despite aging

x: A royal and messianic psalm attributed to or for Solomon, closing Book II of the Psalter. It prays that the king would govern with God's own justice, defending the poor and crushing oppressors, so that he endures as long as the sun and moon and refreshes the land like rain on mown grass (vv. 1-7). His dominion is pictured stretching from sea to sea and to the ends of the earth, with foreign kings bringing tribute and all nations bowing before him (vv. 8-11), because he rescues the needy and those who have no helper and redeems them from violence (vv. 12-14). The psalm envisions lasting prosperity and a name that endures forever, with all nations calling him blessed (vv. 15-17). It closes with a doxology praising the LORD, whose glory fills the whole earth, followed by the editorial note that the prayers of David are ended (vv. 18-20).
h: He Shall Have Dominion from Sea to Sea (vv.5-11)
His Name Shall Endure for Ever (vv.15-17)
m: The ideal king, justice for the poor, universal dominion, prosperity under righteous rule, the everlasting kingdom, all nations blessed

x: A wisdom psalm of Asaph, opening Book III of the Psalter and part of the Asaph collection (Psalms 73-83). The psalmist confesses that his feet nearly slipped when he envied the prosperity of the arrogant, who seem free of struggle, grow fat and proud, and mock God with impunity while their wealth increases (vv. 1-12). He nearly concluded that keeping a pure heart had been pointless, since he faced trouble and discipline every morning (vv. 13-14), until he entered God's sanctuary and finally understood the wicked's true end — set on slippery ground and swept away suddenly like a dream (vv. 15-20). Recognizing his own bitterness as senseless, he affirms that God still holds his hand and guides him, climaxing in the declaration that God alone, not heaven or earth, is his true desire and portion forever (vv. 21-26). Those who abandon God perish, but for the psalmist nearness to God is…
h: Truly God Is Good to Israel (v.1)
Until I Went into the Sanctuary (vv.17-20)
Whom Have I in Heaven but Thee (vv.23-28)
m: The prosperity of the wicked, the suffering of the righteous, envy and doubt, the sanctuary as turning point, God as ultimate portion, nearness to God as supreme good

x: A communal lament of Asaph, mourning the destruction of the temple, likely by an invading enemy such as Babylon. The psalmist asks why God has cast off his people forever and pleads with him to remember Zion, now that adversaries have burned the sanctuary and destroyed its carved work with axes (vv. 1-8). With no prophet left to say how long this will last, he asks how long God's name will be scorned and urges God to act (vv. 9-11). He then recalls God's ancient acts of power — splitting the sea, crushing the heads of Leviathan, opening springs and rivers, and fixing the boundaries of day, night, and seasons (vv. 12-17) — as grounds for hope. He appeals to God to remember his covenant and the reproach against his name, not to abandon the poor and oppressed to their enemies, and to rise up and defend his own cause against those who mock him without end (vv. 18-23).
h: Why Hast Thou Cast Us Off For Ever (vv.1-3)
They Have Set Up Their Ensigns (vv.4-8)
There Is No More Any Prophet (vv.9-11)
m: Destruction of the temple, God's apparent absence, "how long?", covenant faithfulness appealed to, God's power over creation, cry for divine intervention

x: A psalm of judgment attributed to Asaph. It opens with thanks that God's name is near and his wonders are declared (v. 1), then God himself speaks, announcing that at his appointed time he will judge with fairness and warning the arrogant and wicked not to boast or raise a defiant horn (vv. 2-5). True exaltation comes from God alone, not from any direction on earth, since he is the judge who humbles one and lifts up another (vv. 6-7). A cup of foaming wine in the LORD's hand pictures the judgment the wicked must drink to the dregs (v. 8). The psalmist vows to praise the God of Jacob forever, who will cut off the strength of the wicked while exalting the righteous (vv. 9-10).
h: Unto Thee, O God, Do We Give Thanks (v.1)
Promotion Cometh Neither from the East nor from the West (vv.6-8)
All the Horns of the Wicked Will I Cut Off (vv.9-10)
m: God as sovereign judge, divine timing ("the set time"), the cup of God's wrath, God alone exalts and brings down, warning against pride

x: A Song of Zion celebrating God's victory over hostile armies, Asaph declares that God is known in Judah, with his dwelling place established in Zion, and that he has broken the weapons of war there (vv. 1-3). Even the mightiest warriors were left powerless once God rebuked them, their chariots and horses cast into a deep sleep (vv. 4-6). The psalm reflects on God's awesome, fearsome power to judge and to save the meek of the earth, noting that even human wrath will ultimately serve to display his glory (vv. 7-10). It closes with a call to bring vows and gifts to this God who humbles the pride of rulers and is to be feared by every king (vv. 11-12).
h: Thou Art More Glorious Than the Mountains of Prey (vv.4-6)
Who May Stand in Thy Sight (vv.7-9)
The Wrath of Man Shall Praise Thee (v.10)
Vow, and Pay unto the LORD (vv.11-12)
m: God's victory from Zion, divine warrior, the fear of God, human wrath serving God's purposes, God as judge over all the earth

x: A psalm of lament that turns to remembrance, Asaph describes crying out to God in the night, so troubled that he cannot even speak, and wondering aloud whether God's mercy and promises have failed for good (vv. 1-9). He then deliberately shifts his focus, choosing to remember the years of God's past faithfulness and the wonders he has worked (vv. 10-12). The psalm reflects on God's holiness and unmatched greatness, recalling how the waters themselves trembled at his power (vv. 13-16). It closes by retelling the exodus, picturing God's path through the sea and his leading of his people like a flock under Moses and Aaron, even though his footprints were left unseen (vv. 17-20).
h: I Cried unto God with My Voice (vv.1-3)
Will the Lord Cast Off For Ever (vv.7-9)
I Will Remember the Years of the Right Hand (vv.10-12)
Thy Way Is in the Sanctuary (v.13)
Thy Way Is in the Sea (vv.14-20)
m: Sleepless anguish, questioning God's faithfulness, choosing to remember God's works, the Exodus as proof of God's power, God's invisible ways

x: A long historical psalm of instruction, Asaph opens by calling the people to pass down the story of God's works to their children so future generations will not repeat their ancestors' stubborn unfaithfulness (vv. 1-8). He recounts Israel's rebellion in the wilderness despite witnessing miracles like the parting of the sea and water from the rock, including their complaints for food and God's provision of manna and quail (vv. 9-31). Even after repeated judgment, the people kept sinning and only turned back to God superficially, provoking him again and again until he abandoned Shiloh and allowed his people to fall by the sword (vv. 32-64). The psalm closes with God rousing himself like a warrior, rejecting Ephraim, and instead choosing the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, and David his servant to shepherd Israel with integrity and skill (vv. 65-72).
h: We Will Not Hide Them from Their Children (vv.1-8)
The Children of Ephraim Turned Back (vv.9-11)
Can God Furnish a Table in the Wilderness (vv.17-31)
He, Being Full of Compassion, Forgave (vv.32-39)
He Turned Their Rivers into Blood (vv.40-55)
He Forsook the Tabernacle of Shiloh (vv.56-64)
m: Teaching the next generation, Israel's cycle of rebellion and grace, God's patience and compassion, the Exodus retold, God's choice of David and Judah over Ephraim

x: A communal lament following national disaster, Asaph describes foreign nations invading God's inheritance, defiling the temple, reducing Jerusalem to ruins, and leaving the dead unburied while their blood is poured out like water (vv. 1-4). He cries out asking how long God's anger will last and pleads for God's wrath to fall instead on the nations who do not know him (vv. 5-7). The psalm asks God not to hold past sins against his people, but to act quickly for the sake of his own name and glory, avenging his servants' shed blood (vv. 8-12). It closes with a vow that, once rescued, God's people will give thanks and declare his praise to every generation (v. 13).
h: The Heathen Are Come into Thine Inheritance (vv.1-4)
Pour Out Thy Wrath upon the Heathen (vv.6-7)
Remember Not Against Us Former Iniquities (vv.8-9)
We Thy People Will Praise Thee For Ever (v.13)
m: Temple desecration, Jerusalem's destruction, unburied dead, national shame, God's reputation among the nations, plea for mercy and vengeance, generational praise

x: A communal lament addressed to God as Israel's shepherd, the psalmist pleads for him to lead his people like a flock, shine his face on them, and save them, a refrain repeated three times through the psalm (vv. 1-3, 7, 19). He laments that God has fed his people with tears and made them an object of ridicule to their neighbors (vv. 4-6). The central image is a vine that God brought out of Egypt and planted, which once filled the land and flourished but is now broken down, its hedges torn away and its branches burned (vv. 8-16). The psalm closes with a plea for God to strengthen the man at his right hand and revive his people, promising that they will never turn back from him again (vv. 17-19).
h: Give Ear, O Shepherd of Israel (vv.1-2)
Thou Feedest Them with the Bread of Tears (vv.4-6)
Turn Us Again, O God of Hosts (v.7)
Thou Hast Brought a Vine out of Egypt (vv.8-16)
The Man of Thy Right Hand (vv.17-18)
Turn Us Again, O LORD God of Hosts (v.19)
m: God as Shepherd of Israel, the vine metaphor, national devastation, "restore us" refrain, the shining face of God, prayer for the "man of thy right hand"

x: A festival psalm calling Israel to celebrate with music and song at the appointed feast, a statute instituted from the time God delivered his people out of Egypt (vv. 1-5). The psalm shifts into God's own voice, recalling how he relieved Israel's burdens and tested them at the waters of Meribah, warning them against worshiping any foreign god (vv. 6-10). God laments that his people would not listen and gave them over to their own stubborn hearts and plans (vv. 11-12). The psalm closes with God's wish that Israel had walked in his ways, promising that he would have subdued their enemies and satisfied them with the finest food (vv. 13-16).
h: Sing Aloud unto God Our Strength (vv.1-5a)
I Removed His Shoulder from the Burden (vv.5b-7)
Oh That My People Had Hearkened (vv.13-16)
m: Festival worship, God's voice from Sinai, divine longing for obedience, the tragedy of "would not," God's willingness to bless if only Israel would listen

x: A brief prophetic psalm depicting God presiding over an assembly of judges or rulers, confronting them for showing favoritism to the wicked instead of upholding justice (vv. 1-2). He commands them to defend the poor, the fatherless, and the afflicted, and to rescue the needy from oppression, condemning their ignorance and the moral disorder they have allowed (vv. 3-5). Though these rulers were given great authority, even called "gods," God declares that they will die like any other mortal, falling like any earthly prince (vv. 6-7). The psalm closes with a plea for God himself to rise up and judge the earth, since all nations belong to him (v. 8).
h: God Standeth in the Congregation of the Mighty (v.1)
How Long Will Ye Judge Unjustly (v.2)
They Know Not, Neither Will They Understand (v.5)
Arise, O God, Judge the Earth (v.8)
m: God judging unjust judges, human rulers as "gods," defense of the weak, the foundations of earth shaken by injustice, mortality of corrupt authorities, God inheriting all nations

x: A communal lament calling on God not to stay silent while a coalition of enemy nations conspires to wipe out Israel entirely, so that its name would be remembered no more (vv. 1-8). Asaph names the allied peoples arrayed against Israel — Edom, Moab, Ammon, the Philistines, Tyre, and others — united in their hostility (vv. 5-8). He prays that God would defeat them as he once defeated Midian, Sisera, and Jabin, scattering them like dust and stubble before the wind (vv. 9-15).
