The psalm closes asking that their shame would drive them to seek God's name, so that all people would know that the LORD alone is Most High over all the earth (vv. 16-18).
h: Keep Not Thou Silence, O God (vv.1-4)
Do unto Them as unto the Midianites (vv.9-12)
That Men May Know That Thou Art the Most High (v.18)
m: Enemy coalition against Israel, God's silence, prayer for divine intervention, historical precedents of God's victories, the ultimate purpose: that all may know God is LORD

x: A pilgrimage psalm expressing deep affection for God's dwelling place, the psalmist's soul faints with longing for the courts of the LORD, even envying the sparrows and swallows that nest near the altar (vv. 1-4). He describes the blessing of those who journey toward Zion, finding strength renewed and even hardship transformed into refreshment along the way (vv. 5-7). The psalm turns to prayer for God's anointed king, expressing that a single day in God's courts is worth more than a thousand anywhere else (vv. 8-10). It closes with confidence that the LORD is a sun and shield who withholds no good thing from those who walk uprightly, declaring blessed everyone who simply trusts in him (vv. 11-12).
h: A Doorkeeper in the House of My God (vv.10-12)
m: Longing for God's house, the blessedness of dwelling in God's presence, pilgrimage faith, God as sun and shield, preferring God's courts to worldly comforts

x: A communal prayer for renewed favor, the psalm opens by recalling how God has been gracious to the land before, forgiving his people's iniquity and turning away his anger (vv. 1-3). Building on that memory, the people now ask God to restore them again and to end his displeasure so they can rejoice in him once more (vv. 4-7). The psalmist listens for God's answer, confident that his salvation is near for those who fear him, pictured as mercy and truth meeting together and righteousness and peace embracing (vv. 8-10). It closes with the promise that the LORD will give what is good, the land will yield its harvest, and righteousness will go before him, preparing the way (vv. 11-13).
h: Thou Hast Been Favourable unto Thy Land (vv.1-3)
Turn Us, O God of Our Salvation (vv.4-7)
I Will Hear What God the LORD Will Speak (v.8)
Mercy and Truth Are Met Together (vv.9-13)
m: Past restoration recalled, present distress, prayer for revival, mercy and truth meeting, righteousness and peace kissing — the cross foreshadowed

x: An individual prayer of David, he asks God to bend down and listen, appealing to his own need and devotion while praising God as good, forgiving, and abounding in steadfast love toward all who call on him (vv. 1-7). David declares that no other god compares to the LORD, and that all nations will one day come and worship before him, since he alone works wonders (vv. 8-10). He then asks God to teach him an undivided heart devoted to fearing God's name, promising to praise him fully for rescuing his soul from the depths (vv. 11-13). The psalm closes with a renewed cry for help against proud and violent enemies, appealing again to God's compassion and asking for a visible sign of his favor (vv. 14-17).
h: Bow Down Thine Ear, O LORD (vv.1-5)
In the Day of My Trouble I Will Call (vv.6-7)
Among the Gods There Is None Like unto Thee (vv.8-10)
Unite My Heart to Fear Thy Name (v.11)
The Proud Are Risen Against Me (v.14)
Shew Me a Token for Good (vv.16-17)
m: Poverty and neediness before God, God's character as the basis of prayer, undivided heart, the incomparability of God, all nations worshiping, divine compassion

x: A short Song of Zion celebrating the city's unique place in God's affection, declaring that the LORD loves the gates of Zion more than any other dwelling in all of Israel (vv. 1-3). Remarkably, the psalm envisions God registering people from historically foreign and even hostile nations — Egypt, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, and Ethiopia — as though they too were born in Zion (vv. 4-6). It closes with singers and musicians celebrating together, declaring that all their springs of joy are found in this city (v. 7).
h: His Foundation Is in the Holy Mountains (vv.1-3)
All My Springs Are in Thee (v.7)
m: The glory of Zion, Gentile nations registered as born in Zion, God's universal family, spiritual citizenship, all springs of life flowing from God's city

x: Widely regarded as the darkest lament in the Psalter, the psalmist cries out to God day and night, describing his soul as full of trouble and his life as drawing near to the grave, counted among those already dead (vv. 1-5). He describes God himself as the source of his suffering, laid in the lowest pit under crushing waves of wrath, cut off even from friends and acquaintances (vv. 6-9). He questions whether God's wonders and faithfulness can even be known among the dead, while continuing to pray to him morning after morning (vv. 10-13). Unlike nearly every other psalm, it ends without resolution or praise, closing simply with darkness as his closest companion (vv. 14-18).
h: O LORD God of My Salvation (vv.1-2)
My Life Draweth Nigh unto the Grave (vv.3-5)
Thou Hast Laid Me in the Lowest Pit (vv.6-8)
Mine Eye Mourneth by Reason of Affliction (v.9)
Shall the Dead Arise and Praise Thee (vv.10-12)
Why Castest Thou Off My Soul (vv.13-14)
I Have Been Afflicted from My Youth Up (vv.15-17)
m: Unrelieved suffering, divine wrath experienced, isolation and abandonment, proximity to death, unanswered prayer, faith persisting without resolution

x: A long royal psalm closing Book III of the Psalter, it opens with praise for God's steadfast love and faithfulness, celebrating his covenant promise that David's throne would be established forever (vv. 1-4). The psalm extols God's unmatched power over creation and the sea, and his justice and righteousness as the foundation of his throne (vv. 5-18). It then recounts God's covenant with David in detail — choosing him, anointing him, and promising that his line would endure even if his descendants sinned and were disciplined (vv. 19-37). The tone shifts sharply in the final section as the psalmist laments that God now seems to have rejected and humiliated his anointed king, closing with an anguished appeal for God to remember his former faithfulness (vv. 38-52).
h: I Will Sing of the Mercies of the LORD (vv.1-4)
Who in the Heaven Can Be Compared (vv.5-18)
I Have Found David My Servant (vv.19-37)
m: God's covenant faithfulness (hesed), the Davidic covenant, God's incomparability, the tension between divine promises and present suffering, the apparent failure of God's oath

x: A psalm of Moses opening Book IV of the Psalter, it begins by contrasting God's eternal, timeless existence as humanity's true home with the fleeting, dust-like brevity of human life (vv. 1-6). Moses reflects that human suffering and short lifespans stem from God's response to sin, since he sees even hidden faults clearly (vv. 7-11). Out of that sober reflection comes the well-known prayer to number our days rightly so that wisdom, not waste, fills them (v. 12). The psalm closes with a plea for God's compassion and steadfast love to satisfy his people, replacing their years of hardship with gladness and establishing the work of their hands (vv. 13-17).
h: Thou Hast Been Our Dwelling Place (vv.1-2)
We Spend Our Years as a Tale That Is Told (vv.7-11)
Teach Us to Number Our Days (v.12)
Establish Thou the Work of Our Hands (vv.13-17)
m: God's eternity vs. human brevity, the brevity of life, sin and divine wrath, numbering our days, prayer for God's mercy and the establishment of human work

x: A psalm of trust in God's protection. The psalmist describes whoever dwells in the shelter of the Most High as safe under his care, calling God his refuge and fortress (vv. 1-2). He promises deliverance from hidden traps and plague, assuring that no disaster will overtake the one who makes God his dwelling (vv. 3-10). God's angels are pictured guarding him in all his ways, lifting him up so he does not strike his foot against a stone, and he will tread safely on the lion and serpent (vv. 11-13). The psalm closes with God speaking directly, promising to rescue, protect, answer, and honor the one who loves him, and to satisfy him with long life and salvation (vv. 14-16).
h: He That Dwelleth in the Secret Place (vv.1-2)
The Snare of the Fowler and the Noisome Pestilence (vv.3-8)
Because Thou Hast Made the LORD Thy Habitation (v.9)
He Shall Give His Angels Charge over Thee (vv.10-13)
Because He Hath Set His Love upon Me (vv.14-16)
m: Divine protection, dwelling in God's presence, freedom from fear, angelic guardianship, treading on enemies, God's personal promises to the faithful

x: A psalm for the Sabbath, celebrating it as good to give thanks and sing praise to God morning and evening (vv. 1-3). The psalmist rejoices in God's works, contrasting the senseless person who cannot grasp that though the wicked spring up like grass, they are doomed to everlasting destruction, while the LORD is exalted forever (vv. 4-9). He describes his own strength renewed and his enemies' downfall witnessed firsthand (vv. 10-11), then closes with the image of the righteous flourishing like a palm tree and growing like a cedar of Lebanon, planted in God's house, still bearing fruit and full of sap even in old age as proof that the LORD is upright (vv. 12-15).
h: It Is a Good Thing to Give Thanks (vv.1-3)
The Righteous Shall Flourish like the Palm Tree (vv.12-15)
m: The goodness of thanksgiving, morning lovingkindness and nightly faithfulness, the fate of the wicked vs. flourishing of the righteous, fruitfulness in old age, God as upright rock

x: A short enthronement psalm proclaiming that the LORD reigns, robed in majesty and strength, with his throne established from ancient times (vv. 1-2). Though the floods lift up their voice and pound with great force, the LORD on high is mightier than the noise of many waters and the breakers of the sea (vv. 3-4). The psalm closes by affirming that God's decrees are trustworthy and holiness adorns his house forever (v. 5).
h: The LORD Reigneth, Clothed with Majesty (v.1)
Thy Throne Is Established of Old (v.2)
The Floods Have Lifted Up Their Voice (vv.3-4)
m: The LORD reigns, divine majesty, God's eternal throne, God mightier than chaos waters, the sureness of God's testimonies, holiness befitting His house

x: A lament calling on God, the avenger, to rise up and shine forth against the arrogant wicked who crush his people, kill the widow, the foreigner, and the fatherless, and assume the LORD does not see or care (vv. 1-7). The psalmist rebukes their foolishness, asking whether the one who formed the ear and eye does not hear and see, and pronounces blessing on the person God disciplines and teaches, who is given relief until judgment again becomes just (vv. 8-15). He asks who will stand up for him against evildoers, confessing that without the LORD's help he would have perished, and that God's comfort brought joy amid his anxious thoughts (vv. 16-19). The psalm closes by rejecting any alliance between corrupt rulers and God, affirming the LORD as his fortress who will repay the wicked for their sins and destroy them (vv. 20-23).
h: O LORD God, to Whom Vengeance Belongeth (vv.1-3)
He That Planted the Ear, Shall He Not Hear (vv.8-11)
Blessed Is the Man Whom Thou Chastenest (vv.12-15)
My Foot Slippeth, Thy Mercy Held Me Up (vv.16-19)
The Throne of Iniquity Which Frameth Mischief by a Law (vv.20-21)
m: God of vengeance, cry against oppressors, the folly of thinking God cannot see, blessedness of divine discipline, God's comfort amid anxious thoughts, God as defense and refuge

x: A call to worship followed by a warning. The psalmist invites the assembly to sing joyfully to the LORD, the great God and King above all gods who holds the depths of the earth and made the sea and dry land, and to come before him with thanksgiving, kneeling before their Maker (vv. 1-7a). The tone shifts sharply as God warns against hardening one's heart as Israel did at Meribah and Massah, where the generation that tested him in the wilderness, despite seeing his works, was barred from entering his rest because their hearts went astray (vv. 7b-11); this warning is quoted extensively in Hebrews 3-4.
h: O Come, Let Us Sing unto the LORD (vv.1-2)
A Great King above All Gods (vv.3-5)
To Day If Ye Will Hear His Voice (vv.7b-11)
m: Joyful worship, God as Creator-King, we are His sheep, today hearing God's voice, warning against hardened hearts, Meribah/Massah as negative example, God's rest forfeited

x: An enthronement hymn calling all the earth to sing a new song to the LORD and proclaim his salvation and glory among the nations (vv. 1-3). It contrasts the LORD's greatness with the worthlessness of the idols of the peoples, urging all families of the earth to ascribe him glory and strength and worship him in the splendor of his holiness (vv. 4-9). The nations are told that the LORD reigns and the world stands firm, and all creation — heavens, sea, fields, and forest — is summoned to rejoice before him, for he is coming to judge the earth with righteousness and truth (vv. 10-13).
h: O Sing unto the LORD a New Song (vv.1-3)
All the Gods of the Nations Are Idols (vv.4-6)
Worship the LORD in the Beauty of Holiness (vv.7-9)
Say among the Heathen That the LORD Reigneth (v.10)
For He Cometh to Judge the Earth (vv.11-13)
m: A new song, declaring God's glory among the nations, the LORD above all gods, worship in holiness, creation rejoicing, God coming to judge the earth

x: A psalm celebrating the LORD's kingship — the whole earth and the coastlands are called to rejoice because the LORD reigns (v. 1). His throne rests on righteousness and justice, and his coming is described in storm imagery: clouds, fire, and lightning that make the mountains melt like wax and the earth tremble (vv. 2-5). The heavens declare his righteousness, idol worshippers are put to shame, and every false god is made to bow before him (vv. 6-7), while Zion and the towns of Judah rejoice over his just rule (vv. 8-9). It closes with a charge for those who love the LORD to hate evil, trusting him to guard and deliver his people and to sow light and gladness for the righteous (vv. 10-12).
h: The LORD Reigneth, Let the Earth Rejoice (v.1)
Clouds and Darkness Round About Him (vv.2-6)
Confounded Be All They That Serve Graven Images (v.7)
Ye That Love the LORD, Hate Evil (vv.10-12)
m: The LORD reigns, theophany in fire and lightning, creation trembles before God, shame of idol-worshippers, Zion's gladness, loving the LORD means hating evil, light sown for the righteous

x: A psalm of praise calling for a new song because the LORD has worked salvation with his own right hand and holy arm, displaying his righteousness in full view of the nations (vv. 1-3). All the earth is summoned to shout for joy and make music with harp, trumpet, and horn before the King (vv. 4-6), and even creation joins in — the sea roaring, the rivers clapping their hands, the hills singing together — because the LORD is coming to judge the world with righteousness and fairness (vv. 7-9).
h: His Right Hand Hath Gotten Him the Victory (vv.1-3)
Make a Joyful Noise, All the Earth (vv.4-6)
Let the Floods Clap Their Hands (vv.7-9)
m: New song for new salvation, God's victory by His own power, salvation revealed to all nations, joyful noise with instruments, nature worshipping, God coming to judge with equity

x: An enthronement psalm centered on God's holiness, declaring that the LORD reigns over Zion and all peoples, seated above the cherubim (vv. 1-2). It praises his great and holy name and the justice of his rule, marked by equity and righteousness in Jacob (vv. 3-4), then recalls Moses, Aaron, and Samuel as priests and intercessors who called on the LORD and were answered from the pillar of cloud, even as God forgave them while still holding them accountable (vv. 5-8). The psalm closes with a threefold refrain calling Israel to worship at his footstool and holy hill, for the LORD our God is holy (v. 9).
h: Moses and Aaron Among His Priests (vv.6-7)
Thou Wast a God That Forgavest Them (vv.8-9)
m: The LORD reigns, God's holiness (triple refrain), trembling before God, justice and equity, God answering His servants, forgiveness and consequences

x: A brief psalm of thanksgiving calling all the earth to worship the LORD with joyful singing and gladness (vv. 1-2). It grounds that praise in the truth that the LORD is God, the one who made his people, who belong to him as the sheep of his pasture (v. 3), and invites entry into his gates and courts with thanksgiving and praise (v. 4). It closes by affirming that the LORD is good, his mercy is everlasting, and his faithfulness endures through every generation (v. 5).
h: Know Ye That the LORD He Is God (v.3)
Enter into His Gates with Thanksgiving (v.4)
m: Joyful worship, serving God with gladness, knowing God as Creator and Shepherd, entering His presence with thanksgiving, God's eternal goodness, mercy, and faithfulness

x: A royal psalm in which David pledges to sing of God's mercy and justice and to pursue personal integrity, praying for God's presence as he seeks to walk with a blameless heart within his own house (vv. 1-2). He resolves to refuse anything wicked, to reject perverse and deceitful people, and to have no tolerance for slander, arrogance, or dishonesty among those close to him (vv. 3-5). Instead he will surround himself with the faithful and blameless, while working daily to remove the wicked from his household and from the city of the LORD (vv. 6-8).
h: I Will Sing of Mercy and Judgment (v.1)
I Will Walk Within My House with a Perfect Heart (vv.2-4)
He That Worketh Deceit Shall Not Dwell Within My House (vv.5-7)
m: Integrity of leadership, personal holiness, justice in governance, choosing righteous company, rejecting wickedness, the king's moral commitments

x: A lament of the afflicted, opening with an urgent plea for God to hear his prayer and not hide his face (vv. 1-2). The psalmist describes his suffering in vivid images — days vanishing like smoke, bones burning, a heart withered like grass, and loneliness like a desert owl or a sparrow alone on a roof (vv. 3-11). He turns from his own frailty to God's eternity, pleading for the LORD to arise and rebuild Zion so the nations will fear his name and future generations will praise him (vv. 12-22). The psalm closes by contrasting human mortality with God's changelessness: the earth and heavens will wear out like a garment, but the LORD remains the same, and the children of his servants will endure before him forever (vv. 23-28).
h: Hide Not Thy Face from Me (vv.1-2)
My Days Are Consumed like Smoke (vv.3-11)
Thou Shalt Arise, and Have Mercy upon Zion (vv.12-22)
m: Human frailty and suffering, God's eternality, restoration of Zion, hope for future generations, the unchangeable nature of God, lament turning to confidence

x: A hymn of praise calling the soul to bless the LORD and remember all his benefits — forgiveness, healing, redemption from the pit, and a crown of steadfast love that renews life like the eagle's youth (vv. 1-5). The LORD is described as compassionate and slow to anger, not repaying his people according to their sins but removing their transgressions as far as east is from west, and pitying them as a father pities his children, mindful that they are only dust (vv. 6-14). Human life is fleeting like grass or a flower blown away by the wind, but the LORD's steadfast love and righteousness endure from everlasting to everlasting for those who fear him and keep his covenant (vv. 15-18). The psalm closes with a call for angels, heavenly hosts, and all creation to join in blessing the LORD (vv. 19-22).
h: Bless the LORD, O My Soul (vv.1-2)
The LORD Is Merciful and Gracious (vv.6-10)
As Far as the East Is from the West (vv.11-14)
Bless the LORD, All His Works (vv.19-22)
m: God's compassion and forgiveness, the fatherhood of God, removal of sin, human frailty and God's eternal love, commanding one's soul to worship, God's sovereign rule over all

x: A creation hymn that pictures the LORD robed in light, stretching out the heavens like a tent and riding on the clouds and wind, with the earth set on unshakable foundations and the waters bounded so they cannot return to cover it (vv. 1-9). It moves through the created order in loving detail — springs watering wild animals, birds nesting in the trees, crops and wine and oil provided for people, the moon marking seasons, and lions hunting by night while people labor by day (vv. 10-23). The psalmist marvels at the sheer variety of God's works, including the vast sea teeming with creatures and Leviathan at play, all of them dependent on God to open his hand and provide (vv. 24-30). It closes with praise for God's enduring glory and a resolve to sing to him for life, asking that sinners and the wicked vanish from the earth (vv. 31-35).
h: Thou Hast Set a Bound That They May Not Pass (vv.5-9)
He Sendeth the Springs into the Valleys (vv.10-18)
The Sun Knoweth His Going Down (vv.19-23)
O LORD, How Manifold Are Thy Works (vv.24-26)
I Will Sing unto the LORD as Long as I Live (vv.31-35)
m: God as Creator and Sustainer of all life, the majesty of God in nature, divine providence over all creatures, the order and beauty of creation, dependence of all life on God, praise arising from contemplation of creation

x: A historical psalm of praise urging Israel to give thanks, seek the LORD, and remember his wonders, grounded in the everlasting covenant he swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to give them the land of Canaan (vv. 1-11). It traces God's faithful care through the patriarchs' wanderings, Joseph's rise from slavery and prison to power in Egypt, and Israel's growth into a great nation there (vv. 12-25). The psalm recounts the plagues sent through Moses and Aaron, the exodus with plunder from Egypt, and God's provision of cloud, fire, quail, manna, and water in the wilderness (vv. 26-41). It closes by tying it all to God's remembered promise to Abraham, as he gave Israel the land of the nations so they would keep his statutes and laws (vv. 42-45).
h: Make Known His Deeds Among the People (vv.1-6)
He Hath Remembered His Covenant for Ever (vv.7-11)
He Sent a Man Before Them, Even Joseph (vv.16-22)
Wonders in the Land of Ham (vv.23-36)
He Brought Them Forth with Silver and Gold (vv.37-41)
That They Might Observe His Statutes (vv.42-45)
m: God's faithfulness to His covenant, Israel's history as God's story, the Abrahamic covenant, Joseph's suffering and exaltation, the Exodus plagues, providence through history, remembering God's works

x: A historical psalm of confession closing Book IV, opening with praise for God's enduring goodness before turning to a long, honest recounting of Israel's repeated rebellion (vv. 1-6). Despite seeing God's wonders at the Red Sea, the people forgot his works, grumbled in the wilderness, worshipped the golden calf, despised the promised land, joined themselves to Baal of Peor, and eventually sacrificed their own children to idols in Canaan (vv. 7-39). Each act of rebellion brought God's discipline, yet each time he heard their cry, remembered his covenant, and relented in mercy (vv. 40-46). The psalm ends with a plea for God to gather his scattered people and a doxology blessing the LORD from everlasting to everlasting (vv. 47-48).
h: Remember Me with the Favour Thou Bearest (vv.1-5)
We Have Sinned with Our Fathers (v.6)
They Provoked Him at the Red Sea (vv.7-12)
He Gave Them Their Request, but Sent Leanness (vv.13-15)
They Envied Moses in the Camp (vv.16-18)
They Made a Calf in Horeb (vv.19-23)
He Spake Unadvisedly with His Lips (vv.32-33)
They Were Mingled Among the Heathen (vv.34-39)
Many Times Did He Deliver Them (vv.40-46)
Save Us, and Gather Us from Among the Heathen (vv.47-48)
m: National confession of sin, Israel's repeated rebellion, God's repeated mercy, the cycle of sin and deliverance, intercessory prayer, God's covenant faithfulness despite human unfaithfulness

x: A thanksgiving psalm opening Book V, calling the redeemed of the LORD — those gathered from every direction — to give thanks for his enduring mercy (vv. 1-3). It illustrates that mercy through four scenes of distress and rescue: wanderers lost in the desert, prisoners bound for their rebellion, the sick and foolish near death's door, and sailors caught in a storm at sea — each group cries to the LORD and he delivers them, with a refrain urging thanks for his wonderful works (vv. 4-32). The psalm closes by celebrating God's sovereign reversals — turning fertile land to desert for the wicked and desert to fruitful land for the hungry, humbling princes while lifting up the needy — and calls the wise to take note and understand the LORD's steadfast love (vv. 33-43).
h: Let the Redeemed of the LORD Say So (vv.1-3)
They Wandered in the Wilderness in a Solitary Way (vv.4-9)
Such as Sit in Darkness and in the Shadow of Death (vv.10-16)
He Sent His Word, and Healed Them (vv.17-22)
They That Go Down to the Sea in Ships (vv.23-32)
He Turneth Rivers into a Wilderness (vv.33-42)
Whoso Is Wise Will Observe These Things (v.43)
m: God's deliverance from various troubles, the recurring pattern of distress and rescue, gratitude as duty, God's sovereign control over nature and nations, wisdom in recognizing God's hesed

x: A psalm of confident praise, combining earlier material from Psalms 57 and 60, in which David's heart is steadfast as he resolves to praise God among the nations for a mercy that reaches above the heavens (vv. 1-5). He recalls God's promise to claim and rule over Israel's tribal lands as well as Moab, Edom, and Philistia (vv. 6-9), then asks God to lead his people into victory since human help is worthless (vv. 10-12). The psalm ends on a note of trust: through God alone Israel will act valiantly and tread down its enemies (v. 13).
h: O God, My Heart Is Fixed (vv.1-5)
That Thy Beloved May Be Delivered (v.6)
Thou, O God, Who Hast Cast Us Off (vv.10-11)
Vain Is the Help of Man (vv.12-13)
m: Fixed heart in praise, God's sovereignty over nations, confidence in divine help, the futility of human strength apart from God, praising God among the nations

x: An imprecatory lament in which David, betrayed by an enemy who repays his love and prayers with hatred and lies, calls on God to break his silence and act (vv. 1-5). He pours out an extended, harsh string of curses on his chief accuser — asking for a shortened life, a ruined family, and unrelenting judgment as punishment for the man's cruelty toward the poor and brokenhearted (vv. 6-20). The tone shifts as David describes his own weakness and suffering — poor, wounded, fasting, and mocked — and pleads for God's mercy and rescue for his own sake (vv. 21-25). The psalm ends in confidence that God will shame his accusers, vindicate his servant, and stand at the right hand of the needy to save them (vv. 26-31).
h: Hold Not Thy Peace, O God of My Praise (v.1)
They Have Rewarded Me Evil for Good (vv.2-5)
Let Satan Stand at His Right Hand (vv.6-20)
I Am Gone like the Shadow When It Declineth (vv.21-25)
Let Them Curse, but Bless Thou (vv.26-29)
He Shall Stand at the Right Hand of the Poor (vv.30-31)
m: Unjust accusation, betrayal by those loved, calling on God for justice, imprecation against the wicked, vindication of the innocent, God as defender of the needy

x: A brief but highly quoted Messianic and royal psalm in which the LORD invites David's Lord to sit at his right hand until his enemies are made his footstool (v. 1). It describes this coming King ruling from Zion with a willing army and declares him, by God's own oath, a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek (vv. 2-4). The closing verses picture him executing judgment on hostile nations and kings, triumphant even after a brief, refreshing pause along the way (vv. 5-7).
h: Sit Thou at My Right Hand (v.1)
The Rod of Thy Strength out of Zion (vv.2-3)
A Priest for Ever After the Order of Melchizedek (v.4)
He Shall Judge Among the Heathen (vv.5-7)
m: Christ's deity and lordship, the session of Christ at God's right hand, the eternal priesthood of Melchizedek, the conquest of all enemies, the union of king and priest in the Messiah

x: An acrostic psalm of praise — each line in Hebrew beginning with a successive letter of the alphabet — that celebrates the greatness of God's works, worthy to be studied by all who delight in them (vv. 1-2). It highlights his enduring righteousness, gracious and compassionate character, and faithfulness to remember his covenant by providing for those who fear him (vv. 3-6). His commandments are trustworthy and stand forever, and he has sent redemption to his people (vv. 7-9). The psalm closes with its most famous line: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and his praise endures forever (v. 10).
h: I Will Praise the LORD with My Whole Heart (v.1)
The Works of the LORD Are Great (vv.2-4)
He Will Ever Be Mindful of His Covenant (vv.5-6)
The Fear of the LORD Is the Beginning of Wisdom (vv.9-10)
m: God's works and character, covenant faithfulness, the fear of the LORD as beginning of wisdom, God's provision, redemption, praise in the congregation

x: This acrostic wisdom psalm serves as a companion to Psalm 111, describing the blessed life of the person who fears the LORD and delights in his commands (v. 1). Such a person's descendants are called mighty and blessed (v. 2), his household prospers, and his righteousness endures forever (v. 3). Light breaks into darkness for the upright, who are gracious, compassionate, and just (v. 4), generous in lending and wise in managing their affairs (v. 5). Because their heart is fixed and trusts in the LORD, they are unshaken and unafraid even of bad news, secure until they see their enemies overcome (vv. 6-8). Their generosity to the poor is lasting, and they are honored and exalted (v. 9), while the wicked who witness this prosperity are consumed with envy and frustration, their own desires coming to nothing (v. 10).
h: Blessed Is the Man That Feareth the LORD (v.1)
A Good Man Sheweth Favour, and Lendeth (v.5)
His Heart Is Fixed, Trusting in the LORD (vv.6-8)
He Hath Dispersed, He Hath Given to the Poor (v.9)
The Desire of the Wicked Shall Perish (v.10)
m: The blessed life of the God-fearing person, generosity and righteousness, fearlessness in the face of evil, the contrast between the righteous and the wicked, the legacy of the upright

x: This Hallel psalm of praise opens with a call for God's servants to praise his name continually, from sunrise to sunset and for all time (vv. 1-3). It celebrates the LORD's transcendence — exalted above every nation and even the heavens (v. 4) — paired with his condescension: no one else compares to a God who, though enthroned on high, stoops down to notice what happens in heaven and on earth (vv. 5-6). That humility is shown in concrete acts of reversal: he lifts the poor from the dust and the needy from the ash heap to seat them among princes (vv. 7-8), and he gives the childless woman a home and children, turning her sorrow into joy (v. 9).
h: From the Rising of the Sun unto the Going Down (vv.1-3)
Who Is Like unto the LORD Our God (vv.4-5)
He Raiseth Up the Poor out of the Dust (vv.6-9)
m: God's transcendence and condescension, God's care for the lowly, praise from dawn to dusk, God's incomparability, lifting the poor from the dust, the reversal of fortune

x: This brief Hallel psalm recalls the Exodus, when Israel left Egypt and became God's own sanctuary and dominion (vv. 1-2). Using vivid poetic imagery, it personifies creation reacting to God's presence: the sea flees, the Jordan River turns back, and the mountains and hills skip like frightened animals at the crossing of the Red Sea and Jordan (vv. 3-4). The psalmist then directly questions this fleeing creation — what caused the sea, river, mountains, and hills to react this way (vv. 5-6) — answering that all the earth should tremble before the presence of the LORD, the God of Jacob (v. 7), who once turned solid rock into pools and springs of water in the wilderness (v. 8).
h: When Israel Went Out of Egypt (vv.1-2)
The Sea Saw It, and Fled (vv.3-4)
What Ailed Thee, O Thou Sea (vv.5-6)
The Flint into a Fountain of Waters (vv.7-8)
m: The Exodus as cosmic event, God's presence causing nature to flee, the power of God's presence, poetic personification of creation, the God of Jacob as Lord of all nature

x: This Hallel psalm begins by directing all glory away from Israel and to God alone, for the sake of his covenant love and faithfulness (v. 1), countering the nations' taunt of "where is their God?" with the reminder that God does whatever he pleases from heaven (vv. 2-3). By contrast, the idols of the nations are lifeless objects of silver and gold, with mouths, eyes, ears, and hands that cannot actually speak, see, hear, or act — and those who make and trust them become just as lifeless (vv. 4-8). The psalm then calls Israel, the priestly house of Aaron, and all who fear the LORD to trust in him as their help and shield (vv. 9-11), affirming that God is mindful of his people and will bless them, young and old, and increase their numbers (vv. 12-14). Since the dead cannot praise God, the psalm closes with a vow that the living will bless the LORD forever (vv. 17-18).
h: Not unto Us, but unto Thy Name (vv.1-2)
They Have Mouths, but They Speak Not (vv.3-8)
O Israel, Trust Thou in the LORD (vv.9-11)
He Will Bless Them That Fear the LORD (vv.12-15)
The Dead Praise Not the LORD (vv.16-18)
m: God's glory vs. human glory, the futility of idols, trusting in the living God, the nature of idolatry, God as help and shield, blessing from the Creator

x: This Hallel thanksgiving psalm opens with love and devotion to God for hearing the psalmist's cry (vv. 1-2). He recalls being surrounded by the anguish of death until he called on the LORD for rescue (vv. 3-4), praising God's graciousness, righteousness, and mercy toward the helpless (vv. 5-6). Having been delivered from death, tears, and stumbling, he can now rest and walk confidently before the LORD in the land of the living (vv. 7-9), his faith holding even through affliction (vv. 10-11). Unable to repay God's kindness, he resolves to publicly offer thanksgiving and fulfill his vows before God's people (vv. 12-14, 17-18), noting that the death of God's faithful ones is precious to him (v. 15) and closing with a declaration of devoted service and praise in Jerusalem (vv. 16, 19).
h: I Love the LORD, Because He Hath Heard (vv.1-2)
The Sorrows of Death Compassed Me (vv.3-4)
Return unto Thy Rest, O My Soul (vv.7-9)
I Said in My Haste, All Men Are Liars (vv.10-11)
What Shall I Render unto the LORD (vv.12-19)
m: Love for God because He heard prayer, deliverance from death, rest for the soul, paying vows publicly, the preciousness of saints' deaths to God, gratitude in worship

x: The shortest chapter in the Bible, this psalm is a brief but sweeping call for every nation and people to praise the LORD (v. 1), grounded in the greatness of his steadfast love toward his people and the eternal endurance of his faithfulness (v. 2).
h: O Praise the LORD, All Ye Nations (v.1)
His Merciful Kindness Is Great Toward Us (v.2a)
m: Universal praise from all nations, God's mercy (hesed) toward His people, God's eternal truth, the brevity and completeness of praise

x: This Hallel thanksgiving psalm opens with a call-and-response liturgy in which Israel, the priests, and all who fear the LORD declare that his mercy endures forever (vv. 1-4). The psalmist recalls being answered by God in distress, finding confidence that the LORD's presence removes fear of what people can do to him (vv. 5-7), and concluding it is better to trust God than to rely on human strength or rulers (vv. 8-9). Though surrounded by hostile nations, he overcomes them in the LORD's name (vv. 10-12), and though pushed hard toward failure, the LORD became his strength, song, and salvation (vv. 13-14). Joyful praise fills the camp of the righteous as God's right hand acts victoriously (vv. 15-16), and the psalmist vows to live and declare the LORD's works despite severe discipline (vv. 17-18). He calls for the gates of righteousness to be opened so he can enter and give thanks (vv.…
h: It Is Better to Trust in the LORD (vv.5-18)
Open to Me the Gates of Righteousness (vv.19-21)
The Stone Which the Builders Refused (vv.22-24)
Thou Art My God, and I Will Praise Thee (vv.28-29)
m: God's enduring mercy, trust over human confidence, the rejected stone becoming the cornerstone, the day the LORD has made, Messianic triumph through rejection, processional worship

x: Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the Bible, an elaborate acrostic of 22 stanzas of eight verses each, one per letter of the Hebrew alphabet, with nearly every verse using a synonym for God's revealed word — law, testimonies, precepts, statutes, commandments, judgments, and word. The psalmist opens by blessing those who walk blamelessly and seek the LORD wholeheartedly, and repeatedly asks God to teach him and keep him from wandering (vv. 1-40). He treasures God's word above riches and honey, hiding it in his heart to guard against sin and meditating on it constantly (vv. 11, 97, 103-104). A recurring theme is affliction: the psalmist is mocked and persecuted by the proud, yet insists his suffering was good for him because it drove him deeper into God's statutes (vv. 67, 71, 75, 84-87, 107). He calls God's word a lamp to his feet and a light to his path (v. 105) and calls it his…
h: Aleph: The Undefiled in the Way (vv.1-8)
Beth: Wherewithal Shall a Young Man Cleanse His Way (vv.9-16)
Gimel: I Am a Stranger in the Earth (vv.17-24)
Daleth: My Soul Cleaveth unto the Dust (vv.25-32)
He: Incline My Heart unto Thy Testimonies (vv.33-40)
Vav: I Will Walk at Liberty (vv.41-48)
Zayin: This Is My Comfort in My Affliction (vv.49-56)
Cheth: Thou Art My Portion, O LORD (vv.57-64)
Teth: It Is Good for Me That I Have Been Afflicted (vv.65-72)
Yod: Thy Hands Have Made Me and Fashioned Me (vv.73-80)
Kaph: Like a Bottle in the Smoke (vv.81-88)
Lamed: Thy Word Is Settled in Heaven (vv.89-96)
Mem: O How Love I Thy Law (vv.97-104)
Nun: A Lamp unto My Feet (vv.105-112)
Samekh: Thou Art My Hiding Place and My Shield (vv.113-120)
Ayin: It Is Time for Thee, LORD, to Work (vv.121-128)
Pe: The Entrance of Thy Words Giveth Light (vv.129-136)
Tsade: Thy Word Is Very Pure (vv.137-144)
Qoph: Thou Art Near, O LORD (vv.145-152)
Resh: Plead My Cause, and Deliver Me (vv.153-160)
Shin: Great Peace Have They Which Love Thy Law (vv.161-168)
Tav: I Have Gone Astray like a Lost Sheep (vv.169-176)
m: The supremacy and sufficiency of God's Word, love for God's law, obedience as delight, Scripture as guide/lamp/comfort/ life/treasure, persecution for righteousness, longing for God through His Word, the Word as source of wisdom/purity/freedom

x: A Song of Ascents in which the psalmist recalls crying out to the LORD in distress and being heard, then asks for deliverance from lying lips and a deceitful tongue (vv. 1-2). He warns that the false tongue will be repaid with a warrior's sharp arrows and burning coals (vv. 3-4). He laments living among hostile foreigners in Meshech and Kedar, surrounded by people who hate peace, and grieves that whenever he speaks of peace, they want war (vv. 5-7).
h: In My Distress I Cried unto the LORD (v.1)
Deliver My Soul from Lying Lips (v.2)
What Shall Be Done unto Thee, Thou False Tongue (vv.3-4)
I Am for Peace, but They Are for War (vv.5-7)
m: Deceitful speech, longing for peace among warlike people, the pain of living among the ungodly, crying to God in distress, spiritual exile

x: A Song of Ascents expressing confident trust in the LORD as protector. The psalmist looks to the hills and asks where his help comes from, then affirms that his help comes from the LORD, maker of heaven and earth (vv. 1-2). He declares that the LORD who keeps Israel never slumbers or sleeps, watching over the traveler as a shade at his right hand so that neither sun nor moon can harm him (vv. 3-6). The psalm closes with assurance that the LORD will guard his life and every going out and coming in, now and forever (vv. 7-8).
h: I Will Lift Up Mine Eyes unto the Hills (v.1)
My Help Cometh from the LORD (v.2)
He That Keepeth Israel Shall Neither Slumber nor Sleep (vv.3-4)
Thy Shade upon Thy Right Hand (vv.5-6)
Thy Going Out and Thy Coming In (vv.7-8)
m: God as keeper/protector, divine watchfulness that never sleeps, help from the Creator, protection from all evil, preservation in all circumstances, total security in God

x: A Song of Ascents in which the psalmist rejoices at the invitation to go up to the house of the LORD, and describes standing at last within Jerusalem's gates (vv. 1-2). He praises the city as tightly built together, the place where the tribes go up to give thanks and where the thrones of David's house sit in judgment (vv. 3-5). He calls on the hearers to pray for Jerusalem's peace, promising prosperity to those who love her, and pledges to seek her good for the sake of his family and friends and for the house of the LORD (vv. 6-9).
h: I Was Glad When They Said unto Me (v.1)
Our Feet Shall Stand Within Thy Gates (v.2)
A City That Is Compact Together (vv.3-5)
Pray for the Peace of Jerusalem (vv.6-9)
m: Joy in going to God's house, love for Jerusalem, prayer for peace, unity of God's people, worship as communal destination

x: A Song of Ascents in which the psalmist lifts his eyes to the LORD enthroned in heaven, comparing his posture to a servant watching his master's hand for direction (vv. 1-2). He pleads for mercy, describing how thoroughly he and the people have been filled with the contempt and scorn of the proud and those who are at ease (vv. 3-4).
h: Unto Thee Lift I Up Mine Eyes (v.1)
As the Eyes of Servants unto the Hand of Their Masters (v.2)
Have Mercy upon Us, O LORD (v.3)
The Scorning of Those That Are at Ease (v.4)
m: Looking to God for mercy, patient waiting as a servant, contempt from the proud, humble dependence on God

x: A Song of Ascents in which Israel reflects on what would have happened had the LORD not been on their side when enemies rose against them - they would have been swallowed alive and overwhelmed like a flood (vv. 1-5). The psalmist blesses the LORD for not letting them be torn apart, comparing their rescue to a bird escaping a broken snare (vv. 6-7). The psalm closes by affirming that their help is in the name of the LORD, maker of heaven and earth (v. 8).
h: If It Had Not Been the LORD Who Was on Our Side (vv.1-5)
As a Bird out of the Snare of the Fowlers (vv.6-7)
Our Help Is in the Name of the LORD (v.8)
m: What would have happened without God, divine rescue from overwhelming enemies, escape like a bird from a snare, help in the name of the LORD

x: A Song of Ascents comparing those who trust in the LORD to Mount Zion, immovable and enduring forever, just as the mountains surround Jerusalem (vv. 1-2). The psalmist affirms that the LORD surrounds his people the same way, and that the rule of the wicked will not remain over the land of the righteous, lest the righteous themselves be tempted toward evil (v. 3). He asks God to do good to the upright, while those who turn to crooked ways will be led away with evildoers, and closes with a blessing of peace upon Israel (vv. 4-5).
h: As Mount Zion, Which Cannot Be Removed (v.1)
As the Mountains Are Round About Jerusalem (v.2)
The Rod of the Wicked Shall Not Rest (v.3)
m: The immovability of those who trust God, God surrounding His people like mountains, the scepter of wickedness will not remain, peace upon Israel

x: This Song of Ascents recalls how the LORD's restoration of Zion felt like a dream, filling the people with laughter as even the surrounding nations took notice (vv. 1-3). The psalmist prays for that restoration to continue, likening it to desert streambeds suddenly rushing with water (v. 4). It closes with the assurance that those who sow in tears will reap in joy, and whoever goes out weeping with seed will surely return rejoicing with a full harvest (vv. 5-6).
h: We Were like Them That Dream (vv.1-3)
As the Streams in the South (v.4)
They That Sow in Tears Shall Reap in Joy (vv.5-6)
m: The joy of restoration, laughter and singing at God's deliverance, sowing in tears and reaping in joy, the dream-like quality of answered prayer

x: This Song of Ascents, attributed to Solomon, warns that without the LORD's blessing, building a house or guarding a city is pointless labor, even for those who rise early and stay up late in anxious toil — for God gives rest to those he loves (vv. 1-2). It then calls children a heritage and reward from the LORD, like arrows in a warrior's hand, and pronounces the man blessed whose household is full of them (vv. 3-5).
h: Except the LORD Build the House (v.1)
So He Giveth His Beloved Sleep (v.2)
Children Are an Heritage of the LORD (vv.3-5)
m: The futility of human effort without God, trust vs. anxiety, children as God's blessing, the family as divine gift, rest in God's sovereignty

x: This Song of Ascents blesses everyone who fears the LORD and walks in his ways, promising they will enjoy the fruit of their own labor and prosper (vv. 1-2). Such a man's wife is pictured as a fruitful vine inside his house, and his children like young olive shoots around his table (v. 3). The psalm closes by praying that the LORD will bless him from Zion, let him see Jerusalem's prosperity throughout his life, and live to see his grandchildren, with peace over Israel (vv. 4-6).
h: Blessed Is Every One That Feareth the LORD (v.1)
As a Fruitful Vine by the Sides of Thine House (vv.2-4)
The LORD Shall Bless Thee out of Zion (vv.5-6)
m: The blessing of the God-fearing household, fruitful labor, family as vine and olive shoots, blessing from Zion, prosperity through fearing God

x: This Song of Ascents has Israel recalling a lifetime of affliction from its youth, describing enemies who plowed long furrows across their back, yet never prevailed (vv. 1-3). The psalmist declares the LORD righteous for cutting the ropes of the wicked (v. 4), then prays that those who hate Zion would be turned back and wither like grass on a rooftop — cut down before anyone can even harvest or bless it (vv. 5-8).
h: The Plowers Plowed upon My Back (vv.1-4)
As the Grass upon the Housetops (vv.5-8)
m: Israel's history of persecution, survival through affliction, God cutting the cords of the wicked, judgment on those who hate Zion, resilience of God's people

x: This Song of Ascents opens with the psalmist crying out to the LORD from the depths, pleading for him to listen (vv. 1-2). If the LORD kept a record of sins, no one could stand before him, but forgiveness is found with him, which is why he is revered (vv. 3-4). The psalmist waits for the LORD more eagerly than watchmen wait for morning, urging Israel to hope in him, since with the LORD is steadfast love and full redemption from sin (vv. 5-8).
h: Out of the Depths Have I Cried (vv.1-2)
More Than They That Watch for the Morning (vv.5-6)
m: Crying from the depths, God's forgiveness, waiting on God, hope in God's word, plenteous redemption, the fear that comes from forgiveness

x: In this shortest Song of Ascents, David professes that his heart is not proud and his eyes are not haughty — he no longer chases matters too great or wonderful for him (v. 1). Instead he has calmed and quieted his soul like a weaned child resting with its mother (v. 2). He closes by urging Israel to put its hope in the LORD, now and forever (v. 3).
h: As a Child That Is Weaned of His Mother (v.2)
Let Israel Hope in the LORD (v.3)
m: Humility before God, contentment like a weaned child, quieting the soul, not striving beyond one's place, childlike trust

x: This Song of Ascents recalls David's vow not to rest until he found a dwelling place for the LORD, the mighty God of Jacob (vv. 1-5). It recounts the search for the ark and the people's resolve to worship at God's footstool (vv. 6-9), then turns to intercession for the king, asking God to remember his oath to David that a descendant would always sit on his throne if his children kept the covenant (vv. 10-12). The LORD responds by declaring his everlasting choice of Zion as his resting place, promising to bless its provisions, satisfy its poor, and make David's line flourish while shaming his enemies (vv. 13-18).
h: Until I Find Out a Place for the LORD (vv.1-5)
Arise, O LORD, into Thy Rest (vv.6-9)
The LORD Hath Sworn in Truth unto David (vv.10-12)
m: David's zeal for God's dwelling, the Davidic covenant, God choosing Zion, the anointed king's throne, God's faithful oath, priestly blessing

x: This short Song of Ascents, attributed to David, opens by declaring how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in unity (v. 1). That unity is compared to precious oil poured on Aaron's head, running down his beard and robes, and to the dew of Hermon falling on the mountains of Zion (vv. 2-3a). The psalm closes by noting that it is there, in that unity, that the LORD has commanded his blessing — life forevermore (v. 3b).
h: How Good and How Pleasant It Is (v.1)
The Precious Ointment upon the Head (v.2)
There the LORD Commanded the Blessing (v.3b)
m: The goodness of unity, anointing that flows from head to body, refreshing dew from above, commanded blessing, brethren dwelling together

x: This final Song of Ascents calls on the LORD's servants who stand watch by night in his house to bless him, lifting their hands in the sanctuary (vv. 1-2). It closes with a benediction: may the LORD who made heaven and earth bless you from Zion (v. 3).
h: Which by Night Stand in the House of the LORD (vv.1-2)
m: Night worship, blessing the LORD, lifting hands in the sanctuary, priestly blessing, the Creator who blesses

x: This Hallel psalm calls the LORD's servants who stand in his house to praise his name, because he is good and it is pleasant to sing to him (vv. 1-3). It celebrates his choice of Israel as his own treasured possession and his sovereign power over creation, commanding clouds, lightning, and wind (vv. 4-7). The psalm recounts his mighty acts in the exodus, striking Egypt's firstborn and defeating the kings Sihon and Og to give Israel their land (vv. 8-12). It contrasts the LORD's enduring name with the lifeless idols of the nations, which have mouths, eyes, and ears but cannot speak, see, or hear (vv. 13-18), closing with a call for Israel, Aaron, and Levi to bless the LORD from Zion (vv. 19-21).
h: He Bringeth the Wind out of His Treasuries (vv.5-7)
Sihon King of the Amorites, and Og King of Bashan (vv.8-12)
Thy Name, O LORD, Endureth for Ever (vv.13-14)
They That Make Them Are like unto Them (vv.15-18)
Bless the LORD, O House of Israel (vv.19-21)
m: God's sovereignty over nature and nations, the superiority of the LORD over idols, God's covenant name, praise as the calling of His servants, the futility of idolatry

x: Known as the Great Hallel, this psalm is a litany of thanksgiving in which every verse ends with the refrain "his steadfast love endures forever." It moves through God's greatness as creator of the heavens, sun, moon, and stars (vv. 1-9), his mighty acts in the exodus — striking Egypt's firstborn, parting the Red Sea, and drowning Pharaoh's army (vv. 10-15) — his guidance of Israel through the wilderness and defeat of the kings Sihon and Og to give them the land (vv. 16-22), and his continued remembrance of his people in their weakness, providing food for all creatures (vv. 23-26).
h: The God of Gods, the Lord of Lords (vv.1-3)
To Him That by Wisdom Made the Heavens (vv.4-9)
With a Strong Hand, and with a Stretched Out Arm (vv.10-22)
Who Remembered Us in Our Low Estate (vv.23-26)
m: God's mercy (hesed) enduring forever — repeated 26 times, God as Creator, God as Redeemer from Egypt, God as Provider, the connection between mercy and every divine act

x: This lament pictures the exiles sitting by the rivers of Babylon, weeping as they remember Zion, their harps hanging silent on the willow trees (vv. 1-2). Their captors mock them, demanding songs of joy, but the exiles ask how they could sing the LORD's song in a foreign land (vv. 3-4). The psalmist vows never to forget Jerusalem, calling curses on himself if he lets it fade from his highest joy (vv. 5-6), then closes with a fierce prayer against Edom and Babylon for their cruelty, including a jarring call for vengeance on Babylon's children (vv. 7-9).
h: If I Forget Thee, O Jerusalem (vv.5-6)
O Daughter of Babylon, Who Art to Be Destroyed (vv.7-9)
m: The pain of exile, inability to sing in a foreign land, memory of Jerusalem, longing for homeland, the raw emotion of loss, imprecation against Babylon and Edom

x: In this thanksgiving psalm, David praises the LORD with his whole heart, bowing toward his temple and praising him for his steadfast love and faithfulness, since God has exalted his word above all else (vv. 1-2). He recalls how the LORD answered him and strengthened his soul when he cried out (v. 3), and anticipates kings of the earth praising the LORD once they hear his words (vv. 4-5). Though the LORD is exalted, he takes notice of the lowly while keeping the proud at a distance (v. 6). David closes confident that even amid trouble, God will preserve him and complete the work he has begun, since his steadfast love endures forever (vv. 7-8).
h: Before the Gods Will I Sing Praise (vv.1-3)
All the Kings of the Earth Shall Praise Thee (vv.4-5)
He Hath Respect unto the Lowly (v.6)
The LORD Will Perfect That Which Concerneth Me (vv.7-8)
m: Wholehearted praise, God's faithfulness to His word, answered prayer bringing boldness, God's regard for the lowly, the LORD perfecting what concerns His people

x: David marvels that the LORD has searched him and knows him completely — his sitting, rising, and every thought before he speaks it (vv. 1-6). He reflects on God's inescapable presence, noting there is nowhere he could flee, whether to the heavens, the depths, or the far side of the sea, where God's hand would still lead him (vv. 7-12). He praises God for forming him in his mother's womb, calling himself fearfully and wonderfully made, with every one of his days written in God's book before they began (vv. 13-18). After voicing his hatred for those who oppose God (vv. 19-22), he closes by inviting God to search his own heart and lead him in the way everlasting (vv. 23-24).
h: Thou Hast Searched Me, and Known Me (vv.1-6)
Whither Shall I Go from Thy Spirit (vv.7-12)
I Hate Them with Perfect Hatred (vv.19-22)
Search Me, O God, and Know My Heart (vv.23-24)
m: God's omniscience (all-knowing), omnipresence (everywhere), creation of human life in the womb, the inescapability of God, being fully known and fully loved, invitation for God to search the heart

x: David prays for deliverance from violent men who plot evil and gather for war, their tongues sharp as serpents with poison on their lips (vv. 1-3). He asks the LORD to guard him from the wicked who have hidden snares and nets for his steps (vv. 4-5), affirming his trust in God as his strength and shield in battle (vv. 6-8). He prays that the trouble his enemies planned would fall back on their own heads, like burning coals or a pit they dug themselves (vv. 9-11), closing with confidence that the LORD upholds the cause of the afflicted and that the righteous will give thanks in his presence (vv. 12-13).
h: Adders' Poison Is Under Their Lips (vv.1-3)
They Have Set Gins for Me (vv.4-5)
Thou Hast Covered My Head in the Day of Battle (vv.6-7)
Let the Mischief of Their Own Lips Cover Them (vv.8-11)
m: Protection from violent and deceitful enemies, the tongue as a weapon, God as defender of the afflicted, imprecation against the wicked, confidence in God's justice

x: David asks the LORD to hear him quickly and to receive his prayer like incense and his lifted hands like an evening offering (vv. 1-2). He asks God to guard his mouth and keep him from being drawn toward evil or the delicacies of wrongdoers (vv. 3-4). He welcomes correction from the righteous as a kindness rather than an injury, even while facing his enemies' schemes (vv. 5-7). David keeps his eyes fixed on the LORD as his refuge, asking to be kept from the snares laid for him and praying that the wicked would fall into their own nets while he escapes (vv. 8-10).
h: Let My Prayer Be Set Forth as Incense (vv.1-2)
Keep the Door of My Lips (vv.3-4)
Let the Wicked Fall into Their Own Nets (vv.6-10)
m: Prayer as incense, guarding the mouth, welcoming righteous correction, refusing the enticements of the wicked, evening worship

x: This lament records David's prayer from the cave, crying aloud to the LORD and pouring out his complaint before him (vv. 1-2). When his spirit grows faint, he notes that God alone knows his path, even though enemies have hidden a trap along his way (v. 3). Looking around, he finds no one who notices him or cares for his soul, so he calls the LORD his refuge and his portion in the land of the living (vv. 4-5). He asks God to listen to his cry, rescue him from stronger persecutors, and free him from his prison so he can praise God's name among the righteous (vv. 6-7).
h: I Poured Out My Complaint Before Him (vv.1-2)
No Man Cared for My Soul (v.4)
My Refuge and My Portion in the Land of the Living (v.5)
Bring My Soul out of Prison (vv.6-7)
m: Complete isolation, God as sole refuge, pouring out complaints before God, no human help available, prayer from confinement, hope for future praise

x: David pleads for the LORD to answer him in faithfulness and righteousness, asking not to be judged as strictly deserved, since no one living is righteous before God (vv. 1-2). He describes an enemy who has crushed him to the ground and left him dwelling in darkness, leaving his spirit overwhelmed and his heart desolate (vv. 3-4). He remembers God's past works and stretches out his hands, thirsting for God like dry ground thirsts for rain (vv. 5-6). David begs God to answer quickly, show him steadfast love and the way to walk, and lead him on level ground for the sake of God's own name and righteousness (vv. 7-12).
h: No Man Living Shall Be Justified (vv.1-2)
As Those That Have Been Long Dead (vv.3-4)
My Soul Thirsteth After Thee, as a Thirsty Land (vv.5-6)
Cause Me to Hear Thy Lovingkindness in the Morning (vv.7-10)
m: Pleading God's faithfulness, no one is righteous, spiritual thirst, remembering past mercies, prayer for guidance, the leading of God's Spirit

x: David blesses the LORD, his rock and strength who trains him for battle, his fortress, shield, and deliverer (vv. 1-2). He marvels that God would take notice of mere mortals, whose days pass like a fleeting shadow (vv. 3-4), and asks God to reach down from heaven, scatter his enemies, and rescue him from the deceit of foreign foes (vv. 5-8). David promises to sing a new song of praise for the God who grants victory to kings (vv. 9-10), then prays for a flourishing nation — sons like healthy plants, daughters like polished pillars, full storehouses, thriving livestock, and no cry of distress in the streets — calling blessed the people whose God is the LORD (vv. 11-15).
h: Which Teacheth My Hands to War (vv.1-2)
Bow Thy Heavens, O LORD, and Come Down (vv.5-8)
I Will Sing a New Song unto Thee (vv.9-11)
Happy Is That People, Whose God Is the LORD (vv.12-15)
m: God as rock and fortress, human frailty and smallness, divine intervention in battle, the vision of a blessed nation, prayer for national prosperity

x: In this acrostic psalm of praise, David vows to extol God as his King every day, declaring that his greatness is unsearchable (vv. 1-3). He anticipates one generation telling the next about God's mighty and glorious works (vv. 4-7), and describes the LORD as gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, and good to all he has made (vv. 8-9). David praises God's everlasting kingdom and his care for those who are falling or bowed down, providing food to every living thing in its season (vv. 10-16). He closes by praising the LORD's righteousness and nearness to all who call on him in truth, promising to fulfill the desires of those who fear him while preserving those who love him (vv. 17-21).
h: One Generation Shall Praise Thy Works to Another (vv.4-7)
His Tender Mercies Are over All His Works (vv.8-9)
Thy Kingdom Is an Everlasting Kingdom (vv.10-13)
The LORD Is Nigh unto All Them That Call upon Him (vv.17-20)
Let All Flesh Bless His Holy Name (v.21)
m: God's greatness beyond comprehension, His kingdom that endures, God's compassion to all creation, His faithfulness and nearness to all who call on Him, declaring God's praise to all generations

x: This Hallel psalm, the first of the final five, opens with the psalmist vowing to praise the LORD as long as he lives (vv. 1-2). He warns against putting trust in princes or any mortal, since their breath departs and their plans perish with them (vv. 3-4). He calls blessed the one whose help is the God of Jacob, the maker of heaven and earth who remains faithful forever (vv. 5-6). The psalm lists the LORD's care for the oppressed, hungry, blind, and bowed down, and his love for the righteous, strangers, orphans, and widows, while overturning the ways of the wicked (vv. 7-9), closing with the declaration that the LORD reigns forever (v. 10).
h: While I Live Will I Praise the LORD (vv.1-2)
Put Not Your Trust in Princes (vv.3-4)
Happy Is He That Hath the God of Jacob for His Help (v.5)
The LORD Shall Reign for Ever (v.10)
m: Lifelong praise, trusting God over princes, God as helper of the helpless, God who executes justice for the oppressed, the Creator who cares for the marginalized

x: This Hallel psalm praises the LORD for rebuilding Jerusalem and gathering Israel's exiles, healing the brokenhearted and binding up their wounds (vv. 1-3). It marvels that the God who numbers and names every star also has understanding beyond measure (vv. 4-5), lifting up the humble while bringing down the wicked (v. 6). The psalm celebrates God's provision through creation — sending rain, growing grass, and feeding animals and ravens — noting that his pleasure is not in military strength but in those who fear him and hope in his steadfast love (vv. 7-11). It closes by praising God for strengthening Jerusalem, sending snow and ice, and revealing his word and statutes uniquely to Israel (vv. 12-20).
h: He Telleth the Number of the Stars (vv.1-6)
He Delighteth Not in the Strength of the Horse (vv.7-11)
He Maketh Peace in Thy Borders (vv.12-14)
He Hath Not Dealt So with Any Nation (vv.19-20)
m: God rebuilds Jerusalem, He heals the brokenhearted, He counts the stars yet cares for individuals, God's power in nature, His delight in those who fear Him, His word running swiftly

x: This cosmic Hallel psalm calls the heavens to praise the LORD — angels, heavenly hosts, sun, moon, and stars, all of which he brought into being by his command and established forever (vv. 1-6). It then summons the earth to praise him too: sea creatures, weather, mountains, trees, wild and tame animals, and every creature that flies or crawls (vv. 7-10). Finally it calls on kings, rulers, and all people, young and old alike, to praise the LORD, whose name alone is exalted above earth and heaven (vv. 11-13), closing by noting that he has raised up strength for his people, a praise for all his saints, and for Israel who is near to him (v. 14).
h: Praise Ye the LORD from the Heavens (vv.1-6)
Praise the LORD from the Earth (vv.7-12)
m: All creation praising God, heaven and earth united in worship, the command for everything to praise, God's name alone exalted, nature as worshiper

x: This Hallel psalm calls Israel to sing a new song to the LORD, rejoicing in their Maker and King with dancing, tambourine, and harp (vv. 1-3). It declares that the LORD delights in his people and adorns the humble with salvation, inviting the saints to rejoice and sing for joy even on their beds (vv. 4-5). The psalm closes with a striking image of the saints carrying praise in their mouths and a double-edged sword in their hands, executing God's judgment on rebellious nations and their kings — an honor given to all his saints (vv. 6-9).
h: Sing unto the LORD a New Song (vv.1-3)
He Will Beautify the Meek with Salvation (v.4)
A Twoedged Sword in Their Hand (vv.5-6)
To Execute upon Them the Judgment Written (vv.7-9)
m: A new song, joy in the Maker, praise through dance and instruments, God's pleasure in His people, the two-edged sword of worship and judgment, the honor of the saints

x: This final psalm is a grand doxology calling for praise of God in his sanctuary and in the heavens above, for his mighty acts and surpassing greatness (vv. 1-2). It calls for praise with trumpet, harp and lyre, tambourine and dancing, strings and pipe, and clashing cymbals (vv. 3-5), closing the entire Psalter with a sweeping call for everything that has breath to praise the LORD (v. 6).
h: Praise Him upon the Loud Cymbals (vv.3-5)
Let Every Thing That Hath Breath Praise the LORD (v.6)
m: Universal praise with every instrument, praise everywhere (sanctuary and sky), praise for who God is and what He's done, everything with breath praising the LORD, the Psalter's climactic conclusion

x: The book opens by naming its purpose — to give wisdom, discipline, and discernment for righteous living (vv. 1-6) — and grounds it all in the fear of the LORD (v. 7). The father urges his son not to follow sinners who ambush the innocent for profit, warning that such greed destroys the one who practices it (vv. 8-19). Wisdom is then personified as a woman crying out publicly in the streets and city gates, pleading with the simple to turn from mockery before disaster strikes, since those who reject her will call for help too late (vv. 20-33).
m: a prologue that states six separate purposes before offering a single proverb, the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge set as the motto the entire book hangs on, sinners' own invitation to violence quoted at length precisely because it sounds like belonging rather than crime, Wisdom…

x: The father tells his son that if he treasures wisdom's commands and searches for insight as eagerly as for silver or hidden treasure, he will come to understand the fear of the LORD and find the knowledge of God (vv. 1-5). This wisdom comes from the LORD himself, who stores up sound judgment for the upright and guards the path of justice (vv. 6-9). Once wisdom enters the heart it protects him from wicked men who delight in evil speech (vv. 10-15), and from the immoral woman who abandons her marriage vows and leads to death (vv. 16-19). The chapter closes by promising that the upright will inhabit the land while the wicked are cut off from it (vv. 20-22).
h: Walking in the Way of the Good (vv.20-22)
m: an entire chapter built as one twenty-two-verse conditional sentence, four verses of effortful verbs, receive, hide, incline, cry, before a single promise is given, wisdom described as both a gift God gives and a treasure a man must dig for like silver, protection offered against two dangers in…

x: The son is urged to keep his father's teaching, to trust the LORD completely rather than lean on his own understanding, and to honor him with his wealth, with the promise that his paths will be made straight and his barns will overflow (vv. 1-10). He must not resent the LORD's discipline, since it comes from fatherly love (vv. 11-12). Wisdom is praised as more valuable than silver or jewels, bringing long life, riches, honor, and peace, and as the very means by which the LORD founded the earth (vv. 13-20). The chapter ends with practical commands not to withhold good from those who deserve it, not to plot harm against a trusting neighbor, and not to envy a violent man, since the LORD blesses the humble and honest (vv. 27-35).
h: Blessings of Obedience: Life, Peace, Favour (vv.1-10)
m: five of the most quoted sentences in the book packed into ten opening verses, each pairing an instruction with a promise, trust in the LORD with all thine heart tied directly to having thy paths directed, divine discipline reframed as evidence of love rather than of rejection, for whom the LORD…

x: The father again urges his sons to get wisdom and understanding above all else, recalling how his own father taught him the same lesson (vv. 1-9). He sets before them two paths — the way of the righteous, which grows brighter like the dawn, and the way of the wicked, who cannot sleep until they have caused someone to stumble (vv. 10-19). He tells them to guard their heart above everything else, since it is the source of all of life's direction, and to keep their eyes, mouth, and feet fixed on the straight path, turning aside from evil (vv. 20-27).
h: Guard Your Heart and Walk Straight (vv.20-27)
m: wisdom passed down three explicit generations, David to Solomon to Solomon's own son, quoted directly rather than merely asserted, a road pictured as the central image of the chapter, four separate commands to avoid the same wicked path, avoid it, pass not by it, turn from it, pass away, two paths…

x: The chapter warns against the seductive woman whose lips drip honey but whose end is as bitter as wormwood and as sharp as a two-edged sword, leading down to death (vv. 1-6). The son is told to keep his way far from her house, lest he lose his strength, wealth, and reputation to strangers and end in bitter regret (vv. 7-14). Instead he is urged to find satisfaction in the wife of his youth, rejoicing in her love as in a fountain reserved for him alone (vv. 15-19). The chapter closes with the reminder that the LORD sees every path a man walks, and that the wicked are ensnared by their own sin (vv. 20-23).
m: a warning whose entire logic rests on the gap between how something sounds and where it actually ends, her lips drop as an honeycomb, but her end is bitter as wormwood, a command that is purely spatial and admits no negotiation, remove thy way far from her, and come not nigh the door of her house…

x: Solomon warns against carelessly pledging surety for another person's debt, urging urgent action to free yourself before the obligation snares you (vv. 1-5). He sends the lazy man to study the ant, which stores up food with no overseer forcing it to work, warning that a little more sleep leads to poverty arriving like an armed robber (vv. 6-11). A troublemaker is marked by shifty gestures and a lying mouth that stirs up conflict, and the LORD is said to hate seven things, including pride, lying, and sowing discord among brothers (vv. 12-19). The chapter closes with an extended warning against adultery, framed by parental instruction and pictured as fire no man can carry without being burned, leaving a reproach that never fully fades (vv. 20-35).
m: four separate dangers gathered into a single varied chapter, foolish loan pledges urged to be escaped through the same verbs used to describe fleeing a hunter or a fowler, an ant sent as the sole teacher of diligence, having no guide, overseer, or ruler, provideth her meat in the summer, a…

x: The father urges his son to treasure his teaching as a guard against the seductive stranger, holding wisdom close like a sister to stay grounded (vv. 1-5). He then recounts watching from his window a naive young man wander toward a seductress's corner at twilight (vv. 6-9). She meets him dressed to entice, bold and restless, luring him with talk of fulfilled vows, a perfumed bed, and her husband's absence on a long trip (vv. 10-20). Smooth talk wins him over, and he follows her the way an ox walks to slaughter, unaware it will cost him his life (vv. 21-23). The father closes by begging his sons to avoid her paths, since she has brought down many strong men and her house leads straight to death (vv. 24-27).
m: the longest continuous narrative in the entire book of Proverbs told from a window at twilight, wisdom urged to be held as close as family, thou art my sister, and understanding my kinswoman, specifically as protection against what follows, a seduction narrated in unhurried, cinematic detail down…

x: Wisdom personified calls out publicly at the city gates, inviting the simple and foolish to gain understanding (vv. 1-5). She insists her words are true and righteous, worth more than silver, gold, or rubies, and that kings and rulers govern justly only through her (vv. 6-16). Those who love and seek her are rewarded with lasting wealth and righteousness (vv. 17-21). She then describes being present with God before creation, brought forth before the mountains and seas, rejoicing daily in his presence and in humanity (vv. 22-31). The chapter closes with her appeal to be heard daily, promising that whoever finds her finds life, while whoever rejects her brings ruin on themselves (vv. 32-36).
h: Wisdom's Origin and Role in Creation (vv.22-31)
m: Wisdom speaking for herself in an extended first-person address unlike anywhere else in the book, a public call issued from the very gates and crossroads where business is actually done rather than from anywhere hidden, a claim placed underneath government itself, by me kings reign, and princes…

x: Wisdom builds a grand house with seven pillars, prepares a feast, and sends her servants to invite the simple to eat and gain understanding (vv. 1-6). Correcting a mocker only brings scorn, but a wise person welcomes correction and grows from it (vv. 7-9). True wisdom begins with reverence for the LORD and brings a longer, fuller life, while scorning it brings consequences the scorner alone must bear (vv. 10-12). Folly is pictured as a loud, undisciplined woman who sits at her door offering the same invitation, tempting the simple with stolen water and secret bread that seem sweet in the moment (vv. 13-17). Her guests never realize her house leads to death, and everyone who enters ends up among the dead (v. 18).
m: two women, Wisdom and Folly, each building a house and each calling out from the highest places of the city using nearly identical words, whoso is simple, let him turn in hither, a banquet fully prepared, animals killed, wine mingled, servants sent, set against a banquet built on nothing but theft…

x: This chapter opens Solomon's collection of short, standalone proverbs, mostly contrasting the righteous and the wicked in pairs (v. 1). Diligence brings wealth while a slack hand brings poverty, and gathering at the right time marks a wise son (vv. 4-5). Speech recurs as a major theme: a righteous mouth is a well of life worth more than silver, while too many words invite sin and a lying tongue eventually gets cut off (vv. 11, 19-21, 31-32). Love is said to cover over offenses, while hatred stirs up conflict (v. 12). The fear of the LORD prolongs life, and the righteous are pictured as an everlasting foundation, while the wicked vanish like a passing storm and their hope comes to nothing (vv. 25, 27-30).
h: The Righteous and the Wicked Contrasted (vv.1-14)
What the Righteous Gain and the Wicked Lose (vv.25-32)
m: a literary transition marked cleanly in its own opening verse, the proverbs of Solomon, moving from nine chapters of discourse into individual two-line contrasts built almost entirely on the word but, the tongue appearing in eleven of thirty-two verses, from the mouth of the righteous as a well of…

x: Solomon opens with God's demand for honest business dealings, calling dishonest scales detestable and just weights delightful to him (v. 1). Pride precedes disgrace while humility carries wisdom, and personal integrity guides the upright while the wicked are ultimately destroyed by their own wrongdoing (vv. 2-6). A city thrives when the righteous prosper, gossip destroys neighbors, and trustworthy people keep confidences while many advisors bring safety (vv. 9-14). Generosity is repeatedly praised: the one who gives freely still grows richer, while the stingy person heads toward poverty, and whoever refreshes others will be refreshed in return (vv. 24-25). The chapter closes by warning that trusting in riches leads to a fall, while the righteous flourish like a green branch, and whoever wins souls is called wise (vv. 28, 30).
h: Counsel, Surety and the Company Kept (vv.12-21)
Generosity, Greed and the Fruit of the Righteous (vv.22-31)
m: commerce opened with a specific business practice named outright, a false balance is abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight, a civic claim unusual for the collection, by the blessing of the upright the city is exalted, treating private virtue as having public effect, in the…

x: Solomon opens by saying that loving instruction reflects a love of knowledge, while hating correction is foolish (v. 1). A good wife is her husband's pride, but a disgraceful one saps his strength (v. 4), and the righteous, unlike the wicked, are firmly established and produce lasting fruit (vv. 3, 7, 12). Speech is a major theme again: truthful lips endure while lying lips are detestable to the LORD and only last a moment, and words can wound like a sword or bring healing (vv. 17-19, 22). Diligence brings satisfaction and authority, while laziness leaves a person empty-handed, unable even to enjoy what he catches (vv. 11, 24, 27). The chapter closes by affirming that the path of righteousness leads to life, with no death found along it (v. 28).
h: The Virtuous Wife, Words and Roots (vv.1-14)
Diligence, Anxiety and the Way of Life (vv.23-28)
m: correction opened directly, whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge, but he that hateth reproof is brutish, a virtuous woman called a crown to her husband while her opposite is named rottenness in his bones, speech pictured as both weapon and rescue, the words of the wicked lie in wait for blood…

x: A wise son listens to his father's instruction, while a mocker refuses correction, and careful speech is repeatedly tied to a well-guarded life (vv. 1-3). The lazy person craves and gets nothing, while diligence brings prosperity, and wealth gained by dishonest shortcuts shrinks away while wealth earned through labor grows (vv. 4, 11). Hope delayed makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is like a tree of life, and refusing correction leads to poverty and shame while welcoming it leads to honor (vv. 12-13, 18). Companionship matters: walking with the wise makes a person wise, while associating with fools brings harm (v. 20). The chapter closes on parental discipline, teaching that withholding correction from a child is a form of hatred, while loving discipline is applied early (v. 24).
m: a son who hears instruction set against a scorner who will not from the very first verse, two observations about money placed deliberately against each other, the ransom of a man's life are his riches, and there is that maketh himself rich, yet hath nothing, hope deferred maketh the heart sick, but…

x: A wise woman builds up her household while a foolish one tears it down with her own hands, and the chapter repeatedly ties character to the tongue, contrasting faithful and false witnesses (vv. 1, 5, 25). A path can look right to a person and still end in death, warning against trusting mere appearances (v. 12), and the naive believe anything while the prudent think carefully about their steps (v. 15). Treatment of the poor becomes a moral test: oppressing the poor insults their Maker, while showing them kindness honors him (v. 31). The fear of the LORD is described as a source of strong confidence and a fountain of life that helps a person avoid deadly traps (vv. 26-27). The chapter closes by noting that righteousness elevates a nation while sin brings it disgrace (v. 34).
h: The House, the Heart and the Simple (vv.1-14)
Poverty, Anger and the Fear of the LORD (vv.15-27)
