m: building and demolition opening the chapter, every wise woman buildeth her house, but the foolish plucketh it down with her hands, a warning against self-assurance repeated twice in the whole book, there is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death, a loneliest…

x: A gentle answer defuses anger while harsh words provoke it, opening a chapter heavy on wise, timely speech versus foolish outbursts (vv. 1-2, 4, 23, 28). The LORD is described as watching everything, everywhere, seeing both good and evil, and hearing the prayers of the righteous while staying distant from the wicked (vv. 3, 29). A cheerful heart is praised for producing a glad face and a steady spirit, and love in a poor household is said to beat wealth mixed with strife or hatred (vv. 13, 15-17). The wise pursue correction and counsel, knowing that plans fail without advice but succeed with many counselors, while fools despise instruction to their own harm (vv. 22, 32). The chapter ends by tying humility to the fear of the LORD, the true foundation of wisdom and the path to honor (v. 33).
h: The Soft Answer and the Watching Eyes (vv.1-15)
Pride, Instruction and the Answer of the Heart (vv.24-33)
m: the best-known verse in the whole collection opening the chapter, a soft answer turneth away wrath, but grievous words stir up anger, God named as the watching observer rather than only the judge, the eyes of the LORD are in every place, beholding the evil and the good, two better-than sayings that…

x: Solomon opens with a strong theme of divine sovereignty: people plan their steps, but the LORD directs them, weighs the heart, and even the wicked exist within his purposes (vv. 1-4, 9). Honest business dealings, like true scales and weights, belong to him, and committing one's work to him brings stability (vv. 3, 11). Several verses focus on kings, noting that righteous speech pleases them and that a wise person knows how to calm royal anger and gain favor (vv. 10, 13-15). Pride is condemned as leading to a fall, while humility is praised as better than sharing plunder with the proud, and pleasant, wise words are compared to sweet, healing honeycomb (vv. 18-19, 24). The chapter closes by valuing patience over strength, since ruling one's own temper outranks conquering a city, even though the LORD governs every outcome, down to the casting of lots (vv. 32-33).
h: Kings, Pride and the Way of Life (vv.10-22)
m: the densest theological cluster in the whole collection, six of nine opening verses naming the LORD directly, a man's heart deviseth his way, but the LORD directeth his steps, court wisdom assuming a reader near power, the wrath of a king is as messengers of death, the single most quoted verse in…

x: Solomon says a quiet meal beats a feast filled with conflict, and that the LORD tests hearts the way fire refines silver and gold (vv. 1, 3). Covering an offense builds love, but repeating it drives friends apart, and starting a quarrel is compared to letting water break through a dam, so it is best avoided from the start (vv. 9, 14). True friendship is praised as constant, with a real friend or brother sticking close through hard times, while foolish agreements like careless pledges bring trouble (vv. 17-18). A cheerful heart is described as good medicine, while a broken spirit saps strength, and a foolish child brings grief to both parents (vv. 21-22, 25). The chapter closes by praising restrained speech, noting that even a fool who stays silent can be mistaken for wise (vv. 27-28).
h: Fools, Friends and the Merry Heart (vv.15-28)
m: an opening preference for less rather than more, better is a dry morsel, and quietness therewith, than an house full of sacrifices with strife, the fining pot for silver and the furnace for gold set beside the LORD who trieth the hearts, one of Scripture's great friendship verses, a friend loveth…

x: Solomon opens by warning that a person who isolates himself pursues only his own desires and rejects sound judgment, unlike a fool who talks just to reveal his own mind (vv. 1-2). Careless, hasty speech is condemned: a fool's mouth invites trouble, gossip wounds deeply, and answering before listening is called foolish and shameful (vv. 6-8, 13). The LORD's name is pictured as a strong tower where the righteous find safety, while the rich mistakenly trust their wealth as their own fortress (vv. 10-11). Pride precedes a fall while humility precedes honor, and an offended brother is said to be harder to win back than a fortified city (vv. 12, 19). The tongue holds enormous power over life and death, and the chapter closes by praising a good wife as a gift from the LORD and a loyal friend as closer than a brother (vv. 20-22, 24).
h: The Isolated Man, the Tongue and the Name (vv.1-12)
m: a man who has withdrawn from community pursuing his own desire against all sound wisdom, judging a matter before hearing it named outright as folly and shame, two images of refuge placed deliberately unequal, the name of the LORD is a strong tower, and the rich man's wealth is his strong city, one…

x: This collection of proverbs opens by valuing integrity over cleverness, warning that a poor person who walks with integrity is better than a fool who twists his words, and that zeal without knowledge or hasty decisions lead a person astray (vv. 1-2). A person's own folly ruins his way, yet his heart still rages against the Lord as if God were to blame (v. 3). Several proverbs contrast wealth and poverty in relationships: riches multiply friends and flattery draws favor-seekers, while the poor are shunned even by family, and a false witness or liar will not go unpunished (vv. 4-9). The chapter warns that luxury does not suit a fool and it is worse still for a servant to rule over princes, while good sense produces patience and the glory of overlooking an offense (vv. 10-11). A king's fury is likened to a lion's roar and his favor to dew on the grass, while a foolish son ruins his father…
h: Instruction, Kindness and the Fear of the LORD (vv.15-29)
m: integrity preferred over cleverness from the opening verse, better is the poor that walketh in his integrity, than he that is perverse in his lips, poverty's effect on friendship stated without any moralizing, wealth maketh many friends, but the poor is separated from his neighbour, the…

x: This chapter gathers wisdom on a wide range of subjects, opening with a warning that wine and strong drink lead the deceived astray (v. 1). It touches on the sluggard who refuses to plow in season and has nothing to show at harvest (v. 4), the rarity of genuinely faithful people despite many claiming loyalty (v. 6), and the universal question of who can honestly claim a clean heart (v. 9). Several verses address just kingship and justice (vv. 2, 8, 26, 28), while others condemn dishonest weights and measures as detestable to the Lord (vv. 10, 23). The chapter closes with reminders that the Lord directs a person's steps (v. 24) and that vengeance belongs to him, not to us (v. 22).
h: Wine, Kings and the Clean Heart (vv.1-11)
Trade, Counsel and the Hasty Inheritance (vv.12-21)
Vengeance Left to God, and the King's Sifting (vv.22-30)
m: a warning about alcohol stated without any softening, wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging, a question that comes as near to a doctrine of universal guilt as the collection gets, who can say, I have made my heart clean, I am pure from my sin, the sharpest piece of market observation in the…

x: This chapter's proverbs circle around God's sovereignty over human plans, opening with the striking claim that the king's heart is like a stream of water in the Lord's hand, directed wherever he pleases (v. 1). Doing what is right and just is valued above religious sacrifice (v. 3), and living with a quarrelsome spouse is likened to a leaky roof in a storm or cramped quarters on a rooftop (vv. 9, 19). The chapter warns that the sluggard's own laziness will be his ruin, craving all day while refusing to work (vv. 25-26). It closes by declaring that no wisdom, understanding, or plan can succeed against the Lord, and that while a horse may be prepared for battle, victory itself belongs to him (vv. 30-31).
h: The King's Heart and the Weighing of Ways (vv.1-8)
The Housetop Corner and the Price of Pleasure (vv.9-20)
Guarded Speech, and the Horse Prepared for Battle (vv.21-31)
m: the boldest sovereignty claim in the whole collection opening the chapter, the king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water, he turneth it whithersoever he will, a priority the prophets spent entire books arguing, to do justice and judgment is more acceptable to the LORD than…

x: This chapter closes the first Solomonic collection (vv. 1-16) and opens the "words of the wise" (vv. 17-29), moving through a range of practical sayings. A good name is valued above great riches (v. 1), and children raised in the right path are promised they will not depart from it later in life (v. 6). The proverbs also observe that the rich rule over the poor and the borrower is servant to the lender (v. 7), while repeatedly warning against exploiting the poor or the fatherless, since the Lord himself will take up their case (vv. 16, 22-23). The chapter ends by promising that a person skilled in his work will stand before kings rather than obscure men (v. 29).
h: The Last of the Solomonic Couplets (vv.1-16)
The Words of the Wise Begin (vv.17-29)
m: the final sixteen verses of the first great Solomonic collection weighted heavily toward money and class, the rich and poor meet together, the LORD is the maker of them all, a sentence that has described debt ever since it was written, the borrower is servant to the lender, the single most quoted…

x: Continuing the "words of the wise," this chapter ranges across self-discipline and relationships. It opens with counsel on restraint when dining with a ruler and a warning not to wear yourself out chasing riches, since wealth can sprout wings and fly away like an eagle (vv. 1-5). Readers are told not to eat the bread of a stingy host, whose hospitality is not what it seems (vv. 6-8), and parents are urged to discipline their children and find joy in a wise son or daughter (vv. 13-16, 22-25). The chapter warns against envying sinners and urges continual fear of the Lord instead (v. 17), and it closes with the Bible's most vivid extended portrait of a drunkard, whose eyes see strange things and who wakes only to crave another drink (vv. 29-35).
h: At a Ruler's Table, and Riches That Fly Away (vv.1-11)
Winebibbers, Gluttons and the Deep Ditch (vv.19-28)
m: a meal at a ruler's table treated as a test rather than a courtesy, riches said to make themselves wings and fly away as an eagle toward heaven the moment a man labours to be rich, correction offered from a father's own hope of being gladdened rather than from mere enforcement, a request that…

x: This chapter concludes the "words of the wise" with counsel on integrity and diligence. It notes that a house is built through wisdom and its rooms filled with rare treasures through knowledge (vv. 3-4), while a person who faints in adversity has little strength to begin with (v. 10). Readers are urged to rescue those being led away to death rather than claim ignorance of their plight (vv. 11-12), and warned not to gloat over a fallen enemy, since the Lord may turn his anger toward the one who rejoices (vv. 17-18). The chapter also calls for impartial judgment in disputes (vv. 23-26) and closes with a first-person parable: walking past the sluggard's overgrown, wall-crumbling field, the writer draws a lesson about how a little more sleep leads straight to poverty (vv. 30-34).
h: The House Built by Wisdom, and the Duty to Rescue (vv.1-12)
The Just Man Rising Again, and the End of the Wicked (vv.13-22)
A Further Word to the Wise, and the Sluggard's Field (vv.23-34)
m: wisdom's own house-building language from chapter nine reused for human strength, through wisdom is an house builded, and by understanding it is established, character measured in the shortest sentence in the book, if thou faint in the day of adversity, thy strength is small, an obligation to…

x: This chapter opens the second Solomonic collection, copied out by King Hezekiah's scribes some two hundred fifty years after Solomon's reign (v. 1), and its proverbs range widely across kingship, speech, and self-control. It contrasts the glory of God in concealing a matter with the glory of kings in searching it out, and counsels removing the wicked from a king's presence to establish his throne (vv. 2-7). On speech, a word fitly spoken is compared to apples of gold in settings of silver, and a wise rebuke to an attentive ear is like a gold earring (vv. 11-15). The chapter urges moderation, warning against eating too much honey and comparing a man without self-control to a city with broken-down walls (vv. 16-17, 28), and it calls for kindness to a hungry enemy, feeding him bread and giving him water to drink (vv. 21-22).
h: Hezekiah's Men, the King's Court and Words Fitly Spoken (vv.1-14)
Honey, Neighbors and Coals of Fire (vv.15-28)
m: an editorial note found nowhere else quite like it in the Old Testament, these are also proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out roughly two and a half centuries after they were first spoken, court material built around the glory of concealing versus the honour of…

x: This chapter groups proverbs around three character types: the fool, the sluggard, and the troublemaker. Honor fits a fool as poorly as snow falling in summer (v. 1), and Scripture holds two opposite responses to folly in tension — sometimes silence, sometimes a firm answer (vv. 4-5). A fool who repeats his own mistakes is compared to a dog returning to its vomit (v. 11), and a man convinced of his own wisdom is called more hopeless than a fool (v. 12). The sluggard invents imaginary dangers to avoid work (v. 13) and is too lazy even to feed himself (v. 15), yet still considers himself wise (v. 16). The closing verses expose gossips and troublemakers, warning that flattering speech can mask a hateful, deceitful heart destined to be exposed (vv. 17-28).
h: The Fool, Answered and Not Answered (vv.1-12)
The Meddler, the Talebearer and the Flattering Mouth (vv.17-28)
m: three character types organized into deliberate blocks, the fool, the sluggard and the troublemaker, rather than scattered individually, two verses placed side by side that appear to contradict each other on purpose, answer not a fool according to his folly and immediately answer a fool according…

x: This chapter mixes proverbs on humility, friendship, and stewardship. Boasting about tomorrow is foolish since no one controls what a day brings (v. 1), and praise is better received from someone else's mouth than one's own (v. 2). A friend's honest correction, though painful, is trustworthy, while an enemy's flattery is not (v. 6), and open rebuke beats love kept hidden (v. 5). True friendship sharpens character the way iron sharpens iron (v. 17), and nearby neighbors can prove more valuable in a crisis than distant family (v. 10). Human desire is compared to the grave — never satisfied (v. 20) — and a person's true character is revealed by how they handle praise, much as fire refines silver and gold (v. 21). The chapter closes urging diligent care of one's flocks and resources, since riches do not last forever (vv. 23-27).
h: Iron Sharpening Iron, and the State of the Flocks (vv.15-27)
m: a limit on planning stated outright, boast not thyself of tomorrow, for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth, the fullest and most unsentimental treatment of friendship anywhere in the book, faithful are the wounds of a friend, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful, character described as…

x: This chapter contrasts the righteous and the wicked across leadership, wealth, and honesty. The wicked flee even when no one pursues them, while the righteous stand bold as a lion (v. 1), and a nation's stability depends on leaders with real understanding rather than oppressive rulers who prey on the poor like a roaring lion (vv. 2, 15-16). An honest poor person is better off than a rich one of crooked character (v. 6), and hiding sin brings no success, while confessing and forsaking it brings mercy (v. 13). Steady reverence for God is called blessed, but a hardened heart leads to ruin (v. 14). Diligent work on one's own land brings plenty, while chasing empty pursuits brings poverty (v. 19), and rushing to get rich only invites trouble (vv. 20, 22). The chapter favors honest rebuke over flattery (v. 23), trust in God over self-reliance (vv. 25-26), and generosity to the poor over…
h: Bold as a Lion, and Sin Confessed (vv.1-14)
Hasty Riches, Self-Trust and the Rising of the Wicked (vv.15-28)
m: bearing contrasted rather than outcome from the opening verse, the wicked flee when no man pursueth, but the righteous are bold as a lion, governance and money woven through nearly every antithetical couplet, a condition the rest of the Bible builds a whole doctrine on, he that covereth his sins…

x: This chapter continues contrasting the righteous and the wicked, with special attention to leadership and discipline. Those who repeatedly resist correction face sudden, irreversible ruin (v. 1), and a nation's mood rises or falls with the character of its rulers (v. 2). Bribery undermines justice while fair judgment establishes a land (v. 4), and a king who judges the poor faithfully secures a lasting throne (v. 14). Wise people turn away wrath while scorners stir up an entire city (v. 8), and a fool blurts out everything he thinks while a wise person holds back (v. 11). The chapter urges disciplined child-rearing, warning that an undisciplined child brings shame while correction brings peace (vv. 15, 17), and states that people without vision or guidance perish, while those who keep God's law are blessed (v. 18). It closes contrasting pride, which brings a person low, with humility…
h: The Hardened Neck, and Rulers Who Hear (vv.1-14)
The Rod, the Vision and the Fear of Man (vv.15-27)
m: the single point past which correction stops working named outright, he that being often reproved hardeneth his neck shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy, public life running through the chapter more than any other in the collection, when the righteous are in authority, the people…

x: This chapter records the sayings of Agur son of Jakeh, opening with a humble confession that he lacks understanding of God's ways (vv. 1-4) and an affirmation that every word of God is trustworthy, not to be added to (vv. 5-6). Agur prays for honesty and modest provision — neither poverty nor riches — so he is not tempted to deny God or to steal (vv. 7-9). The rest of the chapter is built from numerical proverbs grouped in sets of "three, even four": generations marked by pride and cruelty to the poor (vv. 11-14); things never satisfied, like the grave and a barren womb (vv. 15-16); mysteries too wonderful to grasp, including the way of a man with a young woman, likened to an adulterous woman who denies wrongdoing (vv. 18-20); things the earth cannot bear, such as a well-fed fool or an unloved woman who marries (vv. 21-23); small creatures that are remarkably wise, like ants and spiders…
h: The Sufficiency and Purity of Scripture (vv.5-6)
The Eye That Mocks a Father (v.17)
The Four Small but Wise Creatures (vv.24-28)
m: an unknown author, Agur son of Jakeh, opening not with instruction but with a confession of ignorance, surely I am more brutish than any man, questions no answer in the collection has actually addressed, who hath gathered the wind in his fists, the only prayer in the entire book, give me neither…

x: King Lemuel recounts the wisdom his mother taught him about the dangers of wine, injustice, and misused strength for a king, and the responsibility to defend the poor and needy (vv. 1-9). The chapter closes with an acrostic poem, each verse beginning with a successive Hebrew letter, praising a capable, God-fearing wife — valued far above jewels, industrious in trade and household management, generous to the poor, wise in speech, and honored by her husband and children (vv. 10-31). Verse 30 sets the poem's true standard: charm and beauty are fleeting, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised.
h: A Mother's Oracle to a King (vv.1-2)
Give Not Thy Strength Unto Women (v.3)
It Is Not for Kings to Drink Wine (vv.4-7)
Plead the Cause of the Dumb (vv.8-9)
Her Worth and Her Husband's Trust (vv.10-12)
Her Praise and the Fear of the LORD (vv.28-31)
m: the book's final chapter attributed entirely to a mother instructing her son the king, three times naming their relationship before a single piece of advice is given, what, my son, and what, the son of my womb, wine withheld specifically from a ruler who might forget the law and pervert judgment…

x: The Preacher — identified as Solomon, son of David and king in Jerusalem — opens by declaring that everything is fleeting and produces no lasting gain (vv. 1-3). He points to nature's endless repeating cycles — generations pass, the sun rises and sets, rivers flow to a sea that never fills — as proof nothing under the sun is truly new (vv. 4-11). Applying his mind to search out wisdom about all that happens under heaven, he calls it a heavy burden God has given people to struggle with (v. 13). He concludes that human effort is like chasing the wind, that what is crooked cannot be straightened, and that increased wisdom only brings increased grief and sorrow (vv. 14-18).
h: Title and Thesis: All Is Vanity (vv.1-2)
The Question: What Profit Hath a Man? (v.3)
m: A thesis stated before any argument, life measured under the sun, cycles that go nowhere and are never full, and wisdom pursued to the point where it increases grief

x: The Preacher tests pleasure, laughter, and wine, then throws himself into great building projects, gardens, pools, servants, livestock, silver and gold, and every entertainment money could buy, denying himself nothing his eyes desired (vv. 1-10). Surveying it all, he judges it profitless, though he notes wisdom does exceed folly as light exceeds darkness (vv. 11-13). Still, the same death overtakes the wise and the foolish alike, so he despairs of his labor, knowing he must leave it all to a successor who may prove wise or foolish (vv. 14-21). He concludes that there is nothing better than to eat, drink, and find enjoyment in one's work, recognizing this capacity as a gift from God's hand (vv. 22-26).
h: The Experiment with Pleasure and Works (vv.1-11)
Eat, Drink, and Enjoy: from God (vv.24-26)
m: Pleasure tested deliberately and found empty, works on a royal scale that still end in someone else's hands, wisdom conceded to be better than folly and still ending in the same grave, and a first conclusion that eating and drinking are a gift

x: The Preacher opens with a poem cataloging the appointed seasons of life — birth and death, planting and uprooting, weeping and laughing, war and peace — showing that God has fitted a proper time to every human activity (vv. 1-8). He affirms that God makes everything fitting in its season and has placed a sense of eternity in the human heart, yet in a way that keeps people from grasping the full scope of His work from start to finish (vv. 9-11). Because that scope stays hidden, he concludes the best course is to rejoice, do good, and enjoy the fruit of one's labor as God's gift, since what God does is fixed and unchangeable and meant to inspire reverence (vv. 12-14). Even where courts should render justice, he sees wickedness instead, yet trusts that God will judge both the righteous and the wicked in His own time (vv. 15-17). He closes by noting that people and animals share the same…
h: The Poem of Times and Seasons (vv.1-8)
m: Fourteen pairs of opposites nobody chooses, eternity set in the human heart without the ability to see the whole, injustice observed rather than explained, and death leveling man with beast

x: The Preacher observes the tears of the oppressed, who have no comforter while power rests with their oppressors, leading him to say the dead — and even the unborn — are better off than those forced to witness such evil (vv. 1-3). He notes that skillful labor is often driven by envy of one's neighbor, that the fool folds his hands in idleness, and that a little rest with quiet is better than toil that only chases the wind (vv. 4-6). He describes a lonely man endlessly laboring for wealth with no heir or companion, then contrasts this with the value of companionship — two can help each other up, keep each other warm, and resist an attacker where one alone would fail (vv. 7-12). He closes by noting that a poor but wise youth is better than an old, foolish king who refuses advice, yet even a popular successor is eventually forgotten by those who come after (vv. 13-16).
m: Oppression seen with no comforter, rivalry named as the engine of achievement, isolation described as misery, two better than one and three strands hard to break, and popularity that does not outlast a generation

x: The Preacher urges caution when approaching God's house — listening is better than offering the thoughtless sacrifice of fools, and words spoken before God should be few and never rash, since vows once made must be paid (vv. 1-7). He notes that oppression of the poor by officials should not surprise anyone, since layers of authority protect each other, though the land ultimately benefits everyone including the king (vv. 8-9). He warns that loving money never satisfies, that more possessions only mean more people to feed from them, and that the rich man's abundance often steals his sleep while the laborer rests easy (vv. 10-12). Describing a man who hoards wealth only to lose it in misfortune, leaving his heir nothing, the Preacher reminds readers that everyone leaves this world as naked as they entered it (vv. 13-17). He concludes that the good and fitting response is to eat, drink, and…
m: Fewer words in God's house, vows better unmade than unkept, money that never satisfies the one who loves it, sleep as the labourer's advantage over the rich, and a portion received rather than earned

x: The Preacher identifies a painful evil: God may give a person riches, wealth, and honor lacking nothing they desire, yet withhold the ability to enjoy it, so a stranger ends up consuming it instead (vv. 1-2). He declares that even a man who fathers a hundred children and lives many years is worse off than a stillborn child if his soul finds no satisfaction and he receives no proper burial, since the stillborn at least finds rest (vv. 3-6). He observes that all human labor is ultimately for the mouth, yet appetite is never filled, and that the wise gain no lasting advantage over the fool since both share the same fate (vv. 7-9). He closes by noting that what happens has already been determined and named, no one can contend with one mightier than themselves, and no one truly knows what is good for a person during their fleeting, shadow-like life or what will follow after them (vv. 10-12).
m: Wealth held without the capacity to enjoy it, a stillborn child called better off, appetite that outruns supply, and the question of who knows what is good left open

x: The Preacher opens with a series of paradoxes: a good reputation outlasts fine perfume, and the day of death can be better than the day of birth, because mourning teaches the heart what feasting cannot (vv. 1-6). He warns that extortion corrupts even a wise man and a bribe corrupts judgment, that patience is better than pride, and that it is not wise to long nostalgically for days gone by (vv. 7-10). Wisdom, he says, is as valuable as an inheritance and preserves the life of the one who has it, yet he also observes that God has paired prosperity with adversity so that no one can predict the future (vv. 11-14). He notes the troubling reality that righteous people sometimes perish young while the wicked live long, and cautions against extremes of self-righteousness or wickedness alike, since perfect righteousness is beyond any person's reach (vv. 15-22). Searching further for wisdom, he…
h: Better Than: The Value of Sorrow (vv.1-12)
The Strength and Limits of Wisdom (vv.19-22)
m: A funeral preferred to a feast, sorrow treated as more instructive than laughter, a warning against being either too righteous or too wicked, and a search that concludes people were made upright and have sought out inventions

x: The Preacher praises wisdom for brightening a person's countenance, then counsels obedience to the king's command since royal authority is absolute and no one can question it (vv. 1-4). He advises that the wise heart knows there is a right time and way to act, even though people cannot know the future or the timing of their own death, and that no one escapes life's ultimate battle (vv. 5-8). He grapples with the troubling fact that the wicked are sometimes honored and forgotten in peace at their burial, and that because judgment on evil is delayed, people's hearts grow bold to do wrong (vv. 9-11). Still, he affirms that ultimately it will go well for those who fear God, and not well for the wicked, even though on earth the righteous sometimes suffer as the wicked prosper and vice versa (vv. 12-14). He closes by commending enjoyment of food, drink, and labor as life's fitting portion…
m: Authority obeyed without illusions about it, sentences delayed until the heart is set on evil, the fear of God distinguished from outcomes, and God's work declared beyond finding out

x: The Preacher affirms that the righteous and the wise are in God's hand, though no one can know from human experience whether they meet with love or hatred, since the same fate — death — comes to everyone regardless of righteousness, wickedness, or ritual observance (vv. 1-3). He values even the humblest living creature over the mightiest of the dead, since the dead have no further knowledge, reward, or memory (vv. 4-6). He therefore counsels enjoying bread and wine with a joyful heart, dressing well, and living joyfully with one's spouse, since such enjoyment is the portion God gives for this life, and there is no work, planning, or wisdom left in the grave (vv. 7-10). He observes that speed, strength, and skill do not guarantee success since time and chance affect everyone, and illustrates this with a poor wise man who saved a besieged city yet was quickly forgotten (vv. 11-16). He…
h: Go Thy Way, Eat Thy Bread (vv.7-10)
m: One event happening to the righteous and the wicked alike, the living told to eat and drink and work because the dead cannot, time and chance overriding swiftness and strength, and a poor wise man whose city forgot him

x: The Preacher observes that a small amount of folly can outweigh great wisdom and honor, the way dead flies spoil fine perfume, and contrasts the wise heart with the foolish one that betrays itself even while walking down the road (vv. 1-3). He advises meeting a ruler's anger with composure rather than resignation, and laments seeing the social order inverted, with fools placed in high positions while the competent are overlooked (vv. 4-7). He offers a string of proverbs on the risks of everyday tasks like digging pits or quarrying stone, the value of sharpening one's tools and skill, and the danger of careless or excessive speech (vv. 8-14). He notes that a fool's labor exhausts him because he doesn't even know the way to town, and pronounces trouble on a land ruled by immature leadership but blessing on one ruled with discipline (vv. 15-17). He closes with warnings against laziness…
h: A Dead Fly in the Ointment (vv.1-3)
m: A dead fly spoiling the ointment, composure recommended before a ruler's anger, hazards attached to ordinary work, a fool's own words consuming him, and a land judged by the character of its rulers

x: The Preacher urges bold, generous action — sending one's resources out freely and diversifying efforts among several ventures, since no one can predict what disaster might come (vv. 1-2). He observes that natural events like rainfall and a falling tree follow their own course beyond human control, and that a farmer too preoccupied with watching the wind and clouds will never sow or reap (vv. 3-4). Since people cannot understand the mystery of how life forms in the womb any more than they understand God's work as a whole, he counsels sowing seed both morning and evening without knowing in advance which effort will succeed (vv. 5-6). He closes by encouraging the young to enjoy life's light and their youthful years fully, while remembering that God will hold them accountable for how they live and that both youth and life itself pass quickly (vv. 7-10).
h: Cast Thy Bread upon the Waters (vv.1-2)
He That Observeth the Wind Shall Not Sow (vv.3-6)
m: Bread cast on waters without knowing the return, sowing continued because the weather cannot be predicted, light called sweet, youth told to rejoice, and judgment named in the same breath

x: The Preacher urges the young to remember their Creator before old age arrives and the years bring no pleasure (v. 1). He then paints an extended picture of the body's decline in old age — using imagery of a darkening sky, trembling guards, failing grinders, closing doors, and fading strength — to describe eyes, limbs, teeth, and senses giving way, hair turning white like almond blossoms, and desire itself fading, all before a person goes to their eternal home and mourners gather in the streets (vv. 2-5). He describes death itself as a silver cord snapping and a golden bowl shattering, when the body returns to dust and the spirit returns to God who gave it (vv. 6-7). Reaffirming that everything is fleeting, he notes that as Preacher he carefully taught the people, weighing and arranging many wise sayings meant to guide and even prod like a herdsman's goad (vv. 8-11). He warns against…
h: The Conclusion of the Whole Matter (vv.13-14)
m: A creator to be remembered before the body fails, old age described through a failing household, words called goads and nails, many books declared wearying, and a whole duty stated in two clauses

x: The Song opens with the Bride longing for her Beloved's kisses and love, which she says is better than wine (vv. 1-4). She explains to the Daughters of Jerusalem that though sun-darkened from tending vineyards, she considers herself lovely, and asks where he pastures his flock so she can find him (vv. 5-8). He compares her beauty to a prized mare among Pharaoh's chariots and praises her ornamented cheeks and neck (vv. 9-11). She in turn describes him as fragrant myrrh and henna blossoms while they are near each other (vv. 12-14). The chapter closes with the couple exchanging tender compliments, delighting in each other and their surroundings (vv. 15-17).
h: The Bride: Draw Me, We Will Run After Thee (vv.2-4)
The Bride: I Am Black, but Comely (vv.5-7)
The Bridegroom: As a Company of Horses (vv.8-11)
The Bride: A Bundle of Myrrh (vv.12-14)
Mutual Praise: Our Bed Is Green (vv.15-17)
m: A working woman rather than a princess, longing stated before the beloved appears, self-consciousness about her sun-darkened skin, and admiration that begins at once and runs both ways

x: The Bride compares herself to a common wildflower, and her Beloved calls her a lily among thorns, while she likens him to a fruit tree offering shade and sweetness (vv. 1-3). She recalls being brought to the banquet hall under his banner of love, so lovesick she asks to be revived, and she charges the Daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up love before its time (vv. 4-7). She then hears her Beloved's voice and pictures him bounding over the hills, calling her to come away now that winter has passed and spring has arrived (vv. 8-13). He longs to see her face and hear her voice, and she asks him to catch the little foxes spoiling their vineyards (v. 15). The chapter closes with her confident claim that they belong to each other and her invitation for him to return swiftly, like a gazelle on the mountains (vv. 16-17).
h: The Rose of Sharon and the Lily (vv.1-3)
The Bride: His Banner Over Me Was Love (vv.4-7)
Rise Up, My Love: The Winter Is Past (vv.10-14)
m: Spring as the reason to come away, a banner of love over the banqueting house, a beloved compared to a gazelle on the mountains, and small foxes named as the threat to a vineyard in bloom

x: At night the Bride searches the city for her Beloved after failing to find him beside her, encountering the watchmen before finally finding him and bringing him to her mother's house, unwilling to let him go (vv. 1-4). She again charges the Daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken love before its time (v. 5). The scene shifts to Solomon's magnificent wedding procession approaching from the wilderness like a column of smoke, surrounded by sixty mighty warriors for protection (vv. 6-8). His ornate carriage, built of Lebanon's finest wood and adorned with gold, silver, and purple, is described in detail (vv. 9-10). The chapter closes with an invitation for the daughters of Zion to see King Solomon in his wedding crown, crowned on the day of his gladness (v. 11).
h: By Night on My Bed I Sought Him (vv.1-3)
I Found Him: Charge to the Daughters (vv.4-5)
Who Is This Coming Out of the Wilderness? (vv.6-8)
m: A search through the streets at night, the watchmen met on the way, a charge laid on the daughters of Jerusalem, and a royal procession out of the wilderness

x: The Bridegroom praises the Bride from head to toe in a series of vivid comparisons — her eyes like doves, her hair like a flock of goats, her teeth like shorn sheep, and her neck like the tower of David — declaring her altogether beautiful and without flaw (vv. 1-7). He invites her to come away with him from the mountains (v. 8) and describes how her love has captured his heart, sweeter than wine, her lips dripping honey (vv. 9-11). He calls her a locked garden and a sealed fountain, an orchard of choice fruit and spices, a well of living water (vv. 12-15). The chapter ends with the Bride inviting the winds to spread her garden's fragrance and welcoming her Beloved to come into his garden and enjoy its fruit, delicately picturing the couple's full union (v. 16).
h: The Bridegroom: Thou Art Fair, My Love (vv.1-5)
Until the Day Break: No Spot in Thee (vv.6-7)
A Garden Enclosed, a Fountain Sealed (vv.12-15)
The Bride: Let My Beloved Come (v.16)
m: Praise catalogued feature by feature in the manner of a wasf, an unqualified “no spot in thee”, a garden described as enclosed and a fountain as sealed, and an invitation that answers the praise

x: The Bridegroom responds that he has come into his garden and enjoyed its fruit, and he invites friends to eat and drink freely with the couple (v. 1). At night the Bride hears her Beloved knocking, but she hesitates to rise and open the door, and by the time she does he has already left (vv. 2-6). Searching for him through the city, she is struck and stripped of her veil by the watchmen, and she pleads with the Daughters of Jerusalem to tell him, if they find him, that she is faint with love (vv. 7-8). When they ask what makes her beloved better than any other, she answers with an admiring description of him from head to toe — radiant, outstanding among ten thousand, with hair black as a raven, eyes like doves, and a form like polished ivory — concluding that he is altogether lovely (vv. 9-16).
h: The Bridegroom: I Am Come into My Garden (v.1)
The Bride: I Sleep, but My Heart Waketh (vv.2-6)
The Daughters Ask: What Is Thy Beloved? (v.9)
The Bride: My Beloved Is White and Ruddy (vv.10-16)
m: A knock at the door answered too late, a search that ends in being struck by the watchmen, a question from the daughters that invites the answer, and a description of the beloved from head to feet

x: When the Daughters of Jerusalem ask where her Beloved has gone, the Bride explains he has gone down to his garden to graze among the lilies, reaffirming that she belongs to him and he to her (vv. 1-3). He responds with renewed praise, comparing her beauty to great cities and declaring that though he could have countless queens and concubines, she alone is perfect and unique — the favorite of her mother and admired by all who see her (vv. 4-10). The Bride recalls wandering down to the orchard, where she was suddenly overtaken by longing for her beloved (vv. 11-12). The chapter closes with others calling for the Shulammite to return so they might look upon her (v. 13).
h: The Bridegroom: Terrible as an Army with Banners (vv.4-9)
Who Is She That Looketh Forth? (v.10)
The Bride: I Went Down into the Garden (vv.11-13)
m: A question about where the beloved has gone, beauty called terrible as an army with banners, one singled out from sixty queens, and a return to the garden and the nut trees

x: The Bridegroom praises the Bride's beauty from her feet to her head, comparing her to a palm tree and her form to clusters of grapes, in the most elaborate description in the book (vv. 1-9). The Bride responds that she belongs to her Beloved and his desire is for her (v. 10). She invites him to go with her to the countryside and vineyards, to see whether the vines have budded, promising to give him her love there (vv. 11-12). The chapter closes with her describing the fragrant mandrakes and the choice fruits, both new and old, that she has kept in store for him (v. 13).
h: How Beautiful Are Thy Feet with Shoes (vv.1-5)
This Thy Stature Is Like a Palm Tree (vv.6-9)
I Am My Beloved's, and His Desire Is Toward Me (vv.10-11)
Let Us Get Up Early to the Vineyards (vv.12-13)
m: Praise running from feet upward, the reverse of chapter 4, a stature likened to a palm tree, mutual belonging stated plainly, and an invitation out to the vineyards and villages

x: The Bride wishes her Beloved were like a brother so she could show affection openly without shame, and she again charges against stirring up love prematurely (vv. 1-4). Recalling where she awakened him, she declares love as strong as death and jealousy as fierce as the grave, insisting that no flood can quench love and no wealth could ever buy it (vv. 5-7). Her brothers recall protecting her purity in her youth, and she affirms that she has kept herself for him and found peace in his eyes (vv. 8-10). Solomon's own vineyard is contrasted with the Bride's, which she offers freely (vv. 11-12). The Song closes with her companions listening for her voice and her final invitation for her Beloved to come quickly, like a gazelle on the mountains of spices (vv. 13-14).
h: O That Thou Wert as My Brother (vv.1-4)
Who Is This That Cometh Up? (v.5)
m: A wish for affection that need not hide, love declared strong as death and jealousy cruel as the grave, a price that cannot be paid, a younger sister to be guarded, and a closing call to make haste

x: Isaiah's opening vision summons heaven and earth to witness Judah's rebellion — a nation that no longer recognizes its own Master, sick from head to foot despite constant religious activity (vv. 2-6). Jerusalem sits besieged and stripped, spared only because the LORD left a small remnant (vv. 7-9). God declares their sacrifices, festivals, and prayers worthless while their hands are covered in blood and injustice, and calls them instead to wash themselves by defending the fatherless and the widow (vv. 11-17). He invites them to reason together: sins like scarlet can become white as snow if they are willing and obedient, but refusal brings the sword (vv. 18-20). The chapter closes mourning how the once-faithful city has turned corrupt, promising God will purge away the dross and restore righteous judges, while unrepentant idolaters wither like a garden without water (vv. 21-31).
h: From the Sole of the Foot to the Head (vv.5-9)
I Delight Not in the Blood of Bullocks (vv.10-15)
I Will Purely Purge Away Thy Dross (vv.24-31)
m: God's lawsuit against His people, the futility of empty religion, the offer of grace amid judgment, the purification of Zion

x: Isaiah looks ahead to the last days, when the mountain of the LORD's house will stand highest of all and the nations will stream to it to learn God's ways and turn their weapons into farm tools (vv. 2-4). He then contrasts that future glory with Judah's present idolatry — the land is full of foreign customs, silver, horses, and handmade idols, and its people bow down to their own works (vv. 6-9). Isaiah calls them to hide from the terror of the LORD when he rises to shatter every proud and lofty thing — towers, ships, cedars, and human pride alike (vv. 10-17). Idols will be thrown to the moles and bats as people flee into caves, for that day belongs to the LORD alone; humanity's own breath gives it no basis to boast (vv. 18-22).
h: The Mountain of the LORD's House (vv.1-4)
Let Us Walk in the Light (v.5)
Full of the Customs of the East (vv.6-9)
m: The future exaltation of Zion, nations drawn to God's word, swords beaten into plowshares, the terrifying Day of the LORD against all pride and idolatry

x: God announces he is stripping Jerusalem and Judah of every stabilizing support — food, water, warriors, judges, elders, and skilled leaders — leaving the nation to be ruled by children and the incompetent (vv. 1-5). Society collapses into such disorder that no one wants the burden of leadership (vv. 6-9), though Isaiah pauses to affirm that it will go well for the righteous and badly for the wicked (vv. 10-11). He indicts the leaders for crushing the poor and grinding down the needy (vv. 12-15), then turns to the proud women of Zion, who parade in vanity and jewelry; God will replace their finery with baldness, sackcloth, and shame as the men fall in battle and the city itself sits desolate on the ground (vv. 16-26).
h: They Declare Their Sin as Sodom (vv.8-9)
Ye Grind the Faces of the Poor (vv.12-15)
m: God removes competent leaders as judgment, social collapse when the righteous are taken away, the sin of oppressing the poor, the pride of wealthy women exposed and judged

x: The devastation of chapter 3 continues into the opening verse, where so many men have died that seven women beg to attach themselves to one man just to escape the stigma of being unmarried (v. 1). But the tone shifts sharply: in that day the Branch of the LORD will be beautiful and glorious, and the survivors left in Zion will be called holy (vv. 2-3). Once the LORD washes away Jerusalem's filth and bloodshed by a spirit of judgment and burning, he will cover Mount Zion with a cloud and smoke by day and a flaming fire by night, echoing the exodus, providing shelter from heat, storm, and rain (vv. 4-6).
h: He That Is Left Shall Be Called Holy (v.3)
The Spirit of Judgment and of Burning (v.4)
A Cloud by Day, a Fire by Night (vv.5-6)
m: The remnant who survive judgment, the Branch of the LORD, purification through a "spirit of burning," the return of God's glory-cloud over Zion, new exodus imagery

x: Isaiah sings a love song about a vineyard that his friend planted on fertile ground, cleared of stones, and fitted with a tower and winepress, expecting good grapes but getting only wild ones (vv. 1-2). He explains the vineyard is the house of Israel, and after listing everything done for it, announces that God will remove its protection and let it be trampled, overgrown, and rained on no more, because he looked for justice and found only oppression and bloodshed (vv. 3-7). Six woes follow: against those who grab up land and leave others homeless (v. 8), those who chase strong drink from morning to night (vv. 11-12), those who mock God to hurry his judgment (vv. 18-19), those who call evil good and good evil (v. 20), those who are wise in their own eyes (v. 21), and those who take bribes to acquit the guilty (vv. 22-23). The chapter ends with God's anger still unsatisfied, summoning a…
h: Woe to Those Who Join House to House (vv.8-10)
Woe to Those Who Rise Early for Drink (vv.11-17)
Woe to Those Who Draw Iniquity with a Cord (vv.18-19)
Woe to Those Who Call Evil Good (v.20)
Woe to the Wise in Their Own Eyes (v.21)
Woe to Those Who Justify the Wicked for Reward (vv.22-23)
m: God's investment in Israel unrewarded, the Song of the Vineyard, six woes against specific sins, God whistling for distant nations as instruments of judgment

x: In the year King Uzziah dies, Isaiah sees the Lord seated on a high throne, his robe filling the temple, while seraphim call to one another that the whole earth is full of his glory, and the doorposts shake with smoke (vv. 1-4). Overwhelmed by his own sinfulness in the presence of such holiness, Isaiah cries out that he is ruined, but a seraph touches his lips with a coal from the altar and declares his guilt taken away (vv. 5-7). When the LORD asks who will go, Isaiah volunteers, and is sent to a people who will hear but not understand, whose hearts God will let grow calloused as judgment (vv. 8-10). Isaiah asks how long, and is told until the land is left utterly desolate — yet even then, a tenth will remain, a holy seed, like a stump that still holds life (vv. 11-13).
h: In the Year That King Uzziah Died (vv.1-4)
Woe Is Me, for I Am Undone (vv.5-7)
How Long, and the Holy Seed (vv.11-13)
m: The holiness of God, human sinfulness exposed by divine glory, cleansing through substitutionary atonement (the coal from the altar), prophetic commissioning, judicial hardening

x: When Syria and Israel join forces against Jerusalem during the Syro-Ephraimite crisis, God sends Isaiah to meet King Ahaz and tell him not to fear these two "smoldering stumps," for their plan will not succeed (vv. 1-9). God offers Ahaz any sign he wants, but Ahaz refuses, hiding behind false piety (vv. 10-12). Isaiah rebukes him and gives a sign anyway: a young woman will conceive and bear a son named Immanuel, meaning "God with us," and before the boy is old enough to know right from wrong, both threatening kings will be gone (vv. 13-16). Isaiah then warns that God will bring days of trouble on Judah itself through the king of Assyria, turning the land to briers and thorns (vv. 17-25).
m: Faith tested by political crisis, the offer of a sign refused, the virgin birth prophecy, Immanuel ("God with us"), Assyria as God's razor shaving Judah bare

x: God tells Isaiah to name his newborn son Maher-shalal-hash-baz, meaning "quick to the plunder, swift to the spoil," as a sign that Assyria will soon strip Damascus and Samaria of their wealth (vv. 1-4). Because the people rejected the gently flowing waters of Shiloah and instead trusted in Syria and Israel, God will bring the mighty flood of the Assyrian river against them, sweeping through Judah until it reaches up to the neck (vv. 5-8). Isaiah warns against joining any human conspiracy for safety and calls the people instead to fear the LORD alone, who will be either a sanctuary or a stone people stumble over (vv. 9-15). He resolves to bind up his teaching among his disciples and wait for the LORD, even while God hides his face from Israel (vv. 16-18). The chapter ends warning that those who consult mediums instead of God's law will wander in hunger, curse their king, and be driven…
h: The Waters of Shiloah, and the Waters of the River (vv.5-8)
Take Counsel Together, and It Shall Come to Nought (vv.9-10)
To the Law and to the Testimony (vv.19-22)
m: The named child as prophetic sign, Assyria as God's flood overflowing Judah, the Immanuel connection ("thy land, O Immanuel"), the stumbling stone, rejecting spiritists for God's word, darkness for those who refuse the light

x: Light breaks over Galilee after deep darkness, promising joy like the joy of harvest as God shatters the oppressor's yoke the way he once defeated Midian (vv. 1-4). A child is born who will carry the government on his shoulders, called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace, ruling forever on David's throne with justice and righteousness (vv. 6-7). Yet the second half of the chapter turns back to present judgment: because of Israel's pride and refusal to turn back to God, he will cut off leaders and people alike in a single day, and even civil war will break out between Manasseh and Ephraim (vv. 8-21). Four times the chapter repeats that despite all this, God's anger has not been satisfied and his hand remains stretched out still (vv. 12, 17, 21).
h: The Joy of Harvest, and the Burning of Boots (vv.3-5)
Unto Us a Child Is Born (vv.6-7)
The Bricks Are Fallen, We Will Build with Hewn Stones (vv.8-12)
m: Light after darkness, the messianic child with divine titles, the endless increase of His government, God's repeated judgment against Israel's pride ("for all this his anger is not turned away, his hand is stretched out still")

x: Isaiah opens with a woe against those who write unjust laws to rob the poor, the fatherless, and widows, warning they will have no one to help them on the day of reckoning (vv. 1-4). He then names Assyria as the rod of God's anger, sent to punish a godless nation, though Assyria itself intends only conquest and boasts that it has conquered kingdoms by its own strength and wisdom (vv. 5-14). Isaiah rebukes that arrogance with an image of an axe boasting against the one who swings it, and warns that God will send leanness on Assyria's strength and burn its glory like fire (vv. 15-19). In that day a remnant of Israel will stop leaning on the nation that struck them and lean on the LORD instead, and though Israel is as numerous as sand, only a remnant will return (vv. 20-23). The chapter closes describing Assyria's invading army advancing city by city toward Jerusalem, until God fells it…
h: Woe unto Them That Decree Unrighteous Decrees (vv.1-4)
Assyria, the Rod of Mine Anger (vv.5-11)
Shall the Axe Boast Against Him That Heweth (vv.12-19)
Be Not Afraid of the Assyrian (vv.24-27)
The Assyrian March, Town by Town (vv.28-34)
m: Woe to unjust legislators, Assyria as God's unwitting instrument, Assyria's arrogance judged, the tool doesn't boast against the hand, the remnant returns, the Assyrian advance halted

x: A shoot will grow from the stump of Jesse, resting under the Spirit of the LORD — a spirit of wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, and the fear of the LORD — enabling him to judge rightly rather than by outward appearance, defending the poor and the meek (vv. 1-5). Under his reign, natural enemies live together in peace: the wolf with the lamb, the leopard with the goat, and a little child leads them, because the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea (vv. 6-9). This root of Jesse will stand as a rallying banner for the nations, and God will reach out a second time to gather his scattered people from Assyria, Egypt, and the far corners of the earth (vv. 10-12). Old rivalries between Ephraim and Judah will end, their enemies will be subdued, and God will dry a path through the sea for the remnant's return, echoing the exodus from Egypt (vv. 13-16).
h: A Rod Out of the Stem of Jesse (v.1)
The Spirit of the LORD Shall Rest upon Him (v.2)
He Shall Not Judge After the Sight of His Eyes (vv.3-5)
The Wolf Also Shall Dwell with the Lamb (vv.6-9)
A Second Time, and a Highway (vv.11-16)
m: The Branch from Jesse's root, the sevenfold Spirit, righteous judgment, the peaceable kingdom (wolf and lamb), the second exodus gathering, reunification of Israel and Judah

x: This short psalm closes the "Book of Immanuel" (chapters 7-12) with a song of thanksgiving for the salvation just promised. The redeemed declare that though God was once angry, his anger has turned away and he has become their comfort, their strength, and their song (vv. 1-2). They will draw water joyfully from the wells of salvation, call on his name, and make his deeds known among the nations (vv. 3-4). The chapter ends with a call for Zion's people to sing and shout, for the Holy One of Israel is great in their midst (vv. 5-6).
h: O LORD, I Will Praise Thee (vv.1-3)
Declare His Doings Among the People (vv.4-6)
m: Thanksgiving after deliverance, God's anger turned away, God as salvation and strength, drawing water from wells of salvation, declaring God's deeds among the nations

x: This oracle against Babylon opens the long series of judgments on the nations (chapters 13-23). God summons a mustered army from a distant land to carry out his anger, and the Day of the LORD approaches with cruelty, terror, and cosmic upheaval — the sun, moon, and stars going dark (vv. 1-10). God will punish the whole world for its evil, humble the arrogant, and make human life rarer than fine gold (vv. 11-12). The heavens will shake and the earth will be shaken from its place as invaders — identified as the Medes — show no mercy, even to children (vv. 13-18). Proud Babylon, the jewel of kingdoms, will be overthrown like Sodom and Gomorrah, left forever uninhabited and haunted by wild creatures (vv. 19-22).
m: God summons warriors for judgment, the Day of the LORD as cosmic devastation, Babylon's pride destroyed, Babylon as perpetually desolate, the Medes as God's agents

x: Israel's coming restoration opens the chapter: God will again choose Jacob, settle His people in their own land, and give them rest from bondage, with other nations even joining and serving them (vv. 1-2). Verses 3-23 form a taunt song against the fallen king of Babylon, mocking his descent from proud self-exaltation — boasting he would rise above the stars and rival the Most High — down to humiliation in Sheol, stripped of splendor and denied burial. A brief oracle against Assyria follows, declaring God's purpose to break its yoke (vv. 24-27), and the chapter closes with a warning to Philistia not to celebrate a fallen enemy, since a greater threat is still coming (vv. 28-32).
h: The LORD Will Have Mercy on Jacob (vv.1-2)
The Taunt-Song Against the King of Babylon (vv.3-11)
How Art Thou Fallen from Heaven (vv.12-15)
m: Israel's future restoration, the king of Babylon's fall, the "Lucifer" passage (pride aspiring to God's throne and cast down to Sheol), God's purpose against Assyria, Philistia warned

x: This oracle pronounces judgment on Moab, opening with the sudden nighttime destruction of its cities Ar and Kir (v. 1). Moab's people go up to their high places to weep, shave their heads in mourning, and cry out in the streets and on rooftops as the news spreads from town to town — Heshbon, Elealeh, Jahaz, Medeba (vv. 2-4). Isaiah himself is moved with grief for Moab, describing refugees fleeing south toward Zoar and Horonaim with their wealth loaded on donkeys while the waters of Nimrim dry up and the land lies desolate (vv. 5-7). The wailing echoes across Moab's entire border, and the chapter ends warning that even greater disaster awaits those who survive (vv. 8-9).
m: Sudden overnight destruction, national lamentation, refugees fleeing, the prophet's compassion for the judged nation, water and vegetation dried up

x: Moab's fugitives are urged to send tribute to Judah's ruler and seek asylum in Zion, with Isaiah pleading that Judah shelter the outcasts and hide the wanderers (vv. 1-4). He then looks ahead to a future throne established in steadfast love, occupied by a ruler from David's line who judges with justice and seeks righteousness (v. 5). But Moab's proud arrogance blocks any real repentance, so the prophet mourns instead over the ruined vineyards of Heshbon and Sibmah and the silenced joy of the harvest (vv. 6-11). The chapter closes with a specific timetable: within three years Moab's glory will be brought to contempt, leaving only a small, feeble remnant (vv. 12-14).
h: Send the Lamb, and Hide the Outcasts (vv.1-5)
m: Refugees seeking asylum, the messianic throne of justice, Moab's pride as the barrier to mercy, the prophet's grief for Moab, a three-year countdown to judgment

x: Isaiah pronounces a joint burden on Damascus, capital of Syria, and on Ephraim (the northern kingdom), which had allied together against Judah — Damascus will cease to be a city and Ephraim's strength will vanish with it, leaving only a remnant like the last few olives shaken from a tree (vv. 1-6). In that day, the text says, people will finally look to their Maker instead of the altars and idol poles they built with their own hands, since Israel has forgotten the God of its salvation despite tending false gods that yield only a harvest of sorrow (vv. 7-11). The chapter closes with a vision of raging nations rushing in like a roaring sea, only to be rebuked and driven off by morning — the fitting portion of those who plunder God's people (vv. 12-14).
h: The Remnant Turns to Their Maker (vv.7-8)
m: The Syro-Ephraimite alliance punished, the fall of Damascus, Ephraim's parallel judgment, a remnant turning back to God, the futility of idol-worship, the roar of hostile nations

x: Isaiah addresses a distant, powerful nation beyond the rivers of Cush, whose swift messengers travel by papyrus boats to warn a people feared far and wide (vv. 1-2). All the peoples of the earth are told to watch for a signal raised on the mountains and listen for a trumpet blast (v. 3). The Lord explains that he will quietly watch from his dwelling, undisturbed as shimmering heat or dew in harvest season, while events unfold on his own timing (v. 4). Just before harvest, he will cut off the flourishing branches like a vinedresser pruning ripening shoots, leaving them for birds and animals (vv. 5-6). In the end, this same feared and powerful nation will bring an offering to the Lord of Hosts at Mount Zion (v. 7).
h: The Land Beyond the Rivers of Cush (vv.1-2)
m: God's sovereignty over distant nations, the image of God as a quiet observer who acts at the right moment, pruning before harvest, nations bringing tribute to Zion

x: The Lord comes swiftly against Egypt, causing its idols to tremble and its people to lose heart (v. 1). He turns Egyptians against each other in civil strife, confuses their plans, and drives them to consult idols and mediums instead of him (vv. 2-3), then hands them over to a harsh ruler (v. 4). The Nile dries up, ruining fishermen and linen workers alike (vv. 5-10), while the once-wise counselors of Zoan and Pharaoh are exposed as fools who have led Egypt astray like a drunk stumbling in his own vomit (vv. 11-15). Egypt trembles before the Lord's raised hand and fears even the mention of Judah (vv. 16-17). Remarkably, the chapter then turns to hope: Egyptian cities will worship the Lord, an altar will stand within Egypt, and when they cry out he will send a deliverer, make himself known to them, strike and heal them, and receive their worship (vv. 18-22). It closes with a highway…
h: Five Cities Speak the Language of Canaan (vv.16-18)
An Altar to the LORD in Egypt (vv.19-22)
The Highway, and Egypt My People (vv.23-25)
m: God's sovereignty over the world's greatest civilization, civil war and confusion, the failure of human wisdom and false religion, judgment leading to conversion, the stunning future unity of Egypt-Assyria-Israel

x: Isaiah is told to strip off his sackcloth and sandals and go bare and barefoot for three years, becoming a walking object lesson for Judah (vv. 1-3). The sign points to what is coming: Assyria's king will lead the Egyptians and Cushites into exile stripped and barefoot in the same humiliating way (vv. 4-5). Watching this, the people of the coastland realize the nations they were counting on for protection cannot even protect themselves, leaving them to ask how they will now escape (vv. 5-6). The episode drives home Isaiah's larger point across these chapters: political alliances are no substitute for trusting God.
m: Embodied prophecy, the humiliation of Egypt and Cush, the folly of trusting in human alliances, Assyria as God's instrument, a dated prophecy (year of Assyrian conquest of Ashdod)

x: This chapter gathers three short, urgent oracles. First, Isaiah sees a vision of Babylon's sudden fall under siege from Elam and Media, and the news leaves him physically shaken with dread even as he relays the command to keep watch (vv. 1-5). A watchman set on a tower waits through the night and finally reports that Babylon has fallen and her idols lie shattered on the ground (vv. 6-9). Two brief oracles follow: a cryptic exchange with Edom, called Dumah, about how much longer the night of trouble will last, and a warning that within a year Arabia's glory and its warriors will be swept away (vv. 11-17).
m: The fall of Babylon to Medo-Persia, the watchman motif, the emotional toll on the prophet, Edom's uncertain future, Arabia's fleeting glory

x: Isaiah addresses Jerusalem itself, calling it the Valley of Vision, and rebukes the city for throwing a rooftop party and getting drunk on false confidence instead of weeping and repenting as disaster approaches (vv. 1-5). He weeps bitterly over the coming destruction and warns that self-reliant preparations, like checking the armory or building reservoirs, mean nothing without turning to God (vv. 8-13). The oracle then turns personal: Shebna, a royal steward who has built himself an impressive tomb, will be thrown out of office and hauled off into exile (vv. 15-19). In his place God will raise up Eliakim, a faithful servant given the key of David's house, a position of trust later understood as a picture of Christ's authority (vv. 20-25).
h: Ye Looked to the Armour, Not to the Maker (vv.8b-11)
m: Jerusalem's inappropriate revelry in the face of judgment, the failure of human military preparations, the sin of "eat and drink for tomorrow we die," the removal of a corrupt official, Eliakim as a type of Christ, the key of David

x: Isaiah pronounces judgment on Tyre, the great trading power of Phoenicia, calling on the ships of Tarshish to wail because the harbor and its wealth are being wiped out (vv. 1-5). The proud city that once crowned its merchants like princes will be humbled, its markets scattered, its glory brought down as Egypt's had been before it (vv. 8-14). The chapter then adds an unusual twist: after seventy years of obscurity, Tyre will return to business much like a forgotten prostitute plying her trade again, but eventually its profits will be dedicated to the LORD instead of hoarded for itself (vv. 15-18).
h: Behold the Land of the Chaldeans (vv.13-14)
Seventy Years, and the Hire Made Holy (vv.15-18)
m: The fall of commercial pride, wealth as a false god, the 70-year desolation, Tyre as a "harlot" (commerce without God), the ultimate dedication of trade profits to God's purposes

x: Isaiah widens his lens from single nations to the whole earth, announcing a coming judgment that will empty the land and scatter its people regardless of status, because humanity has defiled the earth and broken its everlasting covenant with God (vv. 1-6). Joy disappears from the land as the wine, the music, and the city gates all fall silent, while a scattered remnant lifts up songs of praise to the LORD from the ends of the earth (vv. 7-16). Isaiah himself confesses his own dread and weakness in the face of what is coming, describing traps and terror closing in from every side (v. 16). The chapter builds to a cosmic climax: God will punish the powers of heaven and the kings of earth together, shutting them up as prisoners, before the moon is confounded and the sun ashamed, because the LORD of hosts reigns in glory on Mount Zion before his elders (vv. 21-23).
h: A Remnant Sings, and the Prophet Does Not (vv.14-16a)
My Leanness, and the Cosmic Collapse (vv.16b-20)
The LORD Shall Reign in Mount Zion (vv.21-23)
m: Universal judgment (not just one nation), the broken everlasting covenant, cosmic upheaval, the earth cursed by sin, a singing remnant amid desolation, the LORD reigns on Zion

x: Following the devastation of chapter 24, Isaiah bursts into praise, thanking God for turning a fortified enemy city into a ruin while proving to be a refuge and strength for the poor and needy caught in the storm (vv. 1-5). He then describes a lavish feast of rich food and fine wine that the LORD will prepare on his mountain for all peoples, not Israel alone (v. 6). At that feast God will remove the veil of death that covers every nation, swallow up death itself forever, and personally wipe away every tear (vv. 7-8). The chapter ends with people declaring that this is the God they waited for, alongside a warning that Moab, standing in for all proud opposition to God, will be trampled down like straw in a dunghill (vv. 9-12).
h: O LORD, Thou Art My God (vv.1-5)
This Is Our God, We Have Waited for Him (v.9)
m: Praise for God's faithfulness, the destruction of the proud city, God as shelter for the poor, the messianic banquet for all peoples, the destruction of death, tears wiped away, Moab's pride crushed

x: Isaiah presents a song to be sung in Judah once God's deliverance arrives, celebrating a strong city whose walls and defenses are salvation itself, open to any righteous, faithful nation that wants to enter (vv. 1-2). He declares that God keeps in perfect peace anyone whose mind stays fixed on him, because trusting in the LORD means trusting an everlasting rock, while he humbles the proud, lofty city and lets the oppressed and needy trample it underfoot (vv. 3-6). The path of the righteous is described as level and just, and Isaiah confesses that his soul longs for God through the night, adding that only when God's judgments reach the earth do people learn righteousness (vv. 7-10). He asks God to establish peace for them since every good thing they have accomplished ultimately comes from his hand, then acknowledges that other lords have ruled over them but only the LORD's name will be…
h: The Way of the Just Is Uprightness (vv.7-9)
The Wicked Learn Nothing from Grace (v.10)
Thou Wilt Ordain Peace for Us (vv.11-15)
We Have Not Wrought Any Deliverance (vv.16-18)
Hide Thyself Until the Indignation Be Past (vv.20-21)
m: God's strong city vs. the lofty city, perfect peace for the trusting mind, waiting on God in the night, the futility of human effort without God, the dew of resurrection, hiding during God's indignation

x: Isaiah pictures God defeating Leviathan, a monstrous sea serpent symbolizing the chaotic, hostile powers arrayed against him, punishing it with his fierce and mighty sword (v. 1). He then shifts to the image of Israel as a pleasant vineyard that God personally waters and guards night and day, promising that thorns and briers, standing for hostile enemies, will be burned up if they oppose him, but peace is available to anyone who takes refuge in him (vv. 2-5). Israel's own discipline is measured and purposeful, unlike the harsher judgment poured out on her enemies, meant to purge idolatry rather than destroy the nation outright (vv. 7-9). The chapter closes with a picture of restoration: a great trumpet sounds, and the scattered exiles of Israel, from Assyria to Egypt, are gathered home to worship God in Jerusalem (vv. 12-13).
h: A Vineyard, Kept Night and Day (vv.2-6)
m: The slaying of Leviathan, God's vineyard protected and fruitful, measured discipline vs. total destruction, the gathering of the scattered, the great trumpet

x: Isaiah opens with a warning to the drunken leaders of Ephraim, the northern kingdom, whose proud, fading crown of splendor is about to be trampled underfoot like a wilted flower (vv. 1-4). He then turns to Judah's own leaders, priests and prophets who are just as drunk and stumble over their own teaching, mocking Isaiah's message as fit only for babies (vv. 7-13). Because they have struck what amounts to a covenant with death, trusting in lies and a false shelter, God announces he is laying a tested, precious cornerstone in Zion, promising that whoever trusts in it will not be shaken (vv. 14-16). Their false refuge will be swept away by hail and flood, but Isaiah closes with a farming parable: a wise farmer does not plow forever or thresh forever, and God's dealings with his people follow the same purposeful, measured wisdom (vv. 23-29).
h: The Refuge of Lies Swept Away (vv.17-22)
m: Drunkenness (literal and spiritual), the rejected word of God, the "covenant with death," the precious cornerstone in Zion, God's strange work, the farmer parable

x: The Lord pronounces judgment on Ariel, Jerusalem, the city of David, even while its feasts and sacrifices continue as usual (v. 1). He will bring distress and siege against it until its voice sounds like a ghost whispering from the dust (vv. 2-4). Yet the horde besieging the city will vanish suddenly, like a dream that disappears the moment its dreamer wakes (vv. 5-8). The people are spiritually numb, as if drunk without wine, their prophets and seers blinded so that God's revelation becomes like a sealed book no one can read (vv. 9-12). The Lord condemns their empty worship — lips honoring him while hearts stay far away, reverence merely learned by rote (v. 13) — and promises a work of judgment that will confound human wisdom and expose those who question his authority as though he were ignorant clay questioning its potter (vv. 14-16). A reversal follows: forests become farmland, the…
h: This People Draw Near with Their Mouth (vv.13-14)
Woe to Those Who Hide Their Counsel (vv.15-16)
m: Ariel (Jerusalem as God's altar-hearth), siege and deliverance, spiritual blindness, lip-service religion, the sealed book, the failure of human wisdom, the coming transformation

x: Isaiah confronts Judah's leaders for making an alliance with Egypt without consulting God, calling them rebellious children who compound their sin by seeking shelter and shade from Pharaoh instead of from the LORD (vv. 1-3). He warns that Egypt's help will prove worthless and shameful, gaining Judah nothing but disgrace (vv. 5-7). The people don't even want to hear the truth — they tell the prophets to stop confronting them and speak comforting illusions instead (vv. 9-11). Yet God still waits to be gracious, promising that once they turn back to him he will give them a Teacher they can follow with their own ears, guiding them onto the right path (vv. 18-21). The chapter ends with a vivid picture of the LORD striking down Assyria with the sound of his voice, like a consuming fire prepared long ago (vv. 27-33).
h: Thine Ears Shall Hear a Voice Behind Thee (vv.19-22)
m: The folly of trusting Egypt, rejection of the prophetic word, God's patience ("He waits to be gracious"), the coming Teacher, the destruction of idols, God's fury against Assyria, the Topheth prepared for the Assyrian king

x: Isaiah pronounces judgment on those who run to Egypt for military help, trusting horses and chariots instead of seeking the Lord (v. 1). God, who is also wise, will bring the disaster he has promised against both the evildoers and their allies (v. 2), reminding them that the Egyptians are merely human and their horses flesh, not spirit — so when he acts, helper and helped will stumble together (v. 3). Like a lion guarding its prey, undeterred by a crowd of shepherds, the Lord will come down to fight for Mount Zion, and like a bird hovering over its nest he will defend and rescue Jerusalem (vv. 4-5). Isaiah calls the deeply rebellious people to return to God and cast away the idols they made (vv. 6-7). Assyria will then fall as if by an unseen sword, its young men fleeing and its officers panicking at Zion's banner, because the Lord's fire burns in Zion and his furnace in Jerusalem (vv.…
h: Woe to Them That Go Down to Egypt (vv.1-3)
As a Lion, and as Birds Flying (vv.4-5)
m: The folly of trusting Egypt's military, horses vs. the Holy Spirit, God as a lion defending His prey, God as protective birds over Jerusalem, the call to turn from idols, Assyria's supernatural defeat

x: Isaiah looks ahead to a king who will reign in righteousness, with leaders who rule justly, each one like shelter from wind and storm, like water in a dry land (vv. 1-2). Under this reign, clear sight and hearing replace spiritual blindness, the rash gain understanding, and moral categories are no longer confused — fools are no longer called noble and stingy people are no longer called generous (vv. 3-8). Isaiah then warns complacent, carefree women that their comfort is about to end: within about a year, harvest will fail and mourning will follow, so they should strip off their fine clothes and put on sackcloth (vv. 9-12). Thorns will overtake the land, the city's joyful houses will empty, and its towers will stand abandoned until wild donkeys and grazing flocks take them over (vv. 13-14). This desolation lasts only until the Spirit is poured out from on high, turning the wilderness…
h: A King Shall Reign in Righteousness (vv.1-2)
The Vile Person Shall No More Be Called Liberal (vv.3-8)
m: The righteous king, spiritual sight restored, the exposure of fools and knaves, complacent women warned, the Spirit poured from on high, justice dwelling in the wilderness, peace as the fruit of righteousness

x: Isaiah pronounces judgment on a treacherous destroyer, understood as Assyria, warning that the one who betrays others without being betrayed will itself be betrayed once its destruction is complete (v. 1). He prays for God's grace and strength each morning in this time of trouble (v. 2), describing how nations scatter and plunder is seized the instant the Lord rises in power (vv. 3-4). The Lord is exalted, filling Zion with justice and becoming his people's stability, wisdom, and treasure (vv. 5-6), even as the land mourns around them — roads abandoned, agreements broken, Lebanon, Sharon, and Carmel withering (vv. 7-9). God announces he will now act, and his enemies' plans will burn like stubble, consumed by their own hostility (vv. 10-12). Both near and far are called to witness his power, and the sinners in Zion tremble, asking who can survive his consuming presence (vv. 13-14). The…
h: O LORD, Be Gracious unto Us (vv.2-6)
Who Shall Dwell with Everlasting Burnings (vv.14-16)
m: The destroyer destroyed, prayer for God to rise up, sinners trembling in Zion, the character of those who survive, seeing the King in His beauty, the land of broad rivers, God as judge-lawgiver-king-savior

x: Isaiah summons all nations and peoples to hear a sweeping oracle of judgment (vv. 1-2), as the LORD's anger falls on their armies and the heavens themselves are rolled up like a scroll while the stars fall (vv. 3-4). The LORD's sword, sated with blood, descends particularly on Edom, whose land becomes a great slaughter and sacrifice at Bozrah (vv. 5-7), for this is the day of vengeance owed to Zion's cause (v. 8). Edom's streams turn to pitch and its soil to burning sulfur, its ruin lasting generation after generation with no one passing through (vv. 9-10). Wild and desert creatures — the porcupine, owl, jackal, and hawk — take permanent possession of the abandoned land, each finding its place exactly as decreed (vv. 11-17).
m: Universal judgment on all nations, cosmic upheaval (stars falling, heavens rolled up), God's sword of vengeance, Edom as representative of all enemies, total desolation, the Book of the LORD

x: Isaiah pictures the wilderness and desert bursting into bloom and rejoicing as they behold the glory of the LORD (vv. 1-2). The weak are told to take courage because God himself is coming to save them (vv. 3-4), and when he comes the blind will see, the deaf hear, the lame leap, and the mute sing, while waters break out across the desert (vv. 5-7). A clear highway called the Way of Holiness will run through this transformed land, safe from predators and impassable to the unclean, reserved for the redeemed (vv. 8-9). Those the LORD has ransomed will travel it home to Zion with everlasting joy, as sorrow and sighing disappear (v. 10).
h: The Eyes of the Blind Shall Be Opened (vv.5-6a)
m: Creation restored, physical healing, the Holy Way, the ransomed returning to Zion, everlasting joy, no predator on the road, the desert blooming
