x: The narrative shifts to history: in Hezekiah's fourteenth year, Assyria's king Sennacherib captures Judah's fortified cities and sends his field commander with a large army to Jerusalem (vv. 1-2). Hezekiah's officials meet him at the city wall, and the commander delivers a taunting speech questioning where Hezekiah's confidence lies, mocking reliance on Egypt as a broken reed and dismissing trust in the LORD as no different from trust in any other god the Assyrians have already conquered (vv. 3-10, 18-20). Asked to speak in Aramaic so the people on the wall won't understand, he instead raises his voice in Hebrew, deliberately trying to frighten the population into surrendering rather than facing a siege (vv. 11-17). The people stay silent as Hezekiah had commanded, and his officials return to him with torn clothes, grieved by the blasphemy they've heard (vv. 21-22).
h: Is It Not the LORD Whose High Places He Has Taken Away (vv.7-10)
He Cried with a Loud Voice in the Jews' Language (vv.13-20)
m: Faith tested by overwhelming military threat, psychological warfare against faith, the enemy's strategy of undermining trust in God, Hezekiah's initial response of silence

x: When King Hezekiah hears the Assyrian threats, he tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth, and goes into the temple, sending word to Isaiah through officials dressed the same way (vv. 1-4). Isaiah answers that Hezekiah should not fear the blasphemy he has heard, for the Lord will put a rumor in the Assyrian king's ear that sends him back to his own land, where he will die by the sword (vv. 5-7). Sennacherib, hearing that Tirhakah of Cush is coming against him, sends Hezekiah a letter repeating his taunts and questioning whether God can save Jerusalem any better than the gods of nations Assyria has already destroyed (vv. 8-13). Hezekiah takes the letter into the temple, spreads it before the Lord, and prays, acknowledging God alone as Creator and asking him to save Jerusalem so all the earth will know he is the Lord (vv. 14-20). Isaiah sends back a lengthy answer: God has decreed that…
h: Be Not Afraid of the Words (vv.5-7)
The Sign of What Grows by Itself (vv.30-32)
He Shall Not Come into This City (vv.33-35)
m: Prayer as warfare, God defending His own reputation, the mockery of the living God answered, the angel of the LORD's devastating intervention, the sign of natural recovery

x: Hezekiah becomes deathly ill, and Isaiah tells him to put his house in order because he will not recover (v. 1). Hezekiah turns his face to the wall, prays, and weeps bitterly, reminding God of his faithful walk (vv. 2-3). Before Isaiah has even left the palace, the LORD sends him back with a message: he has heard Hezekiah's prayer and seen his tears, and will add fifteen years to his life and deliver the city from Assyria (vv. 4-6). As a sign that the promise is trustworthy, the shadow on Ahaz's stairway goes backward ten steps (vv. 7-8). The chapter closes with Hezekiah's own psalm of thanksgiving, reflecting on the nearness of death, his anguish, and his gratitude that God in love has kept him from the pit of destruction (vv. 9-20), followed by a brief note on the fig poultice used to treat his boil and his earlier question about the sign (vv. 21-22).
m: Mortality and the prayer for life, God's willingness to respond to prayer, the sign of the reversed shadow, Hezekiah's psalm of gratitude, the bitterness of near-death and the sweetness of recovery

x: Envoys from Babylon's king Merodach-baladan arrive with letters and a gift for Hezekiah after hearing of his illness and recovery, and Hezekiah welcomes them gladly (v. 1). Flattered by the attention, he shows them everything in his treasury — silver, gold, spices, oil, weapons — holding nothing back (v. 2). Isaiah then asks Hezekiah what the visitors saw and where they came from, and Hezekiah answers plainly that he showed them all his treasures (vv. 3-4). Isaiah responds with a sobering prophecy: everything in the palace will one day be carried off to Babylon, and some of Hezekiah's own descendants will be taken as eunuchs in the Babylonian court (vv. 5-7). Hezekiah accepts the word as good, relieved that peace and security will last through his own lifetime (v. 8). The chapter closes out Isaiah's first major section, turning the book's focus from the Assyrian threat toward the coming…
m: The pride of displaying wealth, Babylon's first contact with Judah, the prophetic preview of exile, Hezekiah's troubling response, the hinge between Isaiah 1-39 and 40-66

x: Isaiah opens the book's second major section with a call to comfort God's people, announcing that Jerusalem's hard service is over and her sin has been paid for (vv. 1-2). A voice cries out to prepare a highway for the LORD in the wilderness, leveling every valley and mountain so that his glory will be revealed to all people (vv. 3-5). All human strength and beauty are as fleeting as grass that withers, but God's word stands forever (vv. 6-8). Zion is told to lift up her voice and announce God's coming with power, tending his flock like a shepherd who gathers the lambs in his arms (vv. 9-11). The LORD's greatness is set against the smallness of the nations and the futility of idols carved by human hands, since he measures the oceans in his palm and calls each star by name (vv. 12-26). Israel's complaint that God has overlooked her way is answered with the assurance that the everlasting…
h: O Zion, That Bringest Good Tidings (vv.9-11)
To Whom Then Will Ye Liken God (vv.18-20)
Why Sayest Thou, My Way Is Hid (vv.27-28)
They Shall Mount Up with Wings (vv.29-31)
m: Comfort after judgment, the voice in the wilderness (John the Baptist), the transience of humanity vs. the permanence of God's word, the incomparable greatness of God, mounting up with eagle's wings

x: The LORD summons the coastlands and nations to court, asking who stirred up one from the east — Cyrus — giving him victory over nations before him (vv. 1-4). Watching the nations panic and turn to idol-making for help, God reassures Israel not to fear, since he has chosen and will strengthen, help, and uphold them with his righteous right hand (vv. 5-10). Those who oppose Israel will be put to shame and come to nothing, while the LORD will make weak Israel into a threshing instrument able to crush mountains (vv. 11-16). He promises to answer the poor and needy, opening rivers on bare heights and streams in the desert (vv. 17-20). The LORD then challenges the idols to predict the future or explain the past, declaring that they and their makers are nothing, while he alone stirs up the one who will call on his name (vv. 21-29).
h: They Helped Every One His Neighbour (vv.5-7)
Fear Thou Not, for I Am with Thee (vv.10-13)
I Will Open Rivers in High Places (vv.17-20)
m: God's sovereignty over history (raising up Cyrus), the courtroom challenge to idols, Israel as God's chosen servant, "Fear not — I am with you," God as redeemer and helper, the futility of idol-manufacture

x: God introduces his chosen servant, upheld and Spirit-filled, who will bring justice to the nations gently, without breaking a bruised reed or extinguishing a smoldering wick (vv. 1-4). The LORD who created the heavens and earth declares he has called this servant in righteousness, given as a covenant to the people and a light to the nations, to open blind eyes and free prisoners from darkness (vv. 5-9). A new song of praise rises from the coastlands and the desert as the LORD marches out like a warrior to defeat his enemies (vv. 10-17). Yet Israel herself is described as a servant who is blind and deaf despite having seen much, plundered and looted because she would not walk in the LORD's ways and did not take his law to heart (vv. 18-25).
h: A Covenant of the People, a Light of the Gentiles (vv.5-9)
Sing unto the LORD a New Song (vv.10-17)
Who Is Blind but My Servant (vv.18-25)
m: The Servant's character (gentle, just, persistent), the Servant as a light to the Gentiles, the new song, God as warrior, Israel's blindness despite being God's servant

x: The LORD reassures Israel not to fear, since he created and redeemed them and calls them by name, promising to be with them through waters and fire and to gather his sons and daughters from every direction because they are precious in his sight (vv. 1-7). He calls Israel as his witness that he alone is God, with no other savior before or after him, able to declare things beforehand as no idol can (vv. 8-13). He announces a coming deliverance from Babylon and a new exodus even greater than the first, making a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert (vv. 14-21). Despite Israel's failure to call on him and her burdening him with sins, the LORD declares that he himself blots out her transgressions for his own sake, and invites her to state her case so he might be proved right (vv. 22-28).
h: When Thou Passest Through the Waters (vv.1-7)
Remember Ye Not the Former Things (vv.14-21)
Thou Hast Not Brought Me the Small Cattle (vv.22-24)
I, Even I, Am He That Blotteth Out (vv.25-28)
m: Redemption by name, passing through water and fire, God as Israel's only Savior, the new exodus, witnesses to God's uniqueness, sins blotted out for God's own sake

x: The LORD promises to pour out his Spirit and blessing on Israel's offspring like water on thirsty ground, so that they will flourish and proudly claim to belong to him (vv. 1-5). He again declares himself the first and the last, the only true God, asking who else could have declared things to come as he has (vv. 6-8). Isaiah then mocks idol-makers at length: a craftsman uses half a piece of wood to warm himself and cook his food, then carves the other half into a god to worship, oblivious to the absurdity of bowing before what he made with his own hands (vv. 9-20). Israel is called back to remember these things, since the LORD has blotted out her sins like a cloud and redeemed her (vv. 21-23). The chapter closes with the LORD, who alone stretched out the heavens and formed the earth, naming Cyrus by name as the one who will command Jerusalem to be rebuilt and the temple's foundations to…
h: I Will Pour My Spirit upon Thy Seed (vv.1-5)
I Am the First and I Am the Last (vv.6-8)
He Warmeth Himself, and Saith, Aha (vv.9-20)
m: The Spirit poured on descendants, God as first and last (Alpha and Omega), the absurdity of idol-making, Israel redeemed and not forgotten, Cyrus named as God's shepherd

x: The LORD addresses Cyrus as his anointed, whose hand he holds to subdue nations before him and open doors that cannot be shut, though Cyrus does not yet know the LORD (vv. 1-5). This is so that people from east to west will know there is no other God, since the LORD alone forms light and darkness, makes well-being and calamity (vv. 6-7). He rebukes anyone who would quarrel with their Maker, since the potter shapes the clay and the creature has no right to question the one who formed it (vv. 8-13). The LORD calls himself a God who hides himself yet is the only Savior, inviting the survivors of the nations to turn to him and be saved, since idols bring only shame (vv. 14-22). He swears that every knee will bow to him and every tongue will acknowledge him, and that all of Israel's offspring will be justified and will glory in the LORD (vv. 23-25).
h: Let the Skies Pour Down Righteousness (v.8)
Woe unto Him That Striveth with His Maker (vv.9-13)
They Shall Come After Thee in Chains (vv.14-17)
I Have Not Spoken in Secret (vv.18-19)
m: Cyrus as God's "anointed," God's absolute sovereignty over good and evil, the potter and clay, every knee bowing, the hidden God who saves, Israel's everlasting salvation

x: Isaiah pictures Babylon's gods Bel and Nebo bowed down, loaded onto weary beasts of burden and carried off into captivity, unable even to save themselves (vv. 1-2). In contrast, the LORD reminds Israel that he has carried them from birth and will keep carrying them even to old age, since he alone is God and there is no one like him (vv. 3-5). He contrasts himself with idols that people pay goldsmiths to make and must be carried because they cannot move or answer when called (vv. 6-7). The LORD calls Israel to remember this and take it to heart, declaring the end from the beginning and calling a man from the east — Cyrus — to accomplish his purpose (vv. 8-11). He closes by telling the stubborn-hearted that his righteousness and salvation are near and will not delay (vv. 12-13).
h: I Have Made, and I Will Bear (vv.3-4)
To Whom Will Ye Liken Me (vv.5-7)
Declaring the End from the Beginning (vv.8-11)
m: Fallen gods vs. the carrying God, idols carried vs. God who carries, declaring the end from the beginning, God's purpose stands, the ravenous bird from the east (Cyrus)

x: Isaiah delivers a taunt-song against Babylon, pictured as a pampered virgin daughter told to come down from her throne and sit in the dust, grinding grain like a common slave and exposed to shame (vv. 1-3). The LORD explains that though he used Babylon as an instrument to punish his people, Babylon showed them no mercy and grew proud, boasting that she would never be a widow or lose her children (vv. 4-9). Trusting in her wickedness and her reliance on sorcery and astrology, she believed no one could see her or hold her accountable, but disaster will come upon her suddenly, in a single day, which none of her spells or star-gazers will be able to avert (vv. 9-15).
h: Come Down and Sit in the Dust (vv.1-4)
Thou Didst Shew Them No Mercy (vv.5-7)
I Am, and None Else Beside Me (vv.8-9)
m: Babylon's pride and fall, from throne to millstone, cruelty without mercy, the failure of sorcery and astrology, sudden destruction, no one to save

x: God confronts stubborn, hard-hearted Israel, reminding them that he announced events long before they happened precisely so they couldn't credit their idols with the outcome (vv. 3-5). Now he says he is declaring new things, previously hidden, because he has refined Israel in the furnace of affliction rather than simply cutting them off, holding back his anger for the sake of his own name and reputation (vv. 9-11). He points to the ally he has raised up to carry out his purpose against Babylon, widely understood as Cyrus, and urges the people to pay close attention (vv. 14-16). The chapter closes with a joyful call to leave Babylon and announce far and wide that the LORD has redeemed his people, paired with a sober reminder that the wicked will find no peace (vv. 20-22).
h: Which Swear by the Name of the LORD, but Not in Truth (vv.1-5)
For My Name's Sake Will I Defer (vv.9-11)
I Am the First, and I Am the Last (vv.12-16)
m: Israel's stubbornness despite prophecy, new things declared, refined in affliction, God's name/reputation as motive, the call to leave Babylon, no peace for the wicked

x: The Servant speaks in the first person, describing how God called him before birth, named him while still in the womb, and shaped him like a sharpened arrow kept ready in a quiver (vv. 1-2). Though he confesses feeling like his labor has been for nothing, God tells him his mission is bigger than restoring Israel alone — he is appointed to be a light to the nations, carrying God's salvation to the ends of the earth (vv. 4-6). God promises that kings and princes will one day bow before him, and that captives and prisoners will be freed and led out through green pastures (vv. 7-11). When Zion complains that the LORD has forgotten and abandoned her, God answers that he could no more forget her than a mother could forget her nursing child, since he has her permanently engraved on the palms of his hands (vv. 14-16).
h: Zion Hath Said, The LORD Hath Forsaken Me (v.14)
Can a Woman Forget Her Sucking Child (vv.15-16)
m: The Servant's calling from the womb, apparent failure redeemed by larger mission, light to the Gentiles, Zion not forgotten, engraved on God's palms, children returning

x: The chapter opens with God reminding Israel that their exile is the result of their own sin, not any failure or weakness on his part to save (vv. 1-2). The Servant then speaks, describing how God has given him a well-taught tongue to sustain the weary with a timely word, and how he wakens him morning by morning to listen like a disciple (vv. 4-5). Rather than resisting mistreatment, he offers his back to those who strike him and his face to those who pull out his beard and spit on him, refusing to hide his face from shame because he trusts God to vindicate him (vv. 5-7). The chapter closes with an appeal: those who fear the LORD and walk in darkness should trust in God's name, while those who try to light their own way by their own fire will end up lying down in torment (vv. 10-11).
h: Where Is the Bill of Divorce (vv.1-3)
The Lord GOD Hath Opened Mine Ear (vv.4-9)
m: God didn't divorce Israel, the Servant's obedient ear, suffering willingly endured, face set like flint, trust in God amid opposition, the danger of self-made light

x: Isaiah calls three times for those pursuing righteousness to listen, pointing them back to Abraham and Sarah as proof that God can take one person and multiply them into a great people (vv. 1-2). He promises that the LORD will comfort Zion's ruins and turn her wilderness into a garden, because his righteousness and salvation are near and will last forever, even after the heavens and earth wear out (vv. 3-8). The people cry out for God's arm to awaken and act as it did when it dried up the sea for the exodus generation to cross (vv. 9-11). God responds with sympathy but also authority, reminding them that he is their comforter and that a mere human oppressor is nothing to fear (vv. 12-16). Finally he calls Jerusalem itself to wake up and rise, promising to remove the cup of his wrath from her hand and place it instead into the hands of her tormentors (vv. 17-23).
h: Fear Ye Not the Reproach of Men (vv.7-8)
Awake, O Arm of the LORD (vv.9-11)
I, Even I, Am He That Comforteth You (vv.12-16)
The Cup Taken Out of Thy Hand (vv.17-23)
m: Look to your origins (Abraham/Sarah), God's comfort for Zion, everlasting salvation, "Awake, awake" (calling God and Zion to action), the cup of wrath transferred from Israel to her enemies, Rahab/the sea-dragon defeated

x: Zion is called to wake up, put on strength and beautiful garments, and shake off the dust and chains of captivity, because the unclean will no longer enter her gates (vv. 1-2). Isaiah describes messengers running across the mountains with good news of peace and salvation, declaring that God reigns, and pictures the watchmen of Jerusalem breaking into song together as they see the LORD returning to Zion with their own eyes (vv. 7-8). God calls his people to leave captivity behind, carrying the vessels of the LORD but without haste, since he goes ahead of them and behind them (vv. 11-12). The chapter ends by introducing the Servant, announcing that he will act wisely and be highly exalted, though many will be appalled at him first because his appearance will be marred beyond recognition (vv. 13-15).
h: Behold, My Servant Shall Deal Prudently (vv.13-15)
m: Zion's awakening, liberation from captivity, beautiful feet bringing good news, God reigns, departure from Babylon, the Servant exalted yet marred beyond recognition

x: Isaiah opens by asking who would believe this report and to whom the Lord's power has been revealed (v. 1). He describes a servant who grows up in obscurity, like a small plant pushing through dry ground, someone with no outward qualities that would draw attention or admiration (v. 2). People turn away from him, treating him as unimportant and undesirable, someone who carries ongoing sorrow and a familiarity with hardship that others prefer not to look at (v. 3). Yet what looks like divine punishment for his own guilt is actually him absorbing sickness and suffering that belonged to others (v. 4); his wounds and the punishment he bears become the means by which wandering, wayward people are restored, since everyone had gone their own direction like scattered sheep and God placed the weight of that collective wrongdoing on him (vv. 5-6). Mistreated and afflicted, he offers no protest…
h: He Was Wounded for Our Transgressions (vv.4-6)
As a Sheep Before Her Shearers (vv.7-9)
m: Substitutionary atonement, the Servant despised yet exalted, bearing others' sins, silent before slaughter, death with transgressors yet burial with the rich, justifying many, interceding for transgressors

x: Following the Servant's suffering in chapter 53, Isaiah pictures a barren woman bursting into song because she will have more children than a woman who was never childless, telling her to enlarge her tent because her descendants will spread out and possess whole nations (vv. 1-3). God addresses Zion as a wife briefly forsaken in anger but now gathered back with everlasting love and compassion (vv. 6-8). He compares his commitment to the promise he made to Noah never to flood the earth again, vowing that his steadfast love and covenant of peace will never be removed, even if mountains and hills give way (vv. 9-10). The chapter closes with a picture of a city rebuilt with precious stones and children taught directly by the LORD, along with the well-known assurance that no weapon formed against her will succeed (vv. 11-17).
h: All Thy Children Taught of the LORD (v.13)
m: The barren woman multiplied, enlarging the tent, God as husband, brief anger vs. everlasting kindness, the covenant of peace (like Noah's rainbow), children taught by the LORD, no weapon shall prosper

x: Isaiah issues an open invitation to everyone who is thirsty to come freely to the water, wine, and milk God offers, urging them to stop spending their resources on what doesn't satisfy and instead listen so their souls can truly live (vv. 1-3). He calls the people to seek the LORD while he can be found and to turn from their sinful ways, promising abundant forgiveness (vv. 6-7). God reminds them that his thoughts and ways are far higher than theirs, and that just as rain waters the earth and makes it fruitful, his word will not return to him empty but will accomplish exactly what he sends it to do (vv. 8-11). The chapter closes with a picture of creation itself celebrating Israel's release, with mountains and hills bursting into song and thorn bushes replaced by flourishing trees, becoming a lasting sign of God's covenant (vv. 12-13).
h: Seek Ye the LORD While He May Be Found (vv.6-7)
My Thoughts Are Not Your Thoughts (vv.8-9)
Ye Shall Go Out with Joy (vv.12-13)
m: Free salvation for the thirsty, the everlasting Davidic covenant, God's word always accomplishes its purpose, God's thoughts higher than ours, the joy of exodus/creation

x: God announces that his salvation is coming soon and calls his people to keep justice and righteousness in response, promising blessing to anyone, including foreigners and eunuchs, who holds fast to his covenant and keeps the Sabbath, regardless of what excluded them before (vv. 1-5). His house, he says, will be called a house of prayer for all peoples, not for Israel alone, and he will gather still more besides the outcasts already gathered (vv. 6-8). The tone then shifts sharply: Isaiah pictures Israel's watchmen as blind, silent, and lazy, more interested in sleep and their own appetites than warning the people, while the nation's leaders are compared to greedy shepherds who look only after their own profit (vv. 9-12).
m: Radical inclusion (foreigners, eunuchs), the Sabbath as covenant sign, a house of prayer for all people, the failure of Israel's watchmen/shepherds, leaders as blind dogs

x: Isaiah observes that the righteous and devout are dying without anyone taking it to heart, even though their death actually spares them from the evil still to come (vv. 1-2). He then turns sharply to expose Israel's spiritual unfaithfulness, describing idol worship carried out under every green tree and on every high hill, using the language of adultery to capture how far the people have strayed from God (vv. 3-10). Despite this, God says he has been patient and silent, though his patience has limits (vv. 11-13). The chapter's tone then turns tender: God dwells with the humble and contrite, promising to revive their spirit, heal those who have wandered, and create genuine peace for those far off and near, closing with the same warning found elsewhere that the wicked will find no such peace (vv. 15-21).
h: Of Whom Hast Thou Been Afraid (vv.11-13)
Peace to the Far and to the Near (vv.17-19)
m: The righteous dying unnoticed, spiritual adultery, God as the lofty One who dwells with the lowly, revival for the contrite, peace for far and near, no peace for the wicked

x: Israel complains that they have fasted faithfully and God hasn't noticed, but God answers that their fasting really serves their own interests while being paired with exploiting workers and stirring up conflict (vv. 1-4). He describes the fasting he actually wants: freeing the oppressed, sharing food with the hungry, providing shelter for the homeless, and clothing the naked, rather than putting on a show of humility (vv. 6-7). If they do this, he promises their light will break forth like the dawn, their healing will come quickly, and God will answer when they call (vv. 8-9). The chapter closes by connecting this same kind of practical, others-focused obedience to honoring the Sabbath, promising that those who do so will be called repairers of broken walls and restorers of streets to live in (vv. 12-14).
h: Then Shall Thy Light Break Forth (vv.8-12)
If Thou Turn Away Thy Foot (vv.13-14)
m: False fasting (self-serving religion), true fasting (justice and mercy), the conditions for answered prayer, light breaking forth, Sabbath delight, repairing the breach

x: Isaiah opens by insisting that the exile is not due to God's inability to save but to the people's own sin, which has separated them from him (vv. 1-2). A sweeping catalog exposes their violence, lies, and injustice (vv. 3-8), prompting communal confession (vv. 9-15). Seeing no one willing to intervene, God himself takes up the cause, arming himself with righteousness as a breastplate and salvation as a helmet (vv. 16-17) before coming as Redeemer to Zion for those who turn from sin (v. 20). The chapter closes with God's covenant promise that his Spirit and his words will never depart from his people or their descendants (v. 21).
h: Their Webs Shall Not Become Garments (vv.3-8)
He Put On Righteousness as a Breastplate (vv.16b-19)
The Redeemer Shall Come to Zion (v.20)
m: Sin as separation from God, the catalog of human wickedness, no human intercessor found, God arms Himself as warrior, the Redeemer comes to Zion, the Spirit-and-Word covenant

x: Isaiah calls Zion to rise and shine, for the Lord's glory has dawned on her even as darkness covers the rest of the earth (vv. 1-3). Nations and kings stream toward her light, and her scattered children return from afar bringing the wealth of the nations as tribute (vv. 4-9). Foreigners rebuild her walls and serve her, for though she was once forsaken she will now be called an eternal excellence, her gates open day and night to receive the nations in peace (vv. 10-18). The Lord himself replaces the sun and moon as Zion's everlasting light, ending her days of mourning, and her smallest family multiplies into a mighty nation (vv. 19-22).
h: Strangers Shall Build Up Thy Walls (vv.10-14)
A Little One Shall Become a Thousand (vv.21-22)
m: Light in darkness, nations streaming to Zion, wealth of nations brought, God as eternal light, no more violence, gates always open, the least becoming great

x: Isaiah speaks as the Spirit-anointed Servant, sent to bring good news to the poor, bind up the brokenhearted, proclaim liberty to captives, and announce the Lord's favor — the year of Jubilee (vv. 1-2), a passage Jesus later read aloud in the Nazareth synagogue and declared fulfilled in himself (Luke 4:16-21). Those who mourn receive beauty instead of ashes and praise instead of despair, and they rebuild the ruins of generations past (vv. 3-4). God's people become priests and ministers named among the nations, sustained by others' wealth (vv. 5-6), and God promises them an everlasting covenant because he loves justice and hates wrongdoing (vv. 7-9). The chapter closes with the speaker rejoicing like a bridegroom, clothed in salvation and righteousness, as God causes righteousness and praise to spring up before all nations (vv. 10-11).
h: The Spirit of the Lord GOD Is upon Me (vv.1-3)
They Shall Build the Old Wastes (vv.4-5)
Ye Shall Be Named the Priests of the LORD (vv.6-7)
m: The Spirit-anointed Messiah, good news to the poor, liberty to captives, the Year of Jubilee, beauty for ashes, the garment of praise, rebuilding ruins, priests of God, everlasting covenant, salvation and righteousness as garments

x: Isaiah (or the Lord himself) vows not to stay silent until Jerusalem's righteousness shines like a blazing torch and the nations see her vindication (vv. 1-3). Zion receives new names — no longer "Forsaken" and "Desolate" but "Hephzibah" (My Delight Is in Her) and "Beulah" (Married) — as God rejoices over her the way a bridegroom rejoices over a bride (vv. 4-5). Watchmen are posted on the walls and told to give the Lord no rest until he establishes Jerusalem as a praise in the earth (vv. 6-7). God swears an oath that her grain and wine will never again be plundered by enemies (vv. 8-9), and the chapter closes with a call to prepare the highway and lift a banner, announcing that the Redeemer is coming for his people (vv. 10-12).
h: For Zion's Sake I Will Not Hold My Peace (vv.1-3)
Ye That Make Mention of the LORD, Keep Not Silence (vv.6-7)
Prepare the Way of the People (vv.10-12)
m: Relentless intercession, Zion's new name, God's delight in His people, the marriage metaphor, watchmen who never rest, giving God no rest until He acts, the highway prepared

x: Isaiah pictures a lone figure striding from Edom with garments stained crimson, identified as the Lord, who has trodden the winepress of judgment alone because no one else would help (vv. 1-6). The tone then shifts to grateful remembrance of God's past kindnesses and the deliverance he gave Israel out of love and pity (vv. 7-9), followed by the sobering admission that Israel rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit, turning him into their enemy (vv. 10-14). The chapter ends with an anguished prayer pleading for God to look down from heaven, asking where his zeal and compassion have gone and appealing to him as Father and Redeemer to return for his servants' sake (vv. 15-19).
h: They Rebelled and Vexed His Holy Spirit (vv.10-14)
m: God as lone warrior, the winepress of judgment, garments dipped in blood, remembering God's past mercies, the Holy Spirit grieved, "thou art our Father," prayer for God's return

x: The prayer begun in 63:15 continues with a passionate plea for God to tear open the heavens and come down in power as he has in the past (vv. 1-3), for no eye has ever seen a God like him who acts on behalf of those who wait for him (v. 4). The prayer turns to confession: the people are all unclean, their righteous deeds like filthy rags, and they wither like leaves carried off by their sin (vv. 5-7). Yet they appeal to God as Father and themselves as clay in the hands of their Potter (v. 8), pleading with him not to remember their iniquity forever or stay angry, but to look on the ruined cities that bear his name (vv. 9-12).
h: Oh That Thou Wouldest Rend the Heavens (vv.1-3)
All Our Righteousnesses Are as Filthy Rags (vv.5-7)
m: Prayer for God to rend the heavens, the incomparable God who acts for those who wait, universal uncleanness, filthy rags righteousness, fading like autumn leaves, God as Father and Potter, appeal for mercy

x: Isaiah records God's answer to the prayer of chapters 63-64: he was found by a nation that was not even seeking him, a foretaste of Gentile inclusion later cited in Romans 10:20, even while Israel provoked him with idolatry and rebellion (vv. 1-7). Still, God promises to preserve a faithful remnant, like good wine found in a cluster of grapes not to be destroyed along with the rest (vv. 8-12), and he draws a sharp contrast between his obedient servants, who will eat, drink, and rejoice, and the rebels, who will hunger, thirst, and be put to shame (vv. 13-16). The chapter climaxes with the promise of new heavens and a new earth, where weeping and crying are no more, people enjoy long life and the work of their hands, and even the wolf and the lamb feed together in peace (vv. 17-25).
h: I Am Found of Them That Sought Me Not (v.1)
I Have Spread Out My Hands All the Day (vv.2-7)
As the New Wine in the Cluster (vv.8-12)
Ye Shall Leave Your Name for a Curse (vv.13-16)
New Heavens and a New Earth (vv.17-25)
m: Gentiles finding God, Israel's rebellion, the faithful remnant preserved, judgment on the unfaithful, new heavens and new earth, joy replacing sorrow, long life, peace in nature

x: The Lord declares that heaven is his throne and earth his footstool, so no physical temple could ever contain him; what he values instead is a humble and broken spirit that trembles at his word (vv. 1-2). He rejects hollow, hypocritical worship — even sacrifices offered by people clinging to their own sinful choices are treated as no better than violence or idolatry — and warns that he will bring on them the very fears they dread, because they refused to listen when he called (vv. 3-4). He speaks comfort to those who tremble at his word and have been mocked by their own people, promising vindication while their opponents are put to shame, and warns of coming judgment on his enemies (vv. 5-6). Using the image of childbirth, God says Zion will bring forth a nation suddenly and without prolonged labor, since he who opens the womb will not fail to bring the birth to completion (vv. 7-9).…
h: He That Killeth an Ox, as If He Slew a Man (vv.3-4)
Before She Travailed, She Brought Forth (vv.7-9)
As One Whom His Mother Comforteth (vv.10-14)
The LORD Will Come with Fire (vv.15-17)
I Will Send Them unto the Nations (vv.18-21)
From One New Moon to Another (vv.22-24)
m: Heaven as throne / earth as footstool, God looks to the humble, Zion's miraculous birth, God's final coming in fire, all nations gathered, all flesh worships, the everlasting contrast between the redeemed and the lost

x: Before Jeremiah was formed in the womb, God set him apart and appointed him a prophet to the nations (vv. 4-5). Jeremiah objects that he is only a youth, but God tells him not to be afraid and touches his mouth, putting His words there and giving him authority to uproot and tear down, and to build and plant (vv. 6-10). Two confirming visions follow: an almond branch, signifying that God is watching over His word to perform it (vv. 11-12), and a boiling pot tilting away from the north, picturing the disaster about to come from that direction (vv. 13-16). God warns Jeremiah that Judah's kings, officials, priests, and people will fight against him, but promises to make him strong as a fortified wall so they cannot overcome him (vv. 17-19).
h: The Priest's Son from Anathoth, and Forty Years of Kings (vv.1-3)
A Defenced City, an Iron Pillar (vv.17-19)
m: Predestined calling, God's sovereignty over nations, prophetic authority from God (not self), the cost of prophetic ministry, the watching God, judgment from the north

x: This is God's opening indictment of Israel through Jeremiah, framed as a marriage gone wrong. God recalls Israel's early devotion to Him in the wilderness, like a bride's first love (vv. 2-3), then charges the nation with an inexplicable betrayal: they abandoned Him, the spring of living water, and dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water (vv. 11-13). The chapter catalogs Israel's spiritual unfaithfulness, chasing after foreign gods and alliances with Egypt and Assyria, comparing it to a wild donkey in heat and a prostitute who has forgotten shame (vv. 20-25, 33-36). Despite the evidence, Israel insists it is innocent (v. 35), and God warns that its own wickedness will correct it (v. 19).
h: What Iniquity Have Your Fathers Found in Me (vv.4-8)
Two Evils, and the Broken Cisterns (vv.9-13)
Egypt and Assyria, and Wickedness That Corrects Itself (vv.14-19)
The Noble Vine, and the Wild Ass (vv.20-25)
Trees, Stones, and the Number of Thy Cities (vv.26-37)
m: Israel's early love forsaken, God as a fountain abandoned, broken cisterns that fail, spiritual adultery with idols, "Where is the LORD?" no longer asked, even the priests don't seek God

x: God continues the marriage metaphor, now comparing Israel and Judah to two unfaithful sisters. Israel, the northern kingdom, was sent away for her adultery with idols, yet Judah, her sister, witnessed this and was not afraid, playing the harlot too (vv. 6-10), making treacherous Judah worse than faithless Israel because she had the warning and ignored it (v. 11). Even so, God pleads for Israel's return, promising mercy rather than anger if she will only acknowledge her guilt (vv. 12-14, 22). The chapter closes with a vision of future restoration, where God gives shepherds after His own heart and Judah and Israel are reunited (vv. 14-18), followed by a corporate confession of sin and shame (vv. 21-25).
h: Shepherds, and the Ark Not Missed (vv.15-18)
Why Do You Not Call Me Father (vv.19-25)
m: Spiritual adultery as divorce-worthy, Judah worse than Israel (they had the warning), God's plea for return, the future reunification of Israel and Judah, the ark no longer needed, Jerusalem as God's throne

x: God calls Judah to genuine, inward repentance, not mere ritual, saying they must circumcise their hearts (vv. 1-4). Then the alarm sounds: a trumpet, a disaster from the north, an invading force coming to make the land desolate (vv. 5-9). Jeremiah receives a terrifying vision of undoing, the earth waste and void, mountains quaking, birds fled, cities in ruins, echoing the language of creation in reverse (vv. 23-26). Overwhelmed, the prophet cries out in anguish over what he sees coming, and Jerusalem itself is pictured as a woman dressed for disaster, doomed by lovers who will in fact seek her life (vv. 19-21, 29-31).
h: Blow the Trumpet, the Lion Is Come Up (vv.5-9)
Thou Hast Greatly Deceived This People (v.10)
A Dry Wind, Not to Fan (vv.11-18)
m: Heart circumcision (not external), the approaching army from the north, creation reversed (de-creation), the prophet's personal anguish, Judah's foolishness, daughter Zion in labor

x: God tells Jeremiah to search Jerusalem's streets for even one person who deals honestly and seeks the truth, promising to pardon the city if such a person can be found (v. 1), but none exists, among rich or poor (vv. 4-5). The people swear falsely, refuse correction, and deny that God will ever act in judgment (vv. 2, 3, 12). Jeremiah describes a people with eyes but no sight, a rebellious and stubborn heart that has turned away, and asks rhetorically whether God will not punish such a nation (vv. 21, 23, 29). A foreign nation from far away is coming to devour their harvest and their children (vv. 15-17), because the prophets prophesy falsely, the priests rule by their own authority, and the people love it that way (vv. 30-31).
h: A Nation Whose Language You Do Not Know (vv.15-19)
A Wonderful Thing in the Land (vv.26-31)
m: Not one honest person in Jerusalem, refusal to repent despite discipline, false prophets saying "no judgment," a nation that has completely revolted, willful spiritual blindness

x: Jerusalem is called to flee as an enemy from the north advances, described as cruel and merciless, arrayed for battle against the daughter of Zion (vv. 1, 22-23). God's word is poured out like fire that cannot be contained on a people who refuse to listen (vv. 10-11). The prophet urges the nation to stand at the crossroads and ask for the ancient, good way, but they refuse to walk in it, and reject the watchmen God sent to warn them (vv. 16-17). Because their worship is hollow, God rejects their sacrifices and sets a stumbling block before them, so that both parents and children, neighbors and friends, will perish together (vv. 20-21).
h: Flee, and the Mount Cast Against the City (vv.1-8)
Glean Thoroughly, and Ears That Cannot Hear (vv.9-12)
Peace, Peace, When There Is No Peace (vv.13-15)
A People from the North Country (vv.22-26)
m: Flee Jerusalem, the approaching siege, God's word as fire, the old paths rejected, empty sacrifices, the refiner who finds only dross, the enemy from the north described

x: In the well-known Temple Sermon, Jeremiah stands at the gate of the temple and warns the people not to trust in deceptive words claiming the temple itself guarantees their safety (vv. 1-4). The presence of the temple will not protect a people who steal, murder, commit adultery, and burn incense to Baal, then come and stand before God as though rescued, going right back to those same practices (vv. 9-10). God points back to Shiloh, where His dwelling place was destroyed because of Israel's wickedness, warning that Jerusalem's temple will meet the same fate (vv. 12-14). He also condemns the worship of the "queen of heaven" carried out by whole families (vv. 17-18), and tells Jeremiah to stop interceding for this people, because their judgment is already decided (v. 16).
h: Topheth, and the Valley of Slaughter (vv.29-34)
m: False trust in the temple, the "temple of the LORD" as a magical incantation, God demands justice not ritual, Shiloh as precedent, God refuses to hear prayer for them, the Queen of Heaven, Topheth/child sacrifice

x: God declares that even the bones of the dead, kings, officials, priests, prophets, and people, will be dug up and exposed to the sun, moon, and stars they had worshipped instead of being properly buried (vv. 1-2). Judah refuses to turn back despite every warning, clinging to deceit rather than repentance (vv. 4-6), and even the migratory birds know their appointed seasons, yet God's people do not recognize His timing of judgment (v. 7). Scribes have falsified the law with their pen, so-called wise men have rejected God's word, and prophets and priests alike heal the wound of the people superficially, declaring peace when there is none (vv. 8-11). Jeremiah, overcome with grief, laments that the harvest season has ended without deliverance and asks whether there is no remedy, no healer, for his people's suffering (vv. 20-22).
h: Bones Brought Out of the Graves (vv.1-3)
The Lying Pen of the Scribes (vv.8-9)
No Grapes, and Serpents That Will Not Be Charmed (vv.13-17)
Is There No Balm in Gilead (vv.18-22)
m: The dishonored dead, unnatural stubbornness (animals are smarter), the lying scribes, the deceptive peace-cry repeated, missed harvest (too late for salvation), the balm of Gilead, the weeping prophet

x: Jeremiah wishes his head were a spring and his eyes a fountain so he could weep continually for his people, who are about to be destroyed for their corruption (vv. 1-2). He describes a society where neighbors deceive one another, no one speaks truthfully, and everyone's tongue is like a deadly weapon (vv. 3-8). God announces coming devastation severe enough that professional mourners must be summoned to teach the daughters wailing, because death has entered every home (vv. 17-21). The chapter closes with a call not to boast in wisdom, strength, or wealth, but instead to boast only in truly knowing and understanding God, who delights in steadfast love, justice, and righteousness (vv. 23-24).
h: A Fountain of Tears, and a Lodge in the Wilderness (vv.1-2)
Let Not the Wise Man Glory (vv.23-24)
m: The weeping prophet, pervasive deception, tongues as deadly weapons, coming desolation, the call for mourning women, true vs. false glory, circumcision of flesh vs. heart

x: This chapter is a sharp satire against idol worship: craftsmen cut a tree, carve it, and decorate it with silver and gold, then nail it down so it cannot topple over, yet the resulting idol cannot speak, walk, or do anything, good or bad, on its own (vv. 3-5). This lifeless craftsmanship is set against the living God, who made the heavens and the earth by His wisdom and power, and before whom the nations tremble (vv. 10-13). Jeremiah responds with a prayer, admitting that human beings cannot direct their own steps and asking God to correct His people gently rather than in fierce anger (vv. 23-24), while calling down judgment on the nations that have devoured Jacob (v. 25).
h: Learn Not the Way of the Heathen (vv.1-2)
The Idol That Has to Be Fastened Down (vv.3-5)
Silver from Tarshish, Gold from Uphaz (vv.8-9)
The Living God, and the One Verse in Aramaic (vv.10-16)
m: The absurdity of idol-worship, the incomparable living God, "there is none like thee," idols as scarecrows, God as Creator vs. manufactured gods, Jeremiah's prayer for correction in measure

x: God reminds Judah of the covenant made when He brought their ancestors out of Egypt, a covenant that required obedience and promised blessing, but that this generation, like their fathers, has broken (vv. 1-8). A widespread conspiracy of rebellion runs through Judah and Jerusalem, and the people have returned to the sins of their ancestors, following other gods (vv. 9-10). Because of this, God again tells Jeremiah not to intercede for the people, since He will not listen to their cries when disaster comes (vv. 11, 14). The chapter ends with Jeremiah discovering that the men of his own hometown, Anathoth, are conspiring to kill him and silence his preaching, comparing him to a tree they intend to destroy along with its fruit (vv. 18-21).
h: A Conspiracy Among the Men of Judah (vv.9-13)
m: The broken covenant, "cursed be the man that obeyeth not," don't pray for them (repeated), the conspiracy against Jeremiah from his own town, the cost of faithful ministry

x: Jeremiah brings a bold complaint to God, asking why the wicked prosper and traitors thrive in comfort while he himself suffers for righteousness (vv. 1-2). God's reply challenges him further: if he is worn out competing with men on foot, how will he compete with horses; if he stumbles in safe country, what will he do in the dangerous thickets along the Jordan (v. 5)? God then declares that He has abandoned His own house and given His beloved people into the hand of their enemies because of their wickedness (vv. 7-8), while also promising that the surrounding nations who plundered Israel's inheritance will themselves be uprooted, though any who genuinely learn to follow God will be restored among His people (vv. 14-17).
h: Why Does the Way of the Wicked Prosper (vv.1-4)
If Thou Hast Run with the Footmen (vv.5-6)
Even the Neighbors May Be Restored (vv.14-17)
m: The theodicy question (why do wicked prosper?), God's challenge to Jeremiah (prepare for worse), God's grief over His own judgment, the desolation of the pleasant land, future hope for surrounding nations

x: God instructs Jeremiah to buy a linen loincloth, wear it, and later bury it by a river, where it rots into something useless, illustrating how Israel, once bound closely to God like that garment to His body, has become ruined through pride and refusal to listen (vv. 1-11). A related parable about wine jars follows, picturing the whole population, from the king down, being filled with drunken confusion in judgment (vv. 12-14). Jeremiah pleads with the people to give glory to God before darkness falls, warning that continued pride will bring captivity (vv. 15-19), and the chapter closes with the prophet weeping in secret because God's flock is being carried off (vv. 15-17).
h: To the King and the Queen Mother (vv.18-19)
Can the Ethiopian Change His Skin (vv.20-27)
m: The ruined girdle (Israel's ruined intimacy with God), pride as the cause of ruin, the wineskin parable (drunken judgment), the impossibility of changing ingrained sin, captivity coming

x: A severe drought strikes Judah, so severe that nobles send servants for water in vain, farmers are ashamed at the parched ground, and even wild donkeys and deer abandon their young for lack of food (vv. 1-6). Jeremiah intercedes on the nation's behalf, but God tells him not to pray for their welfare, because judgment by sword, famine, and plague is already decreed (vv. 11-12). False prophets have been promising peace and freedom from disaster in God's name, but God says He never sent or commanded them, and that these prophets will themselves be consumed by the very sword and famine they denied (vv. 13-16). Jeremiah closes in anguished prayer, confessing the nation's guilt and asking God not to break His covenant with them (vv. 19-22).
h: The Prophets Who Said Ye Shall Not See the Sword (vv.13-16)
Mine Eyes Run Down with Tears (vv.17-18)
m: Drought as divine judgment, intercessory prayer rejected, false prophets exposed, the contrast between Jeremiah's genuine intercession and false prophets' empty promises, God's sovereignty over weather

x: God tells Jeremiah that even if Moses and Samuel stood before Him pleading, He would not turn His heart toward this people, and appoints four means of destruction: the sword, dogs, birds, and wild beasts (vv. 1-3). Jeremiah offers one of his rawest personal complaints, lamenting that he was ever born, since his calling has brought him nothing but strife and reproach even though he never joined in the people's mockery (vv. 10, 17). He accuses God of being like an unreliable stream that dries up, and God responds by calling him to repent of this despair, promising that if he returns to faithful speech, God will make him like a fortified bronze wall against his opponents, who will not prevail against him (vv. 18-20).
h: Though Moses and Samuel Stood Before Me (vv.1-4)
Who Shall Go Aside to Ask How Thou Doest (vv.5-9)
If Thou Return, Then Will I Bring Thee Again (vv.19-21)
m: Even Moses/Samuel can't intercede, four forms of destruction, Jeremiah's deep personal crisis, accusation against God, God's conditional restoration of the prophet, Jeremiah as a fortified wall

x: God forbids Jeremiah to marry or have children, to attend funerals, or to join in celebrations, because his isolated life itself becomes a living sign that ordinary life in Judah is about to end, death will come so widely that the dead will go unburied and unmourned, and singing and feasting will cease from the land (vv. 1-9). When the people ask why such disaster is coming, the answer is that their ancestors and now they themselves have forsaken God and worshipped other gods, refusing to keep His law (vv. 10-13). Yet the chapter closes with a striking promise: a day will come when Israel's future rescue and regathering from all the lands of exile will eclipse in memory even the exodus from Egypt (vv. 14-15).
h: Thou Shalt Not Take Thee a Wife (vv.1-4)
Wherefore Hath the LORD Pronounced This Evil (vv.10-13)
m: Jeremiah's celibacy as prophetic sign, no marriage/ mourning/feasting in Judah's future, the question "why?" answered, judgment for forsaking God, the coming new exodus, future Gentile conversion

x: The chapter opens by describing Judah's sin as permanently etched into their hearts and altars (vv. 1-2), and contrasts those who trust in mere human strength, who are like a shrub in the desert, with those who trust in God, who are like a tree planted by water, unaffected by drought (vv. 5-8). It observes that the human heart is deceitful and hard to know, but that God searches it and rewards each person according to their conduct (vv. 9-10). Jeremiah prays for vindication against those who persecute him (vv. 14-18), then delivers a sermon at the city gates calling the people to honor the Sabbath by not carrying burdens for work, promising blessing for obedience and unquenchable fire for disobedience (vv. 19-27).
h: Graven with a Pen of Iron (vv.1-4)
The Partridge That Sitteth on Eggs (v.11)
The Hope of Israel, and the Fountain (vv.12-13)
Heal Me, and Let Them Be Confounded (vv.14-18)
The Sabbath Sermon in the Gate (vv.19-27)
m: The incurably wicked heart, cursed vs. blessed (trust in man vs. trust in God), the tree by waters, God as heart-searcher, Jeremiah's prayer for vindication, Sabbath faithfulness as covenant test

x: God sends Jeremiah down to a potter's house, where he watches the potter reshape a marred piece of clay into a different, useful vessel (vv. 1-4). This becomes an illustration of God's sovereign right over nations: if He announces judgment on a nation and it turns from evil, He will relent, and if He announces blessing on a nation and it turns to evil, He will withhold the good He intended (vv. 6-10). Judah refuses this warning, insisting they will keep following their own plans and stubborn hearts regardless (v. 12), and in response plots against Jeremiah, hoping to silence him with false charges (vv. 18-20). Jeremiah, in turn, prays that God will bring judgment on his enemies rather than heed their scheme (vv. 21-23).
h: As the Clay Is in the Potter's Hand (vv.5-10)
But They Said, There Is No Hope (vv.11-12)
Will a Man Leave the Snow of Lebanon (vv.13-17)
Come, and Let Us Devise Devices (v.18)
The Hardest Prayer in the Book (vv.19-23)
m: God as potter, nations as clay, conditional prophecy (judgment can be revoked), the people's stubborn refusal, the plot against Jeremiah, the prophet's imprecatory prayer

x: God instructs Jeremiah to buy a clay jar from a potter and take it, along with elders and priests, to the Valley of Ben-Hinnom, where he publicly smashes the jar, declaring that God will break this people and city just as the jar has been broken, beyond repair (vv. 1-2, 10-11). Because of the idolatrous and even child-sacrificing worship carried out there, the valley will be renamed the Valley of Slaughter, and it will become a burial ground because there is no other room (vv. 4-6, 11). Unlike the reworkable clay on the wheel in chapter 18, this fired and hardened vessel cannot be reshaped, only shattered, picturing a point of judgment that can no longer be averted (vv. 10-11). Jeremiah then returns and repeats the same message of coming disaster publicly in the temple court (vv. 14-15).
m: The irreparably broken vessel, Topheth and child sacrifice, the Valley of Slaughter, judgment beyond repair, the contrast with chapter 18's reformable clay

x: Pashhur, a priest and temple official, has Jeremiah beaten and placed in stocks overnight for his prophecies (vv. 1-2). Upon his release, Jeremiah renames him "Terror on Every Side," declaring that Pashhur and his household will go into captivity in Babylon and die there (vv. 3-6). The chapter then turns to Jeremiah's most anguished personal lament: he complains that God has overpowered and mocked him, that speaking God's word brings him only ridicule, yet he cannot hold it in because it burns like fire within him (vv. 7-9). In his lowest moment, he curses the day of his birth and wishes he had died in the womb rather than live to see only trouble and sorrow (vv. 14-18).
h: Pashhur Smote Jeremiah, and Put Him in the Stocks (vv.1-2)
O LORD, Thou Hast Deceived Me (vv.7-10)
But the LORD Is with Me (vv.11-13)
Cursed Be the Day Wherein I Was Born (vv.14-18)
m: Physical persecution by religious authorities, God's word as fire in the bones, the prophet's suicidal despair, cursing the day of birth, the tension between calling and despair

x: As Nebuchadnezzar's army besieges Jerusalem, King Zedekiah sends officials to ask Jeremiah to inquire of God, hoping for a miraculous deliverance like those of the past (vv. 1-2). Jeremiah's answer is devastating: rather than help Jerusalem, God Himself will fight against the city with outstretched hand and mighty arm, gathering its own weapons uselessly against the invaders (vv. 4-6). The people are given only two options: stay in the city and die by sword, famine, and plague, or surrender to the Babylonians and live (vv. 8-10). The chapter closes with a warning to the royal house to execute justice, since without it, God's fiery judgment will consume the palace itself (vv. 11-14).
h: I Myself Will Fight Against You (vv.3-7)
The Way of Life and the Way of Death (vv.8-10)
m: No miraculous deliverance this time, God fights against His own city, surrender as the path of life, resistance as the path of death, the choice before each individual

x: God directs an oracle to the royal house of David, calling the king to do justice and righteousness or watch the dynasty's house become a ruin (vv. 1-5). Three kings receive specific pronouncements: Shallum (Jehoahaz), taken captive and never to return; Jehoiakim, condemned for building his palace through unpaid labor and injustice, who will die dishonored and unmourned; and Coniah (Jehoiachin), described as a signet ring God will tear off, whose descendants will never again sit on David's throne (vv. 10-12, 13-19, 24-30). Throughout, the chapter contrasts King Josiah's righteous rule, in which he judged the cause of the poor and needy, with the injustice of his successors (vv. 15-17).
h: Do Justice, and This House Shall Not Be a Desolation (vv.1-9)
Woe to the Builder of the Paneled House (vv.13-19)
m: Justice as the condition for monarchy's survival, three kings judged, Jehoiakim's exploitation of workers, Coniah/Jehoiachin's rejection and exile, the broken Davidic line

x: God pronounces woe on the shepherds, Judah's leaders, who have scattered and destroyed His flock instead of caring for it, and promises to gather the remnant Himself and raise up faithful shepherds in their place (vv. 1-4). He then promises a righteous Branch from David's line, a king who will reign wisely and be called "The LORD Is Our Righteousness" (vv. 5-6). The rest of the chapter condemns the false prophets at length: they commit adultery, strengthen the hands of evildoers, speak visions from their own imagination rather than from God, and steal words from one another while claiming divine authority (vv. 14, 16, 25-30). God insists He is a God who is near as well as far off, seeing and judging even secret sins (vv. 23-24).
h: Woe to the Pastors That Scatter (vv.1-4)
Both Prophet and Priest Are Profane (vv.9-15)
They Speak a Vision of Their Own Heart (vv.16-22)
Dreams, and the Word Like a Hammer (vv.25-32)
m: Failed shepherds vs. the coming Shepherd-King, the Righteous Branch from David, "The LORD Our Righteousness," false prophets' comprehensive corruption, distinguishing true from false prophecy, God sees everything

x: God shows Jeremiah a vision of two baskets of figs set before the temple: one basket holds very good figs, the other very bad, rotten figs (vv. 1-3). Surprisingly, the good figs represent the exiles already taken to Babylon with King Jehoiachin, whom God will watch over for their good, bring back to the land, and give hearts to know Him (vv. 4-7). The bad figs represent King Zedekiah, his officials, and those remaining in Jerusalem or fleeing to Egypt, whom God will make an object of horror and destruction among the nations (vv. 8-10). The vision overturns the assumption that those who stayed behind were the fortunate ones.
h: Two Baskets of Figs Set Before the Temple (v.1)
One Basket Very Good, the Other Very Bad (vv.2-3)
The Good Figs Are the Exiles (vv.4-7)
The Bad Figs Are Those Who Remain (vv.8-10)
m: The exiles as God's hope (not punishment), those remaining as the doomed (not privileged), God's heart toward the first deportees, the promise of return and restoration, counterintuitive divine assessment

x: Jeremiah reviews twenty-three years of preaching that the people refused to heed, despite God's persistent sending of prophets (vv. 1-7). Because of their disobedience, God announces that Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar will conquer the land and the people will serve Babylon for seventy years, after which Babylon itself will be punished for its own guilt (vv. 8-14). Jeremiah is then shown a symbolic cup of God's wrath that he must make all the surrounding nations drink, beginning with Jerusalem and Judah and extending outward to the ends of the earth, including Babylon itself under the code name Sheshach (vv. 15-26). The chapter closes with a vivid picture of God's judgment sweeping across the whole earth like a storm, from nation to nation (vv. 30-33).
h: The Cup of the Wine of This Fury (vv.15-29)
The LORD Shall Roar from on High (vv.30-38)
m: 23 years of rejected prophecy, the 70-year Babylon exile, Babylon's own judgment after 70 years, the cup of wrath passed to all nations, universal judgment

x: This chapter narrates Jeremiah's trial after he delivers the temple sermon recorded in chapter 7. Priests, prophets, and people seize him in the temple and demand his death for prophesying that the temple and city would be destroyed like Shiloh (vv. 7-9). Jeremiah defends himself before the officials, insisting that God sent him and urging the people to repent so that God might relent of the disaster He has pronounced (vv. 12-13). The officials and elders side with Jeremiah, citing the earlier precedent of the prophet Micah, who prophesied doom against Jerusalem under King Hezekiah without being executed (vv. 16-19); but the chapter also records that another prophet, Uriah, was hunted down and killed for delivering the same message (vv. 20-23).
h: The Verdict, and the Micah Precedent (vv.16-19)
m: The cost of truth-telling, religious authorities opposing God's prophet, the trial process, the precedent of Micah, God's protection through unlikely allies, the murder of Uriah

x: God instructs Jeremiah to make a wooden yoke, wear it, and send similar yokes to the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon, with the message that God has given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, and that any nation that submits to Babylon's yoke will be allowed to remain in its land, while resistance means destruction (vv. 2-8). Jeremiah warns Judah's own king and people not to listen to prophets, diviners, and dreamers who claim they will not serve Babylon, since those prophets are lying (vv. 9-10, 12-15). Regarding the temple vessels not yet taken to Babylon, God declares that they too will be carried off and will remain there until He decides to bring them back (vv. 19-22).
h: To Zedekiah, Serve Him and Live (vv.12-15)
To the Priests, the Vessels Will Not Come Back Yet (vv.16-22)
m: Nebuchadnezzar as God's "servant," submit to Babylon or die, false prophets opposing submission, the temple vessels going to Babylon, God's sovereignty over all nations

x: The false prophet Hananiah publicly confronts Jeremiah in the temple, breaks the wooden yoke off Jeremiah's neck, and declares that within two years God will break Babylon's power, return the temple vessels, and bring King Jehoiachin and the exiles home (vv. 1-4, 10-11). Jeremiah initially responds that he hopes Hananiah's words are true, but later returns with a harsher message from God: the wooden yoke has been replaced with an iron one, symbolizing an unbreakable Babylonian dominance, and Hananiah himself will die within the year for making the people trust in a lie (vv. 13-16). The chapter closes by noting that Hananiah died two months later, exactly as Jeremiah had said (v. 17).
m: False prophecy vs. true prophecy, the test of prophetic authenticity, the wooden yoke replaced by iron, the death of a false prophet, Hananiah's two-year timeline vs. God's seventy-year timeline

x: This chapter records Jeremiah's letter sent to the Jewish exiles already living in Babylon. He instructs them to settle in for the long term, building houses, planting gardens, marrying, and seeking the welfare of the city where they have been sent, since their own welfare depends on it (vv. 4-7). God promises that after seventy years He will fulfill His good word and bring them back, adding the well-known assurance that He knows the plans He has for them, plans for their welfare and not for disaster, to give them a future and a hope (vv. 10-11). The people are told to call on God and seek Him with their whole heart, and He will be found by them and restore their fortunes (vv. 12-14). The chapter closes by condemning specific false prophets among the exiles, including Ahab, Zedekiah, and Shemaiah, who are prophesying lies and will be punished (vv. 21-23, 31-32).
h: Build Houses, Plant Gardens, Seek the Peace of the City (vv.4-7)
Let Not Your Prophets Deceive You (vv.8-9)
Seventy Years, and the Thoughts of Peace (vv.10-14)
m: Settling into exile (not resisting it), praying for Babylon's welfare, God's plans for hope and a future, the 70-year timeline, false prophets in Babylon, seeking God with your whole heart

x: This chapter opens the "Book of Consolation" (chapters 30-33), a sustained turn from judgment to hope. God commands Jeremiah to write down promises that He will restore the fortunes of both Israel and Judah and bring them back to the land given to their ancestors (vv. 1-3). A time of unprecedented distress is coming, described as "Jacob's trouble", yet the people will be saved out of it, and God will break the yoke of foreign oppression from their neck (vv. 5-8). God promises to raise up a Davidic ruler over them, to heal their wounds though other nations considered them beyond hope, and to punish those who devoured them (vv. 9-11, 16-17). The chapter closes reaffirming that in latter days the people will fully understand this covenant relationship, God as their God and they as His people (v. 22).
h: Write All the Words in a Book (vv.1-3)
Fear Thou Not, O My Servant Jacob (vv.10-11)
Thy Wound Is Incurable, and I Will Heal It (vv.12-17)
The City Builded Upon Her Own Heap (vv.18-22)
m: Restoration promised, Jacob's trouble and deliverance, the yoke broken, the Davidic king raised, God as physician, the fierce storm of judgment passing, restoration of the covenant relationship

x: This chapter contains the celebrated promise of a new covenant. God declares an everlasting love for His people and promises to rebuild and replant them (vv. 3-4). Rachel is pictured weeping for her exiled children, but told to stop, because they will return from the enemy's land (vv. 15-17). God then announces that the days are coming when He will make a new covenant with Israel and Judah, unlike the covenant made at the exodus which they broke, this time He will put His law within them and write it on their hearts, so that everyone will know Him personally, from the least to the greatest, and their sins will be remembered no more (vv. 31-34). The chapter closes affirming that God's covenant with Israel is as fixed as the created order itself, and that the rebuilt city will be holy to the LORD forever (vv. 35-40).
h: A Woman Shall Compass a Man (vv.21-22)
As Long as Sun and Moon (vv.35-37)
The Whole Valley Shall Be Holy (vv.38-40)
m: Everlasting love, the return of Israel and Judah, Rachel weeping (quoted in Matthew 2), the new covenant written on hearts, sins forgotten, individual accountability, the permanence of Israel (as permanent as sun and moon)

x: With the Babylonian siege closing in and Jeremiah imprisoned in the palace courtyard, God commands him to buy a field from his cousin Hanamel in Anathoth, an act of confidence in future restoration even as the city is about to fall (vv. 6-12). Jeremiah has the deed sealed and preserved in a clay jar, and God explains that this is a sign that houses, fields, and vineyards will again be bought and sold in the land (vv. 13-15). Jeremiah then prays, acknowledging God's great power and the certainty of coming judgment for the nation's long history of provoking Him to anger (vv. 17-35). God responds that nothing is too difficult for Him, and though He is bringing disaster now, He will also gather His people back, give them one heart and one way, and make an everlasting covenant with them (vv. 36-41).
h: Is Any Thing Too Hard for Me (vv.26-35)
m: Faith action during disaster, investing in God's future promises, Jeremiah's great prayer, "nothing too hard for God," the certainty of both judgment and restoration

x: While Jeremiah is still confined during the siege, God invites him to call out and be shown great and hidden things he does not yet know (v. 3). God promises that Jerusalem will be healed and restored, its ruins rebuilt, and its former joy and celebration returned in full (vv. 6-11). Flocks will again pasture safely in the land, and cities of Judah will again know prosperity (vv. 12-13). Central to the chapter is the promise of a righteous Branch to spring from David, executing justice, along with an assurance that the Levitical priesthood will never lack someone to serve before God, both promises anchored to the fixed, unbreakable order of day and night (vv. 14-22).
h: I Will Bring It Health and Cure (vv.4-9)
The Voice of the Bridegroom Again (vv.10-13)
m: "Call unto me and I will answer," hidden things revealed, healing and restoration, the Branch of Righteousness, the Davidic and Levitical covenants as certain as day/night, permanent priesthood and kingship

x: As Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem, God tells Zedekiah through Jeremiah that the city will fall and he will be captured, but that he will die in relative peace rather than by the sword (vv. 1-5). The chapter then describes a covenant crisis: Zedekiah led the people to free their Hebrew slaves as the law required after six years of service, but once the Babylonian siege temporarily lifted, the slaveholders took their freed servants back into bondage (vv. 8-11). God's anger is sharp: because they proclaimed freedom and then revoked it, He will proclaim a different kind of "freedom" for them, freedom to die by sword, plague, and famine (vv. 15-17).
h: To Zedekiah, Thou Shalt Not Escape (vv.1-7)
The Covenant to Release the Slaves (vv.8-11)
Ye Turned and Polluted My Name (vv.12-16)
I Proclaim a Liberty for You (vv.17-22)
m: Zedekiah's fate prophesied, the slave-release covenant broken, liberty proclaimed and revoked, God's "liberty" of judgment, hypocrisy exposed

x: God uses the Rechabite family as a living object lesson for Judah. For over two hundred years, this clan has faithfully kept the command of their ancestor Jonadab to drink no wine, build no houses, and live as nomads (vv. 6-10). When Jeremiah brings them into the temple and sets wine before them, they refuse it without hesitation, honoring their father's instruction (vv. 5-6, 8). God contrasts this unwavering human loyalty with Judah's repeated refusal to obey Him despite His persistent warnings through the prophets (vv. 14-16). Because of their faithfulness, the Rechabites are promised that their family line will never fail to have someone serving before God (v. 19).
h: Bring the Rechabites into the House of the LORD (vv.1-5)
They Obeyed, and You Have Not (vv.12-17)
Jonadab Shall Not Want a Man (vv.18-19)
m: Faithfulness to ancestral commands, the Rechabites' obedience vs. Judah's disobedience, human obedience shaming divine disobedience, the reward for faithfulness

x: God tells Jeremiah to have Baruch write down all the prophecies given over the years onto a single scroll, in hope that hearing it might turn the people from their evil ways (vv. 1-3). Baruch reads the scroll publicly in the temple, and when officials hear it, they are alarmed and bring it to King Jehoiakim (vv. 9-16). The king, unmoved, cuts the scroll into pieces column by column and burns it in the fire pot as it is read to him, showing no fear despite the pleas of some officials (vv. 21-25). God tells Jeremiah to rewrite the scroll with all the same words, adding further judgment specifically against Jehoiakim, whose line will not continue on David's throne because of this act (vv. 27-32).
h: Write All the Words in a Roll (vv.1-4)
The Officials Hear, and Advise Him to Hide (vv.11-19)
The King Cuts It Up and Burns It (vv.20-26)
Write It Again, and Add More (vv.27-32)
m: God's word preserved in writing, the public reading of Scripture, the king's contempt for God's word, you can't destroy God's word by burning it, Baruch the faithful scribe

x: When the approach of Pharaoh's army temporarily forces Babylon to lift its siege of Jerusalem, King Zedekiah secretly sends messengers asking Jeremiah to pray for the nation (vv. 1-3). Jeremiah's answer is that the Babylonians will indeed return and burn the city, and warns the people not to deceive themselves into thinking otherwise (vv. 7-10). While attempting to leave the city to attend to property in his territory, Jeremiah is arrested on suspicion of deserting to the Babylonians, beaten, and imprisoned in a dungeon (vv. 11-15). Zedekiah later has him brought secretly for another private consultation, but receives the same unwelcome message and only softens Jeremiah's conditions of imprisonment (vv. 17-21).
h: Egypt Comes Up, and the Chaldeans Depart (vv.1-5)
m: False hope from Egypt's intervention, consistent prophecy under pressure, false accusation, imprisonment, Zedekiah's weakness (believes Jeremiah but won't act publicly)

x: Officials accuse Jeremiah of demoralizing the soldiers and remaining population with his message and demand his execution, and Zedekiah, unwilling to oppose them, hands Jeremiah over (vv. 4-5). They lower him into a muddy cistern where he begins to sink, but Ebed-Melech, a Cushite official in the palace, intervenes and, with the king's permission, pulls him out using ropes and rags to cushion his arms (vv. 6-13). Zedekiah meets with Jeremiah once more in secret, receiving the same counsel to surrender to Babylon in order to live, but the king admits he fears how his own officials, who have already defected, might treat him, and so does not act on the advice (vv. 14-23).
m: Prophet thrown into cistern (death intended), rescue by a foreign servant, Zedekiah's cowardice, the final offer to surrender, fear of man vs. fear of God

x: Jerusalem finally falls after an eighteen-month siege, as the Babylonian army breaches the city walls (vv. 1-3). Zedekiah attempts to flee by night but is captured near Jericho; his sons are executed before his eyes, which are then put out, and he is bound and taken to Babylon (vv. 4-7). The city and temple are burned, and most of the remaining population is taken into exile, though the poorest are left in the land (vv. 8-10). Nebuchadnezzar personally orders Jeremiah's release and protection, and Ebed-Melech, who had rescued Jeremiah earlier, is promised that his life will be spared because he trusted in God (vv. 11-18).
h: The City Burned, and the Poor Given the Fields (vv.8-10)
m: Prophecy fulfilled (exactly as Jeremiah predicted for 40 years), Zedekiah's fate, the prophet protected by the enemy, Ebed-Melech rewarded for faith, the end of Judah's monarchy

x: After Jerusalem's fall, the captain of the guard releases Jeremiah at Ramah and gives him the choice to go to Babylon or remain in the land; Jeremiah chooses to stay and settles with Gedaliah, the governor Babylon has appointed over the remaining Judeans (vv. 1-6). Scattered Judean survivors and soldiers gradually return and gather around Gedaliah, and for a time the land experiences a measure of peace and even harvests wine and summer fruit (vv. 7-12). But Johanan warns Gedaliah that Ishmael, a member of the royal family, has been sent by the king of Ammon to assassinate him, and offers to eliminate the threat secretly (vv. 13-15). Gedaliah refuses to believe the warning and takes no action (v. 16).
m: Jeremiah freed, Gedaliah's brief governance, temporary peace, the assassination plot warned but ignored, Judean remnant gathering

x: Ishmael assassinates Gedaliah during a meal at Mizpah, along with the Judeans and Babylonian soldiers present with him, then throws their bodies into a cistern (vv. 1-3, 7). He goes on to kill a group of pilgrims traveling to the temple and takes the rest of the population at Mizpah captive, heading toward Ammon (vv. 4-10). Johanan and other military commanders pursue Ishmael, rescue the captives at the pool of Gibeon, but Ishmael and a handful of men escape to Ammon (vv. 11-15). Fearing Babylonian reprisal for Gedaliah's murder, the surviving remnant gathers near Bethlehem, intending to flee to Egypt (vv. 16-18).
h: The Pilgrims Killed at the Pit (vv.4-9)
m: Betrayal at a feast, massacre of innocents, the remnant's fear of Babylonian retaliation, the pull toward Egypt, violence breeding more violence

x: The remnant, including Johanan, asks Jeremiah to seek God's guidance, promising in advance to obey whatever answer comes, whether favorable or not (vv. 1-6). After ten days, Jeremiah delivers God's response: remain in the land and God will build them up and show them mercy from the king of Babylon, but if they go to Egypt, the very sword and famine they fear will overtake them there instead (vv. 7-17). Jeremiah confronts them directly, accusing them of having already decided to go to Egypt and merely deceiving themselves by asking for guidance they never intended to follow, since they had claimed they would obey and now will not (vv. 19-22).
h: Pray for Us, and We Will Obey (vv.1-6)
If Ye Abide in This Land (vv.8-12)
If Ye Say, We Will Go into Egypt (vv.13-18)
m: Asking for God's guidance with no intention of following it, the 10-day wait for God's word, stay vs. go to Egypt, God promising to replant if they stay, the people's pre-decided hearts

x: Rejecting Jeremiah's word, the remnant, led by Johanan and other officers, accuses Jeremiah and Baruch of lying and forces them, along with the rest of the people, to go down into Egypt (vv. 1-7). Once in Tahpanhes, God instructs Jeremiah to bury large stones at the entrance of Pharaoh's palace as a sign, declaring that Nebuchadnezzar will one day set his throne on that very spot and extend his conquest over Egypt (vv. 8-11). The chapter closes with the warning that Babylon will also plunder Egypt's temples and idols, showing that the sword the remnant fled from will ultimately overtake them anyway (vv. 12-13).
h: They Went into Egypt, and Took Jeremiah (vv.4-7)
The Stones Hid in the Clay (vv.8-13)
m: Disobedience despite clear guidance, the accusation against Jeremiah (Baruch manipulated you!), forced migration to Egypt, God's judgment reaching into Egypt, Nebuchadnezzar called "my servant" again

x: In what is presented as Jeremiah's final recorded message, delivered to Judean refugees scattered throughout Egypt, he confronts them for reviving worship of the "queen of heaven," the very idolatry that brought Jerusalem's destruction (vv. 1-6, 15-17). The people respond defiantly, insisting they will continue burning incense to this goddess, claiming that life was actually better when they worshipped her and worse since they stopped (vv. 16-18). Jeremiah pronounces that this remnant in Egypt will be consumed by sword and famine until almost none remain, with only a tiny number ever returning to Judah (vv. 27-28). As a confirming sign, God announces that Pharaoh Hophra will be delivered into the hands of his enemies, just as Zedekiah had been (v. 30).
h: We Will Certainly Burn Incense to the Queen of Heaven (vv.15-19)
m: Return to idolatry in Egypt, the "queen of heaven" worship defended by the people, the people's twisted logic ("things were better when we worshipped idols"), Jeremiah's final word of judgment, the sign: Pharaoh Hophra will fall

x: The shortest chapter in the book is a brief, personal message directed to Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, originally given years earlier when Baruch wrote out Jeremiah's scroll (v. 1). Baruch has expressed exhaustion and grief, feeling that God has added sorrow to his suffering and left him no rest (v. 3). God's answer reminds Baruch that He is tearing down what He built and uprooting what He planted throughout the whole land, and asks whether Baruch should be seeking great things for himself in such a time, instructing him not to (vv. 4-5).
