Even so, God promises to preserve Baruch's life wherever he goes, though it will be like escaping with nothing else (v. 5).
h: Seek Not Great Things for Thyself (vv.4-5)
m: The faithful scribe's personal crisis, "seek not great things for thyself," God preserving life amid catastrophe, expectations adjusted to the era

x: This chapter opens a series of oracles against foreign nations (chapters 46-51), beginning with Egypt. The first oracle describes Egypt's crushing defeat by Nebuchadnezzar's forces at Carchemish in 605 BC, picturing Egypt's mighty army fleeing in terror and confusion (vv. 2-12). The second oracle foretells a future Babylonian invasion of Egypt itself, striking its cities and gods (vv. 13-26). The chapter closes with a message of comfort to Israel in contrast to the nations under judgment: God will one day save His servant Jacob from exile, though He will still discipline the nation in just measure (vv. 27-28).
h: Fear Not, O My Servant Jacob (vv.27-28)
m: Egypt's military pride humbled, the Battle of Carchemish, Nebuchadnezzar as God's instrument against Egypt, the failure of Egypt's famed army, comfort for Israel amid universal judgment

x: This oracle is directed against the Philistines, describing an overwhelming flood-like force advancing from the north, Babylon's army, that will overrun the coastal cities before the Philistines can even prepare their defenses (vv. 1-4). Gaza and Ashkelon are named as facing destruction, their people driven to grief and self-mourning (vv. 5-7). Even Tyre and Sidon, whom the Philistines might have looked to for aid, will be unable to help, since the same sword is coming for the whole coastland (v. 4). The oracle closes asking how long the sword of the LORD will continue before it can rest, implying that judgment is not yet finished (v. 7).
h: Waters Rise Out of the North (vv.1-4)
How Long Wilt Thou Be Quiet (vv.5-7)
m: Flood imagery for invasion, the coastal cities destroyed, no helper remains, the sword of the LORD unsheathed

x: This is the longest oracle against a single nation in the book, directed at Moab. City after city of Moab is named as facing destruction, and Moab's strength and pride are described as being broken like a shattered horn and a crushed arm (vv. 1-25). The underlying cause of judgment is identified: Moab has lived at ease and settled undisturbed, like wine left on its dregs, never having been poured out from vessel to vessel and refined through hardship (v. 11). Its deeper sin is trusting in its own achievements and treasures, and above all its arrogance, Moab's pride, insolence, and boastfulness are explicitly named as the reason for its downfall (vv. 7, 29-30). Even so, the chapter closes with a promise that Moab's fortunes will be restored in days to come (v. 47).
h: Woe unto Nebo, City by City (vv.1-10)
Never Emptied from Vessel to Vessel (vv.11-13)
Yet Will I Bring Again the Captivity of Moab (vv.45-47)
m: Moab's complacent ease as the cause of ruin, pride as the defining sin, city-by-city devastation, the prophet's grief for Moab, the wine metaphor (never poured/refined), future restoration promised

x: This chapter gathers five shorter oracles against five different nations: Ammon, condemned for seizing Israelite territory (vv. 1-6); Edom, whose pride in its rocky, elevated strongholds will not save it from being brought down (vv. 7-22); Damascus, which will be consumed by fire and left in panic (vv. 23-27); the nomadic peoples of Kedar and Hazor, who will be plundered and scattered (vv. 28-33); and Elam, whose bow, symbol of its military strength, will be broken and whose people will be scattered to every wind (vv. 34-39). Edom's oracle is by far the longest, dwelling on the futility of trusting in natural defenses against God's judgment. Even so, both Ammon and Elam are promised eventual restoration of their fortunes (vv. 6, 39).
m: God's sovereignty over all nations, pride in fortifications exposed, each nation's specific sin addressed, Nebuchadnezzar as universal instrument, restoration promised to some

x: This chapter begins the lengthy oracle against Babylon, spanning chapters 50-51, announcing that Babylon itself, along with its gods Bel and Marduk, will be humiliated and shattered, just as it once shattered other nations (vv. 1-3). A nation from the north will bring desolation on Babylon, while Israel and Judah, though presently scattered, will come back weeping, seeking the way to Zion and reaffirming an everlasting covenant with God (vv. 3-5). God is described as the people's strong Redeemer, certain to plead their cause and give the Babylonians no rest in return for the violence they inflicted (vv. 33-34). Babylon's fundamental sin is identified as arrogance and defiance against the Holy One of Israel (v. 29).
h: Babylon Is Taken, Bel Is Confounded (vv.1-3)
Flee Out of the Midst of Babylon (vv.8-10)
Go Up Against the Land of Merathaim (vv.21-32)
A People Shall Come from the North (vv.41-46)
m: Babylon's fall announced, Israel's return, God as Redeemer/Avenger, Babylon's pride judged, a nation from the north (Medo-Persia), the cup reversed on Babylon

x: The oracle against Babylon continues and reaches its climax, describing God's vengeance on the empire that destroyed His temple and scattered His people (vv. 11, 24). Babylon is described as having once been a gold cup in God's hand, an instrument He used to intoxicate and judge the nations, but which will now itself be broken (v. 7). Its judgment is portrayed as reaching all the way to heaven and touching the skies, underscoring its severity and totality (v. 9). The chapter concludes with Jeremiah instructing the officer Seraiah to read this scroll of judgment aloud once he reaches Babylon, then tie a stone to it and throw it into the Euphrates River, declaring that Babylon will sink in the same way, never to rise again (vv. 59-64).
h: He Hath Made the Earth by His Power (vv.15-19)
As Babylon Hath Caused the Slain (vv.49-53)
The Broad Walls Shall Be Utterly Broken (vv.54-58)
The Book Cast into the Euphrates (vv.59-64)
m: Babylon as God's instrument now judged, vengeance for the temple, the golden cup now rejected, "flee from Babylon" (God's people must leave), the Medes as instruments against Babylon, the scroll cast into the Euphrates

x: This closing chapter is a historical appendix, largely paralleling the account in 2 Kings, recounting Zedekiah's rebellion against Babylon and the resulting siege and fall of Jerusalem (vv. 1-11). It describes the burning of the temple and city, the demolition of the walls, and the deportation of the population, along with a list of the numbers taken into exile over several successive years (vv. 12-30). The temple's bronze pillars, sea, and other furnishings are catalogued in detail before being carried off to Babylon (vv. 17-23). The chapter ends on an unexpected note of hope: years later, the Babylonian king Evil-Merodach releases the exiled King Jehoiachin from prison, restores him to a position of honor, and provides for him at the royal table for the rest of his life (vv. 31-34).
h: The Breach, the Flight and the Capture (vv.6-11)
m: Prophecy fulfilled (everything Jeremiah predicted came true), the temple destroyed, the Davidic monarchy ended (seemingly), yet Jehoiachin's release — a spark of hope for David's line

x: Jerusalem is pictured as a widowed queen, once great among the nations, now sitting alone and weeping through the night with no one to comfort her (vv. 1-2). Her roads mourn empty of pilgrims, her gates are desolate, and her priests groan, since her enemies now rule over her because of her many transgressions (vv. 4-5). Zion's princes are like starving deer with no pasture, and her adversaries mock her downfall, gloating over her exposed shame (vv. 6-7). The city herself speaks, calling out to anyone passing by to consider whether any sorrow compares to hers, and acknowledging that the Lord has afflicted her for her own rebellion (v. 12). The chapter closes with Jerusalem appealing to God to look on her distress and to bring the same judgment on her enemies that He has brought on her (vv. 20-22).
h: Jerusalem the Widow: Alone and Weeping (vv.1-7)
Her Sin Exposed, and No Comforter (vv.8-11)
The City Speaks: Is It Nothing to You? (vv.12-16)
God Is Righteous; I Have Rebelled (vv.17-22)
m: The desolation of Jerusalem, the absence of comfort, the consequences of persistent sin, God's righteous judgment, the city personified as a weeping woman, loneliness and shame after judgment

x: In His anger the Lord Himself is pictured as the one who tears down Jerusalem's walls and strongholds, acting toward His own people as an enemy would (vv. 1-5). He destroys the tabernacle, ends the appointed feasts and Sabbaths, and rejects His own altar and sanctuary, so that her prophets no longer receive visions from Him (vv. 6-9). Elders sit in silence with dust on their heads, and children and infants faint from hunger in the streets, crying to their mothers for food that isn't there (vv. 10-12). The prophets are blamed for failing to expose the nation's sin, while passersby and enemies mock the fallen city (vv. 14-16). The chapter ends with a wrenching appeal for the Lord to look at the suffering He has caused, including mothers driven to eat their own children in the siege (vv. 20-22).
h: God as the Destroyer: He Hath Swallowed Up (vv.1-8)
The Silence: No Vision, No Law, No King (vv.9-10)
What Can I Say? Ruin Beyond Comparison (vv.13-14)
Enemies Mocking, and the LORD Has Done It (vv.15-17)
Cry Out in the Night: Mothers and Children (vv.18-22)
m: God as active agent of judgment (not merely passive observer), the destruction of all institutions (temple, law, prophecy), the failure of false prophets, the horror of siege conditions, the appropriateness of grief

x: The speaker describes personal affliction under God's hand in intensely physical terms — darkness, broken bones, walls that hem him in, and prayers that seem to go unheard (vv. 1-9). In the depths of this suffering he suddenly turns to hope, recalling that the Lord's mercies are new every morning and that His faithfulness never fails, and concluding that it is good to wait quietly for the Lord's salvation (vv. 22-26). He counsels patient submission — bearing hardship in youth, sitting in silence, and offering no resistance to one who strikes him — trusting that God does not reject forever and will yet show compassion (vv. 27-33). The chapter turns to confession and self-examination, urging the people to test their ways and return to God, lifting up hearts and hands together in repentance (vv. 40-42). The speaker then recounts his own cry for help from the depths, God's nearness when he…
h: The Man of Affliction: God's Rod (vv.1-18)
This I Recall, Therefore Have I Hope (vv.19-24)
Let Us Search and Turn Again (vv.40-42)
Covered with a Cloud: Continuing Lament (vv.43-54)
Thou Drewest Near: The Cry for Justice (vv.55-66)
m: Personal affliction, the faithfulness of God even in judgment, mercy new every morning, the goodness of waiting on God, hope in the pit of despair, God's sovereignty over both good and evil, the call to self-examination and return

x: Precious things — gold, sacred gems, and Zion's noble sons — are now treated as worthless, showing how far the city has fallen (vv. 1-2). Even jackals nurse their young, but the daughter of Jerusalem has grown cruel like an ostrich in the wilderness, as children beg for bread and water with no one to give it to them (vv. 3-4). Those who once ate delicacies now waste away in the streets, and the famine grows so severe that compassionate mothers cook their own children for food — a judgment described as worse than the sudden destruction of Sodom (vv. 5-10). This fierce anger is attributed to the sins of the city's prophets and priests, who shed innocent blood and were then shunned even by the surrounding nations (vv. 11-15). The king, the Lord's anointed, is captured in the very pits the people had dug, and the chapter closes with a warning to Edom, which gloats now but whose own judgment…
h: Children Starving; Mothers Worse Than Jackals (vv.3-6)
The Nazirites: From Rubies to Coal (vv.7-8)
Better Slain by the Sword Than by Famine (vv.9-12)
Prophets and Priests: Blood in the Streets (vv.13-18)
The Anointed Taken, and Edom's Turn (vv.19-22)
m: The physical horrors of siege and starvation, the reversal of all social order, sin's consequences worse than Sodom, the failure of religious leadership (prophets/priests), the capture of God's anointed, Edom's coming judgment

x: The chapter shifts to a communal prayer as the whole people ask the Lord to remember and see the disgrace that has come upon them (v. 1). They catalog their losses: their inheritance given to strangers, their homes to foreigners, and orphans and widows left without support (vv. 2-3). They must now pay for water and wood that were once free, and they are exhausted from forced labor under foreign rule (vv. 4-5). Women have been violated, princes hanged, elders shown no honor, and even the joy of dancing has turned to mourning (vv. 11-15). The people confess that the crown has fallen from their head because of their sin, yet close by affirming that the Lord reigns forever, pleading with Him to restore them as in days of old even while uncertain whether He has utterly rejected them (vv. 16-22).
h: Remember, O LORD, What Is Come Upon Us (vv.1-3)
Thou Remainest For Ever: Turn Us Again (vv.19-22)
m: Communal suffering and corporate prayer, the loss of inheritance and identity, the consequences falling on the next generation, longing for restoration, the uncertainty of whether God will restore, the permanence of God vs. the transience of human suffering

x: The heavens open and Ezekiel receives one of the most elaborate visions in Scripture. A storm from the north reveals four living creatures, each with four faces and four wings, alongside whirling wheels covered with eyes, an expanse of crystal above them, and on the expanse a throne with a figure like a man surrounded by fire and rainbow light (vv. 4-27). Ezekiel recognizes this as the likeness of the glory of the LORD and falls facedown (v. 28).
h: Date and Place, by the River Chebar (vv.1-3)
The Storm out of the North (v.4)
The Wheels, and a Wheel Within a Wheel (vv.15-21)
The Throne, and the Likeness of a Man Upon It (vv.26-28)
m: God's glory appearing in exile (not just in the temple), the four living creatures, the wheels (omnidirectional divine mobility), God's throne above all creation, the priest becomes prophet

x: God commissions Ezekiel as a prophet, sending him to a rebellious, obstinate Israel whether or not they listen, since even their refusal will prove a prophet has been among them (vv. 1-5). God tells him not to fear the people or their hostility, comparing them to briers, thorns, and scorpions (vv. 6-7). He then shows Ezekiel a scroll covered with writing on both sides, full of lament and mourning and woe, and commands him to eat it before he speaks (vv. 8-10).
h: Son of Man, and the Spirit That Set Him on His Feet (vv.1-2)
The Commission to a Rebellious House (vv.3-5)
The Roll Written Within and Without (vv.8-10)
m: "Son of man" as divine address, sent to a rebellious people, success not guaranteed (just faithfulness), don't fear faces, the scroll of lamentation eaten

x: Ezekiel eats the scroll, and to his surprise it tastes sweet as honey (v. 3). God sends him not to a foreign people who would listen, but to the hard-hearted house of Israel, giving him a resolve as unyielding as their own stubbornness (vv. 4-9). He is carried to the exiles at Tel-abib and sits among them, overwhelmed, for seven days (vv. 14-15). God then appoints him a watchman for Israel: if he warns the wicked and they still perish, he is cleared of guilt, but if he fails to warn them, their blood is on his own hands (vv. 16-21).
h: The Roll Eaten, and Sweet as Honey (vv.1-3)
Sent to Israel, Who Will Not Hearken (vv.4-11)
The Spirit Lifts Him, and He Sits Seven Days (vv.12-15)
The Plain, the Bands, and the Tongue Made Dumb (vv.22-27)
m: The scroll tastes like honey (God's word is sweet even when the message is heavy), the prophet's forehead hardened, the watchman's responsibility, blood-guilt for silence, seven days of stunned silence

x: God commands Ezekiel to enact Jerusalem's coming siege through a series of sign-acts: he draws the city on a clay brick and stages a mock siege against it (vv. 1-3), then lies on his left side for 390 days bearing Israel's iniquity and on his right side for 40 days bearing Judah's (vv. 4-8), rationing meager bread and water and cooking it over dung fuel to dramatize the coming famine (vv. 9-17). His own body becomes a living sermon of the siege and exile to come.
h: The Tile, the Fort and the Iron Pan (vv.1-3)
Three Hundred and Ninety Days on the Left Side (vv.4-5)
Forty Days on the Right Side (vv.6-8)
m: Embodied prophecy, the coming siege of Jerusalem enacted in miniature, measured punishment (day = year), the horror of siege conditions, God's concession to priestly scruples (cow dung instead of human dung)

x: Ezekiel is told to shave his head and beard with a sword and divide the hair into three portions, symbolizing Jerusalem's fate: a third burned inside the model city, a third struck with the sword around it, and a third scattered to the wind (vv. 1-2). A few strands are bound into his garment as a remnant, though even some of these are later burned (vv. 3-4). God declares that because Jerusalem has rebelled against His statutes more than the surrounding nations, He will bring on her judgment unlike any other, including cannibalism during the siege and scattering among the nations (vv. 5-17).
h: The Razor, and the Hair Divided in Three (vv.1-4)
This Is Jerusalem, Worse Than the Nations (vv.5-8)
What Has Not Been Done Before (vv.9-10)
My Fury Accomplished, and My Comfort Taken (vv.13-17)
m: The divided hair (thirds of Jerusalem's population), famine/sword/scattering, a tiny remnant barely preserved, Jerusalem worse than surrounding nations, unprecedented judgment, "then shall they know that I am the LORD"

x: Ezekiel delivers an oracle against the mountains and high places of Israel where idols are worshiped (vv. 1-3). God promises to destroy the altars and incense stands and scatter the bones of the slain around their own idols, leaving the land desolate (vv. 4-7). Yet a remnant will survive in exile among the nations, where they will remember God, be broken over their unfaithfulness, and loathe themselves for their sin (vv. 8-10). The repeated refrain underscores the purpose of the judgment: that Israel will know God is the LORD (vv. 11-14).
h: The Oracle Addressed to the Mountains (vv.1-2)
The High Places Broken, and the Bones Scattered (vv.3-7)
A Remnant That Will Loathe Itself (vv.8-10)
The Gesture, and the Slain Among Their Idols (vv.11-14)
m: The high places of idolatry destroyed, corpses among idols, scattered remnant, the remnant's broken-hearted memory, "they shall know that I am the LORD" (Ezekiel's signature phrase)

x: Ezekiel proclaims that the end has come upon the land of Israel from every direction (vv. 1-4). He describes it with urgent, staccato language: the day is near, doom is dawning, and violence has grown into a rod of wickedness ready to strike (vv. 5-11). Ordinary economic life collapses, since buying and selling lose all meaning when no one will keep what they gain, and silver and gold are thrown into the streets as worthless (vv. 12-19). The chapter ends with the sanctuary itself defiled and the land handed over to foreign plunderers (vv. 20-27).
h: An End Upon the Four Corners of the Land (vv.1-4)
The Trumpet Blown, and Nobody Goes (vv.14-18)
The Chain, and the Collapse of Every Office (vv.23-27)
m: The finality of judgment ("the end"), economic collapse (silver useless), violence blossoming like a rod, all normal activity suspended, the Day of the LORD

x: In a vision, God transports Ezekiel to Jerusalem's temple and shows him four escalating abominations happening within its courts. He sees the idol that provokes God's jealousy standing at the north gate (vv. 3-6), seventy elders burning incense to images carved on the walls in darkness (vv. 7-13), women weeping for the god Tammuz at the temple's north gate (v. 14), and twenty-five men facing east to worship the sun with their backs to the temple itself (vv. 15-16). Each scene is worse than the last, and God tells Ezekiel there is more to see (v. 17).
h: The Image of Jealousy at the Gate (vv.5-6)
The Chamber of Imagery, and the Seventy Elders (vv.7-13)
Sun Worship with Their Backs to the Temple (vv.16-18)
m: Idolatry inside God's temple, escalating abominations (each worse than the last), the elders' secret worship, pagan religion in the holy place, the cause of God's departure

x: God summons six executioners and a scribe dressed in linen carrying a writing kit (vv. 1-2). The scribe is sent through Jerusalem to mark the foreheads of everyone who grieves over the city's abominations (v. 4). The executioners are then commanded to kill everyone without that mark, showing no pity, beginning at the sanctuary itself (vv. 5-7); the slaughter starts with the elders standing before the temple. As the killing spreads, Ezekiel cries out and asks whether God intends to destroy the entire remnant of Israel (v. 8).
h: The Glory at the Threshold, and the Mark on the Foreheads (vv.3-4)
The Slaughter, Beginning at the Sanctuary (vv.5-7)
m: The mark of preservation (those who grieve sin), judgment starting at the sanctuary, no sparing (old, young, women, children), the righteous remnant marked, God's response to Ezekiel's protest

x: Ezekiel again sees the throne-chariot vision from chapter 1, now positioned above the cherubim at the temple (vv. 1-8). Burning coals from among the cherubim are scattered over Jerusalem by the man in linen, symbolizing judgment on the city (vv. 2, 6-7). The glory of the LORD rises from the cherubim, pauses at the temple's threshold, and then moves toward the east gate (vv. 4, 18-19) — God is departing His own house.
h: Coals of Fire Taken from Between the Cherubim (vv.1-8)
The Wheels, the Faces and the Eyes (vv.9-14)
The Same Creatures He Saw by Chebar (vv.15-17)
The Glory Goes to the East Gate (vv.18-22)
m: The glory of God leaving the temple, cherubim identified (= living creatures of ch.1), coals of fire scattered (judgment on Jerusalem), the mobile throne positioned to depart

x: Ezekiel sees twenty-five leaders at the temple's east gate giving wicked counsel, comparing the city to a cooking pot that will protect them like meat inside it (vv. 1-3). God condemns their false sense of security, and as Ezekiel prophesies against them, one leader, Pelatiah, drops dead (vv. 4-13). God then promises the exiles that though scattered among the nations, He will be a sanctuary to them and will one day give them a unified heart and a new spirit in place of their heart of stone (vv. 14-21). The chapter closes with the glory of the LORD departing the city and coming to rest on the mountain east of Jerusalem (vv. 22-23).
h: The Five and Twenty Men at the East Gate (vv.1-4)
Pelatiah Dies, and Ezekiel Cries Out (v.13)
A Little Sanctuary in the Countries (vv.14-16)
A New Heart and a New Spirit (vv.17-21)
The Glory Departs to the Mountain on the East (vv.22-25)
m: Wicked leadership giving false security, God as sanctuary in exile, the new heart promise, the glory departing to the Mount of Olives, the vision ends

x: Ezekiel performs two more sign-acts. First, in daylight he packs baggage as if going into exile, then at evening digs through the wall and leaves with his face covered, enacting how Zedekiah will flee Jerusalem yet be captured and taken to Babylon without seeing it, since he will be blinded (vv. 1-13; cf. 2 Kings 25:4-7). Second, he eats his food trembling and with anxiety, dramatizing the terror residents of Jerusalem will feel during the coming siege (vv. 17-20). God also confronts a popular proverb claiming that time is dragging on and every vision is failing to come true, insisting instead that the days of fulfillment are near (vv. 21-28).
h: The Exile's Baggage, and the Hole in the Wall (vv.1-7)
The Prince Shall Not See the Land (vv.8-16)
The Other Proverb, About the Distant Future (vv.26-28)
m: The prince's escape enacted (Zedekiah), "eyes but sees not" (Babylon but won't see it = blinding), eating in terror (siege conditions), the false proverb rejected ("vision fails"), no more delay

x: God pronounces judgment on Israel's false prophets, who speak from their own imagination and have seen nothing true, yet proclaim peace when there is no peace (vv. 1-7). He compares them to foxes among ruins, doing nothing to repair the breach, and to builders who cover a flimsy wall with whitewash rather than sound material — a wall God will expose by sending storm, hail, and wind to knock it down (vv. 8-16). The chapter closes with a similar condemnation of women who practice divination, using charms and veils to ensnare people's lives for personal gain, whom God vows to expose and free their victims from (vv. 17-23).
h: Prophets Who Follow Their Own Spirit (vv.1-7)
The Untempered Mortar, and the Wall That Falls (vv.8-16)
The Women with Pillows and Kerchiefs (vv.17-23)
m: Prophesying from one's own heart (not God's word), "peace when there is no peace," the whitewashed wall metaphor, God tearing down false assurances, female occult practitioners condemned

x: Elders of Israel come to sit before Ezekiel to inquire of the LORD, but God tells him these men have set up idols in their hearts and refuses to answer them until they repent (vv. 1-8). He describes four severe judgments — sword, famine, wild beasts, and plague — and declares that even if Noah, Daniel, and Job were present in the land, their righteousness would save only themselves, not their sons or daughters (vv. 12-20). Yet God promises that a remnant will survive each judgment and be brought out to the exiles, whose conduct will prove that God's judgment on Jerusalem was justified (vv. 21-23).
h: Elders with Idols in Their Hearts (vv.1-5)
Noah, Daniel and Job Could Not Deliver Them (vv.12-20)
m: Internal idolatry (heart-idols vs. physical statues), God refusing to answer double-minded inquirers, even the most righteous cannot save others by their merit alone, four judgments (sword, famine, beasts, pestilence)

x: God gives Ezekiel a brief parable about the wood of a grapevine, asking whether it is more useful than any other wood — unfit even for a peg to hang something on, and good for nothing but fuel (vv. 1-5). Since a vine's only value is its fruit, a vine that fails to produce fruit has no worth at all. Jerusalem, God says, is like that useless vine wood: having failed to bear fruit for Him, she is fit only to be consumed by fire (vv. 6-8).
h: What Is the Vine Branch Good For (vv.1-3)
m: Israel as vine, vine wood's sole value = fruit, without fruit = fuel for fire, Jerusalem's purposeless existence apart from God

x: In the longest chapter of Ezekiel, Jerusalem's history is told as an extended allegory: an abandoned infant of Canaanite origin, left to die, whom God rescues, raises, and eventually marries, adorning her with royal splendor (vv. 1-14). She grows unfaithful, however, using her God-given beauty to pursue other nations and their gods, and is judged worse than a prostitute because she gives her favors away rather than being paid for them (vv. 15-34). God pronounces on her the judgment an adulterous wife deserves, comparing her guilt to that of her sister cities Samaria and Sodom, who by comparison seem less corrupt (vv. 35-52). Yet the chapter closes with God remembering His covenant with her from her youth and promising to establish an everlasting covenant despite her unfaithfulness (vv. 53-63).
h: The Abandoned Infant, and Canaanite Parentage (vv.1-5)
The Covenant, the Clothing and the Renown (vv.8-14)
The Sentence, Carried Out by Those She Paid (vv.35-43)
Worse Than Samaria, Worse Than Sodom (vv.44-52)
The Everlasting Covenant, and Remembering with Shame (vv.53-63)
m: Jerusalem's Canaanite origins (no natural superiority), God's grace in choosing/raising her, unfaithfulness worse than prostitution, judgment proportional to privilege, yet an everlasting covenant promised

x: Ezekiel tells a parable of two eagles and a vine: a great eagle, representing Babylon and Nebuchadnezzar, breaks off the top of a cedar, representing King Jehoiachin, and carries it to Babylon, then plants a seed from the land that grows into a low, spreading vine, representing Zedekiah (vv. 1-6). That vine turns instead toward a second eagle, Egypt, seeking water and support, and God asks whether it will prosper — the answer is no, it will be uprooted for breaking its covenant (vv. 7-21). The chapter closes with a promise that God Himself will plant a tender sprig on a high mountain, where it will grow into a noble cedar sheltering every kind of bird, a picture of the coming Messianic kingdom (vv. 22-24).
h: The Riddle of the Two Eagles and the Vine (vv.1-10)
The Interpretation, and the Broken Oath (vv.11-21)
The Tender Twig Planted on the Mountain (vv.22-24)
m: Political allegory (Babylon, Zedekiah, Egypt), covenant-breaking punished, the futility of trusting Egypt against Babylon, God's own planting of the Messiah

x: God addresses a popular proverb blaming children for their fathers' sins, declaring instead that the soul who sins is the one who will die (vv. 1-4). Through three case studies — a righteous father, his wicked son, and that son's righteous son — Ezekiel shows that each person is judged by his own conduct, not his parent's or child's (vv. 5-20). God adds that a wicked person who turns from sin will live, while a righteous person who turns to sin will die, since He takes no pleasure in anyone's death and calls the house of Israel to repent and live (vv. 21-32).
h: The Proverb About Sour Grapes Withdrawn (vv.1-4)
The Wicked Who Turns Shall Live (vv.21-23)
The Righteous Who Turns Shall Die (v.24)
m: Individual (not inherited) guilt, the sour grapes proverb rejected, righteousness defined by behavior, the wicked can repent and live, the righteous can fall and die, God takes no pleasure in death, "turn and live"

x: Ezekiel raises a funeral lament for the princes of Israel using two vivid images. First, a lioness raises cubs who become young lions, but each is caught in a pit and dragged away in chains, one to Egypt and one to Babylon (vv. 1-9). Second, Israel is pictured as a fruitful vine planted by abundant waters, whose strong branches — its kings — are torn off and used as scepters, until the vine itself is uprooted, withered by the east wind, and set on fire (vv. 10-14). The chapter mourns the loss of royal potential destroyed by sin and foreign conquest.
h: The Lioness and Her First Whelp (vv.1-4)
The Lioness and Her Second Whelp (vv.5-9)
The Vine Plucked Up and Planted in the Wilderness (vv.10-14)
m: The lioness and her cubs, royal failure, the vine uprooted, the death of a dynasty, lamentation over wasted potential, sovereign judgment on kings

x: Elders of Israel come to inquire of the LORD, but God refuses to be consulted by them until they face their history (vv. 1-3). He rehearses Israel's repeated rebellions in Egypt, in the wilderness, and in the promised land, showing a pattern of idolatry at every stage (vv. 4-32). Yet at each point of deserved judgment, God held back destruction for the sake of His own name and reputation among the nations (vv. 9, 14, 22). The chapter closes with God's promise to purge the rebels in a future gathering and restore a purified remnant through a second exodus (vv. 33-44).
h: The Elders Come, and Get No Answer (vv.1-4)
The Second Generation, and Statutes That Were Not Good (vv.18-26)
The Second Exodus, and the Purge (vv.33-38)
The Fire in the Forest of the South (vv.45-49)
m: Israel's repeated rebellions, God's restraint "for my name's sake," idolatry in every generation, the purging of rebels, a second exodus, God's holiness vindicated

x: God commands Ezekiel to sigh deeply before the people as a sign of coming disaster, then delivers a dramatic song about a sword sharpened and polished for slaughter against Jerusalem (vv. 1-17). Nebuchadnezzar is shown standing at a crossroads, using divination — shaking arrows, consulting idols, examining a liver — to decide whether to attack Jerusalem or Ammon, and the lot falls on Jerusalem (vv. 18-23). The chapter culminates in the overthrow of Judah's crown and throne, with a promise that everything will be overturned until the one to whom it rightfully belongs finally comes (vv. 25-27). A closing oracle condemns Ammon to the same fate by the sword.
h: A Sword Drawn Out of Its Sheath (vv.1-7)
Nebuchadnezzar at the Parting of the Way (vv.18-23)
m: The unsheathed sword of the LORD, Ezekiel's sighing as a sign-act, the sword sharpened for slaughter, Nebuchadnezzar at the crossroads, divination overruled by sovereignty, the crown removed, "until he come whose right it is"

x: Jerusalem is condemned as a bloody city, and her sins are catalogued in devastating detail: bloodshed, idolatry, sexual immorality, oppression of the vulnerable, profaning the Sabbath, and corruption at every level of society (vv. 1-16). God likens the nation to metal in a furnace, refined by judgment because it has become dross (vv. 17-22). He then declares that prophets, priests, princes, and common people have all failed in their duty (vv. 23-29). The chapter climaxes with God searching for just one person to stand in the gap and intercede for the land, but finding no one (v. 30), leaving judgment as the only remaining option (v. 31).
h: The Bloody City, and Her Sins Catalogued (vv.1-16)
The Furnace, and Israel as Dross (vv.17-22)
Every Class Indicted, and No Man in the Gap (vv.23-31)
m: Jerusalem as "the bloody city," comprehensive sin catalogue, corruption at every social level, the smelting furnace of judgment, no intercessor found, leadership failure

x: Ezekiel tells the allegory of two sisters, Oholah, representing Samaria, the northern kingdom, and Oholibah, representing Jerusalem, the southern kingdom, both pictured as wives who commit spiritual adultery through political alliances and idolatry, first with Assyria, then Egypt, then Babylon (vv. 1-21). Oholah is judged and destroyed for her unfaithfulness, yet Oholibah watches her sister's fate and becomes even worse (vv. 9-11). God sentences Oholibah to be handed over to the very nations she pursued as lovers, who will strip, mutilate, and destroy her, while a closing section reiterates the sisters' shared guilt in explicit terms (vv. 22-49).
m: Spiritual adultery through political alliances, two sisters representing two kingdoms, unfaithfulness despite witnessing judgment, escalating sin, the lovers become the executioners, jealous judgment of a betrayed God

x: God reveals to Ezekiel the exact day Nebuchadnezzar's siege of Jerusalem begins and marks it with two devastating signs (vv. 1-2). First, he tells the parable of a corroded boiling pot representing Jerusalem, whose filth cannot be cleansed and so must be set empty over the fire until it burns away (vv. 3-14). Second, in the most personal sign-act of the book, God takes the life of Ezekiel's beloved wife and forbids him to mourn her publicly, in the ordinary way (vv. 15-24). His restrained grief becomes a preview of how the exiles will react with stunned silence when news arrives that Jerusalem has fallen (vv. 25-27).
h: The Boiling Pot, Corroded Beyond Cleaning (vv.3-14)
When the News Comes, Thou Shalt Speak (vv.25-27)
m: The siege begins, the corroded pot that cannot be cleaned, judgment by fire, the death of Ezekiel's wife, forbidden mourning as a sign, the end of Ezekiel's silence, the most costly prophecy

x: The oracles against the surrounding nations begin as God turns His attention from Jerusalem to four neighboring peoples who rejoiced over Judah's fall: Ammon (vv. 1-7), Moab (vv. 8-11), Edom (vv. 12-14), and Philistia (vv. 15-17). Each receives a specific charge and a specific sentence of judgment. Their sin is not merely idolatry but the gloating, mocking satisfaction they took in watching God's people suffer. In judging them, God shows He still defends His own people even while disciplining them.
h: Moab, and Judah Treated as One Nation Among Many (vv.8-11)
Edom, and Vengeance Against a Brother (vv.12-14)
m: God judges those who rejoice over Israel's fall, divine justice for gloating enemies, Ammon's "Aha!," Moab's contempt, Edom's vengeance, Philistia's spite, God vindicates His name among all peoples

x: The oracle against Tyre begins, one of the most detailed prophecies in Scripture. Tyre rejoiced over Jerusalem's fall, hoping to absorb her trade routes (vv. 1-2). God responds with specific judgment: many nations will come against Tyre like waves of the sea, Nebuchadnezzar will besiege the mainland city, its stones and timber will be cast into the sea, and the site will become a bare rock where fishermen spread their nets (vv. 3-14). The chapter closes with the surrounding nations and their rulers mourning Tyre's fall as the once-great city sinks into oblivion (vv. 15-21).
h: The Charge, and the Nations Like Waves (vv.1-6)
The Lament of the Coastland Princes (vv.15-18)
Down to the Pit, and Never Found Again (vv.19-21)
m: Tyre's commercial pride, rejoicing over Jerusalem's fall, waves of nations as judgment, Nebuchadnezzar's siege, stones cast into the sea, the great city silenced, fulfilled prophecy and divine sovereignty

x: A funeral lament for Tyre pictures the city as a magnificent merchant ship. Ezekiel describes the vessel's construction in detail — planks of fir from Senir, masts of cedar from Lebanon, oars of oak from Bashan, ivory-inlaid decks, and sails of fine embroidered linen from Egypt (vv. 1-11). He then catalogues Tyre's vast trading network, listing the many nations that brought goods to her harbors (vv. 12-25). But an east wind wrecks the great ship in the heart of the sea, and her merchants, sailors, and wealth all sink to the bottom, mourned by onlookers on the shore (vv. 26-36).
h: The Ship Built Out of the Whole World (vv.1-11)
The Ship Broken in the East Wind (vv.26-36)
m: Tyre as a perfect ship, the catalogue of nations and trade goods, beauty and craftsmanship, the east wind destruction, the mourning of merchants, pride sunk in the depths, the fragility of commercial empire

x: The oracle against the ruler of Tyre begins by addressing the human prince of Tyre, condemning his pride in claiming to be a god because of his wealth and wisdom (vv. 1-10). It then shifts into a lament over the king of Tyre using language that seems to transcend any human ruler, describing a being who once dwelt in Eden as a guardian cherub, blameless from the day of his creation until sin was found in him, whose heart grew proud because of his beauty and splendor (vv. 11-19). Many interpreters see in this description a picture of Satan's original glory and fall. The chapter concludes with a brief oracle against Sidon and a promise that Israel will be gathered home in security (vv. 20-26).
h: The Prince of Tyre, Who Said I Am a God (vv.1-10)
The King of Tyre, and the Anointed Cherub (vv.11-19)
No More a Pricking Brier for Israel (vv.24-26)
m: The pride of the prince of Tyre, "I am a God," the king of Tyre in Eden, the anointed cherub, perfection corrupted by pride, beauty becoming the cause of the fall, cast from the mountain of God, Satan typology, judgment on Sidon, Israel's restoration promise

x: The oracles against Egypt begin, depicting Pharaoh as a great monster lying in the Nile who arrogantly claims the river as his own creation (vv. 1-3). God promises to put hooks in his jaws, drag him from the water, and scatter Egypt and its people among the nations for forty years (vv. 4-16). Egypt will never again rule over other nations, reduced instead to the lowest of kingdoms. The chapter closes with God giving the land of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar as compensation for his long, costly siege of Tyre (vv. 17-21).
h: The Dragon in the River, and the Staff of Reed (vv.1-7)
Forty Years, and a Base Kingdom (vv.8-16)
Egypt as Wages for the Army at Tyre (vv.17-21)
m: Pharaoh as the great dragon, "My river is mine own," the dragon dragged from the water, Egypt scattered forty years, the basest of kingdoms, Nebuchadnezzar's wages, God's sovereignty over empires

x: Ezekiel applies the day of the LORD to Egypt, announcing a day of clouds and doom for Egypt and her allies — Ethiopia, Libya, Lydia, and other allied peoples (vv. 1-9). Nebuchadnezzar is named as God's chosen instrument to destroy Egypt's idols, scatter her people, and devastate her cities (vv. 10-19). The chapter also pictures God breaking Pharaoh's arms so he can no longer wield a sword, while strengthening the arms of Babylon's king (vv. 20-26). Egypt's pride in her own power is permanently shattered.
h: The Day of the LORD Against Egypt (vv.1-5)
m: The day of the LORD against Egypt, a day of clouds, judgment on Egypt's allies, God's sword given to Nebuchadnezzar, Pharaoh's broken arms, idols destroyed, cities named and judged, Egypt's power permanently ended

x: Pharaoh is compared to a great cedar in Lebanon, the tallest and most magnificent tree in the garden of God, whose top reached the clouds and whose branches sheltered every nation, making even the trees of Eden envious (vv. 1-9). But because its heart grew proud in its height, God handed it over to be cut down and cast into Sheol, mourned by the nations it had sheltered (vv. 10-17). The lesson for Pharaoh is direct: if Assyria, greater than Egypt, could be felled this way, Egypt should expect the same fate (v. 18).
h: Cut Down, and the Nations Gone from Under It (vv.12-14)
Sheol, and the Comfort of Company (vv.15-18)
m: Pharaoh compared to Assyria's cedar, the greatest tree in Eden, pride in height and beauty, God cuts down the tallest tree, descent to Sheol, the lesson of Assyria's fall for Egypt, no tree is too great for God's axe

x: The final two oracles against Egypt begin with a funeral lament over Pharaoh, pictured as a dragon caught in God's net, its blood poured out on the mountains and the sun darkened at its fall (vv. 1-16). The second oracle is one of the most haunting passages in Ezekiel: a guided tour of Sheol where Pharaoh descends and finds the fallen empires already there — Assyria, Elam, Meshech and Tubal, Edom, and the princes of the north and of Sidon — all lying uncircumcised among the slain (vv. 17-32). Egypt joins them in the pit, closing the entire oracles-against-the-nations section with a vision of universal death.
h: The Dragon Taken in a Net (vv.1-10)
The Sword of Babylon, and the Waters Made Deep (vv.11-16)
The Descent, and the Tour of the Pit (vv.17-21)
Meshech and Tubal in the Pit (vv.26-28)
Sidon and the Princes of the North (v.30)
m: Pharaoh's funeral lament, the dragon caught in a net, cosmic darkness at Egypt's fall, descent to Sheol, the catalogue of dead empires, lying with the uncircumcised, the pit as equalizer, the terror of the nations silenced

x: This chapter marks the great turning point of the book. Ezekiel is recommissioned as a watchman, echoing his call in chapter 3, and God reaffirms that each person is judged by their own conduct: the wicked who repent will live, and the righteous who turn to sin will die (vv. 1-20). A fugitive then arrives from Jerusalem with news that the city has fallen, and that same evening Ezekiel's mouth is opened, ending his period of restrained speech (vv. 21-22). The chapter closes with God rebuking the people who flock to hear Ezekiel's words as if he were merely a skilled singer, yet never put his message into practice (vv. 30-33).
h: I Have No Pleasure in the Death of the Wicked (vv.10-20)
Hearers Who Treat It as Entertainment (vv.30-33)
m: The watchman's responsibility, individual moral accountability, "turn ye, turn ye!" — God's desire that the wicked live, the fugitive arrives with news of Jerusalem's fall, Ezekiel's silence broken, hearing without obeying, treating the prophet as entertainment

x: God pronounces judgment on the shepherds of Israel — its leaders — who have fed themselves rather than the flock, neglecting the weak, sick, injured, and scattered sheep (vv. 1-10). Because the shepherds have failed, God declares He will personally search for His sheep, gather them, and feed and heal them Himself (vv. 11-16). He also promises to judge between the fat and lean sheep, protecting the weak from being pushed aside by the strong (vv. 17-22), and to set up one shepherd over them, His servant David, under a covenant of peace that brings security and abundant blessing (vv. 23-31).
h: Woe to the Shepherds Who Feed Themselves (vv.1-6)
A Covenant of Peace, and Showers of Blessing (vv.25-31)
m: Failed leadership indicted, God as personal Shepherd, gathering the scattered, the messianic "David," covenant of peace, blessings restored

x: Ezekiel delivers an oracle against Mount Seir, the territory of Edom, declaring judgment because of Edom's perpetual hatred toward Israel and Judah and her violence against them in their time of calamity (vv. 1-9). Edom is condemned for claiming Israel and Judah's land as her own to possess, and for gloating that their desolation left the land hers to consume (vv. 10-13). Because Edom rejoiced over Israel's emptiness, God will make Edom herself a permanent desolation — the mountain that celebrated another's ruin will itself become ruined (vv. 14-15).
h: Perpetual Hatred, and the Blood Shed at the Calamity (vv.5-9)
m: Edom's perpetual hatred, gloating over Israel's fall, attempting to seize God's land, "These two nations shall be mine," blood-guilt, speaking against the mountains of Israel, God's jealousy for His land, perpetual desolation for perpetual hatred

x: God promises to restore both the land and the people of Israel, first addressing the mountains of Israel and promising they will again be cultivated and inhabited rather than mocked by neighboring nations (vv. 1-15). He then explains that restoration comes not because Israel deserves it, but for the sake of His own holy name, which their exile has profaned among the nations (vv. 16-23). In the most comprehensive new-covenant promise in the book, God pledges to sprinkle clean water on His people, give them a new heart and a new spirit in place of their heart of stone, and put His own Spirit within them so they walk in obedience to Him (vv. 24-32). The chapter closes with a vision of the land made fruitful again, like the garden of Eden (vv. 33-38).
h: To the Mountains of Israel, You Shall Yield Again (vv.1-15)
They Profaned My Name Among the Nations (vv.16-21)
Clean Water, a New Heart, a New Spirit (vv.25-27)
Land, Crops, Cities, and a Flock of Men (vv.28-38)
m: God's name profaned among nations, restoration for God's reputation (not Israel's merit), clean water sprinkled, new heart, new spirit, God's Spirit placed within, obedience enabled supernaturally, the land restored to Eden-like fertility

x: In the vision of the valley of dry bones, God sets Ezekiel down among a vast field of bones and asks whether they can live again (vv. 1-3). Ezekiel prophesies as commanded, and the bones come together, are covered with tendons, flesh, and skin, and finally receive breath from the Spirit, rising as a vast army (vv. 4-10). God interprets the vision: Israel in exile is like these dry bones, but He will open their graves and bring them back to their own land (vv. 11-14). Ezekiel then joins two sticks, representing Judah and Israel, into one piece of wood, symbolizing the reunification of the divided kingdom under one king from David's line (vv. 15-28).
h: One King, One Shepherd, One Everlasting Covenant (vv.24-28)
m: Resurrection of a dead nation, the Spirit as life-giver, national restoration from exile, reunification of divided Israel, one king (Messiah), the everlasting covenant

x: God directs Ezekiel to prophesy against Gog, of the land of Magog, chief prince of Meshech and Tubal (vv. 1-3). A massive coalition from the north — including Persia, Cush, Put, Gomer, and Beth-togarmah — will invade a restored, peaceful Israel in the latter years, drawn by the prospect of plunder (vv. 4-16). God declares that He Himself draws this army in, only to destroy it with earthquake, plague, and fire and brimstone, vindicating His holiness before all the watching nations (vv. 17-23).
h: The Thought That Comes into His Heart (vv.10-13)
That the Heathen May Know Me (vv.14-16)
m: God's sovereignty over hostile nations, the Gog-Magog invasion, divine protection of restored Israel, supernatural judgment, the vindication of God's holiness among the nations

x: The aftermath of Gog's catastrophic defeat is described in vivid detail. God rains destruction on Gog's armies across the mountains of Israel (vv. 1-6), and the devastation is so vast that birds and wild animals feast on the dead for months, Israel burns the enemy's weapons for fuel for seven years, and burial crews spend seven months cleansing the land of corpses (vv. 9-16). The chapter closes with God pouring out His Spirit on the house of Israel and declaring He will never again hide His face from them (vv. 25-29).
h: Seven Months of Burial, and Hamon-gog (vv.11-16)
The Feast for the Birds and Beasts (vv.17-20)
Restoration, and the Spirit Poured Out (vv.25-29)
m: The total destruction of Gog, God's provision from the spoils, the cleansing of the land, the sacrificial feast for birds and beasts, the outpouring of the Spirit, God's permanent faithfulness to Israel

x: In the twenty-fifth year of exile, around 573 BC, Ezekiel is transported in vision to a high mountain in Israel, where a man with a measuring rod and line reveals the dimensions of a magnificent future temple (vv. 1-4). The chapter measures the outer wall and the outer gates on the east, north, and south sides, then the outer court, and finally the inner gates leading to the inner court, laying the framework for the most detailed temple blueprint in Scripture (vv. 5-49).
h: The Date, the Mountain and the Man with the Line (vv.1-4)
The Wall, and the East Gate (vv.5-16)
The Outer Court, and the North and South Gates (vv.17-27)
The Chambers for the Singers, and the Porch (vv.44-49)
m: The future temple, divine measurement and order, holiness expressed in architecture, God's intention to dwell among His people permanently, the precision of God's plans

x: The angelic guide leads Ezekiel deeper into the temple, measuring the inner sanctuary — the holy place and the most holy place (vv. 1-4). The chapter details the surrounding side chambers, the wall decorations of alternating cherubim and palm trees, the wooden altar before the LORD, and the structure at the temple's western end (vv. 5-26). This inner sanctuary is the heart of God's dwelling, the place where heaven meets earth.
h: The Vestibule of the Temple Proper (vv.1-2)
The Most Holy Place Measured, and Not Entered (vv.3-4)
The Side Chambers, in Three Stories (vv.5-11)
Cherubim and Palm Trees on Every Wall (vv.15b-21)
The Wooden Altar Called the Table Before the LORD (v.22)
m: The holy place and most holy place dimensions, the sacred progression from outer to inner, cherubim and palm tree decorations symbolizing Eden restored, the wooden altar as "the table before the LORD"

x: The angelic guide measures the priests' chambers, rooms on the north and south sides of the temple complex where the priests eat the most holy offerings and change out of their sacred garments before entering the outer court (vv. 1-14). The chapter concludes with the overall dimensions of the entire temple enclosure — five hundred reeds square, roughly a mile per side — with a wall separating the holy area from the common (vv. 15-20).
h: The Outer Dimensions, and the Wall Between (vv.15-20)
m: The distinction between holy and common, priestly provisions for ministry, garments of holiness, the separation wall protecting sacred space, God's meticulous care for those who serve Him

x: In the climactic moment of Ezekiel's prophecy, the glory of the LORD — the same glory that departed Jerusalem through the east gate in chapters 10-11 — returns from the east and fills the new temple (vv. 1-5). God declares this to be the place of His throne, where He will dwell among the people of Israel forever, if they put away their idolatry and unfaithfulness (vv. 6-12). The chapter then gives the dimensions and consecration instructions for the great altar of burnt offering, including a seven-day ordination ceremony (vv. 13-27).
h: The Glory Returns from the East (vv.1-5)
This Is My Throne, and My Holy Name (vv.6-9)
Show the House to Israel, That They May Be Ashamed (vv.10-12)
Seven Days to Consecrate the Altar (vv.18-27)
m: The glory of God returning, permanent divine indwelling, God's throne established forever, the altar of burnt offering dimensions and consecration, the call to repentance through the vision of holiness

x: Because the glory has returned through the east gate, God now commands that this gate remain permanently shut, since the LORD Himself has entered by it and it may never be used again (vv. 1-3). The chapter then establishes who may serve in the temple: Levites who strayed into idolatry are demoted to menial duties, while the faithful sons of Zadok alone are permitted to minister at the altar (vv. 4-16). Detailed regulations follow for the priests' clothing, conduct, marriages, and teaching responsibilities, along with their portion of support from the people's offerings (vv. 17-31).
h: The East Gate Shut for Good (vv.1-3)
m: The permanently closed east gate, consequences of faithfulness and unfaithfulness, the Zadokite priesthood elevated, priestly holiness standards, teaching the difference between holy and common

x: God commands that a holy district be set apart within the promised land — a sacred reserve for the temple, the priests, the Levites, and the city — with the prince receiving land on either side of this district (vv. 1-8). The chapter then establishes honest weights and measures, correcting the economic corruption condemned earlier in the book, and prescribes the prince's duty to provide offerings for the appointed feasts, including Passover and the Feast of Tabernacles (vv. 9-25).
h: The Holy Portion of the Land (vv.1-6)
The Offerings Brought to the Prince (vv.13-17)
m: The holy district (sacred geography), just weights and measures, the prince's responsibility for public worship, the restored feasts, God's concern for economic justice alongside spiritual faithfulness

x: This chapter prescribes worship regulations for the prince and the people: Sabbath and new-moon offerings, the opening of the inner east gate specifically for the prince's worship, and directional rules requiring worshipers to exit by a different gate than they entered (vv. 1-10). It also sets out inheritance laws protecting the people's land from being permanently seized by the prince (vv. 16-18) and describes the daily morning burnt offering along with the kitchens where offerings are cooked (vv. 19-24) — the rhythms of worship in God's restored kingdom.
h: The Inner East Gate Opened on Sabbaths (vv.1-3)
In at One Gate, Out at the Other (vv.9-10)
The Prince May Not Take an Inheritance (vv.16-18)
m: Ordered worship rhythms (Sabbath, new moon, daily), the prince's regulated access, the protection of the people's inheritance, the continuous burnt offering, God's concern for both worship and justice in daily governance

x: One of the most striking visions in Scripture: a river flows out from beneath the threshold of the temple, running eastward and growing deeper the farther Ezekiel wades — ankle-deep, knee-deep, waist-deep, and finally too deep to cross (vv. 1-12). The river flows into the Dead Sea and heals its waters, bringing abundant life where before there was only death, and trees line its banks whose leaves never wither and whose fruit never fails, providing food and healing. The chapter closes by marking out the boundaries of the promised land for the restored twelve tribes (vv. 13-23).
h: The Water from Under the Threshold (vv.1-2)
Ankles, Knees, Loins, and Then Swimming (vv.3-5)
Everything Lives Where the River Goes (vv.6-10)
The Stranger Shall Have an Inheritance (vv.21-23)
m: The river of God flowing from His presence, life conquering death, healing of the Dead Sea, supernatural fruitfulness, the boundaries of the restored land, inclusion of sojourners in the inheritance

x: The final chapter of Ezekiel divides the promised land among the twelve tribes in parallel horizontal strips running east to west, with the holy district — containing the temple, the priests' territory, the Levites' territory, and the city — placed at the center (vv. 1-29). The chapter, and the book, close by naming the city's twelve gates after each tribe and giving the city itself a new name meaning the LORD is there (vv. 30-35), a final declaration that after judgment, exile, and restoration, God's abiding presence with His people is now guaranteed.
h: Seven Tribes North of the Holy Portion (vv.1-7)
The Holy Portion, the City, and the Prince's Land (vv.8-22)
Five Tribes South of the Holy Portion (vv.23-29)
Twelve Gates, Named for the Tribes (vv.30-34)
The Name of the City, The LORD Is There (v.35)
m: The equal distribution of the land, the holy district at the nation's center, all twelve tribes restored, God's permanent presence as the nation's defining identity, YHWH- Shammah — "The LORD Is There"

x: In the third year of King Jehoiakim, Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem and carries Daniel and three fellow Hebrew youths into captivity (vv. 1-4). Chosen for three years of training in Babylon's language and literature, they are assigned rich food and wine from the king's table, but Daniel resolves not to defile himself and asks for a ten-day trial of vegetables and water instead (vv. 5-14). At the trial's end the four look healthier than those on the royal diet, so their plain fare continues (vv. 15-16). God gives them knowledge and skill in every branch of learning, and gives Daniel understanding of visions and dreams (v. 17). When presented to Nebuchadnezzar, the four are found ten times wiser than all the magicians and enchanters in his kingdom (vv. 18-20), and Daniel remains in royal service until the first year of King Cyrus (v. 21).
h: Babylon Takes Jerusalem, and the Vessels (vv.1-2)
m: Faithfulness in exile, God's sovereignty over nations, divine wisdom surpassing pagan knowledge, the test of compromise, identity preservation under pressure

x: Nebuchadnezzar is troubled by a dream and demands that his wise men both describe and interpret it or be executed; when they cannot, Daniel asks for time and, after praying with his three friends, receives the mystery in a night vision (vv. 1-19). Daniel praises God for revealing hidden things (vv. 20-23) before describing the king's dream: an immense statue with a head of gold, chest and arms of silver, belly and thighs of bronze, legs of iron, and feet of iron mixed with clay, struck and shattered by a stone cut from a mountain without human hands (vv. 31-35). Daniel interprets the metals as a succession of four kingdoms, the last divided and partly strong, partly brittle (vv. 36-43), while the stone represents a kingdom God will set up that will never be destroyed and will endure forever (vv. 44-45). Nebuchadnezzar falls before Daniel, acknowledges his God, and elevates Daniel and…
h: Daniel Asks for Time, and for Prayer (vv.14-18)
Blessed Be the Name of God For Ever (vv.19-23)
There Is a God in Heaven (vv.24-30)
The Image of Gold, Silver, Brass, Iron (vv.31-35)
m: God's sovereignty over world history, the four world empires, the divine kingdom that destroys all others, God as revealer of mysteries, human kingdoms as temporary

x: Nebuchadnezzar sets up a gold statue on the plain of Dura and commands everyone to bow down to it when the music sounds, on pain of death in a blazing furnace (vv. 1-7). Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refuse, telling the king that the God they serve can deliver them, but that even if He does not, they will still not worship the image (vv. 12-18). Enraged, Nebuchadnezzar has the furnace heated seven times hotter and the three thrown in bound, killing the soldiers who cast them in (vv. 19-22). The king then sees four men walking unbound in the flames, the fourth having the appearance of a divine being, and calls the three out unharmed, without even the smell of smoke on them (vv. 23-27). Nebuchadnezzar praises their God and decrees that no one may speak against Him, then promotes the three in the province of Babylon (vv. 28-30).
h: The Image on the Plain of Dura (vv.1-7)
Seven Times Hotter, and a Fourth in the Fire (vv.19-25)
Not a Hair Singed; the King's Decree (vv.26-30)
m: Idolatry vs. true worship, courage under threat of death, God's presence in the fire (not just from it), the fourth man, faithfulness regardless of outcome

x: Nebuchadnezzar issues this chapter as his own decree to all peoples, testifying to what the Most High has done for him (vv. 1-3). He recounts a dream of a great tree reaching to heaven, visible to the whole earth and sheltering every creature, which a holy watcher orders cut down, leaving only a stump bound with iron and bronze (vv. 4-17). Daniel alone can interpret it: the tree is the king himself, who will be driven from human society to live like an animal for seven periods of time until he acknowledges that the Most High rules over every kingdom and gives it to whomever He wishes (vv. 18-27). Twelve months later, as Nebuchadnezzar boasts over Babylon, the judgment falls exactly as foretold (vv. 28-33). At the end of the appointed time his reason returns, and he blesses and praises God, whose kingdom is everlasting and who is able to humble the proud (vv. 34-37).
h: Twelve Months Later: Is Not This Great Babylon? (vv.28-33)
I Lifted Up Mine Eyes unto Heaven (vv.34-37)
m: Divine humbling of the proud, God's sovereignty over all rulers, the danger of pride, madness as divine judgment, restoration after humbling, the stump of hope

x: Belshazzar throws a great feast and, in his drunkenness, orders the gold and silver vessels taken from Jerusalem's temple be brought in so his guests can drink from them while praising idols of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone (vv. 1-4). A hand suddenly appears and writes on the palace wall, terrifying the king, whose wise men cannot read or explain it (vv. 5-9). At the queen's suggestion Daniel is summoned; he refuses the offered rewards but reads the words MENE, MENE, TEKEL, and PARSIN, declaring that God has numbered the days of Belshazzar's kingdom and brought it to an end, weighed the king and found him lacking, and is dividing his kingdom between the Medes and Persians (vv. 10-28). That very night Belshazzar is killed, and Darius the Mede takes the kingdom (vv. 30-31).
h: Belshazzar's Feast and the Holy Vessels (vv.1-4)
m: The sacrilege of misusing holy things, God's patience running out, divine judgment weighed and measured, the suddenness of divine reckoning, the fall of empires in a single night

x: Under Darius the Mede, Daniel so distinguishes himself as one of three administrators that the king plans to set him over the whole kingdom, provoking jealous rivals to search for a charge against him (vv. 1-4). Finding nothing but his faithfulness to God, they persuade Darius to sign an irrevocable decree forbidding prayer to anyone but the king for thirty days (vv. 5-9). Daniel continues praying toward Jerusalem three times a day as always and is caught and reported, and though troubled, Darius is bound by his own law and has him thrown into the lions' den (vv. 10-18). At dawn Daniel is found unharmed, explaining that God sent an angel to shut the lions' mouths because he was found innocent before Him (vv. 19-23). His accusers and their families are thrown to the lions instead, and Darius decrees that all his subjects must fear the God of Daniel (vv. 24-27).
h: No Fault, Except Concerning His God (vv.4-9)
He Prayed as He Did Aforetime (vv.10-13)
The King Trapped by His Own Law (vv.14-18)
Is Thy God Able to Deliver Thee? (vv.19-24)
m: Faithfulness in prayer despite persecution, God's power over nature, the failure of evil schemes against God's servants, integrity that provokes jealousy, civil disobedience for God's glory

x: In the first year of Belshazzar, Daniel has a night vision of four great beasts rising from a storm-tossed sea: a lion with eagle's wings, a bear raised up on one side, a four-headed winged leopard, and a dreadful, iron-toothed beast with ten horns, among which a boastful little horn rises and uproots three others (vv. 1-8). The scene shifts to heaven, where the Ancient of Days takes His throne amid fire and thousands of attendants, the court sits, and the fourth beast is slain and its body destroyed, while the other beasts have their dominion taken away but their lives extended for a time (vv. 9-12). One like a son of man then comes with the clouds of heaven and is given everlasting dominion, glory, and a kingdom that all peoples will serve and that will never be destroyed (vv. 13-14). Troubled, Daniel asks a heavenly attendant to explain, and is told the four beasts are four kings…
h: Four Beasts Out of the Sea (vv.1-8)
The Ancient of Days Takes His Seat (vv.9-12)
One Like the Son of Man (vv.13-14)
The Fourth Beast and the Little Horn (vv.19-25)
The Kingdom Given to the Saints (vv.26-28)
m: The four world empires as beasts, the Ancient of Days, the Son of Man receiving the kingdom, the little horn's blasphemy, God's ultimate victory, saints possessing the kingdom

x: In the third year of Belshazzar, Daniel sees a two-horned ram, representing Media and Persia, charging west, north, and south unopposed, until a swift goat with a single great horn, representing Greece, comes from the west and shatters it (vv. 1-7, 20-21). At the height of the goat's power its great horn breaks and four horns rise in its place, representing four kingdoms that follow Alexander (vv. 8, 22). From one of these grows a small horn that grows exceedingly great toward the Beautiful Land, throws down some of the stars, magnifies itself against the Prince of the host, halts the daily sacrifice, and desecrates the sanctuary for 2,300 evenings and mornings before it is finally broken (vv. 9-12, 23-25). Daniel is told this refers to a fierce, deceitful king still far in the future — traditionally identified with Antiochus Epiphanes — and is instructed to seal up the vision, since it…
h: The Goat from the West, and the Broken Horn (vv.5-8)
The Little Horn and the Trampled Sanctuary (vv.9-12)
How Long? Two Thousand Three Hundred Days (vv.13-14)
m: The Medo-Persian and Greek empires, Alexander the Great, the four successor kingdoms, Antiochus Epiphanes as a type of Antichrist, the desecration and restoration of the temple, the sovereignty of God over future history

x: In the first year of Darius, Daniel studies Jeremiah's prophecy that Jerusalem's desolation will last seventy years and responds with fasting and a long prayer confessing Israel's sin and pleading for God's mercy on the city and His people (vv. 1-19). While he is still praying, the angel Gabriel arrives and announces a prophecy of seventy sets of seven years decreed for Daniel's people and holy city, to finish transgression, atone for sin, and bring in everlasting righteousness (vv. 20-24). Sixty-nine of those sevens will pass, from the command to rebuild Jerusalem until an anointed ruler comes, after which the Anointed One will be cut off and the city and sanctuary destroyed by the people of a coming ruler (vv. 25-26). That ruler will make a firm covenant for one final seven, but in the middle of it will put an end to sacrifice and offering and set up an abomination, until the decreed…
h: The Plea: For Thine Own Sake (vv.15-19)
m: Corporate confession and repentance, the power of Scripture-driven prayer, God's faithfulness to His word, the precise timeline to Messiah, the cost of sin and the price of atonement, prophetic timetables

x: In the third year of Cyrus, Daniel mourns and fasts for three weeks while seeking understanding of a vision, eating no rich food, meat, or wine (vv. 1-3). Beside the Tigris he sees an overwhelming, radiant heavenly figure that leaves his companions fleeing in terror and leaves him drained of strength, until a hand touches him and steadies him (vv. 4-10). The figure tells Daniel that his prayer was heard on the first day he began seeking understanding, but that the messenger was resisted for twenty-one days by the ruling spirit over the kingdom of Persia, until Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help him (vv. 11-14). Daniel is left speechless and weak, but is strengthened by a touch and told not to be afraid, for he is highly valued (vv. 15-19). The messenger says he must now return to fight against the princes of Persia and Greece, with only Michael standing with him, before…
h: From the First Day Thy Words Were Heard (vv.10-14)
Strengthened Twice, and Told to Be Strong (vv.15-19)
The Prince of Persia, and Michael (vv.20-21)
m: The reality of spiritual warfare, demonic territorial powers, angelic hierarchy (Michael as chief prince), the connection between prayer and heavenly conflict, God's immediate response vs. delayed answer, the invisible war behind visible history

x: An angel reveals to Daniel a long, detailed forecast of conflict between a line of Persian kings and a mighty Greek king, whose empire will fracture into four after his death rather than pass to his descendants (vv. 1-4). The bulk of the chapter traces generations of warfare and shifting alliances between a king of the South (Ptolemaic Egypt) and a king of the North (Seleucid Syria), including invasions, marriages, and betrayals (vv. 5-20). It then focuses at length on a contemptible king who seizes the northern throne through intrigue, invades Egypt, turns back against the holy covenant, desecrates the temple fortress, abolishes the daily sacrifice, and sets up an abomination, while flattering some of God's people into apostasy and driving others to resist and suffer for their faith (vv. 21-35). The narrative then turns to a self-exalting king who honors no god but himself, meets…
h: Persia and the Mighty King of Greece (vv.1-4)
Kings of the South and North (vv.5-20)
A Vile Person Rises by Flattery (vv.21-24)
m: God's foreknowledge of all history, the wars of the Ptolemies and Seleucids, Antiochus Epiphanes as persecutor and type of Antichrist, the faithfulness of "the people that do know their God," the ultimate end-times king of pride

x: At that time, Michael, the great prince who watches over Israel, will arise during a time of distress unmatched in history, and everyone whose name is found written in the book will be delivered (v. 1). The dead will be raised, some to everlasting life and some to shame and everlasting contempt, and the wise who lead others to righteousness will shine like the stars forever (vv. 2-3). Daniel is told to seal up the scroll until the time of the end, when knowledge will increase (v. 4). Asked how long until these wonders are fulfilled, Daniel is told it will be for a time, times, and half a time, ending when the power of the holy people is fully shattered (vv. 5-7). Though he does not understand, Daniel is told the words are sealed until the end, when the wicked will keep acting wickedly but the wise will understand; he is given the numbers 1,290 and 1,335 days, with blessing on those who…
h: They That Be Wise Shall Shine (v.3)
Seal the Book Until the Time of the End (v.4)
How Long? A Time, Times and an Half (vv.5-13)
m: The great tribulation, bodily resurrection, eternal destinies (life vs. contempt), the sealed book, the blessing of patient waiting, Daniel's personal assurance of resurrection, the wise shining like stars

x: Hosea is commanded to marry Gomer, a promiscuous woman, as a living picture of Israel's unfaithfulness to the LORD during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah (vv. 1-3). Their first son, Jezreel, signals coming judgment on the house of Jehu for the bloodshed at Jezreel (vv. 4-5). A daughter, Lo-ruhamah, meaning no mercy, marks God's withdrawal of compassion from Israel (vv. 6-7). A second son, Lo-ammi, meaning not my people, declares the nation is no longer God's covenant people (vv. 8-9). The chapter closes with a reversal: Israel's descendants will become as numerous as the sand of the sea and will again be called children of the living God, reunited with Judah under one head (vv. 10-11).
h: First Child: Jezreel, Judgment on Jehu's House (vv.4-5)
Third Child: Lo-ammi, Not My People (vv.8-9)
m: Spiritual adultery of Israel, God's judgment through symbolic names, the coming restoration despite unfaithfulness, covenant love that persists through betrayal

x: Hosea depicts Israel as an unfaithful wife pursuing other lovers, the Baals, while God is the wronged husband (vv. 1-5). Because she credited her grain, wine, oil, and wealth to Baal rather than to the LORD who actually gave them, God threatens to strip her, expose her lovers as false, and end her feasts and celebrations (vv. 6-13). Yet the chapter turns from judgment to restoration: God will allure her into the wilderness and speak tenderly to her, turning the Valley of Achor into a door of hope (vv. 14-15). She will call God "my husband" instead of "my Baal," and he will betroth her forever in righteousness, justice, steadfast love, and faithfulness (vv. 16-20). The chapter closes with a reversal of the ominous names from chapter 1 — Israel, once called "No Mercy" and "Not My People," will be shown mercy and called "my people," and will answer, "you are my God" (vv. 21-23).
h: The Accusation Against the Unfaithful Wife (vv.1-5)
God's Discipline: Hedging Her Way with Thorns (vv.6-13)
The Great Restoration: Reversal of Judgment Names (vv.21-23)
m: Spiritual adultery exposed, the discipline of love, God's relentless pursuit, covenant renewal and betrothal, the reversal of judgment names

x: God instructs Hosea to seek out and love his wife again, even though she is loved by another man, as a living picture of the LORD's love for Israel despite their turning to other gods (v. 1). Hosea buys her back for fifteen shekels of silver and a measure and a half of barley (v. 2), then tells her she must live with him many days without engaging in prostitution, and he will do likewise toward her (v. 3). This mirrors Israel's coming fate: for many days the nation will have no king, no sacrifice, no idol, and no means of divination (v. 4). But afterward Israel will return and seek the LORD their God and David their king, coming in awe to the LORD and his goodness in the last days (v. 5).
h: The Purchase: Buying Back the Adulterous Wife (v.2)
The Prophetic Parallel: Israel's Long Exile (v.4)
The Promise: Return in the Latter Days (v.5)
m: Redeeming love, the cost of restoration, the long waiting period, future return to the LORD and David's King

x: The LORD brings a legal complaint against Israel because there is no faithfulness, steadfast love, or knowledge of God in the land, only swearing, lying, murder, theft, and adultery (vv. 1-2). As a result the land itself mourns and its creatures waste away (v. 3). God specifically indicts the priests for failing to teach his law, declaring "my people are destroyed for lack of knowledge" and that because they rejected knowledge, he will reject them from serving as priests (vv. 4-6). The people consult wooden idols and are led astray by a spirit of prostitution, sacrificing on hilltops and under trees while their daughters and daughters-in-law fall into sexual sin (vv. 11-13). God warns Judah not to follow Ephraim's example, since Ephraim is joined to idols and given over to stubbornness, drunkenness, and shameless sin (vv. 15-19).
h: Warning to Judah: Do Not Follow Israel (vv.15-19)
m: God's lawsuit against His people, failed priesthood, destruction through ignorance, the spirit of whoredom, like people like priest, creation groaning under human sin

x: God pronounces judgment on Israel's priests, people, and royal house, calling them a snare and a net that has trapped the nation in rebellion (vv. 1-2). Their spirit of prostitution keeps them from knowing the LORD, and Israel's arrogance testifies against them as both Israel and Judah stumble in guilt (vv. 3-5). When they finally seek the LORD with their flocks and herds it will be too late, since he has withdrawn from them because of their unfaithfulness (vv. 6-7). Alarms sound across Ephraim and Judah as God, like a moth or dry rot, slowly consumes them, and Ephraim's turn to Assyria for help proves powerless to heal their wound (vv. 8-13). God declares he will be like a lion tearing his prey and will then withdraw to his place until the people acknowledge their guilt and earnestly seek his face in their distress (vv. 14-15).
h: Triple Indictment: Priests, Israel, Royal House (vv.1-7)
m: God as a lion and a moth, failed alliances with Assyria, pride as the root of destruction, God withdrawing until repentance, seeking God in distress

x: The chapter opens with what appears to be Israel's call to return to the LORD, confidently expecting him to heal what he has torn and to revive them after a short time (vv. 1-3). God responds that their love is fickle, like a morning cloud or dew that vanishes quickly, and that he has used the prophets' words to cut them down in judgment (vv. 4-5). He declares his true desire: steadfast love rather than sacrifice, and knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings (v. 6). Instead they have broken the covenant like Adam, and priests and people alike are stained with treachery and murder (vv. 7-10). The chapter closes noting that a harvest of judgment is appointed for Judah as well, whenever God restores the fortunes of his people (v. 11).
h: God's Lament: Your Love is Like Morning Dew (v.4)
God's True Desire: Mercy, Not Sacrifice (vv.5-6)
m: False repentance that evaporates, the third-day resurrection, God's desire for mercy over sacrifice, the knowledge of God, covenant breaking like Adam

x: Whenever God moves to heal Israel, their sin only becomes more exposed: they deal falsely, thieves break in, and bandits raid outside while the leaders drink themselves sick alongside their princes and scoffers (vv. 1-5). Their hearts burn like a baker's oven, hot with adultery and treachery that consumes their rulers, so that all their kings have fallen and no one calls on the LORD (vv. 6-7). Ephraim is compared to a cake left unturned on the griddle and to a silly, senseless dove flitting between Egypt and Assyria for help instead of seeking God (vv. 8-11). God will spread a net to capture them as discipline, and pronounces woe on them for wailing over grain and wine rather than crying to him from the heart (vv. 12-14). Though he trained and strengthened them, they plot evil against him, turning to worthless alliances so that their princes will fall by the sword and become an object…
h: The Oven: Political Conspiracy and Regicide (vv.3-7)
The Silly Dove: Flitting Between Empires (vv.11-12)
God's Lament: I Would Redeem, But They Rebel (vv.13-16)
m: Internal corruption, political instability, alliances with pagan nations, self-deception and unawareness of decay, God's frustrated love

x: God sounds the alarm like a trumpet, an eagle circling because Israel has broken his covenant and transgressed his law even while claiming to know him (vv. 1-3).
