They set up kings and princes without God's approval and made idols of silver and gold that will lead to their own ruin, including the calf-idol of Samaria that God's anger burns against (vv. 4-6). Having sown the wind, they will reap the whirlwind — their labor yields nothing, and what little it produces will be devoured by foreigners (v. 7). Israel is swallowed up among the nations, having gone to Assyria for help like a wandering donkey and multiplied both alliances and altars, yet all of it only increases their sin (vv. 8-11). Though God wrote out his law for them, they treat it as something foreign, offering sacrifices he will not accept, and Ephraim has forgotten its Maker in favor of building palaces and fortified cities…
h: Sowing the Wind, Reaping the Whirlwind (vv.7-8)
m: Covenant violation, self-made religion, sowing and reaping, forgotten Maker, useless among the nations, the folly of idolatry

x: Hosea warns Israel not to rejoice like other nations, since they have played the prostitute, loving the wages of idolatry more than the LORD, and their harvests and wine will fail (vv. 1-2). Because of this they will not remain in the land but will be scattered to Assyria and Egypt, eating unclean food and unable to worship at the LORD's house (vv. 3-6). The days of punishment have come, and Israel treats God's prophet as a fool and a madman because of the depth of their sin, corrupted as in the days of Gibeah (vv. 7-9). God recalls finding Israel like grapes in the wilderness, but they turned to Baal at Peor and became as detestable as the thing they loved, so their glory will fly away like a bird, leaving them without children (vv. 10-12). The chapter ends with God declaring he will give Ephraim a miscarrying womb and dry breasts because of their wickedness at Gilgal, and Ephraim…
h: No Joy for Israel: The Harvest Will Fail (vv.1-6)
The Days of Punishment Are Here (vv.7-9)
God's Memory: Once Beloved, Now Corrupt (v.10)
m: False joy in harvest festivals, exile from the LORD's land, barrenness as judgment, God's departure, wanderers among nations, past love turned to present grief

x: Israel is described as a lush vine whose growing prosperity only produced more altars and idols, leaving their hearts false and deserving judgment (vv. 1-2). They will admit they have no king because they do not fear the LORD, breaking covenants and letting injustice spring up like poisonous weeds (vv. 3-4). Their calf-idol at Beth-aven will be carried off to Assyria as tribute, and Samaria's king will vanish like a chip of wood on the water, prompting the people to beg the mountains to fall on them and hide their shame (vv. 5-8). God recalls their sin since the days of Gibeah and vows to discipline them for their double iniquity, comparing them to a trained heifer that must now be yoked to hard labor (vv. 9-11). He calls them to break up their fallow ground, sow righteousness, and seek the LORD, since they have instead plowed iniquity and eaten the fruit of lies (vv. 12-13). The…
h: The Luxuriant Vine: Prosperity Breeds Idolatry (vv.1-2)
The Calf Departs: Idols Carried Away (vv.5-8)
The Call: Sow Righteousness, Seek the LORD (vv.9-12)
m: Prosperity misused for idolatry, divided hearts, fallow ground, sowing and reaping, trusting in military might, the call to seek the LORD

x: God recalls his tender fatherly love for Israel from its infancy, calling his son out of Egypt, yet the more he called them the more they wandered off to sacrifice to the Baals (vv. 1-2). He describes teaching Ephraim to walk, healing them, and leading them with cords of kindness and bands of love, though they never recognized his care (vv. 3-4). Because they refuse to return to him, they will instead return to bondage under Assyria, and the sword will devastate their cities as a result of their own schemes (vv. 5-7). Yet God's compassion overrules his anger: he cannot bring himself to give Ephraim up or destroy them like Admah and Zeboiim, since he is God and not man, the Holy One who will not come in wrath (vv. 8-9). The chapter ends with a promise that the people will one day follow the LORD as he roars like a lion, and his children will come trembling home from Egypt and Assyria to…
h: God's Heart Torn: How Can I Give You Up (vv.8-9)
m: God as Father, the pain of unrequited parental love, divine compassion overcoming divine wrath, "I am God and not man," the call from Egypt, future restoration

x: Ephraim is pictured chasing after the wind, multiplying lies and violence, and making alliances with Assyria and Egypt instead of trusting God, while the LORD also brings a charge against Judah (vv. 1-2). God contrasts Israel's present deceit with their ancestor Jacob, who wrestled with his brother in the womb and later strove with God himself, weeping and seeking his favor until he prevailed (vv. 3-4). This becomes the basis for the call to Israel: return to your God, hold on to love and justice, and wait continually for him (vv. 5-6). Yet Ephraim uses dishonest scales and boasts of wealth gained through oppression, insisting no one can find sin in him, even though God has repeatedly warned them through the prophets (vv. 7-10). Their worship at Gilgal and Gilead is denounced as worthless, and the chapter closes recalling how a prophet once brought Israel out of Egypt and guarded them…
h: Ephraim Feeds on Wind: Useless Alliances (v.1)
God's Case Against Jacob and Judah (vv.2-6)
The Jacob Parallel: Served for a Wife (vv.12-13)
m: Feeding on wind, the Jacob story as model and warning, false balances and self-deception, the ministry of prophets, the call to return

x: God recalls that Ephraim once held a position of honor in Israel, but incurred guilt through Baal worship and effectively died (v. 1). Their sin has only grown worse, making metal idols and kissing calf images, so they will vanish like morning mist, dew, or chaff blown away (vv. 2-3). God reminds them he alone has been their God and savior since Egypt, the one who knew and fed them in the wilderness, yet their hearts grew proud and forgot him (vv. 4-6). As a result he will attack them like a lion, leopard, or bear robbed of her cubs, since the kings and rulers they demanded instead of him cannot save them (vv. 7-11). Ephraim's guilt is stored up, and though God pictures the pain of childbirth as a chance for new life, they prove an unwise child who will not be born at the right time (vv. 12-13). The chapter turns to a striking question — "O death, where are your plagues? O grave, where…
h: God's Exclusive Claim: No Saviour Beside Me (vv.4-6)
God as Predator: Lion, Leopard, Bear (vv.7-8)
Sin Stored Up and Birth Pangs Coming (vv.12-13)
The East Wind of Judgment on Samaria (vv.15-16)
m: The progression from exaltation to death through Baal, God as lion/leopard/bear, self-destruction vs. divine help, the defeat of death, the east wind of judgment

x: The book closes with a call for Israel to return to the LORD, since their sin has caused their downfall, and to bring words of genuine repentance instead of empty ritual (vv. 1-2). They are told to stop trusting Assyria, horses, or the work of their own hands, since only in God does the fatherless find mercy (v. 3). In response, God promises to heal their unfaithfulness and love them freely, no longer angry with them (v. 4). He pictures Israel flourishing again like a lily, taking root like the cedars of Lebanon, spreading out with beauty and fragrance, and living fruitfully in his shade (vv. 5-8). The book ends with a wisdom appeal: whoever is wise should understand these things, for the ways of the LORD are right, and the righteous walk in them while transgressors stumble (v. 9).
h: The Final Call: Return to the LORD (vv.1-3)
m: The call to return, words of repentance, God's free love, healing of backsliding, Israel as a flourishing tree, the wisdom of walking in God's ways

x: Joel opens with the word of the Lord describing a locust plague so severe that successive swarms strip the land bare, an event unlike anything the older generation has seen (vv. 1-4). He calls drunkards to weep because the wine supply is cut off, and pictures the land mourning like a young bride grieving her husband, with grain and drink offerings halted at the temple (vv. 5-10). Farmers and vinedressers are told to despair over ruined crops, and priests are urged to lament, call a fast, and gather the people to cry out to the Lord because the great and terrible Day of the Lord is near (vv. 11-15). The chapter closes with a picture of starving livestock and scorched pastures, and Joel himself cries out to God over the devastation caused by drought and fire (vv. 16-20).
h: The Unprecedented Plague: Tell Your Children (vv.1-4)
Call to Mourn: Drunkards, Priests, Farmers (vv.5-12)
Call to Fast and Cry Out (vv.13-14)
The Day of the LORD Is Near (vv.15-18)
Joel's Prayer: Creation Cries to God (vv.19-20)
m: Unprecedented devastation, the call to mourn and fast, creation groaning, the Day of the LORD approaching, total economic and agricultural collapse

x: Joel sounds the alarm that the Day of the Lord is coming, describing an overwhelming army — likely the locust swarm intensified into a picture of invading forces — that darkens the sun and moon and leaves the land like Eden before it and a wasteland behind it (vv. 1-11). God calls the people to return to Him with fasting, weeping, and mourning, urging them to tear their hearts rather than their garments, since He is gracious, merciful, and slow to anger (vv. 12-14). Joel instructs the priests to gather the whole community, including the very young and old, and to intercede for the land (vv. 15-17). In response, the Lord promises to restore the grain, wine, and oil lost to the locusts, to remove the northern army, and to fill His people with abundance (vv. 18-27). The chapter closes with God's promise to pour out His Spirit on all people — sons, daughters, old and young, servants alike —…
h: The Terrifying Army of the LORD (vv.1-11)
Rend Your Hearts, Not Your Garments (vv.12-17)
Signs Before the Day of the LORD (vv.30-31)
m: The invading army (literal/eschatological), rending the heart, God's compassion and relenting, restoration of lost years, the outpouring of the Spirit on all flesh, calling on the name of the LORD

x: When the Lord restores the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem, He will gather all nations into the Valley of Jehoshaphat to judge them for scattering Israel and dividing up its land, including selling captives for slaves and trading children for wine (vv. 1-8). Nations are summoned to prepare for war and beat their farm tools into weapons, but this is actually a call to God's own judgment, since He is the one who will sit to judge them all in the valley (vv. 9-14). The sun, moon, and stars grow dark and the earth shakes as the Lord roars from Zion, yet He remains a refuge for His people (vv. 15-16). Israel will then know the Lord dwells in Zion, and the land will overflow with abundance while Egypt and Edom become desolate for the violence done to Judah (vv. 17-19). The book closes with the promise that Judah and Jerusalem will endure forever, cleansed and secure, because the Lord dwells…
h: God Gathers the Nations to Judgment (vv.1-3)
The Call to War: Nations Against God (vv.9-12)
m: Judgment on nations for mistreating Israel, the Valley of Jehoshaphat, plowshares into swords (reversed), multitudes in the valley of decision, God as refuge, eternal Jerusalem

x: Amos, a shepherd from Tekoa, receives this vision concerning Israel two years before an earthquake, opening with the LORD roaring from Zion (vv. 1-2). He then pronounces judgment on five surrounding nations one by one, using the repeated formula "for three transgressions ... and for four": Damascus for brutalizing Gilead (vv. 3-5), Gaza and Tyre for exiling whole communities into slavery (vv. 6-10), Edom for pursuing his brother Israel with the sword (vv. 11-12), and Ammon for ripping open pregnant women in Gilead (vv. 13-15). Each oracle promises fire that will consume the nation's strongholds and send its king into exile.
h: Amos of Tekoa, Two Years Before the Earthquake (v.1)
m: Universal divine justice, crimes against humanity, the "for three... and for four" formula, fire as judgment, God holds all nations accountable regardless of covenant relationship

x: The judgment oracles continue against Moab, condemned for desecrating the bones of Edom's king (vv. 1-3), and against Judah for rejecting the LORD's law (vv. 4-5). The cycle then closes on Israel itself: sellers trade the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals, and trample the poor into the dust (vv. 6-8). God recalls how He destroyed the Amorites before them and brought Israel out of Egypt, raising up prophets and Nazirites, only to have Israel silence the prophets and corrupt the Nazirites with wine (vv. 9-12). As a result, the LORD declares that not even the swiftest or strongest will escape His judgment on that day (vv. 13-16).
h: I Brought You Up Out of Egypt (vv.9-12)
m: Judgment on Moab and Judah, the climactic indictment of Israel, selling the poor, oppressing the afflicted, silencing prophets, ingratitude for divine deliverance, inescapable judgment

x: God declares that Israel's unique relationship with Him brings greater accountability, not exemption, so He will punish all their sins (v. 2). A series of rhetorical questions establishes that effects have causes — two do not walk together unless agreed, a lion does not roar without prey — building to the point that when the LORD speaks, the prophet must speak also (vv. 3-8). Amos summons surrounding nations to witness the chaos and oppression within Samaria (vv. 9-10), and pronounces that an enemy will surround the land, plunder its fortresses, and topple its winter and summer houses, sparing only a small remnant, like a shepherd rescuing a couple of bones from a lion's mouth (vv. 11-15).
h: Seven Questions: Can Two Walk Together? (vv.3-6)
The Lion Roars; the Prophet Speaks (vv.7-8)
Two Legs and a Piece of an Ear (vv.11-15)
m: Election means responsibility not immunity, cause and effect in judgment, God reveals His plans to prophets, the wealthy who store up violence, luxury destroyed

x: God condemns the wealthy women of Samaria, called "cows of Bashan," who oppress the poor and crush the needy while demanding their husbands bring them drink, warning they will be led away with hooks into exile (vv. 1-3). He mocks Israel's empty religious rituals at Bethel and Gilgal, where they multiply sin even while offering sacrifices and tithes (vv. 4-5). God then recounts five judgments He sent to bring Israel back — hunger, drought, blight and mildew, plague, and military defeat — each followed by the refrain "yet you did not return to me" (vv. 6-11). Because Israel would not repent, God warns them to prepare to meet their God (vv. 12-13).
h: Yet Have Ye Not Returned unto Me (vv.6-11)
m: The "cows of Bashan" — wealthy women who oppress the poor, sarcastic invitation to sin at Bethel, five failed disciplines, "prepare to meet thy God"

x: Amos sings a funeral dirge over Israel, lamenting that the nation has fallen with no one to raise her up (vv. 1-3). He pleads with Israel to seek the LORD and live, rather than seeking the pagan shrines of Bethel, Gilgal, and Beersheba, which will come to nothing (vv. 4-6). He condemns those who turn justice to bitterness, hate honest reproof, and oppress the poor through unfair taxes and bribes (vv. 7-13). Amos calls Israel to hate evil and love good, to let justice roll down like water and righteousness like a never-failing stream (v. 24), warning that their feasts will turn to mourning because worship without justice is meaningless to God (vv. 18-27).
h: A Lamentation: The Virgin of Israel Is Fallen (vv.1-3)
Hate the Evil, Love the Good (vv.14-15)
The Day of the LORD: Darkness, Not Light (vv.18-23)
Let Judgment Run Down as Waters (vv.24-27)
m: Lamentation over Israel's fall, "seek me and live," the God who makes the stars, injustice in the courts, let justice roll down like waters, God hates empty worship, the Day of the LORD as darkness

x: Amos pronounces woe on those complacent in Zion and Samaria who feel secure while ignoring the coming disaster (vv. 1-3). He describes the wealthy lounging on beds of ivory, feasting on choice meat, inventing musical instruments, and drinking wine from bowls, yet feeling no grief over the ruin of their nation (vv. 4-6). Because of this indifference, they will be the first to go into exile, their revelry brought to an end (v. 7). The LORD swears by Himself that He detests the pride of Israel and will hand the city over to an enemy, turning justice into poison and the fruit of righteousness into bitterness (vv. 8-14).
h: Woe to Them That Are at Ease in Zion (vv.1-3)
Ivory Beds and Bowls of Wine (vv.4-6)
The LORD Abhorreth the Excellency of Jacob (vv.8-11)
Horses on Rock, and a Nation Raised Up (vv.12-14)
m: False security, luxury and indifference, "not grieved for the affliction of Joseph," self-congratulation, God abhorring pride, a nation raised up against Israel

x: God shows Amos three visions of judgment — a swarm of locusts and a consuming fire, both of which Amos intercedes against and God relents (vv. 1-6) — followed by a plumb line held against a wall, symbolizing that God will no longer overlook Israel's crookedness (vv. 7-9). Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, reports Amos to King Jeroboam and orders him to flee back to Judah and never prophesy at Bethel again, the king's sanctuary (vv. 10-13). Amos responds that he was no professional prophet but a shepherd and fig grower whom the LORD took and commanded to prophesy to Israel, then pronounces judgment on Amaziah and his family (vv. 14-17).
h: First Vision: Locusts, and God Repents (vv.1-3)
Second Vision: Fire, and God Repents (vv.4-6)
Amaziah: Go, Flee Thou to Judah (vv.10-13)
I Was No Prophet: The LORD Took Me (vv.14-17)
m: God's mercy delaying judgment (twice), the plumbline of absolute standard, confrontation with religious establishment, the calling of a layman-prophet, the cost of speaking truth

x: God shows Amos a basket of ripe summer fruit, a wordplay signaling that the end has come for Israel (vv. 1-3). Amos condemns merchants who cannot wait for the Sabbath to end so they can cheat customers with dishonest scales and sell even the sweepings of the wheat (vv. 4-6). Because of this, God swears He will never forget their deeds, and the land will tremble and mourn as at a funeral (vv. 7-10). God declares a coming famine, not of bread or water, but of hearing His word, so that people will wander in search of it and not find it (vv. 11-14).
h: Fourth Vision: A Basket of Summer Fruit (vv.1-3)
When Will the Sabbath Be Gone? (vv.4-6)
Sworn by the Excellency of Jacob (vv.7-8)
The Sun Going Down at Noon (vv.9-10)
A Famine of Hearing the Words of the LORD (vv.11-14)
m: The ripe fruit of judgment, exploitation of the poor, corrupt merchants, the sun going down at noon, famine of hearing God's Word

x: Amos sees the LORD standing beside the altar, commanding the destruction of the temple and declaring that none who flee — whether digging into the earth or climbing to heaven — will escape His judgment (vv. 1-4). The LORD is shown as sovereign over creation and over nations, having brought up not only Israel from Egypt but also the Philistines and Arameans (vv. 5-7). Though the sinful kingdom will be destroyed, God promises not to totally destroy the house of Jacob, but to sift Israel among the nations like grain in a sieve while none of the good is lost (vv. 8-10). The book closes with the promise to restore David's fallen tent, rebuild its ruins, and bring unprecedented agricultural abundance and lasting restoration to the land (vv. 11-15).
h: Fifth Vision: The Lord Standing upon the Altar (vv.1-4)
Doxology: He That Buildeth His Stories in the Heaven (vv.5-6)
Are Ye Not as the Ethiopians? (vv.7-10)
The Tabernacle of David Raised Up (vv.11-12)
Planted, and No More Pulled Up (vv.13-15)
m: No escape from God, the sifting of Israel, "not the least grain shall fall," the tabernacle of David raised up, Messianic restoration, permanent planting in the land

x: Obadiah's brief vision announces God's judgment on Edom, whose pride in its unreachable mountain refuge will not save it from being brought down (vv. 1-4). Edom's coming destruction will be thorough, plundered by former allies who turn against it and stripped of everything (vv. 5-9). The specific charge is betrayal of family: when Jerusalem fell, Edom stood by, gloated over Judah's disaster, looted the city, and blocked the escape routes of fleeing survivors (vv. 10-14). Because of this, the coming day of the LORD will bring judgment on all nations, and Edom's treatment of Jacob will return on its own head (vv. 15-16). The book closes with hope for Zion's surviving remnant, who will possess the very territory of their enemies, and the declaration that the kingdom ultimately belongs to the LORD (vv. 17-21).
m: Pride before a fall, betrayal of brotherhood, gloating over a brother's ruin, the folly of trusting inaccessible terrain, measure-for-measure recompense, the day of the LORD reaching every nation, and the kingdom belonging to the LORD

x: God commands Jonah to go preach against Nineveh because of its wickedness, but instead Jonah boards a ship at Joppa and flees toward Tarshish, away from the LORD's presence (vv. 1-3). The LORD hurls a violent storm at the ship, and after casting lots identifies Jonah as its cause, the terrified sailors question him and learn he is fleeing the God who made the sea (vv. 4-10). At Jonah's own instruction they reluctantly throw him overboard, the sea instantly grows calm, and the sailors respond by fearing the LORD and offering him sacrifices (vv. 11-16). The LORD then appoints a great fish to swallow Jonah, where he remains three days and three nights (v. 17).
m: Running from God's call, the futility of flight, God's sovereignty over nature, pagan sailors more responsive than God's prophet, and a descent traced downward — into the ship, into sleep, into the sea

x: From inside the fish, Jonah prays to the LORD, describing his own distress as being thrown into the deep and sinking toward the roots of the mountains, cut off from God's presence and certain of drowning (vv. 1-6). He recalls how his life was fading away when he remembered the LORD and prayed toward his holy temple, contrasting himself with those who cling to worthless idols and forfeit God's mercy (vv. 7-8). Jonah vows to offer sacrifice and thanksgiving, declaring that salvation belongs to the LORD alone, and the LORD commands the fish to vomit him out onto dry land (vv. 9-10).
h: God Cast Me Down; God Will Bring Me Up (vv.3-4)
Deliverance: Thou Hast Brought Up My Life (v.6b)
The Confession: Salvation Is of the LORD (v.9)
m: Prayer from the depths, deliverance from death, the temple as an orientation point, remembering God when the soul faints, and the confession that salvation belongs to the LORD

x: The LORD's message comes to Jonah a second time, commissioning him again to go to Nineveh, and this time Jonah obeys, entering the enormous city and proclaiming that it will be overthrown in forty days (vv. 1-4). Remarkably, the Ninevites believe God, and from the greatest to the least they declare a fast and put on sackcloth (v. 5). The king steps down from his throne, exchanges his robe for sackcloth, and issues a decree calling everyone, even the animals, to fast and cry out to God while turning from their evil ways, in hope that he might relent (vv. 6-9). Seeing their repentance, God relents from the judgment he had threatened and does not destroy the city (v. 10).
h: The Second Call: God Speaks Again (vv.1-2)
m: The second chance, obedience after failure, the shortest sermon and the largest revival, corporate repentance from king to cattle, and God relenting from declared judgment

x: Jonah is greatly displeased that God showed mercy to Nineveh, admitting in prayer that this is exactly why he fled toward Tarshish, since he knew God to be gracious, compassionate, and slow to anger, and he asks to die rather than live (vv. 1-3). When the LORD questions his anger, Jonah goes outside the city to watch what will happen, and God appoints a plant to shade him, which pleases him greatly, only for a worm to attack it the next day so that it withers (vv. 4-7). As the sun and a scorching wind beat down on him, Jonah again wishes to die, and when God asks if he is right to be angry about the plant, Jonah insists he is (vv. 8-9). The LORD then reasons that if Jonah can care about a plant he did nothing to grow, God can rightly have compassion on Nineveh, a city of more than 120,000 people who do not know right from wrong (vv. 10-11).
h: Jonah's Anger: I Knew You Were Merciful (vv.1-4)
The Object Lesson: Gourd, Worm, and Wind (vv.6-8)
God's Final Question: Should I Not Spare Nineveh? (vv.9-11)
m: A prophet angry at mercy, God's freedom to show compassion, the object lesson of gourd and worm, comfort valued above souls, and a book that ends on an unanswered question

x: Micah opens with a word from the Lord against Samaria and Jerusalem, given during the reigns of Judah's kings Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah (v. 1). All peoples are summoned to witness as the Lord comes down from His holy temple, melting mountains and splitting valleys before Him (vv. 2-4). This judgment answers Israel and Judah's rebellion, centered in their capitals (v. 5), so Samaria's idols, gathered through spiritual prostitution, will be smashed and the city reduced to rubble (vv. 6-7). Micah mourns barefoot and stripped over the wound reaching Jerusalem's gate (vv. 8-9), then laments town by town as judgment sweeps toward the capital, closing with a call to mourn the coming exile of Judah's children (vv. 10-16).
h: Superscription: The Word to Samaria and Jerusalem (v.1)
The LORD Comes Down: A Theophany (vv.2-5)
The Prophet's Lament, Stripped and Wailing (vv.8-9)
Wordplay on the Towns of the Lowlands (vv.10-16)
m: Divine judgment, theophany, idolatry's consequences, lamentation, national sin

x: Micah pronounces judgment on those who lie awake plotting evil and then carry it out at first light simply because they have the power to do so, seizing fields and houses from their rightful owners through violence (vv. 1-2). Because of this, God is planning disaster for this family of oppressors, a calamity they will not escape or walk away from proudly (v. 3), and on that day people will mock them with a taunt song lamenting how their portion has been stripped away and divided among others (vv. 4-5). The people demand that the prophets stop preaching such warnings, but Micah insists his words bring good to anyone who walks uprightly, even as the people rise up like an enemy against the vulnerable, stripping the peaceable and evicting women and children from their homes (vv. 6-10). The chapter closes with a promise that God will yet gather a scattered remnant of Israel together like…
h: Woe to Those Who Devise Iniquity in Bed (vv.1-2)
I Devise an Evil Against You (vv.3-5)
Prophesy Not: The Silencing of Micah (vv.6-7)
Stripping the Robe, Casting Out Women and Children (vv.8-11)
m: Social injustice, land theft, oppression of the poor, false prophets, remnant hope

x: Micah confronts Israel's leaders, who should uphold justice but instead oppress the people so violently it is likened to stripping their skin and eating their flesh (vv. 1-3); when trouble comes, the Lord will hide His face from them (v. 4). He condemns prophets who cry "peace" for pay but turn on anyone who won't pay them, promising they will lose their visions to darkness and shame (vv. 5-7). By contrast, Micah is filled with the Lord's Spirit and power to expose Jacob's sin (v. 8), rebuking corrupt leaders, priests, and prophets who profit from bribery yet falsely assume the Lord guarantees their safety (vv. 9-11). Because of this corruption, Zion will be plowed like a field and Jerusalem reduced to rubble (v. 12).
h: Rulers Who Eat the Flesh of My People (vv.1-4)
But I Am Full of Power by the Spirit (v.8)
Zion Shall Be Plowed as a Field (v.12)
m: Leadership accountability, corrupt judges, false prophets, true prophetic authority, Jerusalem's coming destruction

x: Micah looks to the last days when the Lord's mountain will be exalted above all others, drawing the nations to learn His ways and be judged by Him, as weapons become farm tools and all nations live at peace (vv. 1-4). While other peoples follow their own gods, Israel will walk with the Lord forever, who promises to gather the lame and afflicted into a strong remnant and reign over them from Zion (vv. 5-8). Zion must first labor in pain and go into exile in Babylon, where the Lord will redeem her from her enemies (vv. 9-10). Though nations gather against Zion to defile her, they don't grasp God's plan to gather them for judgment, and Zion is called to thresh them like grain, dedicating their gain to the Lord (vv. 11-13).
h: The Mountain of the LORD in the Last Days (vv.1-5)
The LORD Shall Reign in Zion (vv.6-8)
Why Dost Thou Cry Out? Babylon Foretold (vv.9-10)
Many Nations Gathered, and a Threshing (vv.11-13)
m: Millennial kingdom, universal peace, swords into plowshares, the remnant restored, Zion exalted, Babylonian exile foretold

x: Israel, under siege, is told that from Bethlehem Ephrathah — though small among Judah's clans — will come a ruler whose origins stretch back to eternity (vv. 1-2). Israel will be given over until this ruler is born, after which the scattered remnant returns; he will shepherd his people in the strength of the Lord and become their peace, even repelling an Assyrian invasion (vv. 3-6). Jacob's remnant will be scattered among the nations, refreshing like dew yet also fierce like a lion tearing its prey, with enemies cut off before them (vv. 7-9). The Lord promises to purge Israel of the false securities they trusted instead of Him — horses, chariots, fortified cities, witchcraft, idols, and sacred poles — and to pour out vengeance on the disobedient nations (vv. 10-15).
h: The Judge Smitten on the Cheek (v.1)
Bethlehem Ephrathah: The Ruler from Everlasting (v.2)
He Shall Stand and Feed, and He Shall Be Peace (vv.4-6)
Dew and Lion, and the Purging of False Securities (vv.7-15)
m: The Bethlehem prophecy, Messiah's eternal origin, shepherd-king, peace, the remnant's dual nature, purification from idolatry

x: The Lord summons Israel to trial before the mountains and hills, asking what He has done to weary them and recalling how He delivered them from Egypt and guided them safely past Balak and Balaam (vv. 1-5). Israel wonders what sacrifice could satisfy God — burnt offerings, thousands of rams, even a firstborn child — but the Lord's true requirement is simply to act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with Him (vv. 6-8). He then indicts the city for dishonest scales, deceitful weights, violence, and lying, warning that sickness and desolation are coming because of their sins (vv. 9-13). They will eat without being filled, sow without reaping, and press olives and grapes without enjoying the oil or wine, because they have followed the corrupt ways of kings Omri and Ahab, bringing reproach on themselves (vv. 14-16).
h: The LORD's Case: Hear, O Mountains (vv.1-2)
What Have I Done to Thee? The Saving Acts Rehearsed (vv.3-5)
Shall I Come with Burnt Offerings? (vv.6-7)
He Hath Shewed Thee What Is Good (v.8)
Wicked Balances, and the Futility Curses (vv.9-16)
m: God's controversy with Israel, true vs. false worship, the requirements of God, social corruption, futility curses, what God truly desires

x: Micah laments that Israel is like a picked-over vineyard with no good fruit left — the godly have vanished and people hunt one another for gain, with even judges and rulers demanding bribes (vv. 1-4). No one can be trusted, not even close family, yet Micah chooses to wait on the Lord, confident God will hear him (vv. 5-7). He tells his enemy not to gloat, for though he falls he will rise, and the Lord will be his light in the darkness until God vindicates him and shames those who mocked his faith (vv. 8-10). A day of rebuilding is coming for Israel even as the land now suffers for its sin, and Micah prays for God to shepherd His people again as in days of old, with wonders like those at the Exodus (vv. 11-15). The nations will watch in fear and humiliation before the Lord (vv. 16-17). The chapter closes in praise of a God unlike any other, who delights to forgive, casts sins into the…
h: Woe Is Me: No Upright Man Remains (vv.1-6)
Therefore I Will Look unto the LORD (v.7)
Rejoice Not Against Me, O Mine Enemy (vv.8-10)
The Day for Building Thy Walls (vv.11-13)
Feed Thy People with Thy Rod (vv.14-17)
Who Is a God Like unto Thee? (vv.18-20)
m: Moral collapse of society, personal faith amid corruption, hope in God's faithfulness, forgiveness of sin, covenant faithfulness, incomparable God

x: Nahum opens with a hymn describing the LORD as jealous and avenging toward his enemies, yet slow to anger and immense in power, marching through the earth in whirlwind and storm (vv. 2-3). Creation itself reacts to his presence — seas dry up, mountains quake, and no one can withstand his fierce anger (vv. 4-6). In contrast, the LORD is good, a refuge in times of trouble for those who trust him (v. 7), even as he vows complete destruction on his adversaries so they will never trouble Judah again (vv. 8-10). The chapter turns to address Nineveh directly, denouncing the wicked plotter who schemes against the LORD and pronouncing an end to that nation's name, idols, and power (vv. 11-14). It closes by announcing good news of peace for Judah, calling the people to keep their festivals now that the wicked oppressor is cut off (v. 15).
h: A Hymn to the Avenging God (vv.2-6)
Good to Those Who Trust Him, an End to the Rest (vv.7-11)
m: God's jealous wrath against oppressors, theophanic power over nature, the goodness of God as refuge, the utter destruction of those who oppose the LORD

x: An unnamed attacker advances on Nineveh, prompting a call to man its defenses, even as the LORD restores the splendor of Jacob and Israel that Assyria had stripped away (vv. 1-2). The assault is pictured in vivid imagery — red-shielded warriors and chariots racing like torches and lightning through the streets — until the city's defenses fail and its river gates give way, collapsing the palace (vv. 3-6). Nineveh's queen is led away captive while her attendants mourn, and the population flees like water draining from a pool, with no one able to rally them (vv. 7-8). Invaders plunder the city's abundant silver and gold, leaving it empty and its people paralyzed with terror (vv. 9-10). Nineveh, once a lions' den that devoured freely, is now hunted down, as the LORD declares himself against it and vows to burn its chariots and silence its messengers forever (vv. 11-13).
h: The Siege Begins, and Jacob's Majesty Returned (vv.1-2)
The Assault: Chariots, Torches, and Panic (vv.3-5)
The Breakthrough: Gates of the Rivers Opened (vv.6-7)
The Flight: Nineveh Emptied Like a Pool (vv.8-10)
The Lion's Den Emptied, and “I Am Against Thee” (vv.11-13)
m: Vivid battle imagery of Nineveh's destruction, the reversal of Assyrian power, God's restoration of Jacob's majesty, the lion's den emptied, divine declaration: "I am against thee"

x: Nahum pronounces woe on the bloodstained city of Nineveh, full of lies and plunder, picturing the chaos of cracking whips, racing chariots, and heaps of corpses from its conquests (vv. 1-3). Its downfall is traced to its seductive, deceptive practices that had enslaved other nations, and the LORD declares himself against it, vowing to expose its shame publicly so no one will mourn its fall (vv. 4-7). Nahum points to the earlier destruction of Thebes as proof that even strong allies like Egypt, Cush, Put, and Libya could not save a great city from judgment, warning Nineveh it will suffer the same fate, its children dashed to pieces and its nobles bound in chains (vv. 8-10). Its fortresses will fall like ripe figs shaken loose, its gates will stand open to enemies, and any siege preparation will prove useless (vv. 11-15). Nahum mocks the city's countless merchants and officials as locusts…
h: The Indictment: Woe to the Bloody City (vv.1-4)
The Precedent: The Fall of Thebes (vv.8-10)
The Application: Nineveh Will Share That Fate (vv.11-13)
m: The bloody city's sins exposed, divine justice as public shaming, the precedent of Thebes' fall, the incurable wound, universal rejoicing at Nineveh's destruction

x: Habakkuk opens by crying out to God, asking how long he must call for help while God seems not to listen, surrounded by violence, injustice, and a law that seems paralyzed (vv. 1-4). God answers that He is doing something the prophet would not believe even if told — raising up the fierce and terrifying Chaldeans (Babylonians) to sweep across the earth as His instrument of judgment (vv. 5-11). This answer only deepens Habakkuk's confusion: he affirms that God is eternal and holy and cannot tolerate evil, yet asks how a righteous God can use a nation more wicked than Judah to punish His own people (vv. 12-13). The chapter closes with Habakkuk picturing the Babylonians as fishermen dragging up nations with a hook, sacrificing to their own military power, and asking whether God will let this go on forever (vv. 14-17).
h: God's First Answer: I Raise Up the Chaldeans (vv.5-11)
The Second Complaint: How Can You Use the Wicked? (vv.12-17)
m: Wrestling with God's silence, the problem of evil and injustice, God's sovereign use of wicked nations, faith in tension with observation, the Chaldean (Babylonian) instrument of judgment

x: The Lord tells Habakkuk to write the vision clearly on tablets so it can be read at a glance, and to wait for it, since it will surely come at its appointed time (vv. 2-3). He contrasts the proud, whose souls are not right within them, with the righteous, who will live by their faithfulness to God (v. 4). God then pronounces a series of five woes against the arrogant Babylonian conqueror: for plundering many nations through greed (vv. 6-8), for building his house through unjust gain (vv. 9-11), for building a city with bloodshed and violence (vv. 12-14), for shaming his neighbors through drunkenness and exposure (vv. 15-17), and for trusting in worthless idols he made with his own hands (vv. 18-19). The chapter closes with a call for all the earth to fall silent before the Lord, who is present in His holy temple (v. 20).
h: The Watchman's Posture: Waiting for an Answer (v.1)
The Just Shall Live by His Faith (vv.4-5)
First and Second Woes: Plunder and Exploitative Gain (vv.6-11)
Fourth and Fifth Woes: Debauchery and Idolatry (vv.15-19)
The LORD in His Temple: Let the Earth Keep Silence (v.20)
m: Waiting on God's word, the pivotal verse: "the just shall live by his faith," five woes against Babylonian excess, the futility of idolatry, the sovereignty of God in His temple

x: Habakkuk's chapter takes the form of a prayer set to music, opening with a plea that God would renew His mighty works in the prophet's own time, and that even in wrath He would remember mercy (vv. 1-2). He describes a theophany of God coming in overwhelming splendor from Teman, with rays of light, plague going before Him, and the earth's ancient mountains shattering at His approach (vv. 3-6). The vision continues with God riding out in His chariots of salvation, splitting rivers, and making the sun and moon stand still, in order to save His people and crush the head of the wicked (vv. 7-15). Habakkuk admits his body trembles at what he has seen and heard, yet resolves to wait quietly for the day of trouble to come upon the invading nation (v. 16). The book closes with Habakkuk's declaration of unshakable faith: even if every crop fails and every flock and herd is gone, he will still…
h: Superscription and a Prayer for Revival (vv.1-2)
m: Theophany and God's power recalled, trembling before divine majesty, faith that triumphs over circumstance, joy independent of provision, God as personal strength

x: Zephaniah, a descendant of King Hezekiah, delivers this message during Josiah's reign (v. 1). The Lord declares He will sweep away every living thing from the earth, reversing creation (vv. 2-3), then turns to Judah, vowing to end Baal worship, star worship, and divided loyalty toward Him (vv. 4-6). The Day of the Lord is pictured as a sacrificial feast where the princes, the king's sons, and the violent and deceitful are judged, with cries of distress rising across Jerusalem (vv. 7-11). God will search the city with lamps to expose those indifferent to good and evil, stripping away their wealth and homes (vv. 12-13). The chapter closes describing that day as near and devastating, when silver and gold cannot save anyone from the fire of His jealous wrath (vv. 14-18).
h: The Day of the LORD as Sacrifice (vv.7-11)
The Great Day: Near and Terrible (vv.14-18)
m: Comprehensive cosmic judgment, the Day of the LORD, judgment beginning at God's house, spiritual complacency exposed, the insufficiency of wealth in judgment, God's searching investigation

x: Zephaniah calls the shameless nation to gather and seek the Lord, urging the humble to pursue righteousness and meekness in hopes of shelter on the day of His anger (vv. 1-3). Judgment then falls on Judah's neighbors: Philistia's cities—Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, and Ekron—will be abandoned, and the surviving remnant of Judah will one day possess that coastland (vv. 4-7). Moab and Ammon are condemned for mocking and encroaching on God's people and will become as desolate as Sodom and Gomorrah, while the Lord humbles every false god so that nations everywhere will worship Him (vv. 8-11). Cush will fall by the sword (v. 12), and Assyria's proud capital, Nineveh, will be reduced to a wasteland fit only for grazing flocks and roosting birds, an object of scorn to everyone who passes by (vv. 13-15).
h: Seek the LORD Before the Day (vv.1-3)
Against Moab and Ammon: The East (vv.8-11)
Against Assyria and Nineveh: The North (vv.13-15)
m: The urgency of repentance before judgment, oracles against surrounding nations (Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Cush, Assyria), the fate of those who mock God's people, Nineveh's arrogance exposed

x: Zephaniah pronounces woe on Jerusalem, an oppressive city that refuses correction and will not draw near to God, whose leaders—princes, judges, prophets, and priests—prey on the people and profane what is holy (vv. 1-4). The Lord remains just and displays His justice every morning, yet the city feels no shame, even after watching other nations fall as a warning (vv. 5-7). He calls His people to wait for Him, since He will gather the nations for judgment and later purify their speech so all people call on His name together (vv. 8-10). He will remove the proud and leave a humble, honest remnant who trust in Him and live secure (vv. 11-13). The chapter closes with a joyful call for Zion to sing, for the Lord dwells among them as a mighty Savior who rejoices over them with singing and will gather the outcast and restore their fortunes (vv. 14-20).
h: Patience Exhausted, and “Wait Ye Upon Me” (vv.6-8)
Sing, O Daughter of Zion, and the God Who Sings (vv.14-17)
m: Jerusalem's rebellion indicted, God's justice in the midst of corruption, purification of the nations, the humble remnant preserved, God rejoicing over His people with singing, final restoration and renown

x: In the second year of King Darius, the word of the LORD comes through the prophet Haggai to Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest, rebuking the people for saying the time has not yet come to rebuild the temple while they live in paneled houses of their own (vv. 1-4). Haggai points out that their hard work has produced little because they have prioritized their own houses over God's house — their hardship is a direct consequence of neglecting the temple (vv. 5-11). Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the whole remnant of the people obey the LORD's voice and the words of Haggai, and the people fear the LORD (v. 12). The LORD promises "I am with you," and stirs up the leaders and people to begin rebuilding the temple about three weeks later (vv. 13-15).
h: The Date and the Two Leaders (v.1)
“The Time Is Not Come”: Misplaced Priorities (vv.2-4)
Consider Your Ways: Much Sown, Little Reaped (vv.5-6)
Go Up to the Mountain and Build (vv.7-8)
The People Obeyed, and the Spirit Was Stirred (vv.12-15)
m: Misplaced priorities, divine discipline through economic hardship, obedience and divine presence, the stirring of the Spirit, "Consider your ways"

x: The LORD asks the discouraged builders who remembers the temple's former glory and now sees it as nothing by comparison, then commands them to be strong and to work, for He is with them just as He promised at the exodus (vv. 1-5). He promises to shake the heavens and earth and the nations, so the treasures of all nations will come and fill this house with glory greater than the former, and He will give peace in that place (vv. 6-9). Haggai then teaches through the priests that just as uncleanness is contagious while holiness is not, the people's defiled offerings have kept God's blessing from their crops, but from this day forward He promises to bless them (vv. 10-19). Finally, God promises to overthrow the kingdoms of the nations, and to make Zerubbabel like a signet ring, chosen and treasured by the LORD, a note of messianic hope pointing toward the line of David (vv. 20-23).
h: The Shaking of Nations and the Greater Glory (vv.6-9)
The Lesson of Holiness and Defilement (vv.10-14)
The Turning Point: From This Day I Will Bless (vv.15-19)
m: Encouragement to the discouraged, the latter glory surpassing the former, the shaking of nations, holiness and defilement, the turning point of blessing, Zerubbabel as God's signet ring (Messianic type)

x: Zechariah's first message calls Judah to return to the Lord, since their ancestors ignored the earlier prophets and paid for it (vv. 1-6). Two months later he has a night vision of a rider on a red horse among the myrtle trees, backed by patrol horses reporting that the whole earth is at ease while Jerusalem still lies desolate (vv. 7-11). An angel intercedes, and the Lord answers with comfort, declaring his jealous love for Zion, his anger at the complacent nations, and his promise to rebuild his house and again choose Jerusalem (vv. 12-17). A final vision shows four horns that scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem, confronted by four craftsmen sent to terrify and cast them down (vv. 18-21).
h: The Call to Repentance: Return unto Me (vv.1-6)
The First Night Vision: Horsemen Among the Myrtles (vv.7-11)
The Angel's Intercession and God's Answer (vv.12-17)
The Second Vision: Four Horns and Four Craftsmen (vv.18-21)
m: A call to repentance, God's jealousy for Jerusalem, angelic patrols reporting on the earth, God's comfort and restoration, the four horns and four craftsmen

x: Zechariah sees a man with a measuring line setting out to measure Jerusalem's dimensions (vv. 1-2). An angel reports that Jerusalem will one day be too full of people and livestock for walls, since the Lord himself will be a wall of fire around the city and its inner glory (vv. 3-5). Exiles are urged to flee Babylon before God's judgment falls on the nations that plundered his people, since touching Israel is like touching the pupil of his eye (vv. 6-9). Zion is called to rejoice because the Lord will dwell among her, many nations will join themselves to him, and he will again choose Jerusalem as his own, prompting all flesh to fall silent before him (vv. 10-13).
h: The Third Vision: A Man Measuring Jerusalem (vv.1-2)
The Angel's Message: No Walls Needed (vv.3-5)
The Apple of God's Eye and the Hand Shaken (vv.8-9)
The LORD Comes to Dwell in Zion, and All Flesh Silent (vv.10-13)
m: The future expansion of Jerusalem, God as supernatural protection, the call to flee Babylon, the nations joining the LORD, God dwelling in Zion's midst

x: Joshua the high priest stands before the angel of the Lord with Satan at his side to accuse him, but the Lord rebukes Satan and calls Joshua a stick snatched from the fire (vv. 1-2). Joshua's filthy garments, symbolizing sin, are removed and replaced with clean robes and a turban, picturing his iniquity taken away (vv. 3-5). The angel charges him to walk faithfully in his priestly duties, promising him access among the attendants, then points ahead to a coming servant called the Branch (vv. 6-8). A stone with seven eyes is set before Joshua, and the Lord promises to remove the land's iniquity in a single day, ushering in an age of peace where neighbors invite one another under vine and fig tree (vv. 9-10).
h: Joshua Before the Angel: Satan the Accuser (vv.1-2)
The Clean Turban and Pure Vestments (v.5)
The Branch and the Stone with Seven Eyes (vv.8-9)
m: Satan as accuser, divine justification, filthy garments removed, clean garments bestowed, the Branch promised, iniquity removed in one day, the gospel in the Old Testament

x: An angel wakens Zechariah to a vision of a solid gold lampstand fed by seven lamps and flanked by two olive trees (vv. 1-3). Zechariah asks what it means, and the angel explains it as the Lord's word to Zerubbabel: the temple will be finished not by might or power but by God's Spirit, and the great obstacle before him will become level ground (vv. 4-7). Zerubbabel's hands laid the temple's foundation and will complete it, and no one should despise the day of small beginnings, since the seven lamps represent the eyes of the Lord ranging over the whole earth (vv. 8-10). The two olive trees are identified as the two anointed ones who stand beside the Lord of all the earth, supplying golden oil through the lampstand (vv. 11-14).
h: The Vision: A Golden Lampstand with Olive Trees (vv.1-3)
Zechariah's Question and the Angel's Challenge (vv.4-5)
Not by Might, Nor by Power, But by My Spirit (v.6)
Zerubbabel Will Finish It and the Day of Small Things (vv.8-10)
m: The sufficiency of the Spirit, human weakness and divine power, the day of small things, Zerubbabel's completion of the Temple, continuous supply of God's anointing

x: Zechariah sees a flying scroll, twenty cubits by ten, identified as a curse sweeping the land that will cut off every thief and every false swearer, entering their houses and consuming them completely (vv. 1-4). A second vision follows: a basket goes out representing the iniquity of the whole land, and when its lead cover is lifted a woman named Wickedness is seen sitting inside (vv. 5-8). She is pushed back down and sealed under the lead weight, then carried off by two winged women to Shinar, where a house is built to set the basket on its own base (vv. 9-11). Together the visions picture God actively removing sin and wickedness from the land.
h: The Sixth Vision: The Flying Scroll (vv.1-2)
The Curse Against Theft and False Swearing (vv.3-4)
The Seventh Vision: The Woman in the Ephah (vv.5-8)
m: God's curse against sin, judgment on theft and false oaths, the removal of wickedness from the land, wickedness personified and exiled to Shinar (Babylon)

x: Zechariah sees four chariots with different-colored horses emerge from between two bronze mountains, identified as the four spirits of heaven going out from before the Lord to patrol the earth, with those heading north bringing his Spirit rest there (vv. 1-8). The Lord instructs Zechariah to take silver and gold from returned exiles and make a crown for Joshua the high priest, symbolizing the coming Branch who will build the temple, bear royal honor, and sit as both priest and king in harmonious counsel (vv. 9-13). The crown is kept in the temple as a memorial, and the chapter closes with the promise that people from far away will help build the temple, confirming Zechariah's calling, contingent on the people's obedience (vv. 14-15).
h: The Eighth Vision: Four Chariots from Bronze Mountains (vv.1-3)
The Interpretation: Four Spirits of Heaven (vv.4-8)
The Crown as a Memorial and Those Far Off (vv.14-15)
m: Divine sovereignty over the nations, the four spirits/winds of heaven executing judgment, the Branch as priest-king, the union of priestly and royal offices in one Person, those "far off" joining in building God's temple

x: In the fourth year of King Darius, a delegation from Bethel sends men to the temple to ask the priests and prophets whether they should keep observing the fast that commemorates Jerusalem's destruction (vv. 1-3). The Lord answers through Zechariah by questioning whether their fasting, and even their feasting, over these many decades was ever truly done for him rather than for themselves (vv. 4-7). He reminds them what he had already commanded through the earlier prophets: render true justice, show kindness and compassion, and stop oppressing the widow, the orphan, the foreigner, and the poor (vv. 8-10). Their ancestors refused to listen, hardened their hearts, and ignored the prophets, so the Lord scattered them among the nations and left their once-pleasant land desolate (vv. 11-14).
h: The Delegation's Question: Should We Still Fast? (vv.1-3)
God's Probing Response: Was It Really for Me? (vv.4-6)
The True Requirement: Justice and Mercy (vv.7-10)
The Terrible Consequence: As I Called, They Refused (vv.13-14)
m: Empty ritual versus genuine obedience, self-centered religion exposed, God's true requirements (justice, mercy, compassion), the hard heart that refuses to hear, the consequences of persistent disobedience

x: The Lord declares his zealous love for Zion and his return to dwell in Jerusalem, now to be called the City of Truth, with old men and women safely sitting in its streets while children play (vv. 1-5). He promises to gather his scattered people from east and west to be his own, urging the remnant to take courage as the temple is rebuilt, since the past hardship will give way to prosperity and blessing rather than the curse they had become among the nations (vv. 6-15). They are called to speak truth, render honest judgment, and abandon evil plots and false oaths, since God hates such things, and their sorrowful fasts will turn into joyful feasts (vv. 16-19). The chapter closes with many peoples and strong nations streaming to Jerusalem to seek the Lord, grasping the robe of a Jew and saying they have heard that God is with him (vv. 20-23).
h: The Faithful City: Elderly and Children at Peace (vv.3-5)
Nothing Too Hard, and the Gathering from East and West (vv.6-8)
m: God's jealousy for Zion, the future Jerusalem of peace and prosperity, the reversal of former judgment, ethical requirements for the blessed community, fasts transformed to feasts, the nations drawn to God through Israel

x: An oracle of judgment falls on Israel's neighbors — Hadrach, Damascus, Hamath, Tyre, Sidon, and the Philistine cities — with Tyre's wealth destroyed and the Philistines' pride and pagan practices stripped away, though even a remnant of them will be absorbed into God's people (vv. 1-7). The Lord promises to guard his house from invading armies (v. 8), then delivers the famous promise of Zion's king arriving humble and riding on a donkey, bringing salvation and speaking peace to the nations, with dominion reaching to the ends of the earth (vv. 9-10). Because of his covenant, God frees prisoners from the waterless pit and promises to restore his people double (vv. 11-12). He will make Judah and Ephraim his weapon against Greece, appear over his people like lightning and a trumpet blast, and give them victory as his flock, sparkling like jewels in his land and flourishing on grain and new…
h: Judgment on Damascus, Hamath, Tyre and Sidon (vv.1-4)
The Philistine Cities and a Guard Set on God's House (vv.5-8)
The King on a Donkey and Dominion to the Ends of the Earth (vv.9-10)
Judah as a Bow and Ephraim as an Arrow (vv.13-15)
m: Judgment on Israel's enemies, the triumphal entry of the humble King, the Prince of Peace, prisoners of hope set free, God as warrior and protector, Messianic kingdom dominion

x: The people are told to ask the Lord, not idols or false diviners, for rain, since it is God who sends the storms that make the fields grow (vv. 1-2). His anger burns against the false shepherds who led Judah astray, but he will care for his flock personally, making them like a mighty warhorse and the source of every leader and weapon they need (vv. 3-4). Strengthened by God, Judah and Joseph will fight victoriously and rejoice as though never rejected, remembering the Lord even in distant lands and returning to him (vv. 5-9). God will regather his scattered people from Egypt and Assyria into Gilead and Lebanon, drying up the sea before them and humbling their oppressors as he strengthens them to walk in his name (vv. 10-12).
h: Ask the LORD for Rain, Not Idols (vv.1-2)
Anger Against the Shepherds and Strength from Judah (vv.3-5)
The Full Restoration of Judah and Ephraim (vv.6-7)
God Whistles for His Scattered People (vv.8-10)
Through the Sea and Strengthened in His Name (vv.11-12)
m: God as the true source of rain and blessing, false shepherds condemned, God's anger against worthless leaders, the cornerstone/tent peg/battle bow from Judah, the regathering of Ephraim and Judah, divine redemption and strengthening

x: A cry of lament opens the chapter as Lebanon's cedars, Bashan's oaks, and the shepherds themselves are told to wail over coming devastation on the land's rulers and glory (vv. 1-3). The Lord commands Zechariah to shepherd a flock marked for slaughter, mistreated by greedy buyers and careless shepherds, since God will no longer pity the land and will let its people fall into each other's hands (vv. 4-6). Zechariah takes up two staffs, Favor and Union, to tend the flock, but grows weary of the people and breaks the first staff, ending the covenant God had made with them (vv. 7-11). Paid a mere thirty pieces of silver for his labor, he throws the money to the potter in the Lord's house, then breaks the second staff, severing the brotherhood between Judah and Israel (vv. 12-14). The chapter closes with a warning about a worthless shepherd who abandons the flock instead of caring for it…
h: The Shepherd of the Doomed Flock (vv.4-7)
The Shepherd Rejected by the Flock (vv.8-9)
The Staff Beauty Broken: Covenant Annulled (vv.10-11)
Thirty Pieces of Silver and the Breaking of Bands (vv.12-14)
The Rise of the Foolish Shepherd (vv.15-17)
m: The Good Shepherd rejected, the flock doomed to slaughter, the breaking of covenant, thirty pieces of silver (the price of Messiah's betrayal), the foolish shepherd who destroys the flock, judgment for rejecting the true Shepherd

x: The Lord, who formed the heavens, earth, and human spirit, declares Jerusalem will become an intoxicating cup and an immovable stone that injures every nation that lays siege to it (vv. 1-3). He will strike enemy cavalry with panic and blindness while defending Judah, and Jerusalem's leaders and inhabitants will become like fire consuming the surrounding peoples, restored securely to their place (vv. 4-7). The Lord will shield Jerusalem so that even its weakest citizen is like David, and the house of David is like God himself (v. 8), determined to destroy every nation that attacks the city (v. 9). Most significantly, God will pour out a spirit of grace on the house of David and Jerusalem, and the people will look on the one they have pierced, mourning for him with the grief of losing an only child, a sorrow spreading through every family in the land (vv. 10-14).
h: Jerusalem a Cup of Staggering and a Heavy Stone (vv.2-3)
The Weak Made Strong and the Nations Destroyed (vv.7-9)
The Spirit Poured Out: Looking on the Pierced One (v.10)
The Great Mourning, Every Family Apart (vv.11-14)
m: Jerusalem as an immovable burden stone, God's supernatural defense of His people, the spirit of grace poured out, Israel looking on Him whom they pierced, national repentance and mourning, the deity of Christ implied

x: A fountain will be opened for the house of David and the people of Jerusalem to cleanse them from sin and impurity, and God will remove the names of idols from the land along with the false prophets and the unclean spirit (vv. 1-2). Any who still try to prophesy falsely will be exposed and rejected even by their own parents, and prophets will abandon the prophet's garb and claim instead to be farmers rather than admit what they are (vv. 3-6). God then calls for a sword to strike his own shepherd, scattering the sheep, while he turns his hand against the little ones (v. 7). Two-thirds of the people in the land will perish, but God will bring the remaining third through fire, refining them like silver and gold until they call on his name and are recognized again as his own people (vv. 8-9).
h: The Fountain Opened for Sin and Uncleanness (v.1)
The Purging of Idols and False Prophets (vv.2-6)
The Sword Against the Shepherd and the Scattered Sheep (v.7)
Two Parts Cut Off and the Third Refined (vv.8-9)
m: A fountain opened for cleansing from sin, the end of idolatry and false prophecy, the shepherd struck by God's own sword, the sheep scattered, the remnant refined through fire, covenant restoration

x: The Day of the Lord brings a final siege of Jerusalem in which the city is plundered and half its people taken captive, but then the Lord himself goes out to fight for the city, his feet splitting the Mount of Olives in two and opening a valley of escape (vv. 1-5). That day will be unlike any other, ending in light at evening, with living water flowing from Jerusalem toward both seas as the Lord becomes king over all the earth (vv. 6-9). Jerusalem will be raised up and secure, while the attacking nations are struck with a horrifying plague and thrown into panic against each other, their wealth left for Judah to gather (vv. 10-15). Survivors from every nation will then go up yearly to worship the King and keep the Feast of Tabernacles, with drought or plague striking any nation that refuses (vv. 16-19). Finally, everything in Jerusalem, down to the bells on the horses and the ordinary…
h: The Nations Gathered and the City Taken (vv.1-2)
The LORD Goes Forth and His Feet on the Mount of Olives (vv.3-5)
A Day Neither Day Nor Night, and Living Waters (vv.6-8)
The LORD King Over All the Earth (v.9)
The Land Made Plain and Jerusalem Safely Inhabited (vv.10-11)
The Nations Keep the Feast of Tabernacles (vv.16-19)
Holiness on the Bells of the Horses (vv.20-21)
m: The final siege of Jerusalem, the LORD's physical return to earth, the Mount of Olives split, living waters flowing from Jerusalem, the LORD as King over all the earth, universal holiness, the nations worshipping God

x: Malachi opens with the Lord declaring His love for Israel, contrasting His choice of Jacob with His judgment on Esau's descendants, Edom, whose rebuilding efforts He will keep tearing down (vv. 1-5). He then confronts the priests for dishonoring Him despite claiming to be His people, pointing out that they offer blind, lame, and sick animals on His altar — sacrifices they would never dare present to a governor (vv. 6-9). God says He takes no pleasure in such offerings and would rather the temple doors be shut than see worship offered without reverence, declaring that His name will be great among the nations even while Israel profanes it (vv. 10-12). The chapter closes with a warning that those who vow a good animal but sacrifice a defective one are cursed, since the Lord is a great King whose name is to be feared among the nations (vv. 13-14).
h: Superscription: The Burden of the Word (v.1)
First Disputation: I Have Loved You (vv.2-5)
My Name Great Among the Nations (vv.10-11)
Weariness, and a Curse on the Deceiver (vv.12-14)
m: God's sovereign electing love, the ingratitude of Israel, contemptible worship from contemptuous priests, offering God the leftovers, God's name great among the nations, the contrast between Israel's dishonor and Gentile worship

x: The Lord warns the priests that if they refuse to honor Him, He will curse their blessings and spread the refuse of their festival sacrifices on their faces (vv. 1-3). He contrasts their unfaithfulness with His covenant with Levi, whose ancestor walked with Him in reverence and taught the truth faithfully, whereas the current priests have turned aside, caused people to stumble, and shown partiality in their teaching (vv. 4-9). Malachi then rebukes the wider people for breaking faith with one another and with the covenant of their ancestors, specifically calling out those who have married foreign wives devoted to other gods, and those who cover the altar with tears because the Lord no longer accepts their offerings (vv. 10-13). He explains this is because they have broken faith with the wife of their youth despite God being witness to that covenant, and declares that God hates the…
h: The Covenant with Levi and the Ideal Priest (vv.5-7)
Priests Who Cause Others to Stumble (vv.8-9)
Faithlessness to Brothers, and Foreign Marriage (vv.10-12)
Faithlessness in Marriage, and Wearying the LORD (vv.13-17)
m: The failure of the priesthood, the ideal priest versus the corrupt priest, marriage as covenant, God's hatred of divorce, faithlessness between brothers, wearying God with moral relativism

x: The Lord promises to send a messenger to prepare the way before Him, followed by His own sudden coming to the temple, a day compared to a refiner's fire that will purify the sons of Levi so their offerings become acceptable again (vv. 1-4). He warns He will draw near for judgment against sorcerers, adulterers, false witnesses, and those who oppress workers, widows, orphans, and foreigners (v. 5). Because God does not change, Israel has not been consumed despite generations of turning away from His commands, and He calls the people to return to Him (vv. 6-7). He accuses them of robbing Him by withholding tithes and offerings, and invites them to test Him by bringing the full tithe, promising to pour out blessing and rebuke the pests devouring their crops (vv. 8-12). Malachi then answers those who claim serving God is pointless by noting that a book of remembrance is being kept for those…
h: The Messenger, and the Lord Coming to His Temple (v.1)
The Refiner's Fire: Who Shall Stand? (vv.2-5)
I Change Not, and Return to Me (vv.6-7)
The Cynics and the Book of Remembrance (vv.13-18)
m: The forerunner preparing the way, the Lord suddenly coming to His Temple, refining fire, God's unchanging character, robbing God in tithes, the open windows of heaven, the book of remembrance for the faithful, God's treasured possession

x: Malachi closes his prophecy with a warning that the coming day will burn like a furnace, consuming the arrogant and evildoers completely, leaving them neither root nor branch (v. 1). For those who fear God's name, however, the sun of righteousness will rise with healing, and they will go out rejoicing like calves released from the stall, trampling down the wicked (vv. 2-3). The people are told to remember the law given to Moses at Horeb (v. 4), and the book ends with God's promise to send the prophet Elijah before the great and dreadful Day of the Lord, so that he may turn the hearts of fathers and children toward each other and prevent the land from being struck with judgment (vv. 5-6).
h: The Day Burning Like an Oven (v.1)
The Sun of Righteousness, with Healing (vv.2-3)
Elijah Is Coming, and the Last Word (vv.5-6)
m: The coming day burning like an oven, judgment on the arrogant, the Sun of righteousness with healing, the faithful leaping like calves, remembering the law of Moses, Elijah's return, the turning of hearts, the OT's final word

x: Matthew opens with a genealogy tracing Jesus' lineage from Abraham through David to Joseph, arranged in three sets of fourteen generations to present him as Israel's promised Messiah (vv. 1-17). The account then turns to Mary, found to be pregnant by the Holy Spirit before her marriage to Joseph, and Joseph's plan to quietly end the engagement (vv. 18-19). An angel appears to Joseph in a dream, telling him not to be afraid to take Mary as his wife and to name the child Jesus, because he will save his people from their sins (vv. 20-21). Matthew notes this fulfills Isaiah's prophecy of a virgin bearing a son called Immanuel, God with us, and Joseph obeys, taking Mary home and naming the child at his birth (vv. 22-25).
m: a genealogy opening the entire Gospel as a legal document rather than a story, three groups of fourteen imposed deliberately on the record rather than found in it, four women named by choice, Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and the wife of Uriah, before Mary breaks the pattern of the whole list entirely, a…

x: Wise men from the east arrive in Jerusalem seeking the newborn king of the Jews, prompting a troubled Herod to learn from the chief priests that the Messiah is to be born in Bethlehem (vv. 1-6). Herod secretly sends the magi to find the child under the pretense of wanting to worship him; the star leads them to Jesus, they present gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh, and are then warned in a dream to avoid Herod on their way home (vv. 7-12). An angel warns Joseph to flee to Egypt with Mary and Jesus, and when Herod realizes he has been outwitted he orders the massacre of Bethlehem's boys age two and under, fulfilling Jeremiah's prophecy of Rachel weeping for her children (vv. 13-18). After Herod dies, an angel again guides Joseph, who settles the family in Nazareth rather than Judea, fulfilling the prophecy that the Messiah would be called a Nazarene (vv. 19-23).
h: The Wise Men from the East (vv.1-12)
m: astrologers from outside Israel reading a star correctly and then asking the wrong man for directions, Herod's own scholars naming the exact town of Bethlehem from Micah without a single one of them making the five-mile trip, a request for a report that Matthew frames as a lie before it is even…

x: John the Baptist appears in the wilderness of Judea, preaching repentance and the nearness of the kingdom of heaven, dressed in camel's hair and eating locusts and wild honey, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy of a voice crying in the wilderness (vv. 1-6). Crowds from Jerusalem and Judea come to be baptized, but when John sees Pharisees and Sadducees approaching he rebukes them as a brood of vipers, warning that descent from Abraham will not spare them from judgment and that one mightier than himself is coming who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire (vv. 7-12). Jesus comes from Galilee to be baptized by John, who initially objects that he himself needs to be baptized by Jesus, but Jesus insists it is fitting to fulfill all righteousness (vv. 13-15). As Jesus comes up from the water, the heavens open, the Spirit descends on him like a dove, and a voice from heaven declares him God's…
m: a two-word message translated with its reason attached, repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand, a wilderness prophet dressed deliberately like Elijah drawing crowds out of Jerusalem and all Judea, Pharisees and Sadducees met with a different sermon than the crowd, O generation of vipers, a…

x: The Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness, where he fasts forty days and is tempted three times by the devil — to turn stones to bread, to throw himself from the temple, and to worship Satan in exchange for the kingdoms of the world — answering each temptation with Scripture until the devil leaves him (vv. 1-11). Hearing that John the Baptist has been arrested, Jesus withdraws to Capernaum in Galilee, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy that a great light would dawn on that region (vv. 12-16). He begins preaching that people should repent because the kingdom of heaven has come near, then calls the fishermen Peter, Andrew, James, and John to leave their nets and follow him as fishers of men (vv. 17-22). Jesus travels through Galilee teaching in synagogues, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom, and healing every disease, drawing large crowds from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea…
h: All Galilee, and the Great Multitudes (vv.23-25)
m: temptation following baptism not by accident but by the Spirit's own leading, forty days of fasting deliberately echoing Israel's forty years in the wilderness, three temptations answered every time from the very book of Deuteronomy that once described Israel failing the same tests, two pairs of…

x: Jesus goes up on a mountain and delivers the Beatitudes, pronouncing blessing on the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the gentle, those hungry for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, peacemakers, and those persecuted for righteousness' sake (vv. 3-12). He calls his disciples the salt of the earth and the light of the world, meant to be visible rather than hidden (vv. 13-16). Jesus explains that he has come not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, and that true righteousness must exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees (vv. 17-20). He then reinterprets several commandments, tracing anger back to the root of murder and lust back to the root of adultery, and addresses divorce, oaths, and retaliation, telling his followers to turn the other cheek rather than seek revenge (vv. 21-42). The chapter closes with the call to love one's enemies and pray for those who persecute them…
h: Not to Destroy, But to Fulfil (vv.17-20)
m: nine blessings delivered from a mountain in a teacher's posture, each pairing a condition nobody would choose with a promise attached to it, salt and light offered as two images for the same uselessness if withheld, a claim stronger than the objection it answers, I am not come to destroy, but to…

x: Jesus warns against practicing righteousness to be seen by others, instructing that giving to the needy, prayer, and fasting should be done privately, trusting that the Father who sees in secret will reward them openly (vv. 1-18). He gives his disciples a model prayer addressing God as Father and seeking his kingdom and will, daily provision, forgiveness, and deliverance from temptation, then stresses that forgiving others is tied to receiving forgiveness (vv. 9-15). He tells them to store up treasures in heaven rather than on earth, describes the eye as the lamp of the body, and warns that no one can serve both God and money (vv. 19-24). The chapter closes with Jesus urging his listeners not to be anxious about food or clothing, pointing to the birds and the lilies as evidence of the Father's care, and calling them to seek God's kingdom first, trusting that each day's needs will be met…
h: Do Not Your Alms Before Men (vv.1-8)
m: three religious duties, alms, prayer and fasting, each given the identical choice between a reward already received before men and a reward from the Father who seeth in secret, a model prayer covering worship, submission, dependence, forgiveness and protection in a single short pattern, the one…

x: Jesus warns against judging others hypocritically, using the image of a speck and a beam to show that self-examination must come before correcting someone else's fault, and cautions against giving what is holy to those who will trample it (vv. 1-6). He teaches his disciples to ask, seek, and knock, trusting that the Father gives good gifts to those who ask him, and summarizes the Law and Prophets in the command to treat others as they wish to be treated (vv. 7-12). Jesus calls his listeners to enter through the narrow gate rather than the easy, crowded road to destruction, and warns them to identify false prophets by their fruit rather than their appearance (vv. 13-20). He cautions that not everyone who calls him Lord will enter the kingdom of heaven, only those who do the Father's will, and closes with the parable of two builders — one wise, whose house on rock survives the storm, and…
h: The Strait Gate and the False Prophets (vv.13-23)
m: judging forbidden on the ground of reciprocity rather than relativism, with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again, a mote and a beam turned into a joke with a serious end, a rule stated positively for once rather than negatively, all things whatsoever ye would that men should do…

x: Jesus comes down from the mountain and heals a leper who worships him, then heals a Roman centurion's paralyzed servant from a distance, commending the centurion's faith as greater than any he had found in Israel (vv. 1-13). He heals Peter's mother-in-law of a fever and, that evening, drives out spirits and heals many who are sick, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy that he would bear their diseases (vv. 14-17). When a scribe offers to follow him and a disciple asks to bury his father first, Jesus describes the cost of discipleship, noting that the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (vv. 18-22). Crossing the sea, Jesus calms a violent storm after his frightened disciples wake him, and on the other side he casts a legion of demons out of two men into a herd of pigs, which rushes into the sea, prompting the townspeople to beg him to leave (vv. 23-34).
h: Peter's Wife's Mother, and the Cost (vv.14-22)
m: a leper touched despite every social and religious barrier that made him untouchable, a Roman centurion whose understanding of authority produces the only faith in the Gospels that makes Jesus marvel, a mother-in-law healed with a touch and rising immediately to serve, two would-be followers…

x: Jesus forgives and heals a paralyzed man, showing the scribes who accuse him of blasphemy that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins (vv. 1-8). He calls the tax collector Matthew to follow him, then eats with tax collectors and sinners, telling the objecting Pharisees that he came to call sinners, not the righteous, comparing himself to a physician for the sick (vv. 9-13). When asked why his disciples don't fast like John's, Jesus explains that mourning is out of place while the bridegroom is present, and illustrates the point with new cloth on old garments and new wine in old wineskins (vv. 14-17). He raises a synagogue leader's daughter from death and heals a woman who touches his garment after twelve years of bleeding, then gives sight to two blind men and casts a demon out of a mute man, astonishing the crowds while the Pharisees credit the demons' prince (vv.…
h: Why Eateth Your Master with Publicans (vv.10-15)
The Ruler's Daughter and the Woman (vv.18-26)
Two Blind Men, and a Dumb Man (vv.27-34)
m: sins forgiven before legs are healed, addressing the deeper need first and proving the authority to do either, Matthew himself called from a tax booth with two words and answering with an immediate dinner party, two objections answered with two quotations, mercy and not sacrifice for the Pharisees…

x: Jesus commissions the twelve apostles, naming them (vv. 1-4), and sends them to the lost sheep of Israel with authority over disease and demons, instructing them to preach that the kingdom of heaven is near, heal freely, travel light, and rely on worthy hosts (vv. 5-15). He warns that they will be sent out like sheep among wolves, dragged before rulers, and betrayed even by family, but the Spirit will supply their words and those who endure to the end will be saved (vv. 16-23). He tells them not to fear those who can kill only the body, since sparrows and the hairs of their heads are under the Father's care, and that following Him brings division as well as peace, requiring them to love Him above family and take up their cross to find true life (vv. 24-39). He closes by promising a reward for anyone who welcomes His messengers, down to a cup of cold water given in His name (vv. 40-42).
h: Fear Not Them Which Kill the Body (vv.26-33)
