m: twelve named in pairs, one labeled by his old job and one by his eventual betrayal, a mission deliberately narrowed at this stage to the lost sheep of the house of Israel that Matthew will later reverse entirely, dependence commanded down to the smallest detail, no gold, no scrip, no second coat, a…

x: John the Baptist, now imprisoned, sends disciples to ask whether Jesus is truly the promised Messiah, and Jesus points to his healings and preaching to the poor as proof (vv. 2-6). He then praises John as the greatest of the prophets and the promised Elijah, though even the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he (vv. 7-14). Jesus rebukes his generation for rejecting both John's austerity and his own table fellowship, likening them to sulking children in the marketplace (vv. 16-19), then pronounces judgment on unrepentant Galilean towns like Chorazin and Capernaum for failing to respond to his miracles (vv. 20-24). He thanks the Father for revealing himself to the humble rather than the wise (vv. 25-27), and closes with his gracious invitation for the weary and burdened to come to him and find rest for their souls (vv. 28-30).
h: Come Unto Me, All Ye That Labour (vv.25-30)
m: a formula that closes every one of Matthew's five discourses used here for the first time, a bold prophet now imprisoned and doubting whether he had gotten it right, three questions about what the crowds went out to see building to an unqualified verdict on John immediately relativized in the very…

x: Conflict over the Sabbath opens the chapter as the Pharisees challenge Jesus over his disciples plucking grain and his healing a man's withered hand in the synagogue, prompting them to plot his death (vv. 1-14). Jesus withdraws and quietly fulfills Isaiah's prophecy of the humble servant (vv. 15-21), then heals a demon-possessed man who was blind and mute, leading the Pharisees to accuse him of casting out demons by the power of Satan (vv. 22-24). He answers that a divided kingdom cannot stand and warns that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is the one unforgivable sin (vv. 25-32). When the religious leaders demand a miraculous sign, he points instead to the sign of Jonah, foretelling his own death and resurrection, and warns that Nineveh and the queen of the South will condemn this unbelieving generation (vv. 38-42). He closes by describing the danger of a reformed but empty life and…
h: He Shall Not Strive Nor Cry (vv.15-30)
By Thy Words Thou Shalt Be Judged (vv.33-42)
The Empty House, and Who Is My Mother (vv.43-50)
m: two sabbath disputes both answered from precedent rather than principle, David eating the showbread and priests working in the temple, before two claims are made that are larger than either argument requires, one greater than the temple and Lord even of the sabbath, the longest Old Testament…

x: Jesus sits by the sea and teaches the crowds from a boat, beginning with the parable of the sower: seed falls on the path and is eaten by birds, on rocky ground and springs up but withers for lack of root, among thorns and is choked, and on good soil where it yields thirty, sixty, or a hundredfold (vv. 1-9). When the disciples ask why he teaches in parables, Jesus explains that they have been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom while others have not, fulfilling Isaiah's words about people who see and hear without perceiving, and he calls his disciples blessed for what they are given to see (vv. 10-17). He then interprets the sower: the seed is the word, and the four soils represent a hearer who does not understand and loses the word to the devil, one who receives it with joy but falls away under trial, one whose faith is choked by worldly cares and the love of wealth, and one who…
h: The Sower Explained, and the Tares (vv.18-30)
Mustard Seed, Leaven, and the Parables Explained (vv.31-43)
m: a sower parable told from a boat without a word of interpretation, four soils and four outcomes closing on who hath ears to hear, let him hear, parables explained as an act of both grace and judgment, revealing to the open and confirming the blindness of those already closed, a private…

x: Herod Antipas hears reports of Jesus and fears John the Baptist has been raised from the dead, prompting Matthew to recount how Herod had John beheaded to satisfy a rash oath made to Herodias' daughter (vv. 1-12). Jesus withdraws by boat, but when crowds follow him he has compassion on them, healing the sick and then feeding five thousand men, besides women and children, with five loaves and two fish (vv. 13-21). That night he sends the disciples ahead by boat and comes to them walking on the sea; Peter asks to come to him and briefly walks on the water himself before doubt sets in and he begins to sink, and Jesus catches him and calms the wind (vv. 22-32). The disciples in the boat worship him as the Son of God (v. 33), and when they land at Gennesaret, crowds bring the sick to him, and all who touch even the fringe of his garment are healed (vv. 34-36).
h: The Death of John the Baptist (vv.1-12)
The Feeding of the Five Thousand (vv.13-21)
m: John's death told as a flashback triggered by Herod's guilty conscience, a rash oath at a birthday party sealing a prophet's fate that Herod himself lacked the will to order sooner, five thousand men fed from five loaves and two fishes after Jesus is moved with compassion rather than sending the…

x: Scribes and Pharisees confront Jesus for letting his disciples ignore the tradition of the elders regarding handwashing, and Jesus counters that they themselves nullify God's commands for the sake of their traditions, citing Isaiah's charge that they honor God with their lips while their hearts are far from him (vv. 1-9). He then teaches the crowds and disciples that it is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the heart — evil thoughts, murder, theft, and slander (vv. 10-20). A Canaanite woman from the region of Tyre and Sidon begs him to heal her demon-tormented daughter, and though he initially tests her, he commends her great faith and grants her request (vv. 21-28). Jesus heals a great crowd by the Sea of Galilee (vv. 29-31), and, moved with compassion for the hungry multitude, feeds four thousand men and their families with seven loaves and a few…
h: Not That Which Goeth Into the Mouth (vv.10-20)
m: a hand-washing dispute turned into a countercharge that the Pharisees' own tradition voids God's actual commandment, corban exposed as a loophole that lets religious devotion excuse abandoning aging parents, a principle announced to the crowd, not that which goeth into the mouth defileth a man, but…

x: The Pharisees and Sadducees demand a sign from heaven, but Jesus refuses and warns his disciples instead to beware the leaven — the corrupting teaching — of the Pharisees and Sadducees (vv. 1-12). At Caesarea Philippi he asks who people say he is, and Peter declares him the Christ, the Son of the living God; Jesus blesses Peter for this Father-given revelation and says he will build his church on this confession, giving Peter the keys of the kingdom (vv. 13-20). From that point Jesus begins telling his disciples plainly that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer, be killed, and rise on the third day, and when Peter objects, Jesus sharply rebukes him for thinking merely human thoughts rather than God's (vv. 21-23). He then tells all his disciples that anyone who would follow him must deny himself and take up his cross, warning that whoever tries to save his life will lose it, and asking what…
h: A Sign, and the Leaven of the Pharisees (vv.1-12)
Whom Say Ye That I Am (vv.13-17,19-20)
m: Pharisees and Sadducees together demanding a sign answered by mocking their own competence at reading weather, a warning about leaven that the disciples take as a comment on forgotten bread until Matthew supplies what they missed, a question asked in two stages at a city built around pagan worship…

x: Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain, where he is transfigured before them, his face shining like the sun and his clothes turning white as light, as Moses and Elijah appear speaking with him and a voice from heaven again declares him God's beloved Son (vv. 1-8). As they come down, Jesus tells them not to speak of it until after his resurrection and explains that John the Baptist already fulfilled the coming of Elijah (vv. 9-13). At the foot of the mountain he heals a boy tormented by a demon that the disciples had been unable to cast out, attributing their failure to little faith and saying that faith even as small as a mustard seed can move mountains (vv. 14-21). Jesus again predicts to his disciples that he will be betrayed, killed, and raised on the third day, filling them with grief (vv. 22-23). The chapter closes with Jesus, to avoid giving offense over the temple…
h: The Boy the Disciples Could Not Heal (vv.14-21)
m: three disciples taken up a mountain and shown a glory breaking through ordinary human form, his face did shine as the sun, Moses and Elijah appearing beside him before a voice repeats the words from the baptism with one addition, hear ye him, a boy the disciples cannot heal met first with…

x: When the disciples ask who is greatest in the kingdom of heaven, Jesus calls a child to himself and says that only those who humble themselves like children will enter the kingdom at all, and that welcoming such a child is welcoming him (vv. 1-5). He warns severely against causing one of these little ones to sin, saying it would be better to be drowned than to cause such stumbling, and urges radical measures to avoid sin (vv. 6-9). Through the parable of the lost sheep, he shows that the Father is unwilling that any of these little ones should perish (vv. 10-14). Jesus then lays out a process for confronting a sinning brother — privately, then with witnesses, then before the church — and promises his presence wherever two or three gather in his name (vv. 15-20). When Peter asks how many times he must forgive, Jesus answers not seven times but seventy times seven, and illustrates the…
h: Where Two or Three Are Gathered (vv.18-22)
The Parable of the Unforgiving Servant (vv.23-35)
m: a child called into the middle of the room to answer a question about greatness, the most violent language in the whole Gospel aimed at anyone who causes one of these little ones to offend, a shepherd's arithmetic applied to a single lost sheep out of ninety-nine, an explicit three-step process for…

x: Pharisees test Jesus by asking about divorce, and he responds that God's original design joined man and woman as one flesh and that Moses permitted divorce only because of hardness of heart, adding that divorcing one's wife except for sexual immorality and remarrying commits adultery (vv. 1-9). When the disciples react that it is better not to marry, Jesus speaks of those who remain single for the kingdom's sake (vv. 10-12). He welcomes little children brought to him despite the disciples' objections, saying the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these (vv. 13-15). A rich young man asks what he must do to inherit eternal life, and when told to keep the commandments and then to sell his possessions and follow Jesus, he goes away sorrowful because of his great wealth, prompting Jesus to say it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the…
m: a test question about divorce answered by going behind Moses to Genesis itself, what therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder, Moses' provision named a concession to hardness of heart rather than a permission, disciples rebuking people who bring children to Jesus for the second…

x: Jesus tells the parable of the workers in the vineyard, in which a landowner pays laborers hired at the end of the day the same wage as those who worked since morning, illustrating God's sovereign generosity and the principle that the last will be first, and the first last (vv. 1-16). He again predicts to the Twelve that he will be delivered to the chief priests, condemned, mocked, and crucified, and will rise on the third day (vv. 17-19). The mother of James and John asks that her sons sit at Jesus' right and left in his kingdom, and Jesus responds that such positions belong to the Father to assign, and teaches the Twelve that greatness in his kingdom means becoming a servant, since the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many (vv. 20-28). As he leaves Jericho, two blind men cry out for mercy, and Jesus, moved with compassion, touches…
h: The Third Prediction, and the Cup (vv.17-24)
m: a parable found only in Matthew existing specifically to unsettle the promise Peter has just been given, laborers hired at dawn and at the eleventh hour all paid the same penny, a complaint answered not by denying unfairness but by asking is thine eye evil, because I am good, the most detailed…

x: Jesus sends two disciples to bring a donkey and its colt so he can enter Jerusalem riding on them, fulfilling Zechariah's prophecy of a humble king, as the crowds spread their cloaks and branches and shout Hosanna (vv. 1-11). He enters the temple and drives out the money changers and merchants, declaring it a house of prayer that they have made a den of robbers, and heals the blind and lame who come to him there (vv. 12-17). The next morning, finding a fig tree with no fruit, he curses it and it withers at once, using the moment to teach the disciples about faith that does not doubt (vv. 18-22). When the chief priests and elders question his authority, he answers with a counter-question about John's baptism that they refuse to answer (vv. 23-27), then tells the parable of the two sons to expose their false obedience (vv. 28-32) and the parable of the wicked tenants, who kill the…
h: The Temple, and the Fig Tree (vv.12-22)
By What Authority, and Two Sons (vv.23-32)
m: detailed arrangements given in advance for a donkey and colt, fulfilling Zechariah's prophecy of a king who comes in peace rather than in war, a crowd shouting Hosanna to the son of David, a royal acclamation the city itself cannot quite explain, calling him only Jesus the prophet of Nazareth of…

x: Jesus tells the parable of a king's wedding feast for his son, in which invited guests refuse to come and even kill the king's servants, so the king destroys them and instead fills the banquet with people gathered from the streets, though one man without a wedding garment is cast out (vv. 1-14). The Pharisees try to trap him over paying taxes to Caesar, and he answers that they should render to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's (vv. 15-22). The Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, pose a question about a woman married to seven brothers, and Jesus corrects their misunderstanding of both Scripture and God's power, declaring that God is the God of the living (vv. 23-33). A lawyer asks which commandment is greatest, and Jesus names loving God with all one's heart, soul, and mind as the first, and loving one's neighbor as oneself as the second, on which hang all the Law and…
h: The Sadducees, and the Great Commandment (vv.23-40)
m: a wedding feast parable ending in a detail unique to Matthew, a guest without a wedding garment cast out even after the doors were thrown open to bad and good alike, an unnatural alliance between Pharisees and Herodians setting a tax trap with no safe answer, a coin's image drawn out to produce the…

x: Jesus warns the crowds and his disciples against the hypocrisy of the scribes and Pharisees, who teach the law but do not practice it and burden others while seeking honor, titles, and the best seats for themselves (vv. 1-12). He then pronounces seven scathing woes against the scribes and Pharisees: for shutting people out of the kingdom (v. 13), for making converts into sons of hell (v. 15), for elevating trivial oaths and neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness while meticulously tithing garden herbs (vv. 16-23), for straining out a gnat while swallowing a camel (v. 24), for cleaning the outside of the cup while remaining full of greed and self-indulgence within (vv. 25-26), for resembling whitewashed tombs that look beautiful outside but are full of dead bones and uncleanness within (vv. 27-28), and for building tombs for the prophets while being the spiritual heirs of those who…
m: instruction to obey the scribes and Pharisees paired immediately with a warning not to imitate their works, the charge being inconsistency rather than error, three titles forbidden to the disciples, Rabbi, father and master, seven specific woes rather than general abuse, straining a gnat and…

x: Jesus predicts that the temple's buildings will be utterly thrown down, and when the disciples ask privately about the sign of his coming and the end of the age, he begins the Olivet Discourse, warning of false messiahs, wars, famines, and earthquakes as only the beginning of birth pains, and of persecution, betrayal, and the gospel being preached to all nations before the end comes (vv. 1-14). He warns of the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place and describes a tribulation unlike any before, urging those in Judea to flee immediately and warning against false christs and false prophets performing signs (vv. 15-28). After that tribulation, he says, the sun and moon will darken and the Son of Man will appear in the sky with power and great glory, sending his angels to gather his elect (vv. 29-31). Using the parable of the fig tree, he says these signs mean the end is near…
h: The Fig Tree, and No Man Knoweth (vv.29-44)
m: a prediction that not one stone shall be left upon another answered by three joined questions about timing and signs, wars, famines and earthquakes named explicitly as only the beginning of sorrows rather than the end, a specific sign, the abomination of desolation, triggering practical…

x: Jesus tells the parable of the ten virgins awaiting a bridegroom, five wise and prepared with extra oil and five foolish who run out, teaching the disciples to watch, since they do not know the day or hour of his return (vv. 1-13). In the parable of the talents, a master entrusts his servants with different sums of money before departing, and rewards the two who invested and multiplied what they were given while condemning the one who buried his talent out of fear as wicked and lazy (vv. 14-30). Jesus then describes the final judgment, when the Son of Man will come in glory and separate all nations as a shepherd separates sheep from goats, welcoming the righteous into the kingdom because they fed, clothed, welcomed, and visited him in the person of the least of his brothers, and sending away those who failed to do so into eternal punishment (vv. 31-46).
m: five wise and five foolish virgins differing only in oil kept in reserve, all ten having slept, the failure being unpreparedness for delay rather than wakefulness itself, three servants given unequal sums and judged identically for what they do with them rather than how much they receive, a buried…

x: The chief priests plot to kill Jesus while a woman anoints him with costly ointment at Bethany in preparation for his burial, an act Jesus commends even as Judas Iscariot goes to the chief priests and agrees to betray him for thirty pieces of silver (vv. 1-16). At the Passover meal, Jesus identifies his betrayer, then institutes the Lord's Supper, giving the bread and cup as symbols of his body and blood poured out for the forgiveness of sins (vv. 17-30). On the way to the Mount of Olives he predicts that all the disciples will fall away and that Peter will deny him three times that very night (vv. 31-35). In Gethsemane, Jesus prays in anguish that the cup might pass from him while yielding to the Father's will, though Peter, James, and John repeatedly fall asleep instead of watching with him (vv. 36-46). Judas arrives with an armed crowd and betrays Jesus with a kiss; Jesus is arrested…
h: The Plot, and the Anointing at Bethany (vv.1-16)
m: the longest chapter in the whole Gospel opening with a plot dated carefully to avoid an uproar during the feast, an anointing at Bethany defended as preparation for burial against an objection costed in exact terms, thirty pieces of silver recorded only by Matthew as the price of betrayal, the same…

x: The chief priests hand Jesus over to Pilate, and Judas, overcome with remorse, returns the thirty pieces of silver and hangs himself, the money later used to buy the potter's field (vv. 1-10). Before Pilate, Jesus makes no defense, and though Pilate's wife warns him and Pilate himself finds no fault in Jesus, the crowd — stirred up by the chief priests — demands the release of the criminal Barabbas instead and calls for Jesus to be crucified, taking his blood upon themselves (vv. 11-26). Roman soldiers mock Jesus with a crown of thorns and a purple robe before leading him to Golgotha, where he is crucified between two criminals while onlookers and religious leaders jeer at him to save himself (vv. 27-44). From noon until three, darkness covers the land, and Jesus cries out in anguish before giving up his spirit, at which point the temple curtain is torn in two, the earth shakes, and a…
m: Judas's fate told only in this Gospel, a confession offered and refused, see thou to that, before silver bought a field, Pilate's own wife sending a warning during the hearing that he chooses to ignore, hands washed in front of the crowd changing nothing about the verdict already decided, a…

x: On the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary come to the tomb and find it opened by an angel, who tells them Jesus has risen just as he said and sends them to tell the disciples he is going ahead of them to Galilee (vv. 1-7). Jesus himself meets the women on their way, and they worship him and take hold of his feet (vv. 8-10). Meanwhile, the guards report what happened to the chief priests, who bribe them to spread the false story that the disciples stole the body while they slept (vv. 11-15). The eleven disciples meet Jesus on a mountain in Galilee, where, though some still doubt, he declares that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him and commissions them to make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything he commanded, promising to be with them always, to…
h: The Angel, and the Empty Tomb (vv.1-10)
m: an earthquake and a descending angel recorded only in this Gospel, guards left shaking and as dead men, a message reduced to four short clauses, fear not, he is not here, he is risen, come see the place, women leaving with fear and great joy held together rather than resolved into one, worship and…

x: Mark opens by introducing John the Baptist, who preaches repentance and baptism in the wilderness in fulfillment of prophecy (vv. 1-8). Jesus is baptized, the Spirit descends on Him like a dove, and a voice from heaven declares Him God's beloved Son (vv. 9-11), after which He is tempted by Satan in the wilderness for forty days (vv. 12-13). Returning to Galilee, He announces that the kingdom of God has come near and calls Simon, Andrew, James, and John to follow Him (vv. 14-20). In Capernaum He teaches with striking authority, casts out an unclean spirit, and heals Simon's mother-in-law and many others (vv. 21-34). Early the next morning He withdraws to pray, then tells His disciples they must carry His message to other towns, and the chapter closes with the healing of a leper (vv. 35-45).
h: Baptism and Temptation in Five Verses (vv.9-13)
A Whole City at the Door (vv.29-34)
The Leper Who Would Not Keep Quiet (vv.40-45)
m: A gospel that starts without a genealogy or a nativity, John in the wilderness, baptism and temptation compressed into five verses, four fishermen called at once, authority recognized before it is explained, and a healed leper whose talking shuts Jesus out of the towns

x: Jesus returns to Capernaum, where four men lower a paralyzed friend through the roof; He forgives the man's sins and heals him, demonstrating His authority as the Son of Man (vv. 1-12). He calls the tax collector Levi to follow Him and dines with tax collectors and sinners, drawing criticism from the scribes and Pharisees (vv. 13-17). Asked why His disciples don't fast, Jesus describes Himself as the bridegroom and uses the images of new cloth and new wine to show that His arrival brings something new (vv. 18-22). The chapter closes with two Sabbath controversies: His disciples pick grain in the fields, and Jesus declares that the Sabbath was made for humanity, not humanity for the Sabbath, identifying Himself as Lord even of the Sabbath (vv. 23-28).
m: A paralytic's sins forgiven before his legs are healed, scribes who reason correctly about who can forgive sins and stop short of the conclusion, a tax collector's table chosen deliberately over the righteous, new cloth and new wine refused a home in old containers, and the sabbath declared made…

x: Jesus heals a man's withered hand in the synagogue on the Sabbath, provoking the Pharisees and Herodians to begin plotting His death (vv. 1-6). Large crowds follow Him from across the region for healing, and He appoints twelve apostles to be with Him and to preach and cast out demons (vv. 7-19). When His family sets out to restrain Him, thinking Him out of His mind, scribes from Jerusalem accuse Him of casting out demons by the power of Beelzebul (vv. 20-22). Jesus answers that a divided kingdom cannot stand and warns that blaspheming the Holy Spirit is an unforgivable, eternal sin (vv. 23-30). When His mother and brothers arrive looking for Him, He declares that whoever does the will of God is His true brother and sister and mother (vv. 31-35).
m: A withered hand used as a trap before it is used as a healing, the one place in the Gospels where Jesus is described as angry, Pharisees and Herodians allied against a common threat despite being natural enemies, twelve chosen to be with Him before being sent out for Him, and a family standing…

x: Teaching from a boat beside the Sea of Galilee, Jesus tells the parable of the sower and explains privately to His disciples that the seed represents the word of God received in different kinds of soil (vv. 1-20). He follows with the parables of the lamp, the seed growing secretly, and the mustard seed, each showing how the kingdom of God begins small and hidden yet inevitably produces a harvest or great growth (vv. 21-32). That evening, crossing the lake, a violent storm arises while Jesus sleeps; He rebukes the wind and waves with a word, and they instantly grow calm, leaving His awestruck disciples wondering who this is that even the wind and sea obey (vv. 35-41).
h: Nothing Hid That Shall Not Be Manifested (vv.21-25)
m: A sower parable called foundational to understanding every other parable, four soils sorting hearers by what happens after the seed lands, a seed that grows while the farmer sleeps and does not know how, a mustard seed's disproportion between its start and its finish, and a storm rebuked with two…

x: Crossing to the region of the Gerasenes, Jesus frees a man possessed by a legion of demons, sending them into a herd of pigs that rushes into the sea, though the townspeople ask Him to leave (vv. 1-20). Back in Galilee, a synagogue leader named Jairus begs Jesus to heal his dying daughter (vv. 21-24). On the way, a woman who has suffered a twelve-year hemorrhage touches His garment and is instantly healed, and Jesus commends her faith (vv. 25-34). Though word comes that the girl has died, Jesus continues to the house, takes her by the hand, and raises her back to life, astonishing everyone present (vv. 35-43).
h: The Woman with the Issue of Blood (vv.25-34)
m: A legion of demons overpowered by a single word after no one else could help, a synagogue ruler kneeling in public because his daughter is dying, an interruption on the way that costs precious time yet ends in a name, daughter spoken to a woman healed after twelve years of isolation, and Talitha…

x: Jesus is rejected by His own hometown of Nazareth, where the people take offense at Him despite His wisdom and mighty works (vv. 1-6). He sends the twelve out in pairs with authority over unclean spirits, instructing them to travel light (vv. 7-13). This prompts an account of Herod's beheading of John the Baptist at his stepdaughter's request (vv. 14-29). When the apostles return, Jesus feeds a crowd of five thousand with five loaves and two fish, with twelve baskets left over (vv. 30-44). He then sends the disciples ahead by boat, walks out to them on the sea during a storm, and calms their fear, and the chapter closes with more healings at Gennesaret (vv. 45-56).
h: The Twelve Sent Out Two by Two (vv.7-13)
The Death of John the Baptist (vv.14-29)
Gennesaret and the Border of His Garment (vv.53-56)
m: A hometown that cannot see past the carpenter it thinks it knows, twelve sent in pairs with a packing list that is mostly prohibitions, John's death told as a flashback about a king trapped by his own rash promise, five loaves and two fish stretched to feed a multitude, and hearts still hardened…

x: When the Pharisees and scribes criticize Jesus' disciples for eating with unwashed hands, He confronts their elevation of human tradition over God's commandment and teaches that true defilement comes from within the heart, not from what enters the body (vv. 1-23). Traveling into Gentile territory near Tyre, He heals the demon-possessed daughter of a Syrophoenician woman after she persistently pleads her case (vv. 24-30). In the Decapolis, Jesus heals a deaf man with a speech impediment, touching his ears and tongue, and though He orders silence, the crowds spread the news all the more (vv. 31-37).
h: The Heart as the Source of Sin (vv.20-23)
m: A hand-washing tradition used to nullify a command Moses actually gave, honoring God with the lips while the heart stays far away, thirteen sins traced to what comes out of a man rather than what goes in, a Gentile woman who accepts the insult and argues from inside it, and Ephphatha spoken…

x: Jesus feeds four thousand people with seven loaves and a few small fish, then warns His disciples to beware the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod after they miss the point of His earlier miracles (vv. 1-21). At Bethsaida He heals a blind man in two stages, restoring his sight gradually (vv. 22-26). Near Caesarea Philippi, Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ (vv. 27-30), after which Jesus gives the first prediction of His coming suffering, death, and resurrection and rebukes Peter for resisting it (vv. 31-33). He then teaches the crowd that anyone who would follow Him must deny himself, take up his cross, and be willing to lose his life for the gospel's sake (vv. 34-38).
h: The Feeding of the Four Thousand (vv.1-10)
m: A second feeding recorded without embarrassment at its resemblance to the first, a sign refused to a generation with a sigh deep in the spirit, a warning about leaven mistaken for a comment on forgotten bread, a blind man healed in two stages that mirrors the disciples' own half-understanding, and…

x: Jesus is transfigured on a mountain before Peter, James, and John, His clothes becoming dazzling white as He speaks with Moses and Elijah while a voice from heaven again identifies Him as God's Son (vv. 1-13). Descending, He casts out a demon from a boy that His disciples could not, telling them the feat requires prayer (vv. 14-29). After a second prediction of His death and resurrection, He finds the disciples arguing about who is greatest and teaches that true greatness means becoming servant of all, welcoming a child as an example (vv. 30-37). He then addresses an outsider casting out demons in His name and closes with severe warnings against causing others to stumble, urging His followers to deal radically with sin (vv. 38-50).
h: The Greatest Is Servant of All (vv.30-37)
He That Is Not Against Us (vv.38-41)
Offend Not One of These Little Ones (vv.42-50)
m: Glory breaking through six days after a saying about not tasting death, a father's confession that he believes and needs help for his unbelief in the same breath, a second passion prediction met with fear rather than questions, a child taken in Jesus' arms as the answer to an argument about…

x: Jesus teaches that God's original design for marriage makes divorce a departure from His intent (vv. 1-12), then rebukes His disciples for turning away children and blesses them instead (vv. 13-16). A rich young man asks how to inherit eternal life but walks away sorrowful when told to sell his possessions, prompting Jesus to teach how hard it is for the wealthy to enter the kingdom (vv. 17-27). Jesus promises reward for those who have left everything to follow Him (vv. 28-31) and gives a third, more detailed prediction of His death and resurrection (vv. 32-34). When James and John ask for places of honor, He teaches that greatness in His kingdom means serving others, since the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and to give His life as a ransom for many (vv. 35-45). The chapter ends as Jesus restores sight to the blind beggar Bartimaeus outside Jericho (vv. 46-52).
h: A Camel Through a Needle's Eye (vv.23-31)
James and John Ask for Glory (vv.35-45)
m: Divorce answered by going behind Moses' concession to Genesis itself, Jesus much displeased that children were being turned away, a rich man Jesus is said to have loved even as he asks him to give everything away, a saying about a camel and a needle's eye repeated because of how it was received…

x: Jesus enters Jerusalem to crowds shouting praise and spreading cloaks and branches before Him, fulfilling messianic expectation as He rides in on a colt (vv. 1-11). The next day, on the way from Bethany, He curses a fig tree that has leaves but no fruit (vv. 12-14), then drives the money changers and merchants from the temple, condemning them for turning a house of prayer into a den of robbers (vv. 15-19). Passing the fig tree again, the disciples find it withered, prompting Jesus to teach on the power of faith-filled prayer and the need to forgive others (vv. 20-26). When the chief priests, scribes, and elders challenge His authority, Jesus answers with a question about John's baptism that leaves them unable to respond (vv. 27-33).
m: A fig tree cursed and a temple cleansed with one story wrapped around the other, leaves without fruit read as a verdict on Israel's worship, a question about authority answered with a counter-question about John's baptism, both sides caught reasoning out loud about what answer is safe rather than…

x: Jesus tells the parable of the wicked tenants who kill the vineyard owner's son, a picture of Israel's rejection of God's messengers and ultimately His Son (vv. 1-12). Religious leaders try to trap Him with questions about paying taxes to Caesar and about marriage in the resurrection, but He answers both in a way that silences them (vv. 13-27). Asked which commandment is greatest, Jesus names loving God with all one's heart and loving one's neighbor as oneself (vv. 28-34). He then raises a question about the Messiah's identity as David's son and Lord (vv. 35-37), warns against the scribes' love of status and their exploitation of widows (vv. 38-40), and commends a poor widow whose two small coins given at the temple treasury represent greater sacrifice than the large gifts of the wealthy (vv. 41-44).
m: A vineyard parable told to men who recognize themselves in it before it ends, render to Caesar drawn from a coin's own image rather than given as a rule, resurrection defended against two errors named separately, a scribe told he is not far from the kingdom which is not the same as being in it, and…

x: As they leave the temple, Jesus predicts its complete destruction, prompting His disciples to ask for signs of when this and His return will happen (vv. 1-4). He warns of false messiahs, wars, and persecution as birth pains preceding the end, and tells His followers they will be brought before authorities to testify (vv. 5-13). He describes a coming abomination of desolation and unprecedented tribulation that will require immediate flight (vv. 14-23), followed by cosmic signs and the visible return of the Son of Man in power and glory to gather His elect (vv. 24-27). Using the fig tree as an illustration, He teaches that these signs mean His coming is near, though the exact day and hour are known to no one but the Father (vv. 28-32). The chapter closes with a call to stay alert and watchful, since no one knows when the master of the house will return (vv. 33-37).
h: The Question on the Mount of Olives (vv.3-4)
Take Heed: Deceivers, Wars, and Birth Pangs (vv.5-13)
The Son of Man Coming in Clouds (vv.24-27)
The Fig Tree and This Generation (vv.28-31)
No Man Knows the Day: Watch (vv.32-37)
m: A question prompted by admiration of the temple, deception named as the first danger, tribulation described as birth pangs rather than the end, the Son of Man coming in clouds, a day the Son himself does not know, and watchfulness as the whole practical application

x: As plots against Jesus intensify, a woman anoints Him with costly perfume at Bethany in preparation for His burial, while Judas Iscariot arranges with the chief priests to betray Him (vv. 1-11). At the Passover meal, Jesus predicts that one of the Twelve will betray Him and institutes what becomes the Lord's Supper, giving the bread and cup as symbols of His body and blood poured out for many (vv. 12-25). After singing a hymn, they go to the Mount of Olives, where Jesus predicts that all the disciples will fall away and that Peter will deny Him three times that very night (vv. 26-31). In Gethsemane, Jesus prays in anguish for the cup to pass while His disciples repeatedly fall asleep, until Judas arrives with an armed crowd and betrays Him with a kiss, leading to His arrest as the disciples scatter (vv. 32-52). Jesus is brought before the Sanhedrin, where false testimony fails to…
h: The Plot, and the Anointing at Bethany (vv.1-11)
The Arrest, and the Young Man Who Fled (vv.43-52)
m: An anointing framed by a plot, betrayal named at the table, a cup and a covenant, Gethsemane prayed in Aramaic, a disciple who runs out of his clothes, the plainest claim to deity in the Gospel, and Peter warming himself at the enemy's fire

x: Jesus is delivered to Pilate, who questions Him and offers to release Him, but the crowd, incited by the chief priests, demands the release of Barabbas instead and calls for Jesus to be crucified (vv. 1-15). Roman soldiers mock Jesus as a false king, dressing Him in a purple robe and a crown of thorns, before leading Him out to Golgotha, where Simon of Cyrene is compelled to carry His cross (vv. 16-21). Jesus is crucified between two criminals while soldiers cast lots for His clothes and passersby, chief priests, and even the criminals hurl insults at Him (vv. 22-32). Darkness covers the land from noon until three, when Jesus cries out and dies; at that moment the temple curtain is torn in two, and a Roman centurion declares that this man truly was the Son of God (vv. 33-39). The chapter closes as Joseph of Arimathea receives permission to take Jesus' body and lays it in a new tomb…
h: Darkness and the Cry from the Cross (vv.33-38)
m: A charge that changes from blasphemy to kingship on the way to Pilate, a governor surprised into silence by a defendant who will not defend himself, Barabbas released as a failure of nerve Mark names outright, a mock coronation where kneeling is recorded as worship, and a centurion's confession…

x: Early on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and other women come to the tomb with spices, wondering who will roll away the stone, only to find it already open and empty (vv. 1-4). A young man dressed in white tells them Jesus has risen and instructs them to tell the disciples and Peter that He is going ahead of them to Galilee, but the women flee in fear and say nothing to anyone (vv. 5-8). In the passage traditionally included as the longer ending, the risen Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene, to two disciples on the road, and to the Eleven, rebuking their unbelief before commissioning them to go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature, and He is then taken up into heaven (vv. 9-20).
m: Spices bought and a stone already rolled away before the question about it is finished, an errand that names one disciple specifically among the rest, the earliest manuscripts ending on fear and silence rather than resolution, a longer ending debated for centuries as possibly not Mark's own hand…

x: Gabriel appears to the priest Zechariah in the temple, announcing that his barren wife Elizabeth will bear a son, John, who will prepare the way of the Lord (vv. 5-17); when Zechariah doubts, he is struck mute (vv. 18-20). Six months later Gabriel visits the virgin Mary in Nazareth, announcing that she will conceive by the Holy Spirit and bear the Son of God, Jesus (vv. 26-35). Mary visits Elizabeth, whose unborn child leaps for joy, and responds with the Magnificat, praising God for exalting the humble (vv. 39-55). John is born, Zechariah's speech returns, and he prophesies over his son in the Benedictus, celebrating a Savior from David's line who will guide Israel into peace (vv. 57-79). The chapter closes noting John's growth in the wilderness (v. 80).
h: Gabriel and Zechariah in the Temple (vv.5-25)
The Birth and Naming of John (vv.57-66)
m: The only Gospel to open with a formal preface, two annunciations set against each other, an old priest silenced for asking and a young girl commended for asking, two songs preserved nowhere else, and a naming that breaks with the family

x: A census under Caesar Augustus brings Joseph and the pregnant Mary to Bethlehem, where she gives birth to Jesus and lays him in a feeding trough because there is no room at the inn (vv. 1-7). An angel announces the good news to shepherds in the fields, and a multitude of angels praises God; the shepherds go and see, then spread the word (vv. 8-20). At eight days Jesus is circumcised and named, and at the temple the devout Simeon and the prophetess Anna recognize him as the promised redemption of Israel (vv. 21-38). Twelve years later, on a family trip to Jerusalem for Passover, Jesus stays behind in the temple; his parents find him after three days, astonishing the teachers with his understanding, and he explains he had to be in his Father's house (vv. 41-49). He returns to Nazareth and grows in wisdom and favor with God and people (vv. 51-52).
m: a birth dated by an administrative decree rather than by any angel or star, a couple traveling only because a government required it and a firstborn laid in a feeding trough for lack of room, an announcement made not to kings or scholars but to shepherds working a night shift, a sign they can…

x: John the Baptist begins his ministry in the wilderness, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy of one preparing the way of the Lord (vv. 1-6). He preaches repentance to the crowds, warning against relying on descent from Abraham, and gives specific instructions to different groups: sharing with the needy, tax collectors collecting no more than required, and soldiers being content with their wages and avoiding extortion (vv. 7-14). He points ahead to one mightier than himself who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire (vv. 15-17), and Luke notes Herod later imprisons John (vv. 19-20). Jesus is baptized, and as he prays, the heavens open, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father's voice declares him his beloved Son (vv. 21-22). The chapter closes with Jesus' genealogy traced backward through David and Abraham all the way to Adam, the son of God (vv. 23-38).
m: a historian's precision naming seven office-holders from Caesar down to the high priests before saying the word of God came to none of them but to John, Isaiah quoted at greater length than any other Gospel keeps, all flesh shall see the salvation of God, practical instructions unique to Luke given…

x: Full of the Holy Spirit, Jesus is led into the wilderness where he fasts forty days and resists three temptations from the devil — to turn stones to bread, to gain the world's kingdoms by worshiping Satan, and to test God by leaping from the temple — answering each with Scripture (vv. 1-13). Returning to Galilee, he teaches in the synagogues, then in Nazareth reads from Isaiah 61 and declares the prophecy of good news to the poor fulfilled in himself (vv. 14-21). When he cites God's past mercy to Gentiles over Israelites, the hometown crowd turns violent and tries to throw him off a cliff, but he passes through them unharmed (vv. 22-30). In Capernaum he casts out an unclean spirit in the synagogue, heals Simon's mother-in-law of a fever, and heals many more at sunset, demonstrating his authority over sickness and demons before withdrawing to pray and continuing his preaching tour (vv.…
h: In the Power of the Spirit (vv.14-15)
Simon's Wife's Mother, and the Many (vv.38-44)
m: temptation following the Spirit's own leading rather than any accident, three temptations ending with the temple rather than the kingdoms, Jerusalem left as the last word because Jerusalem is where this whole Gospel is heading, a homecoming sermon at Nazareth that reads Isaiah aloud and stops…

x: Jesus teaches from Simon Peter's boat, then tells him to let down his nets, resulting in a catch so large it nearly sinks two boats; Peter, awestruck, falls before him, and Jesus calls him and his partners James and John to become fishers of people (vv. 1-11). Jesus cleanses a man full of leprosy with a touch (vv. 12-16), then, at a house packed with Pharisees and teachers of the law, heals a paralyzed man lowered through the roof, first forgiving his sins to prove his authority to do so, provoking accusations of blasphemy (vv. 17-26). He calls the tax collector Levi, dines with sinners at his house, and answers Pharisee objections by saying he came to call sinners, not the righteous (vv. 27-32). Questioned about fasting, he explains that his presence is like a wedding, and teaches that his new teaching cannot simply be patched onto old forms, like new wine needing new wineskins (vv.…
h: The Paralytic Let Down Through the Roof (vv.17-26)
Levi Called, and a Party for Sinners (vv.27-32)
m: A fisherman told his trade by a carpenter, conviction rather than delight as the response to power, a roof opened to reach Jesus, forgiveness offered before healing, a tax collector who throws a party, and new wine that will not go into old skins

x: Jesus defends his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath and heals a man's withered hand on the Sabbath, declaring himself Lord of the Sabbath and provoking the Pharisees' rage (vv. 1-11). After a night of prayer, he chooses twelve apostles from his disciples (vv. 12-16), then, before a great crowd, delivers the Sermon on the Plain: blessings on the poor, hungry, weeping, and persecuted, paired with woes on the rich, full, and well-regarded (vv. 20-26). He commands radical love for enemies, generosity without expectation of return, and mercy instead of judgment (vv. 27-38), then warns against hypocrisy in correcting others and teaches that good and bad fruit reveal the heart (vv. 39-45). The chapter closes with the parable of two builders: the one who hears and obeys Jesus' words is like a house founded on rock, secure against the storm, while the one who does not is like a house…
h: A Night of Prayer, and the Twelve Chosen (vv.12-16)
The Blind Guide, the Beam, and the Tree (vv.39-45)
m: Two Sabbath confrontations, a night of prayer before choosing twelve men, blessings paired with woes found only here, poverty and hunger named without spiritualizing, love of enemies as the distinguishing mark, and two builders distinguished by what they dug

x: Jesus heals a Roman centurion's dying servant from a distance, marveling at the centurion's faith, greater than any he found in Israel (vv. 1-10). At Nain he raises a widow's only son from death, moved by compassion, prompting the crowd to declare a great prophet has arisen (vv. 11-17). When John the Baptist's disciples ask if Jesus is the promised one, he points to his healings and preaching as fulfillment of prophecy, and praises John as the greatest born of women while noting the least in the kingdom is greater still (vv. 18-28). At a Pharisee's dinner, a sinful woman washes Jesus' feet with her tears and anoints them, and Jesus tells the parable of two forgiven debtors to show that her great love flows from having been forgiven much, declaring her sins forgiven and her faith the source of her salvation (vv. 36-50).
h: Art Thou He That Should Come (vv.18-28)
m: a centurion who never appears in person, reasoning from military chain of command rather than personal merit, say in a word, and my servant shall be healed, drawing the strongest compliment Jesus pays anyone in the Gospels, a widow's only son raised at Nain without anyone even asking, compassion…

x: Jesus tells the parable of the sower, explaining that the seed is God's word and the soils represent different responses to it, and teaches that revealed truth is meant to be shared, not hidden (vv. 1-18). When his mother and brothers seek him, he redefines family as those who hear and do God's word (vv. 19-21). Crossing the lake, he calms a violent storm with a word, astonishing the disciples (vv. 22-25), then delivers a man possessed by a legion of demons, sending them into a herd of pigs that rushes into the water (vv. 26-39). Returning, he heals a woman who touches his cloak after twelve years of bleeding, commending her faith (vv. 40-48), and raises Jairus' twelve-year-old daughter from death, telling her parents she is only sleeping before taking her by the hand (vv. 49-56) — together showing his authority over nature, demons, sickness, and death.
h: Nothing Hid That Shall Not Be Known (vv.16-21)
The Woman and the Ruler's Daughter (vv.40-56)
m: women named outright as financial supporters of the ministry, Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Susanna, a sower parable interpreted soil by soil in terms of what happens to the word rather than to the ground, a family unable to reach Jesus through the crowd answered with a redefinition of family itself…

x: Jesus sends the twelve out with power to heal and preach, instructing them to travel light and depend on hospitality (vv. 1-6), which perplexes Herod, who wonders if Jesus is John the Baptist raised (vv. 7-9). Jesus feeds five thousand from five loaves and two fish, with twelve baskets left over (vv. 10-17), then Peter confesses him as the Christ, after which Jesus predicts his suffering, death, and resurrection and calls disciples to take up their cross daily (vv. 18-27). On a mountain he is transfigured before Peter, John, and James, conversing with Moses and Elijah as the Father's voice again declares him his Son (vv. 28-36). He then heals a boy tormented by a demon the disciples could not cast out (vv. 37-43), again predicts his death, and rebukes the disciples' arguments over greatness, their attempt to stop an outside exorcist, and their wish to call down fire on an inhospitable…
h: Whom Say Ye That I Am (vv.18-27)
The Only Child, and the Second Prediction (vv.37-45)
Who Is Greatest, and the Samaritan Village (vv.46-56)
m: the twelve sent out with a deliberately empty packing list, no staff, no bag, no bread, no money, Herod's own question left hanging unanswered, who is this of whom I hear such things, five thousand fed with twelve baskets left over, one for each disciple who said it could not be done, a question…

x: Jesus sends seventy-two disciples ahead in pairs to towns he intends to visit, instructing them to travel without provisions, heal the sick, and proclaim that the kingdom of God has come near, while pronouncing woe on towns like Chorazin and Bethsaida that reject the message (vv. 1-16). When the seventy-two return rejoicing over their authority over demons, Jesus tells them to rejoice instead that their names are written in heaven, and he thanks the Father for revealing these things to the humble rather than the wise (vv. 17-24). A lawyer asks what is required to inherit eternal life, and after affirming that love of God and neighbor is the answer, Jesus tells the parable of the Good Samaritan to redefine "neighbor" as anyone in need, in contrast to the priest and Levite who pass by (vv. 25-37). The chapter closes at the home of Martha and Mary, where Jesus commends Mary for choosing to…
h: The Seventy Sent Two by Two (vv.1-12)
m: Seventy sent ahead in pairs, towns held more accountable than Sodom, joy redirected from success to enrolment, a lawyer's question turned back on him, a Samaritan made the hero, and one thing needful chosen over much serving

x: Jesus teaches the disciples the Lord's Prayer, then tells the parable of a persistent friend at midnight to show that God delights to answer bold, persistent prayer and gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask (vv. 1-13). After He casts a mute demon out of a man, critics claim He works by the devil's power; Jesus counters that a divided kingdom cannot stand, insists He casts out demons by God's power, and warns that a swept but empty house invites worse spirits back in (vv. 14-26). When the crowd demands a sign, He points to Jonah and declares that someone greater than Jonah and Solomon is here, then calls people to keep their spiritual sight clear (vv. 27-36). Dining with a Pharisee, He denounces the Pharisees and lawyers as hypocrites who polish the outside while neglecting justice and the love of God, provoking their fury (vv. 37-54).
h: Ask, and It Shall Be Given (vv.9-13)
m: a disciple's request prompted simply by watching Jesus pray, Lord, teach us to pray, a shorter version of the same model prayer Matthew records, a persistent friend parable arguing not that God is reluctant but that shameless boldness in prayer is rewarded, three imperatives and three promises…

x: Jesus warns the crowd against the hypocrisy of the Pharisees and tells His disciples not to fear those who can kill the body but to fear God, since even the hairs of their heads are numbered (vv. 1-12). Asked to settle an inheritance dispute, He warns against greed with the parable of the rich fool who builds bigger barns but dies before enjoying them, having stored up treasure for himself instead of toward God (vv. 13-21). He tells the disciples not to worry about food or clothing since the Father who feeds ravens and clothes lilies will provide, and to seek God's kingdom first and store treasure in heaven (vv. 22-34). Using pictures of watchful servants and a faithful steward, He calls His followers to stay ready for His return, warns that His coming brings division rather than easy peace, and tells the crowd to read the times and settle matters before judgment (vv. 35-59).
h: Beware the Leaven of the Pharisees (vv.1-3)
Consider the Ravens and the Lilies (vv.22-31)
m: a crowd so thick people trample each other while Jesus addresses his disciples over their heads about the leaven of hypocrisy, fear repeated deliberately three times, persecution, insignificance and provision, each answered by a different aspect of God's own character, an inheritance dispute…

x: Jesus responds to reports of Galileans killed by Pilate and others crushed by a falling tower by insisting tragedy is no proof of greater sin, and calls everyone to repent or perish likewise (vv. 1-5), then tells the parable of a barren fig tree given one more year to bear fruit before being cut down (vv. 6-9). Healing a woman bent double for eighteen years on the Sabbath, He answers the indignant synagogue ruler by noting that even animals are watered on the Sabbath (vv. 10-17). He compares the kingdom of God to a mustard seed that grows into a large tree and to leaven that works through dough (vv. 18-21). Journeying toward Jerusalem, He warns that entering the kingdom requires striving through a narrow door, since many who assume familiarity with Him will be shut out while people from every direction feast in God's kingdom (vv. 22-30). Told that Herod wants to kill Him, He presses on…
h: The Galileans and the Tower of Siloam (vv.1-5)
The Mustard Seed and the Leaven (vv.18-22)
m: two recent tragedies, Galileans killed by Pilate and eighteen crushed by a falling tower, used not to explain suffering but to press the urgency of repentance, a barren fig tree granted one more year of grace by an interceding vinedresser before judgment falls, a woman bent double for eighteen…

x: At a Sabbath dinner in a Pharisee's home, Jesus heals a man with dropsy after asking whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath, silencing His critics (vv. 1-6). Watching guests jockey for the best seats, He tells them to take the lowest place and let the host promote them, and instructs His host to invite the poor and disabled rather than those who can repay the favor (vv. 7-14). Responding to a comment about feasting in God's kingdom, He tells the parable of a great banquet whose invited guests all make excuses, so the host fills his house with the poor, crippled, and outcast from the streets instead (vv. 15-24). Turning to the crowds following Him, He lays out the cost of discipleship in stark terms — loving Him above family and even life itself, carrying one's own cross, and counting the cost like a builder or a king weighing whether to go to war before committing everything to…
h: Sit Not Down in the Highest Room (vv.7-14)
m: a man with dropsy healed at a Sabbath dinner after Jesus asks the lawfulness question himself before anyone else can raise it, seating advice built entirely around status, sit not down in the highest room, paired with an instruction to the host to invite guests who can never repay the favor, the…

x: When tax collectors and sinners gather to hear Jesus and the Pharisees grumble that He welcomes them, He answers with three parables about God's joy over the lost (vv. 1-3). A shepherd leaves ninety-nine sheep to find the one that wandered off, and a woman sweeps her house to find one lost coin, each picturing heaven's joy over a single repentant sinner (vv. 4-10). A father divides his estate between two sons; the younger squanders his share in reckless living far from home and ends up feeding pigs before he comes to his senses and heads home to beg for a servant's place (vv. 11-19). His father sees him from a distance, runs to embrace him, and restores him fully with a robe, ring, and a celebration feast (vv. 20-24). The older son refuses to join in, resentful that his obedience has never been rewarded this way, but his father assures him that everything he has is still his and that…
h: The Lost Sheep and the Lost Coin (vv.1-10)
m: three parables told in direct response to a single complaint, this man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them, a shepherd who leaves ninety-nine to search for one lost sheep and a woman who sweeps her whole house for one lost coin, both stories ending in the same near-identical interpretation, joy…

x: Jesus tells the parable of the shrewd manager, who, facing dismissal for wasting his master's possessions, reduces what several debtors owe so they will welcome him once he's out of a job — and is commended for his shrewdness, prompting Jesus to urge using worldly wealth to secure eternal welcome and to warn that no one can serve both God and money (vv. 1-13). The money-loving Pharisees ridicule him, so Jesus tells them that what people value highly is detestable to God, and affirms that not even the smallest stroke of the Law will pass away (vv. 14-18). He then tells of a rich man who lived in luxury while the beggar Lazarus lay at his gate longing for scraps; both die, and their situations reverse — Lazarus is comforted at Abraham's side while the rich man suffers in torment, separated by a chasm no one can cross (vv. 19-26). When the rich man begs Abraham to warn his five brothers…
h: The Law and the Prophets Until John (vv.14-18)
m: a dishonest manager commended not for his dishonesty but for his shrewdness in securing his own future before it is too late, Pharisees derided for their love of money answered with a single word explaining their contempt, covetous, a warning that what is highly esteemed among men is abomination in…

x: Jesus warns His disciples against causing others to sin and calls them to forgive a repentant brother repeatedly, even seven times a day (vv. 1-4). When the apostles ask Him to increase their faith, He says even faith the size of a mustard seed could uproot a tree, then illustrates humble obedience with the picture of a servant who does his duty without expecting thanks (vv. 5-10). Traveling toward Jerusalem, He heals ten lepers, but only one, a Samaritan, returns to thank Him, prompting Jesus to note how few give glory to God (vv. 11-19). Asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God will come, He says it does not arrive with visible signs but is already among them, then warns His disciples that the day of the Son of Man will come suddenly, like lightning, after He first suffers and is rejected (vv. 20-25). He compares that day to the sudden judgment in the days of Noah and Lot…
h: Offenses, Forgiveness, and Faith as a Grain (vv.1-6)
m: a millstone warning against causing a little one to stumble followed immediately by forgiveness given no limit at all, seven times in a day, the only recorded request in the Gospels for more faith answered not with a bigger portion but with a mustard seed's worth properly used, a servant's…

x: Jesus tells the parable of a persistent widow and an unjust judge to teach His disciples to keep praying without giving up, asking whether He will find faith on earth when He returns (vv. 1-8). He then contrasts a self-righteous Pharisee's prayer with a tax collector's humble plea for mercy, declaring that the humbled one, not the proud one, goes home justified (vv. 9-14). When people bring children to Him and the disciples try to turn them away, Jesus welcomes them, saying the kingdom belongs to those who receive it like a child (vv. 15-17). A rich ruler asks what he must do to inherit eternal life; when Jesus tells him to sell everything and follow Him, the man leaves sorrowful, and Jesus says it is nearly impossible for the wealthy to enter the kingdom apart from God's power, though Peter notes the disciples have already left everything to follow Him (vv. 18-30). Jesus then privately…
h: The Pharisee and the Tax Collector (vv.9-14)
The Rich Ruler, and the Camel (vv.18-30)
The Third Prediction, and the Blind Man (vv.31-43)
m: an unjust judge who fears neither God nor man finally granting justice purely because a widow will not stop asking, a Pharisee praying about his own accomplishments set against a tax collector who cannot even lift his eyes, God be merciful to me a sinner, children brought and rebuked by the…

x: In Jericho, the short tax collector Zacchaeus climbs a tree to see Jesus, who invites Himself to his house; Zacchaeus repents by giving half his goods to the poor and repaying anyone he defrauded fourfold, and Jesus declares that salvation has come to his house (vv. 1-10). Because the crowd expects the kingdom to appear immediately, Jesus tells the parable of a nobleman who entrusts money to his servants before leaving to receive a kingdom, rewarding those who invested it well and condemning the servant who hid his portion out of fear (vv. 11-27). He then approaches Jerusalem, sends disciples for a colt, and rides in as the crowds spread their cloaks and praise God, prompting Him to say the stones would cry out if the people fell silent (vv. 28-40). Seeing the city, He weeps over Jerusalem's coming destruction because it failed to recognize the time of its visitation (vv. 41-44).…
m: a wealthy, hated tax collector climbing a tree in a humiliating act just to see Jesus, an immediate self-invitation followed by radical, voluntary restitution, half my goods to the poor and fourfold to anyone I have cheated, a nobleman parable explained in advance as an answer to a mistaken…

x: When the chief priests and elders demand to know by what authority Jesus acts, He counters by asking whether John's baptism was from heaven or from men, and their refusal to answer lets Him withhold His answer too (vv. 1-8). He tells the parable of tenants who beat and kill the servants a vineyard owner sends for his share of the fruit and finally murder his own son, warning the leaders that the vineyard will be taken from them and given to others (vv. 9-19). Spies sent to trap Him ask whether it is lawful to pay taxes to Caesar; Jesus has them produce a coin and tells them to give Caesar what is Caesar's and God what is God's, leaving them speechless (vv. 20-26). Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, pose a case about a woman widowed by seven brothers to mock the idea of life after death; Jesus answers that the resurrected neither marry nor die, and that God's word to Moses at the bush…
h: David's Son, and Beware of the Scribes (vv.41-47)
m: a counter-question about John's baptism that traps the very men demanding to know Jesus' own authority, a parable of wicked tenants who beat the servants and finally kill the son, aimed unmistakably at the leaders listening to it, a tax question with no safe answer resolved by transcending the trap…

x: Watching people give at the temple treasury, Jesus praises a poor widow's two small coins as a greater gift than the wealthy donations because she gave out of her poverty everything she had (vv. 1-4). When His disciples admire the temple's beauty, He predicts its total destruction and, asked for a sign, warns them not to be misled by false messiahs or alarmed by wars, since the end will not come immediately (vv. 5-9). He describes coming persecution, betrayal even by family, and hatred for His name, promising the disciples wisdom to answer their accusers and assuring them that their souls will ultimately be preserved through patient endurance (vv. 10-19). He foretells Jerusalem's siege and destruction by armies, urging those in Judea to flee to the mountains, and describes cosmic signs and distress among the nations that will precede the Son of Man's coming in power and glory (vv.…
h: Signs, the Fig Tree, and Watch Ye (vv.25-38)
m: a poor widow's two small coins named worth more than every large gift given from abundance, admiration for the temple's stonework answered flatly, not one stone shall be left upon another, wars, earthquakes and famines named explicitly as things that must happen without yet being the end, a…

x: With the religious leaders plotting his death (vv. 1-2), Satan enters Judas, who agrees to betray Jesus for money (vv. 3-6). Jesus sends Peter and John to prepare the Passover (vv. 7-13), then eats it with the Twelve, instituting the Lord's Supper by identifying the bread and cup as his body and blood given in a new covenant (vv. 14-20). He predicts his betrayal, settles a dispute among the disciples over who is greatest by calling them to serve rather than rule (vv. 24-27), and warns Peter that Satan will sift him and he will deny Jesus three times, though his faith will ultimately hold (vv. 31-34). Jesus then withdraws to the Mount of Olives, where in anguished prayer he asks the Father to remove the cup yet submits to his will, sweating drops like blood as an angel strengthens him (vv. 39-44). Judas betrays him with a kiss and he is arrested after healing the ear of the high priest's…
m: Satan entering Judas at the very moment the plot against Jesus finds an insider, an insider whose betrayal is arranged with money mentioned but not yet counted, two cups over a Passover meal Jesus says he has desired with desire to eat, a betrayal announced after the meal rather than before so the…

x: The council brings Jesus before Pilate, who finds no basis for a charge (vv. 1-4), then sends him to Herod after learning he is a Galilean; Herod mocks him and returns him to Pilate, and the two former enemies become friends that day (vv. 6-12). Pilate repeatedly declares Jesus innocent and seeks to release him, but the crowd, stirred by the chief priests, demands the murderer Barabbas instead and shouts for Jesus to be crucified until Pilate gives in (vv. 13-25). On the way to Calvary, Simon of Cyrene is made to carry the cross, and Jesus warns the weeping women of Jerusalem of coming judgment (vv. 26-31). Crucified between two criminals, Jesus asks the Father to forgive his executioners and promises paradise to the repentant criminal who asks to be remembered (vv. 34-43). Darkness covers the land and the temple veil tears as Jesus commits his spirit to the Father and dies, prompting…
h: The Road, and the Daughters of Jerusalem (vv.26-31)
Joseph, and the Sabbath Drawing On (vv.50-56)
m: three political charges brought before Pilate, one of them demonstrably false, answered with a verdict delivered in the trial's first five verses, I find no fault in this man, a trial before Herod found only in Luke in which Jesus simply refuses to perform or even speak, three separate declarations…

x: The women arrive at the tomb early Sunday and find the stone rolled away and the body gone; two angels announce that Jesus has risen, just as he foretold, and the women report this to the eleven, though the apostles dismiss it as nonsense even as Peter runs to check the empty tomb (vv. 1-12). That same day two disciples walking to Emmaus are joined by the risen Jesus, whom they fail to recognize; he walks them through the Scriptures concerning the Christ's suffering and glory, and they finally recognize him as he breaks bread with them, at which point he vanishes (vv. 13-31). They rush back to Jerusalem and find the eleven already saying the Lord has appeared to Simon (vv. 33-34). Jesus then appears among the gathered disciples, showing his hands and feet and eating fish to prove he is not a ghost (vv. 36-43). He opens their minds to understand that the Christ's suffering, resurrection…
m: women arriving with spices to find the stone already rolled away, two men in shining garments answering with a question rather than an announcement, why seek ye the living among the dead, the eleven dismissing the report as idle tales while Peter alone goes to check for himself, two disciples on…

x: John opens with the prologue declaring that the Word existed eternally with God and was God, that all things were made through Him, and that life and light are found in Him alone (vv. 1-5). The Word becomes flesh and dwells among humanity, full of grace and truth, and no one has ever seen God except the only Son who has made Him known (vv. 14-18). John the Baptist denies being the Christ, Elijah, or the Prophet, and identifies himself as the voice preparing the way for the Lord (vv. 19-28). The next day John points to Jesus as the Lamb of God and testifies to seeing the Spirit descend on Him at His baptism (vv. 29-34). Andrew, Peter, Philip, and Nathanael are then called as Jesus' first disciples, and Nathanael confesses Him as the Son of God and King of Israel (vv. 35-49). The chapter closes with Jesus promising that His disciples will see even greater things, heaven opened and angels…
h: In the Beginning Was the Word (vv.1-5)
A Man Sent to Bear Witness (vv.6-13)
m: A prologue that starts before Genesis does, the Word made flesh and dwelling among us, a forerunner who defines himself by what he is not, a lamb identified before anything is explained, and disciples gathered by invitation

x: At a wedding in Cana, Jesus turns water into wine at His mother's request, performing His first sign and revealing His glory so that His disciples believe in Him (vv. 1-11). He then travels to Jerusalem for Passover and drives the money changers and animal sellers out of the temple, declaring zeal for His Father's house (vv. 13-17). When the Jewish leaders demand a sign to justify this, Jesus speaks of destroying and raising up "this temple" in three days, words His disciples only understood after the resurrection as referring to His own body (vv. 18-22). Many in Jerusalem believe in Him because of the signs He performs, but Jesus does not entrust Himself to them, since He knows what is in every person (vv. 23-25).
m: Water turned to wine at a wedding on the third day, a mother's confidence and a son's stated hour, a whip made deliberately, and a temple whose destruction and raising is offered as the only sign

x: Jesus tells the Pharisee Nicodemus that no one can see or enter the kingdom of God without being born again — born of water and the Spirit, not merely of the flesh (vv. 3-7). He compares the Spirit's work to the wind, unseen but unmistakable in its effects (v. 8), then explains that just as Moses lifted up the bronze serpent in the wilderness, the Son of Man must be lifted up so that everyone who believes in Him receives eternal life (vv. 14-15). Verses 16-17 summarize the gospel: God sent His Son not to condemn the world but to save it, out of love for the world. The chapter closes with John the Baptist's disciples growing jealous of Jesus' rising popularity, and John responding that his own role must now diminish as Jesus' increases (vv. 25-30).
h: For God So Loved the World (vv.16-21)
m: A ruler who comes at night, birth described as something that happens to a person, a bronze serpent read as a foreshadowing, the most quoted verse in Scripture, and a forerunner content to decrease

x: Traveling through Samaria, Jesus stops at Jacob's well and asks a Samaritan woman for water, crossing both ethnic and gender barriers of His day (vv. 1-9). He offers her living water that becomes a spring welling up to eternal life, then reveals His knowledge of her five past husbands, prompting her to recognize Him as a prophet (vv. 10-19). When she raises the question of proper worship, Jesus explains that true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth rather than at a particular location, and openly identifies Himself as the Messiah (vv. 20-26). She returns to her town and many Samaritans come to believe in Jesus, some confessing Him as the Savior of the world (vv. 28-42). The chapter closes with Jesus healing a royal official's son from a distance, His second sign in Galilee (vv. 46-54).
m: A route taken through Samaria by necessity, a request for water from a woman at the wrong hour, worship relocated from a mountain to spirit and truth, a harvest already white, and a healing at a distance

x: At the Pool of Bethesda in Jerusalem, Jesus heals a man who has been an invalid for thirty-eight years, telling him to pick up his mat and walk, and does so on the Sabbath (vv. 1-9). This draws persecution from the Jewish leaders, and when Jesus responds that His Father is always working and He too is working, they seek to kill Him for effectively claiming equality with God (vv. 16-18). Jesus then teaches that the Son does only what He sees the Father doing, that the Father has given the Son authority to give life and to execute judgment, and that a coming hour will see the dead rise at His voice (vv. 19-29). He points to multiple witnesses to His identity — John the Baptist, His own works, the Father, and the Scriptures — and rebukes the leaders for studying the Scriptures yet refusing to come to Him for life (vv. 31-40).
h: The Dead Shall Hear His Voice (vv.25-30)
m: A man waiting thirty-eight years by a pool, a healing that starts the hostility, work claimed on the Sabbath because the Father works, resurrection and judgment given to the Son, and four witnesses called

x: Jesus feeds a crowd of five thousand with five loaves and two fish, then withdraws alone while His disciples cross the sea, where He comes to them walking on the water (vv. 1-21). When the crowd catches up the next day, Jesus tells them to seek the food that endures to eternal life rather than bread that perishes, and declares Himself the bread of life who came down from heaven, whom anyone may eat and never hunger or die (vv. 26-51). He presses the image further, saying that eating His flesh and drinking His blood is necessary for eternal life, language so difficult that many of His disciples turn back and no longer follow Him (vv. 53-66). When Jesus asks the Twelve if they too will leave, Peter confesses that Jesus alone has the words of eternal life, though Jesus notes that one among them — a reference to Judas — is a devil (vv. 67-71).
h: Eat My Flesh, Drink My Blood (vv.52-59)
m: Five thousand fed from a boy's lunch, a crowd wanting a king who provides, walking on water, bread from heaven contrasted with manna, teaching hard enough to empty the room, and a question left with the twelve

x: Jesus initially declines to go up publicly to the Feast of Tabernacles with His brothers, who do not yet believe in Him, but later goes up in secret (vv. 1-10). Midway through the feast He teaches in the temple, astonishing the crowds since He has no formal training, and tells them His teaching comes from the One who sent Him (vv. 14-16). The crowd is sharply divided over who He is, and when temple officers are sent to arrest Him they return empty-handed, saying no one has ever spoken the way He does (vv. 32-46). On the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus cries out that anyone who is thirsty should come to Him and drink, promising that rivers of living water — a reference to the Spirit believers would later receive — would flow from within those who believe in Him (vv. 37-39). Nicodemus, a member of the council, mildly objects to condemning Jesus without a hearing (vv. 50-51).
h: Teaching in the Midst of the Feast (vv.14-24)
m: Brothers who do not believe issuing a challenge, timing repeatedly called not yet come, a cry on the last day of the feast about thirst, officers who return without an arrest, and one Pharisee asking about due process

x: Jesus is presented with a woman caught in adultery and challenged to condemn her, but tells her accusers that whoever is without sin may cast the first stone; when they all leave, He tells her to go and sin no more (vv. 1-11). He then declares Himself the light of the world, promising that whoever follows Him will not walk in darkness (v. 12), which leads to a lengthy dispute with the Pharisees over the validity of His testimony and His origin from above rather than below (vv. 13-24). Jesus warns that whoever sins is a slave to sin and that only the Son can truly set someone free, then confronts the Pharisees' claim to Abraham as their father, telling them their actual father is the devil since they seek to kill Him (vv. 34-47). The exchange culminates when Jesus declares, using the divine name, that He existed before Abraham was born, prompting the crowd to try to stone Him (vv. 56-59).
h: I Am the Light of the World (vv.12-20)
Ye Shall Die in Your Sins (vv.21-30)
The Truth Shall Make You Free (vv.31-38)
m: A trap set by quoting Moses that dismantles itself against the ground, light of the world declared during the feast where the great lamps were lit, freedom claimed by people who deny they were ever in bondage, paternity argued down to the hardest sentence spoken to anyone in the Gospels, and before…

x: Jesus heals a man born blind by anointing his eyes with mud and sending him to wash in the Pool of Siloam, explaining that the man's blindness was not caused by anyone's sin but was an opportunity for God's work to be displayed (vv. 1-7). The healing on the Sabbath draws Pharisees who interrogate the man and his parents, and the man's understanding of Jesus deepens through the questioning — from calling Him simply "the man called Jesus" to identifying Him as a prophet sent from God (vv. 8-33).
