When the man is thrown out of the synagogue for defending Jesus, Jesus finds him, reveals Himself as the Son of Man, and the man worships Him (vv. 34-38). Jesus closes by explaining that He came into the world for judgment, so that the spiritually blind might see and those who claim to see would be shown their blindness — a rebuke aimed at the Pharisees (vv. 39-41).
h: Neither This Man Nor His Parents (vv.1-5)
Dost Thou Believe on the Son of God (vv.35-38)
m: A question about blame refused before the healing even happens, clay made from spittle on the sabbath turned into the real charge, a man's answers escalating from a man called Jesus to the Son of God, parents who answer only what they cannot be blamed for, and sight and blindness reversed until…

x: Jesus describes Himself first as the gate for the sheep and then as the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, contrasting Himself with hired hands who abandon the flock when danger comes (vv. 1-13). He states that He knows His sheep and they know Him, that He has other sheep not of this fold whom He must also bring, and that He lays down His life of His own accord with authority to take it up again (vv. 14-18). At the Feast of Dedication in Jerusalem, Jesus tells the Jews that He and the Father are one, and they pick up stones to kill Him for blasphemy, believing He is making Himself God (vv. 22-33). Jesus defends His claim by appealing to Scripture and pointing to His works as evidence, then withdraws across the Jordan, where many come to believe in Him (vv. 34-42).
h: The Good Shepherd Giveth His Life (vv.11-18)
m: A common sheepfold and a shepherd known by voice, two I AM sayings, a life laid down rather than taken, other sheep not of this fold, and a charge of blasphemy answered from the Psalms

x: When His friend Lazarus falls ill, Jesus deliberately delays His arrival, arriving in Bethany four days after Lazarus has died (vv. 1-17). Martha and Mary each tell Jesus that their brother would not have died if He had been there, and Jesus, though He knows what He is about to do, is deeply moved and weeps at the tomb (vv. 20-35). He declares to Martha that He is the resurrection and the life and that whoever believes in Him will live even though they die (vv. 25-26), then calls Lazarus out of the tomb, and he comes out still bound in graveclothes (vv. 38-44). Many who witness this believe in Jesus, but others report it to the Pharisees, and the Sanhedrin, prompted by Caiaphas' comment that it is better for one man to die for the people, formally plots to kill Him (vv. 45-53).
h: He Whom Thou Lovest Is Sick (vv.1-16)
I Am the Resurrection and the Life (vv.17-27)
Withdrawal to Ephraim and the Passover Watch (vv.53-57)
m: A message that states love and is answered with a deliberate delay, resurrection and life relocated from a doctrine to a person, the shortest verse in the Bible standing beside a death Jesus intends to undo, a stone rolled away against Martha's practical objection, and a council that never disputes…

x: Six days before Passover, Mary anoints Jesus' feet with costly perfume at a dinner in Bethany, and Judas objects under the pretense of caring for the poor (vv. 1-8). The next day Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a donkey's colt to crowds waving palm branches and hailing Him as king, fulfilling an old prophecy about Zion's King (vv. 12-15). When some Greeks ask to see Him, Jesus says His hour has come and compares His coming death to a kernel of wheat that must fall into the ground and die in order to bear fruit (vv. 20-24). A voice from heaven confirms that God has glorified His name, though the crowd mistakes it for thunder (vv. 28-29). The chapter closes with John noting that many still refused to believe despite Jesus' many signs, even as Jesus insists He came as light to save the world, not to judge it (vv. 37-47).
h: He That Hateth His Life Shall Keep It (vv.25-26)
m: An anointing defended as a burial before anyone else understands it that way, a crowd shouting Hosanna for a king who arrives on a donkey, Greeks seeking Jesus made the signal that His hour has finally come, a grain of wheat that must die to multiply, and Isaiah's throne vision read backward as a…

x: At the start of the Last Supper, knowing His hour has come, Jesus rises from the table, wraps a towel around Himself, and washes His disciples' feet as an example of humble service, over Peter's initial protest (vv. 1-11). He explains that He has left them a pattern to follow and pronounces a blessing on those who put it into practice (vv. 12-17). Troubled in spirit, He identifies His betrayer by handing a piece of bread to Judas, who then leaves into the night to carry out his plan (vv. 21-30). After Judas departs, Jesus speaks of His coming glorification and gives a new commandment: His disciples are to love one another the same way He has loved them, a mark by which the world will recognize them (vv. 31-35). The chapter ends with Jesus predicting that Peter, despite his confident vow of loyalty, will deny knowing Him three times before the rooster crows (vv. 36-38).
h: Know Ye What I Have Done (vv.12-17)
One of You Shall Betray Me (vv.18-30)
Now Is the Son of Man Glorified (vv.31-33)
m: A towel and basin used by someone who knows all things have been given into His hands, Peter's refusal reversed to its opposite extreme in the same breath, a sop handed to Judas as an honor at the very moment of betrayal, a new commandment measured by as I have loved you, and a promise of loyalty…

x: Jesus comforts the disciples ahead of His departure, telling them not to be troubled and promising that in His Father's house are many rooms, where He is going to prepare a place for them and will return to take them there (vv. 1-3). When Thomas asks how to know the way, Jesus declares that He himself is the way, the truth, and the life, and that no one comes to the Father except through Him (vv. 5-6). He answers Philip that to have seen Him is to have seen the Father (vv. 8-9), then promises that after He leaves, the Father will send another Counselor, the Spirit of truth, to remain with believers forever (vv. 16-17). Responding to Judas (not Iscariot), Jesus explains that those who love Him and keep His word will be indwelt by Him and the Father, and that the coming Spirit will teach them all things (vv. 22-26). He leaves them His peace, unlike the world's peace, telling them not to…
h: My Peace I Give unto You (vv.25-31)
m: Troubled hearts addressed directly, a house with many rooms, an exclusive claim about the way, another Comforter of the same kind, and a peace distinguished from the world's

x: Jesus describes Himself as the true vine and His Father as the gardener, explaining that fruitless branches are removed while fruitful branches are pruned to bear more (vv. 1-2). He calls the disciples to remain in Him as He remains in them, since apart from Him they can do nothing, while a branch that fails to remain withers and is burned (vv. 4-6). Their fruitfulness glorifies the Father and confirms their discipleship (v. 8), and keeping His commandments keeps them in His love, just as He keeps the Father's commandments (vv. 9-10). Jesus renews His command to love one another, calling the disciples friends rather than servants because He has shared with them all He heard from the Father (vv. 12-15), and reminds them that He chose and appointed them for lasting fruit (v. 16). The chapter closes with a warning that the world will hate them as it hated Him, since they are no longer of…
m: A seventh and final I AM saying that places the hearers inside the image, abide repeated as the word that carries the whole passage, pruning done by the same hand whether or not a branch bears fruit, servants reclassified as friends because everything has been disclosed, and a world's hatred…

x: Jesus warns the disciples that they will be expelled from synagogues and even killed by those who wrongly think they serve God, since His opponents do not know the Father or Him (vv. 1-3). He explains that His departure actually benefits them, because only then will the Counselor come to convict the world of sin, righteousness, and judgment, and guide the disciples into all truth (vv. 7-13). Using the image of a woman's labor pain turning to joy at childbirth, He promises that their present sorrow at His going will likewise turn to lasting joy when they see Him again (vv. 20-22). He tells them that in that day they will ask the Father directly in His name, since the Father Himself loves them for loving and believing in Jesus (vv. 23-27). When the disciples affirm their belief that He came from God, Jesus predicts they will soon scatter and leave Him alone, though the Father remains with…
h: That Ye Should Not Be Offended (vv.1-7)
He Will Guide You Into All Truth (vv.12-15)
m: Departure named as expedient because the Comforter cannot come otherwise, the Spirit's threefold work of convicting the world of sin, righteousness and judgment, truth still withheld because the disciples cannot yet bear it, sorrow compared to labor forgotten in what it produces, and tribulation…

x: In His High Priestly Prayer, Jesus first asks the Father to glorify Him with the glory He shared before the world began, having completed the work the Father gave Him (vv. 1-5). He then prays for His disciples, whom the Father gave Him out of the world and who have kept His word, asking the Father to protect and unify them even though He is leaving the world while they remain in it (vv. 6-13). He does not ask that they be removed from the world but that they be kept from the evil one and sanctified in the truth of God's word (vv. 15-17), and He sends them into the world just as the Father sent Him (v. 18). Finally, He extends His prayer to all future believers who will come to faith through the disciples' testimony, asking that they be perfectly united as He and the Father are one, so that the world may know the Father sent Him and loved them (vv. 20-23). He closes by expressing His…
h: That They All May Be One (vv.20-26)
m: The longest recorded prayer of Jesus, glory asked for and glory shared before the world was, disciples described as given rather than recruited, sanctification through truth, and future believers prayed for by name of category

x: Jesus crosses the Kidron Valley to a garden where Judas leads soldiers and officials to arrest Him; when Jesus identifies Himself as "I am he," the arresting party falls to the ground, and He submits while stopping Peter from defending Him with a sword (vv. 1-11). Bound and taken first to Annas and then to the high priest Caiaphas, Jesus answers questions about His teaching by pointing to His public ministry and is struck for it (vv. 12-23). Meanwhile Peter, warming himself by a fire in the courtyard, denies three times that he knows Jesus, just as the rooster crows (vv. 15-27). Jesus is then led to Pilate's headquarters, where Pilate questions Him about kingship; Jesus explains that His kingdom is not of this world but exists to testify to the truth (vv. 33-37). Unconvinced by the charges, Pilate declares he finds no basis for a charge against Jesus (v. 38), but the crowd rejects…
h: My Kingdom Is Not of This World (vv.33-37)
m: An arrest where Jesus asks the questions and takes the initiative throughout, Peter's sword answered by a question about a cup rather than a rebuke, three denials completed exactly as predicted at the same fire of coals, six trials that never produce evidence only pressure, and a kingdom defined as…

x: Pilate has Jesus flogged and mocked with a crown of thorns and purple robe before presenting Him to the crowd, still finding no basis for a charge (vv. 1-6). Under pressure from the chief priests' claim that Jesus made Himself the Son of God, and fearing accusations of disloyalty to Caesar, Pilate hands Jesus over to be crucified despite his own uncertainty (vv. 7-16). Jesus carries His cross to Golgotha, where He is crucified between two others under an inscription naming Him King of the Jews, while soldiers cast lots for His seamless garment (vv. 17-24). From the cross He entrusts His mother to the care of the disciple He loved (vv. 26-27), then, after receiving sour wine, declares "It is finished" and dies (vv. 28-30). To confirm His death, soldiers pierce His side, producing blood and water, without breaking His legs, fulfilling Scripture (vv. 31-37). Joseph of Arimathea and…
m: A scourging and a crown of thorns, authority described as given from above, a title in three languages that the priests could not get changed, a garment not torn, one word meaning paid in full, and a burial by two secret disciples

x: Mary Magdalene finds the tomb empty early on the first day of the week and runs to tell Peter and the disciple Jesus loved, who race to the tomb and find the linen wrappings but no body (vv. 1-9). After the two disciples leave, Mary lingers weeping and encounters the risen Jesus, whom she initially mistakes for the gardener until He calls her by name; He instructs her to tell the disciples He is ascending to the Father (vv. 11-18). That evening Jesus appears to the disciples behind locked doors, showing them His wounds, granting them peace, and breathing the Holy Spirit on them as He commissions them (vv. 19-23). Thomas, absent that night, refuses to believe without physical proof, but a week later Jesus appears again and invites Thomas to touch His wounds, prompting Thomas's confession, "My Lord and my God" (vv. 24-28). Jesus responds by blessing those who believe without seeing, and…
m: Grave clothes left folded rather than stripped away, a name spoken once turning a mistaken gardener into a witness, peace offered twice with wounds shown between the two greetings, a condition for belief stated bluntly and met without a single recorded touch, and a purpose statement naming exactly…

x: Jesus appears a third time to His disciples by the Sea of Tiberias, where Peter and several others return to fishing but catch nothing overnight; at dawn Jesus, unrecognized on the shore, tells them to cast their net on the other side, producing a massive haul of 153 fish that does not tear the net (vv. 1-11). Once John identifies Him and Peter swims to shore, Jesus shares a breakfast of bread and fish that He has already prepared over a charcoal fire (vv. 9-13). After the meal, Jesus asks Peter three times whether he loves Him, mirroring Peter's three earlier denials, and each time commissions him to care for His sheep, then foretells the kind of death by which Peter will glorify God before repeating the call to "follow me" (vv. 15-19). When Peter asks about the fate of the disciple Jesus loved, Jesus tells him that is not his concern (vv. 20-22). The Gospel closes by identifying that…
h: Cast the Net on the Right Side (vv.1-8)
m: A return to fishing and an unrecognized figure on the shore, a net that does not break, a charcoal fire matching an earlier one, three questions for three denials, and a Gospel that ends by admitting it left things out

x: Luke opens by addressing Theophilus and recalling Jesus' teaching up to his ascension (vv. 1-3). Jesus tells the apostles to wait in Jerusalem for the Father's promise, saying they will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes and will be his witnesses to the ends of the earth (vv. 4-8). He is then taken up into a cloud before their eyes from the Mount of Olives, and two angels promise he will return the same way (vv. 9-11). Back in Jerusalem, the apostles join the women and Jesus' brothers in constant prayer (v. 14), and Peter leads the group in choosing Matthias by lot to replace Judas among the twelve (vv. 15-26).
h: The Former Treatise, and Forty Days (vv.1-3)
It Is Not for You to Know the Times (vv.6-7)
Taken Up, and a Promise of Return (vv.9-11)
Continuing in Prayer with One Accord (vv.12-14)
Peter Reads the Vacancy from Scripture (vv.15-22)
m: A former treatise continued, forty days of instruction, a question about timing redirected, power promised for witness, a visible ascension with a promise of return, and a vacancy filled by lot

x: On the day of Pentecost the disciples are gathered together when a sound like a rushing wind fills the house and tongues of fire rest on each of them, and they begin speaking in other languages (vv. 1-4). Devout Jews from many nations hear their own languages and are amazed, while others mock the disciples as drunk (vv. 5-13). Peter explains this is the fulfillment of Joel's prophecy of the Spirit poured out on all people, then preaches that the Jesus they crucified has been raised and exalted as Lord and Christ (vv. 14-36). Cut to the heart, the crowd asks what to do, and Peter calls them to repent and be baptized for forgiveness of sins (vv. 37-38). About three thousand are added that day, and the believers devote themselves to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, prayer, and sharing everything in common (vv. 41-47).
m: three signs marking the Spirit's arrival at once, sound, sight and speech, real languages heard by every nation gathered in Jerusalem rather than any ecstatic babble, a deliberate reversal of Babel centuries after the fact, Peter's first sermon preached seven weeks after denying Jesus three times…

x: Peter and John go up to the temple at the hour of prayer and heal a man lame from birth who begs at the Beautiful Gate, telling him he has no silver or gold but gives him what he has in the name of Jesus Christ (vv. 1-8). The healed man walks and leaps, praising God, drawing an astonished crowd in Solomon's Portico (vv. 9-11). Peter tells the crowd that they denied the Holy and Righteous One and killed the Author of life, but God raised him, and it is faith in his name that made the man strong (vv. 12-16). He acknowledges they acted in ignorance, fulfilling what the prophets foretold, and calls them to repent and turn back so their sins may be wiped out and times of refreshing may come (vv. 17-21), pointing also to Moses' promised prophet and to Abraham's covenant blessing for all nations (vv. 22-26).
h: The Healing at the Beautiful Gate (vv.1-11)
m: a lame man over forty years old carried daily to beg at a temple gate that Peter and John pass with no money but a name instead, a healing instant and complete enough that the man leaps and holds onto his healers as a crowd gathers, Peter's first move being to refuse the credit, why look ye so…

x: Annoyed that Peter and John are proclaiming the resurrection through Jesus, the Sanhedrin arrests them, though many who heard the message believe, bringing the number of men to about five thousand (vv. 1-4). Before the rulers, Peter declares that the man was healed by the name of Jesus Christ, the stone the builders rejected, and that salvation is found in no one else (vv. 8-12). The council, astonished at the apostles' boldness despite their lack of formal training, cannot deny the miracle and can only warn them to stop speaking in Jesus' name (vv. 13-18). Peter and John reply that they cannot help speaking of what they have seen and heard, and are released (vv. 19-22). Back with the believers, the church prays for boldness, the place is shaken, and all are filled with the Spirit (vv. 23-31), and believers continue sharing everything in common, with Barnabas selling a field and laying…
m: an arrest triggered specifically by preaching the resurrection to a council of Sadducees who denied it existed, a healed man standing in the room as evidence the council cannot argue away, an exclusive claim stated as plainly as anywhere in Scripture, neither is there salvation in any other…

x: Ananias and his wife Sapphira sell property but secretly keep back part of the proceeds while claiming to give it all, and each is confronted by Peter and falls dead for lying to the Holy Spirit, filling the church with great fear (vv. 1-11). The apostles perform many signs and wonders, and the sick are brought out hoping even Peter's shadow might fall on them and heal them (vv. 12-16). The high priest and the Sadducees, filled with jealousy, arrest the apostles, but an angel frees them in the night and sends them back to the temple to keep preaching (vv. 17-21). Hauled before the council again, Peter insists they must obey God rather than men (v. 29). Gamaliel, a respected Pharisee, counsels caution, arguing that if this movement is of man it will fail but if it is of God it cannot be stopped (vv. 34-39). The apostles are flogged and released, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to…
m: the first recorded sin inside the church answered by immediate and severe judgment, a lie not about withholding money but about pretending to have given all of it, an angel opening a prison at night only to send the apostles straight back to the very place that got them arrested, baffled officers…

x: As the number of disciples grows, Greek-speaking widows are being overlooked in the daily distribution of food, so the apostles have the community choose seven men full of the Spirit and wisdom to oversee this ministry, freeing the apostles for prayer and the word (vv. 1-6). The word of God spreads, the number of disciples multiplies greatly, and even many priests become obedient to the faith (v. 7). Stephen, one of the seven, full of grace and power, performs great wonders, but members of a synagogue dispute with him and cannot withstand his wisdom (vv. 8-10). They stir up false witnesses who accuse him of speaking against Moses, the law, and the temple, and drag him before the council, where his face is seen to be like that of an angel (vv. 11-15).
m: a complaint from Greek-speaking believers that their widows were being overlooked in daily food distribution, a solution that hands the selection of seven men entirely to the congregation rather than to the apostles themselves, seven chosen with Greek names drawn directly from the community that…

x: Stephen answers the high priest's charge with a long survey of Israel's history, beginning with God's call of Abraham and moving through the patriarchs and Joseph's betrayal and rise in Egypt (vv. 2-16). He recounts Moses' birth, exile, call at the burning bush, and leadership through the exodus and wilderness, noting that the people repeatedly rejected him and turned to idols like the golden calf (vv. 17-43). He traces the tabernacle and temple, insisting God does not dwell in houses made by hands (vv. 44-50). Turning on his accusers, Stephen charges them with being stiff-necked people who, like their ancestors, resist the Holy Spirit and have now betrayed and murdered the Righteous One (vv. 51-53). Enraged, the council drags him out and stones him while he sees the heavens opened and Jesus standing at God's right hand, and he prays for his killers' forgiveness as he dies; a young man…
m: the longest chapter in the whole book built as an answer to a single question, are these things so, Stephen surveying Israel's history from Abraham through Moses to Solomon to argue that God has always worked outside the established structures, a repeated pattern of Israel rejecting its own chosen…

x: Saul's persecution scatters the Jerusalem believers throughout Judea and Samaria, and those scattered go about preaching the word (vv. 1-4). Philip goes down to a city in Samaria, proclaims Christ, and performs signs, bringing great joy as unclean spirits and the paralyzed and lame are healed (vv. 5-8). Simon, a sorcerer who had amazed the city, believes and is baptized, but when he sees the Spirit given through the apostles' laying on of hands, he tries to buy this power and is sharply rebuked by Peter for thinking God's gift can be purchased (vv. 9-24). An angel sends Philip south to the Gaza road, where he meets an Ethiopian court official reading Isaiah, explains that the passage points to Jesus, and baptizes him after the eunuch believes; the Spirit then carries Philip away to Azotus (vv. 26-40).
m: Saul introduced first by consent and then by violence, entering house after house to commit men and women to prison, a scattering meant to destroy the church instead becoming the very mechanism the book uses to spread it, Philip preaching in Samaria, enemy territory for Jews, and Simon the sorcerer…

x: Saul, still breathing threats against the Lord's disciples, sets out for Damascus with letters authorizing arrests, but a light from heaven strikes him down and a voice asks why he is persecuting him, identifying itself as Jesus (vv. 1-6). Blinded, Saul is led into the city and fasts for three days until Ananias, sent by the Lord despite his fear, lays hands on him, restores his sight, and he is baptized (vv. 7-19). Saul immediately begins proclaiming in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God, astonishing those who knew his reputation, and escapes a plot on his life by being lowered over the city wall in a basket (vv. 20-25). In Jerusalem, Barnabas vouches for him before the wary apostles (vv. 26-30). Meanwhile Peter heals the paralyzed Aeneas in Lydda and raises Dorcas (Tabitha) from death in Joppa, leading many to believe (vv. 32-43).
m: a man breathing out threatenings and slaughter struck blind by a light on the road to Damascus, a question that identifies persecuting the church with persecuting Christ himself, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me, Ananias sent to the very man coming to arrest him and greeting him first with a…

x: In Caesarea, the Gentile centurion Cornelius, a devout man, receives a vision instructing him to send for Peter (vv. 1-8). The next day Peter, praying on a rooftop, falls into a trance and sees a sheet of unclean animals lowered from heaven three times with the command to kill and eat, and a voice tells him not to call unclean what God has made clean (vv. 9-16). As he ponders this, Cornelius's messengers arrive, and the Spirit tells Peter to go with them without hesitation (vv. 17-23). At Cornelius's house, Peter now understands the vision's meaning and declares that God shows no partiality, accepting anyone who fears him and does what is right (vv. 24-35). While he is still speaking, the Holy Spirit falls on all who hear the message, Gentiles included, and they speak in tongues and are baptized, proof that God has extended salvation to the Gentiles as well (vv. 44-48).
h: God Is No Respecter of Persons (vv.34-43)
m: a devout Roman centurion who prays and gives alms yet still needs to hear and believe the gospel to be saved, a sheet of unclean animals lowered three times with a command Peter refuses three times, kill, and eat, a vision about people rather than food, what God hath cleansed, that call not thou…

x: Peter returns to Jerusalem and is criticized by Jewish believers for eating with uncircumcised Gentiles, so he explains the vision and recounts step by step how the Spirit fell on Cornelius's household just as it had on the apostles at the beginning (vv. 1-17). Hearing this, the church falls silent, then glorifies God for granting repentance that leads to life even to the Gentiles (v. 18). Meanwhile believers scattered by persecution reach Antioch and begin preaching to Greeks as well as Jews, and a great number turn to the Lord (vv. 19-21). The Jerusalem church sends Barnabas to investigate, and he encourages the believers and brings Saul from Tarsus to help teach the growing congregation for a year, where the disciples are first called Christians (vv. 22-26). The prophet Agabus predicts a famine, and the Antioch church sends relief to the believers in Judea through Barnabas and Saul…
m: Peter defending his ministry to uncircumcised Gentiles before a critical Jerusalem church by simply recounting what happened rather than arguing theology, a conclusion nobody in the room can refute, what was I, that I could withstand God, believers scattered by persecution reaching Antioch and…

x: King Herod Agrippa executes James the brother of John and, seeing it pleases the Jewish leaders, arrests Peter during the Feast of Unleavened Bread, intending to bring him out for trial after Passover (vv. 1-4). While the church prays earnestly for him, an angel appears in the prison at night, wakes Peter, loosens his chains, and leads him past the guards and through the iron gate, which opens by itself (vv. 5-10). Peter realizes it is real and goes to the house of Mary, mother of John Mark, where the praying believers can hardly believe the servant girl Rhoda's report that he is at the door (vv. 11-17). Herod has the guards executed, then later, accepting the crowd's flattering cries that he speaks with the voice of a god rather than giving glory to God, is struck down by an angel and dies (vv. 20-23). Meanwhile the word of God continues to grow and spread (v. 24).
h: The Word Grew; Barnabas and Saul Return (vv.24-25)
m: a king killing one apostle and arresting a second specifically to gain favor with Jewish leaders, a church praying without ceasing while chains fall off Peter unnoticed by the very guards chained to him, a prayer meeting that refuses to believe its own prayer has been answered when Peter actually…

x: In Antioch, while the church worships and fasts, the Holy Spirit sets apart Barnabas and Saul for the work he has called them to, and the church commissions them with fasting, prayer, and the laying on of hands (vv. 1-3). Sailing to Cyprus, Saul, now called Paul, confronts the sorcerer Elymas, who opposes their preaching, and strikes him blind, leading the proconsul Sergius Paulus to believe (vv. 4-12). The company sails on to Pisidian Antioch, where Paul preaches in the synagogue, surveying Israel's history from the exodus through David to Jesus, and proclaims that through Jesus forgiveness of sins is offered and justification comes by faith, not the law of Moses (vv. 16-41). Many Jews and God-fearing converts follow Paul and Barnabas, but the next week jealous Jewish leaders stir up opposition, so Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles, who rejoice and believe, and the word spreads…
h: The Next Sabbath, and the Envy (vv.42-45)
m: a diverse leadership team fasting and worshipping when the Holy Spirit names two men by name, separate me Barnabas and Saul, a name change marked at the exact moment Saul confronts a sorcerer on Cyprus, then Saul, who also is called Paul, a sermon at Pisidian Antioch following the same shape as…

x: In Iconium, Paul and Barnabas preach and a great number of Jews and Greeks believe, but unbelieving Jews stir up opposition and the city divides until the two flee a plot to stone them (vv. 1-7). In Lystra, Paul heals a man crippled from birth, and the crowds, thinking the gods have come down in human form, try to offer sacrifices to Paul and Barnabas as Zeus and Hermes, whom the two barely restrain by tearing their clothes and pleading with the people to turn to the living God (vv. 8-18). Jews from Antioch and Iconium arrive, turn the crowd against Paul, and stone him, dragging him out of the city for dead, but he gets up and continues on (vv. 19-20). After preaching in Derbe, Paul and Barnabas retrace their steps, strengthening the disciples and appointing elders in each church, teaching that it is through many hardships that believers must enter the kingdom of God, before sailing…
h: Confirming the Souls of the Disciples (vv.20-28)
m: the same pattern repeating at Iconium as at Antioch, a divided city and a planned assault the missionaries simply leave rather than confront, a lame man healed at Lystra prompting a pagan crowd to try to worship Paul and Barnabas as Zeus and Hermes, a sermon to a purely pagan audience built…

x: Certain men from Judea arrive in Antioch teaching that Gentile believers must be circumcised according to the law of Moses to be saved, sparking sharp dispute with Paul and Barnabas, so the church sends them to Jerusalem to bring the question before the apostles and elders (vv. 1-4). Believers from among the Pharisees insist that Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses, prompting a council where, after much debate, Peter rises and recalls how God chose him to bring the gospel to the Gentiles at Cornelius's house, giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did the Jews and cleansing their hearts by faith alone — so why place on new believers a yoke that neither the Jews nor their ancestors could bear, when both groups are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus (vv. 5-11). The assembly falls silent as Barnabas and Paul describe the signs and wonders God worked among the…
m: a controversy striking at the heart of the gospel itself, whether Gentile believers must be circumcised to be saved, three testimonies settling the matter in turn, Peter's account of Gentiles receiving the Spirit without circumcision, Paul and Barnabas's miracles, and James's citation of Amos, a…

x: Paul begins his second missionary journey and adds Timothy to the team in Lystra, circumcising him out of consideration for the Jews in that region (vv. 1-3). Forbidden by the Spirit from preaching in Asia and Bithynia, Paul receives a night vision of a Macedonian man pleading for help, and the group sets sail for Macedonia (vv. 6-10). In Philippi, Lydia, a seller of purple goods, has her heart opened by the Lord and is baptized with her household (vv. 13-15). Paul casts a spirit of divination out of a slave girl, and when her owners lose their profit they drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates, who have them beaten and jailed (vv. 16-24). At midnight, as Paul and Silas pray and sing, an earthquake shakes the prison doors open; the jailer, about to take his own life, is stopped by Paul and asks what he must do to be saved, and he and his household believe and are baptized that night…
m: Timothy circumcised by Paul, of all people, right after the Jerusalem council settled that circumcision cannot be required, a tactic rather than a principle chosen to remove an obstacle among local Jews, the Spirit blocking Asia and Bithynia twice before a vision finally redirects Paul toward…

x: In Thessalonica, Paul reasons from the Scriptures for three Sabbaths that the Messiah had to suffer and rise, and some Jews along with many Greeks and prominent women are persuaded, provoking a mob that drags believers before the city officials (vv. 1-9). Sent on to Berea, Paul finds Jews who examine the Scriptures daily to test his teaching, and many believe, until agitators from Thessalonica stir up trouble there as well (vv. 10-13). Paul travels alone to Athens, deeply troubled by the city's idols while he waits for Silas and Timothy (vv. 15-16). He debates in the synagogue and marketplace, and Epicurean and Stoic philosophers bring him to the Areopagus to explain his teaching (vv. 17-21). There Paul points to an altar inscribed "to an unknown god" and proclaims the Creator who does not dwell in temples made by hands, who gives life to all and has set a day of judgment through the…
h: Thessalonica, and the World Turned Upside Down (vv.1-9)
m: a habitual method stated outright, three sabbaths of reasoning from the scriptures, an accusation the opposition itself supplies rather than Luke, these that have turned the world upside down are come hither also, Bereans held up as the model for every believer, receiving the word eagerly while…

x: Paul arrives in Corinth and partners with Aquila and Priscilla, fellow tentmakers recently expelled from Rome, reasoning in the synagogue every Sabbath (vv. 1-4). When Silas and Timothy arrive, Paul devotes himself fully to preaching that Jesus is the Messiah, and after the Jews reject him he turns to the Gentiles, though the synagogue leader Crispus and his household still believe (vv. 5-8). The Lord encourages Paul in a night vision, telling him not to be afraid because he has many people in that city, and Paul stays eighteen months teaching there (vv. 9-11). When the Jews bring Paul before the proconsul Gallio, Gallio dismisses the charge as a matter of Jewish law and refuses to judge it (vv. 12-17). Paul then sails for Syria, briefly stopping in Ephesus, and eventually returns to Antioch before revisiting the churches of Galatia and Phrygia (vv. 18-23). Meanwhile Apollos, an…
h: Corinth, and the Turn to the Gentiles (vv.1,4-8)
Ephesus, and the Vow at Cenchrea (vv.19-23)
m: a synagogue turned away with a gesture and a sentence, your blood be upon your own heads, from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles, the very next convert being the synagogue's own chief ruler, a vision promising safety and a reason for it, for I have much people in this city, a year and six…

x: Paul arrives in Ephesus and finds disciples who have received only John's baptism; after he explains the difference, they are baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus and receive the Holy Spirit as Paul lays hands on them (vv. 1-7). He teaches boldly in the synagogue for three months, then moves to the hall of Tyrannus, reasoning daily for two years until all of Asia hears the word (vv. 8-10). God performs extraordinary miracles through Paul, healing the sick even through cloths that touched him, while seven sons of a Jewish priest named Sceva try to invoke Jesus' name over a demon-possessed man and are overpowered and humiliated instead (vv. 11-16). Fear falls on the city, many who had practiced magic confess and burn their scrolls publicly, valued at fifty thousand pieces of silver, and the word of the Lord spreads powerfully (vv. 17-20). After Paul resolves to go to Jerusalem and then…
h: Two Years in the School of Tyrannus (vv.8-12)
Paul Purposed to Go to Jerusalem (vv.21-22)
m: twelve disciples found who know only John's baptism and are given the rest of the gospel rather than being rejected for their incomplete knowledge, two years of daily teaching in a lecture hall producing the report that all who dwelt in Asia heard the word, a demon that recognizes Jesus and Paul by…

x: After the uproar in Ephesus, Paul travels through Macedonia and Greece encouraging the believers, then heads back through Macedonia when a plot against him is discovered (vv. 1-6). In Troas, as Paul preaches late into the night, a young man named Eutychus falls asleep, drops from a third-story window, and is taken up dead — but Paul embraces him and restores his life before continuing to teach until daybreak (vv. 7-12). Sailing on, Paul bypasses Ephesus to save time but summons the Ephesian elders to meet him at Miletus (vv. 13-17). There he reminds them of his humble, tearful service among them and declares that he is innocent of anyone's blood, having not shrunk from proclaiming the whole purpose of God (vv. 18-27). He charges them to shepherd the church as overseers, warning that fierce wolves will rise up from among them to distort the truth, and commends them to God and the message…
h: Paul's Farewell to the Ephesian Elders (vv.17-38)
m: a change of route explained in a single clause, when the Jews laid wait for him, seven named traveling companions carrying the collection two entire letters were written to organize, a young man named Eutychus falling asleep in a window during a midnight sermon and falling three stories to his…
d: Paul Speaks to the Ephesian Elders (vv17–38)

x: Paul sails toward Jerusalem, and in Tyre the disciples, prompted by the Spirit, urge him not to go, though he continues on (vv. 1-6). At Caesarea he stays with Philip the evangelist, whose four daughters prophesy, and the prophet Agabus binds his own hands and feet with Paul's belt to symbolize the binding that awaits him in Jerusalem (vv. 8-11). Despite the pleading of his companions, Paul insists he is ready not only to be bound but to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus, and the group submits to the Lord's will (vv. 12-14). In Jerusalem, Paul reports to James and the elders all that God has done among the Gentiles, and they ask him to join four men under a vow and pay their expenses to show he still lives in observance of the law (vv. 17-26). Before the vow is completed, Jews from Asia stir up the crowd, falsely accusing Paul of defiling the temple, and a mob drags him…
h: The Will of the Lord Be Done (vv.13-14)
James, and Four Men Under a Vow (vv.15-26)
May I Speak Unto the People (vv.37-40)
m: cargo details and coastline names surviving only because Luke writes this whole section in the first person as an eyewitness, repeated warnings from believers along the way that bonds and afflictions await Paul in Jerusalem, an answer that refuses the premise that this is only about danger, what…

x: From the barracks steps, Paul addresses the hostile crowd in Aramaic, describing himself as a zealous Jew trained under Gamaliel who once persecuted followers of the Way to the death (vv. 1-5). He recounts his encounter with the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus, the blinding light, and the voice asking why he was persecuting him (vv. 6-11). He describes Ananias restoring his sight, telling him he has been chosen to know God's will and be a witness to all people, and his baptism there in Damascus (vv. 12-16). Paul then recalls a vision in the temple in which the Lord commanded him to leave Jerusalem because the people there would not accept his testimony, and sent him far away to the Gentiles (vv. 17-21). At the mention of the Gentiles, the crowd erupts, demanding his death, and the commander orders Paul flogged to find out why (vv. 22-24). As he is bound for the whip, Paul reveals…
m: a defense won a hearing simply by being spoken in Hebrew, a speech built entirely on common ground, Tarsus, Gamaliel, zeal for the law, before the crowd erupts the instant the word Gentiles is spoken, a chief captain who cannot follow the Hebrew ordering an examination by scourging simply to learn…

x: Before the Sanhedrin, Paul declares he has lived with a clear conscience, and when the high priest orders him struck for it, Paul rebukes him before catching himself for speaking against God's appointed leader (vv. 1-5). Perceiving that the council is divided between Pharisees and Sadducees, Paul calls out that he is on trial over the hope of the resurrection, splitting the assembly into a violent dispute that forces the commander to pull him out by force (vv. 6-10). That night the Lord stands by Paul, telling him to take courage, for as he has testified in Jerusalem he must also testify in Rome (v. 11). More than forty men bind themselves by an oath to kill Paul before eating, but Paul's nephew learns of the plot and reports it, prompting the commander to send Paul under heavy guard to Governor Felix in Caesarea by night (vv. 12-24). The commander's letter explains that he rescued a…
m: a council split in two by a single sentence declaring himself on trial for the hope and resurrection of the dead, Pharisees and Sadducees turning on each other instead of on Paul, a personal appearance by the Lord at Paul's darkest moment naming the destination that guarantees his survival until…
d: Paul Sent to Felix the Governor (vv23–35)

x: Five days later the high priest Ananias comes to Caesarea with the lawyer Tertullus, who flatters Felix and accuses Paul of stirring up riots and desecrating the temple as a ringleader of the Nazarene sect (vv. 1-9). Paul answers that he came to Jerusalem to worship and bring gifts to his nation, was found peacefully in the temple, and that he serves the God of his ancestors according to the Way, believing everything written in the Law and the Prophets, including the resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked (vv. 10-16). He explains he was ceremonially purified in the temple when he was seized, with no crowd or disturbance of his making, and that his true offense is his hope in the resurrection (vv. 17-21). Felix, already well informed about the Way, postpones a decision, and afterward listens to Paul discuss faith in Christ, righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment…
m: a professional orator hired to prosecute Paul opening with three verses of flattery before three charges, only one of which anyone can actually prove, a defense that insists Christianity is the fulfillment of Judaism rather than a departure from it, a governor deferring judgment for a reason Luke…

x: Festus succeeds Felix and travels to Jerusalem, where the chief priests renew their accusations against Paul and ask that he be transferred there, secretly planning to ambush and kill him along the way (vv. 1-3). Festus instead invites the accusers to come to Caesarea, and when the case is heard he asks Paul whether he is willing to stand trial in Jerusalem (vv. 4-9). Paul refuses, insisting he is standing before Caesar's own tribunal, has wronged no one, and formally appeals to Caesar, which Festus grants (vv. 10-12). When King Agrippa and Bernice arrive to pay their respects, Festus lays out Paul's case, admitting he found no charge deserving death and is unsure what to write to the emperor, since Paul's accusers only disputed points about their own religion and someone named Jesus who Paul claims is alive (vv. 13-21). Agrippa asks to hear Paul himself, and the next day, amid great…
m: a new governor waiting only three days before the prosecution raises Paul's case again, a proposed transfer to Jerusalem that Festus does not realize is actually an ambush, repeated hearings producing the same result as before, no accusation of the things that were supposed, an appeal that removes…

x: Given leave to speak, Paul describes his strict upbringing as a Pharisee and his former zeal in persecuting the followers of Jesus, even voting for their deaths and forcing them to blaspheme (vv. 1-11). He recounts his journey to Damascus, the blinding light from heaven, and the voice of Jesus asking why he was persecuting him and commissioning him to open the eyes of Jews and Gentiles alike, turning them from darkness to light (vv. 12-18). Paul explains that he was not disobedient to that heavenly vision, but preached repentance and a turn to God everywhere he went, which is why the Jews seized him in the temple (vv. 19-21). He insists he has said nothing beyond what Moses and the prophets foretold — that the Messiah would suffer, rise first from the dead, and proclaim light to Jews and Gentiles alike (vv. 22-23). Festus interrupts, calling Paul insane from too much learning, but Paul…
m: the third and fullest account of the Damascus road in the whole book, shaped deliberately for a king already expert in Jewish affairs, a past stated without any softening, many of the saints did I shut up in prison, a commission summarized in a single sentence covering the entire gospel, to open…

x: Paul, under guard, sets sail for Rome with the centurion Julius, and as the journey grows dangerous late in the season, Paul warns that continuing will bring disaster, but the centurion trusts the ship's pilot and owner instead (vv. 1-12). A gentle south wind tempts the crew to sail on from Fair Havens, but a violent northeaster soon drives the ship out to sea, forcing the crew to undergird the hull and eventually throw cargo and tackle overboard (vv. 13-19). After many days without sun or stars, all hope of survival is abandoned, until Paul stands up and announces that an angel of God has told him no lives will be lost, though the ship will run aground on an island (vv. 20-26). On the fourteenth night, sensing land is near, the sailors try to escape in the ship's boat, but Paul warns that all must stay aboard to be saved, and the soldiers cut the boat loose (vv. 27-32). Paul urges…
h: Two Hundred Threescore and Sixteen Souls (vv.37-44)
m: the longest sustained eyewitness passage in the whole book, full of the kind of detail only a passenger would keep, Paul's warning against sailing overruled because the centurion trusts the ship's master and owner more than the prisoner, fourteen days without sun or stars and all hope of survival…

x: Shipwrecked on Malta, Paul is bitten by a viper while gathering firewood, and when he suffers no harm the islanders, who first assumed he was a murderer under divine judgment, change their minds and decide he is a god (vv. 1-6). The chief official of the island, Publius, welcomes the survivors, and Paul heals his sick father along with many others on the island, who honor them greatly and supply what they need for the rest of the voyage (vv. 7-10). After three months, Paul sails on to Italy, and believers from Rome come out to meet him along the way, encouraging him as he finally arrives in the city (vv. 11-16). There Paul calls the local Jewish leaders together, explains why he is a prisoner, and testifies about the kingdom of God and Jesus from the Law and the Prophets from morning until evening, persuading some while others disbelieve (vv. 17-24). Echoing Isaiah's warning about a…
m: an island's kindness met with a viper bite the locals read first as guilt and then, when Paul survives it, as divinity, believers walking out thirty and forty miles from Rome to meet a prisoner who has been shipwrecked and held two years without ever being formally charged, six words recording the…

x: Paul introduces himself as a servant of Christ set apart for the gospel, and expresses his eagerness to preach in Rome, saying he is not ashamed of the gospel because it is God's power for salvation to everyone who believes (vv. 1-16). He states the letter's thesis: God's righteousness is revealed through faith, quoting that the righteous will live by faith (v. 17). He then turns to indict humanity — even though God's power and nature are plain in creation, people suppressed the truth, exchanged God's glory for idols, and were given over by God to dishonorable desires and a corrupted mind (vv. 18-28). The chapter closes with a list of the resulting sins, ending with the sobering note that people not only do these things but approve of others who do them too (vv. 29-32).
m: A one-sentence introduction that names the gospel before Paul names himself, an obligation felt toward Greeks and Barbarians before Rome has ever been visited, the just shall live by faith set down as the thesis before the letter argues for it, idols exchanged for the glory of an incorruptible God…
d: The Righteous Shall Live by Faith (vv16–17)

x: Paul turns to the self-righteous judge, showing that anyone who condemns others for sins they themselves commit is equally guilty and cannot escape God's judgment (vv. 1-3). He warns that God's kindness is meant to lead people to repentance, not to be presumed upon, and that God will repay everyone impartially according to their deeds, Jew and Gentile alike (vv. 4-11). Having the law does not excuse anyone — only those who do the law are justified, and even Gentiles without the law show its work in their consciences (vv. 12-16). Paul then confronts the Jew who boasts in the law but breaks it, arguing that such hypocrisy dishonors God's name among the nations (vv. 17-24). He concludes that true circumcision is not an outward, physical mark but a matter of the heart accomplished by the Spirit (vv. 25-29).
m: A moralist condemned by the same standard he uses to condemn pagans, judging another named a way of confessing the same guilt rather than escaping it, the Law's possession shown worthless the moment it is broken, circumcision relocated to the heart and the spirit rather than the flesh, and no…

x: Paul asks what advantage the Jew has, answering that they were entrusted with God's very words, though some were unfaithful — yet human unfaithfulness cannot cancel God's faithfulness (vv. 1-8). He stacks up Old Testament quotations to prove that no one is righteous, no one seeks God, and the whole world is guilty and silenced before him (vv. 9-20). But now, apart from the law, God's righteousness has been revealed through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe, since all have sinned and fall short of God's glory (vv. 21-23). Believers are justified freely by grace through the redemption in Christ, whom God presented as a sacrifice of atonement through faith in his blood, demonstrating that God is both just and the one who justifies those who believe (vv. 24-26). This leaves no room for boasting, since a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law (vv. 27-31).
h: What Advantage Then Hath the Jew (vv.1-8)
The Righteousness of God Without the Law (vv.21-26)
m: Objections raised by Paul himself before anyone else can raise them, a string of Old Testament quotations stopping every mouth at once, but now marking the hinge of the whole letter after three chapters of indictment, justification, redemption and propitiation drawn from three different worlds in…
d: The Righteousness of God Through Faith (vv21–31)

x: Paul asks what Abraham discovered about justification, and answers that Abraham believed God and it was credited to him as righteousness, not because he earned it through works (vv. 1-5). David likewise describes the blessedness of the one to whom God credits righteousness apart from works, whose sins are forgiven and not counted against him (vv. 6-8). Paul stresses that this crediting happened while Abraham was still uncircumcised, making him the father of all who believe, whether circumcised or not, since the promise came through the righteousness of faith rather than the law (vv. 9-17). Though he was old and Sarah's womb was as good as dead, Abraham did not waver in unbelief but grew strong in faith, fully persuaded God could do what he promised (vv. 18-22). Paul closes by applying this to believers today, who are likewise credited righteous through faith in the God who raised Jesus…
m: Abraham believing God and having it counted for righteousness before circumcision or law existed, David's forgiveness cited as proof that works were never the ground even for Israel's own king, a date made to carry the whole argument about circumcision as sign rather than cause, hope believed…

x: Paul explains that since believers are justified by faith, they now have peace with God and access to grace, rejoicing even in sufferings because suffering produces endurance, character, and hope, all sustained by God's love poured into their hearts through the Spirit (vv. 1-5). He highlights that Christ died for the ungodly while they were still sinners, a rare kind of love that guarantees believers will be saved from wrath and reconciled to God through Christ's life (vv. 6-11). Paul then draws a parallel between Adam and Christ — through one man's sin, death entered and spread to everyone, but through one man's obedience, grace and righteousness are offered to many (vv. 12-19). He notes that the law was added to increase awareness of sin, but wherever sin increased, grace increased even more, so that grace now reigns through righteousness leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ…
m: Peace with God named first among five results that flow from justification, access into grace and hope of glory listed alongside a purpose found even in suffering, Adam and Christ set up as two representative heads for the whole of humanity, condemnation through one traced against justification…
d: Death in Adam, Life in Christ (vv12–21)

x: Paul asks whether believers should keep sinning so that grace may increase, and answers emphatically no — those baptized into Christ were baptized into his death and are raised to walk in newness of life (vv. 1-4). Because their old self was crucified with Christ, they are no longer enslaved to sin, and are called to consider themselves dead to sin but alive to God (vv. 5-11). Paul urges them not to let sin reign in their bodies but to offer themselves to God as instruments of righteousness, since sin has no dominion over those under grace rather than law (vv. 12-14). He explains that everyone is a slave to whatever they obey, either sin leading to death or obedience leading to righteousness, and having been freed from sin they are now slaves to righteousness and holiness (vv. 15-22). The chapter closes with the summary statement that the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God…
m: An objection about grace and continued sin answered before it can even be finished, union with Christ's death offered as identity rather than willpower, reckon named as the first imperative and treated as arithmetic rather than effort, a slave metaphor apologized for even as it is used, and wages…
d: Dead to Sin, Alive to Christ (vv1–14)

x: Paul uses the analogy of marriage to explain that believers have died to the law through the body of Christ, freeing them to belong to Christ and bear fruit for God rather than serving in the old way of the written code (vv. 1-6). He clarifies that the law itself is not sin, but it revealed his sin — apart from the law he would not have known what it meant to covet — and sin used the commandment to produce every kind of wrongdoing in him (vv. 7-11). Paul affirms that the law is holy, righteous, and good, and describes his ongoing struggle: he does not do the good he wants but keeps doing the evil he does not want, showing sin still living in him (vv. 12-20). He identifies a principle at work — when he wants to do good, evil is right there with him, waging war against his mind and holding him captive (vv. 21-23). He cries out for deliverance from this body of death, and thanks God for…
m: Marriage law used to argue that death dissolves an obligation the living cannot escape, the law called holy and just and good even as sin uses it as a weapon, coveting aroused by the very command that forbids it, a war between wanting the good and doing the evil described from the inside, and a cry…

x: Paul opens by declaring that believers in Christ Jesus are free from condemnation, because the Spirit's law of life has set them free from the law of sin and death (vv. 1-2). Those who live according to the Spirit, rather than the flesh, are led as God's own children and given a spirit of adoption that lets them call God "Father" (vv. 14-16). Present sufferings are set against future glory, with all creation groaning for its own liberation, and the Spirit interceding for believers with groanings too deep for words (vv. 18-27). Paul closes with the assurance that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him (v. 28), and that nothing in all creation — not death, life, angels, or any power — can separate believers from the love of God in Christ Jesus (vv. 31-39).
m: No condemnation declared as a relocation of judgment rather than its cancellation, nineteen mentions of the Spirit answering a struggle that had only one in the chapter before, Abba, Father left standing in Aramaic inside a Greek letter to a Latin city, a golden chain of five links all spoken of in…

x: Paul expresses deep sorrow and anguish over his fellow Israelites, even wishing he could be cursed in their place, since they possess the adoption, the covenants, the law, and the promises, and descended from the patriarchs and from Christ himself (vv. 1-5). He argues that God's word has not failed, because not all who descend from Israel are true Israel — God's promise works through his sovereign choice, as shown when he chose Jacob over Esau before either had done anything (vv. 6-13). Paul defends God's justice by pointing to his declaration that he will have mercy on whom he chooses, comparing God to a potter who has the right to shape the clay as he wills, whether for honor or dishonor (vv. 14-23). He explains that God called people from among both Jews and Gentiles, fulfilling the prophecy that those who were not his people would be called his children, though only a remnant of…
h: Vessels of Mercy, Called from the Gentiles (vv.24-29)
m: Paul's willingness to be accursed for brothers he has just finished grieving over, Isaac chosen over Ishmael and Jacob over Esau before either had done good or evil, a potter's authority over clay answering an objection about fairness before it is fully raised, Hosea and Isaiah both quoted to…

x: Paul shares his heartfelt desire and prayer that Israel would be saved, noting that they have zeal for God but not according to knowledge, since they sought to establish their own righteousness instead of submitting to God's (vv. 1-3). He declares that Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes, contrasting the righteousness of the law with the righteousness of faith, which does not require impossible feats but simply says the word is near, in the mouth and in the heart (vv. 4-8). Paul states that confessing Jesus as Lord and believing God raised him from the dead brings salvation, and that there is no distinction between Jew and Greek since the same Lord is generous to all who call on him (vv. 9-13). He then reasons that people cannot call on, believe in, or hear about someone without a preacher being sent, concluding that faith comes through hearing the…
m: Zeal without knowledge diagnosed as Israel's problem rather than a lack of sincerity, Moses quoted for both ways of righteousness he is used to argue, no ascent to heaven or descent to the deep required because the word is already near, a chain of necessity running backward from calling to being…
d: The Message of Salvation to All (vv5–21)

x: Paul asks whether God has rejected his people and answers no, pointing to himself as an Israelite and to the remnant chosen by grace, just as God preserved seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal in Elijah's day (vv. 1-6). He explains that Israel as a whole did not obtain what it sought, but the elect did, while the rest were hardened, and that Israel's stumbling opened the door of salvation to the Gentiles in order to provoke Israel to jealousy (vv. 7-14). Paul uses the image of an olive tree, warning Gentile believers, who were grafted in as wild branches, not to boast against the natural branches, since God is able to graft the natural branches back in if they do not persist in unbelief (vv. 15-24). He reveals the mystery that a partial hardening has come on Israel until the full number of Gentiles comes in, and that all Israel will be saved, since God's gifts and calling are…
m: Paul's own believing as the proof Israel has not been cast away entirely, an indirect strategy that provokes jealousy through Gentile salvation rather than bypassing Israel, an olive tree with natural branches broken off and wild branches grafted in, a mystery revealed so the Gentiles will not be…

x: Paul urges believers, in view of God's mercy, to offer their bodies as a living and holy sacrifice as their true act of worship, refusing to be shaped by the world but instead transformed through the renewal of their minds so they can discern God's good and perfect will (vv. 1-2). He calls each person to think of themselves with sober judgment rather than pride, according to the measure of faith God has given (v. 3), comparing the church to a body with many members and different functions, so that believers who are many form one body in Christ, belonging to one another (vv. 4-5). He lists gifts that differ by God's grace — prophesying, serving, teaching, encouraging, giving generously, leading diligently, and showing mercy cheerfully — and urges each person to exercise their gift accordingly (vv. 6-8). Paul then gives a rapid string of instructions for genuine love: hate evil, cling to…
h: Present Your Bodies a Living Sacrifice (vv.1-2)
Bless, Weep, and Be Not Wise in Your Own Conceits (vv.14-16)
m: Mercies as the ground of obedience, bodies presented as a living sacrifice, a renewed mind against conformity, gifts measured by faith and exercised in a body, and love worked out as far as the treatment of enemies

x: Paul instructs believers to submit to governing authorities, since they are established by God and serve as his agents to restrain evil and promote good (vv. 1-7). He then reduces every commandment to a single debt that is never fully paid off — the obligation to love one's neighbor, since love does no harm and so fulfills the law (vv. 8-10). The chapter closes with an urgent call to wake from spiritual sleep, since salvation is nearer now than when they first believed (vv. 11-12). Paul urges believers to cast off the deeds of darkness and put on the armor of light, living decently rather than in indulgence or strife, and to clothe themselves with the Lord Jesus Christ instead of making provision for sinful desires (vv. 13-14).
m: Governing authorities named ministers of God ordained to restrain evil, submission taught as the general principle rather than an absolute overriding obedience to God, love named the only debt that never finishes being paid, an ethic given an actual deadline with the night far spent, and clothing…

x: Paul addresses disputes among believers over disputable matters like food and observing certain days, urging the "strong" not to despise the "weak" and the "weak" not to judge the "strong," since both are serving the Lord according to their conscience (vv. 1-6). He reminds them that none of us lives to ourselves, and every believer will one day stand before God's judgment seat and give an account, so there is no place for judging a fellow servant (vv. 7-12). Even where a believer has freedom, that freedom should never be exercised in a way that causes a weaker brother to stumble, because the kingdom of God is not about food and drink but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit (vv. 13-19). Paul closes by warning that whatever is not done in faith is sin, so believers should act only according to a clear conscience (vv. 20-23).
h: The Doxology as Some Manuscripts Place It (vv.24-26)
m: Strong and weak believers commanded not to judge or despise each other over disputable matters, a day and a meal both referred to the Lord rather than argued to a single correct practice, none of us living to himself grounded in an accounting each believer gives for themselves alone, liberty…
d: Do Not Pass Judgment on One Another (vv1–12)
Do Not Cause Another to Stumble (vv13–23)

x: Paul continues the theme of unity, urging the strong to bear with the weaknesses of the weak rather than pleasing themselves, following the example of Christ, who did not please himself either (vv. 1-3). He prays that God would grant the Roman believers unity of mind so that together, Jew and Gentile, they might glorify God with one voice, since Christ welcomed both groups for God's glory (vv. 5-9), and offers a benediction that the God of hope would fill them with joy and peace as they trust him (v. 13). Paul then describes his calling as a pioneer missionary who preaches only where Christ has not already been named, a work now fulfilled from Jerusalem to Illyricum (vv. 18-22). He shares his plan to visit Rome on his way to Spain, but first to deliver a financial collection from Gentile churches to the poor believers in Jerusalem, and asks for prayer for safety and refreshment along…
m: The strong asked to bear the weak by Christ's own example of not pleasing himself, Christ named a minister to the circumcision and a mercy to the Gentiles in the same careful sentence, four Old Testament quotations stacked from every part of the Hebrew Bible to put Jew and Gentile in one sentence…
d: Christ the Hope of Jews and Gentiles (vv8–13)
Paul the Minister to the Gentiles (vv14–21)

x: Paul closes the letter with an extended list of personal greetings to more than two dozen believers in Rome, including Phoebe, who carried the letter and is commended as a servant of the church, and Priscilla and Aquila, his co-workers (vv. 1-16). He then warns sharply against those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to sound teaching, deceiving the naive with smooth talk while serving their own appetites, and urges believers to be wise about what is good and innocent of what is evil (vv. 17-20). Greetings follow from Paul's own companions, including Timothy and Tertius, who wrote down the letter as Paul dictated it (vv. 21-24). The letter ends with a doxology celebrating the gospel as God's long-hidden mystery, now revealed through the prophetic writings and made known to all nations to bring about the obedience of faith, giving glory to the only wise God through Jesus…
m: Twenty-six people greeted by name in a church Paul had never visited, women named prominently including a deacon, a couple where the wife is listed first, and an apostle called Junia, a warning against smooth talkers slipped into a chapter otherwise made of greetings, a secretary who signs his own…

x: Paul greets the church at Corinth as those sanctified and called to be saints, thanking God for the grace and spiritual gifts they have received in Christ (vv. 1-9). He then appeals for unity, having heard of quarrels forming around Paul, Apollos, Cephas, and Christ himself (vv. 10-13). He recalls that his calling was to preach the gospel, not to impress with eloquent wisdom, since the message of the cross seems foolish to those who are perishing but is God's power to those being saved (vv. 14-18). God has overturned worldly wisdom, choosing what is foolish, weak, and lowly in the world's eyes to shame the wise and strong (vv. 19-29). Believers' standing comes from God alone, who made Christ their wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption, so that anyone who boasts should boast only in the Lord (vv. 30-31).
h: The Divisions: I Am of Paul (vv.10-17)
The Preaching of the Cross Is Foolishness (vv.18-21)
Christ Crucified: Stumbling Block and Foolishness (vv.22-25)
m: Called saints in a divided church, factions named after their favorite teacher, baptism as a side issue, the cross as folly to those perishing, and God choosing what the world counts as nothing
d: Christ the Wisdom and Power of God (vv18–31)

x: Paul recalls that when he first came to Corinth, he deliberately set aside eloquence and clever argument, resolving to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ crucified, preaching in weakness and fear so their faith would rest on God's power rather than human wisdom (vv. 1-5). Yet he does speak wisdom to the mature — not the wisdom of this age's rulers, but God's hidden wisdom, planned before the ages, which those rulers failed to recognize when they crucified the Lord of glory (vv. 6-8). No eye or ear has grasped what God has prepared for those who love him, but God has revealed it through the Spirit, who searches even the depths of God (vv. 9-11). Because believers have received God's Spirit rather than the world's spirit, they can understand what God has freely given them, expressing spiritual truths in Spirit-taught words (vv. 12-13). The natural person cannot accept these…
h: The Natural and the Spiritual Man (vv.11-16)
m: Paul's own arrival described in weakness and fear so that faith would rest in power rather than eloquence, a hidden wisdom eye has not seen and ear has not heard, the Spirit named as the only means by which the things of God can be received, a natural man unable to know what is spiritually…

x: Paul says he could not address the Corinthians as spiritually mature but had to treat them as infants in Christ, feeding them milk rather than solid food because they were still unready, as shown by their ongoing jealousy and quarreling (vv. 1-3). Their slogans of loyalty to Paul or Apollos prove they are thinking in merely human terms, when in truth he and Apollos are only servants through whom the Corinthians believed — one planted, another watered, but God alone gave the growth (vv. 4-7). Paul describes himself as a skilled builder who laid the foundation of Jesus Christ, on which others now build, and warns that each person's work will be tested by fire on the day of judgment — some will be rewarded, others will suffer loss though still be saved (vv. 8-15). He reminds them that together they are God's temple, indwelt by his Spirit, and that anyone who destroys that temple will…
m: Envying and strife diagnosed as evidence of spiritual infancy rather than sophistication, Paul planting and Apollos watering while only God gives the increase, Christ named the only foundation before any building material is judged, fire testing every man's work with loss possible even where…

x: Paul instructs the Corinthians to regard him and his fellow workers as servants of Christ entrusted with God's mysteries, whose only requirement is faithfulness, and he refuses to be swayed by human judgment since it is the Lord who will judge him (vv. 1-5). He applies this to himself and Apollos as an example, warning against the arrogance that favors one leader over another, since anything they have was given by God, not achieved on their own (vv. 6-7). He contrasts the Corinthians' sense of having already arrived — reigning like kings — with the apostles' ongoing suffering: hunger, homelessness, hard labor, and public contempt for Christ's sake (vv. 8-13). Paul frames this rebuke as fatherly correction, reminding them that he became their spiritual father through the gospel and sent Timothy to reinforce his teaching (vv. 14-17). He warns the arrogant among them that he will soon test…
h: As My Beloved Sons I Warn You (vv.14-21)
m: Apostles described as stewards managing what belongs to someone else, Paul declining to judge even himself and leaving that to the Lord, a devastating irony set between the Corinthians reigning as kings and the apostles going hungry and despised, fatherhood claimed on grounds no other teacher in…

x: Paul addresses a report of sexual immorality in the church worse than what even pagans tolerate — a man involved with his father's wife — and is shocked that the church is proud rather than grieved, when they should have already removed him (vv. 1-2). Though physically absent, Paul has already passed judgment and instructs the church, when gathered in the Lord's authority, to hand the man over to Satan for the destruction of his flesh so that his spirit may be saved (vv. 3-5). He warns that tolerating this sin is like a small amount of yeast working through an entire batch of dough, and urges them to clear out the old sinful influence, since Christ, their Passover lamb, has already been sacrificed (vv. 6-8). He clarifies an earlier instruction not to associate with sexually immoral people: he did not mean avoiding unbelievers entirely, which is impossible, but refusing fellowship with…
m: A sin not even named among the Gentiles met with pride instead of mourning, deliverance to Satan aimed at saving the spirit rather than merely punishing the flesh, a little leaven argued to leaven the whole lump, an earlier instruction corrected and narrowed to a brother rather than the world…

x: Paul rebukes believers for taking their disputes before pagan judges instead of settling them within the church, reminding them that they will one day judge the world and even angels, so surely they can handle everyday disagreements (vv. 1-6). He says it would be better to simply accept being wronged than to sue a fellow believer, and warns that the wrongdoing itself grieves God (vv. 7-8). He then lists behaviors — including sexual immorality, idolatry, theft, drunkenness, and greed — that will keep people from inheriting God's kingdom, reminding the Corinthians that some of them once lived this way but have been washed, sanctified, and justified in Jesus' name and by the Spirit (vv. 9-11). Paul explains that while many things may be technically permissible, not everything is beneficial, and believers should not be mastered by anything, since the body is meant for the Lord, not for…
m: Lawsuits between believers taken to pagan courts when saints will one day judge the world and angels, being wronged preferred to wronging a brother, a vice list ending in a reminder that this is what some of them used to be, all things lawful answered by not all things being profitable, and the…

x: Responding to questions the Corinthians had written to him, Paul addresses marriage, teaching that husbands and wives should give each other their due and not withhold intimacy except briefly by mutual consent for prayer (vv. 1-6). He wishes all had his gift of singleness but recognizes it is not given to everyone, and tells the unmarried and widowed that it is fine to remain single or to marry if they cannot control desire (vv. 7-9). He relays the Lord's instruction that married believers should not divorce, and his own guidance that a believer married to an unbeliever should stay in the marriage unless the unbeliever chooses to leave, since God has called believers to peace (vv. 10-16). His broader principle is that each person should remain in the situation God called them to, whether circumcised or not, slave or free, since outward status matters far less than keeping God's commands…
h: Let Him Do What He Will (vv.36-40)
m: Marriage and singleness both named gifts rather than one ranked above the other, divorce addressed separately for two believers and for a believer married to an unbeliever, remaining in the calling one was called in argued twice from circumcision and once from slavery, advice about virgins offered…

x: Paul turns to the question of eating food sacrificed to idols, cautioning that knowledge alone tends to make people arrogant, while love builds others up, and that anyone who thinks they know something fully still has more to learn (vv. 1-3). He affirms that idols have no real existence and there is only one God the Father and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things exist (vv. 4-6). But not everyone shares this understanding — some believers, out of a weak conscience formed by their past experience with idols, are defiled if they eat such food thinking it is dedicated to a real god (v. 7). Food itself does not bring anyone closer to or further from God, but Paul warns that the "strong" believer's freedom can become a stumbling block that damages a weaker believer's conscience, in effect sinning against that brother and against Christ himself, who died for him (vv. 8-12). Paul…
m: Knowledge that puffs up set against love that builds up, one God and one Lord confessed before any question about meat is settled, an idol declared nothing at all in the world while a weaker conscience is still taken seriously, a strong believer's freedom capable of emboldening a weak one toward…

x: Paul defends his apostolic authority, pointing to his eyewitness encounter with the risen Christ and the Corinthians themselves as proof of his ministry, and argues from common sense, Old Testament law, and the temple system that gospel workers have a right to material support from those they serve (vv. 1-14). Yet he has deliberately not used this right, preferring to preach the gospel free of charge so that no one can accuse him of doing it for profit, since preaching itself is simply an obligation laid on him (vv. 15-18). Though free from everyone, Paul has made himself a servant to all, adapting his approach to Jews, to those under the law, to those without the law, and to the weak, becoming all things to all people so that he might save some by every possible means (vv. 19-22). He compares this discipline to an athlete training for a race, exercising self-control in all things to…
m: Real rights established from common sense, the Law and Jesus' own command before any of them are surrendered, none of those rights actually used so no accusation of financial motive could stick, becoming all things to all men kept inside a chapter about surrendering rights rather than convictions…

x: Paul points to Israel's wilderness generation as a warning: though they were all under the cloud, passed through the sea, and shared spiritual food and drink from the Rock, which was Christ, most of them were still struck down by God for their disobedience (vv. 1-5). He lists their failures — idolatry, sexual immorality, testing Christ, and grumbling — as examples written down to warn believers living in the last days, concluding that anyone who thinks they are standing firm should be careful not to fall (vv. 6-12).
