He assures them that God is faithful and will not let them be tempted beyond what they can bear, always providing a way out (v. 13). From there Paul warns against idolatry directly, arguing that sharing the Lord's cup and bread at communion creates a real spiritual participation that cannot be mixed with participation in pagan sacrifices (vv. 14-22). He closes with practical…
h: All to the Glory of God (vv.23-33)
m: Israel's wilderness privileges shown insufficient to prevent its wilderness failures, let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall, a way of escape promised through temptation rather than around it, one loaf making many eaters one body used to argue what sharing an idol's table also…
d: Do All to the Glory of God (vv23–33)

x: Paul addresses order in worship, first instructing on head coverings — arguing from the relationship between Christ, man, and woman, and from the created order, that men should pray and prophesy with heads uncovered while women should have their heads covered as a sign of proper honor, though he adds that men and women are mutually interdependent in the Lord (vv. 1-16). He then sharply corrects abuse of the Lord's Supper: the Corinthians' gatherings were doing more harm than good because factions had emerged and some ate and drank to excess while others went hungry (vv. 17-22). Paul recounts the tradition he received from the Lord — on the night of his betrayal, Jesus took bread and the cup, identifying them with his body and blood and instructing his followers to do this in remembrance of him until he comes (vv. 23-26). He warns that eating and drinking without recognizing the…
m: Imitation of Paul as he imitates Christ governing a passage about coverings that follows, a cultural sign of married status read as either respectability or rebellion depending on whether it is worn, the Lord's Supper turned into a divisive meal where the wealthy eat while the poor go hungry, the…

x: Paul teaches that the same Spirit who enables believers to confess Jesus as Lord also distributes a variety of spiritual gifts, all given for the common good, ranging from wisdom and knowledge to faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, tongues, and interpretation (vv. 1-11). He compares the church to a human body: just as the body has many parts that function as one, so believers, though many, were baptized by one Spirit into one body, whether Jew or Gentile, slave or free (vv. 12-13). No part can claim independence from the body just because it differs from another part, and no part can dismiss another as unnecessary — God arranged the body's members exactly as he wanted, giving special honor to the parts that seem weaker (vv. 14-24). This design ensures there is no division in the body, and that all members care for one another, suffering and rejoicing together (vv. 25-26). Paul reminds…
h: God Hath Set Some in the Church (vv.28-31)
m: A test for spiritual utterance stated by its content, Jesus is Lord, rather than its intensity, the same Spirit, Lord and God behind gifts, ministries and workings that differ, a body with many members none of which may say it does not belong, less honourable parts given more abundant honour rather…

x: Known as the love chapter, this passage opens with Paul insisting that without love, even the most impressive spiritual gifts and sacrifices are worthless — eloquent speech becomes noise, and prophecy, knowledge, faith, generosity, even martyrdom accomplish nothing apart from love (vv. 1-3). He then describes love's character: it is patient and kind, free of envy, boasting, and arrogance; it does not dishonor others, insist on its own way, or become easily angered, and it keeps no record of wrongs (vv. 4-5). Love finds no joy in wrongdoing but rejoices in truth, and it bears, believes, hopes, and endures through everything (vv. 6-7). Paul contrasts love's permanence with the temporary nature of spiritual gifts — prophecy, tongues, and knowledge will all pass away because present knowledge is only partial, like a child's limited understanding compared to an adult's, or a dim reflection…
h: What Love Does and Does Not Do (vv.4-7)
m: Gifts without love reduced to nothing, love defined by what it does rather than what it feels, patience and kindness listed before anything impressive, prophecy and knowledge described as temporary, and seeing face to face rather than in a mirror

x: Paul urges the Corinthians to pursue love while also desiring spiritual gifts, especially prophecy, because prophecy speaks intelligibly to build up the church while speaking in tongues without interpretation edifies only the speaker (vv. 1-5). He illustrates the need for clarity with musical instruments and military trumpets, arguing that unintelligible speech is useless for communication, and that anyone speaking in tongues in the assembly should pray for the ability to interpret (vv. 6-13). He explains that praying only with the spirit leaves the mind unfruitful, so he insists on praying and singing with understanding as well, since an outsider cannot say "Amen" to something they cannot comprehend (vv. 14-19). Paul reasons that tongues function as a sign mainly for unbelievers while prophecy builds up believers and can even convict an outsider who hears their heart's secrets exposed…
m: Prophecy preferred over tongues in corporate worship because it edifies the whole church rather than only the speaker, five words with understanding weighed against ten thousand in an unknown tongue, tongues limited to two or three speakers and required to be interpreted, God named not the author…

x: Known as the resurrection chapter, Paul reminds the Corinthians of the gospel he preached to them — that Christ died for sins according to Scripture, was buried, and rose on the third day, appearing to Peter, the Twelve, more than five hundred believers at once, James, and finally to Paul himself (vv. 1-8). He acknowledges his own unworthiness as a former persecutor of the church but credits God's grace for his transformation and ministry (vv. 9-11). Paul then confronts those denying the resurrection of the dead, arguing that if there is no resurrection, then Christ himself was not raised, making the apostles' preaching empty, the Corinthians' faith worthless, and believers who have died simply lost (vv. 12-19). But Christ has indeed been raised, the first of a coming harvest, guaranteeing that in Christ all will be made alive just as in Adam all die, with Christ ultimately handing the…
m: The gospel reduced to three facts and two scripture-anchored qualifiers, a chain of consequences traced out fully if Christ is not risen, Christ named firstfruits so that His resurrection is the beginning of the harvest rather than a separate event, a resurrection body compared to a seed sown in…

x: Paul gives instructions for a collection being gathered for the believers in Jerusalem, asking the Corinthians to set aside money weekly so funds are ready when he arrives, and to appoint trusted representatives to carry the gift (vv. 1-4). He outlines his travel plans, intending to pass through Macedonia before possibly staying with the Corinthians for a time, while remaining in Ephesus until Pentecost because of the ministry opportunity there despite strong opposition (vv. 5-9). He asks the church to welcome Timothy without fear and to send him on his way in peace, and explains that Apollos was unwilling to visit them now but will come when he has opportunity (vv. 10-12). Paul closes with a series of exhortations to stay alert, stand firm in the faith, act with courage and strength, and do everything in love (vv. 13-14). He commends the household of Stephanas for their service, asks…
h: Watch Ye, Stand Fast, and the Greeting in His Own Hand (vv.13-24)
m: A collection organized as systematic and weekly giving rather than a single impulsive gift, a great door opened at Ephesus in the same breath as many adversaries, Apollos declining an invitation from the very church that had formed a party around him, five imperatives gathered under one that…

x: Paul, writing with Timothy to the church at Corinth and all the saints in Achaia, opens by praising God as the Father of mercies who comforts believers in every trouble so they can comfort others facing the same (vv. 1-7). He recalls a severe affliction in Asia that pressed him beyond his own strength, teaching him to rely on God who raises the dead rather than on himself, and thanks the Corinthians for their prayers on his behalf (vv. 8-11). He defends the sincerity of his conduct and his reason for changing travel plans, explaining he delayed visiting to spare them another painful encounter (vv. 12-17, 23-24). Paul closes the chapter by affirming that God's promises are never uncertain, since every promise finds its "Yes" in Christ, and that God has sealed believers with the Holy Spirit as a guarantee of what is to come (vv. 18-22).
h: Greeting to the Church and All Achaia (vv.1-2)
m: Comfort received explicitly so it can be passed to others in trouble, a trouble in Asia named only by its effect, a clear conscience offered as the one boast Paul allows himself, yea and amen argued from Paul's own reliability up to God's, and an explicit refusal to have dominion over their faith

x: Paul explains he decided against another painful visit and instead wrote to them through many tears, not to cause sadness but to show his deep love for them (vv. 1-4). Regarding the individual who caused grief, he says the discipline already given by the majority is enough, and now urges the church to forgive and comfort him so he is not overwhelmed by excessive sorrow, reaffirming their love for him so Satan cannot gain an advantage through unforgiveness (vv. 5-11). He recounts arriving in Troas with an open door to preach the gospel, yet having no peace of mind because he could not find Titus, so he went on to Macedonia (vv. 12-13). The chapter closes with Paul giving thanks to God, who leads believers in triumphal procession in Christ and spreads the knowledge of Him everywhere, describing believers as the fragrance of Christ — an aroma of life to those being saved and of death to…
h: No Rest in My Spirit at Troas (vv.12-13)
m: A visit canceled to avoid the very scene a letter was meant to prevent, tears named as the letter's true composition rather than its rebuke, forgiveness commanded for a repentant man lest sorrow swallow him whole, a sentence left broken off at Troas and not resumed until chapter seven, and a…

x: Paul asks whether he needs a letter of recommendation, since the Corinthians themselves are his letter, written by the Spirit not on stone but on human hearts, known and read by everyone (vv. 1-3). His confidence comes not from his own sufficiency but from God, who made him a minister of a new covenant of the Spirit rather than the letter, for the letter kills but the Spirit gives life (vv. 4-6). He argues that if the old covenant, which brought condemnation and was fading away, still came with glory so great that Israel could not look at Moses' radiant face, the new covenant of the Spirit and righteousness must carry far greater, unfading glory (vv. 7-11). Because of this hope, Paul speaks with boldness, unlike Moses who veiled his face; even now a veil remains over hearts when the old covenant is read, lifted only when a person turns to Christ (vv. 12-16). Where the Spirit of the Lord…
m: Changed lives offered as a letter of commendation written without ink, an old covenant of glory that still brought condemnation set against a new covenant that brings righteousness, sufficiency for the ministry located outside the minister before any comparison begins, a veil removed only when a…

x: Paul explains that having this ministry by God's mercy, he does not lose heart, and has renounced deceptive methods in favor of openly proclaiming the truth (vv. 1-2). He acknowledges the gospel remains veiled only to those who are perishing, whose minds the god of this age has blinded to keep them from seeing the light of Christ's glory, since God is the one who shines light into believers' hearts (vv. 3-6). He describes believers as carrying this treasure in jars of clay, so that the power is clearly God's and not their own, and lists the paradox of being afflicted but not crushed, struck down but not destroyed (vv. 7-10). Though outwardly wasting away, Paul says believers are inwardly renewed daily, because present light affliction is producing an eternal weight of glory far beyond comparison (vv. 11-17). The chapter closes with the reminder to fix attention not on what is seen…
m: A ministry held without resorting to craftiness or a deceitful use of the word, a god of this world blinding minds rather than an argument simply failing to persuade, treasure deliberately kept in earthen vessels so the power is credited to God, four pairs of pressures each conceded and each denied…

x: Paul explains that our earthly body is like a temporary tent, and though we groan under its weakness, we long for the eternal, heavenly dwelling God has prepared, walking now by faith rather than sight (vv. 1-7). Since everyone will one day stand before Christ's judgment seat to give account, Paul's aim is simply to please the Lord (vv. 8-10). Christ's love, not human approval, compels his ministry, and he no longer judges anyone by outward appearances (vv. 11-16). Anyone in Christ becomes a new creation, the old life gone and a new one begun (v. 17). God reconciled the world to himself through Christ without counting people's sins against them, entrusting believers with that message and making them his ambassadors, pleading with others to be reconciled to God (vv. 18-20). Finally, God made the sinless Christ to be sin for us so we might become his righteousness (v. 21).
h: The Love of Christ Constraineth Us (vv.11-16)
m: A body compared to a tent groaning for a building not made with hands, love constraining a ministry between only two possible motives, a new creature declared rather than an old one merely improved, reconciliation described twice in three verses as both a ministry and a message not of Paul's own…

x: Paul, as God's co-worker, urges the Corinthians not to receive God's grace without effect, noting that now is the accepted time of salvation (vv. 1-2). He lists the hardships and contrasting realities that mark his authentic ministry - afflictions, honor and dishonor, sorrow and joy, poverty and abundance - all endured through purity, patience, and genuine love (vv. 3-10). Paul opens his heart wide to the Corinthians and asks them to do the same, since any restraint lies on their side, not his (vv. 11-13). He then warns against being mismatched with unbelievers, since righteousness and wickedness, light and darkness, God and idols have nothing in common (vv. 14-16). Quoting Old Testament promises, he calls believers to separate from what is unclean, since God has promised to dwell among them as Father to his own sons and daughters (vv. 17-18).
m: Grace that can be received in vain if the moment it is offered is allowed to pass, ministry credentials built from suffering rather than comfort, paradoxes stacked one after another as though the world's verdict and reality can both be spoken at once, an enlarged heart met by a restriction Paul…
d: The Temple of the Living God (vv14–18)

x: Paul urges the Corinthians, in light of God's promises, to cleanse themselves from every impurity of body and spirit and pursue holiness (v. 1). He asks them to make room for him in their hearts, insisting he has wronged no one, and expresses deep affection despite the conflict and fear he faced in Macedonia (vv. 2-5). God comforted him through Titus's arrival, who reported the Corinthians' longing, mourning, and zeal for Paul (vv. 6-7). Though his earlier severe letter caused pain, Paul explains it produced godly sorrow leading to repentance rather than the death worldly sorrow brings, and their resulting earnestness proves their sincerity (vv. 8-11). He concludes that his purpose was to reveal their genuine care for him before God, and he rejoices in Titus's refreshed spirit and his own full confidence in the church (vv. 12-16).
h: Comforted by the Coming of Titus (vv.5-9)
m: A sentence broken off in chapter two picked up again with an honest account of no rest and fears within, comfort arriving by an arrival rather than an insight, godly sorrow distinguished from worldly sorrow by what each one produces, seven results of genuine repentance listed as active rather than…
d: The Temple of the Living God (v1)

x: Paul highlights the Macedonian churches as an example of generosity, noting that despite severe trial and deep poverty, their overflowing joy produced abundant giving, even beyond their means and entirely of their own will (vv. 1-5). He urges Titus to help the Corinthians complete the same grace of giving they had begun, since they already excel in faith, speech, knowledge, and love (vv. 6-7). Paul points to Christ himself as the ultimate model of generosity, who though rich became poor for their sake so they might become rich (v. 9). He advises them to follow through on their earlier willingness, giving according to what they have, so that abundance and need are balanced among believers, as with Israel's manna (vv. 10-15). Finally, Paul commends Titus and two other trusted brothers who will carry the gift, taking care to handle the funds with full transparency before both God and…
h: Proving the Sincerity of Your Love (vv.6-8)
m: Macedonian churches giving beyond their power out of deep poverty rather than surplus, giving themselves to the Lord named as the act that precedes giving their money, Christ's own poverty offered as the pattern for a collection rather than as an illustration, willingness measured against ability…

x: Paul says it is almost unnecessary to write further about the collection for the saints, since he has already boasted to the Macedonians about the Corinthians' eagerness, which in turn stirred many others to give (vv. 1-2). Still, he sends the brothers ahead to make sure the gift is ready in advance, so it will be given generously rather than grudgingly, and so neither he nor the Corinthians are embarrassed if Macedonians arrive and find them unprepared (vv. 3-5). He teaches that giving is like sowing seed: whoever sows sparingly reaps sparingly, and whoever sows generously reaps generously, and each person should give as he decides in his heart, not reluctantly, since God loves a cheerful giver (vv. 6-7). God is able to supply all they need so they can abound in every good work, and their generosity will produce overflowing thanksgiving to God and prayers on their behalf (vv. 8-14).…
h: Sent Ahead, That It Be Not of Necessity (vv.1-5)
m: A chapter written to say a letter was unnecessary, sowing bountifully and sparingly set against each other as the whole of the principle, a cheerful giver preferred to a grudging one regardless of the amount given, five alls describing a sufficiency so complete it can always abound to every good…

x: Paul appeals to the Corinthians by Christ's gentleness, asking them not to force him to be as bold in person as he can be in his letters against those who accuse him of acting by merely human standards (vv. 1-2). Though he lives in the flesh, his ministry weapons are not fleshly but divinely powerful, tearing down arguments and every proud obstacle raised against the knowledge of God, and bringing every thought into obedience to Christ (vv. 3-6). He urges the Corinthians to stop judging by outward appearance, since he belongs to Christ as much as anyone claiming special authority, and his authority was given for building them up, not tearing them down (vv. 7-11). Refusing to compare himself with those who commend themselves, Paul boasts only within the ministry God assigned him, hoping their growing faith will let his work expand further (vv. 12-16). True approval, he concludes, comes…
h: Base in Presence, Bold When Absent (vv.1-2)
The Authority the Lord Hath Given (vv.6-9)
m: Critics quoted before they are answered rather than paraphrased, weapons of warfare declared not carnal though mighty enough to pull down strongholds, authority claimed for building up and immediately limited against tearing down, an accusation about a weak presence and a contemptible speech met…

x: Paul asks the Corinthians to bear with a bit of foolish boasting, explaining that his jealousy for them is godly, since he has promised them to Christ as a pure bride and fears their minds being led astray from simple devotion to Christ, just as the serpent deceived Eve (vv. 1-3). He notes they readily tolerate outsiders preaching a different Jesus, spirit, or gospel, even though he is in no way inferior to the leading apostles despite his plain speech (vv. 4-6). He defends preaching to them free of charge, supported instead by other churches, and vows to keep doing so to undercut rivals who boast of matching his ministry (vv. 7-12). He calls these rivals false apostles disguised as servants of Christ, just as Satan disguises himself as an angel of light (vv. 13-15). Reluctantly playing the fool, Paul matches his opponents' boasting, listing his Jewish heritage alongside a grueling…
m: A fool's speech Paul names as folly before he ever begins it, jealousy compared to a father guarding a bride's purity rather than a rival defending territory, refusing payment turned from an insult into a boast about robbing other churches instead, Satan transformed into an angel of light offered…

x: Paul reluctantly turns to visions and revelations, describing a man - clearly himself - caught up into paradise fourteen years earlier who heard things too sacred to repeat (vv. 1-4). Rather than boast in that experience, he boasts in his weaknesses, explaining that a painful thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan, was given to keep him from becoming conceited (vv. 5-7). Though he pleaded three times for its removal, the Lord answered that his grace is sufficient and his power is made perfect in weakness, so Paul embraces weakness that Christ's power may rest on him (vv. 8-10). He notes the Corinthians should have defended him themselves, given the signs and wonders performed among them, and reaffirms he will not burden them financially on his coming third visit, since he seeks them, not their money (vv. 11-18). He closes fearing he will find quarreling, jealousy, and unrepented sin…
h: I Seek Not Yours, But You (vv.14-18)
Lest I Find You Not Such As I Would (vv.19-21)
m: A vision of paradise told in the third person by a man reluctant to boast even about what is true, a thorn in the flesh refused removal three times and answered with sufficient grace instead, signs of an apostle claimed once and briefly rather than dwelt on, a fear of finding envyings and strife…

x: Paul announces this will be his third visit, warning that on the testimony of multiple witnesses he will no longer spare those who remain unrepentant (vv. 1-2). Since the Corinthians want proof that Christ speaks through him, he reminds them that Christ, though crucified in weakness, lives by God's power, and Paul's own weakness likewise carries God's power toward them (vv. 3-4). He urges them to examine themselves to see whether they are truly in the faith, confident Christ is in them unless they fail the test (vv. 5-6). Paul prays they will do what is right regardless of his own reputation, since he can do nothing against the truth, only for it, and he would rather appear weak while they are strong and mature (vv. 7-9). He writes this in advance so his presence will not require severity, since his authority is for building up, not tearing down (v. 10). The letter closes with…
h: We Pray That Ye Do No Evil (vv.6-10)
Be Perfect, Be of Good Comfort (vv.11-13)
m: A third visit announced under the same rule of two or three witnesses used for legal testimony, self-examination turned back onto the readers instead of onto Paul's own credentials, a willingness to appear disapproved himself so long as the Corinthians do what is right, four short imperatives…

x: Paul insists his apostleship comes not from men but directly from Jesus Christ and God the Father, and greets the Galatian churches with grace and peace (vv. 1-5). He expresses astonishment that they are so quickly deserting the true gospel for a distorted one, and pronounces a curse on anyone — even himself or an angel — who preaches a different gospel (vv. 6-9). Seeking human approval, he says, would disqualify him as a servant of Christ (v. 10), and he insists the gospel he preaches came not from any human source but by revelation from Jesus Christ (vv. 11-12), recalling how he once violently persecuted the church while zealous for Jewish tradition (vv. 13-14). He describes how God, who set him apart before birth, called him by grace to reveal his Son in him and to preach to the Gentiles, and how he did not consult anyone but went to Arabia before returning to Damascus (vv. 15-17).…
h: Greeting: An Apostle Not Sent by Men (vv.1-5)
No Other Gospel: Astonishment in Place of Thanksgiving (vv.6-9)
His Former Life in the Jews' Religion (vv.13-14)
Separated from the Womb, Sent to the Gentiles (vv.15-17)
Three Years Later, Fifteen Days with Peter (vv.18-20)
Unknown by Face, Glorified in Report (vv.21-24)
m: Apostleship received directly rather than through men, a gospel that admits no alternative, astonishment in place of thanksgiving, a former life of zeal in Judaism, and a chronology offered as evidence of independence

x: Paul describes returning to Jerusalem fourteen years after his conversion, laying his gospel before the apostles there and finding that Titus, though Greek, was not compelled to be circumcised (vv. 1-5). James, Peter, and John recognize Paul's calling to the Gentiles and add nothing to his message, asking only that he remember the poor (vv. 6-10). When Peter later visits Antioch and withdraws from eating with Gentiles out of fear of the circumcision party, Paul publicly confronts his hypocrisy (vv. 11-14), then explains that justification comes through faith in Christ, not the law, and that he now lives by faith in the Son of God who loved him and gave himself for him (vv. 15-21).
m: A private meeting in Jerusalem that adds nothing to Paul's gospel, right hands of fellowship extended by men called pillars, Peter withdrawn from Gentile believers out of fear rather than conviction, a public rebuke delivered to an apostle's face, and a confession that it is no longer I who live…

x: Paul rebukes the Galatians for abandoning faith after receiving the Spirit through hearing with faith rather than works of the law (vv. 1-5). He points to Abraham, who believed God and was credited with righteousness, showing that those who have faith are Abraham's true children (vv. 6-9). Because no one is justified by keeping the law, Christ redeemed believers from its curse by becoming a curse for them, so the blessing of Abraham might reach the Gentiles (vv. 10-14). The law, given centuries after God's promise to Abraham, cannot cancel that promise; instead it served as a guardian until Christ came (vv. 15-25). Now, through faith and baptism into Christ, all believers are one in him and heirs according to the promise (vv. 26-29).
h: The Argument from the Law's Purpose (vv.19-25)
m: Experience of the Spirit cited as evidence before any argument from scripture, Abraham believing God 430 years before the law existed, a curse and a promise both quoted from the law against itself, the law described as a schoolmaster rather than a permanent guardian, and neither Jew nor Greek, bond…
d: By Faith, or by Works of the Law? (vv1–9)
The Righteous Shall Live by Faith (vv10–14)

x: Paul explains that an heir under guardians is no better than a slave until the appointed time, but God sent his Son to redeem those under the law, so that believers receive adoption as sons, with the Spirit crying "Abba, Father" in their hearts — making each one an heir rather than a slave (vv. 1-7). He asks why the Galatians, having known God, would turn back to weak and worthless practices tied to observing special days and seasons (vv. 8-11), then appeals to their earlier warm welcome of him despite his physical weakness, contrasting it with false teachers courting their favor for selfish ends (vv. 12-20). He closes with the allegory of Hagar and Sarah, showing believers are children of the free woman and the promise, not of slavery (vv. 21-31).
m: An heir no different from a slave until the appointed time, adoption sealed by the Spirit crying Abba, Father, a personal appeal that recalls eyes the Galatians would once have plucked out for him, weak and beggarly elements traded back for days and months and years, and two women read as two…

x: Paul opens by declaring that Christ has set believers free and urges them to stand firm rather than submit again to slavery, warning that accepting circumcision as a requirement severs them from Christ and obligates them to keep the whole law (vv. 1-6). He rebukes whoever has hindered their progress, comparing false teaching to leaven spreading through the whole batch (vv. 7-12), and calls them to use their freedom to serve one another in love, since the whole law is fulfilled in loving one's neighbor (vv. 13-15). Walking by the Spirit rather than the flesh keeps believers from sinful desires; he contrasts the works of the flesh with the fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control — noting that those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh (vv. 16-26).
m: Liberty declared before any instruction on how to use it, circumcision accepted as salvation shown to obligate the whole law, freedom fulfilled in serving one another rather than the flesh, works of the flesh and fruit of the Spirit listed as two harvests rather than two rule-books, and a flesh…
d: Keep in Step with the Spirit (vv16–26)

x: Paul instructs believers to gently restore anyone caught in sin, watching themselves, and to bear one another's burdens in fulfillment of the law of Christ, while still taking responsibility for their own work (vv. 1-5). He urges sharing good things with teachers and warns that God is not mocked — whatever one sows, one reaps, so believers should not grow weary in doing good, especially toward fellow believers (vv. 6-10). Paul contrasts false teachers who push circumcision to avoid persecution and boast in the flesh with his own determination to boast only in the cross of Christ, through which the world is crucified to him (vv. 11-16). He closes by pointing to the marks he bears for Jesus and blessing them with grace (vv. 17-18).
m: A fallen brother restored gently by those aware of their own vulnerability, burdens borne as the law of Christ rather than an optional kindness, sowing to the flesh or to the Spirit named as the whole of the choice, Paul's own large handwriting offered as proof he wrote this closing himself, and…

x: Paul greets the believers at Ephesus and breaks into praise of God for the spiritual blessings given in Christ — chosen before the world's foundation, predestined for adoption as sons, and given redemption and forgiveness through Christ's blood (vv. 1-7). God has revealed the mystery of His will: to unite all things in heaven and earth in Christ, and in Him believers have obtained an inheritance, sealed with the promised Holy Spirit as a guarantee of what's to come (vv. 8-14). Paul then tells them he constantly thanks God for their faith and love, praying that God would give them wisdom to know Him better — the hope of His calling, the riches of His inheritance in the saints, and the greatness of His power toward believers (vv. 15-19). That power is the same power God used to raise Christ from the dead and seat him far above every authority, making him head over all things for the…
h: Chosen Before the Foundation of the World (vv.3-6)
The Mystery Made Known: All Things Gathered Up (vv.9-10)
An Inheritance Obtained, a Spirit Given as Deposit (vv.11-14)
Paul's Prayer: Eyes to See What Is Already True (vv.15-19)
The Measure of the Power: Raised and Seated (vv.20-23)
m: Blessing chosen before the foundation of the world, adoption and redemption, the mystery of all things gathered up in Christ, the Spirit given as a deposit, and power measured by the resurrection

x: Paul reminds the Ephesians that they were once spiritually dead, following the world and their own sinful desires, deserving God's wrath like everyone else (vv. 1-3). But God, rich in mercy, made them alive together with Christ, raising and seating them with him in the heavenly realms — saved by grace through faith, not by works, so that no one can boast (vv. 4-9). They are God's workmanship, created for the good works He prepared in advance (v. 10). Paul recalls that Gentile believers were once excluded from Israel's covenants and without hope, but Christ's blood has now brought them near, tearing down the wall of hostility between Jew and Gentile and creating one new humanity reconciled to God through the cross (vv. 11-16). Christ preached peace to both, giving all believers access to the Father through one Spirit, so that Gentiles are no longer outsiders but fellow citizens in God's…
m: Spiritual death described as a condition by nature rather than a series of choices, but God interrupting the sentence at its worst point, salvation by grace through faith set apart from works while still leading to them, a dividing wall broken down between Jew and Gentile, and one new man built…

x: Paul, a prisoner for the sake of the Gentiles, describes the mystery God revealed to him: Gentiles are now fellow heirs with Israel, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise through the gospel (vv. 1-6). Though he counts himself the least of all saints, he was made a minister of this gospel to preach Christ's unsearchable riches and to display God's wisdom, hidden for ages, now made known through the church to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms (vv. 7-11). In Christ, believers have boldness and confident access to God, so Paul urges the Ephesians not to lose heart over his sufferings on their behalf (vv. 12-13). He then prays that they would be strengthened by the Spirit, that Christ would dwell in their hearts by faith, and that, rooted in love, they would grasp the full extent of Christ's love and be filled with the fullness of God (vv. 14-19). He closes…
m: A sentence begun and abandoned until Paul can explain why his imprisonment is for the Gentiles, a mystery defined as three fellow-words — heirs, members, partakers — held in complete equality, Paul naming himself less than the least of all saints as his own credential, a prayer for strength and…
d: The Mystery of the Gospel Revealed (vv1–13)

x: Paul urges believers to walk worthy of their calling, striving for unity through the one body, one hope, one Lord, one faith, and one baptism they share (vv. 1-6). Christ gave gifted leaders — apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers — to equip the saints for ministry and build up the body until all reach maturity, measured by the fullness of Christ (vv. 7-13). This keeps believers from being tossed about by false teaching; instead, speaking truth in love, they grow up into Christ as each part of the body does its work (vv. 14-16). Paul then tells them to put off their old, corrupted self and put on the new self, created after God in righteousness and holiness, rather than living as the Gentiles do in futile, darkened thinking (vv. 17-24). He closes with practical instructions: speak truth, handle anger without sinning, work honestly rather than steal, avoid corrupt talk…
h: Put Off the Old, Put On the New (vv.17-24)
m: A single therefore that turns three chapters of doctrine into a command to walk worthy, seven ones offered as the ground of unity rather than uniformity, gifted leaders given to equip the saints rather than to do the work for them, an old self put off and a new self put on like changing clothes…
d: Unity in the Body of Christ (vv1–16)

x: Paul calls believers to imitate God and walk in love as Christ did, avoiding sexual immorality, impurity, greed, and coarse talk that have no place among God's people and invite His wrath (vv. 1-7). Once darkness, they are now light in the Lord and should live as children of light, exposing rather than joining the fruitless works of darkness, waking up to the light Christ gives (vv. 8-14). He urges them to walk wisely, make the most of their time, and be filled with the Spirit instead of wine — singing, giving thanks, and submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ (vv. 15-21). Wives are told to submit to their husbands as to the Lord, while husbands are told to love their wives sacrificially, as Christ loved the church and gave himself to cleanse and present her without blemish (vv. 22-27). Husbands should love their wives as their own bodies, since the two become one flesh —…
m: Believers called not merely to have been in darkness but to have been darkness itself, redeeming the time set alongside being filled with the Spirit as the same command, singing and thanksgiving and mutual submission offered as evidence rather than instruction, marriage read backward from Christ…

x: Paul addresses household relationships: children are to obey and honor their parents (vv. 1-3), fathers are to raise their children in the Lord's instruction rather than provoke them (v. 4), and servants are to work for their masters wholeheartedly as though serving Christ, while masters are to treat their servants the same way, since God shows no favoritism (vv. 5-9). He then calls believers to be strong in the Lord and put on the full armor of God, since the real struggle is against spiritual powers, not flesh and blood (vv. 10-13). He lists the armor's pieces — the belt of truth, breastplate of righteousness, readiness from the gospel of peace, shield of faith, helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, the word of God (vv. 14-17) — and urges constant prayer, including prayer for himself to boldly proclaim the gospel despite being a prisoner for it (vv. 18-20). He closes by…
m: A household code that reaches children and servants before it reaches armor, obedience commanded of children as the first command carrying a promise, mutual accountability planted between masters and servants who share one Master in heaven, warfare named against principalities rather than people…

x: Paul and Timothy greet the believers at Philippi, along with their overseers and deacons (vv. 1-2). Paul thanks God for their partnership in the gospel and expresses confidence that God will finish the good work He began in them, praying their love would grow in knowledge so they can discern what matters and remain pure until Christ returns (vv. 3-11). He explains that his imprisonment has actually advanced the gospel, emboldening others to preach fearlessly, whether from good motives or rivalry — either way, Paul rejoices that Christ is proclaimed (vv. 12-18). Confident he will be delivered, Paul declares that living means Christ and dying means gain, torn between departing to be with Christ or remaining to help the Philippians grow (vv. 19-26). He closes by urging them to live worthy of the gospel, standing firm together in one spirit and unafraid of their opponents, since suffering…
h: Partakers of Grace, in Bonds and in Defence (vv.7-8)
The Gospel Advanced by a Chain (vv.12-14)
To Live Is Christ, To Die Is Gain (vv.19-26)
Citizens Standing Fast, Given the Gift of Suffering (vv.27-30)
m: Partnership in the gospel from the first day, a good work God will finish, imprisonment turned to advance, rivals preaching Christ from mixed motives, life and death both gain, and suffering described as a gift

x: Paul appeals for unity among the Philippians, urging them to be of one mind, act without selfish ambition, and consider others more important than themselves (vv. 1-4). He points to the example of Christ, who though equal with God, emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and humbled himself to death on a cross — so God exalted him above every name, that every knee would bow and every tongue confess him Lord (vv. 5-11). Paul then urges them to work out their salvation with reverence, since God is at work in them, doing everything without complaining so they shine as lights in a corrupt world (vv. 12-16). Rejoicing even in possible martyrdom, Paul plans to send Timothy soon to check on them and hopes to visit himself (vv. 17-24). In the meantime he sends back Epaphroditus, who nearly died serving Paul on their behalf, asking the church to welcome him with honor (vv. 25-30).
m: Unity appealed to on the ground of humility rather than agreement, a hymn tracing Christ from equality with God down to a cross and back up to the name above every name, salvation worked out rather than worked for, two men — Timothy and Epaphroditus — offered as living examples of the pattern the…

x: Paul tells the Philippians to rejoice in the Lord and warns them against false teachers who insist on circumcision, since true worship comes through the Spirit rather than confidence in the flesh (vv. 1-3). He then lists his own impressive religious credentials — a Hebrew of Hebrews, a zealous Pharisee, legally blameless — only to count them all as loss compared to the surpassing value of knowing Christ (vv. 4-8). Paul wants to be found in Christ with a righteousness that comes from faith, to know the power of Christ's resurrection and share in his sufferings, and so attain the resurrection from the dead (vv. 9-11). Though not yet perfect, he presses on toward the goal, forgetting what lies behind and straining for the prize of God's heavenly call (vv. 12-16). He urges the Philippians to imitate him rather than the enemies of the cross who are focused on earthly things, since believers'…
m: Judaizers named dogs in a deliberate reversal of a slur, an impressive Jewish pedigree listed in full before being called refuse, righteousness sought as a gift received by faith rather than earned by the law, a race run by a man who insists he has not yet arrived, and citizenship claimed in heaven…

x: Paul urges the Philippians to stand firm in the Lord and calls on Euodia and Syntyche, two women who had labored with him, to settle their disagreement (vv. 1-3). He commands them to rejoice always, be gentle toward others, and replace anxiety with prayer and thanksgiving, promising that God's peace will guard their hearts and minds (vv. 4-7). He tells them to focus their thoughts on whatever is true, honorable, and pure, and to practice what they've learned from him (vv. 8-9). Paul thanks them for renewing their support of him, explaining that he has learned contentment in any circumstance — abundance or need — because he can do all things through Christ's strength (vv. 10-13). He commends the Philippians as the only church that partnered with him financially from the start, most recently through Epaphroditus, and assures them God will supply all their needs from his riches in Christ…
m: Two named women in conflict addressed by name rather than left anonymous, joy commanded rather than merely encouraged, anxiety answered with prayer and thanksgiving rather than argued away, contentment described as something learned rather than natural to Paul, and greetings closing from converts…

x: Paul and Timothy greet the Colossians, thanking God for their faith, love, and hope in a gospel already bearing fruit throughout the world (vv. 1-8). Paul prays they would grow in the knowledge of God's will, recalling how God rescued believers from darkness into his Son's kingdom, granting redemption and forgiveness (vv. 9-14). The chapter's center is a hymn on Christ's supremacy: he is the image of the invisible God, existed before all things, holds creation together, and is head of the church, since God's fullness dwells in him and all things are reconciled through his death (vv. 15-20). Paul calls the Colossians to remain firm in that faith (vv. 21-23), then describes his own suffering for the church and his labor to reveal Christ dwelling within believers as their hope of glory (vv. 24-29).
h: Greeting to a Church He Had Not Seen (vv.1-2)
Faith, Love, and a Hope Laid Up (vv.3-8)
Prayer: Filled with Knowledge, Walking Worthy (vv.9-12)
The Image of the Invisible God (vv.15-17)
Head of the Body, Firstborn from the Dead (vv.18-20)
Once Enemies, Now to Be Presented Holy (vv.21-23)
Christ in You: The Mystery Now Revealed (vv.24-29)
m: A church Paul had never visited, faith and love resting on hope laid up in heaven, transfer out of darkness into a kingdom, Christ as image and firstborn holding creation together, reconciliation through the blood of the cross, and a mystery now disclosed

x: Paul voices his deep concern for the Colossians and the Laodiceans, praying they would be united in love and reach full understanding of the mystery of God, which is Christ, in whom all wisdom and knowledge are hidden (vv. 1-5). He urges them to keep walking in Christ as they first received him, warning against hollow philosophy and human tradition, since God's fullness dwells bodily in Christ and believers are made complete in him (vv. 6-10). Through faith they have been spiritually circumcised, buried with Christ in baptism, and raised to new life, their sins forgiven and the debt of the law canceled at the cross, where Christ disarmed every rival power (vv. 11-15). Paul then warns against being judged over food, festivals, or Sabbaths, mere shadows of Christ, or deceived by false humility and angel worship that lets go of Christ as head of the body, asking why those who died with him…
m: Completeness in Christ argued against four distinct rivals in turn, philosophy named first among the threats, festivals and sabbaths called shadows of a substance already present, angel worship diagnosed as a loss of connection to the Head, and rules against touching and tasting shown to have no…

x: Since believers have been raised with Christ, Paul tells them to set their minds on things above, for their life is now hidden with Christ in God (vv. 1-4). He calls them to put to death earthly desires like sexual immorality and greed, and to put away anger, malice, and lying now that they have put off the old self and put on the new self, renewed in the image of its Creator, where distinctions like Greek and Jew no longer matter because Christ is all and in all (vv. 5-11). As God's chosen and beloved people, they are to clothe themselves with compassion, kindness, humility, patience, and forgiveness, and above all with love, which binds everything together in perfect unity (vv. 12-14). The peace of Christ should rule their hearts, and the word of Christ should dwell in them richly through teaching and singing, with everything done in the name of the Lord Jesus (vv. 15-17). The chapter…
m: A life already hidden with Christ in God before it is described, two catalogued lists of sins put off before any list of virtues is put on, love named above every other virtue rather than merely included among them, a household code applied to wives and husbands, children and fathers, servants and…

x: Paul closes the letter with instructions for masters to treat their servants fairly, since they too answer to a Master in heaven (v. 1), and urges the Colossians to persist in prayer, including prayer for his own gospel ministry while imprisoned, and to live wisely and speak graciously toward outsiders (vv. 2-6). He commends Tychicus and Onesimus, who will carry news and encouragement to the church (vv. 7-9), and passes along greetings from his coworkers Aristarchus, Mark, and Jesus called Justus, followed by Epaphras, who prays earnestly that the Colossians would stand mature and fully assured in God's will (vv. 10-13). Luke and Demas also send greetings (v. 14), and Paul asks that the letter be shared with the church at Laodicea and read alongside a letter from there, while urging Archippus to complete the ministry entrusted to him (vv. 15-17). Paul signs off in his own hand, asking…
m: A master's duty completing a household code rather than left as an afterthought, speech asked to be gracious and seasoned with salt toward outsiders, a network of named co-workers filling out the early church's map, Mark's restoration to fellowship despite the break of Acts 15, and Demas greeted…

x: Paul, Silas, and Timothy greet the Thessalonian church and open by thanking God for them, remembering their work of faith, labor of love, and endurance inspired by hope in Jesus Christ (vv. 1-3). Paul notes that the gospel came to them not in word only but in power, in the Holy Spirit, and with full conviction, and that they received the message with joy despite affliction, becoming examples to believers throughout Macedonia and Achaia (vv. 5-7). Their faith became so well known that Paul says he no longer needs to say anything about it, since others report how the Thessalonians turned from idols to serve the living and true God (vv. 8-9). The chapter closes by noting that they now wait for God's Son from heaven, whom He raised from the dead, and who delivers believers from the coming wrath (v. 10).
h: Work of Faith, Labour of Love, Patience of Hope (vv.2-3)
m: Faith, love and hope shown in work, labour and patience, election evidenced by the gospel's effect, imitation producing further imitation, a report that traveled ahead of the apostles, and a turn from idols to serving and waiting

x: Paul reminds the Thessalonians that his visit was not without purpose, and that despite earlier suffering and opposition in Philippi, he and his companions spoke the gospel boldly amid much conflict (vv. 1-2). He insists his appeal came from pure motives, not error, impurity, or trickery, and that he sought to please God rather than people, avoiding flattery and any pretext for greed (vv. 3-5). Though he had the right to be supported as an apostle, Paul was gentle among them like a nursing mother caring for her children, and worked night and day so as not to be a financial burden while he preached (vv. 6-9). He describes exhorting, comforting, and urging each of them individually the way a father deals with his own children, so they would live lives worthy of God (vv. 10-12). The chapter closes with Paul recalling their joyful reception of the gospel as God's word, their suffering at…
m: A ministry defended point by point against a slander it never states outright, boldness claimed despite suffering already endured at Philippi, gentleness compared to a nursing mother and burden compared to a father, a word received as God's own rather than as merely human, and Paul calling himself…
d: Paul's Longing to See Them Again (vv17–20)

x: Unable to bear being separated from the Thessalonians any longer, Paul sent Timothy from Athens to strengthen and encourage their faith amid the persecutions he had warned them to expect (vv. 1-4). Paul explains he sent Timothy because he feared the tempter had somehow undermined their faith, which would have made his labor among them wasted (v. 5). Timothy's return brought good news of their faith and love, and word that they remember Paul fondly and long to see him just as he longs to see them, which comforted Paul in his own distress (vv. 6-7). Paul prays earnestly night and day to see them again and to complete what is lacking in their faith (vv. 9-10). He closes by praying that the Lord would direct his way back to them and cause their love to increase for one another and for everyone, strengthening their hearts to be blameless in holiness at Christ's coming (vv. 11-13).
m: An uncertainty Paul says he could no longer bear, Timothy sent alone to a church still under the persecution Paul had already warned them about, good news received as though it were Paul's own life restored, a prayer for a path back measured alongside a prayer for their holiness, and love asked to…
d: Paul's Longing to See Them Again (vv1–5)

x: Paul urges the Thessalonians to keep living in a way that pleases God, specifically calling them to sexual purity — each controlling his own body in holiness and honor rather than in the passion common among those who don't know God (vv. 1-5). He warns against wronging a brother in this matter, since the Lord avenges such sins, and reminds them that God has called them to holiness, not impurity (vv. 6-8). On brotherly love he says they hardly need instruction since God Himself has taught them, but urges them to keep growing in it, living quietly, minding their own business, and working with their hands so they depend on no one (vv. 9-12). Paul then comforts them about believers who have died, teaching that just as Jesus died and rose, God will bring back with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in Him (vv. 13-14). He describes the Lord's return in dramatic terms — descending from heaven…
m: Sanctification named as God's will in so many words rather than left implied, sexual conduct governed by not defrauding a brother rather than only personal restraint, ambition redirected toward a quiet life and working with one's own hands, grief answered with information rather than only comfort…

x: Paul explains that the Day of the Lord will come unexpectedly, like a thief in the night, bringing sudden destruction on those who feel safe and secure (vv. 1-3). But since the Thessalonians are children of light and of the day, they are not to be taken by surprise, and should stay alert and sober rather than sleeping or getting drunk like others do (vv. 4-7). Instead they are to arm themselves with faith, love, and the hope of salvation, since God appointed them for salvation through Jesus Christ, not for wrath (vv. 8-9). Paul then gives a series of rapid instructions: respect church leaders, live in peace, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and repay no one evil for evil (vv. 12-15). He closes with short commands to rejoice continually, pray constantly, give thanks in every circumstance, not quench the Spirit, test everything, and hold fast to what is good, followed by a…
m: A day arriving as a thief for those who say peace and safety, children of light distinguished from the day by category rather than by watchfulness alone, a run of short commands fired with almost no elaboration between them, the Spirit named as something that can be quenched by neglect, and a…

x: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy greet the church and give thanks for the Thessalonians' growing faith and increasing love for one another amid the persecutions and afflictions they are enduring (vv. 1-4). Paul explains that their suffering is evidence of God's righteous judgment, in which He will repay affliction to those who trouble them and grant relief to the afflicted when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with His mighty angels in blazing fire (vv. 5-8). Those who do not know God and disobey the gospel will suffer eternal destruction, shut out from His presence, while Jesus will be glorified among His saints on that day (vv. 9-10). Paul closes with a prayer that God would make them worthy of His calling and fulfill their every good purpose, so that Jesus' name would be glorified in them (vv. 11-12).
m: Faith growing and love abounding under persecution, present suffering as evidence rather than contradiction, the revelation of Christ in flaming fire, judgment described as recompense, and a prayer that God would count them worthy

x: Paul urges the Thessalonians not to be quickly shaken or alarmed by any claim, even one supposedly from him, that the Day of the Lord has already come (vv. 1-2). He explains that day cannot come until the rebellion occurs and the man of lawlessness is revealed, who exalts himself above every so-called god and sets himself up in God's temple, proclaiming himself to be God (vv. 3-4). Paul notes that a restraining force currently holds this figure back, but once removed, the lawless one will be revealed, empowered by Satan with counterfeit signs and wonders that deceive those who are perishing because they refused to love the truth (vv. 5-10). Because of this, God will send a powerful delusion so they believe the lie and are condemned (vv. 11-12). Paul thanks God for choosing the Thessalonians for salvation and urges them to stand firm in the teaching they were given (vv. 13-17).
m: A forged letter or claimed prophecy spreading panic that the Day had already come, a falling away and a man of sin required before it can arrive, something currently restraining what is not yet revealed, a strong delusion sent on those who refused to love the truth, and a people called and chosen…

x: Paul asks the church to pray that the Lord's message would spread rapidly and that he and his companions would be delivered from wicked and evil people (vv. 1-2). He expresses confidence that the Lord will strengthen and protect them, and prays that their hearts would be directed into God's love and Christ's perseverance (vv. 3-5). Paul commands the church, in the name of the Lord Jesus, to keep away from believers who are idle and refuse to follow the teaching they received from him, reminding them that he and his companions worked to support themselves rather than take anyone's bread without paying for it, so that anyone unwilling to work should not eat (vv. 6-10). He instructs the idle to settle down and earn their own living, and tells the church not to grow weary in doing good, but to warn the disorderly as a fellow believer rather than an enemy (vv. 11-15). He closes with a prayer…
m: A prayer request for deliverance from unreasonable men before any command is given, idleness treated as a discipline problem rather than a doctrine problem, Paul's own labor offered as the standard rather than only the argument, a rule that ties eating to working, and withdrawal from a disorderly…

x: Paul opens by reminding Timothy why he left him in Ephesus: to stop certain men from teaching false doctrine and chasing myths and genealogies instead of the love that flows from a pure heart, good conscience, and sincere faith (vv. 1-7). He explains that the law is good when used rightly, aimed at the lawless and sinful, and is consistent with the gospel of God's glory entrusted to him (vv. 8-11). Paul then recalls his own testimony as a former blasphemer and persecutor who was shown mercy and appointed to service, calling himself the worst of sinners as an example of Christ's patience, and breaks into praise of God as the eternal, immortal, invisible King (vv. 12-17). He closes by charging Timothy to fight the good fight, holding on to faith and a clear conscience, warning that Hymenaeus and Alexander have already shipwrecked their faith by rejecting it (vv. 18-20).
h: The End of the Commandment Is Love (vv.5-7)
Chief of Sinners, Pattern of Mercy (vv.15-17)
War a Good Warfare: Faith Shipwrecked (vv.18-20)
m: A charge to stay and correct, endless genealogies set against love from a pure heart, the lawful use of the law, Paul as chief of sinners and pattern of mercy, and faith either held or shipwrecked
d: Christ Jesus Came to Save Sinners (vv12–20)

x: Paul urges that prayers, intercessions, and thanksgiving be offered for everyone, including kings and those in authority, so believers can live peaceful and godly lives, since God desires all people to be saved and come to know the truth (vv. 1-4). He grounds this in the truth that there is one God and one mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all, a message Paul was appointed to preach as apostle to the Gentiles (vv. 5-7). He then instructs men to pray without anger or arguing, women to dress modestly and pursue good works rather than showy adornment, and women to learn in quietness and submission rather than teaching or exercising authority over men in the assembly, pointing to the order of creation and the deception of Eve (vv. 8-14). The chapter closes with the promise that women will be preserved through childbearing if they…
m: Prayer urged for all men and specifically for rulers before any other instruction, one mediator and one ransom stated against a backdrop of many, modesty in dress set against costly adornment as the real point of contrast, teaching authority restricted and grounded in the order of creation rather…

x: Paul lists the qualifications for an overseer, requiring a man of good character who is above reproach, faithful to his wife, self-controlled, hospitable, able to teach, not a heavy drinker or lover of money, and one who manages his own household well (vv. 1-7). He then sets similar standards for deacons and their wives, calling for dignity, sincerity, and a clear conscience, with deacons first being tested before they serve (vv. 8-13). Paul explains he is writing so that Timothy will know how people ought to conduct themselves in God's household, which he calls the pillar and foundation of the truth (vv. 14-15). The chapter closes with an early hymn confessing the mystery of godliness: Christ revealed in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, and taken up in glory (v. 16).
m: Qualifications for overseers built almost entirely from character rather than skill, a new convert excluded by rule rather than by suspicion, deacons held to a nearly identical standard as a second office, the church named the pillar and ground of the truth, and a hymn of six lines rising out of a…

x: Paul warns that in later times some will abandon the faith, following deceptive spirits and demonic teaching that forbids marriage and certain foods — things God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who know the truth (vv. 1-5). He tells Timothy that pointing these things out to the believers will mark him as a good servant of Christ, and urges him to train himself in godliness rather than chase godless myths, since godliness holds promise for both this life and the one to come (vv. 6-10). Timothy is told not to let anyone look down on him for his youth but to set an example in speech, conduct, love, faith, and purity, and to devote himself to public reading of Scripture, exhortation, and teaching (vv. 11-13). Paul closes by telling him not to neglect the gift he was given, to give himself fully to these things, and to watch his life and doctrine closely for the sake of…
m: Apostasy predicted explicitly by the Spirit rather than merely feared, asceticism corrected by declaring creation good and received with thanksgiving, godliness commended as profitable for this life and not only the next, youth defended by example rather than by argument, and a charge to watch…
d: Some Will Depart from the Faith (vv1–5)
A Good Servant of Christ Jesus (vv6–16)

x: Paul instructs Timothy to treat older men as fathers, younger men as brothers, and women as mothers and sisters, with complete purity (vv. 1-2). He gives detailed guidance on caring for widows, distinguishing those truly alone who should be supported by the church from those with family who should be cared for at home, and encouraging younger widows to remarry and manage their households (vv. 3-16). Elders who lead well, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching, deserve double honor and fair pay, and any accusation against an elder requires two or three witnesses, with public rebuke reserved for those who persist in sin (vv. 17-20). Paul charges Timothy to remain impartial, to avoid appointing leaders hastily, to keep himself pure, and to take a little wine for his frequent stomach ailments, closing with the observation that people's sins and good deeds are not always…
m: Correction addressed by age and relation rather than by rank, a formal list of widows with real qualifications for enrollment, family responsibility placed ahead of the church's own resources, elders granted double honour while also held to a public standard of accountability, and a personal note…

x: Paul instructs slaves to honor their masters, warns against those who teach otherwise for personal gain, and identifies the love of money — not money itself — as a root of all kinds of evil that has led some away from the faith (vv. 1-10). He calls godliness paired with contentment great gain, noting that believers brought nothing into the world and can take nothing out, so food and covering should be enough (vv. 6-8). Timothy is charged to flee these temptations and instead pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance, and gentleness, to fight the good fight of faith, and to keep the command he has received without fault until Christ appears, a charge Paul reinforces with praise to God as the only sovereign Ruler (vv. 11-16). He instructs the wealthy not to trust in their riches but in God, and to be generous and ready to share, storing up treasure for the life to come (vv.…
m: Servants instructed to honor believing masters more rather than less, gain mistaken for godliness named as the error underneath the false teaching, contentment paired with godliness as great gain against a love of money called a root of all evil, a charge to fight the good fight framed by a…
d: Fight the Good Fight of Faith (vv11–21)

x: Paul greets Timothy, his beloved son in the faith, and recalls praying for him constantly, longing to see him, and remembering the sincere faith passed down from his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice (vv. 1-5). He urges Timothy to fan into flame the gift of God given through Paul's laying on of hands, since God has given believers a spirit not of fear but of power, love, and self-discipline (vv. 6-7). Timothy should not be ashamed of the gospel or of Paul's imprisonment, but share in suffering for it, relying on God who saved and called believers by His own grace, now revealed through Christ's appearing, who abolished death and brought life to light (vv. 8-10). Paul, though suffering for his appointed role as preacher and teacher, is unashamed because he trusts God to guard what he's entrusted to Him (vv. 11-12), and he charges Timothy to hold to sound teaching and guard that same good…
h: Not Fear, But Power, Love, and a Sound Mind (v.7)
Be Not Ashamed of the Testimony (vv.8-11)
I Know Whom I Have Believed (v.12)
Onesiphorus, and Those Who Turned Away (vv.15-18)
m: Faith inherited through a grandmother and a mother, a gift needing to be stirred into flame, power and love and a sound mind against fear, a deposit committed and kept, and companions who turned away while one man did not
d: Guard the Deposit Entrusted to You (vv3–18)

x: Paul urges Timothy to draw strength from the grace found in Christ and to pass on what he has learned to faithful men who can teach others in turn (vv. 1-2). He compares the Christian life to a soldier who avoids civilian entanglements, an athlete who competes by the rules, and a hardworking farmer who is first to share in the harvest (vv. 3-7). He points Timothy back to the risen Christ as the center of his gospel, for which he suffers imprisonment, though God's word itself cannot be chained, and quotes a trustworthy saying about sharing in Christ's death, life, and reign (vv. 8-13). Timothy is charged to avoid quarrels over words, to rightly handle the word of truth, and to steer clear of empty chatter like that of Hymenaeus and Philetus, who wrongly claimed the resurrection had already happened (vv. 14-19). Using the image of a large house with vessels of varying value, Paul urges…
m: A chain of transmission carried through four generations, endurance argued from a soldier, an athlete and a farmer, a word of God that stays free even when the man who preaches it is chained, a workman who must rightly divide the word of truth, and a servant who corrects opponents gently in hope…
d: A Good Soldier of Christ Jesus (vv1–13)

x: Paul warns that the last days will bring difficult times marked by people who are self-centered, greedy, boastful, disobedient, unloving, and lovers of pleasure rather than of God, holding to outward religion while denying its power, and he tells Timothy to avoid them (vv. 1-5). He describes false teachers who exploit vulnerable people, comparing them to Jannes and Jambres who opposed Moses, though their folly will eventually be exposed (vv. 6-9). By contrast, Paul points to his own teaching, conduct, and suffering, which Timothy has closely observed, noting that all who live godly lives in Christ will face persecution while evil people grow worse (vv. 10-13). He reminds Timothy of the sacred writings he has known from childhood, able to give wisdom for salvation through faith in Christ, and declares that all Scripture is inspired by God and useful for teaching, rebuke, correction, and…
m: Eighteen vices used to describe the last days rather than a distant future, a form of godliness that denies its own power, persecution promised to everyone who lives godly rather than reserved for the unusual case, scripture named as both the source of wisdom for salvation and the tool that equips…
d: All Scripture Is Breathed Out by God (vv10–17)

x: Paul solemnly charges Timothy, before God and Christ the coming judge, to preach the word faithfully and correct, rebuke, and encourage with patience, since a time is coming when people will reject sound teaching for teachers who tell them what they want to hear (vv. 1-5). Sensing his death is near, Paul declares that he has fought the good fight, finished the race, and kept the faith, with a crown of righteousness awaiting him and all who love Christ's return (vv. 6-8). He asks Timothy to come quickly, noting that Demas deserted him for love of the world while others scattered, leaving only Luke with him, and he asks for Mark and for his cloak, books, and parchments left at Troas (vv. 9-13). He warns of harm done by Alexander the metalworker, and recalls that though no one stood with him at his first defense, the Lord stood by him, strengthened him, and rescued him, and will preserve…
m: A charge delivered before God and Christ as if in a courtroom, itching ears preferred to sound doctrine, a life summarized in three perfect-tense verbs before the sentence is passed, a crown offered to everyone who loves Christ's appearing and not to Paul alone, and a list of deserters and…

x: Paul identifies himself as a servant of God and apostle of Jesus Christ, sent to build up the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth, in hope of eternal life promised before time began (vv. 1-3). He greets Titus, left on Crete to set things in order and appoint elders in every town (vv. 4-5), then lists an elder's qualifications — blameless, faithful in marriage and family, self-controlled, hospitable, and able to teach sound doctrine while refuting opponents (vv. 6-9). He warns of many rebellious, deceptive teachers, especially from the circumcision party, quoting a Cretan poet's blunt assessment of his own people before urging Titus to rebuke them sharply so they remain sound in the faith (vv. 10-13). Paul closes by contrasting the purity of those who trust God with the defiled conscience of those who claim to know him yet deny him by their actions (vv. 14-16).
h: Greeting: Truth That Leads to Godliness (vv.1-4)
Left in Crete to Finish What Was Lacking (v.5)
Vain Talkers Whose Mouths Must Be Stopped (vv.10-11)
A Cretan Prophet, and a Sharp Diagnosis (vv.12-14)
To the Pure All Things Are Pure (vv.15-16)
m: Truth defined by the godliness it produces, a task left unfinished on purpose, elders qualified by character and household, a bishop able to hold and to refute, and a local proverb turned into a diagnosis
d: Rebuke Those Who Contradict Sound Doctrine (vv10–16)

x: Paul tells Titus to teach what fits sound doctrine (v. 1), then describes how each group in the church should live: older men self-controlled and sound in faith, older women reverent and equipped to mentor younger women toward loving their husbands and children, young men self-controlled, and Titus himself a model of good works and sound speech (vv. 2-8). Servants are told to be submissive and trustworthy so they honor God's teaching in every way (vv. 9-10). This godly living flows from God's grace, which has appeared bringing salvation to all people and training believers to reject ungodliness and live uprightly while awaiting Christ's return (vv. 11-13). Christ gave himself to redeem people from sin and purify a people devoted to good works (v. 14), and Titus is charged to teach and correct with full authority, letting no one disregard him (v. 15).
m: Instruction sorted by age and household rather than delivered in general, sound doctrine judged by the life it produces, grace appearing as a teacher of self-control rather than only a rescue, a peculiar people purified and zealous of good works, and doctrine handed to one man to speak aloud where…

x: Paul instructs Titus to remind believers to submit to civil authorities, stay ready for good work, and treat everyone with gentleness, recalling that they themselves were once foolish, disobedient, and enslaved to sin (vv. 1-3). But when God's kindness and love appeared, he saved them — not because of their own righteous deeds but because of his mercy — through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit, poured out generously through Jesus Christ (vv. 4-6). Justified by grace, believers become heirs with hope of eternal life, and Paul wants Titus to insist on this so that those who believe stay devoted to good works (vv. 7-8). He warns Titus to avoid foolish arguments, genealogies, and quarrels about the law, and to reject a divisive person after two warnings (vv. 9-11). Paul closes with travel plans, instructions to help Zenas and Apollos, a reminder to keep learning good…
m: Obedience to pagan magistrates commanded rather than debated, a former life catalogued without excuse, salvation by mercy against a works clause it explicitly rules out, the Spirit poured out and renewal named as regeneration, and a letter that ends in errands and unfinished travel plans
d: Be Ready for Every Good Work (vv1–11)

x: Paul, writing as a prisoner, greets Philemon, his wife Apphia, Archippus, and the church that meets in Philemon's house, and gives thanks for Philemon's love and faith toward the Lord and all the saints (vv. 1-7). Rather than command him, Paul appeals on the basis of love on behalf of Onesimus, Philemon's runaway slave who became Paul's spiritual son during his imprisonment and whom Paul is now sending back (vv. 8-12). Paul explains that he would have liked to keep Onesimus for himself but wanted Philemon's consent, suggesting that Onesimus's departure may have providentially resulted in Philemon receiving him back forever, no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother (vv. 13-16). He asks Philemon to welcome Onesimus as he would welcome Paul himself, offering to personally repay any debt or wrong Onesimus caused, and expresses confidence that Philemon will do even more than asked (vv.…
h: Greeting: A Prisoner, Not an Apostle (vv.1-3)
Thanksgiving: Naming What Is Already True (vv.4-7)
The Request: Receive Him as a Brother (vv.8-16)
m: Intercession for another, a slave received as a brother, moral persuasion instead of apostolic command, the gospel reshaping a household, and a debt voluntarily assumed

x: The author contrasts God's past revelation through the prophets, given at many times and in various ways, with his final revelation through his Son (vv. 1-2), who reflects God's own glory and bears the very stamp of his nature, upholding the universe by his word and now seated at God's right hand after purifying people from sin (v. 3). A series of Old Testament quotations then establishes the Son's superiority to angels: he alone is called God's Son and is worshiped by angels (vv. 4-6), his throne and reign are eternal while creation itself will wear out and be discarded like an old garment (vv. 8-12), and he sits enthroned while angels remain merely serving spirits sent to assist those who will inherit salvation (vv. 13-14).
h: God Has Spoken by His Son (vv.1-2a)
Seven Things True of the Son (vv.2b-3)
m: The Son as God's final word, seven Old Testament citations establishing His superiority to angels, creation and inheritance held by the same person, and a throne that does not pass

x: The author warns against drifting away from what has been heard, since the message once given through angels carried binding consequences — making it far more serious to neglect the salvation announced by the Lord and confirmed by those who heard him, with God adding his own testimony through signs, wonders, and gifts of the Spirit (vv. 1-4). Quoting Psalm 8, he notes that humanity, not angels, was given dominion over the world to come, and though we don't yet see that fully realized, we do see Jesus — made lower than the angels for a time and now crowned with glory because he tasted death for everyone (vv. 5-9). It was fitting for God to perfect the founder of salvation through suffering, since Jesus and those he saves share one origin (vv. 10-13). By sharing fully in flesh and blood, he defeated the one who held the power of death and freed those enslaved by fear of dying, becoming a…
m: A first warning naming drifting rather than rebellion as the real danger, the world to come subjected to man rather than to angels, a Son made lower than the angels for the specific purpose of tasting death, brethren claimed rather than merely subjects addressed, and temptation endured so help…

x: The author calls believers, who share in a heavenly calling, to consider Jesus as the apostle and high priest of their confession, faithful to God just as Moses was faithful in God's house — though Jesus, as the house's builder, deserves greater honor than Moses, who was only a servant within it (vv. 1-6). Quoting Psalm 95, he warns readers not to harden their hearts as Israel did in the wilderness, when that generation tested God for forty years despite seeing his works, provoking him to swear they would never enter his rest (vv. 7-11). He urges believers to watch that no one develops an unbelieving heart that turns away from the living God, but to encourage one another daily so that none are hardened by sin's deceitfulness (vv. 12-13). Sharing in Christ depends on holding firm to the end, and the chapter closes by tracing Israel's failure to enter God's rest back to unbelief (vv.…
m: A house compared to its builder to argue for a Son greater than a servant, Moses honored fully before being surpassed, a second warning drawn from Israel's forty years rather than from a new offense, hardening traced to unbelief rather than to circumstance, and daily exhortation urged as the remedy…
d: A Rest for the People of God (vv7–19)

x: The author warns that although the promise of entering God's rest still stands, believers should fear falling short as the wilderness generation did, since the good news reached them too but failed to benefit them because they did not receive it in faith (vv. 1-2). Those who believe do enter that rest, which God established when he rested on the seventh day after finishing creation, yet the rest remained open after that generation's disobedience, since God later designates a new "today" through David long after Joshua had settled Israel in the land (vv. 3-8). A Sabbath rest therefore still remains for God's people, and believers are urged to strive to enter it, resting from their own works as God did from his, so that no one falls through the same disobedience (vv. 9-11). God's word is described as living and active, sharper than any double-edged sword, able to judge the heart's…
