This portrait of diligence pictures willing hands and real physical strength, not reluctant obligation. Good work, done willingly, actually builds strength rather than just draining it. Is your current work approached with willing hands, or with reluctant obligation?

Paul pictures a future testing of the quality of work built on Christ, not just its quantity. It's worth asking not just how much you're producing, but what kind of work will actually survive that fire. Is your current work built to last, or just built to look busy in the moment?

The wall got built because the people 'had a mind to work' — motivation and will, not just capability. Plenty of capable people never finish anything because the will isn't there. What capability do you have that's sitting unused because the will to actually work hasn't kicked in?

Paul frames good works as something learned, practiced, and devoted to — not a spontaneous occasional gesture. Fruitfulness comes from deliberate habit, not just good intentions. What urgent need around you could your devoted, practiced good work actually meet?

Work became hard after the fall — this isn't how it was designed to feel. When your labor feels like toil and struggle, it's not a sign something's wrong with you; it's the reality every worker since Eden has faced. Where does your work currently feel most like toil, and can you bring that honestly to God?

This proverb contrasts two very different relationships to work — one chosen and leading somewhere, the other imposed and going nowhere. Diligence isn't just morally better; it actually shapes your trajectory. Where has a lack of diligence left you more controlled by circumstances than you'd like to be?

Paul holds two things together that seem contradictory — work it out, and it's God working in you. Your effort and God's work aren't competing; your effort is actually powered by His work underneath it. Where have you been trying to work something out in your own strength, forgetting God is working in you too?

Ruth didn't wait for provision to arrive — she went out and worked for it, in humble, unglamorous labor gleaning leftover grain. Her diligence in an ordinary task became the doorway to her whole future. What unglamorous task in front of you might actually be the doorway to something bigger, the way Ruth's gleaning was?

The sluggard here isn't described as lacking desire — he craves plenty, he just never acts on it. Diligence is what turns craving into actually receiving. What have you been craving without actually putting in the diligent work to reach it?

Nehemiah names the problem honestly before calling people to act — clear-eyed about the trouble, and clear-eyed about the work needed. Honest assessment tends to produce real motivation, more than vague optimism does. What 'wall' in your life needs an honest assessment before you can strengthen your hands to rebuild it?

Paul quotes an agricultural principle to make a point about honoring those who labor for others — even an ox gets to eat from what it works for. Fair honor for labor isn't a modern idea; it's built into Scripture from the start. Is there someone whose labor for you or your community deserves more honor than they're currently receiving?

This simple verse sits inside a psalm celebrating the whole rhythm of creation — sunrise, sunset, and ordinary human labor woven right into that same rhythm as something natural and good, not separate from it. Do you experience your daily work as part of creation's good rhythm, or as an interruption to it?

The Preacher circles back again to this same simple conclusion — rejoice in your work, because that's genuinely your portion. Not everything can be known or controlled, but the work in front of you can be enjoyed. What would change if you focused on rejoicing in today's work instead of worrying about what comes after?

The psalmist describes God's works as worth studying, not just admiring from a distance. There's a discipline of paying close attention to what God has done, the same way a craftsman studies excellent work. What work of God in your own life is worth studying more closely, not just glancing at?

This proverb contrasts patient, diligent planning with hasty shortcuts — not because haste is inherently evil, but because it tends to skip the steps that actually lead somewhere solid. Where have you been tempted toward a hasty shortcut instead of diligent, patient planning?

God's own evaluation of His finished work was simple satisfaction — very good. There's something worth imitating in pausing to actually recognize when work is genuinely good, rather than always rushing to the next task. What finished work in your own life have you never paused to actually call good?

Paul doesn't rank these gifts — service and mercy sit right alongside prophecy and teaching, each valuable in its own lane. Whatever work God has gifted you for, it's not lesser just because it's less visible. Have you undervalued a gift you've been given because it seems less visible than someone else's?

Paul remembers this church by three linked qualities — work born from faith, labor born from love, and steadfastness born from hope. Real spiritual fruit tends to show up as active work, not just internal feeling. If someone described you the way Paul describes this church, what would your 'work of faith' and 'labor of love' actually look like?

Before the people worked, God stirred their spirits — motivation itself is described as something God supplies, not just something you have to manufacture on your own. Where do you need God to stir your spirit before you'll have the motivation to actually begin?

Closing this month of work and diligence, this verse promises that none of it goes unnoticed by God — not the visible accomplishments, and not the quiet, ongoing service to others either. What quiet work or service have you done this month that felt unnoticed, but that God promises He hasn't overlooked?

The psalmist doesn't just call individual verses true — he says the whole sum of Scripture, taken together, is truth. It's meant to be trusted as a coherent whole, not just mined for isolated favorite lines. Is there a part of Scripture's 'sum' you tend to avoid because it's less comfortable than your favorite verses?

Paul reminds Timothy of a lifelong, familial acquaintance with Scripture — not a single dramatic encounter, but years of steady exposure that shaped him toward wisdom. How could you build the same kind of lifelong, steady acquaintance with Scripture into your own household?

This short verse places God's word beyond the reach of shifting circumstances or changing opinions — fixed in the heavens, unmoved by whatever happens on earth. What's shifting in your life right now that you need to anchor against something unshakably fixed?

Isaiah contrasts the word of God with the most fragile, temporary things in nature — grass and flowers, gone within a season. Everything else fades; this alone stands. What are you currently investing heavily in that's more like fading grass than God's enduring word?

Jesus makes an audacious claim here — even the physical universe is described as temporary compared to His own words. That's not a small thing to say about anything, let alone spoken words. Is your confidence built on something that will pass away, or on the words Jesus says never will?

Peter is careful to say Scripture's origin wasn't human invention — the writers were carried along, not simply expressing their own ideas. Its authority rests on where it actually came from. Do you approach Scripture as human opinion you can take or leave, or as something the Spirit carried the writers to produce?

This image of refined silver — purified repeatedly, until nothing impure remains — describes the purity of God's words. Nothing false or corrupted has survived the process. Where have you doubted the purity of God's word because of how imperfectly people have sometimes represented it?

John identifies Jesus Himself as the Word — not just a messenger delivering words, but the Word made flesh, present at creation itself. Scripture ultimately points to a person, not just a text. Do you relate to Scripture mainly as information to master, or as an introduction to the living Word Himself?

Paul states the universal problem plainly — all have sinned — and then the universal solution just as plainly: justified as a gift, not earned. This pairing is the hinge the whole gospel turns on. Have you been living like justification is still something to earn, rather than a gift already given?

God tells Habakkuk to write the vision down plainly, so it could be read and understood clearly, even while its fulfillment was still delayed. Truth worth having is worth writing down clearly enough to be trusted while you wait. What promise of God are you still waiting on, and how does having it written plainly help you wait?

God's law had been lost, forgotten, buried in the temple itself — and its rediscovery sparked genuine national reform. Sometimes revival starts simply with finding what was already there, just neglected. What part of Scripture feels like it's been buried and forgotten in your own spiritual life?

This wasn't reading for its own sake — the leaders made sure the meaning was clear, so ordinary people could actually understand what they were hearing. Scripture was always meant to be understood, not just recited. Do you read Scripture to check a box, or to actually understand and be changed by it?

Even Israel's future kings were commanded to personally copy and daily read God's law — power didn't exempt anyone from ongoing dependence on Scripture. No amount of authority replaces the need to keep reading. Has any success or authority in your life quietly reduced how often you turn to Scripture?

David stacks up benefit after benefit — reviving, making wise, bringing joy. Scripture isn't described here as a burden to bear, but as something that actively restores whoever engages it. When did Scripture last actually revive something in you, rather than just inform you?

Peter describes new birth as coming through this specific seed — the living and abiding word, not anything perishable. Whatever else gave you life in this world, spiritual life traces back to this imperishable source. Can you trace your own spiritual birth back to a specific encounter with God's word?

Jeremiah pictures Scripture as food, actually eaten and absorbed, not just glanced at. That kind of internalizing takes more than a quick read — it takes real digestion, chewing on it until it becomes joy. What would it look like for you to 'eat' Scripture this week, rather than just skim it?

Paul describes sound doctrine as a deposit to guard, something entrusted that requires active protection, not passive holding. Truth received has to be actively defended against drift and dilution. Where have you let sound teaching quietly drift, without actively guarding it?

This isn't dutiful obligation — it's love, described as constant meditation running through an entire day. The psalmist's relationship with Scripture sounds more like devotion than discipline. Does your engagement with Scripture feel more like duty, or like the love this verse describes?

The Bereans didn't just accept Paul's teaching because he was Paul — they tested it against Scripture themselves, daily. Eagerness and careful examination weren't in tension for them; they went together. Is there a teaching you've accepted uncritically that you should actually test against Scripture yourself?

Paul ties faith directly to hearing the word — not a feeling that arrives independently, but something that grows specifically through exposure to Christ's word. Faith rarely deepens apart from Scripture. Has your faith been stagnant lately because your exposure to God's word has thinned out?

God promises His word always accomplishes something — never wasted, never returning empty. Even when you can't see the fruit yet, the word you've received or shared is still doing its work. Where have you assumed God's word 'didn't work' when it may simply still be accomplishing its purpose, unseen?

Paul sets a boundary here — not going beyond what is written — specifically to prevent pride and division. Staying rooted in Scripture, rather than personal opinion, protects unity as much as it protects truth. Where have you gone beyond what Scripture actually says, adding your own opinion as though it carried the same weight?

Scripture isn't described as a static document but as living and active — something that actually does something to whoever engages it, cutting through to what's really going on underneath. What has Scripture recently exposed in you that you'd rather have kept hidden, even from yourself?

Ezra's pattern here is worth noticing — study, then do, then teach. Understanding came before obedience, and obedience came before teaching others. The order matters; each step builds on the last. Which step are you skipping — studying deeply, actually doing it, or teaching what you've learned?

This proverb pairs trust in God's word with a warning against adding to it — Scripture's authority isn't something to supplement with your own additions, however well-intentioned. Where have you added your own rules or assumptions to Scripture, treating them as though God said them too?

Paul repeats the same point twice in a single sentence, almost as if anticipating how easily it gets forgotten — justified by faith, not by works. This truth needs restating because it's so easy to quietly slide back toward earning it. Where have you been quietly sliding back toward earning your standing with God through works?

Jesus met the tempter's offer of physical bread with a deeper claim about what actually sustains a person. Real nourishment, He says, comes from something words alone can supply — but only God's words. Are you feeding your soul with God's word as consistently as you feed your body?

Paul, who had impressive religious credentials by any human measure, still calls his own righteousness insufficient compared to what comes through faith alone. If Paul needed this exchange, so does everyone else. What personal 'righteousness' or achievement have you been quietly relying on instead of Christ's?

Paul ties the same creative power that spoke light into existence at creation to the light now shining in a believer's heart. The same God who said 'let there be light' is the one illuminating your understanding today. Where do you still feel in the dark, needing the same creative light God spoke at the beginning?

Paul's instruction is short and direct — teaching should match sound doctrine, not personal preference or popular opinion. As Reformation Day approaches, this is worth remembering: truth doesn't bend to what's fashionable. Where have you softened sound doctrine to make it more palatable or popular?

This is the verse that reportedly gripped Martin Luther and helped spark the Reformation — the righteous shall live by faith, not by earning it through works. On this day, it's worth remembering that the gospel's power was never about human effort; it was always a gift received by faith. Has your own faith drifted toward relying on effort, when this verse says the righteous live by faith alone?

David invites experience, not just belief — taste and see, not merely hear about. Some things about God's goodness are only fully known by actually leaning into Him, not just agreeing with facts about Him. Where have you been agreeing that God is good without actually tasting and experiencing it lately?

John is careful to get the direction right — love didn't start with us reaching toward God, it started with Him reaching toward us first. Every human love, at its best, is a response, not the origin. Are you relating to God as though your love for Him came first, forgetting His love reached you first?

David commits to actively recounting God's deeds — not just feeling grateful in passing, but deliberately naming and remembering them out loud. Gratitude grows stronger when it's spoken, not just felt. What specific 'wonderful deed' of God could you recount out loud today, rather than just feel quietly grateful for?

Paul bursts into worship here after chapters of dense theological argument — sometimes the right response to understanding more about God isn't more analysis, but simply awe. When did theology or study of God last actually move you to worship, rather than just information?

David opens and closes this psalm with the exact same line — a name so majestic it bookends everything in between. Whatever else the psalm explores, it starts and ends anchored in the same wonder. What would change if you started and ended today the way this psalm does — fixed on God's majestic name?

Paul calls Christ's resurrection the 'firstfruits' — the first of a larger harvest still to come. His rising wasn't a solitary miracle; it's the down payment on what's promised for everyone in Him. Does your hope for your own future rest confidently on Christ being the firstfruits of what's to come?

This psalm ties gladness directly to identity — we are His, made by Him, which is exactly why joyful worship makes sense. Belonging to God is the foundation joy stands on. Does your service to God feel like obligation or gladness right now?

Moses distills a massive body of law down to this simple summary — fear, walk, love, serve, wholeheartedly. When the requirements feel overwhelming, this is the actual center of it all. Have you made following God more complicated than this simple summary Moses gives?

David declares this after recounting a lifetime of battles, narrow escapes, and hard-won victories — his confidence in God wasn't theoretical, it was tested and proven across real danger. What tested season of your life has proven God to be your rock, not just an idea you hold?

Israel was told not to measure the battle by the size of the opposing army, but by the presence of the God who fought alongside them. As we approach a day honoring those who served, this is worth remembering — courage isn't the absence of fear, it's trust in who goes with you. What battle are you facing where you've been measuring the opposition instead of remembering who goes with you?

Today honors those who have served in defense of others, often at great cost. This verse credits God as the one who trains and strengthens for battle — a fitting reminder that courage and skill in service are gifts worth honoring, not taking for granted. Do you know a veteran you could specifically thank or check in on today?

Paul describes governing authority, including its power to protect and defend, as ultimately serving God's purposes for good. Legitimate protection and defense have a place in God's ordering of the world, not just in human strategy. How do you think about the role of protection and defense in a God-ordered world?

This is a psalm of blessing spoken over someone else, not a personal prayer — a reminder that we're called to intercede for others facing trouble, not just pray for ourselves. Who is facing a 'day of trouble' right now that you could specifically bless and intercede for?

Jesus doesn't just command love — He sets the standard by His own example, 'as I have loved you.' That standard is high enough that it can't be reduced to mere niceness; it points toward sacrifice. Where has your love for someone fallen short of 'as I have loved you'?

This proverb closes a loophole — it's not enough to avoid actively harming someone; withholding good you're able to give is its own kind of failure. What good is currently within your power to give that you've been withholding from someone?

God doesn't just promise help from a distance here — He describes actively holding your hand, present and near, not just observing from far off. Do you experience God's help as distant assistance, or as this verse describes — a hand actually holding yours?

David prays this while giving away enormous wealth for the temple's construction — his generosity flowed directly from recognizing that everything, including what he was giving, already belonged to God. Does your generosity flow from recognizing God's ownership, or from a sense that you're giving away what's truly yours?

The psalmist describes God as the one 'who hears prayer' — a title, almost, as central to who He is as any other. Prayer isn't shouted into an empty sky; it's received by someone who listens. Do you pray like someone confident they're being heard, or like someone unsure anyone's listening?

This offering of firstfruits was meant to be brought with rejoicing, not grim obligation. Gratitude expressed through giving was designed to feel like celebration, not a tax. Does your giving to God feel more like joyful firstfruits, or reluctant obligation?

The psalmist's joy is specific — tied to actual works of God's hands, not vague positivity. Naming what God has specifically done tends to produce deeper joy than general gratitude. What specific work of God's hands, not just a general blessing, has genuinely made you glad recently?

Paul defines great gain not as accumulation but as contentment paired with godliness — a strikingly modest bar by worldly standards, and yet Paul calls it genuine wealth. By Paul's definition of 'great gain,' are you actually wealthy right now?

The psalmist's thanksgiving is a response to an actual reversal — mourning genuinely turned into dancing, not just wished for. Real gratitude often traces back to a specific turnaround, not abstract positivity. What mourning has God turned into dancing in your own story that deserves ongoing thanksgiving?

Paul says to give thanks 'always and for everything' — not selectively, only for the easy things, but genuinely all of it. That's a much higher bar than most thanksgiving lists usually reach for. What's the hardest thing in your life right now to actually give thanks for?

The invitation here isn't reserved for the spiritually elite — 'all the earth' is called to shout for joy. Worship this wide-open assumes everyone has reason to praise, not just a select few. What's holding you back from shouting for joy, rather than a quieter, more reserved kind of praise?

This simple call to thanksgiving grounds itself in two things — God's goodness and His steadfast love that endures forever, not in circumstances that come and go. Whatever this year has held, both of those remain true today. As you gather today, what specific evidence of God's steadfast love this year is worth naming out loud?

Paul's thanksgiving here is specifically for other people — not his own blessings, but the grace visible in someone else's life. Gratitude aimed outward, at what God is doing in others, is its own kind of thanksgiving. Who in your life could you specifically thank God for today, the way Paul does here?

Paul pictures believers as part of a triumphal procession — not spectators of God's victory, but participants carried along in it, spreading its fragrance wherever they go. Where has God carried you along in His victory recently, rather than leaving you to fight alone?

As Advent begins, this verse ties hope directly to Scripture — not a vague optimism, but a hope built on what's actually been written and promised. The whole season ahead is anchored in a hope with real substance behind it. What promise from Scripture is anchoring your hope as this season of waiting begins?

Every name in this famous prophecy points to a different facet of who was coming — counselor, God, father, prince of peace. As Advent begins, it's worth sitting with the sheer weight of what was actually promised here. Which of these names — Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace — do you need most right now?

Closing this month, Paul names hope itself as something actively waited for — not passive resignation, but expectant waiting for a promised appearing. Advent's waiting isn't empty; it's aimed at something certain. What would it look like for your waiting this Advent to be active and expectant, not just passive?

David opens this psalm with a deliberate act — lifting up his soul, not just his requests. As December begins, it's a good pattern to imitate: start the month by actually lifting your whole self toward God, not just asking for things. What would it look like to lift up your soul to God today, rather than just your usual requests?

God is described here as actually listening to the conversations of those who feared Him, keeping a record. Ordinary conversation about God isn't wasted — it's noticed and remembered. When did you last have a conversation about God worth being remembered?

Mary's news came with fear attached — an angel appearing, an impossible pregnancy announced. The angel doesn't pretend the news isn't overwhelming; he simply tells her not to let fear be the final word. What overwhelming news or calling is God asking you not to be afraid of right now?

Micah's promised ruler leads not through force but through shepherding — strength expressed as care, not domination. This is the kind of King the whole Advent season points toward. Does your image of Christ's rule look more like shepherding or domination?

The peace this season celebrates wasn't achieved through negotiation or compromise — it was made through the cross. Real peace with God cost something enormous, which is exactly why it's worth pausing to receive today. Where in your life is there still unrest that this peace, made through the cross, is meant to reach?

God's plan for the world's rescue began in an obscure town, with an ordinary young woman, through an unglamorous betrothal. Greatness in God's story rarely starts where you'd expect to look for it. Where might God be planning something significant in a circumstance of your life that looks entirely ordinary right now?

This is the simple gladness of anticipating worship together — not obligation, but genuine eagerness. It's worth asking whether gathering with God's people still stirs that same gladness in you. Does going to worship still stir gladness in you, or has it become routine?

Joseph's own fear and confusion get addressed directly and personally — God didn't leave him guessing about what to do next. Even in an unprecedented, world-altering situation, God gave Joseph clear direction. Where are you, like Joseph, considering things anxiously without yet having clear direction from God?

This promise, spoken in the garden immediately after the fall, is the very first hint of the rescue that would eventually arrive at Christmas. The whole Advent story actually starts here, thousands of years earlier than Bethlehem. Does it change your view of Christmas to know the promise of a Savior goes all the way back to Genesis 3?

The angel's explanation to Mary doesn't fully explain how — it simply names who is at work: the Holy Spirit, the power of the Most High. Some mysteries in faith are meant to be trusted, not fully solved. What mystery of faith have you been demanding to fully understand before you'll trust it?

The invitation here is to break forth — not restrained, careful praise, but joy that bursts out. As Advent's next candle approaches, this is a good day to let worship be a little less contained. What's kept your praise more restrained than this verse's 'break forth' invites?

Peter describes a joy that doesn't depend on physically seeing Jesus — inexpressible joy, available even now, even without sight. Advent joy isn't nostalgia for a story long past; it's a present, real experience. Would you describe your current joy in Christ as inexpressible, or has it grown quieter than that?

The announcement of the Messiah's birth went first to shepherds — low-status, overlooked workers, not to kings or religious leaders. God's biggest news often arrives first to the people the world pays least attention to. Where might you be overlooking someone God actually wants to reach with good news, the way He reached these shepherds?

The prophet pictures salvation as clothing — put on, worn, visible. Righteousness here isn't earned fabric you wove yourself; it's a robe you've been covered with as a gift. Are you still trying to weave your own robe of righteousness instead of wearing the one you've already been given?

This joy was so full it was heard far away, beyond the immediate community itself. Real joy in God has a way of carrying, of being noticed by people who aren't even part of the celebration. Would people outside your immediate circle be able to hear your joy in God 'far away,' the way this verse describes?

Heaven's own response to the incarnation was an eruption of praise — a multitude, not a single voice. The birth of Christ was significant enough to fill the sky with worship. Has the familiarity of the Christmas story dulled your own sense of how significant this event actually was?

This isn't quiet, contemplative worship — it's clapping, shouting, loud. There's a place in Scripture for exuberant, physical, unrestrained celebration of God, not only reflective stillness. When did you last let your worship be loud and physically expressive, not just quiet and internal?

The wise men had traveled a long, uncertain distance following only a star — and their joy at finally arriving was exceeding, overflowing. Long journeys of faith often end in a joy proportional to how long the wait actually was. What long journey of faith are you still on, and can you trust the exceeding joy waiting at the end of it?

Paul is deliberately extreme here — even the most impressive spiritual gifts and sacrifices amount to nothing without love underneath them. As Advent's final candle is lit, this is the theme the whole season has been building toward. What gift, sacrifice, or achievement in your life needs love underneath it that's currently missing?

God's love for Israel wasn't earned by their size, strength, or impressiveness — it simply is because He loves them. There's no deeper explanation offered, and none needed. Have you been searching for a reason God loves you, when Scripture says the reason is simply that He does?

This love is described as everlasting — not a love that started recently or might expire, but one stretching backward and forward without limit. His continued faithfulness follows directly from that everlasting love. Have you been treating God's love as conditional, when Scripture calls it everlasting?

The shepherds didn't simply believe the angels' message — they went, with haste, to see for themselves. Real faith tends to move; it doesn't just nod along from a distance. What has God shown you that you've agreed with but never actually gone to see or act on?

This psalm pictures gates commanded to lift up for a King's arrival — a fitting image just before Christmas, as the King of glory arrives not through conquered gates, but through a humble manger. What gate in your own heart still needs to be lifted for Christ to fully enter?

A massive, impersonal imperial decree became the exact mechanism God used to move Mary and Joseph to Bethlehem, fulfilling a prophecy spoken centuries earlier. Even the ordinary machinery of world events was quietly serving God's precise plan. What 'decree' or circumstance beyond your control might actually be moving you exactly where God intends?

The King of the universe arrived without a proper room, wrapped in ordinary cloth, laid in a feeding trough. The humility of this moment is easy to soften with familiarity — today is worth pausing to feel the weight of it again. Have you prepared a real place for Christ in your own life, or has He arrived, like that first night, to find no room?

These wise men traveled from far outside Israel to worship a King who wasn't even their own — a preview of the gospel eventually reaching every nation, not just one. Is there a group of people you've subtly excluded from deserving to hear this good news?

Mary's response to the overwhelming events of Christ's birth wasn't to explain them immediately or move on quickly — she treasured and pondered. Some experiences of God deserve to be held quietly before they're fully understood or spoken. What has God done recently that you've rushed past instead of treasuring and pondering, the way Mary did?

This right — to become children of God — isn't automatic for everyone; it's given specifically to those who receive and believe. Christmas's gift has to actually be received to become yours. Have you actually received this gift personally, or admired it from a distance without receiving it?

Even the announcement of judgment is framed here as cause for gladness — because it's righteous, faithful judgment, not something to dread. As the year winds down, that's worth remembering: God's final word over your life is trustworthy, not terrifying. Does the idea of God's judgment fill you with dread or with the gladness this psalm describes?

The psalmist commits to increasing hope and praise, not diminishing — 'yet more and more,' even as circumstances change around him. As this year closes, that's a fitting posture to carry into the next one. Has your hope and praise grown or shrunk over this past year, and what would it take to move it toward 'more and more'?

As this year closes and a new one begins, this verse is worth carrying forward: you are known by name, redeemed, and claimed. Whatever the new year holds, that identity doesn't reset — it's already secure. Looking back on this past year of daily devotionals, what has God taught you about being called by name and belonging to Him?
